definition: Taken by surprise; startled.
note: Old English onbæc meant 'to the back'. 'Taken aback' was first a sailing term, for a ship whose sails were suddenly pressed back against the mast.
hints: Usually comes after 'taken'.
How a sudden surprise leaves you.
example: Taken aback by the caustic remarks.

definition: To lower someone in rank or dignity.
note: From Old French, built from a Latin word for 'low'. To abase yourself is to make yourself small in front of someone.
hints: Grovelling does this to you.
It lowers rather than raises.
origin: Middle French abaisser, from Old French abaissier
example: They find a secret delight in abasing themselves before men of violence.

definition: To become less intense; to die down.
note: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down'. Storms, fevers and anger all abate.
hints: What a storm does as it passes.
The opposite of building up.
origin: Anglo-Norman abatre, from Latin battere; in English since the 14th century

definition: A building where monks or nuns live and worship.
note: From Old French abaie, ultimately from the Aramaic abba, 'father', via the title of the man who ran it.
hints: Monks might live in one.
Westminster has a famous one.
origin: Old French abaïe, from Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia

definition: The head of a monastery.
note: From Latin abbas, from Aramaic abba, 'father'. The monks' leader was, in name, their father.
hints: Leader of a religious house.
His title once meant 'father'.
origin: Old English abbat, from Aramaic אבא
example: The newly appointed abbot decided to take a tour of the abbey with the cardinal's emissary.

definition: To hate something deeply.
note: From Latin abhorrere, 'to shrink back in horror', with the same root as horror.
hints: Stronger than mere dislike.
Shares a root with horror.
origin: Middle French abhorrer, from Latin abhorreō
example: As a staunch pacifist, she abhors all forms of violence.

definition: To put up with; to tolerate.
note: From Old English abidan, 'to wait'. 'Abode', a place you wait in, comes from the same word.
hints: Often follows 'can't'.
To tolerate, or to obey a rule.

definition: On a ship, train or plane.
note: From a- plus board, meaning the side of a ship.
hints: On a ship, train or plane.
Said when everyone has boarded.
example: We all went aboard the ship.

definition: A home; the place where someone lives.
note: Once meant the act of waiting. A place you stay in came to be named after the staying.
hints: A rather grand word for home.
Related to a word meaning to stay.

definition: To stop something before it is finished.
note: From Latin aboriri, 'to miscarry', from ab- 'away' and oriri 'to arise'. Missions and computer tasks are aborted too.
hints: Mission control might shout it.
To call something off part-way.
example: Abort the process running on my computer.

definition: To exist in large numbers.
note: From Latin abundare, 'to overflow'. Wildflowers abound in meadows.
hints: Wildflowers do it across a spring meadow.
Rumours do it when the whole town is gossiping.
origin: Old French abonder, from Latin abundāre
example: Wild animals abound wherever man does not stake his claim.

definition: Concerning; on the subject of.
note: Old English onbutan meant 'on the outside of'. Going around something became talking around it.
hints: What a story is said to be.
Also means roughly, as with numbers.

definition: Higher than; over.
note: From Old English abufan, 'on top'. 'Above board' comes from card players keeping their hands visible over the table.
hints: The opposite of below.
Where the sky is, from the ground.

definition: In or to another country.
note: From a- plus broad, so it first meant widely or out in the open.
hints: Travel overseas.
Where a holiday often takes you.
example: They had never travelled abroad.

definition: Sudden and unexpected, sometimes rudely so.
note: From Latin abruptus, 'broken off'. An abrupt end is one that snaps off rather than fading.
hints: Describes a stop in the middle of a sentence.
A sudden brake that throws passengers forward.
example: Came to an abrupt stop.

definition: Not present.
note: From Latin absens, 'being away'.
hints: Missing from a roll call.
Away when expected to be there.
origin: Middle French absent, from Latin absens
example: When they were able to return to the clinic some months later, certain pieces of equipment were absent.

definition: To soak up, or to take in.
note: From Latin absorbere, 'to swallow up'.
hints: What a sponge does.
Take in information.
origin: Middle French absorber, from Latin absorbeō

definition: Wildly unreasonable or silly.
note: From Latin absurdus, 'out of tune'.
hints: Camus wrote about its philosophy.
Ridiculous and illogical.
origin: Middle French absurde, from Latin absurdus
example: The absurd excuse that the dog ate his homework.

definition: Cruel or improper treatment, or misuse.
note: From Latin abusus, 'used up' or 'misused'. It began as a word for wrong use before it meant cruelty.
hints: Misuse of something, or someone.
Power can be put to this.
origin: Old French abus, from Latin abūsus
example: The child showed signs of physical abuse.

definition: A person who treats someone cruelly or misuses something.
note: Formed from abuse plus -er. The root verb meant to use wrongly, and the cruelty sense grew from that.
hints: Mentioned in news reports and support-line leaflets.
Might be paired with the word substance, as in drug or alcohol.
example: Abusers often cross the line between respect and disrespect.

definition: A seemingly bottomless chasm.
note: From Greek abussos, 'bottomless', from a- 'not' and bussos 'depth'.
hints: Nietzsche warned it stares back.
A drop with no visible floor.
origin: Late Latin abyssus, from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος
example: When you gaze into the abyss, the abyss also gazes into you.

definition: A way of pronouncing a language, or emphasis.
note: From Latin accentus, 'song added to speech'.
hints: Southern drawl.
A mark above a letter.
origin: Medieval Latin accentus, from Latin accentus

definition: To receive willingly or agree to.
note: From Latin acceptare, 'to take willingly'.
hints: Say yes to an offer.
The opposite of refuse.
origin: Old French accepter, from Latin acceptō
example: Please accept my present.

definition: A way in, or the right to use something.
note: From Latin accessus, 'a coming to'.
hints: A key gives you this.
Permission to enter or use.
origin: Middle French acces, from Latin accessus
example: The door provides access to the premises.

definition: Agreement, or to grant.
note: From Old French acorder, 'to bring into harmony', from Latin cor, 'heart'.
hints: A peace deal between nations.
Harmony between opinions.

definition: To say someone has done wrong.
note: From Latin accusare, 'to call to account'.
hints: Charge with a crime.
Blame for a fault.
origin: Old French acuser, from Latin accūsō

definition: Containing acid; sharp or sour.
note: From acid plus -ic. A solution is acidic if its pH is below 7.
hints: Lemon juice is this.
Litmus paper turns red in this.

definition: The nut of the oak tree.
note: From Old English æcern, originally any wild fruit. The spelling bent towards 'oak' and 'corn' later.
hints: Squirrels bury these.
Great oaks are said to grow from it.
example: Children collect acorns that have fallen from an oak tree.

definition: Sharp and bitter in smell or taste.
note: From Latin acer, 'sharp'. It was shaped to look like 'acid' by people who assumed the two were related.
hints: Smoke can have this quality.
It catches the back of your throat.
example: The acrid smell of burning rubber.

definition: From one side to the other.
note: From Middle English a cros, 'in a cross form'.
hints: Over to the far side.
Bridges take you this way.
example: The football field was 300 feet across.

definition: The doing of something, or a deed.
note: From Latin actio, from agere, 'to do'.
hints: What a director shouts to start filming.
What a film director calls out.
origin: Old French aucion, from Latin āctiō(n)

definition: Busy and moving, or involved.
note: From Latin activus, 'practical', from agere, 'to do'.
hints: A volcano earns this label while it can still erupt.
Always on the move and engaged.
origin: Old French actif, from Latin āctīv(us)

definition: Someone who performs a role on stage or screen.
note: From Latin, 'a doer', from agere 'to do'. In law it once meant the person who brings a case.
hints: Works with scripts and directors.
Plays someone they are not.

definition: Real, not imagined.
note: From Latin actualis, 'relating to action', from agere.
hints: As it truly is.
Not a guess.
origin: Anglo-Norman actuel, from Latin actus; in English since the 14th century

definition: Severe and sudden; or sharp.
note: From Latin acutus, 'sharpened'. An acute angle is a sharp one, and an acute illness strikes quickly.
hints: Describes an angle under ninety degrees.
Sudden and severe, in medicine.

definition: An old saying held to be true.
note: From Latin adagium, a proverb. 'A stitch in time' is one.
hints: A proverb by another name.
Old wisdom in a short sentence.
origin: Middle French adage, from Latin adā̆gium
example: There must always be two parties to a quarrel, says the old adage.

definition: To change to suit new conditions.
note: From Latin adaptare, 'to fit to'. Darwin's species and novels turned into films both do it.
hints: What species do to survive.
A book may be this for the screen.
example: Adapt our native cuisine to the available food resources of the new country.

definition: A venomous snake and Britain's only native one.
note: From Middle English nadder, where 'a nadder' was misheard as 'an adder'.
hints: A snake with a zigzag back.
A viper found in British heathland.

definition: A person who cannot stop doing or using something, especially a harmful drug.
note: From Latin addicere, 'to assign or devote'. Originally it meant someone given over to a habit, good or bad.
hints: Someone who cannot stop, whether it is gambling or caffeine.
Often follows a word like 'coffee' or 'sugar' in casual speech.
example: He is an addict when it comes to chocolate cookies.

definition: Very skilled at something.
note: From Latin adeptus, 'having attained'. Alchemists used it of anyone who had cracked the secret of gold.
hints: Highly skilled.
Alchemists claimed the title.

definition: To stick firmly to a surface, or to follow a rule faithfully.
note: From Latin adhaerere, 'to cling to'. Glue and rule-followers both do it.
hints: What tape does to paper, and what a loyal follower does to rules.
Stickers and bylaws have this in common.
example: Wax adhered to his finger.

definition: A French farewell used in English.
note: From Old French a Dieu, 'to God'. It was a goodbye entrusting someone to God's care.
hints: A literary way to say goodbye.
A French farewell.
origin: Old French adieu, from Medieval Latin ad Deum
example: He bade her adieu forever.

definition: Spanish for goodbye.
note: Borrowed from Spanish adiós, 'to God', and a doublet of adieu.
hints: A farewell borrowed from Spanish.
Said when leaving, south of the border.

definition: To change slightly to fit.
note: From Old French ajuster, 'to bring closer'.
hints: Set a chair to the right height.
Fine-tune a setting a little.
origin: Middle French adjuster, from Latin iuxta
example: Most immigrants adjust quickly to a new community.

definition: Administrative work; the paperwork side of things.
note: A clipping of administration. On the internet it also names whoever runs a forum or server.
hints: Forms, filing and emails.
The person who can ban you from a server.
example: There's a lot of admin involved in the birth of a child.

definition: To respect or enjoy looking at something.
note: From Latin admirari, 'to wonder at'.
hints: Look at a painting with delight.
Regard with respect.
origin: Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror

definition: To confess; or to let someone in.
note: From Latin admittere, 'to send to'. A ticket admits you; a guilty person admits fault.
hints: What a ticket does at the door.
To own up to something.
origin: Old French admettre, from Latin admittō

definition: Sun-dried brick made of clay and straw.
note: From Spanish, via Arabic, from a Coptic word for brick, which goes back to ancient Egyptian. Few English words are older.
hints: Common building material in the American Southwest.
Mud brick dried in the sun.
example: Many people in Texas and New Mexico live in adobe houses.

definition: To take on as your own.
note: From Latin adoptare, 'to choose for oneself', from optare 'to choose'.
hints: Parents may do this with a child.
You can also do it with an idea.
origin: Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō

definition: To love and admire deeply.
note: From Latin adorare, 'to speak to', meaning to pray. It was a word for worship before it was a word for fondness.
hints: Stronger than like.
Once meant to worship.
origin: Old French adorer, from Latin adōrō
example: It is obvious to everyone that Gerry adores Heather.

definition: To decorate or make beautiful.
note: From Latin adornare, 'to furnish', the same root as ornate and ornament.
hints: What jewellery does to a person.
Related to ornament.
example: A gallery of paintings was adorned with the works of some of the great masters.

definition: Floating with no direction or mooring.
note: From a- plus drift. It describes a boat that has lost its anchor or power, or a person without purpose.
hints: A lifeboat without oars.
Someone with no plan after leaving school.

definition: A fully grown person or animal.
note: From Latin adultus, 'grown up'. Adolescent comes from the same verb: one is growing, the other has grown.
hints: No longer a child.
Shares a root with adolescent.

definition: The arrival of something important, such as a new era; also the weeks before Christmas.
note: From Latin adventus, 'arrival'. The Christian season counts down the days to Christmas.
hints: Often paired with 'the' and a new technology.
A calendar with little doors counts down to this.
example: The advent of the computer.

definition: An advertisement, in British speech.
note: Clipped from advertisement. Britons spot them during commercial breaks.
hints: What a British person calls a commercial.
An ad break fills with these.

definition: A suggestion about what to do.
note: From Old French avis, from Latin ad visum, 'according to what is seen'.
hints: Guidance from a friend.
What an agony aunt gives.
origin: Old French avis, from Latin vīsus

definition: To give someone guidance.
note: From Old French aviser, 'to look at'.
hints: What a counsellor does.
Offer a suggestion.
origin: Old French aviser, from Late Latin advisō

definition: Protection or sponsorship.
note: From Greek aigis, the shield of Zeus and Athena. 'Under the aegis of' means under the protection of.
hints: The shield of a Greek god.
Protection, in a formal phrase.
origin: Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́δες

definition: Of the air; or a radio or TV antenna.
note: From Latin aerius, from Greek aer, 'air'.
hints: View from a drone.
Pick up a TV signal.
origin: Ancient Greek ἀέριος; in English since the 16th century

definition: A matter of business, or a secret relationship.
note: From Old French afaire, 'to do', from a faire.
hints: A state one.
A scandalous relationship.
origin: Old French afaire, from Latin ad-

definition: To influence something.
note: From Latin afficere, 'to work on'.
hints: Often confused with effect.
Has an impact on.
example: The experience affected me deeply.

definition: To state that something is true; to confirm.
note: From Latin affirmare, from ad (to) and firmus (firm). To affirm is to make something firm.
hints: A witness who doesn't wish to swear on a book may do it in court.
To say yes with confidence.
origin: Old French afermer, from Latin affirmare

definition: To attach; or a prefix or suffix.
note: From Latin affixus, 'fastened to'. Grammar borrowed it for the bits fastened onto words.
hints: Un- and -ness are examples.
To stick one thing to another.

definition: To have enough money for.
note: From Old English geforthian, 'to carry out'.
hints: Can you pay for it?
Have the means.
example: I think we can afford the extra hour it will take. We can only afford to buy a small car at the moment.

definition: On fire.
note: Simply a- 'on' plus fire, like ablaze. It is used about passions as often as buildings.
hints: Burning, in a literary way.
A heart might be described this way.
example: Forests set ablaze (or afire) by lightning.

definition: Floating on water; or staying financially solvent.
note: From a- plus float. Keeping a business afloat means barely avoiding going under.
hints: A raft or boat is this after launching.
A struggling shop manages to stay so.

definition: Happening or being planned.
note: Literally 'on foot'. Sherlock Holmes made 'the game is afoot' famous, borrowing it from Shakespeare.
hints: Holmes says the game is this.
Something is being planned.

definition: In conflict with; in trouble with.
note: From a- plus foul. Ships ran afoul of each other when their rigging tangled.
hints: Usually followed by 'of the law'.
Tangled up in trouble.
example: He had a knack for running afoul of the law.

definition: Feeling fear.
note: From affray, an old word for to frighten.
hints: Feeling frightened or uneasy.
Reluctant, as in 'I'm sorry to say'.
origin: Anglo-Norman afrayer, from Old French effreer

definition: Later than; following.
note: From Old English æfter. 'Aftermath' first meant a second crop of grass mown after the first.
hints: The opposite of before.
Comes later in time.

definition: Once more.
note: From Old English ongean, 'back'. 'Against' grew from the same word.
hints: One more time.
Encore means roughly this.
example: Be sure to look over your paper again before you hand it in.

definition: With the mouth wide open in wonder.
note: A- plus gape. Its first known use is in Milton's Paradise Lost, in 1667.
hints: Jaw hanging open.
Milton is credited with it.
example: We stood there agape with wonder.

definition: A banded, semi-precious stone.
note: From Greek achates, named after the river in Sicily where the stone was found.
hints: Marbles were once made of it.
A banded gemstone.
origin: Middle French agathe, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης
example: I find agates really pretty.

definition: A spiky desert plant used to make tequila and syrup.
note: From the Greek Agave, a name meaning 'noble' or 'illustrious'.
hints: The plant tequila comes from.
Succulent with sharp leaves in Mexico.

definition: An organisation providing a service; or the capacity to act.
note: From Latin agentia, from agere, 'to do'.
hints: A travel firm or government body.
A company that finds jobs or booking.
origin: Medieval Latin agentia, from Latin agēns

definition: A list of items to be discussed.
note: From Latin agenda, 'things to be done'.
hints: What is printed for a meeting.
Plan of items.

definition: Someone who acts on another's behalf.
note: From Latin agens, 'doing'. A secret agent and a chemical agent both make things happen.
hints: Spies and estate brokers are both called this.
Someone who acts for you.
example: He worked as an agent for the government.

definition: Trouble or aggressive behaviour, in British slang.
note: A clipping of aggravation or aggression plus -o.
hints: Gets you into a fight at a football match.
Hostile bother.
example: Move along, lads; we don't want any aggro.

definition: Able to move quickly and easily.
note: From Latin agilis, 'nimble', from agere 'to drive'. Software teams adopted it in 2001.
hints: Gymnasts and goats are this.
Quick on your feet.

definition: Glowing with light, warmth or happiness.
note: A- plus glow, like afire and ablaze. Faces are aglow as often as fires.
hints: Lit up warmly.
A happy face might be this.
example: The heater is aglow with a beautiful orange color.

definition: Extreme physical or mental pain.
note: From Greek agonia, 'struggle', from agon, an athletic contest. The pain came from the effort.
hints: Severe suffering.
Its Greek root meant a contest.
example: When the weight fell on her foot, she cried out in agony.

definition: A public square or market in ancient Greece.
note: Greek for 'gathering place'. Agoraphobia is a fear of open, public spaces.
hints: Athenians gathered here.
Hidden in a word for fearing crowds.

definition: To share an opinion.
note: From Old French a gré, 'to one's liking', from Latin gratum, 'pleasing'.
hints: What two people do when they see eye to eye.
Nodding usually signals it.
origin: Old French agreer, from Latin ad
example: All parties agree in the expediency of the law.

definition: In front; in the future.
note: A- plus head, probably first a sailor's word for beyond the ship's bow.
hints: Further forward.
The opposite of behind.
example: The island was directly ahead.

definition: Someone who helps or assists.
note: Built from aid plus the -er ending, so it simply means a person who aids. The word is rare and mostly turns up in the phrase 'aiders and abettors'.
hints: A person doing a helping job.
Often paired with 'abettors' in legal language.

definition: Slang for all right.
note: A contraction of all right that suits informal speech.
hints: Casual way to agree.
A shortened okay.

definition: In poor health; or struggling.
note: From the verb ail, from Old English eglan, 'to trouble'. Companies and economies are called this as well as people.
hints: The word a news story uses for a sick king.
An economy in trouble might be called this.

definition: The passage by which air gets to the lungs; also a regular route flown by aircraft.
note: Formed from air plus way.
hints: A first-aid lesson stresses keeping it clear.
A choking person has a blocked one.

definition: A passage between rows of seats or shelves.
note: From Old French ele, 'wing', from Latin ala. It meant the side wings of a church before it meant a walkway.
hints: Supermarkets and planes have them.
Brides walk down one.

definition: A warning of danger, or the device that sounds it.
note: From Italian all'arme, 'to arms!', the cry raised when an enemy appeared.
hints: It wakes you in the morning.
Once a call to grab weapons.
origin: Middle French alarme, from Latin arma

definition: Although.
note: From the Middle English phrase al be it, 'although it be'.
hints: A formal way of saying even though.
Introduces a concession.

definition: A person or animal born without normal colour pigment.
note: From Portuguese and Spanish albino, from Latin albus, 'white'. It was first used by Portuguese explorers describing people they saw in Africa.
hints: White fur and pink eyes in a rabbit.
Moby Dick is a white whale like this.

definition: A collection of recordings, or a book for photos.
note: Latin for a blank white tablet, from albus 'white'. Romans posted public notices on one.
hints: Musicians release these.
Its Latin root meant white.

definition: A tree that grows in wet ground.
note: From Old English alor. It is in the birch family and has small cones.
hints: A tree of wet riverbanks.
A relative of the birch.

definition: Watchful and ready.
note: From Italian all'erta, 'on the lookout', from erta, a high lookout post.
hints: Fully awake and watchful.
Lifeguards should be this.

definition: Simple water plants such as seaweed and pond scum.
note: Plural of Latin alga, 'seaweed'. They produce much of the oxygen in the air.
hints: Turns a pond green.
Seaweed belongs here.
example: Ducks feed on worms, crustaceans, aquatic insects, and algae.

definition: Relating to algae.
note: From Latin alga, 'seaweed'.
hints: Describes a green bloom on a pond.
Pond scum, adjective-style.

definition: A false or alternative name.
note: Latin for 'at another time'. Spies and criminals use them.
hints: A name used by a spy.
What 'also known as' introduces.

definition: A being from another world; or anything foreign.
note: From Latin alienus, 'belonging to another', from alius, 'other'.
hints: Science fiction is full of them.
From somewhere else entirely.
origin: Old French alien, from Latin alius

definition: To bring into a line.
note: From French aligner, from Latin linea, 'line'. Text, wheels and stars can all be aligned.
hints: What you do with text in a document.
To line things up.
origin: Middle French aligner, from Latin lineare

definition: Similar; in the same way.
note: From Old English gelic, 'similar', related to the word like.
hints: Twins often look this way.
Similar to each other.
example: Twins are physically alike, that is, similar-looking people on the outside.

definition: An old spelling of align.
note: Formed from a- plus line, an old form of align.
hints: To straighten something into a row.
Archaic version of a word for lining up.

definition: Living; not dead.
note: From Old English on life, literally 'in life'. The a- in many such words is a worn-down 'on'.
hints: The opposite of dead.
Full of energy, or simply breathing.

definition: To calm or lessen a fear or worry.
note: From Old English alecgan, 'to lay down'. You lay a fear to rest.
hints: What reassurance does to fears.
To put a worry to rest.

definition: To claim that something is true without proof.
note: From Middle English aleggen, probably from Old French alleguer.
hints: A newspaper uses it before a trial ends.
What a prosecutor says before evidence is heard.
origin: Old French alleguer, from Latin ex
example: The agency alleged that my credit history had problems.

definition: A narrow passage between buildings.
note: From Old French alee, 'a going', from aller 'to go'. A bowling alley is a long narrow lane too.
hints: Cats and bins live in one.
Bowling happens in one.
example: The parking lot to my friend's apartment building is in the alley.

definition: To give out as a share.
note: From Old French aloter, 'to divide by lot'. Shares were once settled by drawing lots.
hints: What you do with time or seats.
To share out portions.

definition: To let something happen.
note: From Old French alouer, which blended two Latin verbs, one for praise and one for placing.
hints: To give permission.
Parents decide what to do this with.
origin: Anglo-Norman allouer, from Medieval Latin allocō

definition: A metal made by mixing two or more metals.
note: From Old French aloi, from a Latin word for binding together. Bronze is copper and tin.
hints: Brass and bronze are examples.
Metals melted together.
origin: Middle French alloy, from Latin alligō
example: Brass is an alloy of zinc and copper.

definition: The quality of being attractive or tempting.
note: From Old French alurer, 'to attract', built from a- and leurre, 'lure'.
hints: Perfume adverts promise it.
A distant island holds it for the bored office worker.

definition: The edible seed of a tree, used whole, in milk or in marzipan.
note: From Old French almande, from Greek amygdale. It is technically a seed rather than a true nut.
hints: The nut inside marzipan.
A pale nut milked as an alternative to dairy.
origin: Old French almande, from Arabic ال

definition: Nearly but not quite.
note: From Old English ealmaest, 'nearly all'.
hints: Falling just short.
Close to, but not entirely.
example: Almost all people went there.

definition: Up in the air.
note: From Old Norse a lopti, 'in the sky'. Sailors used it for anything up the mast.
hints: Up in the rigging, to a sailor.
Held up high.
example: Eagles were soaring aloft.

definition: A Hawaiian greeting and farewell.
note: Borrowed from Hawaiian, meaning love and compassion. It is used to say hello and goodbye.
hints: A word of welcome in Hawaii.
Said as a lei is placed round the neck.
origin: Hawaiian aloha; in English since the 19th century
example: An image of a fat American tourist wearing an aloha shirt pops up.

definition: By yourself.
note: From all plus one, 'wholly one'. 'Lonely' was later formed from it by dropping the a-.
hints: Without company.
'Lonely' was clipped from it.

definition: Moving in a line beside something.
note: From Old English andlang, 'extending opposite'. You walk along a beach.
hints: How you walk a riverbank.
Coming with others: tagging this.

definition: Distant and cool towards others.
note: A sailing term: to keep a ship's head 'a loof', to windward, away from the shore.
hints: Standoffish.
Its root is a sailing command.

definition: In a voice others can hear.
note: Simply a- plus loud. Reading aloud was normal; silent reading once astonished people.
hints: Not silently.
How you read to a child.
example: Try speaking aloud rather than whispering.

definition: The first letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Phoenician aleph, 'ox', whose letter was drawn as an ox head. Turn our A upside down and you can still see the horns.
hints: Comes before beta.
Software releases begin with it.
origin: Ancient Greek ἄλφα, from Phoenician 𐤀

definition: Relating to high mountains, especially the Alps.
note: From Latin Alpinus, 'of the Alps'. Alpine skiing and plants share the name.
hints: A type of skiing, or plants above the tree line.
Edelweiss grows in this kind of meadow.

definition: A table used for religious offerings or ceremonies.
note: From Latin altare, likely related to altus, 'high'. Weddings take place in front of one.
hints: Couples stand before one to marry.
A raised table in a church.
origin: Old English altar, from Latin altāre

definition: To change.
note: From Latin alter, 'the other'. Altering something makes it other than it was.
hints: Tailors do it to trousers.
To make different.
example: The advent of the automobile may have altered the growth pattern of the city.

definition: Former students of a school or university.
note: Latin plural of alumnus, 'foster child', from alere, 'to nourish'.
hints: Graduates return to reunions.
Old boys and girls of a college.

definition: At every time; without exception.
note: From Old English ealne weg, 'all the way'.
hints: The opposite of never.
Every single time.
example: God is always the same.

definition: To gather a large amount.
note: From French amasser, 'to heap up', from masse, 'mass'.
hints: What hoarders do with things.
To pile up over time.

definition: To astonish.
note: Middle English amasen meant to bewilder. 'Maze' is the same word: a place made to bewilder you.
hints: What magicians aim to do.
Related to a puzzle of paths.
origin: Old English āmasian, from Middle English amase; in English since the 16th century
example: He was amazed when he found that the girl was a robot.

definition: Greatly surprised.
note: From amaze, from Old English amasian, 'to stupefy'.
hints: Wide-eyed with wonder.
Stunned by something wonderful.

definition: A tall, strong woman warrior; also a South American river.
note: From Greek Amazon, a mythical race of women warriors. The river was named after them by Spanish explorers.
hints: Warrior woman of Greek myth.
The world's largest river by volume.
example: Although the evidence for real Amazons is thin, women athletes are often dubbed amazons.

definition: Fossilised tree resin, or its golden-orange colour.
note: From Arabic anbar, which first meant ambergris from whales. The name slid onto the resin.
hints: Insects are found trapped in it.
The middle traffic light.
origin: Old French aumbre, from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭭𐭡𐭫; in English since the 15th century

definition: The scope or bounds of something.
note: From Latin ambitus, 'a going round'.
hints: The limits of someone's authority.
Falls within or beyond it.
example: These issues should fall within the ambit of the talks.

definition: To walk slowly and easily.
note: From Old French ambler, 'to walk like a horse', from Latin ambulare 'to walk'.
hints: A relaxed stroll.
Ambulance shares its root.
origin: Old French ambler, from Latin ambulō
example: They decided to amble along the beach at sunset.

definition: A surprise attack from a hidden spot.
note: From Old French embuscher, 'to place in the bush'. The idea is lying in wait among trees.
hints: What bandits spring on a stagecoach.
A trap set along a narrow forest road.

definition: To change to make better.
note: From Latin emendare, 'to remove a fault'. The US Constitution has twenty-seven of them.
hints: Constitutions get these.
To correct a text.
origin: Old French amender, from Latin ēmendō

definition: In the middle of; surrounded by.
note: From amid plus -s plus -t, a spelling that grew on the end of the word. It sounds older than amid.
hints: Can be found in the chaos or the crowd.
A poetic variant of 'in the middle of'.

definition: A female friend, in Spanish.
note: Borrowed directly from Spanish amiga.
hints: Spanish word for a girl's pal.
Feminine form of amigo.

definition: Relating to a chemical group found in proteins.
note: From amine, from ammonia, ultimately from the Egyptian god Amun. Proteins are made of acids named for it.
hints: A type of acid in proteins.
A word in the building blocks of life.

definition: Wrong or out of place.
note: A- plus miss. 'Something is amiss' means something has missed its mark.
hints: Something is not right.
Often follows 'something is'.

definition: Friendly relations.
note: From Old French amistie, from Latin amicus, 'friend'.
hints: Friendship between nations.
Its Latin root is friend.
origin: Old French amisté, from Latin amīcus

definition: Surrounded by; in the company of.
note: From Old English on gemang, 'in a crowd'.
hints: In the middle of a group.
Similar to amid.
origin: Old English amang, from Old English onġemang

definition: A quantity of something.
note: From Old French amonter, 'to go up'.
hints: The sum of anything.
Total, such as a bill.
origin: Old French amonter, from Latin ad montem
example: Pour a small amount of water into the dish.

definition: More than enough.
note: From Latin amplus, 'large, spacious'. Amplify comes from the same root.
hints: Plenty, with room to spare.
Related to amplify.
origin: Middle French ample, from Latin amplus
example: Had ample food for the party.

definition: In a way that is more than enough.
note: From ample, from Latin amplus, 'large'. To be amply rewarded is to get plenty.
hints: Generously or fully.
How a debt might be repaid.
example: The evidence amply (or fully) confirms our suspicions.

definition: To make someone laugh or smile.
note: From Old French amuser, 'to divert attention'. It first meant to fool or distract someone.
hints: What a clown tries to do.
Its old meaning was to distract.
example: The clown amused the children.

definition: Entertained or finding something funny.
note: From Old French amuser, 'to divert', which grew from a word for staring idly. It once meant to distract or mislead.
hints: How a queen was famously not.
A smile on a face after a joke.
example: The children chased one another in a circle in front of their amused parents.

definition: Using continuous signals rather than digital ones.
note: From Greek analogos, 'proportionate'.
hints: A clock with hands.
Vinyl records and old dial watches belong to this world.
origin: French analogue, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος

definition: A heavy device that holds a ship in place; also a news presenter.
note: From Greek ankyra, 'hook'.
hints: Dropped overboard to hold a boat.
Reads the evening news.
origin: Old English ancor, from Ancient Greek ἄγκυρα

definition: A condition in which the blood lacks enough red cells or haemoglobin, causing tiredness.
note: From Greek anaimia, built from an-, 'not', and haima, 'blood'.
hints: Iron-rich foods like spinach are suggested to prevent it.
Pale skin and tiredness might lead a doctor to test for it.

definition: A heavenly messenger.
note: From Greek angelos, 'messenger'. Angels were defined by their job, carrying word from God.
hints: Tops many Christmas trees.
Its Greek root meant messenger.
origin: Old English anġel, from Anglo-Norman angele

definition: A strong feeling of displeasure.
note: From Old Norse angr, 'grief'. It meant sorrow before it meant rage.
hints: What a temper unleashes.
Seeing red is this.
example: You need to control your anger.

definition: The space between two lines that meet.
note: From Latin angulus, 'corner'. Angling for fish comes from a different word meaning hook.
hints: Measured in degrees.
A protractor measures it.
origin: Middle French angle, from Latin angulus

definition: Feeling or showing anger.
note: From anger, which in Old Norse meant grief or trouble.
hints: Cross, or worse than cross.
How you feel when wronged.
example: His face became angry.

definition: The soul or inner self.
note: Latin for 'breath' or 'soul'. Jung used it for the inner feminine side of a man's psyche.
hints: Latin for the breath of life.
A word in Jungian psychology.
origin: Latin anima; in English since the 20th century

definition: A living creature that is not a plant.
note: From Latin animal, from anima, 'breath' or 'soul'.
hints: Dog, cat or horse.
Latin for a thing with breath.
origin: Old French animal, from Latin animal
example: Humans, like other animals, need air to breathe and food to eat.

definition: Japanese animated film and television.
note: A Japanese clipping of the English 'animation'. English borrowed the clipped word back.
hints: Studio Ghibli makes it.
Animation from Japan.
origin: Japanese アニメ, from Latin animātiō
example: I can draw an anime version of you, if you want.

definition: A negatively charged ion.
note: From Greek ana, 'up', as it moves towards the positive electrode.
hints: Chemistry term for an atom with extra electrons.
Moves toward the anode.
example: An oxyanion is an anion that contains the element oxygen.

definition: A plant whose seeds taste of liquorice.
note: From Greek anison, via Latin and Old French.
hints: Flavour of ouzo and sambuca.
Seeds that taste like black liquorice.
origin: Old French anis, from Egyptian jnst

definition: The joint between the foot and the leg.
note: From Old English ancleow. The bones were once compared to an angle or bend.
hints: Easy to twist.
Where a sock ends.

definition: A year-by-year record of events; historical records in general.
note: From Latin annales libri, 'yearly books', from annus, 'year'. 'In the annals of history' means in the permanent record.
hints: A monk's chronicle written one year at a time.
Grand historians say something is recorded in these, always plural.
origin: Middle French annales, from Latin annālēs librī

definition: An extra building attached to a main one; or to take over territory.
note: From Latin annexus, 'joined to'. Countries annex land; hotels have annexes.
hints: An extension of a building.
What empires do to land.

definition: To irritate.
note: From Old French anoier, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred'. Ennui shares the root.
hints: What a buzzing fly does.
Shares a root with ennui.
origin: Old French anoier, from Latin odium
example: Marc loved his sister, but when she annoyed him he wanted to switch her off.

definition: Happening once a year.
note: From Latin annualis, from annus, 'year'.
hints: Yearly event.
Like a birthday or a flower that blooms once.
origin: Late Latin annuālem, from Latin annālis

definition: To declare legally invalid.
note: From Latin annullare, 'to make nothing', from nullus.
hints: What can happen to a marriage.
Related to null.
origin: Old French anuller, from Latin annullō
example: The contract was annulled.

definition: The positive electrode of a battery or cell.
note: Coined in 1834 for Michael Faraday, from Greek ana 'up' and hodos 'way'.
hints: Partner of the cathode.
Faraday asked for the word.

definition: A reply, or the solution to a problem.
note: From Old English andswaru, 'a swearing in return', built from and- 'against'.
hints: Written in the box beside a numbered exam item.
What a quiz demands.
origin: Old English andswaru, from Old English swerian
example: I waited several days for his answer.

definition: A rousing song of loyalty or praise.
note: From Old English antefn, from Greek antiphona, 'sung in response'.
hints: Sung before a match.
Musical emblem of a country.
origin: Old English antefn, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα
example: The choir sang a selection of Christmas anthems at the service just before the big day.

definition: Playful and silly behaviour.
note: From Italian antico, 'ancient', used for the strange creatures painted on Roman walls.
hints: Usually plural: silly capers.
Grotesque old paintings gave it its name.

definition: Restless and fidgety.
note: From ants plus -y, as in having ants in your pants.
hints: Can't sit still while waiting.
Nervously impatient.
example: They said that they were getting antsy.

definition: A heavy iron block on which metal is hammered.
note: From Old English anfilt, 'something beaten on'. One of the ear's tiny bones is named after it.
hints: A blacksmith's essential.
Cartoon villains drop these.

definition: In any case, or carelessly.
note: From any plus how. It is also used to move a conversation on.
hints: A way to change subject in a chat.
A word that signals returning to the point.

definition: Any person at all.
note: Made from any and one.
hints: No one in particular.
A word for 'whoever'.
example: Almost anyone can change a light bulb.

definition: In any case; regardless.
note: Formed from any and way.
hints: Used to change the subject or dismiss an objection.
A word for 'all the same'.
origin: any + way; in English since the 19th century

definition: The main artery leaving the heart.
note: From Greek aorte, 'that which is hung up'. Aristotle named it.
hints: The body's largest artery.
Carries blood away from the heart.
example: The aorta is a critical part of the circulatory system.

definition: Relating to the main artery leaving the heart.
note: From aorta plus -ic. The word is used in terms like aortic valve.
hints: A doctor might check its valve with a stethoscope.
A cardiac surgeon replaces its valve.
example: Tom suffered an aortic dissection and passed away.

definition: Quickly.
note: From Old French a pas, 'at a step', so it first suggested a steady walking speed.
hints: Fast, in an old-fashioned way.
Poets say work goes on this way.
example: Construction of the new offices is proceeding apace.

definition: Separated by distance.
note: From French a part, 'to the side'.
hints: Not together.
How couples feel when separated.
origin: Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem
example: These towns are many miles apart.

definition: A complete lack of interest or concern.
note: From Greek apatheia, 'without feeling'. Stoic philosophers saw it as freedom from passion, but the modern word is negative.
hints: Low turnout at an election is blamed on voter ___.
A shrug where there should be an opinion.
origin: French apathie, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια

definition: A small sap-sucking insect.
note: Linnaeus coined aphis in 1758, possibly misreading the Greek word for bug.
hints: Ladybirds eat them.
A garden pest on roses.
origin: New Latin aphis, from Ancient Greek ἀφειδής
example: My roses are covered in aphids, to say nothing of the ants!

definition: For each one; each.
note: Formed from a plus piece, so the sense is literally 'a piece', meaning one for every item.
hints: Tacked on after a price when everyone pays the same amount.
Three friends buy two tickets each, at five dollars for every one.
origin: Anglo-Norman pece, from Old French pece
example: These melons cost a dollar apiece.

definition: A temporary pause in breathing, often during sleep.
note: From Greek apnoia, 'without breath'.
hints: A sleep disorder.
Breathing stops for a while.
origin: New Latin apnoea, from Ancient Greek ἄπνοια
example: Sleep apnea occurs most often when sleeping in a supine position.

definition: A request for help, or an attraction; also a request to a higher court.
note: From Latin appellare, 'to address'.
hints: A plea for money, or charm.
What a convicted person might lodge.

definition: To come into view or seem.
note: From Latin apparere, 'to come in sight'.
hints: Come into sight, as a ghost might.
Seem to be, or come into view.
example: He suddenly appeared at the wedding.

definition: A round fruit with crisp flesh.
note: Old English æppel meant any fruit. The fruit in Eden is never named as an apple.
hints: Keeps the doctor away.
Newton watched one fall.
origin: Old English æppel; in English since the 9th century

definition: To put on; or to request formally.
note: From Latin applicare, 'to fold onto'. You apply paint, and apply for a job.
hints: You do it for a job.
What you do with sunscreen.
example: Apply a magnetic field here.

definition: A garment worn over clothes to keep them clean.
note: Originally 'a napron'. People heard 'an apron', and the n moved across. Napkin keeps it.
hints: Worn while cooking.
It lost its first letter to 'an'.
origin: Old French napperon, from Latin mappa
example: She tied an apron around her waist before cooking dinner.

definition: In a fitting way.
note: From apt, from Latin aptus, 'fitted'.
hints: Done in a fitting way.
How a well-chosen name suits.
example: It is aptly said that necessity is the mother of invention.

definition: A shady garden shelter covered in climbing plants.
note: From Old French erbier, 'herb garden'. People later linked it to Latin arbor, 'tree'.
hints: Vines and roses climb it.
A shady garden nook.
origin: Old French erbier, from Latin arbor
example: The arbor provided a shady resting place in the park.

definition: A passage with arches, or a place for video games.
note: From French arcade, from Latin arcus, 'bow' or 'arch'.
hints: Pac-Man cabinets.
A covered row of shops.

definition: A person who shoots with a bow and arrow.
note: From Old French archier, from Latin arcus, 'bow'.
hints: Robin Hood was one.
Fires arrows at a target.
origin: Old French archier, from Latin arcus

definition: Passionate and eager.
note: From Latin ardere, 'to burn'. An ardent fan is one who burns with enthusiasm.
hints: Describes a devoted fan or lover.
Burning, in a figurative sense, with zeal.

definition: An enclosed area for sport or shows.
note: Latin for 'sand'. Roman arenas were strewn with it to soak up the blood.
hints: Gladiators fought in one.
Its Latin root meant sand.
origin: Latin arēna, from Old Latin hasēna
example: A large crowd filled the seats of the arena.

definition: An inert gas that makes up about one percent of air.
note: From Greek argos, 'idle', because it hardly reacts. It fills light bulbs.
hints: A gas that fills a bulb.
A noble gas in the air.
example: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are noble gases.

definition: To disagree with words.
note: From Latin arguere, 'to make clear'. It was once about proving a point, not fighting.
hints: What lawyers do in court.
Not quite agreeing.
origin: Old French arguer, from Latin arguere
example: He also argued for stronger methods to be used against China.

definition: To come into being; to get up.
note: From Old English arisan, 'to rise'.
hints: What problems tend to do.
To stand up, in older English.

definition: A large fleet of warships.
note: Borrowed from Spanish armada, 'fleet', from Latin arma, 'arms' or weapons. It is a doublet of army.
hints: Spain sent one against England in 1588.
Storms and English fire ships wrecked it.
example: We watched an armada of storm clouds advancing across the horizon.

definition: Protective covering worn in battle.
note: From Latin armatura, 'equipment', from arma, 'weapons'.
hints: Knights clanked in it.
Shares a root with army.

definition: A place where weapons are stored; also a collection of weapons.
note: The American spelling of armoury, from arms in the sense of weapons.
hints: Soldiers sign out rifles from one on a base.
In some cities these big brick halls double as event spaces.

definition: A distinctive, usually pleasant smell.
note: From Greek aroma, 'spice'. In Latin it was used in the plural for spices and sweet herbs.
hints: Coffee and fresh bread have one.
A pleasant smell drifting out.
origin: Late Latin arōmata, from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα
example: I love the aroma of cinnamon.

definition: On every side of, or approximately.
note: From a- plus round, and in use since Middle English.
hints: Circling something, or roughly speaking.
Surrounding, in all directions.
origin: Old English a-, from Middle English round

definition: A large woven tapestry hung on a wall.
note: Named after the French city of Arras, a famous centre for tapestry in the Middle Ages. In Hamlet, Polonius hides behind one.
hints: Polonius hid behind one in Hamlet.
Wall hanging named for a French town.

definition: An impressive range or display of things.
note: From Old French areer, 'to put in order'. Programmers use it for an ordered list of values.
hints: A wide, orderly display.
A list of values, to a programmer.
example: It was a bewildering array of books.

definition: To seize someone for a crime; or to stop something.
note: From Old French arester, 'to stop', from Latin restare, 'to remain'.
hints: What police do to a suspect.
Halt, as with a heart.
origin: Old French areste, from Latin ad-; in English since the 14th century

definition: To reach a destination.
note: From Old French ariver, 'to come to shore', from Latin ripa, 'shore'.
hints: Come to the end of a journey.
Its root meant reaching the bank.
origin: Old French ariver, from Latin rīpa
example: She arrived home at 7 o'clock.

definition: A pointed shaft shot from a bow.
note: From Old English earh. Its shape now points the way on every sign and screen.
hints: Cupid fires them.
A bow sends it flying.

definition: The crime of deliberately setting fire to property.
note: From Old French arsoun, from Latin ardere, 'to burn'. Ardent shares the root.
hints: A crime involving fire.
Investigators look for accelerants.
origin: Old French arson, from Latin ardeō
example: The British term for arson is fire-raising.

definition: A tube carrying blood from the heart; also a main road.
note: From Greek arteria, which the ancients thought carried air, as with the windpipe. The road sense is a metaphor.
hints: What a surgeon might clear when it is clogged.
Also a major motorway into a city.
origin: Old French artaire, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ

definition: A person who makes art.
note: From French artiste, from Latin ars, 'skill'.
hints: Paints or sculpts.
Someone with a studio and a brush.
origin: French artiste, from Late Latin artista
example: An artist uses many tubes of paint to make a large painting.

definition: Showily artistic or bohemian.
note: An American form of arty, from arts plus -y. Often said with a slight eye-roll.
hints: Like a beret-wearing gallery crowd.
Arty, with an eye-roll.

definition: To go up; to climb or rise.
note: From Latin ascendere, built from ad, 'to', and scandere, 'to climb'.
hints: Mountaineers do it, and so does a rocket after liftoff.
Angels and balloons do this, but never a stone dropped from a bridge.
origin: Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō

definition: A climb upward.
note: Formed from ascend, on the model of descend and descent. Mountaineers talk about the ascent of a peak.
hints: What a climber records on the way up a mountain.
The opposite journey is called a descent.
example: He made a tedious ascent of Mont Blanc.

definition: A wide silk tie looped under the chin.
note: Named after Royal Ascot, the racecourse where fashionable men wore them.
hints: A cravat by another name.
Named after a racecourse.

definition: Pale grey, especially from shock or illness.
note: From ash plus -en, 'made of ash'. Faces turn ashen with fright.
hints: How a frightened face looks.
The colour of something burnt out.
example: A face turned ashen.

definition: On or onto land from the water.
note: From a- plus shore. Castaways are washed this way.
hints: Where a shipwreck survivor ends up.
What a sailor goes on leave.
example: We invited them ashore.

definition: To one side; or a remark made quietly.
note: From Old English on side. In theatre, an aside is spoken to the audience, unheard by the others on stage.
hints: Actors speak one to the audience.
Out of the way.
example: Move aside, please, so that these people can come through.

definition: Not straight; crooked.
note: A- plus skew. A picture on a wall can hang this way.
hints: Not hanging straight.
Wonky, off-kilter.

definition: In a state of sleep.
note: From a- plus sleep.
hints: Not awake at the moment.
Resting with your eyes closed.
example: I was asleep when you called.

definition: One part or feature of something.
note: From Latin aspectus, 'a looking at'.
hints: A facet of a problem.
A particular way something looks.

definition: A tree with leaves that tremble in the breeze.
note: From Old English aespe. Its leaves flutter even in light wind.
hints: A tree with quaking leaves.
A tree whose leaves turn gold in a Colorado autumn.
origin: Old English æspen, from Old English æspe

definition: To aim at a high goal.
note: From Latin aspirare, 'to breathe upon', also 'to strive'. A breathing metaphor, tied to the root of spirit.
hints: What a child who dreams of being an astronaut does.
Shares a root with the word for breath.
origin: Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō
example: Aspire to be a person that everyone enjoys interacting with.

definition: A test of a metal's purity.
note: From Old French assai, 'trial'. Essay comes from the same word: an essay is an attempt.
hints: Gold is tested this way.
Shares a root with essay.
origin: Anglo-Norman assai, from Old French essai

definition: Agreement or approval; or to agree.
note: From Old French assentir, from Latin assentire, 'to agree'. A king gave royal assent to make a bill law.
hints: A monarch gives royal one to a bill.
A nod of the head.
origin: Old French assent, from Latin assentiō
example: I will give this act my assent.

definition: To state something firmly and confidently.
note: From Latin asserere, 'to claim or lay hands on'. To assert yourself is to speak up.
hints: What you do when you stand up for your rights.
A programmer's check that something must hold true.
example: He would often assert that there was life on other planets.

definition: To judge the value or quality of something.
note: From Latin assidere, 'to sit beside', as a judge's assistant.
hints: Estimate worth.
Evaluate a situation.
origin: Old French assesser, from Latin assessus
example: He assessed the situation.

definition: Things of value that a person or company owns.
note: From Anglo-French asetz, 'enough', from Latin ad satis.
hints: Property and savings on a balance sheet.
Accountants list them on one side of the ledger, debts on the other.
origin: Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez
example: Assets have earning power or some other value to their owner.

definition: To give someone a task or share of something.
note: From Latin assignare, 'to mark out for someone'. A teacher gives homework this way.
hints: What a manager does when handing out jobs.
A computer language does this to a variable.
origin: Old French assigner, from Latin assignō

definition: To help, or in sport, a pass that leads to a goal.
note: From Latin assistere, 'to stand by'.
hints: To lend a helping hand.
A basketball pass that sets up a basket.
origin: Old French assister, from Latin assistō

definition: To take for granted.
note: From Latin assumere, 'to take up'.
hints: Suppose without proof.
What a famous saying says makes an ass of you and me.
example: Mr. Jones will assume the position of a lifeguard until a proper replacement is found.

definition: To promise or to make certain.
note: From Old French asseürer, from sur, 'sure'.
hints: Give confidence to someone.
Make someone feel certain.
origin: Old French asseurer, from Latin ad-

definition: A daisy-like plant with star-shaped flowers.
note: From Latin and Greek for 'star', and a cousin of the word star itself.
hints: A flower named for the shape of its petals.
Late-summer bloom with a yellow centre and ray petals.
origin: Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ

definition: A condition that causes difficulty breathing.
note: From Greek asthma, 'panting'.
hints: An inhaler treats it.
Wheezing attacks.
origin: Medieval Latin asthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα
example: My daughter, as a child, often suffered from asthma attacks.

definition: Relating to the stars.
note: From Late Latin astralis, from Latin astrum, 'star'. Mystics later used it for a supposed spirit realm beyond the body.
hints: Mystics speak of travelling in this plane.
A body that supposedly floats out of you in meditation.
origin: Late Latin astrālis, from Ancient Greek ἄστρον

definition: Off the right path, or into error.
note: From Old French estraier, from medieval Latin meaning 'to wander beyond'. It shares a root with stray.
hints: What a plan does when it goes wrong.
Sheep might be led this way, or a young person.
origin: Old French estraier, from Latin extra
example: He was led astray.

definition: Quick to see what matters, and shrewd.
note: From Latin astutus, from astus, 'craft'.
hints: A detective's observation might be called this.
Describes a negotiator who spots the weak point.
example: The goldsmith was astute and cunning, and knew very well what kind of bird it was.

definition: Refuge, or protection given to refugees.
note: From Greek asylon, 'refuge', literally 'not subject to seizure'.
hints: Sanctuary for the persecuted.
An old word for a hospital for the mentally ill.

definition: A book of maps.
note: From Greek Atlas, the Titan who held up the sky. Mercator used the word for a book of maps in the sixteenth century.
hints: A bound collection of maps.
A Titan from Greek myth who held the sky.

definition: A ring-shaped coral island around a lagoon.
note: From Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, where the country is made of them.
hints: A ring of coral.
The Maldives are built of them.
example: The Maldive Islands include one of the world's largest atolls.

definition: Relating to atoms or nuclear energy.
note: From atom plus -ic; atom is from Greek atomos, 'uncuttable'.
hints: Describes a famous type of bomb.
Concerning tiny particles of matter.

definition: To make amends for a wrong.
note: From 'at one'. To atone was to bring two sides into harmony again.
hints: Make up for a sin.
Literally 'at one'.
example: He tried to atone for his mistakes by working harder.

definition: A large open hall inside a building, often with a glass roof.
note: From Latin atrium, 'entry hall', possibly from Etruscan. In a Roman house it was a central court open to the sky.
hints: A shopping mall or hotel lobby might have one.
Pompeii's villas had one with a pool for rain.

definition: To fasten or join.
note: From Old French atachier, 'to fasten'.
hints: Clip one thing to another.
Add a file to an email.
example: You need to attach the carabiner to your harness.

definition: To strike with force, or an assault.
note: From Italian attaccare, 'to join battle'. It is related to attach.
hints: A sudden assault.
What a lion does to prey.
example: This species of snake will only attack humans if it feels threatened.

definition: To reach or achieve something, often after effort.
note: From Old French ataindre, from Latin attingere, 'to touch upon'. A goal can be attained.
hints: What a mountaineer does at the summit.
A degree or a high rank is this after long effort.
origin: Anglo-Norman ataindre, from Old French ataindre

definition: To be present at, or to pay attention.
note: From Latin attendere, 'to stretch toward'.
hints: Go to a meeting.
Be there, or look after someone.
origin: Old French atendre, from Latin attendere
example: She attends class regularly.

definition: To declare that something is true.
note: From Latin attestari, 'to bear witness'. A notary attests that a signature is real.
hints: A witness signs a will to this effect.
Documents sworn to by an official.
origin: Middle French attester, from Latin attestor
example: When will the appraiser attest the date of the painting?

definition: The space just below a roof.
note: From Attica, the region around Athens: its architectural style used a decorated top storey.
hints: Old boxes are stored up there.
Named after the region around Athens.
origin: French attique, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός
example: We went up to the attic to look for the boxes containing our childhood keepsakes.

definition: Clothing, especially formal or special clothes.
note: From Old French atirier, 'to put in order'. Invitations specify black-tie.
hints: A word on a formal invitation naming the dress code.
What a dress code regulates.
example: He was wearing his formal attire.

definition: A reddish-brown colour, especially of hair.
note: From Old French auborne, 'blond', from Latin alburnus, 'whitish', and later confused with brown.
hints: Hair colour between red and brown.
Originally meant a pale shade.

definition: An official check of accounts.
note: From Latin auditus, 'hearing'. Accounts were once read aloud to the examiner.
hints: Accountants dread or perform it.
Its root means hearing.

definition: A tool with a spiral blade for drilling holes.
note: The spelling comes from a mistaken split of 'a nauger' into 'an auger', from Old English nafugar, 'nave spear'.
hints: A corkscrew-shaped boring tool.
Used to drill into wood or ice.

definition: To be a sign of what will happen.
note: A Roman augur foretold the future from the flight of birds. Inauguration began with one.
hints: Things may bode well or ill this way.
Romans read birds to do it.

definition: Dignified and impressive; also the eighth month, with a capital.
note: From Latin augustus, 'venerable', which gave the month its name after Emperor Augustus.
hints: Majestic in bearing.
The month named after a Roman emperor.

definition: Affectionate word for aunt or an older woman.
note: A pet form of aunt, with the diminutive -ie ending. In Britain 'Auntie' is also a nickname for the BBC.
hints: What a child calls a parent's sister.
British nickname for the national broadcaster.

definition: An aunt, or an affectionate name for an older woman.
note: A pet form of aunt. In many cultures it is used for any respected older woman.
hints: Your parent's sister.
A fond name for an older woman.
example: Aunty Kelly treated us to ice cream today.

definition: Relating to the ear or to hearing.
note: From Latin auris, 'ear'. It sounds the same as oral but concerns listening, not speaking.
hints: A near-homophone of a mouth word.
Concerning what you hear.
example: An animal with a very sensitive aural apparatus.

definition: Coloured lights in the polar sky.
note: From Latin Aurora, goddess of dawn.
hints: The northern lights.
Named for a Roman dawn goddess.

definition: The writer of a book or article.
note: From Latin auctor, 'originator'. It is related to authority.
hints: Writes novels.
Name on a book jacket.

definition: A developmental condition affecting communication and social interaction.
note: From Greek autos, 'self', coined in the early 1900s.
hints: A spectrum of neurodevelopment.
Named from a Greek word for self.
origin: German Autismus, from Ancient Greek αὐτός
example: Having autism is much better than dying of polio or measles.

definition: The season between summer and winter.
note: From Latin autumnus. The American term is fall.
hints: Leaves turn brown.
Harvest season.
origin: Middle French automne, from Latin autumnāre

definition: Use or benefit.
note: From Old French valoir, 'to be worth'. 'To no avail' means it did no good.
hints: Efforts that achieve nothing are said to be 'to no' this.
Of use or help.
origin: Old French a; in English since the 15th century

definition: A sailor's command to stop.
note: Probably from Dutch houd vast, 'hold fast'.
hints: Pirates in cartoons shout it.
Nautical word to halt.

definition: An online character that represents you; or a Hindu deity in bodily form.
note: From Sanskrit avatara, 'descent'.
hints: A profile picture in a game.
Vishnu has ten.

definition: To take revenge for a wrong done to someone.
note: From Old French avengier, from Latin vindicare, 'to claim'. It is used when revenge is for another's sake.
hints: A hero in a film swears to do it after a murder.
Marvel's team of heroes took its name from someone who does it.
example: My arms avenge my heartache in the hug they can finally have.

definition: A broad street, often with trees.
note: From French avenue, 'a way of approach'.
hints: Fifth one in New York.
A tree-lined road.

definition: Strongly unwilling or opposed.
note: From Latin aversus, 'turned away', from avertere. It is almost always followed by 'to'.
hints: Usually followed by 'to', as in someone cautious about taking chances.
A person who avoids gambles is described as risk-this.
example: Averse to taking risks.

definition: To turn away; to prevent.
note: From Latin avertere, 'to turn from'. You avert your eyes, or a disaster.
hints: What you do with your eyes from a horror.
To stop something bad happening.
origin: Old French avertir, from Latin āvertere
example: They averted their eyes when the King entered.

definition: Relating to birds.
note: From Latin avis, 'bird'. Aviation comes from the same root.
hints: Bird flu is this kind of influenza.
Related to aviation.

definition: To stay away from.
note: From Old French esvuidier, 'to empty out'. Void shares the root.
hints: What you do with an ex in the street.
To steer clear.
example: I try to avoid the company of gamblers.

definition: To wait for.
note: From Old French awaitier, 'to lie in wait'.
hints: What you do for news.
A grand way to wait.
example: The children eagerly awaited the cake at the birthday party.

definition: Not asleep.
note: From Old English awacan, 'to arise'. Two older verbs, one for waking up and one for being up, merged into it.
hints: The opposite of asleep.
Eyes open in the morning.

definition: To wake up, or to rouse someone from sleep.
note: From Old English awæcnan. It also means to stir a feeling, as in an awakening of conscience.
hints: What Sleeping Beauty finally does after a hundred years.
Used for a feeling suddenly stirred within you.

definition: A prize given for achievement.
note: From Old French awarder, 'to observe, then decide'. It began as a judge's decision.
hints: An Oscar is one.
A prize or ruling.
origin: Anglo-Norman awarder, from Medieval Latin wardare

definition: Knowing about something.
note: From Old English gewær, 'watchful'. Wary shares the root.
hints: Conscious of something.
Related to wary.

definition: Flooded or covered with water.
note: A- plus wash. A rock is awash when waves just cover it.
hints: Flooded, literally or with something.
A city might be this with tourists.
example: The main deck was afloat (or awash).

definition: Very bad.
note: Awe plus -ful. It once meant full of awe, inspiring wonder, before it slid to dreadful.
hints: Terrible, or very bad.
It once meant inspiring wonder.
example: The smell of my socks is awful.

definition: For a short time.
note: From the Old English phrase ane hwile, 'a while'.
hints: Stay a little longer.
For some moments.
example: Sit down and stay awhile.

definition: Relating to an axis.
note: From Latin axis, 'axle'. An axial line runs down the centre of something.
hints: Along a central line.
The Earth's tilt is this.

definition: A statement accepted as true without proof.
note: From Greek axioma, 'what is thought worthy'. Euclid's geometry is built on five.
hints: A self-evident truth.
Euclid started from them.
origin: Middle French axiome, from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα

definition: A proposed subatomic particle.
note: Coined by physicist Frank Wilczek in 1978, who named it after a brand of laundry detergent because it 'cleaned up' a problem.
hints: A hypothetical particle.
Named after a laundry detergent.

definition: A shrub with showy spring flowers.
note: From Greek azaleos, 'dry', because it was said to grow in dry soil.
hints: Blooms bright pink in Japanese gardens.
A relative of the rhododendron.
origin: translingual Azalea, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος
example: Several gardeners look after the azaleas in the park.

definition: Bright blue, like a clear sky.
note: From Arabic lazaward, 'lapis lazuli', the blue stone. The first letter fell off in Old French.
hints: The colour of a cloudless sky.
Named after a blue stone.
origin: Old French azur, from Classical Persian لاجورد

definition: A confusion of many voices.
note: From the Tower of Babel in the Bible, where people suddenly spoke many languages. It means a noisy muddle.
hints: A confusing mix of tongues.
A biblical tower where languages were scrambled.

definition: A reserve, or a copy of data.
note: From the phrase back up.
hints: A second copy of a file.
A spare plan if the first fails.

definition: Cured meat from the back and sides of a pig.
note: From Old French bacon, 'back meat'. Bringing home the bacon first meant winning a prize.
hints: Sizzles in a breakfast pan.
Sizzling slices of pork.

definition: A tough or impressive person, in slang.
note: From bad plus ass, American slang from the mid-1900s.
hints: A hero in an action film.
Cool and tough.

definition: A small sign worn to show identity or achievement.
note: Of uncertain origin; first used for heraldic symbols showing whose household you served.
hints: Scouts sew them on sleeves.
A police officer shows one.
origin: Anglo-Norman bage, from Old Saxon bāg

definition: A stocky black and white striped animal that lives in a sett; or to nag someone.
note: From Middle English bageard, perhaps meaning marked by a badge, its white blaze. To badger someone is to pester them.
hints: A Wind in the Willows character.
What you do when you keep asking again and again.

definition: In a poor or unsatisfactory way.
note: Bad plus -ly. To want something badly is to want it very much.
hints: Not well at all.
How you want something you crave.
example: The car runs badly.

definition: A ring-shaped bread roll, boiled then baked.
note: From Yiddish beygl, from a German word for ring or bracelet.
hints: Often eaten with cream cheese.
A bread roll with a hole.
origin: Yiddish בייגל, from Old High German boug

definition: Loose and hanging away from the body.
note: Bag plus -y. Baggy jeans had a revival in the nineties and again in the 2020s.
hints: Not tight-fitting.
Nineties jeans were this.

definition: The outer courtyard of a medieval castle.
note: From Old French baille, 'enclosure', as in motte and bailey.
hints: Part of a Norman fortress.
Wall-enclosed yard beside a mound.
origin: Old French baile, from Latin bacula

definition: Someone who makes bread and cakes.
note: From Old English bæcere. A baker's dozen is thirteen, an extra loaf against short weight.
hints: Works at dawn with ovens.
Their dozen is thirteen.

definition: A shop or building where bread and cakes are made and sold.
note: From bake plus -ery. It replaced the older word 'bakehouse'.
hints: Where the morning smells come from on a high street.
A baguette is bought here.
example: I don't buy my bread at the supermarket. I go to the bakery.

definition: A bald person, informally.
note: From bald plus -y, a teasing nickname.
hints: Hairless head, teasingly.
A nickname for someone with no hair.
example: His elaborate comb over doesn't conceal the fact that he's a baldy.

definition: A machine that packs hay or straw into bales.
note: From bale, a bundle. Farmers tow them behind tractors.
hints: Farm machine for hay.
Turns loose straw into blocks.
example: Farmer Jones is in straits because his baler is broken down and he's got three fields of hay ready to bale.

definition: A song or poem that tells a story, often a slow romantic one.
note: From Old Occitan ballada, 'a song for dancing', from Late Latin ballare, 'to dance'. The meaning shifted from dance tune to story song.
hints: Folk singers pass down tales of outlaws in this form.
A slow love song at the end of a pop album.
origin: French ballade, from Late Latin ballare
example: On Friday nights, the roller rink had a time-block called "Lovers' Lap" when they played nothing but ballads on the overhead speakers.

definition: A classical dance form.
note: From French ballet, from Italian balletto, 'little dance'.
hints: Swan Lake is an example.
Dancers on pointe.
origin: French ballet, from Late Latin ballō

definition: A vote, or the paper used to cast one.
note: From Italian ballotta, 'little ball', as voters once used small balls.
hints: Cast it in an election.
Paper marked in a booth.
origin: Italian balota, from Middle French balote

definition: A mild, old-fashioned British intensifier.
note: An altered form of bloody, softened for polite company.
hints: Something an old colonel might say.
Gentle replacement for a stronger word.
example: What a bally (or blinking) nuisance.

definition: Pleasantly warm.
note: From balm, a soothing ointment. A balmy evening soothes like one.
hints: Warm summer evenings are this.
Soothingly mild weather.
example: Balmy days and nights.

definition: A very light wood used for model aeroplanes.
note: Spanish for raft; the tree's light timber was used to build rafts.
hints: Wood for model planes.
One of the lightest woods in the world.

definition: A fast-growing tall grass with hollow stems used in building and furniture.
note: The word came into English from Malay or Dutch, with a root probably from Dravidian languages. Pandas famously eat it.
hints: A giant panda's main meal.
Scaffolding in parts of Asia is made from it.

definition: Boring and unoriginal.
note: From Old French ban, 'compulsory feudal service'. Shared by everyone, so commonplace.
hints: Trite and predictable.
Common to the point of boredom.
example: The movie’s dialogue was predictable and banal.

definition: A long curved yellow fruit.
note: From Wolof or another West African language, via Spanish or Portuguese.
hints: Monkeys love it.
Yellow fruit you peel.

definition: A robber, especially one who lives outside the law.
note: From Italian bandito, 'outlawed', from bandire, 'to ban'. An outlaw was literally someone put under a ban.
hints: Western films show masked ones riding off with the loot.
A one-armed gambling machine has a nickname starting with this word.
origin: Italian bandito, from Late Latin bannīre

definition: To toss around, as words or ideas.
note: From a French word for striking a ball back and forth at tennis.
hints: Often paired with words or names.
Pass back and forth, as a rumour might be.

definition: To send someone away and forbid their return.
note: From Old French banir, 'to proclaim', from a Germanic word related to ban. You can banish a worry too.
hints: A king might do so to a rival.
What Napoleon suffered on Elba.
origin: Old French baniss-, from Old English bannan
example: He was banished from the kingdom for his crimes.

definition: A stringed instrument with a round drum-like body.
note: Brought to America by enslaved West Africans, from an instrument like the akonting.
hints: Bluegrass leans on its twang.
Has a drum-like body.
example: I come from Alabama with my banjo on my knee...

definition: A person who works at a bank.
note: From bank plus -er.
hints: Handles customers' money.
Works with loans.

definition: A flag or a large strip of cloth bearing a slogan.
note: From Old French baniere, from a Germanic word for a signal.
hints: Hung above a crowd at a protest.
A flag carried into battle.

definition: Playful, teasing talk.
note: The origin is unknown; it appeared in London slang in the 1600s. Jokes among friends are described this way.
hints: What mates at the pub trade.
Friendly teasing between colleagues.

definition: A person who cuts men's hair.
note: From Old French barbe, 'beard', from Latin barba.
hints: Trims hair and beards.
A shop with a striped pole.

definition: Australian informal for a barbecue.
note: Clipped from barbecue with -ie added. Australians use it for the grill and the party.
hints: Where Aussies throw a prawn, in the old advert.
A cookout in the Australian backyard.

definition: Only just.
note: From bare plus -ly, meaning openly, then scarcely.
hints: By a hair's breadth.
Almost not at all.
example: I barely got to the store.

definition: A flat-bottomed boat for carrying goods on rivers.
note: From Old French barge, via Latin barca, 'small boat'. To barge in is to push in clumsily.
hints: Floats slowly down a canal.
To push rudely into a room.
origin: Old French barge, from Egyptian bꜣjrb-bA-A-y:r*Z1-P1

definition: A person who shouts to attract customers; or a dog that barks.
note: From bark plus -er. Fairground ones shouted at passers-by.
hints: A carnival worker calling 'Step right up!'
A noisy dog by the gate.
example: Bob had amassed a considerable stockpile of double entendres from his days working as a barker for a strip joint.

definition: A cereal grain used for food, beer and whisky.
note: From Old English baerlic, meaning barley-like. It was among the first crops farmed.
hints: Malted, it becomes the base of beer and whisky.
A soup grain often paired with lamb.

definition: British slang for a noisy argument.
note: The origin is unknown. It is sometimes confused with rhyming slang.
hints: A loud row between neighbours over a fence.
What a fight at the pub might be called.

definition: A nobleman of the lowest rank; or a powerful businessman.
note: From Old French barun, 'man, warrior'. Robber barons were the ruthless tycoons of the 1800s.
hints: Media or oil tycoons are called this.
The lowest rank of peer.
origin: Old French baron, from Latin barōnem

definition: The handrail dancers hold while exercising.
note: Borrowed from French barre, 'bar'. Ballet dancers warm up at it.
hints: A rail dancers hold to warm up.
Where ballet students stretch.

definition: A round wooden container; also the tube of a gun.
note: From Old French baril, of uncertain origin.
hints: What wine is aged in.
Part of a gun.
origin: Anglo-Norman baril, from Old French baril

definition: Unable to produce plants or fruit, and so empty.
note: From Anglo-Norman baraigne, of uncertain origin. It describes both poor soil and, in older use, people unable to have children.
hints: A desert or a bare rock face is this.
Land too poor to grow a crop is described this way.

definition: A burial mound; also a wheeled cart for carrying loads.
note: From Old English beorg, 'hill' or 'mound'. The cart sense is a separate word, from Old English bearwe, related to bear.
hints: Archaeologists dig into ancient ones on English downs.
In Tolkien, a creature haunts the Downs near one.

definition: To trade goods or services without using money.
note: From Old French barater, 'to cheat' or exchange. It is how markets worked before coins.
hints: Trading eggs for a haircut.
How people traded before currency existed.

definition: Forming the base; fundamental.
note: From base. Your basal metabolic rate is what your body burns at rest.
hints: At the base of something.
A metabolic rate at rest.
example: This is the basal idea.

definition: An aromatic herb used in cooking.
note: From Greek basilikon, 'royal'. It was considered a herb fit for kings.
hints: Key in pesto.
Its Greek name meant royal.
origin: Middle French basile, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν

definition: A bowl for washing, or a large dip in land.
note: From Old French bacin, from Latin baccinum, 'water vessel'.
hints: A sink is one.
A river drains into one.

definition: The foundation or starting point for something.
note: From Greek basis, 'step' or 'pedestal'. Base shares the root.
hints: Facts form this for an argument.
The grounds for something.
origin: Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις
example: He worked on an interim basis.

definition: A woven container.
note: From Anglo-Norman basket, of unknown origin.
hints: Carry picnic food in it.
Shopping one.

definition: A quantity made at one time.
note: From Old English, 'something baked'. A batch was first the bread from a single firing.
hints: Cookies come out of the oven in one.
A group made together.
