definition: To wash in water, or swim.
note: From Old English baþian. Sunbathing borrowed it for lying in light.
hints: To soak in water.
Sunlight can do it to a room.

definition: A way of dyeing cloth by covering patterns with wax.
note: From Javanese bathik. Indonesia is the best-known home of the craft.
hints: Cloth patterned with wax and dye.
Indonesian fabric art.

definition: An officer's personal servant in the British army.
note: From bat, a packhorse, from Old French bat, 'pack saddle', plus man. It has nothing to do with the flying mammal.
hints: A soldier's servant.
Superhero shares the word.
origin: French bât, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω

definition: A short stick used by a conductor, relay runner or officer.
note: From French bâton, 'stick'. Passing the baton means handing over responsibility.
hints: Relay runners pass it.
A conductor waves it.

definition: To strike repeatedly and hard; also a runny mixture of flour, eggs and milk.
note: From Old French batre, 'to beat'. The mix is named for being beaten, and the baseball player for hitting.
hints: What waves do to a sea wall.
What pancakes and fish and chips begin as.
example: The firemen battered down the door.

definition: A fight between armed forces.
note: From Old French bataille, from Latin battuere, 'to beat'.
hints: Waterloo was a famous one.
A contest of strength.
origin: Old French bataille, from Latin battuō

definition: Slightly mad.
note: From 'bats in the belfry', for a head full of fluttering thoughts.
hints: Eccentric, a bit dotty.
Bats in the belfry.

definition: Humorously rude about sex.
note: From bawd, an old word for a brothel keeper. Shakespeare's comedies are full of bawdy jokes.
hints: Like a saucy seaside postcard.
Rude in a cheerful way.

definition: A slow, marshy creek in the southern United States.
note: From Louisiana French, from Choctaw bayuk, 'creek'.
hints: Louisiana is full of them.
Alligators drift through one.
origin: Louisiana French bayou, from Choctaw bayuk
example: Bayous are common in Gulf Coast areas of the southern United States of America.

definition: A market with many small shops or stalls, especially in the Middle East.
note: From Persian bazar, via Turkish and Italian into English. A charity fair at a church is also called this.
hints: Istanbul's Grand one has thousands of shops.
Where you haggle over spices and carpets.
origin: Middle French bazar, from Persian بازار

definition: A sandy or pebbly shore.
note: From Old English bæce, 'stream'. It came to mean the shingle by the water, then the whole shore.
hints: Where sandcastles get built.
Sand, towels and waves.

definition: A signal light or fire.
note: From Old English beacen, 'sign'.
hints: A fire on a hill warned of invasion.
A lighthouse is one.

definition: Small, round and gleaming, like beads.
note: Bead plus -y. 'Keeping a beady eye' on something means watching it closely.
hints: Describes a suspicious bird's eyes.
Said of a sharp watchful stare, small and bright.

definition: A small hound with floppy ears and a keen nose.
note: Of uncertain origin; one suggested source is a French phrase meaning 'open throat'. The Royal Navy ship that carried Darwin had this name.
hints: Snoopy is a cartoon one.
Used by customs to sniff luggage for food.

definition: Hair growing on the chin and cheeks.
note: From Old English beard. To beard someone once meant to confront them face to face.
hints: Grows on a chin.
Santa has a white one.

definition: A person who carries or brings something.
note: From Old English berere, a carrier, built from bear plus -er. It turns up in 'pallbearer' and 'standard-bearer' too.
hints: Brings a message, a cheque or a coffin.
Appears in 'pall' and 'torch' compounds.
example: The bond was marked `payable to bearer'.

definition: A large wild animal; or a brutal person.
note: From Latin bestia, 'animal'. Bestial and beastly share it.
hints: Beauty's companion.
A wild creature.

definition: Defeated, or struck repeatedly.
note: The past participle of beat.
hints: Lost to a rival.
As in a path much walked.

definition: Someone or something that beats, such as a kitchen whisk.
note: From Old English beatere, 'a boxer or fighter', from beat plus -er. It also names the man who flushes game birds towards the guns.
hints: Mixers have two of these.
Drives pheasants out of the bushes at a shoot.

definition: A fine example, especially in Australian speech.
note: A clipping of beauty.
hints: Australian exclamation of approval.
Short word for something splendid.
example: His roses were beauties.

definition: The quality of being very pleasing to see.
note: From Old French biaute, from Latin bellus, 'pretty'.
hints: Lies in the eye of the beholder.
A thing that is lovely.
origin: Old French beauté, from Latin bellus

definition: A large rodent that builds dams.
note: From Old English beofor, from a root meaning 'brown'. Its fur once drove a huge trade in hats.
hints: A dam-building rodent with a flat tail.
The national animal of Canada.

definition: A fast, complex style of jazz from the 1940s.
note: Imitative of the sound of its rhythm. Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie shaped it.
hints: Fast, tricky jazz of the 1940s.
Charlie Parker's style of jazz.

definition: To begin to be, or to suit someone.
note: From Old English becuman, 'to come about'.
hints: Turn into something new.
Also what a dress can do for its wearer.
origin: Old English becuman; in English since the 12th century
example: She became a doctor when she was 25.

definition: A tree with smooth grey bark.
note: From Old English bece. Book may share an ancient root, perhaps from runes carved on beech tablets.
hints: A smooth-barked tree.
Its wood may have given us book.

definition: Muscular and solid.
note: Beef plus -y. It moved from meat to muscle to anything robust.
hints: A bodybuilder looks this way.
Bulky and strong.
example: The barman was a big, beefy guy with his sleeves rolled up and tattoos on his arms.

definition: An insect with hard wing cases.
note: From Old English bitula, 'little biter'. Volkswagen made a famous car named after it.
hints: A small round car by Volkswagen shares its name.
A scarab in Egyptian art is one.

definition: To be suitable for.
note: Be- plus fit. 'As befits a king' means as is proper for one.
hints: Suitable to someone's status.
Fits in a sentence such as 'behaviour that suits a queen'.
example: He spoke with eloquence befitting a king.

definition: Earlier than, or in front of.
note: From Old English beforan, 'in front of', combining be- and foran.
hints: The opposite of after.
Earlier in time, or in front in place.
example: I want this done before Monday.

definition: To father a child; or to cause.
note: From Old English begietan, 'to get'. Biblical family lists are long chains of it.
hints: Violence is said to do this to violence.
Old word for fathering.
example: The King intends to beget a child within the next five years.

definition: A person who asks others for money or food.
note: From Middle English beggere, formed from beg plus the agent ending.
hints: A proverb says that ones in need can't be choosers.
A poor man sitting on a street corner with a cup.
origin: Old French begart, from Middle Dutch beggaert

definition: To start.
note: From Old English beginnan, of uncertain deeper origin.
hints: A starting pistol or a raised conductor's baton signals you to do it.
What you do at the start.

definition: A title for a Muslim noblewoman in South Asia.
note: A title used in South Asia, reaching English through Urdu and Persian.
hints: A royal or noble woman in Pakistan or India.
Title for a lady of rank.

definition: Having started; the past participle of begin.
note: The past participle of begin, from Old English begunnen. It needs a helper such as 'has' or 'had', unlike 'began'.
hints: A form that follows 'has' or 'had'.
What a job is once you have started it.

definition: Interest or support on someone's part.
note: From Middle English on his halve, 'on his side'.
hints: Speak on someone's account.
Used in a phrase with 'on'.
example: She appeared on behalf of the U.N. Secretary General at a conference held in behalf of the world's children.

definition: To act in a certain way, especially well.
note: From be- plus have, 'to carry oneself'.
hints: What a parent asks a child to do.
Conduct yourself politely.

definition: At the back of, or late.
note: From Old English behindan.
hints: Not in front.
Trailing, or in the rear.

definition: To look at, or to see.
note: From Old English behaldan, 'to hold'.
hints: Biblical word for look.
An old command to see something.
example: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!

definition: A pale sandy colour.
note: Borrowed from French, where it described the colour of undyed wool. It is a neutral shade.
hints: A bland pale brown.
The colour of undyed wool.

definition: A living creature; or existence.
note: Formed from be plus -ing around the 1300s.
hints: Humans and aliens are both these.
Existence itself.

definition: To let gas out from the stomach noisily.
note: From Old English bealcian, an imitation of the sound.
hints: A burp, more loudly.
Chimneys do it with smoke too.

definition: To give a false impression of.
note: Old English belecgan, 'to surround', later 'to tell lies about'.
hints: A calm face may do this to nerves.
To disguise or contradict.
origin: Old English belēogan; in English since the 17th century
example: Her smooth complexion and dark hair belie her actual age.

definition: Acceptance that something is true.
note: From Old English geleafa, related to love and leave.
hints: Faith in a thing.
What you hold to be so.
example: It's my belief that the thief is somebody known to us.

definition: A beautiful woman, especially the most admired at a party.
note: French for 'beautiful'. 'The belle of the ball' is the night's star.
hints: Of the ball, traditionally.
French for beautiful.
example: In her new dress she felt like the belle of the ball.

definition: The stomach area of the body.
note: From Old English belg, 'bag'. Bellows shares the root.
hints: A certain kind of dancer moves it.
Related to bellows.
example: My belly was full of wine.

definition: To be a part of something or in its right place.
note: From be- plus an old word for to go along with.
hints: Fit in a place.
Be the property of someone.
example: I don’t belong to the Southside Crew.

definition: Lower than; under.
note: Be- plus low. Sailors go below to leave the deck.
hints: The opposite of above.
Under something.

definition: A long seat for several people.
note: From Old English benc. Judges sit on one, so 'the bench' means judges.
hints: Parks are full of them.
Players wait on it during a match.

definition: A heavy drinking session; also something that bends.
note: The 'bender' as a binge dates from the 1840s, but its exact origin is unclear. It is also the name of the robot in Futurama.
hints: Slang for a long night out that lasts for days.
A robot in Futurama is named this.
example: He's been out on a bender with his mates.

definition: Able to bend easily.
note: From bend plus -y. A British bus with a flexible middle is called this.
hints: Flexible, like a rubber ruler.
A nickname for an articulated bus.

definition: Gentle, kindly, or harmless, as in a tumour.
note: From Latin benignus, 'kind', from bene, 'well', and genus, 'kind'. Doctors use it for a non-cancerous growth.
hints: What a doctor hopes to hear about a lump.
Said of a mild climate or a kindly smile.
origin: Old French benigne, from Latin benignus

definition: A Japanese packed lunch in a compartmented box.
note: Borrowed from Japanese bentō.
hints: Lunch box with neat little compartments.
Japanese packed meal.

definition: A soft, round, flat cap.
note: From French béret, from a Gascon word for cap.
hints: Classic headwear for French painters.
A soft flat hat.
example: The latest variation of the classic tinfoil hat is the tinfoil beret.

definition: A large military rucksack.
note: Short for Bergen rucksack, possibly named for a Norwegian inventor, Ole Bergan. It is common in British army slang.
hints: Soldiers carry their kit in one on long marches.
Associated with Norwegian origins and British troops.
example: Bergen is known as the city between the seven mountains.

definition: A small, juicy fruit.
note: From Old English berie. Botanists count bananas as berries and strawberries as not.
hints: Bananas count as one, botanically.
Small, juicy and often red.

definition: A bed on a ship or train; or a ship's mooring place.
note: Possibly from bear, as in the room needed to steer clear. 'Give a wide berth' means keep away.
hints: Give someone a wide one.
A bunk on a ship.

definition: A hard mineral that includes emerald and aquamarine.
note: From Greek beryllos. Emeralds and aquamarines are gem varieties.
hints: The mineral behind emerald.
A stone that may be green or blue.
origin: Old French beril, from Prakrit 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑀼𑀮𑀺𑀅

definition: To trouble persistently.
note: From Old English besettan, 'to surround'. A city could be beset by enemies.
hints: Troubles do it from all sides.
Plagued by problems.

definition: At the side of, or next to.
note: From Old English be sidan, 'by the side'.
hints: Next to something.
At your elbow.

definition: A leaf or nut chewed as a stimulant in South and Southeast Asia.
note: From Portuguese, from Malayalam vettila. Chewing it stains the teeth red.
hints: Chewed across South Asia.
Stains the mouth red.

definition: To break someone's trust, especially by helping their enemies.
note: From Middle English betrayen, built from be- and the Old French word for 'hand over'. Judas is its most famous example.
hints: Judas did it for thirty pieces of silver.
A spy who sells secrets does this to their country.

definition: A small, brightly coloured freshwater fish, also called a fighting fish.
note: From the genus name Betta. Males are famous for aggression towards each other.
hints: A colourful fish often kept alone in a bowl.
Siamese fighting fish go by this name.

definition: Of higher quality or more suitable.
note: From Old English betera, comparative of an old word related to boot, meaning advantage.
hints: What 'good' becomes when compared.
Superior to what came first.

definition: A sloping edge.
note: From Old French baivel, from bayer, 'to gape'. Mirrors often have them.
hints: A slanted edge on glass.
Mirrors are often given one.

definition: To be on guard.
note: From be plus ware, an old word for careful.
hints: Sign at a dog's gate.
Warning to take care.
example: Beware of telephone salesmen.

definition: On the far side of; past.
note: From Old English begeondan.
hints: Past the limits.
Further than far.
example: No swimming beyond this point.

definition: The ring holding the glass of a watch or a gem.
note: From French biseau, 'sloping edge'.
hints: Frames a watch face.
Holds a gemstone in place.
example: The bezel on that old iPhone model was white.

definition: An authoritative book on a subject.
note: From Greek biblia, 'books'. 'The angler's bible' borrows the idea of the definitive text.
hints: A must-have reference book.
Its Greek root means books.

definition: The muscle at the front of the upper arm.
note: From Latin biceps, 'two-headed', for its two attachment points. Bicep is a modern back-formation.
hints: Flexed to show strength.
Its Latin root meant two-headed.

definition: The muscle at the front of the upper arm.
note: From Latin biceps, 'two-headed', from bis and caput. The muscle starts as two heads at the shoulder.
hints: Flexed to show off strength.
Bulges when you curl a dumbbell.
example: When men go to the gym it seems they really work their biceps.

definition: A person who offers a price at an auction.
note: From bid plus -er. The highest one wins the lot.
hints: The one who raises a paddle at Sotheby's.
The winner gets the hammer to fall in their favour.
example: The highest bidder shall get the house.

definition: A fussy or gossipy old woman.
note: From Biddy, a pet form of Bridget. It became slang for any older woman.
hints: An old busybody.
From a pet form of Bridget.

definition: A low basin for washing the lower body.
note: From French bidet, which originally meant a small horse.
hints: Fixture in French bathrooms.
Its name means pony in French.
example: And it has to have a bathroom with a bidet.

definition: Larger.
note: The comparative of big, whose origin is uncertain.
hints: Of greater size than another.
Compared with something else, greater.
example: The stalk is a little bigger around than your little finger.

definition: A wide bay or a bend in the coast; also a loop in a rope.
note: From Old English byht, 'bend'. It sounds like bite and rhymes with night.
hints: The Great Australian one is a huge curve of coast.
Part of a rope, or an open bay.

definition: An intolerant person with fixed prejudices.
note: From French bigot. A popular story traces it to Normans swearing 'bi God', but nobody is sure.
hints: Intolerant of others' views.
Narrow-minded to a fault.
origin: French bigot, from Middle English bi God
example: It is useless to reason with a bigot.

definition: Small and elegant; also a jewel.
note: Borrowed from French bijou, 'jewel'.
hints: A tiny, stylish flat might be called this.
French word for a trinket or small jewel.

definition: A person who rides a motorbike or bicycle.
note: From bike plus -er. It has meant a motorcycle rider since the mid-twentieth century.
hints: Wears a leather jacket and rides a motorbike.
A cyclist who takes to the road.
example: The police are going all out to keep down the rioting bikers.

definition: A two-piece swimsuit.
note: Named for Bikini Atoll, where atomic tests took place in 1946, as the design was said to be explosive.
hints: Worn at the beach.
Named after a Pacific atoll.

definition: The bottom of a ship's hull; or nonsense.
note: Probably a variant of bulge. The water that collects there is foul, hence nonsense.
hints: Dirty water at the bottom of a ship.
Rubbish talk.

definition: A pretty but unintelligent person, in a mocking slang.
note: Borrowed from Italian bimbo, 'little child', and first used of a man.
hints: Mocking word, once used of men.
Italian for baby.
example: The only difference between a bimbo and a prostitute is payment.

definition: Made of two parts; a number system using only 0 and 1.
note: From Latin binarius, 'consisting of two'.
hints: The code computers use.
Two-state system.
example: Two ingredients are combined in a binary poison.

definition: A cover or folder that holds loose papers; or something that binds.
note: From bind plus -er. Ring binders are standard in offices and schools.
hints: Holds loose pages in a ring clip.
A school folder crammed with worksheets.

definition: A game of chance played with numbered cards.
note: Probably from bing, a ringing sound. It is also shouted when something works out.
hints: Two little ducks, twenty-two.
Shouted when you win.
example: He plays bingo with his family on Saturdays.

definition: A large natural community, such as desert or rainforest.
note: Bio- plus -ome, coined by ecologists in 1916.
hints: The tundra is one.
A large ecological community.
example: You can find different mobs on different biomes.

definition: A film telling the true life story of a person.
note: A clipping of biographical picture.
hints: Rami Malek played Freddie Mercury in one.
Actors often win Oscars for these.

definition: The removal of a small tissue sample to be examined for disease.
note: From Greek bios 'life' plus opsis 'sight', literally a look at living tissue.
hints: A doctor takes one from a suspicious lump.
A tissue sample sent to a lab to check for cancer.
example: We will need to perform a biopsy to determine whether the tumour is malignant or benign.

definition: All the living things in a particular region.
note: From Greek bios, 'life'.
hints: Plants and animals of an area together.
The sum of a region's life forms.
origin: New Latin biota, from Ancient Greek βιοτή
example: For a start, we have a very incomplete knowledge of the earth's biota.

definition: A small bird; or one stroke under par at a golf hole.
note: From bird plus -ie. The golf sense arose in early 20th-century America, where 'bird' meant something excellent.
hints: What a golfer hopes to score on a hole.
A badminton shuttlecock has this nickname.
example: Aw, that's a cute little birdie. Is it a budgie?

definition: The start of life.
note: From Old Norse byrth. Bear, as in to carry a child, shares the root.
hints: Celebrated each year afterward.
The start of a life.
example: They divorced after the birth of the child.

definition: A senior Christian clergyman; also a chess piece.
note: From Greek episkopos, 'overseer'.
hints: Moves diagonally on a board.
A church leader in a mitre.
origin: Old English bisċop, from Vulgar Latin

definition: A large wild ox with a shaggy mane.
note: From Latin bison, a Germanic word for wild ox.
hints: Roamed the great plains.
Often called a buffalo.
origin: Middle French bison, from Latin bisōn
example: The reserve named Białowieża Forest is famous for its bison.

definition: A small, casual restaurant, usually French.
note: From French bistro, whose origin is unknown. A popular story says Russian soldiers in Paris in 1814 shouted 'bystro', 'quickly', but historians doubt it.
hints: A Parisian café with small round tables.
Chalkboard menu and checked tablecloths.
example: In this bistro, there's always a lot of students.

definition: Past participle of bite; having been nipped by teeth or an insect.
note: From Old English biten, the past participle of bite. 'Once bitten, twice shy' says a bad experience makes you cautious.
hints: Where a mosquito or dog may have left a mark.
What a snake victim has been.
example: My dog has never bitten anyone before.

definition: Having a sharp, unpleasant taste, or resentful.
note: From Old English bitere, related to bite.
hints: Coffee or dark chocolate.
Angry and sour.
example: The coffee tasted bitter.

definition: Made up of small, unconnected bits.
note: Bit plus -y. Itty-bitty adds a rhyme for extra smallness.
hints: Disjointed, in fragments.
Itty plus it means tiny.

definition: The darkest colour.
note: From Old English blæc. Old English blac, 'pale, shining', was a different word.
hints: Night's colour.
The colour of soot.

definition: The cutting edge of a knife or tool.
note: From Old English blæd, 'leaf'. A blade of grass kept the older sense.
hints: A knife's sharp part.
A single leaf of grass.

definition: Responsibility for a fault.
note: From Old French blasmer, from the same Latin as blaspheme.
hints: What you place on someone.
Related to blaspheme.
origin: Old French blame, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω

definition: Lacking flavour or interest.
note: From Latin blandus, 'smooth, flattering'. It moved from soothing to dull.
hints: Unseasoned food.
Unremarkable.

definition: Empty; with nothing written.
note: From French blanc, 'white'. A blank page was a white one.
hints: A form left unfilled.
Its French root meant white.

definition: To make a loud harsh sound.
note: From Middle English bleren, 'to wail', imitating the noise.
hints: What car horns do.
Music played far too loud.
example: The trumpet blaring in my ears gave me a headache.

definition: An explosion or strong gust.
note: From Old English blæst, 'blowing'. As slang, a great time.
hints: A loud explosion.
A really fun time.

definition: A large, fierce fire.
note: From Old English blæse, 'torch'. To blaze a trail meant marking trees by cutting away bark.
hints: A raging fire.
To mark a new trail.

definition: A smart jacket, often with a school or club badge.
note: From blaze plus -er. A popular story says it came from the bright red jackets of a Cambridge rowing club.
hints: Part of a school uniform.
Worn with a badge on its chest pocket.
example: He hung his blazer on a hanger because it was really hot.

definition: A chemical that whitens fabric or kills germs; also to remove colour.
note: From Old English blaecan, 'to whiten', related to bleak and the root meaning 'pale'. Laundry and hair dye both use it.
hints: What laundry does to stains and some people do to their hair.
A household cleaner with a sharp smell, kept under the sink.

definition: Cold, bare and depressing.
note: From Old Norse bleikr, 'pale'. Bleach shares the root.
hints: A grey winter moor.
Related to bleach.
example: They escaped across the bleak landscape.

definition: The cry of a sheep or goat.
note: From Old English blætan, imitating the sound.
hints: What a lamb does.
To complain in a whiny voice.

definition: To lose blood.
note: From Old English bledan, from blod, 'blood'.
hints: What a cut does.
Colours can do it in the wash.

definition: A short high electronic sound.
note: Imitative. TV used it to cover swear words.
hints: Censors put it over swearing.
A short beep.

definition: To mix together.
note: From Old Norse blanda, 'to mix'. Blond may share the root.
hints: What a smoothie maker does.
A mixture of coffees.
origin: Old English blandan, from Old Norse blanda
example: The colors blend well.

definition: To make holy, or to wish someone well.
note: From Old English bletsian, 'to consecrate with blood', from an old sense of sprinkling or marking. Over time the word lost the blood and kept the holiness.
hints: What you might say after someone sneezes.
A priest might do this to a crowd with a raised hand.

definition: A plant disease that withers crops; also anything that spoils or ruins.
note: Its origin is uncertain. It meant a plant disease long before it came to mean any ruining influence.
hints: The potato famine in Ireland was caused by a famous one.
Planners use it for an abandoned, decaying stretch of a city.

definition: A large, rounded airship with no rigid frame.
note: Historians are unsure of its origin, but a popular theory says it imitates the sound made by thumping the airship's skin.
hints: It floats above stadiums, sometimes carrying a camera.
Cousin of the zeppelin, but squashier.

definition: Unable to see.
note: From Old English blind, a very old Germanic word. It also came to describe things you cannot see through, as with window shades.
hints: Window coverings that roll or slat are named for it.
A person who reads with their fingertips, perhaps.
example: Even a blind hen sometimes finds a grain of corn.

definition: Flashy jewellery.
note: Imitative of the glint of jewellery, popularised by hip-hop in the late 1990s. It means ostentatious display.
hints: Chunky gold chains.
Showy diamonds and gold.
example: The rapper was loaded with bling.

definition: To close and open your eyes quickly.
note: From Middle English blynken, related to an Old English word meaning 'to deceive'. An older sense was a quick glance or gleam of light.
hints: You do it without thinking, thousands of times a day.
A staring contest is lost when you do this.
example: The TV announcer never seems to blink.

definition: Perfect happiness.
note: From Old English bliss, from a word for joy. It was once spelled blis and tied to the idea of gladness or a blithe spirit.
hints: A feeling beyond mere contentment.
Ignorance is said to be this.
example: The afternoon at the spa was utter bliss.

definition: A sudden, overwhelming attack or burst of effort.
note: Clipped from German Blitzkrieg, 'lightning war'. The German word for lightning is Blitz, and English borrowed it as a name for fast attacks.
hints: Football teams use one to rush the quarterback.
London endured a long wartime one of these from the air.
example: We embarked on a publicity blitz, putting posters and flyers all around town.

definition: To swell up with fluid or gas.
note: Perhaps from Middle English blout, 'soft, flexible', from Old Norse. It first meant soft or puffy before it meant swollen.
hints: How you feel after an enormous meal.
Software with too many unneeded features is said to suffer from it.

definition: A man, especially an ordinary one.
note: Its origin is unknown; guesses include Celtic borrowings. It is especially common in British, Australian and Irish English.
hints: A very British word for a guy.
'A decent one', you might say of a friendly fellow.
example: He's a good bloke.

definition: Having pale yellow hair.
note: Borrowed from French, from Old French blont, which came from a Frankish word for a mixed golden colour. The spelling blond is for male hair; the form with an extra e was for female.
hints: Colour of hair that sunshine might lighten.
Dark-haired people sometimes dye their hair this way.
origin: Middle French blond m, from Old French blond

definition: The red liquid pumped around the body by the heart.
note: From Old English blod, a very old Germanic word. It also came to stand for family ties, as in 'bad' or 'blue' kinds.
hints: Flows through your veins.
What you donate in a drive at the hospital.
example: Some insects are known for consuming blood.

definition: A loose shirt, usually worn by women.
note: From French blouse, first a workman's or peasant's smock. English borrowed it in the early 1800s.
hints: Often tucked into a skirt for the office.
A top with buttons and sometimes a ruffled collar.

definition: A person or device that blows; in British slang, a telephone.
note: From blow plus -er. 'Get on the blower' once meant to phone someone, from speaking-tubes in old buildings.
hints: British slang for a phone.
A device that clears leaves from a garden.

definition: Moved or shaped by air; also swollen or out of breath.
note: The past participle of blow, from Old English blawan. The old sense of 'puffed up' survives in words like 'blown glass' and 'full-blown'.
hints: Glass can be shaped this way.
What a candle is once someone has puffed it out.
origin: Old English blāƿen, from Old English blāwan
example: Blown clouds of dust choked the riders.

definition: More blue in colour.
note: The comparative of blue, which came into English from Old French bleu, a word of Germanic origin.
hints: Comparing two skies or two oceans.
The sea is often this on a clear day.

definition: Not sharp; or speaking in a direct, tactless way.
note: From Middle English, possibly Old Norse in origin, linked to a verb meaning 'to shut the eyes'. First used of dull edges, later of dull minds and then plain-speaking people.
hints: A knife that cannot cut well is this.
Honest to the point of rudeness.

definition: Not sharp or clear.
note: From blur plus -y. A shaky photo or tired eyes can be blurry.
hints: A photo taken while walking.
Your vision after taking off your glasses.
example: Everything looks blurry. I think I need a new pair of glasses.

definition: To say something suddenly, without thinking.
note: Possibly imitative of a sudden sound. It has been used for hasty speech for centuries.
hints: A secret often escapes this way.
Done by someone who can't hold back an answer.
example: Please think about your reply and don't just blurt out the first thing that comes to mind.

definition: To turn red in the face from embarrassment.
note: From Middle English blusshen, from Old English blysċan, 'to be red, to shine'. A glance or glow of red once described a sudden look as well.
hints: Compliments might make you do it.
Also a pink cosmetic for the cheeks.
example: The girl blushed when a young man whistled as she walked by.

definition: A long flat piece of wood.
note: From Old English bord, meaning a plank. It grew into a table, meals ('room and board'), a ship's side, and a group of directors around a table.
hints: What you do to get onto a plane or ship.
Chess and Monopoly are played on one.
example: He nailed boards across the windows.

definition: Enlightenment in Buddhism.
note: Sanskrit for 'awakening'. The Buddha reached it beneath a bodhi tree.
hints: The awakening the Buddha reached.
Tree under which the Buddha sat.

definition: Relating to the body.
note: From body plus -ly.
hints: Physical, not mental.
Harm done to a person.
example: His bodily deficiencies were a heavy burden to him.

definition: In Australian slang, an unfashionable person of working-class background.
note: Of uncertain origin; it appeared in Australia in the 1980s.
hints: Australian slang for someone seen as unsophisticated.
A label from Down Under for an unfashionable person.

definition: An evil spirit; or one stroke over par in golf.
note: Probably related to bogle, a Scottish word for a goblin. The golf term comes from a song about a Colonel Bogey.
hints: What a child may fear in the dark.
A golf score one over par.

definition: A set of wheels under a railway carriage.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps a dialect word.
hints: Wheels under a train car.
A rail truck that pivots.

definition: Fake; not genuine.
note: First American slang for counterfeit coin-making equipment, early nineteenth century. It later meant any sham.
hints: A fake coin.
A sham claim.
example: He was arrested for trying to cash a bogus check at the bank.

definition: A device that heats water for a building.
note: From boil plus -er.
hints: Heats a house's radiators.
Part of a steam engine.

definition: In a brave, confident way.
note: From Old English bealdlice, from bold plus -ly. Star Trek's captain goes where no one has gone this way.
hints: Star Trek's captain goes where no one has gone before in this manner.
Without fear or hesitation.
example: The government acted boldly to deal with the outlaw uprising.

definition: A soft lump of chewed food ready to be swallowed; or a large single dose.
note: From Greek bolos, meaning clod or lump.
hints: Mouthful that you're about to swallow.
A big single injection of medicine.
origin: Late Latin bōlus, from Ancient Greek βῶλος

definition: An aircraft that drops bombs, or a short jacket.
note: From bomb plus -er.
hints: A plane in a war film.
A type of leather flying jacket.

definition: One of a pair of small drums played with the hands.
note: From Spanish bongo, the name of these drums of Cuban origin. The same word names a striped African antelope.
hints: Played by hand, usually in pairs.
A beatnik might drum on one.
origin: United States Spanish bongó, from Ekele boungu

definition: A hat tied under the chin; also the hood of a car in British English.
note: From Old French bonet, the name of a material for hats. In Britain, you lift one to check the engine.
hints: Little Bo Peep and Jane Austen's heroines wore one.
A British mechanic props it up to look at the engine.

definition: Scottish word for attractive and pleasant.
note: Probably from Old French bon, 'good', ultimately from Latin bonus. Bonnie Prince Charlie carried the name into history.
hints: Said fondly of a Scottish lass or of 'banks and braes'.
A pretty child in Glasgow might be called this.
origin: Old French bon, from Latin bonus

definition: An extra reward on top of what you expected.
note: Borrowed from Latin bonus, 'good'. It came to mean a good thing added on, such as extra pay.
hints: Paid at year end if the company did well.
An extra level in a video game might be called this.

definition: A silly person; also a tropical seabird.
note: From Spanish bobo, 'fool', from Latin balbus, 'stammering'. The seabird was so named because it seemed foolishly tame and easy to catch.
hints: A trap rigged to catch someone off guard has this word before it.
A bird with blue feet is named for it.

definition: To dance energetically; or a style of piano music.
note: The origins are unclear, but the word was used in African American music in the early 1900s. Boogie-woogie piano used a driving left hand.
hints: What you do on the dance floor to disco.
A rolling piano style from the 1930s.

definition: Someone who arranges bookings for performers or reservations.
note: From book plus -er. In the entertainment industry, bookers arrange acts.
hints: The person who arranges the guests on a talk show.
Someone who fills a theatre's calendar.

definition: Slang for someone from the post-war baby boom; also a loud thing.
note: Short for baby boomer, a person born roughly 1946 to 1964. 'OK boomer' became a dismissive retort in 2019.
hints: The generation after the Second World War.
Taunted by younger people in the phrase 'OK ___'.
example: They expanded the schools for a generation of baby boomers.

definition: To push up or increase something.
note: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the early 1800s. It started as a push upward for someone climbing.
hints: What a pep talk gives to morale.
A helping hand to lift you up.

definition: A small enclosed stall or compartment.
note: From a Norse word meaning 'dwelling'. It first meant a temporary shelter of boughs or tents, later a market stall.
hints: A phone one was once a street fixture.
Where you cast your vote privately.

definition: Treasure taken as loot.
note: From Middle English, from Old French butin and Middle Low German bute, 'share, loot'. Its later slang sense is separate and informal.
hints: What pirates go after.
Plunder carried off from a defeated enemy.
origin: Old French butin, from Middle Low German bǖte

definition: Alcoholic drink.
note: Originally a Northern English dialect form of bowse, a word for drinking deeply. It has been slang for liquor for centuries.
hints: A bottle shop sells it by the bottle.
Casual word for what you drink at a party.

definition: Drinking a lot of alcohol, or full of it.
note: Built from booze plus -y, the adjective ending. It describes people or occasions.
hints: A long and rowdy lunch might be called this.
A drink with plenty of spirits in it.
example: His boozy drinking companions.

definition: A white mineral salt used in cleaning and glassmaking.
note: Through Medieval Latin and Old French from Arabic bawraq, which itself came from Persian. The mineral was traded across the medieval world.
hints: A laundry booster sold in boxes.
A salt of boric acid found in dry lake beds.
origin: Anglo-Norman boreis, from Middle Persian bwlk'

definition: The edge or boundary of something.
note: From Old French bordure, from a word for edge.
hints: The line between two countries.
A flowerbed edge.

definition: Dull and not interesting.
note: From bore plus -ing; the origin of that bore is uncertain.
hints: Makes you yawn.
Tedious and uninteresting.
example: A boring evening with uninteresting people.

definition: Carried or endured; the past participle of bear.
note: From Old English boren, past participle of beran, 'to carry'. It is the form used for carrying and enduring, while the spelling without the e is kept for birth.
hints: Burdens and grudges are carried this way.
A form of bear, as in 'water-' or 'air-' compounds.
origin: Old English boren, from Old English beran

definition: A chemical element with the symbol B.
note: From borax plus carbon. It is used in glass and detergent.
hints: An element in laundry products.
Element number five.
example: How many moles of boron are there in this solution?

definition: To take something with the intention of returning it.
note: From Old English borgian, 'to give a pledge'.
hints: Take a book from a library.
Neighbours do it with a ladder; banks do it with interest.

definition: The chest, or a person's closest circle.
note: From Old English bosm, a very old Germanic word. We hold things close to it, which is how it came to mean one's inner feelings.
hints: A very close pal is called a buddy of this sort.
A mother holds a baby against hers.

definition: A subatomic particle of a kind that includes the Higgs.
note: Named for the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, with the -on ending from electron.
hints: A class of particle named after a physicist.
The Higgs is one.
example: The Higgs boson has been called the God particle.

definition: Fond of ordering other people around.
note: Built from boss, which came from Dutch baas, 'master', plus -y. It is an informal way of saying domineering.
hints: The sort of older sibling who gives all the orders.
Unwanted attitude on a group project.

definition: The scientific study of plants.
note: A back-formation from botanic, which goes back to Greek botane, 'pasture' or 'herb'.
hints: Charles Darwin's friend Joseph Hooker made his name in it.
A university course covering ferns, flowers and photosynthesis.

definition: To do something badly or clumsily.
note: From Middle English bocchen, 'to mend', of uncertain origin. It first meant to patch up, and mending done carelessly gave us the modern meaning.
hints: A poor repair job is this.
A word for ruining a task by sloppy work.
origin: Old English bōtettan, from Middle Dutch botsen

definition: To annoy or take the trouble.
note: Probably from Irish bodhar, 'deaf' or 'bothered'. It first appears in the 1700s.
hints: A small nuisance.
Take the effort.

definition: A narrow-necked container for liquids.
note: From Old French botele, from Latin buttis, 'cask'.
hints: Holds water or wine.
Baby milk may come in one.
origin: Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula
example: Beer is often sold in bottles.

definition: The lowest part of something.
note: From Old English botm.
hints: Where the sea floor lies.
Where the dregs settle in a glass.
example: They started at the bottom of the hill.

definition: A large branch of a tree.
note: From Old English bog, 'shoulder, arm', which shows the branch was compared to a limb of the body. The spelling is a tricky one.
hints: A cradle in the lullaby falls when it breaks.
Heavy with fruit or snow.
example: The bough didn't support his weight and broke off.

definition: To spring back after hitting something.
note: Probably imitative of a thump.
hints: What a ball does on the floor.
Spring up and down.

definition: Springy, or full of lively energy.
note: Formed from bounce plus -y.
hints: A children's castle at a party is named with it.
A puppy's step or a rubber ball can be this.

definition: Tied up, or certain to happen; also heading somewhere.
note: The tied-up sense is the past tense of bind, from Old English bunden. The 'heading for' sense is a separate word, from Old Norse buinn, 'made ready'.
hints: What a prisoner or a parcel might be.
Sometimes followed by 'for' and a destination.

definition: A reward, or generosity.
note: From Old French bonte, 'goodness'.
hints: A reward for catching an outlaw.
A chocolate bar and a mutinous ship share the word.
origin: Anglo-Norman bounté, from Old French bonté

definition: The intestine, or the deep inner part of something.
note: From Old French, from Latin botellus, 'little sausage'. It also names deep inner parts, as in 'the ___s of the ship'.
hints: Part of the digestive tract below the stomach.
Doctors screen it for cancer.
origin: Middle French bouel, from Latin botellus
example: Sami kept kicking Layla until she lost control of her bowels.

definition: A leafy shelter; or a lady's chamber in a castle.
note: From Old English bur, 'dwelling'. A pergola covered in vines can be called it.
hints: A shady arbour in a garden.
A private room in a medieval castle.

definition: A cricketer who delivers the ball; also a round hat.
note: From bowl plus -er. The hat is named for a London hatter named Bowler.
hints: A cricket team's attacking player.
A round hard hat worn in the City of London.

definition: An archer; or the rower closest to the front of a boat.
note: From bow plus -man. English longbowmen won Agincourt.
hints: A medieval soldier at Agincourt.
The oarsman nearest the front of the boat.

definition: A person who fights in a ring wearing gloves.
note: Simply box plus -er. The dog breed was named for the way it seems to spar with its front paws.
hints: Muhammad Ali was a famous one.
A breed of dog with a squashed nose and drooping jowls.

definition: To prepare for something unpleasant; or a support.
note: From Old French brace, 'arm', from Latin bracchium. Arms hold things tight, so the word came to mean a support or a prop.
hints: What you do before an impact on a plane.
Some people wear one on their teeth.
origin: Old French brace, from Latin bracchia
example: All hands, brace for impact!

definition: To weave three strands of hair together.
note: From Old English bregdan, which meant sudden movement, pulling or weaving. The sense of interweaving remained.
hints: A hairstyle with three woven strands.
Also a decorative cord sewn onto uniforms.

definition: A device that slows or stops a vehicle.
note: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a Middle Dutch word for a curb. Many other unrelated things share the spelling.
hints: Press the pedal and the car does this.
Bicycles have hand levers for it.

definition: A limb of a tree, or a division of an organisation.
note: From Old French branche, from Late Latin branca, 'paw'.
hints: Where birds perch.
A local bank office.
origin: Old French branche, from Late Latin branca

definition: A strong spirit distilled from wine or fruit juice.
note: From Dutch brandewijn, 'burnt wine', meaning wine that had been heated to distil it. Cognac is a famous kind.
hints: A warming spirit poured from a decanter after dinner.
Cognac and armagnac are the most celebrated types.

definition: A small dark goose that breeds in the Arctic.
note: Probably from a Scandinavian word. It winters on the coast.
hints: A small dark wild goose.
A sea goose in winter.
origin: Medieval Latin Branta, from Old Norse brandgás

definition: Loud, bold and tactless.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Scots word for a violent onset or attack.
hints: Not a quiet type at all.
A young hotshot who talks over everyone.
example: A brash newcomer disputed the age-old rules for admission to the club.

definition: A yellow alloy of copper and zinc; also trumpets and trombones.
note: From Old English bræs, of uncertain origin. Instruments made of the metal came to be a section of an orchestra.
hints: Trumpets and trombones belong to this section.
Doorknobs are often made of it.

definition: A cry of praise to a woman performer.
note: The Italian feminine of bravo.
hints: Shouted at an opera singer.
What you call out for a diva.

definition: Ready to face danger without fear.
note: From Middle French, borrowed from Italian bravo. It once meant splendid or fine as well as courageous.
hints: Firefighters are said to be this.
The opposite of cowardly.
origin: Middle French brave, from Italian bravo
example: Familiarity with danger makes a brave man braver but less daring.

definition: A shout of praise for a performance.
note: Borrowed from Italian, where it means 'good' or 'skilled'. It shares an origin with the word brave.
hints: Audiences shout it at the end of an opera.
Also the word for the letter B in the radio alphabet.

definition: A noisy fight, usually involving many people.
note: From Middle English braulen, 'to clamour or quarrel', of otherwise uncertain origin.
hints: A pub fight often turns into one.
Messier than a scuffle.

definition: Bold and shameless, or made of brass.
note: From Old English bræsen, 'of brass'. To be brazen was to be hard and shiny as brass, and 'brazen it out' means to bluff boldly.
hints: A thief who robs in daylight.
Said of a lie told to your face.

definition: A gap made by breaking through, or a failure to keep a rule.
note: From Old English brice, 'a breaking'.
hints: A hole in a wall or a broken promise.
Hackers can cause a data one.

definition: A baked food made from flour and water.
note: From Old English bread, a Germanic word. It once meant a piece or morsel, and loaf was the word for the whole.
hints: A baker's chief product.
Slice it for toast or a sandwich.

definition: To split into pieces, or to stop for a rest.
note: From Old English brecan, a very old Germanic verb. It has also come to mean a pause, a lucky chance and a dawn.
hints: What a dropped plate does.
A short rest from work.

definition: A flat-bodied freshwater fish of Europe.
note: From Middle English breme, via Old French and Frankish.
hints: Silver fish caught by anglers.
A deep-bodied river fish.

definition: The upper front part of the body; the chest.
note: From Old English breost.
hints: Chest of a bird.
Part of the body near the heart.

definition: The air taken in and let out of the lungs.
note: From Old English braeth, 'smell' or 'vapour'.
hints: What you hold under water.
What you see on a cold day.
example: I could feel the runner's breath on my shoulder.

definition: To produce young; or a type of animal.
note: From Old English bredan, related to brood. A kind of animal came to be named for how it was bred.
hints: A poodle is one type of dog this way.
Farmers do it with cattle.
example: Pandas rarely breed in captivity.

definition: A light wind; or something easy.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from Spanish or Portuguese.
hints: A gentle wind from the sea.
An easy task.
example: The breeze rustled the papers on her desk.

definition: Pleasantly windy, or cheerful and casual.
note: From breeze plus -y. A breezy person is as light and unbothered as a mild wind.
hints: A word for a seaside afternoon.
Also a manner that treats serious things lightly.

definition: A person or company that makes beer.
note: From brew plus -er. Hops are central to their craft.
hints: Someone who makes beer for a living.
Works with malt, hops and yeast.
example: By that time, Anheuser-Busch was the largest brewer in the region.

definition: A thorny, tangled shrub such as a wild rose.
note: From Old English brer, of unknown further origin. Pipe makers use the wood of a related plant.
hints: Br'er Rabbit was famously thrown into a patch of it.
A thorny tangle that snags your clothes.

definition: A hard block of baked clay used for building.
note: From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bricke, originally a broken piece or tile. The word came to mean a whole block.
hints: The house of the second pig was made of it.
Red blocks stacked with mortar.
example: This wall is made of bricks.

definition: Relating to a bride or a wedding.
note: From Old English brydealo, 'bride ale', the wedding feast. It was once a noun for the party itself.
hints: Describes a gown, shower or suite.
A shop that sells gowns for a wedding.

definition: A woman on her wedding day.
note: From Old English bryd, a Germanic word that has meant a woman about to marry for well over a thousand years.
hints: Walks down the aisle in white.
Throws a bouquet after the ceremony.

definition: A structure spanning a river or road; also a card game.
note: From Old English brycg.
hints: Crosses a river.
A game with a trump suit.

definition: Short in time or in words.
note: From Latin brevis, 'short', through Old French. A legal summary and a set of lawyer's instructions took the name because they were short documents.
hints: A short summary given before a meeting.
Underwear style that is cut short.
origin: Old French brief, from Latin brevis; in English since the 15th century

definition: Giving off much light, or clever.
note: From Old English beorht.
hints: Sunny, or smart.
Full of light.

definition: Very salty water.
note: From Old English brine, a Germanic word for salt water. It later also named the sea itself in poetry.
hints: Pickles are kept in it.
A cucumber soaks in this to become a pickle.

definition: To carry something to a place.
note: From Old English bringan, a very old Germanic verb meaning to carry or lead toward the speaker.
hints: The opposite of take.
Fetch something and come back with it.

definition: The edge of something steep, or the point just before a change.
note: From Middle English, from Old Norse, meaning the edge of a hill or slope. We now use it for the edge of dramatic events.
hints: Someone on this of tears is about to cry.
A cliff has one; so does a crisis.

definition: Salty, like seawater.
note: From brine plus -y. It often describes the taste of oysters or the smell of the sea. Poets also use it as a name for the ocean itself.
hints: What the sea tastes like.
A pickle or an olive has this flavour.

definition: Wide, from side to side.
note: From Old English brad, a very old Germanic word. It also came to mean general, as in 'in broad terms'.
hints: Shoulders on a swimmer might be this.
In the daylight, as in 'in ___ daylight'.
example: A river two miles broad.

definition: An old word for a badger.
note: From Old English broc, 'badger'. It survives as a surname and in countryside names.
hints: An old name for a badger.
A woodland animal with a striped face.

definition: To cook with strong direct heat from above.
note: From Middle English, from Old French bruller, 'to burn'. Another sense is a noisy quarrel, from a different word.
hints: Something an American oven can do at its top setting.
To grill under a hot element.

definition: In pieces, or not working.
note: The past participle of break, from Old English brecan.
hints: Smashed into pieces.
Not working anymore.
example: His neck is broken.

definition: An agent who buys and sells for others.
note: From Anglo-Norman brocour, a wine tapster.
hints: A stock or house go-between.
Arranges a deal.

definition: An alloy of copper and tin; also the colour, or a third-place medal.
note: From Italian bronzo, possibly of Persian origin.
hints: Third-place medal.
Metal of statues and bells.

definition: A piece of jewellery fastened to clothing with a pin.
note: A variant of broach, from Old French broche, 'pointed tool' or pin.
hints: Worn on a lapel or scarf.
Grandmother's heirloom, pinned to her coat.

definition: To worry or sulk; also a group of young birds.
note: From Old English brod, 'breeding, hatching'. The hen sitting over her eggs became a picture of someone sitting and thinking over a problem.
hints: A hen with chicks has one.
What a moody person does alone.

definition: A long-handled brush for sweeping.
note: From Old English brom, 'brushwood'. The household tool took its name from the twigs of a shrub once used to make it.
hints: A witch rides one in stories.
Used to sweep the kitchen floor.

definition: A thin soup made by simmering meat or vegetables in water.
note: From Old English broth, from a Germanic word related to brewing. It is the liquid left after boiling food.
hints: Chicken soup starts with it.
Too many cooks can spoil it, the proverb says.

definition: The colour of chocolate or soil.
note: From Old English brun, a Germanic word. The colour was so named long before it was a name for a bear.
hints: Colour of a typical bear.
Mix red, yellow and blue and you get this.
example: The browns and greens in this painting give it a nice woodsy feel.

definition: To look through casually without a goal.
note: From Old French brouster, 'to nibble buds', used of deer. It later came to cover shoppers and web users.
hints: What you do in a shop without buying.
What a deer does to leaves and shoots.
example: I'm just browsing around.

definition: A bear, in folk tales.
note: From Middle Dutch bruun, 'brown'. It entered English in a translation of the Reynard the Fox legend, where the bear was named Bruin.
hints: Folk name for a brown bear.
A bear in old fables.

definition: A discoloured mark on the skin caused by a knock; also to damage fruit.
note: From Middle English bruisen, which merged an Old English word meaning 'to crush' with an Old French word meaning 'to break'.
hints: A knock to the shin leaves one that turns purple, then yellow.
Apples get them when dropped.
origin: Old English brȳsan, from Anglo-Norman bruiser

definition: A late-morning meal combining breakfast and lunch.
note: A blend of breakfast and lunch, first appearing in an 1895 British article. It spread in the United States by the 1930s.
hints: A leisurely weekend meal with eggs and mimosas.
What you eat if you wake up at ten on a Sunday.
example: I normally have brunch at the café next to work.

definition: The worst part of an impact or attack.
note: From Middle English, meaning a sudden blow or attack. We still speak of bearing it, as the person who takes the hardest hit.
hints: Usually 'bears' or 'takes' comes before it.
The heaviest part of a storm or criticism.
example: Frontline workers bear the brunt of the pandemic’s risk.

definition: A tool with bristles; or to touch lightly in passing.
note: The noun is from Old French and ultimately a word for bristle. A second, separate sense names thick undergrowth.
hints: What you do to your teeth twice a day.
An artist dips one in paint.

definition: Savagely cruel or harsh.
note: From Latin brutus, 'heavy' or 'dull'.
hints: Violent and merciless.
Unfeelingly harsh.
origin: Medieval Latin brutalis, from Latin brūtus
example: The game was brutal, but after a bloodbath he finally won.

definition: A cruel, savage person; also an animal.
note: From Latin brutus, 'dull, stupid, unfeeling', through French. It first described beasts that lack reason.
hints: '___ force' means strength without cleverness.
A thuggish bully.
origin: Middle French brut, from Latin brūtus

definition: A thin film of liquid filled with air.
note: Imitative of the sound of bubbling.
hints: Blown from a wand.
Soapy sphere.

definition: Full of bubbles; also cheerful and lively, or informally, champagne.
note: Formed from bubble plus -y. The bubbles sense came first, and the personality meaning followed.
hints: Popped open at weddings and New Year's Eve.
A person who walks into a room full of energy.
example: Whip the egg white into a bubbly froth.

definition: An open container with a handle.
note: From Anglo-Norman buket.
hints: Carries water.
Sand pail for a child.
origin: Old English bucc, from Anglo-Norman buket
example: I need a bucket to carry the water from the well.

definition: A clasp for a belt or strap; also to bend and give way under pressure.
note: From Old French boucle, from Latin buccula, 'cheek strap' of a helmet. Knees buckle under weight.
hints: The metal clasp on a belt.
What a bridge may do under too heavy a load.
origin: Old French boucle, from Middle English bokelen

definition: A friend or companion.
note: First seen about 1788, of uncertain origin. It may be a child's version of brother.
hints: Someone you might go to the gym with.
Another casual word for pal or mate.

definition: To move slightly.
note: Through Old French bouger, from Latin bullire, 'to boil, bubble'. Movement and bubbling seem to have shared an origin.
hints: A stubborn donkey won't do it.
Said of a door that is stuck fast.
origin: Middle French bouger, from Latin bullīre

definition: A plan for spending money.
note: From Old French bougette, 'little bag', a purse for money.
hints: A spending plan.
Originally a little leather bag.
origin: Old French bougette, from Late Latin bulga
example: The laboratory runs on a budget of a million a year.

definition: Something that cushions or protects; or a machine for polishing.
note: From buff, an old word for a blow or to cushion.
hints: Reduces a shock.
Space for video to preload.

definition: A meal where guests help themselves from dishes laid out; or a sideboard.
note: From Old French buffet, 'side table'. The verb buffet, to knock about, is a separate word.
hints: A hotel breakfast where you load your own plate.
Food spread on a long table at a wedding.
origin: Middle French buffet, from Old French buffet
example: We'll be serving supper buffet style.

definition: A small light carriage or vehicle; or full of faults.
note: Origin unknown for the carriage sense. The adjective means infested with insects or, of software, full of faults.
hints: A baby might be pushed in one.
Software that crashes often is called this.

definition: A small brass horn with no valves.
note: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman bugle, 'young ox'. It was named for the wild ox's horn from which the earliest ones were made.
hints: Soldiers wake to its call.
Taps is played on one.

definition: To make something by putting parts together.
note: From Old English bytlan, 'to build', from a word for a dwelling. It is a very old word for making houses.
hints: Construction workers do it.
Make a house from bricks, perhaps.

definition: Past tense of build; also describes a muscular body.
note: From Middle English bilden, with the past tense shifted from 'builded' to 'built'. Its use for a strong physique is a later figurative sense.
hints: Something a mason has done to a wall.
Comes after 'well' in describing a strong person.

definition: A swelling that sticks out.
note: Through Old French, from Latin bulga, 'leather bag', itself from a Gaulish word. A bulging bag is a good picture of it.
hints: A stuffed pocket makes one.
A battle in the Ardennes was named for a famous one.
origin: Old Northern French boulge, from Late Latin bulga
example: There was a bulge in my pocket where I kept my wallet.

definition: Large and awkward to carry.
note: From bulk plus -y. It is used for things that take up a lot of space without being necessarily heavy.
hints: A winter coat might be called this.
Hard to fit through a door.
example: Don't throw large or bulky items down the garbage chute.

definition: A small projectile fired from a gun.
note: From French boulette, 'little ball'.
hints: Ammunition for a pistol.
Fired from a gun.

definition: Someone who picks on weaker people.
note: In 1530 it was a term of endearment, perhaps from Dutch boel, 'lover, brother'. Over time it changed to mean someone who is a blustering tyrant.
hints: A playground tormentor.
What you call someone who picks on smaller kids.
origin: Dutch boel, from Middle Dutch boel; in English since the late 17th century

definition: Informal word for a disappointing or unfortunate situation.
note: Borrowed from German Bummler, 'loafer'. The modern sense of an unlucky event arose in the 1960s.
hints: Said when it rains on the day of the picnic.
Teenagers say it when plans fall through.
example: Having to stand in line so long was a real bummer.

definition: A guard on a car's front or back; or unusually large.
note: From bump plus -er.
hints: Shields a car in a collision.
A record-breaking harvest.

definition: Rough and uneven.
note: From bump plus -y. A road or a flight can be this way.
hints: A road full of potholes.
A rough ride in a plane.

definition: A group of things clustered together.
note: From Middle English bunche, 'hump, swelling', of uncertain origin. It was first a lump before it was a cluster.
hints: Grapes grow in one.
Flowers tied together make one.
example: A bunch of trees.

definition: A group of things tied together.
note: From Middle Dutch bondel, related to bind.
hints: A bunch wrapped with string.
Wood tied for a fire.
origin: Middle Dutch bondel, from Old English byndele

definition: A strong underground shelter; also a sand trap on a golf course.
note: The origin is uncertain, but an early sense was a bench or chest in Scotland. A coal store aboard a ship was also called this.
hints: Where leaders hide during a war.
A golfer dreads landing in the sand-filled kind.
origin: Scots bunker, from Old Norse bunki
example: The military built a bunker to help evacuate the citizens safely from the bombings.

definition: A rabbit, especially a young one.
note: Formed from a Scottish word, bun, meaning a rabbit's tail, with the -y of affection. It is a pet name.
hints: The Easter one hides eggs.
A fluffy animal with long ears.
origin: Scottish Gaelic bun, from Old Irish bun

definition: A heavy load, or a duty.
note: From Old English byrthen, from beran, 'to bear'.
hints: Weight on a back.
A hard duty.

definition: An office or agency; or a chest of drawers.
note: From French bureau, a coarse cloth that covered desks, then the desk, then the office.
hints: A government office.
A desk with drawers.
origin: French bureau, from Old French burel

definition: A patty in a bun.
note: Short for hamburger, named after the German city of Hamburg.
hints: Fast food classic.
Meat patty in a bread roll.

definition: The placing of a body in the ground.
note: From Old English byrgels.
hints: Takes place at a funeral.
Grave ceremony.
example: His whole family was present at his burial.

definition: Put underground or hidden.
note: The past participle of bury, from Old English byrgan.
hints: Placed in a grave.
Treasure under sand.

definition: Large, strong and heavily built.
note: From Middle English, where it first meant 'tall, stately'. It slowly shifted from grand to brawny.
hints: A bouncer might be this.
A lumberjack's typical build.
example: He’s a big, burly rugby player who works as a landscape gardener.

definition: The part of a stove that makes the flame; or a disposable phone.
note: From burn plus -er. The phone sense comes from burning it after use.
hints: Every stove has four of these.
A throwaway phone in a crime drama is called this.
example: The electric range had one large burner and three smaller one.

definition: Damaged or blackened by fire or heat.
note: A past form of burn, from Old English. 'Burned' and 'burnt' both exist, and 'burnt' is the one more often used as an adjective.
hints: How toast looks when forgotten.
A shade of orange or sienna may start with it.
example: A row of burned houses.

definition: A garment that covers the whole body, including the face.
note: From Persian and Arabic burqa. It reached English through Hindustani.
hints: A long covering garment worn by some women.
Known in Afghanistan.
example: The Taliban forced all women to wear the burqa.

definition: A tunnel or hole dug by an animal to live in.
note: From Middle English borowe, apparently a variant of burgh, 'fortified place'. It is related to the word borough.
hints: Rabbits and badgers dig one.
Alice fell down one.

definition: To break open suddenly.
note: From Old English berstan, a very old Germanic verb. It describes sudden breaking from pressure.
hints: What a balloon does when pricked.
A pipe in winter might do this.

definition: Thick and spreading like a bush.
note: From bush plus -y. It is most often used of eyebrows, beards and tails.
hints: A squirrel's tail is described this way.
Unclipped eyebrows might be this.

definition: A tough fellow, or a person or thing that breaks something.
note: A dialect form of burster. It works as a friendly nickname and is also seen in blockbuster and ghostbuster.
hints: A suffix behind many monster-fighting films.
Something that destroys, like a bunker or crime fighter.

definition: Having a tough, masculine manner or look.
note: Its origin is uncertain; it may be linked to butcher or to a nickname. It dates from the early 1900s.
hints: Slang that began in the early 1900s, often for a rugged look.
Describes a look or manner thought of as rugged.

definition: The chief male servant of a house.
note: From Old French bouteillier, 'bottle bearer'.
hints: Wooster's helper is Jeeves.
Looks after the wine and the door.
origin: Old French buttiler, from Medieval Latin botellārius

definition: A steep isolated hill with a flat top.
note: Borrowed from French, where it means a mound. It is common in the American West, where French trappers named many landforms.
hints: Monument Valley is full of them.
Smaller than a mesa.

definition: A fatty spread made by churning cream.
note: From Old English butere, from Greek bouturon, 'cow cheese'.
hints: Spread on toast.
Churned from cream.
origin: Old English butere, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον

definition: A small disc used to fasten clothing, or a switch you push.
note: From Old French bouton, 'bud' or 'knob'.
hints: Sewn on a shirt.
What you press on a remote.

definition: Plump and healthy-looking, said of a woman.
note: From Middle English buhsum, which originally meant obedient or pliable, then good-natured, then plump.
hints: Old word that began by meaning obliging.
Describes a full-figured look.

definition: A person who purchases something.
note: From buy plus -er. It also names a professional who selects goods for a shop.
hints: The opposite of seller.
'___ beware' warns of a risky purchase.
example: Sellers and buyers are anonymous and very hard to recognize.

definition: The purchase of a controlling share in a company.
note: From the phrasal verb 'buy out'.
hints: A bigger firm may do one to take over a rival.
A worker might accept one to leave the job.
example: Auctions are annoying, so I bought it instantly with a buyout.

definition: A device that makes a buzzing sound as a signal.
note: From buzz, which imitates the sound, plus -er. Quiz shows rely on them for fast answers.
hints: Contestants slam it to answer a quiz question first.
A visitor presses the button at your door and one sounds.
example: If you think you know the answer to the question, hit the buzzer as fast as you can.

definition: Making a buzzing sound or generating excitement.
note: From buzz plus -y.
hints: Like bees, or like a trending topic.
Humming, or full of hype.

definition: A rule made by a local authority or organisation.
note: From Middle English bilawe, partly from Old Norse byjar-log, 'town law'. The by- originally meant a village.
hints: The council passed one about noisy parties.
A rule a club or company writes for itself.
origin: Old English bīlage, from Old Norse býjar

definition: A road that goes around a town, or an operation that reroutes blood.
note: From by plus pass.
hints: Skips the town centre.
Heart surgery reroutes blood this way.

definition: A small secret group plotting together.
note: From French cabale, from Medieval Latin, from Hebrew qabbalah, 'tradition, received teaching'. It took on political meanings in 1600s England.
hints: A hidden group scheming in the shadows.
Conspirators might form one.

definition: A taxi driver.
note: A shortened, friendly form built from cab plus -y. Cab itself is short for cabriolet, a light horse-drawn carriage.
hints: Someone who drives passengers around town.
The person who asks where you are headed.

definition: A small wooden house, or a room on a ship or plane.
note: From Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna, 'hut'. It is the same source as cabana.
hints: Log houses in the woods are called this.
Where the passengers sit on a plane.
origin: Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna

definition: A thick rope or wire.
note: From Old French, from Late Latin capulum, 'rope, halter'. Today it also names a bundle of electrical wire or a TV service.
hints: A bridge may hang from huge steel ones.
Plug your phone into one to charge.
origin: Old Northern French cable, from Latin capiō

definition: The tree whose seeds are used to make chocolate.
note: From Spanish, from Nahuatl cacahuatl. The word cocoa is a variant of the same word.
hints: Chocolate begins as its beans.
Aztecs prized its seeds as a drink.
origin: Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl
example: Cacao can only grow within about 20° north and south of the equator.

definition: A hidden store of things; or saved data for fast access.
note: From French cacher, 'to hide'. French-Canadian trappers used it for hiding places for supplies.
hints: A web browser clears it to free space.
Squirrels keep one of nuts for winter.

definition: A spiny desert plant that stores water in its fat stem.
note: From Greek kaktos, a spiny plant, though the Greek plant was not the American one. Linnaeus later used the name for these New World plants.
hints: Western films show one standing in the desert.
Its spines are leaves that have been made small to save water.
origin: taxonomic name Cactus, from Ancient Greek κάκτος

definition: A small box for tea; or a golfer's assistant.
note: The tea box name comes from kati, a Malay weight, via a pack of tea. The golf helper is a different word, from cadet.
hints: Carries clubs around a golf course.
A box on a table holding tea bags.

definition: A young person training to be an officer.
note: From French, from Gascon capdet, 'little head or chief'. It first meant a younger son, who would not inherit the family estate.
hints: Trained at a military academy.
A trainee officer in uniform.
origin: French cadet, from Late Latin capitellum
example: The officer told the cadet to get back to work.

definition: A small group of trained people; or a framework.
note: From French cadre, 'frame', from Italian quadro. It names the core group of an organisation.
hints: A core group of party activists.
The nucleus of an army.

definition: Cautious and unwilling to give information.
note: Originally American slang, of unknown origin. Some link it to the guarded behaviour of caged animals.
hints: Asked a direct question, he gave a guarded answer.
Evasive when pressed for details.

definition: A pile of stones used as a marker.
note: From Scottish Gaelic carn, from an old Celtic root. They mark graves, paths and mountain summits.
hints: Hikers stack stones to build one.
A small scottish terrier shares the name.
origin: Scots cairn, from Old Irish carn

definition: A person making a phone call, or a visitor.
note: From call plus -er. Old uses meant someone paying a visit.
hints: The voice on the other end of the line.
Someone who rings you when you don't recognise the number.
example: There were so many callers that he finally disconnected the telephone.

definition: In a peaceful, unflustered way.
note: From calm plus -ly. Calm came from Latin cauma, heat of the day, via Greek.
hints: How a pilot is told to announce turbulence.
In a way that avoids a panic.

definition: The ring of green leaf-like sepals around a flower bud.
note: From Greek kalyx, 'husk' or 'pod'.
hints: Protects a flower before it opens.
The green cup beneath a petal.
origin: Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ

definition: A large desert animal with humps.
note: Through Old English and Old French from Latin camelus, from Greek, from a Semitic source. The word is related to the Arabic word jamal.
hints: One with two humps is called Bactrian.
Known for going long without water.
origin: Old English camel, from Old Northern French camel

definition: A brief appearance by a famous person in a film.
note: From Italian cammeo, a carved gem in relief. The film sense is short for 'cameo role', a small part that stands out like a jewel.
hints: Hitchcock did this in his own films.
Also a carved brooch with a profile on it.
origin: Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus

definition: A device for taking photographs.
note: From Latin camera, 'chamber'. A camera obscura was a dark room.
hints: Used to capture a picture.
Named for a room in Latin.
origin: Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα

definition: A person who stays in a tent; or a vehicle fitted for sleeping in.
note: From camp plus -er, from Latin campus, 'field'. In Britain the vehicle is a campervan.
hints: Roasts marshmallows at a campfire.
A van with a bed and small kitchen.

definition: The grounds of a university or college.
note: Latin for 'field'. American colleges began using it for their grounds in the 1700s.
hints: Where students live and study.
Lawn and lecture halls.
example: The campus is sixty hectares in size.

definition: Deliberately exaggerated and kitschy for fun.
note: From camp, an affected style, plus -y.
hints: Old Batman television series are an example.
Over-the-top in a knowing way.
example: Stu liked to watch campy B-movie horror flicks from the 1950s, not because they scared him, but because he found them funny.

definition: A man-made waterway.
note: From Latin canalis, 'channel, pipe', related to canna, 'reed'. It also names a tube inside the body.
hints: Panama and Suez are famous ones.
Venice is full of them.
origin: Middle French canal, from Akkadian 𒄀

definition: A small yellow songbird originally from the Canary Islands.
note: From Spanish canario, named for the islands, which are in turn named for dogs. Miners took them underground to warn of gas.
hints: A bird once carried down coal mines as a warning of gas.
A yellow songbird in a cage.
origin: French canarie, from Latin Canariae insulae

definition: To call off, or cross out.
note: From Latin cancellare, 'to cross out with lattice lines'.
hints: Scrap an event.
What you do with a subscription.

definition: A disease of uncontrolled cell growth; also a crab in astrology.
note: Latin for 'crab'. A popular story says ancient doctors saw a swollen tumour's veins as a crab's legs.
hints: A zodiac sign symbolised by a crab.
A serious illness, named for a crab.
example: Sure, almost everything 'causes cancer' now. That said, I don't go hugging nuclear waste or acting like cancer itself is some conspiracy.

definition: Honest and open, even when it is uncomfortable.
note: From Latin candidus, 'bright white', then 'pure' and 'frank'. A candid photograph catches people unposed.
hints: What a photo is when people don't know it's being taken.
Frank feedback from a trusted friend.

definition: A stick of wax with a wick that burns for light.
note: From Old English candel, from Latin candela, from candere, 'to shine'.
hints: Blown out on a birthday cake.
Gives off a flame for light.
origin: Old English candel, from Latin candeō

definition: Sweet food made with sugar.
note: From Old French sucre candi, 'candied sugar', from Arabic qandi, which came from a Persian word. The first candy was crystallised sugar.
hints: A trick-or-treater collects it.
The thing a lollipop is made of.
origin: Old French sucre candi, from Sanskrit खण्ड

definition: Relating to dogs; also a pointed tooth.
note: From Latin caninus, from canis, 'dog'. The pointed teeth next to the incisors are called canines.
hints: A pointed tooth that tears food.
The pointed teeth beside a human's front incisors are named this.

definition: A tropical plant with broad leaves and bright flowers.
note: From Latin canna, 'reed'. The genus name was borrowed straight into English.
hints: Showy flower in tropical gardens.
Garden plant with banana-like leaves.

definition: A large gun that fires heavy balls.
note: From Italian cannone, 'large tube', from canna, 'reed'.
hints: Fired on a pirate ship.
Gun with a large barrel.
origin: Old French canon, from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾

definition: Is unable to.
note: Joined from can and not.
hints: Is not able to.
Written as one word, unlike its contraction.

definition: Shrewd and careful, especially about money.
note: From a Northern English dialect word, from can in the old sense 'to know'. In Scots usage it can mean careful or lucky.
hints: A sharp-witted person with good judgment.
Good at spotting a bargain.

definition: A light, narrow boat moved with paddles.
note: Entered English in the 1500s from Spanish canoa, which took it from the Taino word for a dugout boat. It was one of the first Caribbean words Europeans borrowed.
hints: Paddled across a calm lake.
Kayak's open-topped cousin.

definition: An accepted body of rules or works.
note: From Latin canon, from Greek kanon, 'measuring rod, rule'. A rod for measuring became a standard for judging.
hints: Sacred texts accepted by a church form one.
The official set of stories in a fictional universe.
origin: Old French canon, from Ancient Greek κανών
example: Canons of polite society.

definition: A covering held over a bed or throne; or the leafy top layer of a forest.
note: From Greek konopeion, a bed with a mosquito net, from konops, 'gnat'. Rainforest tops have the name.
hints: The treetop layer of a rainforest.
A cloth roof over a royal bed.
origin: Old French conopé, from Ancient Greek κώνωψ

definition: One of the main sections of a long poem.
note: From Italian canto, 'song', and a doublet of chant. Dante's Inferno has thirty-four of them.
hints: A chapter of a long epic poem.
Dante divided his Inferno into these.

definition: A small territorial division, especially in Switzerland.
note: From Old French canton, 'corner'. Switzerland has twenty-six of them.
hints: What Zurich and Geneva are part of.
A Swiss state is this.
origin: Middle French canton, from Old French canton

definition: A singer who leads the music in a synagogue or church.
note: From Latin cantor, 'singer', from canere, 'to sing'. It shares a root with chant and incantation.
hints: Leads the congregation in song at a Jewish service.
