The hazzan chants the prayers.
example: The cantor's place in church is on the right of the choir.

definition: A strong cloth used for tents and painting.
note: From Old French canevas, from Latin cannabis, because it was made of hemp.
hints: Artists paint on it.
Tent material.

definition: A deep valley with steep sides.
note: From Spanish canon, 'tube'.
hints: The Grand one is in Arizona.
Carved by a river.

definition: A unit of weight for gemstones.
note: From Italian and Arabic qirat, itself from Greek keration, 'carob seed, small weight'. Carob seeds were once used to weigh gems.
hints: A diamond ring is measured in it.
Gold purity is measured in a related spelling.
origin: Middle French carat, from Ancient Greek κεράτιον

definition: The element found in coal and diamonds.
note: From Latin carbo, 'coal' or 'charcoal'.
hints: Element number six.
Soot and graphite are made of it.

definition: Exercise that raises the heart rate.
note: Clipped from cardiovascular, from Greek kardia, 'heart'. Running and cycling are examples.
hints: What a treadmill session is.
Gym sessions that leave you out of breath.
example: I did some cardio today instead of lifting weights.

definition: A person's working life; also to rush wildly.
note: From French carriere, from Latin for 'road', so a career first meant a racecourse.
hints: A lifelong path of jobs.
Rush about out of control.
origin: French carrière, from Middle French carriere
example: The general had had a distinguished career.

definition: A person who looks after someone ill or old.
note: From care plus -er. In Britain it names a person who looks after a family member.
hints: Someone who looks after an elderly parent.
A person who looks after someone unwell.
example: Have you thought of a job as a carer for disabled people?

definition: Goods carried by a ship, plane or truck.
note: Borrowed from Spanish cargo, 'load, burden', from cargar, 'to load'. It is a close relative of the word charge.
hints: What a freighter hauls.
Shipping containers are packed with it.
origin: Spanish cargo, from Late Latin carricō
example: The plane was overloaded with cargo. It was a cargo of live animals.

definition: A thick floor covering.
note: From Old French carpite, from Latin carpere, 'to pluck', as it was made from shredded cloth.
hints: Covers a living room floor.
Magic one flew in tales.
origin: Old French carpite, from Middle Armenian կարպետ

definition: An orange root vegetable.
note: From Greek karoton through French. A popular story says wartime British propaganda promoted carrots as helping pilots see in the dark.
hints: Bugs Bunny chews on one.
Used with a stick in the phrase about rewards.
origin: Middle French carotte, from Ancient Greek καρωτόν

definition: A group of firms that agree to fix prices and limit competition.
note: Borrowed from German Kartell in the 1870s. Drug gangs are also called this.
hints: Oil producers in OPEC are one.
Drug gangs in crime stories go by this name.
example: Ziri was too busy worrying about some cartel ambush.

definition: A light box or container, usually of cardboard.
note: Borrowed from French, which took it from Italian cartone, 'big card'. It is a doublet of cartoon.
hints: Eggs or milk come in one from the shop.
A box of cigarettes sold by the dozen packs is called this too.

definition: A person who carves; or a large knife for slicing roast meat.
note: From carve plus -er. The word turns up at roast dinners and at woodcarving fairs.
hints: Sits at the head of a table at Sunday lunch.
Makes figures of wood in a workshop.

definition: A place for gambling.
note: From Italian casino, 'little house'.
hints: Roulette is played there.
Las Vegas is full of them.
example: We valeted our car and entered the casino.

definition: A small box for valuables; or a coffin in American usage.
note: Probably from Old French cassette, 'little box'. Shakespeare's Portia puts three of them at the centre of a wooden test.
hints: A small box holding jewels.
In the US, a coffin.

definition: A fixed social class one is born into.
note: From Portuguese or Spanish casta, 'lineage, breed'. Europeans applied it to the hereditary classes of Indian society.
hints: A rigid hereditary social division.
Also a word for a class of ants or bees, such as workers.

definition: A small swivel wheel on furniture, or someone who casts.
note: From cast plus -er, with the wheel sense appearing later. Fine sugar for baking is also spelled this way.
hints: Under an office chair.
A fine kind of sugar, for baking.
example: Many office chairs roll on a set of casters.

definition: A large fortified building.
note: From Old French castel, from Latin castellum, 'fortress'.
hints: Where a king might live with a moat.
A chess piece also called a rook.
origin: Old English castel, from Latin castrum

definition: A small wheel on furniture; also an oil from a plant; and an old word for a beaver hat.
note: From Latin castor, 'beaver', from Greek kastor.
hints: Office chairs roll on them.
A heavy, bitter oil from the plant was once given as medicine.

definition: Relaxed or informal, or by chance.
note: From Latin casualis, from casus, 'chance'.
hints: Friday dress codes in offices often go this way.
Jeans and a T-shirt.
origin: Middle French casuel, from Late Latin cāsuālis

definition: To grab something thrown or moving.
note: From Old Northern French cachier and Latin captare, 'to chase', a relative of capere, 'to take'. It once meant to chase before it meant to seize.
hints: Mitt in baseball does this to a ball.
A hidden drawback, as in 'what's the ___?'
origin: Anglo-Norman cachier, from Latin captāre; in English since the 13th century

definition: Memorable and likely to stick in the mind.
note: From catch plus -y. A tune that sticks in your head is this.
hints: A pop jingle you cannot get out of your head.
What a chorus should be to become a hit.
example: Eric wrote a catchy tune to play on his acoustic guitar while Alyssa plays the drums.

definition: To provide food and drink for an event.
note: From Middle English catour, a shortened form of acatour, 'buyer', from Old French acater, 'to buy'. A caterer was once simply a buyer of provisions.
hints: What a company does for a wedding reception.
To supply for a need, as in 'to ___ to every taste'.
example: I catered for her bat mitzvah.

definition: Cows and bulls kept on farms.
note: From Old French catel, 'property', the same source as chattel.
hints: Herded on ranches.
Livestock of the bovine kind.
example: Many cattle were suffering from a disease called BSE.

definition: Subtly spiteful.
note: From cat plus -y. Cats were long thought of as sly and sharp, so a catty remark has hidden claws.
hints: A remark with a hidden sting.
Gossip that's spiteful rather than kind.

definition: A meeting of party members to choose candidates or policy.
note: The origin is unknown; one theory ties it to an Algonquian word for adviser. Iowa famously holds them.
hints: A US state's party meeting that picks presidential favourites.
A group of legislators from one party.

definition: A waterproof filler used to seal gaps.
note: From Old Northern French cauquer, from Late Latin calicare, 'to fill with limestone', from calx. Ship builders used it to seal the seams between planks.
hints: Seals the gaps around a bathtub.
Sold in tubes and squeezed from a gun.
origin: Old Northern French cauquer, from Late Latin calicāre

definition: Relating to cause and effect.
note: From Latin causalis, from causa, 'cause'. Scientists warn that correlation does not prove a causal link.
hints: Statisticians say correlation does not imply this relationship.
A link in which one thing makes another happen.
origin: Late Latin causalis, from Latin causa
example: There is no causal relationship between eating carrots and seeing in the dark.

definition: A thing that makes something happen.
note: Borrowed from Old French cause, from Latin causa, 'reason, sake, lawsuit'. It once also meant a legal case.
hints: The opposite of effect.
What you fight for if you are an activist.
origin: Old French cause, from Latin causa
example: He had no cause to complain.

definition: A warning or condition attached to a statement.
note: Latin for 'let him beware'. Lawyers used it for a formal notice.
hints: 'Buyer beware' is a related Latin phrase.
Added after 'but' to qualify a promise.
example: A caveat against unfair practices.

definition: A large cave.
note: From Latin caverna, 'hollow place', from cavus, 'hollow'. It is the same root as cave.
hints: Stalactites hang in one.
Deep underground, dripping with echoes.
origin: Old French caverne, from Latin caverna

definition: The salted eggs of a sturgeon, eaten as a luxury food.
note: Through French and Italian from Ottoman Turkish havyar.
hints: Served on tiny blinis with sour cream.
Russian and Iranian ones from the Caspian are the priciest.
origin: Middle French caviar, from Venetan caviaro
example: The black caviar added a touch of luxury to the meal.

definition: To raise petty objections.
note: From Old French caviller, from Latin cavillari, 'to jeer, to reason captiously'. It has long meant a nitpicking complaint.
hints: A fussy complaint about something trivial.
What a nitpicker does over small details.
origin: Old French caviller, from Latin cavillor

definition: A hollow space, especially a hole in a tooth.
note: From Late Latin cavitas, from cavus, 'hollow'. The word is used for body spaces and decayed teeth.
hints: What the dentist drills out of a tooth.
The hollow chest space that holds the lungs.
origin: Middle French cavité, from Late Latin cavitās

definition: To stop.
note: From Old French cesser, from Latin cessare, 'to stop, delay'. It is usually seen in formal wording like 'cease and desist'.
hints: What a ___-fire does to the fighting.
A formal word for stop.
origin: Middle French cesser, from Latin cessō

definition: A tall evergreen tree with fragrant wood.
note: From Latin cedrus, from Greek kedros. The scented wood is used to line chests and closets.
hints: Moths avoid its scent in a wardrobe.
Lebanon's flag shows one.
origin: Old French cedre, from Ancient Greek κέδρος

definition: A famous person.
note: A clipping of celebrity. It is used in magazines and on social media.
hints: A famous face in a magazine.
Someone on a red carpet.

definition: A crunchy green stalk vegetable eaten raw or in soups.
note: From French celeri, from Greek selinon, 'parsley'. Ancient Greeks gave it as a victory crown.
hints: Dipped in peanut butter as a snack.
A stick in a Bloody Mary.
origin: French céleri, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον

definition: An underground room used for storage.
note: From Latin cellarium, a storeroom, from cella. Wine cellars are famous.
hints: Where wine is kept cool and dark.
The part of the house beneath the ground floor.
example: The farmhouse has several additions, added over many decades; it has three cellars, and one of them is older than the other two.

definition: A large stringed instrument played upright between the knees.
note: Short for violoncello, Italian for 'little violone', where violone was a kind of big viol. Cello was a clipped form.
hints: Bigger than a violin but smaller than a double bass.
Played sitting down with a bow.
example: Olga has been playing the cello since she was 8 years old.

definition: A binding powder used to make concrete.
note: From Latin caementum, 'rough stone'.
hints: Mixed to make a sidewalk.
Glue to bond bricks.

definition: A person who removes material considered unfit for the public; or to do so.
note: From Latin censor, the Roman magistrate who counted citizens and judged their morals. Over time, he lent his name to modern editing of the unacceptable.
hints: Blacks out lines from a letter or film.
The Roman official of the same name took the census.

definition: An official count of a population.
note: From Latin census, from censere, 'to assess'. Rome held one every five years.
hints: A government survey of households.
Every ten years in the US.

definition: The middle point of something.
note: From Greek kentron, 'sharp point', such as the fixed point of a compass.
hints: Midpoint of a circle.
Its Greek root meant a compass point.
origin: Middle French centre, from Ancient Greek κέντρον

definition: A grain crop, or a breakfast food made from grain.
note: From Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture.
hints: Eaten with milk.
Named after a harvest goddess.

definition: To rub and make sore.
note: From Old French chaufer, 'to warm', from Latin calefacere. Rubbing makes heat, and so the meaning shifted from warm to irritate.
hints: What a tight collar does to your neck.
To be annoyed by restrictions.
origin: Old French chaufer, from Latin calefacere

definition: The husks separated from grain.
note: From Old English ceaf, a Germanic word. 'Separating the wheat from this' means sorting good from worthless.
hints: What's blown away when grain is threshed.
Worthless stuff set apart from the wheat.
example: To separate out the chaff, early cultures tossed baskets of grain into the air and let the wind blow away the lighter chaff.

definition: A series of connected metal links.
note: From Old French chaine, from Latin catena. It names a bicycle part, a shop group and a connected series of events.
hints: A bicycle has one that goes around the cogs.
A set of linked rings, or a group of shops.
origin: Old French chaeine, from Latin catēna

definition: A seat with a back, for one person.
note: From Old French chaiere, from Latin cathedra, from Greek kathedra, 'seat'. The same Greek word gave us cathedral.
hints: Sits at the dinner table.
Also what a person running a meeting is called.
origin: Old French chaiere, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα
example: All I need to weather a snowstorm is hot coffee, a warm fire, a good book and a comfortable chair.

definition: In yoga and Indian traditions, one of the centres of spiritual energy in the body.
note: Borrowed from Sanskrit cakra, meaning wheel or circle.
hints: Yoga teachers talk about seven of them, from the spine's base to the crown.
Hindu tradition places them along the spine.

definition: A wooden house with a sloping roof, typical of the Alps.
note: Borrowed from French chalet, from a Franco-Provencal word for a herdsman's mountain hut.
hints: Where skiers stay in the mountains.
A holiday cabin with overhanging eaves and carved balconies.
origin: French chalet, from Franco-Provençal çhalè; in English since the late 18th century
example: Anton's chalet is situated on a mountain.

definition: A soft white rock or a stick used for writing on boards.
note: From Old English cealc, from Latin calx, 'limestone'. The white cliffs of Dover are made of it.
hints: A teacher once used it on a blackboard.
Rock gymnasts rub on their hands.
origin: Old English ċealc, from Ancient Greek χάλιξ

definition: A champion; also, informally, a friendly name for a good sport.
note: A clipping of champion, which comes from Latin campus, 'field', the place where fights took place.
hints: Short for a title won in a contest.
What a boxer hopes to be called.

definition: A possibility, or luck.
note: From Old French cheance, 'a falling', from Latin cadere, 'to fall', like the fall of dice.
hints: A roll of the dice, or an opening.
Luck, or an opportunity.
origin: Old French cheance, from Latin cadere

definition: To make or become different.
note: From Old French changier, from Latin cambire, 'to barter'.
hints: Loose coins, or a swap.
Make something different.
origin: Old French changier, from Latin cambīre
example: The tadpole changed into a frog.

definition: To repeat words rhythmically.
note: From Old French chanter, from Latin cantare, 'to sing'. It is a close relative of cant.
hints: What a football crowd does in unison.
Monks do this in a monotone.
origin: Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre
example: The football fans chanted insults at the referee.

definition: Complete disorder.
note: From Greek khaos, 'abyss, void'. The Greeks used it for the empty state before the world was ordered.
hints: A kitchen with a dozen cooks and no plan.
The opposite of order.

definition: A small place of worship.
note: From Old French chapele, from a cloak preserved as a relic at a shrine in France.
hints: Located in a school or hospital.
A small church.
origin: Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella

definition: To demand payment, rush forward, or put electricity into something.
note: From Old French chargier, 'to load', from Latin carrus, 'cart'.
hints: A cavalry rush, a price, or a battery state.
What a phone needs overnight.
origin: Old French chargier, from Latin carrus
example: Will I get charged for this service?

definition: The power to delight others; or a magic spell.
note: From Old French charme, from Latin carmen, 'song, incantation'. Spells were sung before they were attractions.
hints: A lucky one hangs on a bracelet.
'Third time lucky' is said to work like one.
origin: Old French charme, from Latin carmen

definition: To run after something in order to catch it.
note: From Old French chacier, from Latin captare, a relative of capere, 'to take'. It is a cousin of catch.
hints: A dog does it to a squirrel.
Cars do it in action movies.
example: The policeman chased the mugger down the alley.

definition: One who chases, or a drink taken after a stronger one.
note: From Middle English chaser, from Old French chaceor, 'hunter'. A horse that races over fences is also a chaser, and the drink sense arrived later.
hints: A beer after a shot of whisky.
Storm ones follow tornadoes in a van.
origin: Old French chaceür; in English since the 14th century

definition: A deep gap or crack in the ground.
note: From Latin chasma, from Greek khasma, 'abyss, cleft'. It also names a wide gulf between people.
hints: What a bridge is built over.
A deep gorge in the earth.
origin: Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα
example: The pupils of her eyes had the blackness of a deep chasm.

definition: Low in price.
note: From Old English ceap, 'trade, market, value', which is the root of a word for market in many languages. Originally 'good cheap' meant a good bargain.
hints: The opposite of expensive.
Might also describe poor quality.
origin: Old English cēap, from Latin caupō
example: It would have been cheap at twice the price.

definition: To break the rules to gain an advantage.
note: From Middle English acheten, a variant of escheten, from the legal word escheat, the seizure of property that falls to the crown. Officers who did the seizing had a reputation for dishonesty.
hints: What a student does by copying an exam.
To win unfairly.
example: My brother flunked biology because he cheated on his mid-term.

definition: To examine to make sure something is right.
note: Ultimately from Persian shah, 'king', via the chess call of 'check' to the king. It then spread to mean stopping or testing.
hints: Said when the king is threatened in chess.
What you do to an answer before you hand it in.

definition: The soft part of the face below the eye.
note: From Old English ceace, 'jaw'. Cheeky behaviour was named for the impudent way of making faces.
hints: A kiss on the face lands here.
A hamster stuffs food into them.

definition: Boldly disrespectful in a playful, slightly charming way.
note: From cheek, as in impudence, plus -y. The sense comes from saying something to someone's face.
hints: How a child answers back to a teacher with a grin.
Something a grinning child says that a parent half-forgives.
example: If you're cheeky once more, I won't read you a story tonight.

definition: The thin, high sound of a small bird.
note: Imitative of the noise itself.
hints: A chick's noise.
The thin call of a nestling.

definition: A food made from curdled milk.
note: From Old English cese, from Latin caseus.
hints: Cheddar or brie.
What a mouse is cartoonishly fond of.
origin: Old English ċēse, from Latin cāseus

definition: Tasting like cheese; or tacky and overdone.
note: From cheese plus -y. The tacky sense came in the 1800s.
hints: A pizza topping or a corny joke.
Describes pickup lines and old greeting cards.
example: I like to photograph the cheesy carpet patterns found in airports.

definition: A short word for chemotherapy.
note: A clipping of chemotherapy. It uses drugs to treat cancer.
hints: A medical treatment for cancer.
A treatment using drugs on a tumor.

definition: A written order to a bank to pay money.
note: A variant of check, the idea of a control on amounts. The British spelling separates it from the verb.
hints: Written on paper and handed to a payee.
A signed slip torn from a book and handed to a payee.
example: I was not carrying cash, so I wrote a cheque for the amount.

definition: A small round red fruit with a stone.
note: From Old French cherise, which was mistaken for a plural, so cherry was formed by back-formation.
hints: Sits on top of a sundae.
Fruit with a pit.
origin: Anglo-Norman cherise, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον

definition: A board game with kings, queens and pawns.
note: From Old French esches, from the plural of eschec, 'check', from Persian shah, 'king'. The name of the game is simply 'kings'.
hints: Played on sixty-four squares.
The game where you try to checkmate.
origin: Old French eschés, from Old Persian 𐏋

definition: The front of the body between the neck and stomach; or a strong box.
note: From Old English cest, 'box, coffin', from Latin cista. The body part was named as the box that holds the heart and lungs.
hints: Pirates buried treasure in one.
Where your ribs are.
origin: Old English ċest, from Ancient Greek κίστη

definition: Needing a lot of chewing.
note: From chew plus -y. Toffee and tough steak are this way.
hints: Toffee and gummy sweets.
A tough steak.

definition: A baby bird, especially a chicken.
note: From Middle English chike, a variant of chiken. The informal word for a young woman came later.
hints: It hatches from an egg.
Fluffy and yellow in spring.

definition: To scold mildly.
note: From Old English cidan, 'to quarrel, complain'. It carries a gentler, more old-fashioned tone than scold.
hints: A parent might do this to a child who is rude.
To rebuke gently.
example: The teacher chided a student for not doing her homework.

definition: A leader or head of a group.
note: From Old French chef, from Latin caput, 'head'. It is a cousin of the word cap and captain.
hints: The head of a tribe or a fire department.
Main, as in 'the ___ reason'.
example: All firefighters report to the fire chief.

definition: A young human who is not yet an adult.
note: From Old English cild, from a Germanic word that may have meant 'womb'. The plural, children, keeps an odd old ending.
hints: A boy or girl.
Plays in the playground.

definition: A hot pepper, or a stew made with it.
note: Borrowed from Spanish chile, from Nahuatl chilli. The spelling varies, as in chilli or chile.
hints: A spicy pod that makes your mouth burn.
A stew of beans and meat served in a bowl.
origin: Spanish chile, from Classical Nahuatl chīlli

definition: Uncomfortably cold.
note: From chill plus -y. It describes weather and also an unfriendly welcome.
hints: What a morning feels like in late autumn.
A frosty reception is also described this way.
example: I’m getting rather chilly over here – could you shut the window please?

definition: A bell-like ringing sound.
note: From Middle English, possibly from Old French chimbe, 'cymbal', from Latin cymbalum. It first named the cymbal-like sound of bells.
hints: A doorbell might play one.
To join in, as in 'to ___ in'.
origin: Old Northern French chimbe, from Latin cymbalum

definition: A twill cotton fabric; or trousers made from it.
note: From American Spanish chino, 'toasted'. The trousers are casual and hard-wearing.
hints: Smart-casual trousers of cotton twill.
A khaki-coloured trouser.

definition: A short, sharp bird sound.
note: From Middle English, imitative of the sound. It is often used of birds and crickets.
hints: What a cricket does at night.
A small bird's morning sound.

definition: A wedge placed to stop something moving.
note: From Old Northern French choque, 'block, log'. It is used for wheels, boats and barrels.
hints: Put behind the wheel of a parked aircraft.
A wedge that stops a wheel rolling.
origin: Anglo-Norman choque, from Old French çouche

definition: An option; the act of choosing.
note: From Old French chois, from a Germanic word meaning to taste or try.
hints: Pick from the list.
What you have between two doors.
origin: Old French chois, from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽
example: Do I have a choice of what color to paint it?

definition: A group of singers performing together.
note: From Old French quer, from Latin chorus, 'dance, band of singers'. The spelling changed to resemble the Latin.
hints: Sings carols at Christmas.
Part of a church where singers stand.
origin: Old French quer, from Ancient Greek χορός

definition: To be unable to breathe because something blocks the throat.
note: From Old English aceocian, 'to choke'. It also means to panic and fail under pressure.
hints: What a bite of food might make you do.
To fail under pressure, like a golfer on the last hole.
origin: Old English āċēocian, from Old English ċēoce
example: Ever since he choked on a bone, he has refused to eat fish.

definition: To bite or chew noisily.
note: A regional American variant of champ, from Middle English champen, 'to bite'.
hints: What a hungry horse does to hay.
Loud, enthusiastic eating.
example: The dog chomped on the treat and swallowed it in one gulp.

definition: To pick from several options.
note: From Old English ceosan, a verb with cousins across Germanic languages.
hints: Select one of the options.
What a voter does at a ballot box.
example: I chose a nice ripe apple from the fruit bowl.

definition: Relating to or sung by a choir.
note: From Late Latin choralis, from Latin chorus.
hints: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony ends with this kind of finale.
Describes music for many voices rather than one.
origin: Late Latin choralis, from Latin chorus
example: Palestrina wrote choral music for the Catholic church.

definition: A routine household task.
note: From earlier char, Middle English for an odd job or turn, from Old English cierr, 'a turn'. The meaning of a small daily job stuck.
hints: Taking out the rubbish is one.
Something children are assigned for pocket money.
example: I used to enjoy being self-employed, but it's become a bit of a chore recently.

definition: A group of singers, or a repeated part of a song.
note: From Greek khoros, 'dance' or 'band of dancers'.
hints: Sings together.
Repeated part in a pop tune.
origin: Medieval Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός

definition: Past tense of choose.
note: From Old English ceosan, 'to choose', whose past tense was ceas; the modern 'chose' is that past form reshaped. The verb is related to the word 'choice'.
hints: What you did when you picked one.
The past of a word about picking.

definition: Picked out from others.
note: The past participle of choose.
hints: Picked out from among others.
The ones selected.
origin: Old English coren, from Old English ċēosan
example: The chosen candidate accepted the award with pride.

definition: A shiny metal plating.
note: From Greek khroma, 'colour', since chromium compounds are brightly coloured.
hints: Gleaming car bumpers.
Shiny metal used on taps.

definition: Pleasantly plump, especially of a child's cheeks.
note: Recorded from the 1600s and built from chub, a short thick fish also used as a word for a lazy person.
hints: Grandparents like to pinch the cheeks of a baby described this way.
A cherub in a painting is usually drawn this way.
origin: Old Norse kubbr, from Old Norse kumben

definition: To throw carelessly.
note: A variant of chock, meaning a block or lump. As a verb it came to mean toss, and the cut of beef is the same word.
hints: What you do to an old shoe in the bin.
Part of a drill that holds the bit.
origin: Picard Old French chuquier, from Middle Dutch schocken

definition: A fool, or someone easily tricked.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps a blend of chunk and lump. It first meant a blockhead.
hints: A sucker taken in by a scam.
'Don't be a ___,' you might tell a friend.

definition: A thick, solid piece.
note: A variant of chuck, perhaps from chump, with a diminutive ending. It names a thick piece of something.
hints: A big lump of cheese.
A large portion of your salary.

definition: Thick and solid, or containing pieces.
note: From chunk plus -y. It describes soups, knits and sweaters.
hints: A soup with big pieces of vegetables.
A thick knitted jumper in wool.
example: The British Shorthair has a distinctively chunky body, dense coat and broad face.

definition: A building for Christian worship.
note: From Old English cirice, ultimately from Greek kyriakon, 'of the Lord'.
hints: A place with a steeple.
A Sunday gathering place.
origin: Old English ċiriċe, from Ancient Greek κυριακόν; in English since the 9th century
example: There is a lovely little church in the valley.

definition: A slide or sloping channel.
note: Borrowed directly from French chute, 'fall'. It is also a short form of parachute.
hints: A playground slide, or a laundry or rubbish passage.
A sloping channel for sliding things down.

definition: A roll of tobacco leaves for smoking.
note: From Spanish cigarro, of uncertain origin. It is often smoked on special occasions.
hints: Handed out in celebration when a baby is born.
Rolled tobacco that is thicker than a smoke in a paper tube.
example: The tall guy smoking a cigar over there is a famous director.

definition: Something very easy; or a strap on a saddle.
note: From Spanish cincha, 'girth, belt', from Latin cingulum. A tightly fastened strap became a sure thing.
hints: A sure thing, or something simple.
A strap that holds a saddle on a horse.

definition: A place where films are shown, or films as an art.
note: Short for cinematograph, from Greek kinema, 'movement'.
hints: Popcorn is sold here.
Popcorn is sold there.
origin: French cinéma, from Ancient Greek κίνημα

definition: A secret code, or the digit zero.
note: From Old French cifre, from Arabic sifr, 'zero' or 'empty'. Cipher and zero share an origin, and a cipher can also mean a person of no importance.
hints: Used by spies to scramble a message.
Julius Caesar's simple letter-shifting version is the classic example.

definition: Around; approximately, used with dates.
note: Borrowed from Latin circa, 'around', related to circus and circle. Historians write it, often as 'c.', before an uncertain date.
hints: Seen before a date on a museum label.
Abbreviated c. in front of a year.
example: Julius Caesar visited this area circa 50 BC.

definition: A perfectly round shape.
note: From Latin circulus, 'small ring'.
hints: A ring with all points equal distance from the centre.
Wheel shape.
origin: Old French cercle, from Ancient Greek κίρκος
example: The chairs were arranged in a circle.

definition: A travelling show with acrobats, clowns and animals.
note: Latin for 'ring' or 'circle', from the round arenas of Rome.
hints: Big top entertainment.
Named for its circular shape.
origin: Latin circus, from Ancient Greek κρίκος; in English since the late 18th century
example: The circus will be in town next week.

definition: Quoted or mentioned as a source.
note: From Latin citare, 'to summon'. A scholar does it to credit a source.
hints: What a footnote does for a source.
Named as evidence.

definition: The family of fruits including lemons, limes and oranges.
note: From Latin citrus, a citron tree. The vitamin in them helped prevent scurvy.
hints: A group that includes lemons and grapefruit.
Sailors once ate limes to stop scurvy.
origin: Latin citrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος

definition: Relating to a city or its citizens.
note: Borrowed from Latin civicus, 'of a citizen', from civis, 'citizen'. A citizen's duties came to be called civic duties.
hints: Voting is considered a duty of this kind.
A town hall is a ___ building.
example: Thousands of people came to the Civic Center to show off their civic pride.

definition: Polite, or relating to ordinary citizens.
note: From Old French and Latin civilis, 'relating to a citizen', from civis. It contrasts with military or religious matters, and with rude behaviour.
hints: What a courteous but cold conversation might be.
A ___ war is fought between citizens of one country.
origin: Old French civil, from Latin cīvīlis
example: It was very civil of him to stop the argument.

definition: A short, sharp, hard sound.
note: From Middle English clacken, imitative of the noise. It is the sound of two hard things repeatedly knocking.
hints: Heels do it on a tile floor.
Typewriter keys make this noise.

definition: To say that something is true or yours.
note: From Old French clamer, 'to call out', from Latin clamare, 'to cry out'. A claim was once literally a calling out of what you owned.
hints: A miner might stake one.
An insurance customer files one.
origin: Old French clamer, from Latin clāmō

definition: A device that grips things tightly together.
note: From Middle Dutch clampe, 'hook', from a Germanic root related to clasp. It is a tool for holding.
hints: A carpenter holds two boards together with one.
A parking wheel lock is also called this.

definition: A loud ringing metallic sound.
note: From about 1570, imitative of the sound. It resembles the German word Klang.
hints: What a dropped pan does on a tile floor.
A bell strikes it, but harshly.
example: He could hear the clang of distant bells.

definition: A dull heavy metallic sound.
note: Imitative of the sound itself. It is lower and heavier than a clang.
hints: Chains drag across the floor with this noise.
A knight's armour makes it as he walks.

definition: To crash together noisily, or to conflict.
note: Imitative, like crash and smash. It came to mean fights and also colours that do not match.
hints: Two armies meet in one.
Orange and pink might do this.

definition: To grip tightly; or a fastener.
note: From Middle English claspe, a metal catch or hook. The noun and the verb have been in use since the 1300s.
hints: A necklace has one at the back.
To hold hands tightly.

definition: A group of students; or a category or rank.
note: From French classe and Latin classis, a division of Roman citizens. It grew to mean any group sorted by rank or type.
hints: Students sit in it at school.
A social rank, like middle or working.
origin: Middle French classe, from Latin classis

definition: Stylish and elegant.
note: From class plus -y.
hints: Refined taste.
Sophisticated in a quiet way.
example: That's a very classy outfit you're wearing.

definition: A group of words with a subject and verb, or a section of a contract.
note: From Latin clausa, 'a closing'.
hints: Part of a sentence.
One item in a legal document.
origin: Old French clause, from Latin clausus

definition: Free from dirt.
note: From Old English clæne, meaning pure or clear. It once described moral purity too.
hints: What you make a room before guests arrive.
The opposite of dirty.
example: Children with clean shining faces.

definition: Easy to see through, or easy to understand.
note: From Old French cler, from Latin clarus, 'bright, clear'. It describes light, water, and ideas alike.
hints: A window pane that is spotless is this.
Describes skies with no clouds.
origin: Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler
example: The air is clear and clean.

definition: A wedge or strip used for gripping or fastening.
note: From Middle English clete, meaning a wedge or block. Shoes and boats both have them.
hints: A soccer boot has studs of this kind.
A sailor ties a rope around one on the dock.

definition: A split or crack, such as in a chin.
note: From Middle English clift, related to cleave. It names a gap made by splitting.
hints: A dimple in a person's chin is called this.
'In a ___ stick' means trapped in a split in wood.

definition: Priests and ministers as a group.
note: From Old French clergie, from Latin clericus.
hints: Church officials.
Vicars and bishops.
origin: Old French clergie, from Ancient Greek κληρικός
example: Today we brought together clergy from the Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox, and Reformed traditions for ecumenical dialogue.

definition: A member of the clergy.
note: From Late Latin clericus, from Greek kleros, 'lot' or 'inheritance'. The Greek meaning shows a link to those chosen by lot.
hints: A priest, imam or vicar fits the label.
In Dungeons and Dragons, it heals allies with divine magic.
origin: Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός

definition: An office or shop worker who keeps records or serves customers.
note: From Old English clerc, from Late Latin clericus, 'priest, learned man'. Churchmen were once the only ones who could write, so clerk meant scribe.
hints: Takes your payment at a hotel desk.
A shop assistant who rings up sales.
origin: Old English clerc, from Ancient Greek κληρικός

definition: Quick to learn or ingenious.
note: From Middle English cliver, of uncertain origin.
hints: Smart and quick to understand.
A word for sharp-witted.
origin: Norwegian klover, from Old Saxon klibōn
example: You are a clever man...you reason well and your wit is bold.

definition: An overused phrase or idea that has lost its force.
note: From French cliche, a printer's metal plate for repeated printing. Repeated copies of a block gave rise to the idea of a worn expression.
hints: 'Avoid it like the plague' is one.
A film critic complains about a predictable plot twist.

definition: A short, sharp sound; or to press a mouse button.
note: Imitative of the sound, first recorded in the 1500s. Computer use gave it a new life.
hints: What a mouse does when pressed.
The sound a light switch makes.
example: As I turned the key, the lock gave a click and the door opened.

definition: A customer of a professional or business.
note: From Latin cliens, 'follower' or 'dependent'.
hints: A lawyer's customer.
Someone paying for a service.

definition: A steep rock face.
note: From Old English clif, a Germanic word. It named the seaside rock long before the figurative cliff-edge.
hints: The white ones at Dover look over the sea.
A dangerous place to stand near the edge.
example: He stood on a high cliff overlooking the town.

definition: The most intense point of a story or event.
note: From Greek klimax, 'ladder'. A rhetorical ladder of rising points gave the word its sense of a peak.
hints: Where a thriller's tension finally breaks.
The peak of a film before the ending.
origin: Latin clīmax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ

definition: To go up using hands and feet.
note: From Old English climban, from a Germanic root. The b was once pronounced and is now silent.
hints: What you do on a ladder.
Mountaineers do this to reach summits.
example: My legs were so stiff and my arms so sore that this morning I could barely climb out of bed.

definition: To settle something firmly; also, to hold tight in a fight or embrace.
note: A 1500s alteration of clench. To clinch a deal is to fasten it for good.
hints: Boxers lock arms in one when they are tired.
To seal a win or a deal at last.

definition: To hold on tightly.
note: From Old English clingan, 'to adhere, stick together'. It is often used for wet clothes and for people afraid to let go.
hints: A koala does this to a tree.
Wet fabric might do this to skin.

definition: A place for medical treatment.
note: From Greek kline, 'bed', as the first clinics treated patients in bed.
hints: Outpatient facility.
A doctor's practice.
origin: French clinique, from Ancient Greek κλῑνικός

definition: A light ringing sound of glass or metal touching.
note: From Middle English clinken, imitative of the sound. It is also old slang for prison.
hints: The sound when glasses touch in a toast.
Coins in a pocket make it.

definition: A small, closed group of friends who exclude outsiders.
note: Borrowed from French clique, an exclusive group.
hints: Mean Girls shows one in a school cafeteria.
Teenagers form them in high school.

definition: An exact genetic copy of an organism.
note: Coined in botany in 1903 from Greek klon, 'twig'. Plants grown from cuttings were the first clones.
hints: Dolly the sheep was one.
An identical copy of something.

definition: To shut.
note: From Middle English closen, from Old French clos, from Latin clausus. It is a familiar word with several distinct senses.
hints: What you do to a door.
Nearby, as in 'a ___ friend'.
origin: Old English clȳsan, from Latin clausus

definition: Nearer; or someone who finishes a task.
note: From close plus -er.
hints: Nearer in distance or time.
The pitcher who ends a game.

definition: A small room or cupboard for storing clothes.
note: From Old French closet, 'small enclosure', a diminutive of clos.
hints: Where coats are hung.
American word for a wardrobe.
origin: Old French closet, from Latin clausum

definition: A visible mass of water droplets in the sky.
note: From Old English clud, which meant 'rock, hill'. The mass of rain-bearing vapour was likened to a hill in the sky.
hints: It rains from this when it's grey.
A fluffy white one drifts overhead.

definition: Full of clouds; or not clear, as with a liquid.
note: From Old English cludig, 'rocky or hilly', since clouds looked like hills. The sky sense came later.
hints: What a grey, overcast day is.
What a murky drink looks like.

definition: A dried flower bud used as a spice; or a segment of garlic.
note: From Old French clou de girofle, 'nail of the clove tree', since the bud looks like a small nail.
hints: A bud used to stud a ham.
One segment of a bulb of garlic.

definition: A small plant with three leaves, with four a symbol of luck.
note: From Old English clæfre. Three leaves were said to be used by St Patrick to teach the Trinity, according to a popular story.
hints: A four-leaved one is a lucky find.
Bees love its pink and white flower heads.
example: Ladybugs are beetles that like crimson clover and hairy vetch.

definition: A performer in baggy clothes and a red nose.
note: From earlier clowne, 'a rustic, a boor', likely from a Scandinavian source. The meaning shifted from a clumsy peasant to a comic performer.
hints: A circus performer with a red nose.
Someone who acts silly to get laughs.

definition: The noise a hen makes.
note: From Old English cloccian, imitative of the hen's sound. It can also describe a sound of disapproval.
hints: A mother hen calls her chicks with it.
What you do with your tongue to show disapproval.

definition: A tight cluster or lump.
note: From Old English clympre, 'lump or mass of metal', from a Germanic root. It describes things bunched together.
hints: Grass growing in a tuft.
Hair stuck together in a wet mass.
origin: Old English clymppe, from Middle Low German klumpe

definition: Awkward in movement; prone to knocking things over.
note: Possibly from an old word meaning to be numb with cold. It first described stiff fingers.
hints: A person who trips over their own feet.
A waiter who drops the tray.

definition: Past tense of cling; held on tightly.
note: From Old English clinge, to stick together. Wet clothes, children and hopes all get clung to.
hints: How a wet shirt held to skin.
What a koala did to a tree.

definition: To grip tightly; or a car pedal.
note: From Old English clyccan, 'to bend or clench'.
hints: Hold onto your handbag.
Pedal pressed when changing gear.
origin: Old English clyċċan; in English since the 17th century
example: She clutched her purse tightly and walked nervously into the building.

definition: A trainer; or a large carriage or bus.
note: The carriage named for Kocs, a Hungarian town, is a popular theory. It later meant a tutor who carries a student through an exam.
hints: Leads a sports team from the sideline.
A fancy horse-drawn carriage in a fairy tale.
origin: Middle French coche, from Hungarian kocsi

definition: Rough in texture, or crude in manner.
note: Developed from 'course' in the sense of ordinary or usual, and split in spelling around the 1700s.
hints: Sandpaper or table salt can be this, as can language.
A grade of sand or grain that isn't fine.

definition: The land along the sea.
note: From Old French coste, 'rib, side, coast'. The word first meant a side of the body.
hints: Where the land meets the ocean.
To glide without effort, as a bicycle down a hill.
origin: Old French coste; in English since the 14th century
example: The rocky coast of Maine has few beaches.

definition: A hard blue-grey metal, also a deep blue colour.
note: From German Kobalt, a variant of Kobold, 'goblin'. Miners blamed mischievous goblins for its useless ore that spoiled silver smelting.
hints: Used in batteries and to give glass a deep blue.
Named after a goblin by German miners.
example: Some of the cobalt used in phone and laptop batteries is dug out by hand in Congo.

definition: A venomous snake that spreads a hood.
note: From Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra, 'female snake'. It rears up and flattens its neck when threatened.
hints: Snake charmers play to one.
Rudyard Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi fights one.
example: What should you do if you are bitten by a cobra?

definition: Too sure of yourself.
note: From cock, the rooster, plus -y, for the strutting of a male bird. It means arrogant.
hints: Boastful and over-confident.
Strutting like a rooster.

definition: A powder made from cacao seeds; a hot chocolate drink.
note: From Spanish cacao, via Nahuatl. Cocoa came from confusing the word with coco, a spelling Johnson's dictionary helped spread.
hints: Hot drink with marshmallows.
Powder used in baking chocolate cake.
origin: Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl

definition: A silky case spun by a caterpillar to protect it while it changes.
note: From French cocon, a diminutive of coque, 'shell'. People also cocoon themselves in blankets.
hints: Where a caterpillar becomes a moth.
Silk is harvested from the silkworm's one.

definition: Software that compresses and decompresses audio or video.
note: Short for coder-decoder, formed like modem.
hints: Why your video file needs the right one to play.
Squeezes media files into manageable sizes.

definition: A person who writes computer programs.
note: From code, via Old French from Latin codex, a book of wooden tablets.
hints: Someone who writes software.
What a programmer is also called.
example: Tom is a brilliant coder.

definition: An ancient manuscript in book form.
note: Latin for 'tree trunk' or 'book', since early books were made of wooden tablets. It replaced the scroll.
hints: An ancient handwritten book.
What replaced the scroll.

definition: A three-letter unit of genetic code that specifies an amino acid.
note: Coined in the 1960s from code plus the -on ending used for units.
hints: A triplet in DNA or RNA.
Three bases read together by a cell.

definition: A hot drink made from roasted beans.
note: From Arabic qahwa via Turkish and Italian, reaching English in the 1600s.
hints: Morning drink for many.
Brewed from roasted beans.
example: He and his friends used to order coffee whenever they went out.

definition: A box in which a dead person is buried.
note: From Old French cofin, 'basket', from Greek kophinos.
hints: Carried by pallbearers.
Wooden box for a funeral.
origin: Old Northern French cofin, from Ancient Greek κόφινος

definition: A group of people who share something, such as age or a starting year.
note: From Latin cohors, one of the ten units of a Roman legion. Today it is used by researchers and in schools.
hints: A tenth of a Roman legion.
Used in studies tracking a group over many years.
origin: Latin cohors, from Old French cohorte
example: The 18–24 cohort shows a sharp increase in automobile fatalities over the proximate age groupings.

definition: Severe stomach pain, or in babies, long fits of crying.
note: From French colique, from Greek for 'of the colon'.
hints: Why a newborn may cry for hours.
Tummy trouble in infants.
origin: French colique, from Ancient Greek κωλικός

definition: The part of a garment around the neck, or a band worn by an animal.
note: From Latin collare, from collum, 'neck'.
hints: The part of a shirt around the neck.
Worn by a dog.

definition: The punctuation mark that looks like two dots; also part of the bowel.
note: From Latin colon and Greek kolon, 'limb, clause'. The mark was named for a member of a sentence, the bowel for a different Greek word.
hints: Written before a list.
Two dots stacked on top of each other.
origin: Latin cōlon, from Ancient Greek κῶλον

definition: A territory ruled by a distant country, or a group of animals living together.
note: From Latin colonia, 'settlement', from colonus, 'farmer'.
hints: Ants live in one.
Land settled and governed from abroad.

definition: The quality of light that makes red, blue and green different.
note: From Old French color, from Latin color, 'colour, hue'. Spelled colour in British English.
hints: Red or blue, for example.
A crayon box is full of them.

definition: A tall upright pillar, or a vertical list; also a newspaper feature.
note: From Latin columna, 'pillar'.
hints: Holds up a Greek temple.
A vertical row in a table.
origin: Old French columne, from Latin columna

definition: Fighting between armed forces.
note: From Old French combattre, 'to fight with'.
hints: A battle, as soldiers know it.
Soldiers wear boots for it.
origin: Middle French combat, from Latin com-

definition: A short, deep valley, especially in southern England.
note: From Old English cumb, 'valley', and related to Welsh cwm.
hints: Hollow in the hills of Devon.
Old English word for a small valley.

definition: A combination; or a small music group.
note: A clipping of combination plus -o. It names a meal deal and a small jazz band.
hints: A meal with a burger, fries and a drink.
A small jazz group.

definition: A funny play or film.
note: From Greek komoidia, 'revel song'.
hints: Shakespeare wrote many, and they tend to end in weddings.
Makes you laugh.
example: A Midsummer Night's Dream is among Shakespeare's most famous comedies.

definition: Cosy and comfortable.
note: A shortening of comfortable plus -y, dating to the early 1800s. It is a casual, affectionate word.
hints: How a favourite old sweater feels.
A cosy armchair is described this way.
example: The robe and slippers were so warm and comfy she just fell asleep in her chair.

definition: Funny; or a person or book that's funny.
note: From Latin comicus, from Greek komikos, 'of comedy', from komos, 'carousal'. It once referred to stage comedy only.
hints: A stand-up performer is called one.
A cartoon strip in a newspaper.
origin: Latin comicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός; in English since the 16th century

definition: A punctuation mark that marks a short pause.
note: From Latin comma, from Greek komma, 'piece cut off'. It cuts a sentence into smaller parts.
hints: Looks like a tiny curved tail.
What separates items in a list.
origin: Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα

definition: To pledge, or to carry out a crime.
note: From Latin committere, 'to bring together'.
hints: Promise yourself to a cause.
Do something such as an offence.

definition: Shared, widespread or ordinary.
note: From Latin communis, 'shared'.
hints: Seen all the time.
Belonging to everyone, as in a village green.
origin: Anglo-Norman comun, from Old French comun

definition: To force someone to do something.
note: From Latin compellere, 'to drive together'. A court can compel a witness to testify.
hints: A subpoena does this to a witness.
The pull of a good story does it to a reader.
origin: Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere
example: We compel all students to fill out this form.

definition: To obey a rule or request.
note: From Italian complire, 'to fulfil'.
hints: Follow regulations.
Do as you're told.
example: Hopefully you'll comply with traffic regulations after this.

definition: A large spiral sea shell.
note: From Latin concha, from Greek konkhe, 'shell'. Blowing through one makes a loud horn-like note.
hints: In a famous novel, boys use one to call order.
Hold it to your ear to hear the sea.

definition: To agree.
note: From Latin concurrere, 'to run together'.
hints: Judges do it when they reach the same opinion.
Two doctors who reach the same diagnosis do it.
example: The jury concurs with the case put forward by the defence lawyer, that the defendant is undoubtedly innocent.

definition: An apartment you own in a building.
note: Short for condominium. The full word describes a building where each unit has a separate owner.
hints: Shortened word for a flat that is bought, not rented.
Often has a shared pool and gym.
example: Layla was living in a condo with one of her girlfriends.

definition: A thin sheath used in sex to prevent pregnancy and disease.
note: The origin is unknown despite many guesses, including an Italian word for glove. It is widely used in health campaigns.
hints: A common item in public health.
Sold in pharmacies for contraception.
example: They therefore don't concern themselves about using condoms.

definition: To talk things over; also to give an honour or title.
note: From Latin conferre, 'to bring together'.
hints: Delegates do it behind closed doors.
A university does it on a graduate along with a degree.
origin: Middle French conférer, from Latin cōnferō; in English since the 16th century
example: They were in a huddle, conferring about something.

definition: A Latin dance in which people form a line, or a tall drum.
note: From Spanish, linked to the Congo and Africa.
hints: A line of party-goers snaking around a room.
Tall drum played with the hands.

definition: Shaped like or relating to a cone.
note: Borrowed from Ancient Greek konikos, from konos, 'cone'. It appears mostly in mathematics, in the phrase 'conic section'.
hints: A word from geometry class.
What a slice through a cone can be called.

definition: An official who represents their country's interests in a foreign city; also a Roman magistrate.
note: From Latin consul, one of two yearly heads of the Roman Republic. The later diplomatic sense kept the name.
hints: A diplomat based abroad helps citizens with passports.
Rome had two elected each year.
origin: Old English consul, from Latin cōnsul
example: The Roman consul had the camp placed not far from the enemy.

definition: Against or opposed to; also a Nicaraguan rebel.
note: Latin for 'against'. It appears in the phrase 'pros and cons', where con is a short form of it.
hints: Short form of this Latin word turns up in 'pros and cons'.
Latin preposition for 'against'; Reagan-era rebels in Nicaragua took its name.

definition: Curving outward, like the outside of a ball.
note: From Latin convexus, 'arched'. A magnifying glass is a convex lens.
hints: A magnifying lens is this shape.
The opposite of concave.
origin: Middle French convexe, from Latin convexus

definition: To carry or communicate.
note: From Latin conviare, 'to go with'.
hints: Transport goods.
Express a message.

definition: A casual word for conversation.
note: A clipping of conversation, from Latin conversari, 'to live with'. It is used in text.
hints: A chat between friends.
A talk you have in text messages.

definition: A group of vehicles or ships travelling together.
note: From Old French convoier, 'to accompany'.
hints: Lorries moving as a unit.
Escorted supply ships in a war.

definition: An appliance for cooking food, especially the stove in British English.
note: From cook plus -er. In Britain it is the oven and hob; elsewhere, a slow or pressure device.
hints: A pressure one speeds up a stew.
British kitchens have a gas version with oven and hob.
example: Induction cookers use magnets to directly heat pots and pans.

definition: A small, sweet baked treat; or a small file stored by a website.
note: From Dutch koekje, 'little cake'.
hints: Sweet baked snack.
A tracker saved by a browser.

definition: A box that keeps things cold, or less warm.
note: From cool plus -er.
hints: Picnic box with ice.
Less hot than before.

definition: A person who makes barrels.
note: From Middle Dutch or Low German kuper, from kupe, 'tub'. It became a common surname.
hints: A craftsman of casks.
Wine and whisky need his work.

definition: A reddish metal; also a British slang word for a police officer.
note: From Latin cuprum, 'metal of Cyprus', where the metal was mined.
hints: Used in pipes and pennies.
Metal named after an island.
origin: Old English coper, from Ancient Greek Κῠ́προς

definition: A small group of trees.
note: From coppice, contracted in the 1500s. It first meant a small wood grown to be cut regularly.
hints: A small patch of woodland.
Smaller than a forest, bigger than a grove.

definition: The hard, stony skeleton of tiny sea animals.
note: From Old French and Latin corallium, from Greek korallion, probably of Semitic origin. Reefs are built by countless tiny animals.
hints: The Great Barrier Reef is made of it.
A pinkish orange shade as well.

definition: A line of police or guards around an area to keep people out.
note: From Old French cordon, a little cord, from corde. First it was a literal rope or ribbon, which explains the sense of a ring.
hints: Crime scene tape forms one.
Haute cuisine has a bleu one, named after a ribbon.
origin: Middle French cordon, from Old French cordon

definition: A tool for removing the core from fruit.
note: Built from core plus -er, a tool or person that does the action. The same word also names a device for drilling samples out of the earth or ice.
hints: A kitchen gadget for apples.
Pushed through a fruit to remove its middle.
example: Avoiding one-use kitchen utensils, Elton forgoes apple corers, preferring the more versatile paring knife.

definition: A short-legged Welsh herding dog.
note: From Welsh cor, 'dwarf', plus ci, 'dog'. The Queen kept many.
hints: A short-legged dog of the British royal family.
A herding dog with a fox-like face.

definition: Like cork, or spoiled by a bad cork.
note: From cork plus -y. Cork comes from Latin cortex, 'bark'.
hints: Describes wine that smells musty.
Light and springy like bark.

definition: The point where two edges or streets meet.
note: From Old French corne, 'horn', from Latin cornu.
hints: Where two walls meet.
A football kick taken from one.

definition: Cheesy and sentimental.
note: Related to corn, the grain. It was slang for something tired and old-fashioned, as in a joke that's past its best.
hints: A dad's pun might get this label.
A joke so old it makes people groan.
example: The movie was okay, but the love scene was really corny.

definition: The glowing outer layer of the sun, seen in an eclipse.
note: Latin corona means 'crown' or 'wreath'. It also names a type of cigar and a Latin-named virus family.
hints: The glowing outer layer of the sun, visible in an eclipse.
Its Latin root means crown.
origin: Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη

definition: A dead body.
note: From Latin corpus, 'body'.
hints: Found in a murder mystery.
Lifeless body.
origin: Old French cors, from Latin corpus

definition: A large body of written or spoken material, or a body in Latin.
note: Latin for 'body', related to corpse and corps. Linguists build one from texts to study how language is used.
hints: What a dictionary-maker mines for real examples of words.
Linguists use a huge one of texts to see how people really write.

definition: A fenced enclosure for livestock; or to gather people into one place.
note: From Spanish corral, a doublet of kraal. In the old West, famous gunfights took place at one.
hints: Horses are kept in one on a ranch.
The OK one in Tombstone saw a famous gunfight.
example: We had a small corral out back where we kept our pet llama.

definition: A tight undergarment that shapes the waist.
note: From Old French corset, 'little body', from cors. Victorian women laced them tightly.
hints: Held in with stays and laces.
Scarlett O'Hara had hers pulled tight.

definition: The outer layer of the brain or another organ.
note: Latin for 'bark' or rind. The brain's cortex is its wrinkled outer layer.
hints: The wrinkled grey outer layer of the brain.
The word literally meant bark.

definition: Relating to the universe.
note: From Greek kosmikos, from kosmos, 'order'.
hints: Vast in scale.
Rays that come from space.

definition: The universe seen as an ordered whole.
note: From Greek kosmos, 'order' or 'ornament', which also gave us cosmetic. Pythagoras is said to have first used it for the universe.
hints: What Carl Sagan's famous TV series was about.
The orderly universe, the opposite of chaos, to the Greeks.
origin: Ancient Greek κόσμος, from Ancient Greek κόσμοι

definition: Expensive.
note: From cost plus -ly.
hints: High in price.
Describes a mistake that hurts your wallet.

definition: A soft plant fibre used for cloth.
note: From Arabic qutn via Old French.
hints: T-shirt fabric.
White fluffy bolls from a plant.

definition: A sofa.
note: From Old French couche, 'bed', from the verb coucher, 'to lay down'. It is a cousin of the Welsh word cwtch.
hints: A 'potato' is someone who lounges on one.
Where you sit to watch TV.

definition: A large wild cat of the Americas, also known as a puma or mountain lion.
note: Via French from Portuguese, ultimately from a word in the Tupi language of Brazil. The slang meaning of an older woman seeking younger men grew from the animal.
hints: A tawny predator that hunts deer in the Rockies.
Also slang for an older woman who dates younger men.
origin: French couguar, from Old Tupi sûasuarana
example: A cougar is a cat that weighs no less than 170 pounds.

definition: To force air out of the lungs with a harsh sound.
note: From Middle English coughen, imitative of the sound. The gh was once pronounced as a throat sound.
hints: A common sign of a cold.
Syrup is meant to soothe it.
example: Sometimes she coughed up blood.

definition: Used for what was possible or for polite requests.
note: From Old English cuthe, the past of cunnan, 'to be able'. The letter L crept in later by analogy with 'would' and 'should'.
hints: A helper word that politely asks something.
Past form of can.

definition: To say numbers in order; or a nobleman.
note: From Old French conter and Latin computare, 'to reckon together'. The noble title count comes from a different Latin word, comes, 'companion'.
hints: One, two, three.
Sesame Street's vampire loves to do it.
example: The toddler could count to 100.

definition: An administrative region within a country.
note: From Old French conte, the land of a count.
hints: A region within a state or country.
Land once ruled by a count or countess.
example: The county plans to build a new road.

definition: A two-door car with a sloping roof.
note: Borrowed from French coupe, 'cut', from a carriage that was cut short. A shallow stemmed dish has the same spelling.
hints: A sporty two-door car.
A cut-down version of a sedan.
example: Honda's first hybrid was the Insight, a streamlined, small coupe with room for two people and not much more.

definition: Two things together, or a pair of people in a relationship.
note: From Old French cople, from Latin copula, 'bond'.
hints: A pair, romantically or otherwise.
Two together.
origin: Old French couple, from Latin cōpula

definition: A voucher that gives a discount.
note: From French couper, 'to cut', as it was cut from a sheet.
hints: Clipped from a newspaper.
Gives money off a purchase.

definition: A route, a series of lessons, or a part of a meal.
note: From Latin cursus, 'running'.
hints: A path taken, a class, or a dish.
Where a race is run.
origin: Old French cours, from Latin cursus
example: I need to take a French course.

definition: The child of an aunt or uncle.
note: From Old French cosin, from Latin consobrinus.
hints: Related through your parents' siblings.
A relative from a different branch.
origin: Anglo-Norman cosen, from Old French cosin
example: Although we were cousins, we grew up like sisters.

definition: A gathering of witches.
note: From Middle English covent, from Old French and Latin conventum, 'a coming together'. It is the same word as convent, whose spelling changed to mean the witches' version.
hints: Thirteen witches is the traditional number.
A group of witches gathering.
example: Her coven conjures the demons.

definition: To put something over another thing.
note: From Old French covrir, from Latin cooperire, 'to cover completely'. It has many senses, from a lid to a song someone else wrote.
hints: A lid or a blanket does it.
A band plays a version of another's song, called a ___ song.
example: Cover the meat with a lot of gravy.

definition: Secret or hidden.
note: From Old French covert, 'covered'. Spies carry out these operations.
hints: A spy's mission is described this way.
The opposite of overt in a spy novel.
origin: Old French covert, from Latin coopertus
example: Covert actions by the CIA.

definition: To desire something that belongs to someone else.
note: From Old French coveitier, 'to desire'. The Tenth Commandment warns against it.
hints: The Tenth Commandment warns not to do this to a neighbour's goods.
To long enviously for what another person has.
example: As soon as my left eye sees you, my right eye covets you.

definition: A small flock of partridges or quail.
note: From Old French covee, 'a brood', from Latin cubare, 'to lie down'. It describes a family group of game birds.
hints: A hunter flushes a group of quail like this.
A small gathering of game birds.

definition: A person who lacks courage and runs from danger.
note: From Old French coart, perhaps from coue, 'tail', as in an animal with its tail tucked. A popular guess ties it to a frightened hare.
hints: A lion in Oz who learned he had more nerve than he thought.
One who turns tail at the first sign of trouble.

definition: A man who herds cattle on horseback.
note: From cow plus boy.
hints: Rides the range.
Wears a Stetson.

definition: In a shy or playfully evasive way.
note: From coy plus -ly. Coy comes from Old French coi, 'quiet' or 'still', from Latin quietus.
hints: How someone might smile when teased.
Done with a shy, half-hidden look.

definition: A wild dog of North America, related to wolves.
note: Borrowed from Spanish, from Nahuatl coyotl. In the American West it is known for its yips and howls at night.
hints: Howls at dusk in the desert.
Wile E. is the cartoon one who chases the Road Runner.

definition: To break with a sharp sound without splitting apart.
note: From Old English cracian, 'to resound', imitative of the sound. It is both the break and the noise it makes.
hints: A line that appears in a broken egg.
What a whip does.

definition: A small rocking bed for a baby; also the place where something began.
note: From Old English cradol. Greece is called the cradle of democracy.
hints: Rocks a newborn to sleep.
What a place that gave birth to a civilisation is called.

definition: A skill, especially one done by hand.
note: From Old English craeft, 'strength, power, skill'. Strength gave way to skill, and then to a trade or an art.
hints: Knitting is a handmade one.
Also a general word for a small boat or a plane.

definition: Clever in a sly or deceitful way.
note: From Old English cræftig, 'skilful', formed from craft. Craft itself once meant strength or skill, and only later cunning.
hints: A fox in fables earns this label.
Describes a plan with a hidden angle.
example: I have created a perfect plan for capturing that crafty animal.

definition: A painful, sudden tightening of a muscle.
note: From Old French crampe, from a Frankish word meaning bent or hooked. It describes a muscle clenching up.
hints: What swimmers sometimes get in their legs.
A sudden knot in your calf at night.

definition: A tall wading bird, or a machine for lifting.
note: From Old English cran, the bird. The lifting machine was named for its long neck.
hints: A building site has one towering over it.
Origami paper birds are often this.

definition: A handle that turns a shaft; or an odd person.
note: From Old English crencestaef, a weaver's tool, with a Germanic word meaning bent. The grumpy person sense came later.
hints: Turn it to start an old engine.
A grumpy eccentric with strange ideas.

definition: Grumpy and easily irritated.
note: From crank plus -y. A related Middle Low German word meant 'sickly', so the mood may once have been tied to feeling unwell.
hints: Describes a toddler who missed their nap.
Also said of an old machine that won't start properly.
example: He got home from a long day at work tired and cranky.

definition: Of very poor quality.
note: From crap plus -y. Crap is not, as often claimed, named for Thomas Crapper; it is much older.
hints: How a slang user rates a bad day or bad coffee.
An informal put-down for shoddy goods.
example: That is such a crappy car.

definition: To hit something violently with a loud noise.
note: From Middle English crasshen, 'to break into pieces', of uncertain origin. It seems to combine sounds like crack and smash.
hints: What two cars might do at an intersection.
A computer might do this and freeze.
example: Thunder crashed directly overhead.

definition: Crude and insensitive.
note: From Latin crassus, 'thick, dense'. The thickness of a crass person is of manners.
hints: A tasteless remark at a funeral.
Lacking refinement or tact.
origin: Old French cras, from Latin crassus
example: I'm sick of your crass hints.

definition: A large box for moving goods.
note: From Dutch krat, 'basket, box'. It is used for fruit, bottles and pets.
hints: A box of oranges for shipping.
A dog may be trained in a wire one.
origin: Dutch krat, from Middle Dutch cratte

definition: A bowl-shaped hollow, left by an impact or at the mouth of a volcano.
note: From Greek krater, a mixing bowl for wine. The Moon is covered in them.
hints: The Moon's surface is covered in these pits.
The mouth of a volcano.
origin: Latin crātēr, from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ

definition: To want something very badly.
note: From Old English crafian, 'to ask, demand'. Cravings have long been spoken of as demands.
hints: What a pregnant person might do for pickles.
To long for chocolate after dinner.

definition: Shamefully cowardly.
note: From Middle English cravant, possibly from an Old French word meaning 'defeated'.
hints: A knight who runs from battle would earn the label.
Shakespeare used it to describe a coward's heart.

definition: To move along on hands and knees.
note: From Old Norse krafla, 'to claw about, crawl'. A baby does it before walking.
hints: Babies do it before they walk.
A swimming stroke has this name.
example: The crocodile was crawling along the riverbed.

definition: A coloured wax stick for drawing.
note: From French crayon, from craie, 'chalk', from Latin creta.
hints: A child's drawing might use it.
Comes in a box with a built-in sharpener.

definition: A short-lived but intense fashion.
note: From Middle English crasen, 'to shatter', from Old Norse. The meaning moved from smash to a mind that's cracked, then a passing mania.
hints: Fidget spinners were one.
A passing fad that everyone follows.

definition: Mad or wildly irrational.
note: Built from craze, 'to crush', plus -y. Like cracked, it refers to a mind that has broken.
hints: Way to say something is wild or nuts.
What you might call a plan that makes no sense.
example: The game had a crazy ending.

definition: To make a long, squeaky sound.
note: From Middle English creken, from an Old English word meaning to chatter or crash. It is imitative.
hints: Old stairs do it when stepped on.
A rusty hinge on a door.
example: The door creaked when I opened it slowly.

definition: The rich fat that rises to the top of milk.
note: From Old French creme, a blend of Late Latin chrisma, 'ointment', and an older word for the dairy fat. The best of something is the 'cream of the crop'.
hints: Whipped and put on desserts.
Poured into coffee.
origin: Old French creme, from Late Latin crāmum

definition: Smooth and rich, like cream.
note: Simply cream plus -y, from Middle English. Soups, sauces and ice cream earn the label.
hints: A texture word on a soup or pasta sauce menu.
Not chunky, but thick and velvety.

definition: A line made by folding or pressing.
note: From an older word creast, 'ridge', related to crest. In cricket, the crease marks the batter's safe zone.
hints: What an iron removes from a shirt.
A batter stands behind a white line of this name.
example: His pants had a nice sharp crease.

definition: To bring something into being.
note: From Latin creare, 'to make'.
hints: What an artist does.
Make from nothing.
example: The company was created 25 years ago.

definition: Praise for something, or money lent on trust.
note: From Latin creditum, 'something entrusted', from credere, 'to believe'.
hints: What a card lets you spend.
Recognition for work done.
origin: Middle French crédit, from Latin crēditum
example: She already had several performances to her credit.

definition: A statement of beliefs.
note: From Latin credo, 'I believe'. It is the same word as creed, and the opening word of a famous Latin prayer.
hints: A personal motto or guiding belief.
Latin for 'I believe'.
origin: Old French credo, from Latin crēdō

definition: A set of beliefs.
note: From Old English creda, from Latin credo, 'I believe'. It names a statement of faith recited in church.
hints: A formal statement of what a faith holds.
Not a political one but a religious one.
origin: Old English crēda, from Latin crēdō

definition: A small stream.
note: From Middle English crike, from Old Norse kriki, 'bend, nook'. In Britain it means a narrow inlet; in America a stream.
hints: Kids splash and catch tadpoles in it.
Proverbially, you are up one without a paddle.
origin: Old Norse kriki, from Middle Dutch krēke
example: The creek dried up every summer.

definition: Causing an uneasy, shivery feeling.
note: From creep plus -y, as in skin that seems to crawl.
hints: Spooky enough to raise goosebumps.
What a dark empty house feels.
example: I had a creepy-crawly feeling.

definition: A stable language that grew out of a mix of other languages.
note: From Portuguese crioulo, via Spanish and French, meaning born in a colony. Haitian and Jamaican patois are examples.
hints: Haiti has its own.
Louisiana cooking shares its name.

definition: A very thin pancake.
note: Borrowed from French crepe, from Latin crispus, 'curled'. The word also names a crinkled fabric.
hints: Filled with Nutella and folded.
A French thin pancake.

definition: A peppery plant used in salads and sandwiches.
note: From Old English cressa, a Germanic word. Egg and ___ sandwiches are a British classic.
hints: Grows quickly on damp cotton wool.
A peppery green in a sandwich.

definition: A sharp stiffness in the neck or back.
note: From Middle English crike, 'muscular spasm', possibly from Old Norse kriki, 'bend'. It appears in English from the 1400s.
hints: Sleeping badly may give you one in your neck.
A painful kink in your neck.

definition: A person who shouts out public announcements.
note: From Old French crieor, built on the verb crier, 'to cry out'. A town crier once shouted news and proclamations to the public.
hints: Once announced news in the marketplace.
Often rang a bell and shouted 'Oyez'.

definition: An act that breaks the law.
note: From Old French crime, from Latin crimen, 'charge, accusation, offence'. It has stood for lawbreaking for centuries.
hints: What a detective investigates.
Theft or arson, for example.
origin: Old French crime, from Latin crīmen

definition: To press into small folds or ridges.
note: From Middle English crimpen and Middle Dutch crimpen, 'to wrinkle'. It is related to the shrinking verbs.
hints: Pinching the edge of a pie crust.
A hairdresser's tool gives hair a wavy texture.
example: Cornish pasties are crimped during preparation.

definition: To shrink back in embarrassment, disgust or fear.
note: From Middle English crengen, 'to bend or yield', related to crank. In recent slang it also describes something painfully awkward.
hints: What you do when someone tells an awful joke at a wedding.
A reaction to watching an old home video of yourself.
example: He cringed as the bird collided with the window.

definition: A time of great danger or trouble.
note: From Greek krisis, 'decision', from krinein, 'to separate'.
hints: A moment of turning point, as in finance.
An emergency.
origin: Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις
example: They went bankrupt during the economic crisis.

definition: Firm, dry and brittle.
note: From Old English crisp, from Latin crispus, 'curly'. The word first described curled hair, and later things that snap.
hints: Fresh celery is this.
Describes autumn air or a fried potato slice.
origin: Old English crisp, from Latin crispus

definition: Hard and brittle in a pleasing way, usually of food.
note: From crisp plus -y. Middle English crispy meant curly, from Latin crispus.
hints: What fried chicken skin should be.
A texture prized on bacon and roast potatoes.
example: These biscuits are very crispy.

definition: A person who judges works of art, or finds fault.
note: From Greek kritikos, 'able to judge'.
hints: Reviews plays.
Writes about books.
origin: Middle French critique, from Ancient Greek κριτικός

definition: A low, hoarse noise like a frog's.
note: From Middle English, back-formed from an Old English word meaning to croak. It imitates the sound.
hints: A frog's call.
A hoarse voice with a sore throat.

definition: An earthenware pot.
note: From Old English crocc, 'pot, jar'. A slow cooker is named for it.
hints: A slow cooker has this word in its name.
A big pottery pot.

definition: A small farm in Scotland.
note: From Old English croft, 'small field'. Crofters work them in the Highlands.
hints: A small Highland farm.
A tiny rented plot of land.

definition: An old woman, often an unkind picture of one.
note: From Anglo-Norman carogne, related to carrion. It started as an insult meaning an old ewe or worn-out thing.
hints: A hag in a fairy tale.
An old woman who might stir a cauldron.
example: Some triple goddesses have the forms maiden, mother, and crone.

definition: A close friend or associate, often in questionable dealings.
note: Coined in the 1660s from Greek khronios, 'long-lasting', as Cambridge student slang for an old friend. Politicians' friends get this label.
hints: '___ capitalism' favours friends of the powerful.
A buddy who gets favours from you.
example: Barry and Prue would have given him almost anything they had, for he was a great friend and crony of theirs.

definition: A criminal; or a bend or hook.
note: From Old Norse krokr, 'hook'. The criminal sense is from the bent, not straight, character. A shepherd's staff has one too.
hints: A dishonest person.
What a shepherd's staff is curved into.

definition: Angry; or the shape of two lines meeting.
note: From Latin crux, 'cross', through Old Irish and Old English. The angry sense came from 'crossing' someone's wishes.
hints: Annoyed or ill-tempered.
A plus sign is a small one.
origin: Old English cros, from Latin crux
example: They exchanged a few cross words.

definition: The place where the legs meet the body; or any fork shape.
note: Of uncertain origin; perhaps from Middle English crucche, 'crutch', meaning a forked support. A fork in a tree is a crotch as well.
hints: Where a tree trunk divides into branches.
The seam of a pair of trousers.
example: Every mile they rode their crotches felt worse saddlepain.

definition: To bend low with knees bent, close to the ground.
note: From Middle English crouchen, related to crook. Cats crouch before they pounce.
hints: A cat does it before pouncing.
What a sprinter does at the starting line.
example: We crouched behind the low wall until the squad of soldiers had passed by.
