definition: A children's illness with a barking cough.
note: The name probably imitates the sound of the cough. A horse's rump has the same spelling from a different word.
hints: A child's cough that sounds like a seal.
A childhood illness with a barking cough.
origin: Scots croup, from Old English hrōpan

definition: A large group of people together.
note: From Old English crudan, 'to press, drive'. It first meant to push before it meant a mass of people.
hints: Gathers at a football match.
To squeeze together in a small space.
example: A crowd of insects assembled around the flowers.

definition: A ring worn on a monarch's head.
note: From Anglo-Norman corone, from Latin corona, 'wreath', from Greek. It also names the top of the head or a tooth cap.
hints: A queen wears it.
The top of your head.
origin: Anglo-Norman corone, from Ancient Greek κορώνη
example: Treasure recovered from shipwrecks automatically becomes property of the Crown.

definition: Rough and unrefined.
note: From Latin crudus, 'raw, rough'. It is related to cruel. It names oil in its raw state.
hints: Petroleum before refining.
A rough joke in poor taste.

definition: Willing to cause pain or suffering.
note: From Old French cruel and Latin crudelis, 'hard, severe', related to crudus, 'raw'. A cruel person is raw, not softened.
hints: Describes someone who takes pleasure in others' pain.
The opposite of kind.
origin: Old French cruel, from Latin crūdēlis
example: The supervisor was very cruel to Josh, as he would always give Josh the hardest, most degrading work he could find.

definition: A pleasure trip by sea; or to travel at a steady speed.
note: From Dutch kruisen, 'to cross'.
hints: A holiday on a big ship.
Cars use control to keep a speed.

definition: A tiny piece of bread or cake.
note: From Old English cruma, from a Germanic root. The b was added to the spelling later, as in thumb.
hints: What toast leaves on the table.
A little piece a bird might peck.
example: The pigeons were happily pecking at crumbs of bread on the ground.

definition: A mild British exclamation of surprise.
note: A minced oath, softening 'Christ' to a harmless word. It dates from the early 1900s.
hints: British schoolboy exclamation, nothing to do with biscuits.
A mild exclamation like 'goodness'.

definition: To chew or crush something with a loud, crackling sound.
note: Imitative in origin, from the earlier craunch. It also names a squeeze of time or money.
hints: The noise of a fresh apple or snow underfoot.
A word on a cereal box for the sound.

definition: The hard outer layer of bread or pie.
note: From Latin crusta, 'rind, shell', through Old French. It also names the Earth's outer layer.
hints: The hard part of a loaf.
The outer layer of the planet.
origin: Old French cruste, from Latin crusta

definition: An underground room, often beneath a church, used for burials.
note: From Latin crypta, from Greek kryptos, 'hidden'. The word is related to cryptic.
hints: Beneath a cathedral, with tombs inside.
Dracula sleeps in one.
origin: Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός; in English since the 16th century
example: The royal crypt was pilfered by grave robbers long ago.

definition: Short for cryptocurrency, digital money secured by cryptography.
note: Clipped from cryptocurrency, which came from crypto-, Greek kryptos, 'hidden'. Bitcoin is the best known.
hints: What speculators trade instead of stocks.
Bitcoin and Ethereum belong here.

definition: A small cosy space for storage or hiding.
note: From a Middle English word for a stall, plus a diminutive ending.
hints: Where a child hangs a coat at school.
A little nook in a classroom.

definition: Relating to the shape or measure of a cube.
note: From Middle French cubique, from cube plus -ic. Volumes are measured in these units.
hints: A measure of volume, as in 'a ___ metre'.
Shaped like dice.

definition: A bird that lays its eggs in other birds' nests, named for its call.
note: The name imitates its two-note call, and the word came into English via Old French. A cuckoo clock has a little wooden bird that pops out to sound the hours.
hints: A Swiss clock has one that pops out on the hour.
Its chick shoves the host's own eggs out of the nest.

definition: To hold someone close and affectionately.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from an old word for 'to embrace'. It first appears in English in the 1500s.
hints: Done with a pet on the sofa.
Soft toy or a partner at the end of the day.
example: I cuddled the baby.

definition: Soft and pleasant to hold close.
note: From cuddle plus -y. Cuddle itself first appears in the 1500s with unclear origins.
hints: Describes a favourite plush bear.
A word on toy labels, and for puppies.
example: She's got the biggest collection of cuddly toys I've ever seen.

definition: A spice used in curries and chilli.
note: From Old English cymen and Old French cumin, from Latin cuminum, ultimately from a Semitic source. It has been used in cooking for thousands of years.
hints: A warm brown spice in Indian and Mexican dishes.
Seeds from a plant in the parsley family.

definition: The Roman god of love, often shown as a winged child with a bow.
note: From Latin Cupido, 'desire'. His arrows made people fall in love.
hints: A winged archer on valentine cards.
The god who shoots love's arrows.

definition: A cup of tea, in British speech.
note: A contraction of 'cup of', with the tea understood.
hints: What a Brit puts the kettle on for.
Short for a cup of something warm.
example: I walked out in the middle of it. Let's go and have a cuppa.

definition: A junior priest, or to select and arrange items.
note: From Medieval Latin curatus, 'one responsible for care'. The verb sense for museum shows came later.
hints: An assistant to a vicar.
Museum staff do this to an exhibition.

definition: A rule that people must be indoors by a set hour.
note: From Old French couvre-feu, 'cover the fire', the evening signal to put out fires. The fire-covering bell was medieval.
hints: Teenagers sometimes have one set by their parents.
The medieval evening bell once meant 'cover your fires'.
example: The city has been reported calm after a curfew was imposed.

definition: The papal court, or an ancient Roman council.
note: Borrowed from Latin curia, the Roman senate house.
hints: The administrative body of the Vatican.
Roman senate house.

definition: A small unusual object that people collect.
note: A clipping of curiosity, dated 1851. Collectors displayed them in cabinets of curiosities.
hints: A small, odd collectable in a shop.
An antique trinket on a shelf.
example: The quaint little antique shop is full of unique trinkets, knick-knacks, and curios.

definition: Having curls.
note: From curl plus -y. It describes hair or things that twist into spirals.
hints: Hair that's not straight.
A pig's tail is this.
example: They envied her naturally curly hair.

definition: A spiced dish, popular across India and the UK.
note: From Tamil kari, 'sauce', influenced by an older English word cury, 'cooking'. The first English recipe printed was in 1747.
hints: Served with rice or naan.
A fragrant dish with a spicy sauce.

definition: A wish that harm will fall on someone; or a swear word.
note: From Old English curs, of unknown origin. It names both a spell of misfortune and rude language.
hints: A witch casts one on a prince in a tale.
To swear angrily when you stub your toe.

definition: The blinking mark on a screen showing where you are typing.
note: From Latin cursor, 'runner', from currere, 'to run'. It was a sliding part on instruments before computers took it.
hints: Moves when you push a mouse.
Can be an arrow, hand or vertical line.

definition: A smooth bend without corners.
note: From Latin curvus, 'bent', with a root meaning to turn or bend. It has been in English since the 1690s.
hints: A road bends in one.
What a baseball pitcher throws to fool the batter.

definition: Having many smooth bends.
note: From curve plus -y. It describes roads, shapes and figures.
hints: A mountain road with many bends is this.
Winding, with no straight lines.

definition: Comfortable and undemanding, like a soft job.
note: From Hindustani khushi, 'pleasure', which came from Persian. It reached English through British India.
hints: Describes a job with little effort.
An easy, comfortable post.
example: This is a really cushy job. Mostly I just sit around drinking tea.

definition: A usual or traditional way of doing things.
note: From Old French costume, from Latin consuetudo, 'habit'.
hints: A tradition.
Made to order.
example: Much forbidden by elder custom is accepted today.

definition: An attractive or adorable person; also a small, easy-peel orange.
note: From cute plus the -ie ending. Cute itself is a shortening of acute, once meaning 'sharp' and 'clever'.
hints: A friendly pet name.
Also the brand name of a small, easy-peel orange.

definition: A person who makes or sells knives and other cutting tools.
note: From Old French coutelier, from coutel, 'knife'. It is the origin of the surname and shares a root with cutlery.
hints: Sheffield was once famous for them.
Makes knives and forks for the table.
origin: Anglo-Norman cuteler, from Old French coutelier

definition: A point or limit where something stops; also shorts made from trimmed trousers.
note: From the verb phrase cut off. The limit sense arrived by the idea of a line beyond which nothing continues.
hints: A deadline for applications is one.
A pair of denim shorts frayed at the edge is called this.

definition: A tool or person that cuts; or a small fast boat.
note: From cut plus -er.
hints: Pastry shape tool.
A coast guard vessel.

definition: Relating to computers, networks or the internet.
note: Taken from cybernetics, which came from Greek kybernetes, 'steersman'. It is now a stand-alone word.
hints: A prefix-like word about being online.
Often paired with 'security' or 'space'.

definition: A being that is part machine and part living organism.
note: A blend of cybernetic and organism, coined in 1960 by the scientist Manfred Clynes.
hints: Robocop and the Terminator are film examples.
Science fiction's name for a person with built-in machine parts.
example: A cyborg is a cybernetic organism.

definition: A series of events that repeat; or a bicycle.
note: From Late Latin cyclus and Greek kyklos, 'circle'. A cycle is a sequence that goes around and returns to its start.
hints: The washing machine has several settings of this kind.
Water goes through one of evaporation and rain.
origin: Late Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος
example: A cycle of reprisal and retaliation.

definition: Occurring in cycles; or forming a ring of atoms.
note: From Greek kyklikos, from kyklos, 'circle, wheel'.
hints: The seasons follow this pattern.
A chemist uses it for molecules in a ring.
origin: French cyclique, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός
example: The weather had a cyclic pattern of rain and sun.

definition: A person who assumes the worst about people's motives.
note: From Greek kynikos, 'dog-like'. It named a school of ancient Greek philosophers who rejected comforts and conventions.
hints: Expects everyone to be selfish.
Diogenes lived in a barrel and gave his name to the philosophers who shared the label.
origin: Middle French cynique, from Ancient Greek κυνικός

definition: Relating to a cyst, or to a sac in the body.
note: From Greek kystis, 'bladder'. Cystic fibrosis affects the lungs.
hints: Part of the name of a lung disease.
Acne of this type is deep.
origin: Middle French cystique, from Ancient Greek κύστις

definition: A child's word for father.
note: From dad plus the -y ending. It is also used for the biggest or best of something.
hints: What a small child calls their father.
Informal word for dad.

definition: Silly or a little crazy.
note: From daff, an old word for a fool, plus -y.
hints: Famous cartoon duck with this name.
Goofy or scatterbrained.

definition: A short, pointed knife for stabbing.
note: From Old French dague. Shakespeare's Macbeth sees an imaginary one floating before him.
hints: In Macbeth, a ghostly one hovers in the air.
Brutus used one on Caesar, in Shakespeare's play.

definition: Happening every day.
note: From Old English daeglic, from day plus -ly. It is also the name for newspapers that come out every day.
hints: A newspaper that comes out each morning.
Done once every twenty-four hours.

definition: Small, delicate and pretty.
note: From Old French deintie, from Latin dignitas, 'worth'. It is a doublet of dignity.
hints: A teacup with a pattern of roses.
Tiny cakes and teacups are described this way.
origin: Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem

definition: Milk and foods made from it.
note: From Middle English deyerie, from deye, 'dairymaid', plus -erie. The dairymaid made butter and cheese.
hints: Cheese and butter belong in this food group.
A farm or shop section for milk and yoghurt.

definition: A small flower with white petals and a yellow centre.
note: From Old English daeges eage, 'day's eye', because the flower closes at night and opens at dawn.
hints: Children make chains of them.
'She loves me, she loves me not' is played with one.
example: A little nap and, just like that, I'm as fresh as a daisy.

definition: To waste time or move slowly.
note: From Middle English dalien, from Anglo-Norman. It is a cousin of the word delay.
hints: Don't linger on the way home.
To dawdle instead of getting on with things.

definition: Harm done to something.
note: From Old French damage, from Latin damnum, 'loss'.
hints: A dented car shows it.
What a storm leaves behind.
origin: Old French damage, from Latin damnum

definition: An expletive of anger or frustration.
note: A blending of 'damn it', run together as people actually say it. It is a mild curse from a word once taken seriously as condemnation.
hints: What you mutter after stubbing your toe.
Captain Kirk's ship doctor shouted 'Jim!' after it.

definition: To move your body to music.
note: From Old French dancier, of uncertain earlier origin. It has been in English since the 1300s.
hints: What you do at a party.
Ballet and the tango are forms of it.
example: I danced with her all night long.

definition: A person who dances.
note: From dance plus -er.
hints: Performs ballet.
Moves to music.
example: I'm a terrible dancer.

definition: A man who takes great care over his clothes.
note: Borrowed from Scots, of uncertain origin. It may be a pet form of the name Andrew. It also means excellent, as in 'fine and ___'.
hints: A sharply dressed man of fashion.
'Yankee Doodle' called himself one.

definition: The possibility of harm.
note: From Old French dangier, 'power of a lord', from Latin dominium, 'rule'.
hints: Something that could cause harm.
Red signs warn of it.
example: You are in no danger.

definition: A single piece of information.
note: From Latin datum, 'given'. The plural, data, is far more familiar.
hints: The singular of a word usually in the plural.
One fact among many.

definition: To make someone feel afraid or discouraged.
note: From Old French danter, from Latin domitare, 'to tame'. To be daunted was first to be tamed.
hints: A steep mountain might do this to a new climber.
'Nothing ___ed' means unafraid.
origin: Old French danter, from Latin domō
example: The challenges are daunting, but we can overcome them.

definition: A church official ranked beneath a priest, or a lay leader in some churches.
note: From Greek diakonos, 'servant', which is also the root of the word for a minister. Early deacons looked after charity for the poor.
hints: A servant of the congregation in church.
A rank below priest in the Catholic and Anglican churches.
origin: Old English diacon, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος

definition: Likely to cause death.
note: From dead plus -ly.
hints: Likely to cause someone to die.
A poison could be so.

definition: A person who trades, or who hands out cards.
note: From deal plus -er.
hints: A used-car seller.
Hands out cards at a casino.

definition: Very much; or at a high cost.
note: From Old English deorlice. It does double duty: you can love someone this way and pay for a mistake this way.
hints: How a mourner says someone is missed.
A word in a funeral service before 'departed'.

definition: The end of life.
note: From Old English death, from a Germanic root. It has been the most solemn word for the end for over a thousand years.
hints: The Grim Reaper is its figure.
What a funeral marks.

definition: To officially shut someone out or forbid them.
note: From Anglo-Norman debarrer, from de- plus barre, 'bar'. To be debarred is to have a barrier placed against you.
hints: What a rule might do to a rule-breaker.
Keeping someone out of a profession or a place.

definition: A formal argument between sides.
note: From Old French debatre, 'to fight'.
hints: A contest of arguments.
Candidates do it on TV.
example: After a four-hour debate, the committee voted to table the motion.

definition: An amount of money taken from an account.
note: From Latin debitum, 'what is owed', from debere, 'to owe'. It is a cousin of the word debt.
hints: What a purchase makes to your bank balance.
A card swipe at the till triggers one.
origin: Middle French debet, from Latin debitum

definition: Scattered broken pieces left after destruction.
note: From French debris, from debriser, 'to break down'.
hints: Left after an explosion.
Wreckage on the ground.
origin: French débris, from Old French debrisier
example: Much of the debris that washes up on our beaches is plastic.

definition: A person who owes money.
note: From Old French detour, from Latin debitor. The b was added in spelling to look more like Latin.
hints: The one on the wrong side of a loan.
Old prisons held people in this state.
origin: Old French detour, from Latin debitor
example: Debtors are people who cannot re-pay money they owe.

definition: To find and fix faults in software.
note: From de- plus bug. Admiral Grace Hopper's team supposedly found a real moth in a computer in 1947, though the word bug was older.
hints: A programmer does it to fix errors in code.
To remove glitches from a program.

definition: A first public appearance.
note: From French debut, from debuter, 'to begin'. It comes from a word meaning 'goal', as in the first shot at a target.
hints: A singer's first album.
An actor's first film.
origin: French début, from Old Norse bútr

definition: A period of ten years.
note: From Greek dekas, 'a group of ten'.
hints: The nineties, for example.
Ten years long.
origin: Old French decade, from Ancient Greek δεκάς; in English since the 16th century
example: The 1960s was a turbulent decade.

definition: Coffee with most of the caffeine removed.
note: A clipping of decaffeinated.
hints: What you order late at night.
Coffee without the kick.

definition: A sticker that can be transferred to a surface.
note: A clipping of decalcomania, a French craft of transferring pictures. It names a transfer sticker.
hints: A sticker on a car's rear window.
A transfer you rub onto a model plane.

definition: To rot or break down.
note: From Anglo-Norman decaeir, 'to fall away'. It originally meant simply to decrease.
hints: What happens to a tooth with too much sugar.
Slow breakdown of dead plants into soil.

definition: Dishonest behaviour meant to mislead someone.
note: From Old French deceite, from decevoir, itself from Latin decipere, 'to cheat, mislead'.
hints: The heart of a con artist's trade.
A white lie is a small, forgivable version of it.
origin: Old French deceite, from Latin dēcipere

definition: Respectable, adequate or kind.
note: From Latin decens, 'fitting' or 'proper'.
hints: Fairly good, as in a meal.
Behaving correctly.
origin: Middle French décent, from Latin decēns

definition: To make up your mind.
note: From Latin decidere, 'to cut off', from de and caedere.
hints: Settle on a choice.
Its Latin root meant to cut.
origin: Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere
example: You must decide between good and evil.

definition: The style in which a room is decorated.
note: From French decor, from Latin decor, 'beauty, grace'. It is a shortened word for decoration.
hints: A designer chooses it for a house.
The look of a room, from curtains to cushions.
example: Her living room had a lush Persian-style decor.

definition: An official order.
note: From Old French decret, from Latin decretum, 'something decided'.
hints: A king might issue one.
A ruling announced by authority.

definition: To publicly criticise something as bad.
note: Dating from about 1600, from Old French descrier, 'to shout down'. It is a cousin of descry.
hints: An activist might do this at a rally.
To denounce loudly.
origin: Middle French decrier, from Old French descrier
example: The opposition has decried the law as unconstitutional.

definition: To take an amount away from a total.
note: From Latin deducere, 'to lead from'.
hints: A teacher might do this to marks for lateness.
Taxes come out of a paycheque this way.
example: I will deduct the cost of the can of peas from the money I owe you.

definition: To make or become deeper or more intense.
note: Formed from deep plus -en, from Old English deop.
hints: A mystery does it when a new clue fails to fit.
Colours, voices and friendships can all do this.

definition: To a great depth or degree.
note: From deep plus -ly.
hints: To a profound degree.
Reaching far down or in.
example: I am deeply concerned about this matter.

definition: To beat an opponent, or a loss.
note: From Old French desfaire, 'to undo'.
hints: Win against.
Lose, in a battle.

definition: A flaw or imperfection that stops something from working properly.
note: From Latin deficere, 'to fail or fall short'. To defect also means to desert a country, giving up one's side.
hints: A factory recall is usually about one.
A birth one may be congenital.

definition: To protect from attack.
note: From Latin defendere, 'to ward off'.
hints: What a goalkeeper does.
Guard against a threat.

definition: To put off until later.
note: From Middle English differren, 'to postpone', from Latin differre. It is a doublet of differ.
hints: What a student might do with a university place.
To delay, as with a payment.

definition: To state what something means.
note: From Latin definire, 'to set bounds to'.
hints: Give the meaning of a word.
Describe exactly.
origin: Old French definer, from Latin dēfīniō
example: The textbook defined speed as velocity divided by time.

definition: A unit of angle or temperature, or a university award.
note: From Old French degre, 'step', from Latin gradus.
hints: Thermometers show it.
Graduates earn one.
origin: Old French degré, from Latin gradus; in English since the 14th century
example: The game was played in spite of the 40-degree temperature.

definition: To do something as if it's beneath you.
note: From Old French deignier, 'to think worthy', from Latin dignare. It is related to dignity.
hints: A snob won't ___ to speak to servants.
To condescend.
example: May God Almighty deign to hear and grant our prayers.

definition: A god or goddess.
note: From Middle French deite, from Latin deitas, 'divine nature'. It is a formal word for a god.
hints: Zeus was one.
A divine being that is worshipped.
origin: Middle French deité, from Latin deitās; in English since the 14th century
example: This is an image of a deity with the fiery face of the sun.

definition: To remove or erase.
note: From Latin delere, 'to destroy'.
hints: What you press to remove text.
Take out a word.
example: Please delete my name from your list.

definition: Blue and white glazed pottery from the Netherlands.
note: Named after the Dutch city of Delft.
hints: Blue pottery from a Dutch city.
Tin-glazed ware painted with windmills.

definition: A triangular landform where a river meets the sea; or a Greek letter.
note: From Greek delta, borrowed from a Phoenician word for 'door'. The Nile mouth looked like the capital letter triangle.
hints: The Nile ends in one.
A letter of the Greek alphabet shaped like a triangle.
example: The Mississippi River delta.

definition: A huge flood, or an overwhelming amount of something.
note: From Old French deluge, from Latin diluvium. Noah's flood is called the Deluge.
hints: The Bible's flood was this.
An inbox flooded with messages.
origin: Old French deluge, from Latin dīluvium

definition: Luxurious or of superior quality.
note: From French de luxe, 'of luxury'.
hints: A top version of a product.
A fancier edition.
origin: French de luxe, from Latin luxus
example: The band released a deluxe version of their LP, containing bonus tracks and with a personal message by all the members in the sleeve.

definition: To dig deeply, or to search thoroughly.
note: From Old English delfan, 'to dig, burrow'. It is the same root as a ditch dug with a spade, and now it is used for digging into information.
hints: What a researcher does into old records.
To dig into a topic.
example: When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?

definition: To ask for firmly; or the desire for goods.
note: From Latin demandare, 'to entrust'.
hints: Economists pair it with a curve that slopes downward.
Insist on getting something.
origin: Old French demander, from Latin dēmandō
example: I demand an immediate explanation.

definition: The end of something, or a person's death.
note: From Old French demettre, 'to put away'. In law it meant transferring an estate, which is where the death sense grew.
hints: The end of a business or a rock band.
A solemn word for a passing.
origin: Middle French démise, from Middle English dimisen
example: The lack of funding ultimately led to the project's demise.

definition: An evil spirit.
note: From Medieval Latin daemon, from Greek daimon, 'spirit, divine power'. In Greek a daimon wasn't evil; Christianity changed that.
hints: An evil spirit from hell.
Exorcists try to drive them out.
origin: Medieval Latin dēmōn, from Ancient Greek δαίμων; in English since the 10th century

definition: To raise doubts or politely object.
note: From Anglo-Norman demorer and Old French, 'to linger, delay'. To demur was first to hold back.
hints: Said of someone who politely declines.
To hesitate before agreeing.
origin: Anglo-Norman demorer, from Old French demorer

definition: A refusal to admit or accept.
note: From deny plus -al.
hints: A statement that something is untrue.
Not accepting a hard truth.

definition: To be a sign of something; to mean.
note: From Latin denotare, 'to mark out'. A red light denotes danger.
hints: A symbol on a map does this for a feature.
A red flag on a beach does this for danger.
origin: Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare
example: Her smile denoted that she agreed.

definition: Packed closely together.
note: From French dense and Latin densus, 'thick'. It is used of fog, forests and slow-witted people.
hints: A jungle full of thick trees.
Fog that's hard to see through.
origin: Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus

definition: Relating to teeth.
note: From Latin dens, 'tooth'.
hints: Check-ups at a dentist.
A kind of floss is named so.
origin: Middle French dental, from Late Latin dentālis

definition: To leave, especially on a journey.
note: From Old French departir, 'to divide', from Latin de- and partire, 'to part'. Originally it meant to split up.
hints: What a train does at its scheduled time.
Airports show this next to 'arrive' on a board.
origin: Old French departir, from Late Latin departiō

definition: To rely on, or to be determined by something else.
note: From Latin dependere, 'to hang from'.
hints: What an outcome does on the weather.
Rely on someone's help.

definition: To show something in a picture or in words.
note: From Latin depingere, 'to paint'. A painting or film can depict a battle.
hints: A mural or a novel can do this to a scene.
What a portrait does to its sitter.
origin: Latin dēpictus; in English since the early 15th century
example: This scene depicts country life.

definition: To spread out for action.
note: From French deployer, 'to unfold'.
hints: Send troops into position.
Release software to users.

definition: To force a foreigner to leave a country.
note: From French deporter. An older sense, 'to behave', gave us the word 'deportment'.
hints: Immigration authorities may order it.
Sending someone back to their home country.

definition: A storage place, or a bus or railway station.
note: From French depot, from Latin depositum, 'something put down'. It is a doublet of deposit.
hints: Where buses are parked overnight.
A warehouse for supplies.
origin: French dépôt, from Medieval Latin dēpositum

definition: How deep something is.
note: From Old English dieph, from deep plus -th. It forms a noun like width or length.
hints: What a diver measures.
The opposite of height.
example: Measure the depth of the water in this part of the bay.

definition: A person appointed to act for another.
note: From Old French deputer, 'to assign'.
hints: A sheriff's assistant.
Stands in for the boss.
origin: French député, from Late Latin dēputātus
example: The deputy sheriff was promoted after his senior retired.

definition: To cause a train to leave its tracks, or to throw a plan off course.
note: From French dérailler, 'to go off the rails'.
hints: What a train crash does to a service.
A sudden tangent can do it to a meeting.
example: They had planned to derail the trains that carried atomic waste.

definition: A horse race, or a local sports rivalry.
note: The race is named for Edward Smith-Stanley, 12th Earl of Derby. The Epsom race began in 1780.
hints: The Kentucky one is a famous horse race.
A match between two teams of the same city.
example: I bet ten quid that Liverpool would beat Manchester United in the derby match.

definition: To obtain something from a source, or to work out by reasoning.
note: From Latin derivare, 'to draw off water from a stream'. A word's derivation traces its source.
hints: Etymologists trace where a word does this from.
What a mathematician does to a formula from first principles.
origin: Old French deriver, from Latin dērīvō
example: Reading books is the best way to derive knowledge.

definition: A dry, barren region; or to abandon.
note: The land from Latin desertus, 'abandoned'. The verb is the same word.
hints: Sahara or Gobi.
To leave someone behind.
origin: Old French desert, from Latin dēsertum

definition: A plan or drawing, or to create one.
note: From Latin designare, 'to mark out'.
hints: An architect's job.
Plan how something will look.
origin: Old French designer, from Latin designō

definition: A strong wish for something.
note: From Latin desiderare, 'to long for'.
hints: Want, strongly.
Tennessee Williams named a streetcar after this feeling.
origin: Old French desirer, from Latin dēsīderō

definition: To stop doing something.
note: From Latin desistere, 'to leave off'.
hints: Legal letters tell you to cease and do this.
A police officer's firm command to stop.
origin: Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō
example: Please desist from telephoning me at this number.

definition: A small part or fact.
note: From French detail, from de- and tailler, 'to cut', so a detail was a piece cut off.
hints: The fine points that a careful person notices.
One tiny piece of a larger picture.
origin: Middle French détail, from Old French detail
example: It was perfect in all details.

definition: To hold someone back; to keep them in custody for a time.
note: From Old French detenir, from Latin roots meaning 'to hold away'. It is a doublet of detente.
hints: Police or border officers may do it to a suspect.
A teacher does a milder version after the bell.

definition: To find or notice something hidden.
note: From Latin detegere, 'to uncover'.
hints: What an alarm does with smoke.
Spot the signs of a crime.
example: The forensic examiners detected tiny traces of the poison on the suspect's gloves.

definition: To discourage someone from doing something.
note: From Latin deterrere, 'to frighten from', from de- and terrere, 'to frighten'. It is a cousin of terror.
hints: A guard dog might do this to burglars.
The aim of a 'no entry' sign.
example: Their boss deterred them from both taking holidays at the same time, claiming he couldn't manage it all on his own.

definition: A longer or different route taken instead of the usual one.
note: Borrowed from French detour, from detourner, 'to turn away'.
hints: Orange signs send drivers onto one when a road is closed.
A trip taken off the planned path.

definition: A process of ridding the body of toxins.
note: A clipping of detoxification. It's used for diets and for rehab from addiction.
hints: A juice diet, supposedly.
Treatment for someone giving up drink.

definition: A score of forty all in tennis; or a two.
note: From Old French deus, 'two', from Latin duo. It also mildly names the devil, as in 'what the ___!'
hints: A tennis score where either side needs two points to win.
A playing card with two pips.
origin: Old French deus, from Latin duo

definition: A piece of equipment made for a purpose.
note: From Old French devis, 'intention', from Latin dividere, 'to divide'.
hints: A gadget, such as a phone.
A tool or gadget.
origin: Old French devis, from Latin dīvīsus
example: The device is small enough to wear on your wrist.

definition: A fiend; the king of evil.
note: From Greek diabolos, 'slanderer', through Latin and Old English. It names Satan and any very wicked or mischievous person.
hints: Said to wear red with a pitchfork.
A cheeky person might be called a little one.
origin: Old English dēofol, from Ancient Greek διάβολος

definition: To invent or work out a plan or method; also, in law, to leave land in a will.
note: From Old French deviser, 'to divide, arrange', from Latin dividere. The same word split into 'device' for the noun.
hints: A detective does it to trap a suspect.
A lawyer drafting a will uses the legal sense for land.
origin: Old French deviser, from Latin dīvisō

definition: Completely lacking something.
note: From Old French desvuidier, 'to empty out'. It is almost always followed by 'of'.
hints: Always followed by 'of' in a sentence.
A desert is this of water.
example: I went searching for a knife, but the kitchen was devoid of anything sharper than a spoon.

definition: To give your time or effort completely to something.
note: From Latin devovere, 'to dedicate by a vow'. A devotee is a fervent follower.
hints: What you do to a cause that you love.
A person gives their life to a calling in this way.
example: They devoted their lives to following Jesus Christ.

definition: To eat greedily and fast; to consume completely.
note: From Latin devorare, 'to swallow down', from vorare, 'to swallow'.
hints: A hungry wolf does it to its prey.
A keen reader may do it to a book in one weekend.
origin: Old French devorer, from Latin dēvorō
example: He devoured three sandwiches.

definition: Deeply religious and committed.
note: From Latin devotus, 'devoted', from devovere, 'to vow'. It describes people sincerely observing a faith.
hints: A pilgrim who prays several times a day.
Someone who never misses a service.
origin: Old French devot, from Latin dēvōtus

definition: A double-walled vacuum flask for keeping things very cold or hot.
note: Named after the Scottish physicist James Dewar, who invented it in the 1890s.
hints: Lab flask for liquid nitrogen.
A flask named after its Scottish inventor.

definition: On the right-hand side, especially in heraldry.
note: Borrowed from Latin dexter, 'right'. It is the root of dexterity. Its opposite is sinister.
hints: In heraldry, the side a shield bearer would call right.
Its opposite, sinister, once meant left.

definition: In Hindu and Buddhist thought, cosmic law and duty.
note: From Sanskrit dharma, 'that which upholds'. The Buddhist Dharma means the Buddha's teachings.
hints: A word in Buddhism for the Buddha's teaching.
A wheel is its symbol in Buddhism.

definition: A baby's absorbent undergarment, in American English.
note: From Greek diaspros, 'pure white', originally a fine patterned cloth. The cloth sense became the baby sense.
hints: Changed several times a day for an infant.
British speakers call it a nappy.
origin: Old French diapre, from Byzantine Greek δίασπρος

definition: Risky or uncertain.
note: From dice plus -y. A throw of the dice is a gamble.
hints: A risky plan with an uncertain outcome.
Crossing a stormy sea in a small boat.
example: An extremely dicey future on a brave new world of liquid nitrogen, tar, and smog.

definition: A heavy fuel for engines.
note: Named after Rudolf Diesel, who invented the engine in the 1890s.
hints: Fuel for lorries.
Named for a German engineer.
example: They were chagrined to see that the price of diesel had climbed past six dollars a gallon.

definition: To be unlike something else, or to disagree.
note: From Latin differre, 'to carry apart'.
hints: What two critics do when one loves a film and the other hates it.
Two opinions that do not match.
origin: Old French differer, from Latin differō

definition: To break down food, or a summary.
note: From Latin digerere, 'to separate'.
hints: What your stomach does.
A shortened version of a magazine.
example: I cannot digest milk products.

definition: A machine or person that digs.
note: Formed from dig plus -er. In Australia and New Zealand the word became a nickname for soldiers.
hints: A yellow machine with a bucket on a long arm.
Children playing in a sandpit imitate one with a toy.

definition: A single numeral, or a finger or toe.
note: From Latin digitus, 'finger, toe'. People counted on their fingers.
hints: The number 7 is one.
A thumb counts as one.
example: The base-10 number 123.4 has four digits: the hundreds digit is 1, the tens digit is 2, the units digit is 3, and the tenths digit is 4.

definition: Something remarkable of its kind.
note: It survives in 'dilly-dally' and in the phrase 'a real dilly', meaning a standout example. Dictionaries give it only a thin history.
hints: A word that sounds old-fashioned and cheerful.
A pickle might be said to be this.

definition: To make weaker by adding water or another substance.
note: From Latin diluere, 'to wash away', from dis- and luere, 'to wash'.
hints: You do it to squash before pouring a glass.
Cleaning fluids are done so in a bucket.

definition: In a faint or unclear way.
note: Built from dim plus -ly. Dim comes from Old English dimm, 'dark' or 'gloomy'.
hints: How you recall something half forgotten.
The way a poor bulb lights a room.

definition: The currency of several Arab and Balkan countries.
note: Ultimately from the Latin denarius, a Roman coin.
hints: Money in Kuwait.
A coin name descended from Rome.

definition: A small restaurant serving casual meals; or a person eating.
note: From dine plus -er. In America the word was borrowed for cheap restaurants shaped like railway dining cars.
hints: Serves all-day breakfast and milkshakes.
A person sitting at a table in a restaurant.

definition: A wild dog of Australia.
note: Borrowed from Dharug dingu, 'tame dingo'. It was the name the Sydney Aboriginal people gave to it.
hints: A wild dog Down Under.
A baby was famously said to have been taken by one.

definition: Dirty, dull and shabby.
note: From a Kentish dialect word for dirty, of unknown origin. It rhymes with stingy.
hints: A poorly lit and grubby room.
A cheap hotel might be called this.

definition: Eating a meal.
note: From dine plus -ing.
hints: As in a restaurant car.
What guests do at a formal supper.

definition: Small and neat, often charming.
note: Linked to Scots dink, meaning neat or trim, plus -y. Meaning small came later.
hints: Tiny and cute.
Small enough to be endearing.

definition: The main meal of the day.
note: From Old French disner, originally meaning to break a fast, so it began as a morning meal.
hints: Evening meal.
Served at the table around evening.
example: I had an early dinner because the breakfast in this hostel is superb.

definition: A device that lets current flow one way only.
note: From di-, 'two', and -ode, coined in 1919 by William Eccles, after Greek diodos, 'passage through'. LEDs are a type.
hints: A one-way valve for electricity.
LED stands for light-emitting one.

definition: Straight, without detours; or to guide.
note: From Latin directus, 'set straight'.
hints: A film-maker does this to actors.
Not roundabout.

definition: Not clean.
note: From Middle English dirti, from dirt plus -y. It once was dritti, from drit, an old word for excrement.
hints: Describes laundry that needs washing.
Covered in mud.

definition: To take weapons from someone; also to win over by charm.
note: From Old French desarmer, built from des- (undo) and arme (weapon).
hints: A bomb squad specialist does it to a device.
A sincere smile can do it to an angry person.

definition: Dance music of the 1970s, or a club that plays it.
note: A shortening of the French discotheque. A mirrored ball and flares are classic symbols of it.
hints: Gloria Gaynor sang 'I Will Survive' in this style.
A glittering ball hangs over the floor.

definition: Gloomy, depressing or very poor.
note: From Old French dis mals, 'bad days', from Latin dies mali. It originally referred to unlucky days in the medieval calendar.
hints: A rainy, grey Monday.
A performance that earns a terrible score.
origin: Anglo-Norman dismal, from Medieval Latin diēs malī

definition: A sudden feeling of alarm and distress.
note: From Old French esmaier, 'to frighten', whose root meant 'to take away power'. The sense later softened to sudden distress.
hints: The look on your face at seeing a ruined cake.
Said of someone upset by bad news.

definition: To drive away something, such as doubt or fog.
note: From Latin dispellere, 'to drive apart'.
hints: A clear answer might do it to your fears.
What sunshine does to morning mist.
example: The clouds and mist were soon enough dispelled by the sun.

definition: Far from the centre or the point of attachment.
note: From distant, with -al, formed in the 1800s as the opposite of proximal. Your fingertip is distal to your wrist.
hints: Anatomy term for the end of a limb.
The opposite of proximal.

definition: A long narrow channel dug in the ground.
note: From Old English dic, a Germanic word. It is the same word as dyke, and as a verb it means to get rid of something.
hints: A shallow trench beside a road.
To abandon, as in dumping a plan.
example: Digging ditches has long been considered one of the most demanding forms of manual labor.

definition: The same again.
note: From Italian detto, 'said', from Latin dicere, 'to say'. It first appeared in English in 1625, in bookkeeping and lists.
hints: Two small marks in a list mean this.
What you say when you agree with the thing just said.

definition: A short, simple song or poem.
note: From Old French dite, from Latin dictare, 'to dictate'. It first meant a composed poem.
hints: A little tune you might hum.
A catchy little rhyme.
origin: Old French ditie, from Latin dictāre
example: The folk singer introduced an enchanting ditty about nature.

definition: A long low sofa without a back.
note: From Persian and Turkish diwan, a council or its chamber, whose cushioned benches gave the furniture its name.
hints: A low backless couch.
Once a council of state in the Ottoman Empire.
origin: Ottoman Turkish دیوان, from Sumerian 𒁾

definition: A person who goes underwater or jumps head first into water.
note: Built from dive plus -er. It also names water birds that plunge after fish, such as the loon.
hints: Wears a wetsuit and a tank.
Might leap from a high board.

definition: To turn something aside from its course.
note: From Latin divertere, 'to turn in different directions'. It can mean to rerouting traffic or to entertain.
hints: Road signs tell traffic to follow a different route because of repairs.
A conjuror does it to your attention.
origin: Old French divertir, from Latin di-
example: The workers diverted the stream away from the road.

definition: To split into parts.
note: From Latin dividere, 'to force apart'.
hints: What a maths operation does to a number.
Separate into groups.
example: Divide the cake into three equal parts.

definition: Of or like a god; or to guess.
note: From Latin divinus, from divus, 'god'.
hints: Heavenly, or fit for a god.
Prophets can do it.
origin: Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus

definition: Feeling as if everything is spinning.
note: From Old English dysig, 'foolish, stupid'. It started with foolish and moved to giddy.
hints: What a fairground ride might make you.
How you feel after spinning around.

definition: Possible to do.
note: From do plus -able, found in Middle English.
hints: What a manager hopes the deadline is.
Not too hard, but not trivial.

definition: A person trained to treat illness; also a holder of a doctorate.
note: From Latin doctor, 'teacher', from docere, 'to teach'.
hints: Treats patients in a surgery.
Latin for teacher.
example: She is a doctor of philosophy in physics.

definition: To move quickly out of the way.
note: Perhaps from a dialect word meaning to jerk or jog about, of uncertain origin. It also means to evade, as in a question.
hints: A boxer ducks to do this to a punch.
A game of this involves throwing balls at players.
example: He dodged traffic crossing the street.

definition: A person who avoids something, especially a duty.
note: From dodge plus -er. In Dickens, the Artful ___ is the leader of Fagin's pickpockets.
hints: Fagin's gang includes an Artful one in Oliver Twist.
A person who avoids paying taxes or being drafted.

definition: Unreliable or suspicious.
note: From dodge plus -y, first used in the mid 1800s in England. It describes things that seem to be evading honesty.
hints: An unreliable seller of used cars.
Something that looks risky, as with a questionable alibi.
example: Never listen to dodgy advice.

definition: A cute word for a dog.
note: From dog plus -o. It is internet slang, and 'lie doggo' is an older phrase for staying hidden.
hints: An affectionate word for a pet dog online.
A word used in funny captions of pets.
origin: dog + -o; in English since the early 21st century

definition: A little dog; or about dogs.
note: From dog plus -y. It is used for small dogs and for pet-related items.
hints: A child's word for a pet.
A bag for taking leftover food home.

definition: A belief that is held to be undoubtedly true.
note: From Greek dogma, 'opinion, tenet', from dokein, 'to seem good, think'. It once meant any set opinion before it became rigid.
hints: A rigid set of beliefs not open to question.
A church's official teaching.
origin: Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα

definition: The act of carrying something out; also a deed.
note: From do plus -ing, from Old English don. 'Doing' as a noun can also mean someone's responsibility, as in 'it was his own doing'.
hints: Somebody's own deeds are said to be theirs.
A word that ends in -ing and names an action.

definition: The main currency of the US.
note: From Low German daler, from the German thaler, a silver coin from Joachimsthal.
hints: Currency with a buck as slang.
Named after a silver coin from a Bohemian valley.

definition: A territory ruled, or an area of knowledge or the web.
note: From Old French domaine, from Latin dominium, 'property'.
hints: A website's name ending.
A sphere of influence.
example: His domain extended into Europe.

definition: A small rectangular tile marked with dots, used in a game; also a hooded cloak or half-mask.
note: From French, where it was first a hooded garment, itself from Latin dominus, 'lord'. Row-toppling chain reactions gave rise to the 'theory' named after it.
hints: Lined up in a long row, one tap sets them all tumbling.
A cold-war theory predicted countries would fall like this.
origin: French domino, from Medieval Latin domino

definition: To give to a cause.
note: Back-formed from donation, from Latin donare, 'to give'.
hints: Give blood or money.
Charity gift.
example: She donates 100 dollars to Red Cross every year.

definition: A domesticated, long-eared animal related to the horse.
note: Its origin is uncertain; it appeared in the late 1700s as slang. The older word was 'ass'.
hints: Pinning a tail on one is a party game.
Eeyore in Winnie-the-Pooh is one.

definition: A person who gives something, such as blood or money.
note: From Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur. It names someone who gives for a cause.
hints: Gives blood at a clinic.
One who gives an organ or funds.
origin: Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur

definition: A small, round, fried sweet cake, often with a hole.
note: An American spelling of doughnut, which first meant a small ball of fried dough. Dough comes from Old English dah.
hints: Often found in a box at the office.
A ring of fried dough.
example: Just as Ziri grabbed the last donut, Rima slapped his hand.

definition: A casual scribble drawn while thinking about something else.
note: Doodle first meant a fool, from Low German dudeldopp. It later named idle scribbles.
hints: Fills the margins of a notebook in a dull meeting.
Google changes its logo into one on special days.

definition: Something remarkable, often a troublesome thing.
note: Its origin is unknown; it first appears in 1903 and may come from daisy.
hints: A real one is a big problem or a great one.
What a storm of epic proportions might be called.

definition: Silly or slow-witted.
note: From dope plus -y. It is an informal word for a foolish person, also the name of one of the seven dwarfs.
hints: One of the seven dwarfs.
Acting stupid or confused.
example: Tom often has a dopey expression on his face.

definition: A golden fish also called mahi-mahi.
note: From Spanish dorado, 'gilded'. The fish is bright golden-green in the water.
hints: A big game fish with a blunt head and gold-green sides.
The Spanish name means gilded, and the same word names a lost city of gold.

definition: Awkward in an endearing, uncool way.
note: From dork, an American slang word of the 1960s whose origin is uncertain.
hints: Not cool, but harmless about it.
Describes a person who is a bit geeky.

definition: Relating to the back or upper side of an animal.
note: From Latin dorsum, 'back'. A shark's fin is the best-known example.
hints: A shark's fin that breaks the surface.
A fin on the back of a fish.
example: The dorsal fin is the vertical fin on the back of a fish and certain marine mammals.

definition: The amount and frequency of a medicine.
note: From French dose. Pharmacists and doctors specify it on the label.
hints: Written on a medicine label.
What a pharmacist asks you to follow precisely.
example: Why did he give you only a single 500 mg dose? The correct dosage of this antibiotic is one 500 mg tablet twice a day for 10 days.

definition: Mildly mad or eccentric.
note: From dote, perhaps combined with an old word meaning unsteady.
hints: British word for a little batty.
Eccentric, often said fondly.
example: My nan has got dottier and dottier since passing the age of eighty.

definition: Twice as much, or a look-alike.
note: From Old French doble, from Latin duplus, 'twofold'.
hints: Two of something.
A stand-in who looks like an actor.
origin: Old French doble, from Latin duplus

definition: Twice as much; in two ways.
note: From Middle English dowbly, formed from double plus -ly.
hints: Said before 'sure' when you want to be certain.
Describes something twice as true, or twice as bad.
example: My mother was always doubly careful when winding the grandfather clock.

definition: To feel unsure about something.
note: From Old French douter and Latin dubitare, 'to hesitate'. The b was added in spelling to match the Latin.
hints: What you feel when you aren't sure it's true.
'Beyond a reasonable one' is the standard for a guilty verdict.

definition: A jet of water directed at the body; or an insulting word for a person.
note: Borrowed from French, from Italian doccia, 'shower'. In modern slang it is also an insult.
hints: In French it simply means a shower.
In slang, an insult for an obnoxious man.

definition: A thick mix of flour and water that is baked.
note: From Old English dag, a Germanic word related to the word for 'to knead'. It is also slang for money.
hints: Bread begins as this.
A pizza chef tosses it in the air.
example: Pizza dough is very stretchy.

definition: To drench with liquid or to put out a flame with it.
note: Probably from a Scandinavian word for a heavy plunge or thump.
hints: What a bucket of water does to a fire.
To soak in water or put out a flame.

definition: Plain, dull and unfashionable.
note: First appearing around 1581, likely from an earlier word for a poorly dressed woman. It suggests drab or shabby clothing.
hints: A frumpy outfit.
Dressed in old-fashioned, shapeless clothes.

definition: A short wooden peg used to join pieces.
note: From Middle English dowle, of uncertain origin. Carpenters use it to join two boards.
hints: A woodworker uses it to join two boards.
A round wooden rod.

definition: Something depressing; or a drug that slows the body.
note: From down plus -er. A downer is a sedative, and also a letdown, the opposite of an upper.
hints: A bit of news that kills the party mood.
The opposite of an upper.
example: I was sort of expecting it, but it was still a bit of a downer.

definition: Soft and covered with fine feathers or fluff.
note: From down, from Old Norse dunn, 'soft feathers'. It describes a baby bird or a peach's skin.
hints: A newborn chick's coat.
As soft as a duckling.
example: The chick's downy coat of feathers formed almost immediately to keep it warm.

definition: Money or property given when a couple marry.
note: From Anglo-Norman douarie, from Medieval Latin dotarium and Latin dos, 'dowry'. It is related to the word dower.
hints: Property a bride's family gives at a wedding.
Jane Austen's characters worry about them.

definition: Twelve.
note: From Old French dozaine, 'a group of twelve', from doze, 'twelve'. Eggs are often sold this way.
hints: How many eggs in a carton.
A baker's thirteen is one more than it.
origin: Old French dozaine, from Latin duodecim

definition: A first rough version; or a current of cold air.
note: A phonetic spelling of draught, from Middle English draght, 'that which is drawn'. It also means a military call-up.
hints: A first version of an essay.
A cold breeze from an open window.
example: The final draft of the constitution.

definition: A fire-breathing monster of legend.
note: From Greek drakon, 'serpent'.
hints: St George slew one.
Winged beast that hoards treasure.
origin: Old French dragon, from Old English draca

definition: To let liquid flow out.
note: From Old English dreahnian, 'to strain out'. It names both a pipe and the act of emptying.
hints: What the plug hole does to bath water.
Where the water goes when you pull the plug.

definition: A male duck.
note: From Middle English, from an old word for duck. A dragon was once also called this.
hints: The male of a mallard.
A male duck.

definition: Past tense of drink; also slang for a drink.
note: From Old English dranc, past of drincan. The slang noun spelling began as a pronunciation spelling of drink.
hints: What you did when the glass was emptied.
A form of a word about glasses and sips.

definition: To hang cloth loosely.
note: From Old French draper, 'to weave or make cloth', from drap, 'cloth'. It also names a curtain.
hints: To hang fabric over a chair.
How a gown falls from the shoulders.
origin: Old French draper, from Late Latin drappus
example: Drape the statue with a sheet.

definition: Hung or covered loosely with cloth.
note: The past form of drape, which came from Old French draper, 'to weave cloth'.
hints: A coffin may be covered this way with a flag.
Curtains hung in soft folds look like this.

definition: A merchant who sells cloth.
note: From Anglo-Norman draper, from Old French drap, 'cloth'. It survives mainly as a surname and in old shop names.
hints: An old-fashioned trader in fabric and linens.
A merchant of fabrics, as in 'linen and woollen ___'.
origin: Anglo-Norman draper, from Old French drapier

definition: A sliding box in a piece of furniture.
note: From draw plus -er, as it is drawn out.
hints: Cutlery is kept in one.
Pull it out of a desk.

definition: Pulled or sketched; also looking tired and thin.
note: The past participle of draw, from Old English dragan, 'to drag or pull'. A drawn face looks as if pulled thin by worry.
hints: Describes a face after sleepless nights.
What a curtain or a sketch may be.
example: The drawn draperies kept direct sunlight from fading the rug.

definition: A past form of dream.
note: The past tense of dream, with the same -t ending as in 'slept' and 'kept'. Dreamed is more common in American English.
hints: What you did last night while sleeping.
A past tense ending in t, like slept and kept.

definition: Like a dream; vague and soft; or, informally, very attractive.
note: Formed from dream plus -y.
hints: Describes a faraway look on someone staring out the window.
A teenager might use it for a celebrity crush.

definition: Dull, gloomy and depressing.
note: From Old English dreorig, 'sad', from an old Germanic word that originally meant 'bloody'.
hints: A grey drizzly November afternoon.
Poe's raven came on a midnight of this sort.

definition: To dig up mud from a river bed, or to bring something up from the past.
note: From a Middle English word for a drag net. Cooks also dredge fish in flour.
hints: A boat that clears a harbour channel.
Scooping oysters, or coating chicken in flour.
origin: Scots dreg-boat, from Middle Dutch dregghe

definition: A one-piece outfit; or to put clothes on.
note: From Old French dresser, 'to arrange, put in order'. It meant to set straight before it meant to clothe.
hints: A one-piece garment often worn to a wedding.
Salad ___ing goes on lettuce.
example: He wore a bright orange dress to the office yesterday.

definition: Having had its moisture removed.
note: The past tense of dry, from Old English drygan. Preserving food by drying is among the oldest methods known.
hints: Fruit may be preserved this way.
What the laundry was after hours in the sun.

definition: More dry; less wet.
note: The comparative of dry, from Old English dryge. It is also a spelling of a device that dries clothes or hair.
hints: Comparing a desert with a meadow.
A word that follows 'wetter' in a pair.

definition: To be carried slowly by a current.
note: From Middle English drift, 'act of driving', from Old English. Snow banks and slow movement share the name.
hints: What a boat does when its engine is off.
Snow piles up in these in the winter.
example: Drift the boats downstream.

definition: A tool for making holes; or a repeated practice.
note: From Middle Dutch drillen, 'to bore, move in a circle'. The practising sense came from soldiers' repeated exercises.
hints: A dentist uses a small one.
A fire practice at school.

definition: To swallow a liquid.
note: From Old English drincan, from a Germanic verb. It is also the name for the liquid itself.
hints: What you do with a glass of water.
Water or a soda.
example: The patient must drink several liters each day.

definition: To operate a car.
note: From Old English drifan, 'to push, force'. The word first meant to push cattle, not vehicles.
hints: What you do with a steering wheel.
A strong motivation inside a person.
example: Drive a car or bus.

definition: Motivated and ambitious, or moved by a vehicle.
note: The past participle of drive.
hints: Highly motivated.
A car was this to the airport.

definition: A person who operates a vehicle.
note: From drive plus -er.
hints: Sits behind the wheel.
A bus or taxi worker.
example: The driver will make an announcement when the trip is nearing its completion.

definition: A robot, especially one that resembles a person.
note: A clipping of android, popularised by the Star Wars films. It names a fictional robot.
hints: A robot in a space film.
R2-D2, for one.

definition: Amusing in an odd, dry way.
note: From French drole, 'comical', from a Middle French word for a merry rascal. It carries a quirky tone.
hints: A dry, understated sense of humour.
Funny in a quietly peculiar way.
origin: French drôle, from Old Norse troll
example: Very droll, minister.

definition: A low humming noise; or a remote-controlled flying machine.
note: From Old English dran, the male bee. The buzzing sound gave us the sound, and a lazy person was compared to the non-working bee.
hints: A male honeybee that doesn't work.
A small flying camera with spinning blades.

definition: To let saliva run from the mouth.
note: From earlier drule, probably an alteration of drivel. It comes from a word meaning to dribble.
hints: What a hungry dog does at dinner time.
A baby does it when teething.

definition: To hang or sag downward.
note: From Old Norse drupa, 'to droop', related to drip and drop. Plants do it when thirsty.
hints: A flower does it without water.
Eyelids do it when you are sleepy.

definition: Worthless waste material.
note: From Old English dros, 'dregs, sediment'. Metalworkers skim it from molten metal.
hints: What's skimmed off melted metal.
Rubbish left behind after the good part is taken.
origin: Old English drōs, from Old English drōsna

definition: Past tense of drive; also a large moving herd.
note: The past tense comes from Old English drifan. The noun comes from Old English draf, a herd driven along, and survives in 'droves of people'.
hints: What a driver did on the road.
Cattle moved in one of these.

definition: To die from being under water.
note: From Middle English drownen, of obscure origin. It is a verb with a long history of uncertain roots.
hints: What a lifeguard prevents.
To be covered by a flood, or to overwhelm a sound.
example: When I was a baby, I nearly drowned in the bathtub.

definition: A priest in ancient Celtic religion.
note: Via French and Latin Druidae, from Gaulish. The name may mean 'oak-knower', as they were linked with oak trees.
hints: Associated with Stonehenge in popular belief.
A priest of the ancient Celts.

definition: Having had too much alcohol.
note: From Old English druncen, the past participle of drincan. It is both an adjective and a noun.
hints: Wobbly after too many pints.
The opposite of sober.

definition: A machine that removes moisture.
note: From Middle English driere, 'one who dries'. A laundry machine and a hair device both go by it.
hints: Hot machine for wet laundry.
A hairdresser's hot-air device.

definition: In a flat, humorous way with no show of feeling.
note: From dry plus -ly. Dry humour is said to be delivered with a straight face.
hints: The way a deadpan joke is told.
Said with a straight face and no smile.
example: The barfly dryly brushes off suitors.

definition: The territory ruled by a duke or duchess.
note: From Old French duche, from Latin dux, 'leader'. Cornwall and Lancaster are English ones.
hints: The land a duke governs.
Prince Charles held the one in Cornwall.

definition: Fine or lovely, in old-fashioned slang; also a rubber duck.
note: From duck plus -y. As a term of endearment, duck dates back centuries.
hints: Everything is just this, said an old-fashioned optimist.
A bath toy that floats.
example: Farnesworth smiled contentedly as he read the stock ticker; all was ducky on Wall Street.

definition: A boat hollowed from a tree trunk, or a shelter at a baseball field.
note: From dug out. Players sit in the baseball kind below ground level.
hints: Where players wait to bat.
An ancient canoe.

definition: In a lifeless or slow way.
note: Built from dull plus -ly. Dull originally meant 'slow-witted' before it described blades and colours.
hints: How a blunt knife cuts, or a sleepy voice speaks.
Without sparkle or interest.

definition: A foolish person; also the name of a flying elephant.
note: Formed from dumb plus -o. The Disney film made the name famous for an elephant with big ears.
hints: A flying elephant in a Disney film.
Calling someone this is a mild playground jibe.

definition: A model of a person; or a baby's pacifier.
note: From dumb plus -y. The sense of a fake model, like a shop-window figure, is from a mute, silent stand-in.
hints: A ventriloquist's partner.
A fake used in crash testing a car.

definition: Short and stout.
note: First recorded in 1750, of uncertain origin. It may be related to dumpling.
hints: A squat, round figure.
Describes a plump little teapot.

definition: A person who is slow to learn.
note: Named for John Duns Scotus, a medieval Scottish thinker. His followers were mocked after his ideas fell out of favour.
hints: Wore a pointed cap in the corner of a classroom.
A slow learner.
example: Who usually sits on the dunce's seat?

definition: A casual way of saying 'don't know'.
note: A pronunciation spelling of don't know. It is used when speaking casually.
hints: A shrug in words.
A spoken form of 'I do not know'.

definition: A house split into two homes, or a building with two floors.
note: Latin for 'twofold', from duo and plicare, 'to fold'. In North America it usually names a house divided in two, with a door each.
hints: A house with two front doors and two families.
Landlords advertise it as one half of a double.

definition: Throughout a period of time.
note: From the old verb dure, 'to last', from Latin durare.
hints: Over the course of an event.
Used for something happening while a thing is on.

definition: Dim, dark or shadowy in colour.
note: From dusk plus -y. It describes the half-light of evening or a deep, muted shade.
hints: The colour of the sky just after sunset.
A soft, dark shade, like a plum.
example: Gold earrings gleamed against her dusky cheeks.

definition: Covered in fine dry particles.
note: From Old English dustig, from dust plus -y. It describes shelves and old books.
hints: An attic that hasn't been cleaned for years.
A bookshelf nobody touches.
example: A dusty pile of books.

definition: A soft quilt for a bed.
note: From French duvet, 'down', from Old French dumet, meaning the soft feathers of young birds. It was originally filled with down.
hints: British word for a bed cover filled with feathers.
Goes inside a cover and keeps you warm in bed.
origin: French duvet, from Old Norse dúnn
example: He pulled the thick duvet over his head to block out the morning light.

definition: A very small being in fairy tales; or something much smaller than usual.
note: From Old English dweorg, a Germanic word for the small beings of folklore. It also names small stars and plants.
hints: Snow White lives with seven of them.
A small kind of planet, such as Pluto.

definition: To live in a place.
note: From Old English dwellan, which meant 'to lead astray' or 'delay'. The sense of staying in a place came from lingering.
hints: A poetic way to say 'to live'.
To keep thinking about something, as in 'don't ___ on it'.

definition: Approaching death or the end.
note: From die plus -ing. Die comes from Old Norse deyja.
hints: What a fire is as the embers fade.
Last words are often called a person's this.
example: A dying of old hopes.

definition: A machine that makes electricity from motion; also an energetic person.
note: Shortened from dynamo-electric machine, from Greek dynamis, 'power'.
hints: A bicycle light can be powered by one on the wheel.
A tireless worker is called one.
example: I have a keyring with a carabiner with a dynamo lamp.

definition: Keen and impatient to do something.
note: From Old French aigre, 'sharp', from Latin acer. Eager once meant sharp or sour, and keenness came from that sharpness.
hints: A child waiting at a school gate on the last day.
Describes the beaver who is always busy, in a saying.
origin: Old French aigre, from Latin ācrus
example: Eager to travel abroad.

definition: A large bird of prey.
note: From Old French aigle, from Latin aquila. It has long been a symbol of strength and empire.
hints: Appears on the American national seal.
A large raptor with a sharp beak.

definition: Before the usual or expected time.
note: From Old English aerlic, from aer, 'before'. It is related to the word ere.
hints: The bird who gets the worm.
The opposite of late.
example: We finished the project an hour sooner than scheduled, so we left early.

definition: A stand that holds a painting.
note: From Dutch ezel, 'donkey', from Latin asellus, 'young ass'. It was named because it carries a load like a donkey.
hints: An artist's three-legged stand.
What a canvas rests on while painting.
example: The same half-finished painting sat on the artist's easel for years.

definition: Less difficult.
note: The comparative of easy, from Old French aisie.
hints: Not as hard as before.
A comparative adjective.

definition: Without difficulty.
note: From easy plus -ly.
hints: With no trouble at all.
A hard task that feels simple.
example: Individuals without a family network are easily controlled.

definition: Having been consumed as food.
note: The past participle of eat, from Old English eten. The -en ending is a trace of older verb forms.
hints: Said of a meal once it is gone.
Follows 'has' or 'have' after dinner.

definition: A person or animal that eats.
note: From Old English etere, built on the verb eat. It is a common ending in words like 'meat-eater'.
hints: A fussy one is picky.
Also a creature defined by its diet.
example: These apples are good eaters.

definition: The overhanging edge of a roof.
note: From Old English efes, 'edge'. Birds often nest under them.
hints: The part of a roof that hangs over the wall.
Where swallows build nests.
example: The birds are weathering the storm underneath the eaves of the house.

definition: A hard, dark black wood.
note: From Greek ebenos, ultimately from an Egyptian word for the wood. It has been traded since ancient times.
hints: Piano keys were once made from it.
A very dark colour, like polished wood.

definition: A skin condition causing itchy, dry, inflamed patches.
note: From Greek ekzema, 'a boiling out', from ekzein, 'to boil over'. The rash seemed to erupt from the skin.
hints: Creams soothe this itchy rash.
Often begins in babies.
origin: Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμᾰ
example: The 5% topical solution was ineffective at reducing eczema outbreaks.

definition: Swelling caused by fluid trapped in body tissue.
note: From Greek oidema, 'a swelling'. Ankles can swell with it.
hints: Swollen ankles after a long flight.
A medical word for puffiness.
origin: New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα
example: Tom had a cerebral edema.

definition: Safe or fit to eat.
note: From Late Latin edibilis, from edere, 'to eat'. Foragers need to know which mushrooms are this.
hints: What a forager checks about a mushroom.
Flowers on a fancy salad are this.
origin: Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō

definition: To teach or uplift someone morally or mentally.
note: From Old French edifier and Latin aedificare, 'to build'. To edify someone is to build up their mind or character.
hints: A good lecture should do this.
To improve by instruction.
origin: Old French edifier, from Latin aedificare
example: The pastor's sermons may bore you, but they are morally edifying.

definition: A person who prepares writing for publication.
note: From Latin editor, 'one who puts forth', from edere.
hints: Fixes a writer's mistakes.
Works at a newspaper or publisher.
origin: Medieval Latin ēditor, from Late Latin ēditor

definition: A result brought about by a cause.
note: From Latin effectus, from efficere, 'to accomplish'.
hints: The partner of cause.
What happens because of something.
example: The effect of the hurricane was a devastated landscape.

definition: Hard work or attempt.
note: From Old French esfort, from esforcier, 'to force out'.
hints: Exertion put into a task.
Trying hard.
origin: Middle French effort, from Latin ex
example: He got an A for effort.

definition: A white wading bird with long legs.
note: From Anglo-Norman egret, related to the word for heron. The word also names a plume of feathers.
hints: A graceful white bird that stands in water.
A type of heron.
origin: Old Occitan aigreta, from Medieval Latin hairo
example: The playful elephant calf chased egrets through the lush grass of the savannah.

definition: The number after seven.
note: From Old English eahta, from an ancient root shared by many Indo-European languages. It is a very old number word.
hints: A spider has this many legs.
An octopus's arms.

definition: Coming after seventh.
note: From eight plus -th.
hints: Number eight in a line.
A musical note's fraction.

definition: The number after seventy-nine.
note: From Old English hundeahtatig.
hints: Four times twenty, as a score goes.
Eight tens added together.

definition: One or the other of two.
note: From Old English aeghwaether, 'each of two'.
hints: Choose one of two.
A pair's pick.
example: He made me two offers, but I did not accept either.

definition: To force out.
note: From Latin eicere, 'to throw out'. It is used for pilots, discs and troublemakers.
hints: What a pilot does from a damaged plane.
What a bouncer does to a rowdy guest.
origin: Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus

definition: To fill with great joy.
note: From Latin elatus, 'lifted up'. Feeling elated is feeling uplifted.
hints: A win might do this to a team.
To lift someone's spirits high.

definition: The joint in the middle of your arm.
note: From Old English elnboga, 'ell-bow', where ell means the forearm length and bow means a bend. It is literally the bend of the arm.
hints: You can bend it to flex your arm.
What you use to nudge someone gently.

definition: An older person; or the older of two.
note: From Old English eldra, 'older', from a Germanic root. In many communities an elder is a respected senior person.
hints: An older sibling is this.
A respected senior member of a community.

definition: The oldest of a group of siblings.
note: From Old English eldest, superlative of eald.
hints: First-born child.
Oldest child.

definition: To choose by voting.
note: From Latin electus, 'chosen', from eligere, 'to pick out'. It is a cousin of the word select.
hints: What citizens do on voting day.
To pick for office.
example: I elected to have my funds deposited automatically.

definition: A sad poem for someone who has died.
note: From Greek elegeia, a poem in a certain metre, which in time came to mean mournful verse. Thomas Gray wrote a famous one in a country churchyard.
hints: A poem for the dead.
A mournful poem recited at a funeral.
origin: Middle French elegie, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ; in English since the early 16th century
example: What's the difference between an elegy and a eulogy?

definition: The number after ten.
note: From Old English endleofan, 'one left' over after ten.
hints: Number of players on a football team.
One more than ten.

definition: Small, delicate and a bit magical.
note: From Old English elfen, 'elf', from elf plus a feminine ending. It describes features like those of an elf.
hints: Describes small pointed ears and a pixie haircut.
Dainty, like a fairy.
example: She was an elfin creature--graceful and delicate.

definition: To draw out a response or information.
note: From Latin elicere, 'to draw forth'. Do not mix it up with illicit.
hints: A good question might do this to the truth.
A joke tries to do this to laughter.
example: Fred wished to elicit the time of the meeting from Jane.

definition: To leave out a sound or part of a word.
note: From Latin elidere, 'to strike out'. Speakers elide sounds when saying 'cuppa' for 'cup of'.
hints: What we do to a letter when saying 'fish 'n' chips'.
To omit or skip over.
example: This vowel is usually elided before a single consonant.

definition: A magical or miraculous liquid said to cure illness or give long life.
note: Through Medieval Latin from Arabic al-iksir, a word for the philosopher's stone.
hints: Alchemists dreamed of making it.
Sold by travelling quack doctors in old westerns.
origin: Medieval Latin elixir, from Ancient Greek ξηρίον

definition: To run away secretly to get married.
note: From Anglo-Norman aloper, 'to run away', from a Germanic word related to leap. It once simply meant to escape.
hints: Lovers do it without telling their parents.
A secret dash to a wedding chapel.
example: The young couple eloped and got married in Las Vegas.

definition: To escape or avoid someone cleverly.
note: From Latin eludere, 'to evade', from ex- and ludere, 'to play, trick'. It is related to ludicrous and illusion.
hints: A fox does this to the hounds.
How the answer sometimes behaves when you can't remember it.

definition: A message sent by computer.
note: From electronic plus mail. The word electric goes back to Greek elektron, 'amber', since amber was rubbed to produce static.
hints: Sent from one inbox to another.
What you check when you open your computer in the morning.

definition: To go aboard a ship or plane; or to start on a venture.
note: From French embarquer, built from en- and barque, 'small ship'. The journey sense of starting a project came later.
hints: Passengers do this at the dock before the ship sails.
Takes 'on' when it means to begin a big project.
example: All passengers please embark now.

definition: To fix firmly within something.
note: From en- plus bed. It means to set something in a surrounding mass.
hints: A journalist travels with troops as one.
To set a stone firmly in cement.

definition: A symbol that stands for a person, group or idea.
note: From Greek emblema, 'an inlaid decoration'. A country's national one might be an eagle or maple leaf.
hints: A badge on a team jersey.
A maple leaf is Canada's.
origin: Old French embleme, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα
example: The medical trucks were emblazoned with the emblem of the Red Cross.

definition: To give a visible shape to an idea or quality.
note: Formed from em- (in) and body.
hints: A national hero may do it for courage.
A statue might do it for a city's spirit.

definition: An unborn animal or human at an early stage of development.
note: From Greek embryon, 'a young one', built from en 'in' and bryein 'to swell'. In humans, an embryo is called a fetus after about eight weeks.
hints: Forms soon after an egg is fertilised.
A tiny chick inside an egg begins as one.
origin: Medieval Latin embryō, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον

definition: The host of an event who introduces the acts.
note: A pronunciation spelling of the letters MC, short for 'master of ceremonies'. It later also came to mean a rapper.
hints: The person with the microphone at an event.
Introduces the acts at a show.

definition: To come out or appear.
note: From Latin emergere, 'to rise out'.
hints: Butterfly leaving a cocoon.
Come into view.
origin: Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō

definition: A hard, rough mineral used for polishing.
note: From French emeri, from Greek smyris, 'polishing powder'. A cardboard file for nails is named for it.
hints: A nail file's cardboard abrasive.
A gritty mineral for polishing.

definition: To show emotion in an exaggerated way.
note: Back-formed from emotion in the early 20th century.
hints: What a melodramatic actor does.
Display feelings openly, as on stage.

definition: A large group of lands under one ruler.
note: From Latin imperium, 'command'.
hints: Rome built one.
Ruled by an emperor.
origin: Old French empire, from Latin imperium

definition: To give someone a job, or to use.
note: From Old French employer, from Latin implicare, 'to enfold'.
hints: Hire a worker.
Make use of a tool.

definition: Having nothing inside.
note: From Old English aemtig, 'vacant, free, idle', from a word meaning leisure or free time. A person without work had empty hands.
hints: A glass after the last drop.
The opposite of full.
example: Full of empty seats.
