definition: To give someone the means to do something.
note: From en- plus able.
hints: Make possible.
What a switch does to a feature.
example: The coffee enabled me to stay awake during the dull concert.

definition: To make into law, or to act out.
note: From Middle English enacten, from en- and act. It's said of laws and of plays.
hints: A government might do this to a bill.
To perform a scene on stage.
origin: Old French en-, from Latin actum

definition: A hard glossy coating; also the hard surface of teeth.
note: From Anglo-Norman enamailler, 'to put on glaze'. Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
hints: Decays under the attack of sugar and acid.
An old camping mug has a white one chipped at the rim.
origin: Anglo-Norman enamailler, from Early Medieval Latin smaltum

definition: A repeat or extra performance given after the show ends.
note: Borrowed from French, where it means 'again' or 'still'. French audiences actually shout 'bis' instead.
hints: Fans stamp and clap to demand one.
What a band plays after leaving the stage once.
example: Can I get an encore? We want more!

definition: Something that brings another thing to a close.
note: A plain agent noun from end, from Middle English.
hints: A person or thing that finishes.
Sci-fi fans know a famous Orson Scott Card game with this name.

definition: To give money or a gift to support something.
note: From Middle English endowen, 'to provide with assets'. A generous donor might do it for a college.
hints: A rich donor might do this for a university.
To provide with a talent, as 'nature has ___ed her'.

definition: To put up with hardship, or to last.
note: From Latin indurare, 'to harden'.
hints: Survive something painful.
Last through difficult times.
origin: Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō
example: The new secretary had to endure a lot of unprofessional remarks.

definition: A liquid injected into the bowel, for cleaning or for medical treatment.
note: From Greek enienai, 'to send in'.
hints: A medical procedure that sends fluid in.
A Greek word for injection gave its name.
origin: Late Latin enema, from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα

definition: A person or group that is hostile to you.
note: From Old French enemi, from Latin inimicus, 'not a friend'. It is made up of in-, 'not', and amicus, 'friend'.
hints: The opposite of a friend.
A foe in battle.
example: He viewed lawyers as the real enemy.

definition: The capacity to do work; also liveliness.
note: From Greek energeia, 'activity', built from en and ergon, 'work'.
hints: What a battery stores.
Vigour, or what physicists measure in joules.
origin: Middle French énergie, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια
example: Energy can take a wide variety of forms.

definition: To occupy or attract, or to hire.
note: From Old French engager, 'to pledge'.
hints: Get someone's attention.
Get betrothed or start a battle.
origin: Old French engagier, from Old French en-

definition: A machine that turns fuel into motion.
note: From Latin ingenium, 'cleverness', so engine first meant an ingenious device.
hints: What drives a car.
Its Latin root meant skill, not machine.
origin: Anglo-Norman engine, from Old French engin; in English since the 16th century
example: Medieval engines of war.

definition: A person or thing that is puzzling and hard to understand.
note: From Latin aenigma, from Ancient Greek ainigma, 'dark saying' or riddle.
hints: Churchill described Russia as a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside one of these.
Second World War Germany used a famous cipher machine of this name.

definition: To take pleasure in something.
note: From Old French enjoier, 'to give joy, rejoice', from en- and joy. Enjoying something is bringing joy into it.
hints: What you wish a diner before they eat.
To take delight in a film.

definition: To join the armed forces; or to get someone's help.
note: From en- plus list, in the sense of a roll of names. To enlist is to put your name on the roll.
hints: Done at a recruiting office.
Used for getting a friend to help you move house.
example: The army wants potential soldiers to enlist.

definition: A feeling of weary boredom.
note: Borrowed from French, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred', the same root that gave us annoy. It means a restless dissatisfaction.
hints: A French word for listless boredom.
A sense of dull, tired boredom.
origin: French ennui, from Old French enui

definition: As much as is needed.
note: From Old English genog. The gh once stood for a throat sound that has disappeared.
hints: Not too little, not too much.
Sufficient, so you can stop.
example: I'm sick of you complaining! Enough!

definition: To make richer or better in quality.
note: From Old French enrichier, from en- and riche. It can mean adding wealth, nutrients or meaning.
hints: Cereal fortified with vitamins is described this way.
A good teacher can do it to your life.
origin: Anglo-Norman enrichir, from Old French enrichier
example: Hobbies enrich lives.

definition: To sign up as a member or student.
note: From Old French enroller, 'to put on a roll'. It is spelled with a double l in British English.
hints: What you do to join a course.
What a freshman does in September.
example: She had to take a test before she could enroll in the course.

definition: A flag of a ship or nation; also a junior naval officer.
note: From Old French enseigne, from Latin insignia. The Royal Navy's flags are called by it.
hints: The flag flown at the stern of a warship.
A lowly officer in the US Navy.
origin: Old French enseigne, from Latin īnsignia

definition: To follow as a result.
note: From Old French ensuivre, from Latin insequi, 'to follow close upon'. The word is often used in news reports of a chaotic scene.
hints: What happens after a fight breaks out and chaos follows.
To come afterwards.
origin: Latin īnsequere; in English since the 16th century
example: This sentence was born from indecisiveness and ensuing boredom.

definition: To make certain.
note: From Old French enseurer, from en and sur, 'sure'.
hints: Guarantee that something happens.
Make sure of an outcome.
origin: Anglo-Norman enseurer, from Old French seur; in English since the 18th century
example: I use an alarm clock to ensure that I get up on time.

definition: To involve as a necessary result; also to leave land to a fixed line of heirs.
note: From Old French entailler, 'to cut in'. The land law sense restricted an estate to certain heirs in the family.
hints: Taking on a big job may do this, bringing long hours with it.
Jane Austen's Bennet family faced the legal kind with their house.
origin: Old French entaillier, from Latin talea
example: What does this move entail?

definition: To go into a place.
note: From Old French entrer, from Latin intrare, 'to go in'. It also means to type or register something.
hints: A key on your keyboard.
Come in through the door.
origin: Old French entrer, from Latin intrō

definition: To tempt someone with the promise of pleasure or reward.
note: From Old French enticier, 'to stir up', traced back to a Latin phrase meaning 'I set on fire'. Luring someone was first imagined as kindling a fire in them.
hints: What a shop window display tries to do to passers-by.
A baker might use the smell of fresh bread to do it.
example: The brochure hasn't enticed me to go on holiday there.

definition: Whole and complete.
note: From Old French entier, from Latin integer, 'untouched'.
hints: Not just a part of something.
Describes the whole of something.
example: We had the entire building to ourselves for the evening.

definition: Something that exists as a distinct unit.
note: From Latin entitas, from ens, 'being'.
hints: A company is a legal one.
A thing with its own existence.
example: The Church is an entity that has accumulated a lot of wealth.

definition: The act of going in; or a way in.
note: From Old French entree, from Latin intrare. It names a doorway, an item in a list or a contest submission.
hints: A door or gate is one.
A submission to a competition.

definition: A messenger or representative, often of a government.
note: From French envoye, 'sent', from envoyer, 'to send'. The title is for a diplomat ranking just below an ambassador.
hints: Sent abroad with a message from the government.
A diplomat below an ambassador in rank.

definition: A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in living things.
note: From Greek en, 'in', and zyme, 'leaven', coined in 1870s.
hints: Helps digest your food.
Amylase is one in saliva.
example: A kinase is an enzyme which phosphorylates other proteins.

definition: A strong glue that hardens when two parts are mixed.
note: From Greek oxys, 'sharp' and a chemical prefix. It is a hard resin used in adhesives and coatings.
hints: Comes in two tubes that you mix together.
A powerful glue for repairing ceramics.

definition: The same in size, value or rights.
note: From Latin aequalis, from aequus, 'level, even'. Equal means level, like a fair scale.
hints: What the sign made of two lines stands for.
Having the same rights as everyone else.
example: We hold that all men are created equal and are thus equal under the law.

definition: To treat or regard as equal.
note: From Latin aequare, 'to make equal'.
hints: A person who thinks money and happiness are the same does it.
Mathematicians do it between two expressions.

definition: Relating to horses.
note: From Latin equinus, from equus, 'horse'. Vets use it for horse medicine.
hints: A vet who treats horses is this kind.
A word for something horsey.

definition: To supply with what is needed.
note: From French equiper, 'to fit out', first said of ships. It may come from a Norse word for a ship.
hints: To fit out a ship or a team.
To give someone the tools for a job.
origin: French équiper, from Old Norse skipa

definition: Fairness, or the value of an ownership stake.
note: From Latin aequitas, 'evenness', from aequus, 'equal'.
hints: Justice in dealings.
What you own in a house after a mortgage.
origin: Old French equité, from Latin aequitās

definition: To rub out or remove.
note: From Latin eradere, 'to scrape out'. It was first used for scraping words off wax tablets.
hints: What a rubber at the end of a pencil does.
To wipe a file or a whiteboard clean.

definition: Upright and standing straight.
note: From Latin erectus, 'upright', from erigere, 'to raise'. It can also mean to build, as in 'erect a tent'.
hints: To put up a tent.
Standing with straight posture.
example: For a dog, an erect tail indicates aggression.

definition: To wear away slowly.
note: From French eroder and Latin erodere, 'to gnaw away'. Wind and water do it to rock.
hints: What waves do to a cliff over time.
To gradually weaken, as trust might.
example: The cliff is gradually being eroded by the waves.

definition: Worn away gradually by wind, water or time.
note: From Latin erodere, 'to gnaw away'. Cliffs, soil and trust can all be eroded.
hints: A canyon is carved this way by a river.
Cliffs by the sea slowly become this.

definition: A short trip to do a job for someone.
note: From Old English aerende, 'message'. The older sense was a message carried by a messenger.
hints: Dropping off a parcel on your way home.
A boy who runs them for a shopkeeper.

definition: A mistake.
note: From Old French error, from Latin error, 'a wandering about', from errare, 'to wander'. A mistake was seen as wandering off the right path.
hints: A typo is one.
A message that pops up when a program fails.
example: There was a large error in the accounts.

definition: To burst out suddenly.
note: From Latin eruptus, 'broken out', from erumpere, 'to burst out'. It is related to the word rupture.
hints: A volcano does it with lava.
Anger might do it at a dinner table.

definition: To get free from confinement.
note: From Old French eschaper, probably built from a Latin phrase meaning 'out of the cape'.
hints: Break out of jail.
Houdini's speciality.
origin: Old Northern French escaper, from Late Latin cappa
example: The prisoners escaped by jumping over a wall.

definition: Money or property held by a neutral party until a deal is complete.
note: From Old French escroe, 'scrap of parchment', from a Frankish word for a piece. The scrap was the document held in trust.
hints: House buyers' deposits sit in this account.
A third party holds the funds until the closing.
origin: Law French escrowe, from Old French escroe

definition: A short piece of writing on a topic.
note: From Middle French essai, 'a trial or attempt', a meaning the writer Montaigne gave it in the 1500s. An essay was originally an attempt to work out your thoughts.
hints: Students write one for homework.
A short piece of nonfiction prose.
origin: Middle French essay, from Latin exagium

definition: Large landed property, or a person's total wealth.
note: From Old French estat, 'state' or 'condition'.
hints: A country house with grounds.
What a will distributes.
example: The family owned a large estate on Long Island.

definition: Respect and admiration.
note: From Latin aestimare, 'to value'.
hints: Having it high means feeling good about yourself.
Regard held for someone.
origin: Middle French estimer, from Latin aestimō

definition: A kind of chemical compound often with a fruity smell.
note: The name was coined in German, likely as a contraction of a word for vinegar ether. Many fruit flavours are esters.
hints: Chemistry class compound behind fruity smells.
Formed from an acid and an alcohol.
example: Not all esters smell good.

definition: A clear volatile liquid once used as an anaesthetic; or the upper sky.
note: From Greek aither, 'upper air, bright sky'. Ancient thinkers pictured it as the pure air of the heavens.
hints: Old surgeons used it to put patients to sleep.
Something broadcast 'over the ___' goes through the air.
origin: Anglo-Norman ether, from Old French aether

definition: A moral principle that guides behaviour.
note: From Late Latin ethicus, from Greek ethikos, 'moral'. Its plural gives the field of moral philosophy.
hints: A strong work one is a personal value.
A moral rule about right and wrong.
origin: Old French ethique, from Ancient Greek ἠθική
example: The Protestant work ethic.

definition: Principles of right and wrong.
note: From Greek ethika, from ethos, 'character'.
hints: Moral principles.
What a philosopher studies.
origin: Middle French ethique, from Ancient Greek ἠθική

definition: Relating to a shared culture or ancestry.
note: From Greek ethnikos, 'of a nation', from ethnos.
hints: Describes a cultural group.
Describes cuisine of a particular heritage.
origin: Latin ethnicus, from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός

definition: The spirit or values of a community or culture.
note: From Greek ethos, 'character, custom, habit'. Aristotle used it for a speaker's character as a way of persuading.
hints: A company's guiding values.
The characteristic spirit of a culture.
example: Settling down and raising a family was against the ethos of the times.

definition: A short piece of music for practising a skill.
note: Borrowed from French etude, 'study', in the 1830s. Chopin and Liszt wrote famous ones.
hints: Pianists practise one to improve technique.
French for 'study'.

definition: A cry of triumph on suddenly finding an answer.
note: Greek for 'I have found it'. A popular story says Archimedes shouted it from his bath after solving a puzzle about a crown.
hints: Archimedes supposedly yelled it in a bath.
The moment of a sudden flash of insight.

definition: In a smooth, equal or balanced way.
note: From Old English efenlice. It adds -ly to even.
hints: How a cake must be cut to avoid arguments.
How a fair coin should land over many flips.
example: To avoid arguments, he divided the sweets evenly between his two children.

definition: Something that happens, especially a planned occasion.
note: From Latin eventus, 'an occurrence', from evenire, 'to happen, come out'. It is related to the word venture.
hints: A concert or a wedding.
Anything that takes place at a particular time.
origin: Middle French event, from Latin ēventus

definition: Each one of a group, without leaving any out.
note: From Old English aefre aelc, meaning 'ever each'. It is a blend of the words that gave us ever and each.
hints: All of them, one at a time.
A word that often comes before 'single'.
example: Every person is mortal.

definition: To force someone to leave their home.
note: From Latin evictus, 'conquered completely', the same word as evince. In law it meant to recover property by judgment.
hints: What a landlord may do if the rent isn't paid.
To throw tenants out for not paying.
example: The landlord threatened to evict them for nonpayment.

definition: To bring a memory or feeling to mind.
note: From French evoquer and Latin evocare, 'to call out'. It is related to voice.
hints: A smell that takes you back to childhood.
To call up a feeling, as music can.

definition: To develop gradually.
note: From Latin evolvere, 'to unroll'.
hints: How species change over time.
Change step by step.

definition: Precisely correct.
note: From Latin exactus, 'perfected, measured', from exigere, 'to demand, measure'. It is used of measurements and times.
hints: The ___ amount of change needed.
Not approximate.
origin: Latin exāctus, from Middle English exact

definition: To praise highly or raise in rank.
note: From Old French exalter and Latin exaltare, 'to raise up'. It is an elevated word for lifting up.
hints: What worshippers do to their god.
To lift someone to a higher position.
origin: Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō
example: Exalted the humble shoemaker to the rank of King's adviser.

definition: To go beyond a limit.
note: From Latin excedere, 'to go out'.
hints: Drive faster than permitted.
Be greater than expected.
origin: Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō
example: Your password cannot exceed eight characters.

definition: To be outstanding at something.
note: From Latin excellere, 'to rise, surpass', built from ex-, 'out' and a root meaning to be high. Spreadsheets borrowed the name.
hints: To be better than the rest.
What a top student does in class.
origin: Old French exceller, from Latin excellere
example: Suga has a reputation for excelling at alliance-building.

definition: Not including.
note: From Latin exceptus, 'taken out'.
hints: Leave out someone from the group.
A word that sets something aside.
origin: Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus
example: The bad results were excluded from the report.

definition: More than is needed.
note: From Latin excessus, 'a going out'.
hints: Too much of something.
Overindulgence.
origin: Old French exces, from Latin excessus

definition: A tax on certain goods made or sold inside a country; also to cut something out.
note: From Dutch excijs, 'tax', shaped by Latin excisus, 'cut out'. Taxes on alcohol and tobacco are often excise duties.
hints: Duty on whisky and cigarettes.
A surgeon cuts out a tumour; the verb sense.
origin: Middle Dutch excijs, from Old French acceis

definition: To make someone feel enthusiastic or stirred up.
note: From Latin excitare, 'to call forth'. It first meant to arouse any strong feeling.
hints: Fireworks do this to children.
News of a holiday does it to the whole class.
origin: Old French exciter, from Latin excitō
example: The fireworks which opened the festivities excited anyone present.

definition: A reason given to explain a fault, or to forgive.
note: From Latin excusare, 'to free from blame'.
hints: What a late pupil offers.
Pardon me, or a reason for being late.
origin: Old French escuser, from Latin excūsō
example: Tell me why you were late – and I don't want to hear any excuses!

definition: Free from a rule or duty.
note: From Latin exemptus, 'taken out'.
hints: Not required to pay tax.
Excused from a rule.
origin: Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus
example: In their country all women are exempt from military service.

definition: To breathe out.
note: From Latin exhalare, from ex- 'out' and halare 'to breathe'.
hints: What you do after holding your breath.
Yoga teachers tell you to do it slowly.
origin: Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare

definition: Forced absence from your home country.
note: From Old French exil and Latin exilium, from exul, 'banished person'. Napoleon was sent to Elba and later St Helena.
hints: What happens to a banished ruler.
Napoleon spent his last years in it.
origin: Old French essil, from Latin exsilium

definition: To be real, to have being.
note: From French exister and Latin existere, 'to stand forth', from ex- and sistere, 'to set, place'. To exist is to stand out into being.
hints: Dragons are said not to.
To be alive or real.

definition: A mass departure.
note: From Greek exodos, 'a going out'.
hints: Moses led one.
A sudden mass leaving.
origin: Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος

definition: Unusual and from far away.
note: From Greek exotikos, 'from outside'.
hints: A bird from the tropics.
Strange and colourful.
origin: Middle French exotique, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός
example: An exotic hair style.

definition: To become larger.
note: From Latin expandere, 'to spread out'.
hints: Grow bigger.
What a balloon does.
example: His business expanded rapidly.

definition: A person living outside their home country.
note: A clipping of expatriate, from Latin ex, 'out', and patria, 'homeland'. It is used for workers abroad.
hints: A Briton living in Spain.
A worker living overseas.
example: The beautiful island of Bali is home to many freelance expats.

definition: To believe something will happen.
note: From Latin exspectare, 'to look out for'.
hints: What a mother-to-be is said to do.
Look forward to or anticipate.
example: I expect to be able to walk again after getting over my broken leg.

definition: To force out.
note: From Latin expellere, 'to drive out', from ex- and pellere, 'to drive'. Schools and bodies do it.
hints: A school can do it to a student who misbehaves.
To drive away or throw out, as a diplomat.
example: He was expelled from his native country.

definition: Someone with great skill or knowledge.
note: From Latin expertus, 'tried' or 'proved'.
hints: Knows a subject deeply.
A specialist consulted for advice.
origin: Old French expert, from Latin expertus
example: We called in several experts on the subject, but they couldn't reach an agreement.

definition: To come to an end, as a ticket or deadline does; or to die.
note: From Latin expirare, 'to breathe out', since dying was breathing one's last. It still means the end of a time limit.
hints: What milk and passports do on a printed date.
Literally the opposite of inspire, to breathe out.
origin: Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō

definition: To send goods to another country.
note: From Latin exportare, 'to carry away'.
hints: Ports ship out its coffee and cars.
Trade balance sheets set it against its opposite number.
example: The Russians exported Marxism to Africa.

definition: To uncover or reveal.
note: From Old French exposer, 'to set out'.
hints: Bring a secret to light.
Leave skin unprotected from the sun.
origin: Old French exposer, from Latin expōnō

definition: Still existing, not lost or extinct.
note: From Latin extare, 'to stand out'. Only a few manuscripts of some old works are extant.
hints: Of ancient manuscripts, those that have survived.
The opposite of extinct.
example: Specimens of graphic art found among extant barbaric folk.

definition: To stretch out or make longer.
note: From Latin extendere, 'to stretch out'.
hints: Make longer.
Offer an invitation.

definition: The size or range of something.
note: From Latin extentus, 'stretched out'.
hints: How far something reaches.
To what degree.

definition: To praise enthusiastically.
note: From Latin extollere, 'to lift up, raise high'. It is a more formal way of praising.
hints: To sing someone's virtues.
To praise someone highly.
example: Extol the virtues of one's children.

definition: To give off a liquid or a quality in great quantity.
note: From Latin exsudare, 'to sweat out'.
hints: Someone can do this with confidence.
Ooze, as sap from a tree.
example: Wearing that suit, Jasper just exudes class.

definition: To rejoice greatly, especially in triumph.
note: From Middle French exulter and Latin exsultare, 'to leap up', from salire, 'to jump'. It's a joy that makes you leap.
hints: What a winning team does on the pitch.
To rejoice in victory.
origin: Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō
example: Who cannot exult in Spring?

definition: A short story with animals that teaches a lesson.
note: From Old French fable and Latin fabula, 'story', from fari, 'to speak'. Aesop is the best-known author of them.
hints: The tortoise and the hare is one.
A story with a moral at the end.
origin: Old French fable, from Latin fābula

definition: Cloth, or the structure of something.
note: From Latin fabrica, 'workshop', from faber, 'craftsman'.
hints: Cotton or silk.
Social structure of a community.

definition: The front of a building, or a false outward appearance.
note: From French façade, from Italian faccia, 'face'. The figurative sense is a front hiding the truth.
hints: The grand street-facing side of a cathedral.
A cheerful smile that hides sadness.

definition: One of the flat faces of a cut gem; or an aspect.
note: From French facette, 'little face', a diminutive of face. A cut gem sparkles through many small faces.
hints: A diamond cutter polishes each one.
One side of a complex issue.
example: This facet of the diamond was masterfully cut to enhance its value.

definition: Relating to the face; also a beauty treatment.
note: From Latin facies, 'face'.
hints: Expression or recognition feature.
A spa treatment for skin.

definition: One thing that contributes to a result, or a number that divides another.
note: From Latin factor, 'doer', from facere, 'to make'.
hints: A cause that plays a part.
Two and three are of six.
origin: Middle French facteur, from Latin factor
example: The greatest factor in the decision was the need for public transportation.

definition: A slider that raises or lowers volume or lighting.
note: From fade plus -er.
hints: Slides on a mixing desk.
Sound engineers push them up and down.

definition: Weak or barely noticeable; or to pass out briefly.
note: From Old French faint, 'feigned, sluggish', from feindre, 'to feign'. A faint sound is feeble, and a swoon is a failure of strength.
hints: A sound you can barely hear.
To pass out for a moment from heat.
origin: Old French faint, from Latin fingere

definition: Justly, or to a moderate degree.
note: From fair plus -ly.
hints: Quite, or in an even-handed way.
Treated without bias.

definition: A tiny magical creature with wings.
note: From Old French faerie, 'enchantment', from fae, 'fairy', from Latin fata, 'the fates'. It first named the land of fays, then its inhabitants.
hints: Tinker Bell is one.
Visits under your pillow to collect a tooth.
origin: Old French faerie, from Latin fāta

definition: Strong trust or belief.
note: From Old French feid and Latin fides, 'trust, belief'. It is related to the word fidelity.
hints: 'Leap of ___' means trusting without proof.
Religion or deep trust in a person.
origin: Old French fei, from Latin fidem
example: He lost his faith but not his morality.

definition: Someone who pretends to be something they are not.
note: A plain agent noun from fake. The origin of fake itself is uncertain.
hints: A person passing off a counterfeit.
Not the real thing, in human form.

definition: A fast bird of prey.
note: From Old French faucon, from Late Latin falco.
hints: Used in hunting.
Peregrine is one.
origin: Old French falcun, from Late Latin falcō

definition: Having dropped down.
note: The past participle of fall.
hints: Like leaves in autumn.
Killed in battle, in memorials.
example: Fallen leaves covered the forest floor.

definition: Not true or not real.
note: From Old English fals and Latin falsus, 'deceived, mistaken'. It names things untrue or fake.
hints: The opposite of true.
What a lie is.
origin: Old English fals, from Latin falsus

definition: A group of people related by blood or marriage.
note: From Latin familia, meaning household, including servants.
hints: Parents and children together.
Home group; relatives.

definition: An extreme scarcity of food across a region.
note: From Old French famine, from Latin fames, 'hunger'. The Irish Potato version killed a million in the 1840s.
hints: What follows a total crop failure.
The 1840s Irish potato blight caused a great one.
origin: Middle French famine, from Latin fames

definition: Known by many people.
note: From Latin famosus, from fama, 'rumour' or 'reputation'.
hints: Celebrities are this way.
Widely known.
example: We visited Mito Park, which is famous for its plum blossoms.

definition: Elaborate or high-class; or to like.
note: A contraction of fantasy, from Greek phantasia. It first meant the imagination, then a liking, then something elaborate.
hints: A formal restaurant might be this.
Decorated or showy.
origin: Old French fantasie, from Ancient Greek φαντασία

definition: The community of fans of a show, band, game or team.
note: From fan plus -dom, as in kingdom. Fan itself is short for fanatic.
hints: Where Trekkies and Potterheads belong.
The online world of fan fiction and conventions.
example: The furry fandom, like many other fandoms, has its own slang.

definition: A comedy full of ridiculous situations.
note: From French farce, 'stuffing', a cooking term. Comic interludes were 'stuffed' into serious religious plays.
hints: A silly play with slamming doors and mistaken identities.
A ridiculous situation.
origin: Middle French farce, from Latin farciō

definition: A person who grows crops or raises animals.
note: From Old French fermier, a person who leased land.
hints: Works the fields.
Tends fields and livestock.
origin: Old French fermier, from Old English feormere

definition: Quicker; comparative of fast.
note: From Old English faest, which meant firmly fixed before it meant swift.
hints: Moving at greater speed than before.
Quicker than before, as a runner might be.

definition: Causing death.
note: From Middle French fatal, from Latin fatalis, 'of fate'. Something fated could not be escaped.
hints: A ___ error is one that ends everything.
A disease that kills.
origin: Middle French fatal, from Latin fātālis

definition: A male parent.
note: From Old English faeder, a very ancient word shared across Indo-European languages.
hints: Dad, formally.
A male parent, or a priest's title.
example: His father was born in Atlanta.

definition: To understand something deeply; also a unit of water depth.
note: From Old English faethm, 'outstretched arms', the span of arms measuring six feet. To fathom a thing is to sound its depths.
hints: Used by sailors to measure the depth of water.
'Unable to ___' something means you can't understand it.
example: I can’t for the life of me fathom what this means.

definition: Containing a lot of fat.
note: From fat plus -y.
hints: Describes greasy food.
Rich in oil or lard.

definition: A formal legal opinion issued by an Islamic scholar.
note: From Arabic fatwa, 'legal opinion'.
hints: A ruling from a religious authority.
Learned opinion on Islamic law.
origin: Arabic فَتْوَى, from Ottoman Turkish فتوی
example: Popes are soft targets, they don't issue fatwas but only bulls.

definition: A tap that controls the flow of water.
note: From Old French fausset, of uncertain origin. It first meant a peg that plugged a barrel. It is chiefly American.
hints: A kitchen sink fixture.
A drip from one wastes water.
origin: Old French fausset, from Old Norse foss
example: The rain ceased as if a faucet had been turned off.

definition: Blame; or a defect.
note: From Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin fallita, 'shortcoming', related to fail. A fault is a failing.
hints: 'It's not my ___' is a common excuse.
A crack in the earth where earthquakes happen.

definition: Having a defect; not working properly.
note: From fault plus -y. Fault comes from Latin fallere, 'to deceive or fail'.
hints: What a returned toaster might be called.
A switch that sparks or a machine that jams.
example: They replaced the faulty wiring and it has worked fine ever since.

definition: The animals of a region or period.
note: From New Latin, from Fauna, a Roman goddess and sister of Faunus, god of forests. Linnaeus adopted it as a counterpart to flora.
hints: Flora's partner when describing an ecosystem.
All the animals of a place.
origin: New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna; in English since the late 18th century
example: The fauna of China.

definition: A kind act for someone.
note: From Old French favor and Latin favor, from favere, 'to be kind'. 'Ask a ___' means to request a kindness.
hints: Doing someone a good turn.
Something you ask a friend to do for you.
example: He did me a favor when he took the time to drive me home.

definition: A large, special meal.
note: From Old French feste and Latin festa, 'holiday'. It is a cousin of fiesta and festival.
hints: A banquet to celebrate.
Thanksgiving dinner.
origin: Old French feste, from Latin festum

definition: A felt hat with a creased crown and a brim.
note: Named for Fedora, an 1882 play by Victorien Sardou, whose heroine wore such a hat. It became a male fashion later.
hints: Humphrey Bogart wore one in noir films.
Indiana Jones wears one.
origin: Russian Федо́ра, from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος
example: His black fedora hat added a touch of old-fashioned charm.

definition: Weak in strength or effect.
note: From Old French feble, from Latin flebilis, 'worthy of tears'. Something feeble was once pitiable.
hints: An excuse that no one believes.
A frail old man's voice, or a dim light.
example: Though she appeared old and feeble, she could still throw a ball.

definition: One who or that which feeds; also a bird-food dispenser.
note: From feed plus -er. A bird table or a baby bottle can be one.
hints: A hanging container for sunflower seeds in the garden.
A small stream joining a larger river.

definition: A deceptive move meant to mislead an opponent.
note: From French feinte, from feindre, 'to pretend'.
hints: A boxer's fake punch.
A sword thrust that is not meant to land.

definition: Lively, spirited and ready to argue.
note: From feist, a small aggressive dog. The earlier meaning of that word was 'stink'.
hints: Said of a small dog that takes on big ones.
A small woman with a big temper.

definition: Relating to cats, or like a cat.
note: Borrowed from Latin felinus, from feles, 'wildcat' or 'marten'. The word is used in science and also for something sleek and graceful.
hints: A vet's word for a cat.
Lions and tigers belong to this family.

definition: An informal word for a man or a guy.
note: A casual spelling of fellow, which comes from an Old Norse word for a business partner. It sounds like relaxed speech.
hints: A chatty name for a man.
A pal might be called a good one.
example: There's a fellow at the door.

definition: A man or companion, or a member of a learned society.
note: From Old Norse felagi, 'partner in a business'.
hints: A chap, or a university post.
A colleague or peer.
origin: Old English fēolaga, from Old Norse félagi

definition: A serious crime.
note: From Old French felonie, from fel, 'wicked'.
hints: More grave than a misdemeanour.
A crime like robbery or murder.
example: Sami had a felony conviction for writing phoney checks.

definition: Of the sex that bears young or lays eggs.
note: From Old French femelle, from Latin femella, 'young woman'. The spelling was altered to match male.
hints: A box to tick on many forms, next to its counterpart.
A hen or a mare, for example.
origin: Old French femele, from Latin fēmella; in English since the 14th century

definition: A woman, in French; in English, a feminine-presenting person.
note: Borrowed from French femme, 'woman', from Latin femina.
hints: A glamorous schemer in old films is a fatale one.
French for woman, borrowed as slang.
origin: Old French fame; in English since the 19th century

definition: The thigh bone.
note: Borrowed directly from Latin femur, 'thigh'. It is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
hints: Between hip and knee.
The longest bone in your body.
example: The human femur is tougher than concrete.

definition: A barrier around land.
note: Short for defence, from Old French defens. It also names sword fighting and a person who sells stolen goods.
hints: Made of wooden posts around a garden.
Sword fighting takes this name.

definition: A guard over a car's wheel, or a barrier that protects a ship's side.
note: From fend, a short form of defend, plus -er. In Britain the same part of a car is a wing; a fire fender sits by the hearth.
hints: The American name for the bodywork over a car wheel.
Hung over the side of a boat to protect it at the dock.

definition: A boat that carries people across water.
note: From Old English ferian, 'to carry'. The verb came first, before the boat service.
hints: Crosses a river with cars and passengers.
The way to get to an island without a bridge.
origin: Old English ferian, from Old Norse ferja

definition: Intense passion or enthusiasm.
note: From Latin fervor, 'boiling heat', from fervere, 'to boil'. Fervent has the same origin.
hints: Zeal at a political rally.
Heat in emotion.
example: The coach trains his water polo team with fervor.

definition: Relating to an unborn baby in the womb.
note: From fetus plus -al. Fetus is a Latin word meaning 'offspring'. A fetal position is curled up tightly, with knees tucked in.
hints: A curled-up sleeping posture.
Kind of position a worried person may curl into.
example: A fetal "heartbeat" is a more arbitrary standard than viability.

definition: To go and bring back.
note: From Middle English fecchen, 'to get and bring back'. A dog does it with a stick.
hints: What you tell a dog to do with a ball.
To go and bring back something.
example: The dog fetched the hat.

definition: Smelling very bad.
note: From Latin fetidus, from fetere, 'to stink'. It is a literary word for a foul odour.
hints: A swamp can have this smell.
Rotten, like old rubbish.
example: As the lab was filled with a fetid odor, I could tell the synthesis had gone awry.

definition: An object believed to have magical power; or an intense fixation.
note: From Portuguese feitico, 'charm', through French. The sense of obsessive attachment is modern.
hints: An idol thought to hold spirit power.
An obsession focused on a particular object.

definition: An unborn baby in the later stages of pregnancy.
note: A learned borrowing from Latin fetus, 'offspring'. It is a doublet of fawn.
hints: An unborn child.
What a doctor sees on a pregnancy scan.
example: The embryos and fetuses of all mammals look quite similar.

definition: Relating to the medieval system where lords granted land in exchange for service.
note: From Medieval Latin feodalis, from feodum, 'fief', a property. The word appears in phrases like 'feudal lord'.
hints: A peasant owed service to the lord of the manor.
The system in which a knight held land from a baron.
origin: Old French feodal, from Medieval Latin feodalis
example: Our political system was shaped by feudal traditions.

definition: A body temperature higher than normal.
note: From Old English fefer and Latin febris, 'fever'. It is a common sign of illness.
hints: A sign you may have a cold.
A thermometer shows it.
origin: Old English fefer, from Latin febris
example: There has been a rise in my fever. I think I've the flu.

definition: A smaller number of.
note: From few plus -er. The old rule says fewer goes with things you can count.
hints: Used with countable things like apples.
A grammar pedant corrects 'less'.
example: Fewer birds came this year.

definition: A man who is engaged to be married.
note: From French fiancer, 'to promise', from the root of faith. The feminine form is fiancee.
hints: The man a woman has promised to marry.
Wears a new ring and is planning a wedding.
example: Sami thinks his daughter's fiance is responsible for her death.

definition: A complete and embarrassing failure.
note: From Italian fiasco, 'flask'. Why the bottle meant failure is unknown.
hints: A badly organised event that collapses.
Italian for a bottle of Chianti.
origin: Italian fiasco, from French faire fiasco
example: The event turned into a complete fiasco when the power went out.

definition: A thin thread of material; or roughage in food.
note: From French fibre, from Latin fibra. It also describes nutrients that help digestion.
hints: Whole grains are rich in it.
A thin strand, as in cloth or nerves.
example: The microscope showed a single blue fiber stuck to the sole of the shoe.

definition: Changing your mind or loyalty often and without good reason.
note: From Old English ficol, 'deceitful' or 'tricky', so it once carried a sense of cunning as well as inconstancy.
hints: Describes a friend who drops you for a better offer.
Often applied to the weather, or to a crowd's favour.

definition: A plant in the fig family, often grown indoors.
note: Borrowed from Latin ficus, 'fig'. Houseplants like the rubber tree are of this genus.
hints: A potted rubber plant.
In the same genus as the fig.

definition: A violin, especially one played folk-style; also to fidget with something.
note: From Old English fithele, of uncertain origin. The verb sense of idly playing with things grew from the instrument's busy finger-work.
hints: Played at a ceilidh or a barn dance.
In the song, the devil went down to Georgia and beat a boy at it.

definition: An open area of land, often with crops or sports.
note: From Old English feld, 'open country'. It is a very old Germanic word.
hints: Cows graze in it.
Where a football game is played.
example: He longed for the fields of his youth.

definition: An evil spirit; or a wicked person.
note: From Old English feond, 'enemy'. It is related to the word foe's older forms.
hints: A demon in a horror story.
A wicked person; also an obsessive addict, as in 'sweet-toothed ___'.

definition: Wild, violent or intense.
note: From Old French fers, 'wild', from Latin ferus.
hints: A lion's roar.
Strong and aggressive in spirit.
origin: Old French fers, from Latin ferus
example: A fierce storm battered the coast.

definition: Burning, or full of passion.
note: From Middle English fyry, from fyr, 'fire', plus -y. It describes flames or tempers.
hints: Describes a hot-headed temper.
Red like flames.

definition: A festival or celebration, especially in a Spanish-speaking country.
note: From Spanish fiesta, from Late Latin festa, related to feast and festival.
hints: Streets fill with music and dancing in Spain.
A big Mexican party day with piñatas.
origin: Spanish fiesta, from Late Latin festa

definition: Number five in a sequence.
note: From Old English fifta, which came from fif, 'five'. The 'th' ending turns a number into an order.
hints: The one after the fourth.
A music interval, or a bottle size in the US.

definition: The number after forty-nine.
note: From Old English fiftig, from fif plus -tig, meaning 'tens'. Half of one hundred.
hints: Half of a hundred.
A big birthday for many.

definition: To struggle against someone with force.
note: From Old English feohtan, 'to fight, combat', a very old Germanic word. It covers punches, wars and campaigns alike.
hints: Boxers do it in a ring.
A pillow one is a playful kind.

definition: A number, shape or person.
note: From Latin figura, 'shape'.
hints: Digit or silhouette.
Can mean to work out.

definition: A person who files papers or submits documents.
note: From file plus -er. The word file comes from Latin filum, 'thread', because papers were once threaded on a string.
hints: Someone who sorts papers into cabinets.
Submits a tax return on time.

definition: A boneless cut of meat or fish.
note: From French filet, 'thread' or 'small band'. It is a spelling of fillet that keeps its French look.
hints: A tender cut on a fancy menu.
Mignon is the cut that often follows it on menus.

definition: Material used to fill a gap or add bulk.
note: From Old English fyllan with -er. Padded writing and empty chat are called this too.
hints: Used to patch holes in a wall before painting.
Words in an essay that add length but no meaning.

definition: A young female horse.
note: From Old Norse fylja, related to foal. It names a horse that has not yet reached full age.
hints: A young mare, not yet grown.
The female of a foal.
example: The filly was named "Comet" because she was so fast.

definition: Thin and see-through, like a film.
note: From film plus -y. Film comes from Old English filmen, meaning 'membrane' or 'thin skin'.
hints: How a gauzy curtain looks.
A thin layer, like a veil.
example: Filmy wings of a moth.

definition: A device that strains out unwanted particles.
note: From Medieval Latin filtrum, 'felt', which was used for straining liquids.
hints: Coffee goes through one.
Used on a camera lens.

definition: Disgusting dirt.
note: From Old English fylth, from foul plus -th. It is the noun for the quality of being foul.
hints: What a garbage heap is covered in.
Dirt of the most revolting kind.

definition: Extremely dirty.
note: From filth plus -y.
hints: Covered in mud.
Very unclean.
example: As filthy as a pigsty.

definition: Coming at the end.
note: From Old French final and Latin finalis, 'of the end', from finis, 'end'. It is the last of a series.
hints: The last match of a tournament.
The exam at the end of a term.
origin: Old French final, from Latin fīnālis

definition: The last part of a show or piece.
note: From Italian finale, 'last'.
hints: The final act of a show.
Fireworks at the close.

definition: A small seed-eating songbird.
note: From Old English finc, a Germanic word thought to imitate the bird's call. Darwin studied those on the Galapagos.
hints: Darwin made them famous in the Galapagos.
A small, colourful songbird.

definition: A person or thing that finds something.
note: From find plus -er. A viewfinder helps you aim a camera.
hints: In the saying, 'keepers' is the rule for the first one to be this.
Part of a camera you look through.

definition: In very small pieces or with great delicacy.
note: From fine plus -ly. Fine comes from Latin finis, 'end', in the sense of finished or refined.
hints: How a chef is told to chop parsley.
How a violin is carefully tuned.
example: Fledglings can only be fed finely chopped meat.

definition: Of better quality, or thinner and more delicate.
note: The comparative of fine, which came from Old French fin, 'perfect' or 'pure'. The things in life are sometimes called the 'finer things'.
hints: Comparing two cuts of cloth.
The 'things in life' idiom often uses it.

definition: Of the highest quality.
note: The superlative of fine.
hints: Best of the best.
Best of all in quality.

definition: One of the digits on a hand.
note: From Old English finger.
hints: Five on each hand, counting the thumb.
Wears a ring.
example: Her fingers were long and thin.

definition: To bring to an end, or the final coat on a surface.
note: From Latin finire, from finis, 'end'.
hints: Cross the line to do it.
Varnish on a wooden table.
example: He finished the dishes.

definition: Having limits.
note: From Latin finitus, 'bounded'.
hints: Not going on without end.
Bounded, with a set limit.

definition: In a strong, definite manner.
note: From firm plus -ly.
hints: With determination.
Without wobbling.
example: She corrected him firmly but gently.

definition: Coming before all others.
note: From Old English fyrst, a superlative form meaning 'foremost'. It is related to the word for 'fore'.
hints: The one at the front of the line.
Gold medal position.
example: Hancock was first to arrive.

definition: A narrow inlet of the sea in Scotland.
note: From Old Norse fjordr, the same word as fjord. The Firth of Forth is a famous one.
hints: A Scottish sea inlet.
A cousin of a fjord.
origin: Scots firth, from Old Norse fjǫrðr

definition: Relating to government money or taxes.
note: From Latin fiscus, 'treasury', originally a basket for money.
hints: A budget year is named this way.
Concerns public finances.
origin: Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus

definition: A person who fishes; also a weasel-like animal.
note: From Old English fiscere.
hints: Casts a line.
A big mustelid of North American forests.

definition: Smelling of fish; or suspicious.
note: From fish plus -y. The sense of suspicious comes from the smell of something gone off.
hints: A poor alibi may seem this.
Describes a story that doesn't add up.
example: The soup had a fishy smell.

definition: A five-pound note, or five dollars.
note: From five plus the -er ending.
hints: A banknote of small value.
British slang for a note with a monarch on it.
example: "Excuse me, mate. You've dropped a fiver." "Oh. Cheers, mate!"

definition: Someone who arranges things or repairs problems, sometimes shadily.
note: From fix plus -er. In film and journalism, a fixer arranges local contacts for visiting crews. It also names a photographic chemical.
hints: A person who arranges things quietly.
Also a darkroom chemical that sets a photo.

definition: Full of bubbles.
note: From fizz plus -y. The word imitates the sound of bubbles escaping.
hints: A cola is described this way.
Sparkling water is this.
example: Fizzy drinks are also known as carbonated beverages.

definition: A long, narrow sea inlet between steep cliffs.
note: From Norwegian fjord, from Old Norse fjordr, related to ford. Norway is famous for them.
hints: Norway's coast is full of them.
A deep water channel cut by a glacier.
origin: Norwegian fjord, from Old Norse fjǫrðr
example: Slartibartfast's favorite creation was the fjords of Norway.

definition: A press agent; also a barrage of criticism.
note: Used in the US for a publicist, a sense whose origin is uncertain. Do not confuse it with 'flak', the anti-aircraft fire.
hints: Defends a celebrity to reporters.
Spokesperson for hire.

definition: To wave one's arms wildly.
note: From Middle English flayle, a tool for threshing grain, from Old English fligel. A flailing arm swings like that tool.
hints: What you do with your arms when you slip.
A farm tool once used to beat the grain.

definition: A natural talent or stylish ability.
note: From Old French flair, 'scent', from flairier, 'to smell'. A flair was first a nose for something.
hints: Style or a knack for doing things well.
A chef with a natural gift for presentation.
origin: Old French flair, from Latin flāgrō
example: He has a flair for mathematics.

definition: Breaking off in thin pieces; or unreliable.
note: From flake plus -y. The sense of unreliable is informal and describes someone who cancels plans.
hints: A pastry like a croissant is this.
A friend who cancels at the last minute.

definition: The visible, glowing part of a fire.
note: From Old French flamme, from Latin flamma. It also names an old sweetheart.
hints: Flickers from a candle.
What a match lights.
origin: Old French flame, from Latin flammula

definition: The side of an animal or army.
note: From Old French flanc, probably of Frankish origin. A flank steak is cut from the side of the animal.
hints: An army tries to attack the enemy's.
The side of a horse's body.
origin: Old English flanc, from Old French flanc

definition: A sudden brief burst of light.
note: Partly from Middle English flasshen, 'to sprinkle, splash', likely imitative. It also means a very short time.
hints: A camera makes one in the dark.
Lightning does it in a storm.

definition: Showy in a way meant to impress.
note: From flash plus -y. A flash is a sudden brightness, so flashy means eye-catching.
hints: A gold watch and shiny car.
A loud tie that grabs attention.
example: The dancers wore flashy costumes featuring shiny sequins in many vibrant colors.

definition: A narrow-necked bottle.
note: From Old English flasce and Medieval Latin flasco, 'bottle'. It names a lab vessel and a pocket bottle.
hints: A scientist heats one over a flame.
A small metal bottle for a hot drink.
origin: Old English flasce, from Medieval Latin flascō

definition: The taste of something.
note: From Old French flaor, 'smell'.
hints: Vanilla or mint.
Ice cream comes in many.

definition: A tiny spot or mark.
note: From Old Norse flekkr, 'spot'. It is often used for specks of paint or colour.
hints: A tiny speck of paint on a shirt.
A small spot of colour.

definition: A sheep's wool coat, or a soft warm jacket made of fabric like it.
note: From Old English fleos. In the verb sense, to fleece is to swindle someone, as if shearing them like a sheep.
hints: Jason sought the golden one in Greek myth.
A cosy jacket for walkers.

definition: A group of ships or vehicles; or swift.
note: From Old English fleot, 'ship', related to float. The adjective sense, 'swift', has a separate Norse origin.
hints: A navy's ships all together.
A taxi company's cars.

definition: The soft part of a body.
note: From Old English flaesc, a Germanic word. It is the soft tissue covering the bones.
hints: The part of a fruit you eat.
What lies between skin and bone.

definition: A quick light movement or touch.
note: From Middle English flykke, 'a light blow'. It is imitative, like a snap of the fingers.
hints: What you do to a switch.
A film is also called one.
example: He removed the speck of dust with a flick of his finger.

definition: A journey by air, or the act of flying; also a running away.
note: From Old English flyht, related to fly. The 'escape' sense comes from a different word, fleon.
hints: What an airline sells.
A set of stairs, or an escape.
example: He boarded the flight to Miami.

definition: Thin and weak; easily broken.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from flimflam, though that is unproven. It also names the thin paper used for carbon copies.
hints: Describes a cheap umbrella in the wind.
A weak excuse is called by this word.

definition: To throw something carelessly; or a brief affair.
note: From Middle English fling, from a Norse source. Another sense is a brief romance.
hints: To toss a hat in the air.
A short and carefree romance.

definition: A hard grey stone that makes sparks when struck.
note: From Old English flint, a Germanic word. Early fire-lighters and guns used it.
hints: Early people struck it with steel to make a spark.
A stone used with a firestarter.
example: He used flint to make a fire.

definition: Playfully showing romantic interest.
note: From flirt plus -y. Flirt first meant to flick away sharply.
hints: A wink and a smile at a party.
Playful teasing between two people.

definition: To rest on top of liquid without sinking.
note: From Old English flotian, 'to float'. It is related to fleet.
hints: What a cork does in water.
A parade vehicle is called this.

definition: A group of birds or sheep.
note: From Old English flocc, 'group of people or animals'. It was once used for people as well.
hints: Sheep gather in one.
Birds fly in one.

definition: An overflow of water onto land.
note: From Old English flod, related to flow. It also means any overwhelming amount.
hints: Noah's story features a great one.
What heavy rain may cause by a river.

definition: The surface you walk on indoors.
note: From Old English flor, 'floor, pavement, deck'. It also names the level of a building.
hints: Sweepers and mops spend their lives on it.
A level in a tall building.

definition: Soft and drooping, not stiff.
note: From flop plus -y. A floppy disk was a thin square of flexible plastic used to store data.
hints: Bunny ears flop over like this.
A square disk that held files before USB sticks.
example: Floppy disks are noted for their relatively slow speed and small capacity and low price.

definition: The plants of a region.
note: From Latin Flora, a Roman goddess of flowers. It is the plant counterpart of fauna.
hints: Fauna's plant-loving partner.
All the plants of a place.
example: The flora of southern California.

definition: Relating to flowers.
note: From Latin flos, 'flower'.
hints: Pattern on a summer dress.
Scented like blooms.

definition: A thread used to clean between teeth.
note: Of unclear origin, perhaps from French floche, 'tuft of wool'. It also names soft silk fibre.
hints: Dentists tell you to use it daily.
Candy spun from sugar is named for it.

definition: Ground grain, used for baking.
note: The same word as flower, because flour was 'the flower', or finest part, of the meal. The spellings only separated in the 1800s.
hints: What bread is baked from.
Wheat is ground into it.

definition: To openly disregard a rule.
note: Perhaps from Middle English flouten, 'to play the flute', hence to mock. It is often mixed up with flaunt.
hints: A driver may do this to a speed limit.
To show contempt for a law.

definition: The colourful part of a plant that makes seeds.
note: From Old French flor, from Latin flos. Flour was originally the same word, meaning the finest part of the wheat.
hints: A rose, for example.
Same word as flour, once.

definition: Having travelled through the air; the past participle of fly.
note: From Old English flogen, past participle of fleogan, 'to fly'. A bird that has left the nest is said to have this.
hints: What a bird has done once it has left.
Follows 'has' or 'have' for a trip by air.
origin: Old English flogen, from Old English flēogan

definition: Speaking a language smoothly and easily.
note: From Latin fluens, 'flowing'. A fluent speaker sounds like flowing water.
hints: What you hope to be after years abroad.
A native speaker of a language.
example: She's fluent in French.

definition: Soft light material like down.
note: From earlier floow, 'down, nap, lint', from West Flemish. It also means a minor mistake or trivial content.
hints: What a pillow is stuffed with.
A cat's loose hair on a sofa.

definition: Light and soft, like fluff.
note: From fluff plus -y. A cloud, a cat or a pancake can be this.
hints: A kitten's fur, or a pancake.
What a cloud or a cat's coat looks like.
example: I like my scrambled eggs to be light and fluffy in texture.

definition: A substance that flows.
note: From Latin fluidus, from fluere, 'to flow'. It covers liquids and gases.
hints: Water or air is this.
Neither a solid nor held in a fixed shape.

definition: A narrow channel carrying water.
note: From Old French flum and Latin flumen, 'river', from fluere, 'to flow'. Water parks borrowed it for rides.
hints: A log ride at a theme park goes down one.
A man-made channel for carrying water.
origin: Old French flum, from Latin flumen

definition: To fail an exam or class.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to funk or flinch. It is American student slang from the 1800s.
hints: What a student does with a bad grade.
The opposite of pass.
example: He flunked math, again.

definition: A brief burst of snow, wind or sudden activity.
note: Possibly an American blend of flutter and hurry, though it may come from an old word meaning 'scatter'.
hints: Light snow that is gone by lunch.
A burst of activity just before a deadline.
example: He had to close the window against the flurries.

definition: To turn red; or to clean with rushing water.
note: Of uncertain origin; one sense is to startle birds from cover. Flush also means level, or having plenty of money.
hints: What you do to a toilet.
Your face does this when you blush.

definition: A woodwind played by blowing across a hole.
note: From Old French flaute, of uncertain origin. Champagne is served in a tall glass of the same name.
hints: The Pied Piper played one.
A slim wind instrument.
origin: Old French flaute, from Old Provençal flaüt

definition: A close pass by a spacecraft or aircraft.
note: Formed from the phrase fly by.
hints: A probe's quick visit to a planet.
An air show feature, or a space mission's pass.

definition: Something or someone that flies; also a paper handbill.
note: Built from fly plus -er. The paper sense, a leaflet handed out in the street, is a separate later use.
hints: A thin paper handed out on the street.
A frequent one collects airline miles.

definition: Full of foam or froth.
note: From Old English famig, 'frothy', built from foam plus -y. Beer, surf and a shaken soda can all be this.
hints: Describes the head on a beer.
Surf or soap suds might look this way.
example: He jumped overboard into the foamy waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

definition: Relating to a point of attention.
note: From focus plus -al, borrowed from New Latin. It's used for the main point.
hints: A ___ point is the centre of attention.
Describing the main point of a camera lens.

definition: The point of attention or clarity.
note: From Latin focus, 'hearth, fireplace', related to fuel. Kepler used it for the point where light converges.
hints: What you adjust on a camera.
To concentrate on one thing.

definition: Food for farm animals such as hay.
note: From Old English fodor, related to food. Metaphorically, 'cannon fodder' is soldiers sent to die in great numbers.
hints: Stored in a barn for cows over winter.
'Cannon' sometimes comes before it to describe soldiers.

definition: Covered in thick mist; or vague.
note: From fog plus -y, originally meaning 'covered in long grass or marshy'. Foggy now describes mist or confused thoughts.
hints: A morning when you can barely see ahead.
How your memory feels when you're tired.

definition: To pass off something unwanted on someone.
note: Probably from old Dutch vuisten, 'to take in the hand', from vuist, 'fist'.
hints: A seller might do this with a worthless item.
To force an unwanted thing on someone sneakily.

definition: A cover for papers, or a place for files on a computer.
note: From fold plus -er.
hints: Holds documents.
Icon on a desktop.
example: I keep all my schoolwork in a yellow folder.

definition: People, especially family or friends.
note: From Old English folc. The word is casual, and also used for one's parents.
hints: A friendly word for people.
What your parents may be called.
example: They're just country folk.

definition: To go after or behind.
note: From Old English folgian.
hints: Come after in a line.
Tag along behind someone.
example: She left the room and I followed.

definition: A foolish act or idea.
note: From Old French folie, 'madness', from fol, 'mad'. It also names a decorative building with no use.
hints: A rash plan that was bound to fail.
A tower built just for show on an estate.

definition: With affection; in a tender way.
note: Formed from fond plus -ly. Fond once meant foolish, so doing something fondly was doing it foolishly.
hints: How you recall a happy childhood.
A way to sign off a letter to someone dear.
example: I have loved the stars too fondly to be fearful of the night.

definition: A person with a keen interest in good food.
note: From food plus -ie. It was popularised by The Official Foodie Handbook, published in 1984.
hints: Posts pictures of every dish.
Queues for a new restaurant opening.
example: We self-professed foodies liked to meet in restaurants and talk like experts about what we were eating.

definition: Text repeated at the bottom of every page of a document or web page.
note: From foot plus -er. It mirrors header, the matching strip at the top.
hints: Page numbers often sit in it.
The opposite strip from a header on a webpage.

definition: A casual word for football.
note: From foot plus -y. In Australia it means Aussie rules or rugby.
hints: A casual word for a match.
A game on a pitch with goals.

definition: To search about for food, or the food for animals such as horses.
note: From Old French fourage, from fuerre, 'fodder', ultimately from a Frankish word related to the English food.
hints: What squirrels do in autumn.
Mushroom hunters do this in the woods.

definition: A short, bold venture into new territory.
note: From Middle English forrayen, 'to pillage', from a word for a raider. It began as a military raid.
hints: A raid into enemy land.
A first try at a new field, like a chef's into baking.

definition: To order someone not to do something.
note: From Old English forbeodan, with for- meaning 'against' and beodan, 'to command'. 'Heaven forbid' is a wish that something never happen.
hints: What a stern sign saying 'No Entry' does.
A parent who says 'you may not' does it.

definition: Strength or power.
note: From Old French force and Late Latin fortia, from Latin fortis, 'strong'. It also names a push or pull in physics.
hints: What Jedi use in Star Wars.
A push or pull that moves an object.
origin: Old French force, from Latin fortis

definition: A large area covered with trees.
note: From Old French forest, from Latin foris, 'outside', first land set aside as hunting preserve.
hints: Large expanse of trees.
Robin Hood's Sherwood was one.
origin: Old French forest, from Early Medieval Latin forestis

definition: To lose from memory.
note: From Old English forgietan, 'to lose one's hold on'.
hints: Knots in a handkerchief were once tied to avoid doing this.
Where did I leave my keys, you wonder, having done it.
example: I have forgotten most of the things I learned in school.

definition: To do without something.
note: From Middle English forgon, 'to pass up', from Old English forgan. The for- is the same as in forbid.
hints: To skip dessert, for example.
To give up a pleasure.
example: I've had to forgo my student discount in exchange for taking the job.

definition: Following strict rules or fashion; official.
note: From Latin formalis, from forma, 'shape'.
hints: Ballgowns and tuxedos suit this kind of occasion.
Black tie is a dress code for it.
origin: Old French formel, from Latin fōrmālis

definition: The way something is arranged or laid out.
note: From Latin formatus, 'formed', via French.
hints: Layout of a document.
Wiping a disk resets this.
origin: French format, from New Latin liber

definition: Earlier, or the first of two things mentioned.
note: From Middle English formere, a comparative of forme, 'first'.
hints: The opposite of latter.
Used for the earlier of two things.
example: The novel was made into a film in 1943 and again in 1967; I prefer the former version to the latter one.

definition: Something someone does especially well.
note: From French fort, 'strong', influenced by Italian forte, from Latin fortis. In music, it means to play loudly.
hints: Cooking is her ___, you might say.
A musical direction meaning loud.

definition: Onward or outward.
note: From Old English forth, 'forward'. It appears in 'back and ___' and in old phrases like 'go ___ and multiply'.
hints: What goes with 'back and' in a phrase.
The word in 'set ___' on a journey.

definition: The number after thirty-nine.
note: From Old English feowertig, 'four tens'. It is built from four and the old word -tig meaning tens.
hints: Twice twenty.
Ali Baba had that many thieves.

definition: A place or meeting for public discussion.
note: From Latin forum, 'marketplace, public place'. The Roman Forum was the heart of the city. It is also an online discussion board.
hints: A place for open discussion online.
The central square of ancient Rome.

definition: A pit or hollow in the body; also a cat-like predator of Madagascar.
note: Latin for 'ditch'. The animal's name is a separate borrowing from Malagasy.
hints: A depression in a bone.
A ditch, in Latin.

definition: The preserved remains of ancient life in rock.
note: From Latin fossilis, 'dug up'.
hints: What a palaeontologist finds.
An imprint of a trilobite.

definition: To encourage growth, or to raise a child who is not your own.
note: From Old English fostrian, 'to nourish', related to food.
hints: Look after a child in your home temporarily.
Parent who is not the birth one.
example: Foster our children's well-being and education.

definition: Past tense of find; also, to establish an institution.
note: The past tense comes from Old English fand. The verb meaning 'to establish' comes from Latin fundare, 'to lay a base', and is a different word.
hints: What you did once you discovered the lost keys.
A word that also means to start a company.

definition: Coming after third.
note: From Old English feortha.
hints: Number four in a line.
Next after the bronze medal.

definition: A person who hunts wild birds.
note: From Old English fuglere, from fugol, 'bird'. The word fowl is from the same source.
hints: Someone with a net or gun after ducks.
A hunter of wildfowl in old country life.

definition: An entrance hall in a building.
note: Borrowed from French foyer, 'hearth', from Latin focus. In French it first meant the fireplace room where actors warmed up.
hints: The room just inside the front door.
Where a theatre audience gathers at interval.
example: In the foyer is a vending machine selling bars of chocolate.

definition: Weak and easily hurt.
note: From Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis, 'breakable'. It is a cousin of fragile.
hints: An elderly person who needs assistance.
Easily broken or damaged.
origin: Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis

definition: A structure that holds something in place.
note: From Old English framian, 'to be helpful, profit'. The Middle English sense was to construct or put together.
hints: What a picture hangs in.
A bed's supporting structure.

definition: A former unit of money in France and Switzerland.
note: From French franc, 'free', a phrase first stamped on coins. Switzerland still uses it.
hints: Currency in Switzerland.
Money in Paris before the euro.
example: The last 50 franc note, released in 1993, features Saint-Exupéry and a depiction of The Little Prince.

definition: Deliberate trickery for gain.
note: From Old French fraude and Latin fraus, 'deceit, injury'. It has been recorded since 1345.
hints: Selling a fake painting as real is this.
A crime of lying to get money.
origin: Old French fraude, from Latin fraus

definition: Something very unusual.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from a Germanic word meaning quick or bold. It first meant a sudden whim.
hints: A ___ storm hits without warning.
An unusual accident.
example: The two-headed calf was a freak.

definition: Strange or odd, sometimes in a spooky way.
note: From freak plus -y. Freak itself first meant a sudden whim or prank.
hints: A movie where a mother and daughter swap bodies has Friday attached to its name.
Description of a bizarre coincidence.
example: I've heard the props and costumes in this play are quite freaky.

definition: Without restriction.
note: From free plus -ly.
hints: Not held back.
Moving about with no limits.

definition: More free; with fewer limits.
note: The comparative of free, from Old English freo. The same word also names someone who sets another free.
hints: Comparing two kinds of liberty.
A word one might use for a bird out of its cage.

definition: To turn into ice, or to stop moving.
note: From Old English freosan.
hints: What water does at zero degrees.
Stand perfectly still.
example: It didn't freeze this winter, but last winter was very harsh.

definition: A state of wild, uncontrolled excitement.
note: From Greek phrenitis, 'inflammation of the brain'. Feeding sharks are said to enter one.
hints: What a shark attack creates in the water.
What shoppers fall into on a sale's first morning.
origin: Old French frenesie, from Latin phrenesis
example: She went into a cleaning frenzy to prepare for the unexpected guests.

definition: A painting made on wet plaster.
note: From Italian fresco, 'fresh', because the artist paints on fresh plaster. It is a doublet of fresh.
hints: Michelangelo painted one on the Sistine ceiling.
The pigment becomes part of the wall.

definition: New or not stale.
note: From Old English fersc, 'fresh, pure, sweet'. It once described water as well as food.
hints: Bread straight from the oven.
The opposite of stale.
origin: Old English fersċ, from Middle English freshen
example: He followed the fresh hoofprints to find the deer.

definition: A member of certain religious orders who live among the people.
note: From Old French frere, from Latin frater, 'brother'. Friars owned nothing and begged, unlike monks who stayed in one monastery.
hints: Like a monk, but more often out among the public.
Tuck is the famous one in Sherwood Forest.
example: The hooded clouds, like friars, tell their beads in drops of rain.

definition: An appliance that keeps food cold.
note: A clipping of refrigerator.
hints: Cold box in a kitchen.
Where milk is kept.

definition: Cooked in hot oil or fat.
note: The past tense of fry, from Old French frire, from Latin frigere, 'to roast or fry'. In slang it also means worn out.
hints: How chicken or eggs may be served.
Cooked in a pan with oil.

definition: A person you like and trust.
note: From Old English freond, from a verb meaning 'to love'.
hints: A close companion.
Someone who is on your side.
example: He was my best friend at the university.

definition: A sudden feeling of fear.
note: From Old English fyrhto, 'fear'. A fright can also be a ridiculous-looking person.
hints: A jump-scare gives you one.
A person who sees a ghost gets one.

definition: A decorative gathered edge of fabric.
note: Of uncertain origin. 'No-___s' means a plain service without extras.
hints: A pleated edge on a dress.
An unnecessary extra.

definition: A decorative border of loose threads; or the edge of a group.
note: From Old French frenge, from Latin fimbria.
hints: Edge of a scarf.
British word for bangs.
origin: Old French frenge, from Latin fimbriae

definition: To search someone by patting down.
note: From Middle French frisque, 'lively, merry'. A frisky animal skips about, and then to pat someone's clothes was added.
hints: What a security guard may do to you.
To skip about playfully, as a puppy does.
origin: Middle French frisque, from Old High German frisc
example: The police frisked everyone at the airport.

definition: A state of being broken, used in 'on the fritz'.
note: The phrase is first recorded in 1902. Its origin is unknown, though the German name Fritz has been suggested.
hints: What a machine does when it is going wrong.
Found in an idiom about broken machines.

definition: The leaf of a fern or palm.
note: Borrowed from Latin frons, 'leafy branch'. It is usually seen with ferns and palms.
hints: What a palm tree waves.
A large feathery leaf.
example: The centipede scuttled under the fallen palm frond.

definition: The forward-facing part.
note: From Old French front and Latin frons, 'forehead'. The face of something was its forehead.
hints: The opposite of back.
Where a battle line is drawn.
origin: Old French front, from Latin frōns

definition: Covered in frost; very cold; unfriendly.
note: From Old English forstig, formed from forst, 'frost'.
hints: A snowman in a famous song is described this way.
A cold look or reception also earns the label.
example: The frosty pumpkin is the sign of the end of the growing season, soon the greenery will wither and harvest end for the year.

definition: A mass of small bubbles.
note: From Old Norse frodha, 'froth, foam'. It is also used for trivial matters.
hints: The top of a cappuccino.
Sea foam on a wave.

definition: To wrinkle your brow in displeasure.
note: From Middle English frounen, 'to frown', with an old sense of a threatening look. The opposite of a smile.
hints: The opposite of a smile.
What your face does when you're annoyed.
origin: Old French froignier, from Medieval Latin fruncāre

definition: Turned to ice, or stuck in place.
note: The past participle of freeze.
hints: Solid with cold.
Immobile with fear.
example: The mammoth has been frozen for ten thousand years.

definition: Careful with money and avoiding waste.
note: From Latin frugalis, 'thrifty', from the word for fruit or produce. It replaced an English phrase meaning 'spare-handed'.
hints: Describes someone who saves leftovers and clips coupons.
Thrifty and economical, as with a meal.
example: There's a fine line between being frugal and being cheap.

definition: The sweet seed-bearing part of a plant.
note: From Latin fructus, 'enjoyment, produce'. It also means a result, as in the fruits of labour.
hints: An apple or a pear.
What a tree produces.
origin: Old French fruit, from Latin fruitus

definition: Tasting or smelling of fruit.
note: From fruit plus -y. Wine writers use it for a fresh flavour; in British slang it can mean cheeky or suggestive.
hints: A wine described as having berry notes.
A lollipop might come in this flavour.

definition: A pot or machine used for deep-frying.
note: From fry plus -er. An air one cooks with hot air instead of oil.
hints: A kitchen appliance for chips.
Where the chips cook in oil.
example: He learned to work the fryer as part of becoming a competent cook for a commercial kitchen.

definition: A soft, sweet candy; or to avoid being exact.
note: Probably a variant of fadge, 'to fit together'. The verb means to bend facts and the candy sense came from mixing.
hints: Chocolate treat sold in slabs.
To fake or bend the truth.

definition: A piece of music in which voices chase each other.
note: From Italian fuga, 'flight', from Latin fugere, 'to flee'. The voices seem to flee and pursue one another.
hints: Bach wrote famous ones.
A state of amnesia where someone wanders off.

definition: Completely; to the greatest extent.
note: From Old English fullice, built from full plus -ly. It is used to stress that nothing is missing.
hints: Not partly, but the whole way.
Often goes before 'booked' or 'aware'.
example: He is fully capable of meeting his responsibilities.

definition: To handle something clumsily; to drop a ball.
note: Probably from a Scandinavian or Low German word. In American football it means losing the ball after catching it.
hints: Searching for keys in a dark bag.
A running back losing the ball in football.

definition: Relating to fungi.
note: From fungus plus -al. Athlete's foot is a fungal infection.
hints: An infection like athlete's foot is this kind.
Describes mould and mushrooms collectively.
example: Doctors determined that the cause of the itchy rash was fungal rather than bacterial.

definition: Mushrooms, moulds and yeasts, as a group; the plural of fungus.
note: Borrowed from Latin, where fungi is the plural of fungus. Fungi form their own kingdom, separate from plants and animals.
hints: Mushrooms and moulds belong to this group.
The plural of a word for a mushroom.
example: Fungi constitute a completely independent kingdom of life.

definition: A living organism such as a mushroom, mould or yeast.
note: From Latin fungus, 'mushroom'. Fungi are neither plants nor animals.
hints: Toadstools and mildew belong to this kingdom.
Athlete's foot is caused by this.
example: That fungus is deadly, but many others are actually edible.

definition: Stylishly offbeat; or smelly.
note: From funk plus -y. Funk once meant a strong smell, then a style of music with a heavy groove.
hints: Describes music with a heavy bass groove.
Eccentric and cool.
example: She likes funky clothes.

definition: A cone with a tube at the narrow end, used for pouring into small openings.
note: Probably from Old Provencal fonilh, from Latin infundibulum. The word also names a ship's smokestack.
hints: What you use to pour oil into an engine.
A steamship's chimney also goes by this.

definition: Amusing; or strange.
note: From fun plus -y. It describes jokes, but also something odd, as in 'a funny smell'.
hints: What a good joke is.
Odd, as in 'that's ___ - the door was open'.
example: I know you'll enjoy chatting with her — she's really funny and smart.

definition: A wave of public outrage or excitement.
note: From Latin furor, 'rage, madness', from furere, 'to rage'. It is related to the word fury.
hints: The public outcry over a scandal.
A burst of uproar.
origin: Middle French fureur, from Latin furor
example: The story of the princess's affair caused a furor among journalists.
