definition: Covered with soft hair.
note: From fur plus -y. It describes animals and toys.
hints: A teddy bear is.
Soft and covered in fur.
example: His treatment of our furry friends was nothing short of appalling.

definition: A merging, or a nuclear reaction joining atoms.
note: From Latin fusio, 'a pouring', from fundere, 'to pour'.
hints: How the sun makes energy.
A blend of cooking styles.
origin: Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem

definition: Hard to please or too concerned with small details.
note: From fuss plus -y. It describes babies who cry and people who care too much about details.
hints: A child who won't eat vegetables.
Too particular about tiny details.

definition: Pointless, because it cannot succeed.
note: From Latin futilis, 'leaky' or 'easily poured out'. A futile effort is like pouring water into a sieve.
hints: Bailing out a sinking boat with a teaspoon.
The Borg tell their targets that resisting is this.
origin: Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis

definition: A thin Japanese mattress, or a sofa bed in the West.
note: From Japanese futon, itself from a Chinese word for a meditation cushion.
hints: Sofa that folds into a bed.
Japanese bedding laid on the floor.
example: It would be a good idea for you to get out from the futon!

definition: The time yet to come.
note: From Latin futurus, 'about to be'.
hints: What lies ahead.
Tomorrow and beyond.
origin: Old French futur, from Latin futūrus

definition: Covered with soft short fibres; or unclear.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may be from fuzz plus -y, or the other way around. It also describes a blurry picture.
hints: A peach's skin is this way.
A blurry photo is this.
example: His head fuzzed like a dandelion gone to seed.

definition: Talkative.
note: From gab plus -y. Gab is an old word for chatter.
hints: Someone who talks a lot.
A chatterbox.
example: Gabby Pahinui sang in Hawaiian.

definition: The triangular wall at the end of a pitched roof.
note: From Old Norse gafl. Many old houses show one at the front.
hints: The triangle under a sloped roof.
The end wall of a cottage under the ridge.

definition: A small clever device.
note: Of uncertain origin; it was recorded in sailors' use in the 1800s, with a possible link to a French word for a tool.
hints: A handy tool with a clever function.
A cooks' kitchen tool, like an avocado slicer.
example: He bought a neat new gadget for shredding potatoes.

definition: An embarrassing mistake in public.
note: Borrowed from French gaffe, 'blunder', and a doublet of gaff. Politicians dread making one.
hints: Calling someone by the wrong name, perhaps.
A social blunder.
example: He committed a gaffe when he asked whether she was pregnant.

definition: In a cheerful, lively way.
note: Built from gay plus -ly. Gay came from Old French gai, and long meant 'merry' and 'bright'.
hints: How a bright flag might wave.
In a lively and bright mood.
example: How gaily the kids skip and play, whilst I sink into listless repose!

definition: A huge system of stars, such as the Milky Way.
note: From Greek galaxias, 'milky circle', from gala, 'milk'.
hints: Home to billions of stars.
Name comes from the Greek for milk.
origin: Old French galaxie, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας; in English since the 19th century
example: `extragalactic nebula' is a former name for `galaxy'.

definition: A ship's kitchen; also a long, low ship driven by oars.
note: Via Old French and Latin from a Byzantine Greek word for a type of ship. The ship's kitchen sense came from the ship itself.
hints: Where meals are cooked on a boat or aircraft.
Slaves or prisoners once chained themselves to the oars of the ancient kind.
origin: Old French galee, from Ancient Greek γαλέη

definition: A unit of liquid volume.
note: From Anglo-Norman galon, a measure.
hints: Eight pints in Britain.
What a milk jug may hold.

definition: A horse's fastest running pace.
note: From Old French galoper, from a Frankish phrase meaning 'to run well'. It is related to leap.
hints: All four hooves leave the ground.
The Lone Ranger rode off at one.

definition: In great abundance.
note: Borrowed from Irish go leor, 'enough'. Unusually for English, it comes after its noun, as in 'bargains galore'.
hints: Follows its noun, as in bargains.
A buffet might offer food in this amount.
origin: Irish go leor, from Scottish Gaelic gu leòr; in English since the late 17th century

definition: An opening move that risks something for an advantage, or any clever ploy.
note: From Italian gambetto, 'a tripping up', from gamba, 'leg'. The chess sense, where a pawn is sacrificed, gave the general meaning.
hints: A queen's one is a famous chess opening.
A Netflix chess drama is named after one.
example: Her clever gambit gave her an advantage.

definition: To bet money, or to take a risk.
note: Probably from gamen, an old form of game.
hints: What a casino invites you to do.
Take a chance.

definition: A person who plays games, especially video games.
note: From game plus -er. The word now mostly means a video game enthusiast.
hints: Someone with a headset and a console.
A person with high scores.

definition: The third letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: Borrowed from Greek gamma. In science it names rays of high energy.
hints: Comes after alpha and beta.
A type of ray emitted by radioactive material.

definition: The complete range of something.
note: From gamma ut, a medieval note name that meant the lowest note of the scale. It grew to mean the whole range.
hints: 'To run the ___' is to experience everything from one end to the other.
The full range of notes in a scale.
example: A face that expressed a gamut of emotions.

definition: Cannabis, as a slang word.
note: Borrowed from Hindi ganja, from Sanskrit for hemp.
hints: A slang name used in Jamaica.
A word from Hindi for hemp.

definition: A building for keeping cars, or a repair shop.
note: From French garer, 'to shelter'.
hints: Where you park at home.
Mechanics work in one.
origin: French garage, from Old Norse varask

definition: A plot where plants are grown.
note: From Old French jardin, from a Germanic word related to yard.
hints: Roses grow there.
A lawn and flower beds behind a house.

definition: A strong-smelling bulb used in cooking.
note: From Old English garleac, 'spear leek'.
hints: Vampires are said to hate it.
A clove added to pasta sauce.

definition: To gather or collect, such as praise or votes.
note: From Old French gernier, 'granary', from Latin granarium. It was first a place to store grain.
hints: What an actor does with award nominations.
To collect, as a farmer once stored harvest.
origin: Old French gernier, from Latin grānārium

definition: A deep red gemstone; also its colour.
note: From Old French grenat, 'pomegranate-coloured', because the stones resemble pomegranate seeds. It is a doublet of grenade.
hints: The birthstone of January.
Pomegranate seeds share its deep red.

definition: Full of gas.
note: From gas plus -y. It describes a fizzy drink or a bloated stomach.
hints: A can of soda that's been shaken.
Bloated after beans.

definition: To bring together, or to pick.
note: From Old English gaderian.
hints: Bring people or things together.
Pick ripe fruit from a tree.

definition: Short for alligator.
note: A clipping of alligator, from Spanish el lagarto, 'the lizard'. It is also a nickname for a Florida team.
hints: A reptile in a swamp.
A snappy swamp reptile.
example: Stefan went to the canal to see the gators.

definition: Flashy and tasteless.
note: From Middle English gaudi, from a word for an ornament or trinket.
hints: A very bright, over-decorated outfit.
Too flashy for good taste.
origin: Old French gaudie, from Old French gaude
example: They were all trapped out in the gaudiest of clothes.

definition: An instrument for measuring.
note: From Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French gauger, 'to measure'. To gauge is also to estimate someone's mood.
hints: A fuel one shows how much is left.
To estimate how people feel.

definition: Thin and haggard.
note: From Middle English gaunt, 'lean, slender', of uncertain origin. It's used for people who look drawn and hungry.
hints: A face worn from illness.
Looking bony and tired.
example: A nightmare population of gaunt men and skeletal boys.

definition: A thin, see-through fabric.
note: From French gaze, from Arabic qazz, 'silk'. It is used in bandages and curtains.
hints: A bandage wrapped over a cut.
A very light, open-weave cotton.

definition: A small mallet used by a judge or chair.
note: From the Old English gafol, 'tribute, rent', for one sense; the mallet's own origin is uncertain. Auctioneers use one too.
hints: A judge bangs one to call order.
An auctioneer uses it to close a sale.

definition: Awkward and clumsy in movement.
note: From gawk plus -y. A gawky teenager hasn't yet grown into their limbs.
hints: A teenager who has grown too quickly.
All elbows and knees.
example: A gawky lad with long ungainly legs.

definition: More cheerful or brightly coloured; comparative of gay.
note: From gay, which came from Old French gai, 'joyful'.
hints: Merrier in mood.
Brighter and more festive than before.

definition: A person who looks steadily at something.
note: Built from gaze plus -er. Stargazers are the best known kind.
hints: Might be found staring at the sky.
The 'star' kind looks upward at night.

definition: A small, mostly nocturnal lizard with sticky toe pads.
note: English probably took it from Dutch gekko in the 1700s. Many geckos can climb smooth walls and ceilings.
hints: A small lizard found in warm places.
Known for walking up walls and glass.
example: Salamanders are amphibians, whereas geckos are reptiles.

definition: Showing an enthusiastic, slightly awkward devotion to technical or niche interests.
note: Built from geek plus the -y ending. It was once an insult but is now often worn proudly.
hints: Describes someone absorbed in gadgets or fandoms.
Said of a person who loves sci-fi and coding.

definition: Spirit, especially of an age or group, from German.
note: Borrowed from German, and a cousin of ghost.
hints: German word for spirit, as in the spirit of an age.
Cousin of the English word ghost.

definition: Whether a person is male, female or another identity; also a grammatical category.
note: From Old French gendre, 'kind' or 'sort', from Latin genus.
hints: Masculine or feminine in a language.
Shares a root with genre.
origin: Old French gendre, from Latin genere; in English since the 20th century

definition: A magical spirit who grants wishes.
note: From French génie, which was matched to the Arabic jinn. English picked it up through translations of the Arabian Nights.
hints: Lives in a lamp in fairy tales.
Often grants three wishes.
example: The genie remained trapped in the magic lamp for centuries.

definition: A person of extraordinary intellect or talent.
note: From Latin genius, a guardian spirit that watched over each person from birth.
hints: Einstein is called one.
Its Latin root was a protective spirit.
origin: Latin genius, from Old Latin genō
example: He has a genius for interior decorating.

definition: An organism's complete set of genes.
note: A blend of gene and chromosome.
hints: Sequenced in a famous project.
DNA's whole instruction book.
example: The human genome contains approximately three billion chemical base pairs.

definition: A category of art, music or writing with shared style.
note: Borrowed unchanged from French, from the same Latin root as gender and genus.
hints: Western, horror and romance are examples.
A label that sorts books and films.
example: The still life has been a popular genre in painting since the 17th century.

definition: Kind and soft, not rough.
note: From Old French gentil, 'of noble birth'.
hints: A soft touch.
A mild breeze.
origin: Old French gentil, from Latin gentilis

definition: In a soft, mild way.
note: From gentle plus -ly.
hints: Without force.
How you should handle a sleeping baby.

definition: People of good social standing, just below the nobility.
note: From Old French genterie, formed from gent, 'well-born'.
hints: The class of landowners in a Jane Austen novel.
Squires and country landowners belonged to it.
example: Most authors come from petty gentry.

definition: A category in biology between family and species.
note: Latin for 'kind' or 'birth'. In Homo sapiens, Homo is this.
hints: Homo is this for humans.
The first part of a species' scientific name.

definition: An outfit, especially a strange one.
note: From the verb phrase get up, as in to dress oneself up.
hints: A costume you might raise an eyebrow at.
What a clown wears.

definition: A Muslim warrior, especially one honoured for victory.
note: From Arabic for 'raider'.
hints: A historic title for a veteran fighter.
Title taken by some Ottoman rulers.

definition: A district where a minority group lives, originally for Jews in European cities.
note: From Italian ghetto, the name of the Venetian quarter for Jews, first established in 1516.
hints: A historic walled area in Venice.
Area where a group is confined or concentrated.

definition: A spirit said to feed on the dead.
note: Borrowed from French, which got it from Arabic ghul via Persian. It was first a desert demon in Arabic stories.
hints: Haunts graveyards in horror stories.
A creature that robs graves.

definition: A being of enormous size, especially in myth.
note: Through Old French from Latin gigas, which came from Greek gigas, the name of the mythical race that fought the gods.
hints: Jack climbed a beanstalk to meet one.
Anything much bigger than its kind.

definition: Dizzy, or lightheaded with excitement.
note: Middle English gidi once meant mad or possessed by a spirit, long before it became merely dizzy.
hints: How a fast spin on a roundabout can leave you.
Feeling silly with delight.

definition: To laugh in a light, silly way.
note: Probably imitates the sound itself, appearing in English in the early 1500s.
hints: Spreads through a classroom when the teacher makes a slip.
Often stifled behind a hand.
example: The girls giggled when the rock star came into the classroom.

definition: A casual way of saying 'give me'.
note: A written form of the spoken reduction of give me. In sport it can be an easy shot.
hints: A short way to ask for something.
An easy putt in golf.

definition: A spicy root used in cooking, or a reddish-orange colour.
note: From Old English gingifere, from Sanskrit via Greek.
hints: A hot root grated into tea or biscuits.
Also a name for reddish hair.

definition: Seen as typical of girls; also fussily pretty.
note: Built from girl plus -y. Girl itself arrived in Middle English meaning a young person of either sex.
hints: A word for things like pink and glitter.
A description of a sort of style.

definition: The distance around something, such as a tree or a waist.
note: From Old Norse gjord, a band. The original sense was the strap that holds a saddle on a horse.
hints: The measurement around a thick trunk.
The strap that keeps a saddle in place.

definition: Handed over; also taken for granted.
note: The past participle of give, from Old English gifen. As a noun it means something taken as true without proof.
hints: What a present is once handed over.
A word for an assumption you do not question.

definition: A person who gives.
note: From Middle English, built from give plus -er. It is the opposite of a taker.
hints: Someone who donates.
Contrasts with 'taker' in a saying.

definition: A gadget whose name you don't know or can't remember.
note: Its origin is unknown; it turned up in American slang in the early 20th century.
hints: What you call an unnamed device.
A small device of uncertain purpose.
example: There may be some great new gizmo around the corner that you will want to use.

definition: With pleasure; willingly.
note: Glad plus -ly. Glad once meant 'bright' and 'shining' in Old English.
hints: How you accept an invitation you really want.
Often follows 'I would' in a polite reply.
example: I have my limits. If you cross them, I'll gladly walk away.

definition: A quick look.
note: Of uncertain origin; it appears in the 1400s.
hints: Look at your watch briefly.
A brief look at something.

definition: An organ that makes and releases substances such as hormones or sweat.
note: From French glande, tracing to Latin glandula, a small acorn. The Latin word was used for throat glands.
hints: The thyroid is one in your neck.
It secretes something the body needs.
example: I don't think it's right to remove a skunk's scent glands.

definition: A fierce stare, or harsh bright light.
note: From Middle English glaren, probably tied to shining. It was used for brightness before it described angry looks.
hints: What an annoyed person gives you.
Sunlight on a windscreen can cause it.

definition: A shiny coating, as on pottery or a doughnut.
note: From Middle English glasen, from the word glass. Glazed pottery gets a thin glassy surface.
hints: Painted onto clay before it is fired.
What makes a ham or pastry shine.

definition: A soft, brief flash of light.
note: From Middle English glem, a shaft of light or radiance. It can also mean a faint sign, as in a gleam of hope.
hints: What polished silver does in the sun.
A faint light, or a spark in the eye.

definition: To gather bit by bit, as information or leftover grain.
note: Middle English glenen meant to gather the grain left behind by reapers. The sense later widened to picking up facts.
hints: Poor villagers once did this in harvested fields.
Picking up clues from scattered sources.
example: He has gleaned knowledge from various books.

definition: To move smoothly and effortlessly.
note: From Old English glidan. It describes birds and aircraft moving without power.
hints: What an eagle does on rising air.
Skaters do it across ice.

definition: An aircraft with no engine that rides air currents.
note: From glide plus -er. The Wright brothers experimented with these before their powered flight.
hints: Soars on rising warm air.
Gets towed aloft by another plane and released.
example: During reentry and landing, the Space Shuttle is a glider.

definition: A tiny flash of reflected light.
note: Borrowed from Scots glint, likely from Old Norse. It also names a quick sparkle of emotion in the eyes.
hints: The flash from a blade or coin.
A sparkle in someone's eye.
origin: Scots glint, from Middle English glenten

definition: A small fault or hiccup in a system.
note: Probably from Yiddish glitsh, 'a slip'. Astronauts brought it into wide use in the 1960s.
hints: What a computer screen does when it flickers.
A temporary hiccup in a program.

definition: Flashy, showy glamour.
note: Back-formed from glitzy, which comes from German glitzern, 'to glitter'.
hints: Hollywood has plenty of it.
Sparkly and showy in an over-the-top way.

definition: To enjoy your own success or someone else's failure openly.
note: Middle English likely took it from Old Norse glotta, to grin scornfully. It still carries a smug grin.
hints: Winners should not do this.
Rubbing a rival's loss in his face.

definition: Relating to the whole world.
note: From globe plus -al, from Latin globus, 'ball'.
hints: Covering the whole planet.
Warming of this kind affects the entire planet.

definition: A sphere, especially a model of the Earth.
note: Via French from Latin globus, a ball. It is also used for the planet itself.
hints: A spinning map on a stand.
Phileas Fogg raced around one in eighty days.
origin: Middle French globe, from Latin globus

definition: Darkness, or a mood of heavy sadness.
note: From Old English glom, meaning twilight. The dark of dusk became a dark mood.
hints: What a rainy grey day can bring.
Poets call a dim twilight by this name.
example: He struck a match to dispel the gloom.

definition: Dark and depressing, or low in spirits.
note: From gloom plus -y. Gloom itself may be from an old word for twilight.
hints: A grey, rainy afternoon.
Eeyore's outlook on life.
example: The cavern was gloomy.

definition: Great honour and fame won by achievement.
note: Via Old French from Latin gloria, meaning fame or renown.
hints: What soldiers and athletes chase.
Often follows 'hallelujah' or 'days of'.
origin: Old French glorie, from Latin glōria

definition: A shine on a surface, or a brief explanation of a word.
note: The shine sense probably came from a Nordic language. The explanation sense is separate, from Greek glossa, tongue.
hints: Used loosely for a shine on a surface.
A shine on lips, paint or nails.

definition: Smooth and shiny on the surface.
note: From gloss plus -y. The noun 'glossies' means magazines printed on shiny paper.
hints: Describes a magazine cover or freshly painted door.
Photographs come in this finish or matte.

definition: A covering for the hand with separate fingers.
note: From Old English glof. It is an old word, kept almost unchanged for over a thousand years.
hints: Worn to keep hands warm.
Boxers and surgeons both wear them.
example: I wore gloves to keep my hands warm.

definition: A person who makes or sells gloves.
note: From glove plus -er. It survives mostly as a surname.
hints: A craftsperson stitching fine leather hands.
A trade surname from medieval times.

definition: A protein in wheat and other grains that makes dough stretchy.
note: From Latin gluten, 'glue'. Coeliac patients must avoid it.
hints: Bread bakers prize its stretch; some diners avoid it.
A label on pasta may say 'free of' this.
origin: Middle French gluten, from Latin glūten; in English since the 19th century
example: I like English muffins, but they'd have to be gluten free.

definition: A carved symbol or character.
note: Borrowed from French, from Greek gluphe, a carving. Mayan hieroglyphs are a famous example.
hints: Carved on ancient temple walls.
One symbol in a writing system.
origin: French glyphe, from Ancient Greek γλυφή
example: The grid column header displays a sort glyph indicating an ascending or descending ordering.

definition: To grind the teeth together in anger or pain.
note: Origin uncertain, perhaps imitating the sound. The silent g is kept from older spellings.
hints: Teeth do it in a rage.
Paired with 'wailing' in a biblical phrase.

definition: A small bearded creature of folklore, often a garden figure.
note: From New Latin gnomus, a term used by the physician Paracelsus for earth spirits.
hints: Wears a pointed red hat.
Found standing in lawns.
origin: French gnome, from New Latin gnomus

definition: The player who defends the goal.
note: Clipped from goalkeeper or goaltender with -ie added. In ice hockey, they wear heavy padding and a mask.
hints: Wears gloves and a different colour shirt in football.
The last line of defence in front of the net.

definition: A small, mischievous or evil creature in folklore.
note: From Old French gobelin, perhaps related to a German word for house spirit. In fantasy fiction goblins are often greedy and wicked.
hints: Guards the vaults at Gringotts.
A creature in a fairy tale that lives under a bridge.
example: Leave the goblins alone and they'll usually leave you alone.

definition: Devoted to God; pious.
note: From Old English, formed from god plus the -ly ending. It has long described a righteous way of life.
hints: Often said of a very devout person.
The opposite of wicked.

definition: Moving or leaving; also the condition of the ground or progress.
note: From Old English gan, 'to go', with -ing. 'Heavy going' once described muddy ground and came to mean slow progress.
hints: Setting out on a trip.
Ground may be described as 'rough' or 'heavy' for this.

definition: Made of or like gold.
note: From Old English gylden, from gold.
hints: Shiny and yellowish.
Anniversaries reach this at fifty years.
example: The gold dome of the Capitol.

definition: A figure of clay brought to life by magic in Jewish legend.
note: Borrowed from Hebrew golem. The most famous tale concerns a rabbi in Prague.
hints: Made of mud and animated with words.
A lumbering servant that cannot speak.

definition: A person who plays golf.
note: From golf plus -er. The game began in Scotland and the first records are from the 15th century.
hints: Shouts 'fore' before a wild shot.
Tiger Woods is a famous one.
example: Can you tell me, how come that blind golfer is so successful?

definition: A mild old-fashioned cry of surprise.
note: A euphemism for God from the 1700s, softened to avoid swearing.
hints: An exclamation your grandfather might use.
A mild old-fashioned cry of surprise, a softened 'God'.
example: Golly! That was a long trip to California.

definition: An organ that produces reproductive cells, such as an ovary or testis.
note: From Greek gone, 'seed' or 'generation'.
hints: A biology word for an ovary or testis.
Produces eggs or sperm.
origin: New Latin gonadēs, from Ancient Greek γονή
example: I have many times eaten sea urchin gonads as sushi.

definition: Someone or something doomed or beyond saving.
note: From gone plus -er, recorded from around 1850.
hints: Said of a plant that will not recover.
You are this if the cliff crumbles.
example: I'm a goner if this plan doesn't work.

definition: A casual way of saying 'going to'.
note: A contraction of going to, recorded since 1913. It is common in speech and song lyrics.
hints: How people say a future plan, casually.
A relaxed spoken form of a future plan.

definition: Wildly unconventional and subjective, especially in journalism.
note: Coined in 1971 for the writing of Hunter S. Thompson. Its roots are uncertain, with Italian and Spanish words for 'dolt' or 'goose' suggested.
hints: Describes journalism that puts the writer in the story.
Hunter S. Thompson made this style famous.

definition: A treat; or an exclamation of delight.
note: Built from good plus -y, a casual ending. As a noun it means a sweet or small treat; as a cry it is an exclamation of delight.
hints: Something good to eat, in a bag at a party.
A cry a child may make at a treat.

definition: Soft, sticky and messy.
note: Formed from goo plus the -y ending. It can also mean sappy and sentimental.
hints: Describes warm melted cheese or caramel.
A brownie fresh from the oven might be this.

definition: Silly in a harmless, playful way.
note: Built from goof plus -y. It is also the name of a cartoon dog.
hints: Describes a funny grin or a silly walk.
Not serious at all.

definition: A large waterbird with a long neck, related to ducks and swans.
note: From Old English gos, with relatives across the Germanic languages and deeper still. The plural geese is a leftover vowel change.
hints: Flies south in a V formation.
Honks loudly and lays golden eggs in a fable.

definition: A deep narrow valley, or to stuff yourself with food.
note: From Old French, meaning throat. A gorge is a throat cut in the land, and gorging is feeding the throat.
hints: A river may cut one through rock.
What you do at an all-you-can-eat buffet.

definition: The teachings of Jesus, or a style of Christian music.
note: From Old English godspel, 'good news'.
hints: Mark and John wrote one.
Choir music with soul.
origin: Old English godspell, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον

definition: Idle talk about other people, or someone who spreads it.
note: From Old English godsibb, 'godparent', then a close friend, then a chatterer.
hints: Chat about neighbours.
Once meant a godparent.
example: Be careful what you say to him: he’s a bit of a gossip.

definition: Informal for 'got you', said on catching or understanding someone.
note: A spelling of the way 'got you' is run together in speech. It also names a trick that catches someone out, as in 'gotcha journalism'.
hints: Shouted when you catch a friend in a game of tag.
A tricky question meant to trip someone up.

definition: Describing a dark, dramatic style, from medieval architecture to horror fiction.
note: From the Goths, a Germanic people, though the connection is as an insult by Renaissance critics, who thought the style barbaric. Gothic novels came with Frankenstein and Dracula.
hints: The style of cathedrals with pointed arches and flying buttresses.
A dark castle and a pale heroine are in its stories.

definition: A casual way of saying 'have to'.
note: A contraction of got to. It appears in speech and songs.
hints: A spoken form of 'must'.
A relaxed way to say what you must do.
example: I gotta learn this for my exam.

definition: American past participle of get.
note: From get plus -en, preserved in American English though it faded in Britain.
hints: What Americans say instead of got.
Something has been obtained.

definition: To dig or scoop out roughly, or to overcharge.
note: From Old French for a curved chisel. Overcharging sense came later in American use.
hints: A deep scratch in a wooden table.
What a price-hiking seller might do.
origin: Old French gouge, from Late Latin goia

definition: A hard-shelled fruit of a vine, such as a pumpkin relative.
note: Via Anglo-Norman from Latin cucurbita. Dried ones were used as bottles and bowls.
hints: Decorative in autumn displays.
Hollowed and dried for use as a container.

definition: To rule or control a country, organisation or area.
note: From Latin gubernare, 'to steer a ship', borrowed from Greek kybernao. A ruler was thought of as a helmsman.
hints: What presidents and councils are meant to do.
Its root is the same as the word for a ship's steersman.
origin: Old French governer, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω

definition: A level of quality, or a mark given for schoolwork.
note: From Latin gradus, a step. A grade is a step on a ladder of quality.
hints: What you get on a test.
Fifth in a school year.
origin: Middle French grade, from Latin gradus

definition: A machine that levels roads; or a student of a given school year.
note: From grade plus -er. A fifth-grader is a pupil in the fifth year of school.
hints: A big road machine with a long blade.
An American child in a specific school year.
example: Speaking objectively, math can be confusing for 1st graders.

definition: To join a shoot onto another plant, or to engage in corrupt gain.
note: Originally from Greek graphein via the Old French word for a stylus, because a cutting looks like a pen. The corruption sense is later.
hints: Gardeners do it to fruit trees.
Skin is moved in this way in surgery.
origin: Old French greffe, from Ancient Greek γραφείον
example: Graft the cherry tree branch onto the plum tree.

definition: A type of flour made from whole wheat, or a cracker made from it.
note: Named after Sylvester Graham, a 19th-century American minister who promoted whole-grain diets.
hints: Cracker used in s'mores.
Named after a health reformer.

definition: The legendary cup sought by King Arthur's knights.
note: From Old French graal, meaning cup. It now means any object of a long quest.
hints: Subject of a medieval quest.
Holy, in the legend.
origin: Old French graal, from Latin crater
example: Becoming an astronaut was his grail.

definition: Impressive in size or style.
note: Via Old French from Latin grandis, meaning large.
hints: A piano may be this kind.
Slang for a thousand dollars.
example: The bridge is a grand structure.

definition: Large, in Spanish; also a size of coffee.
note: From Spanish and Italian grande, 'big', from Latin grandis.
hints: A mid-sized cup at a coffee chain.
Spanish for large.

definition: A country house with farm buildings; also a farmers' association in the US.
note: From Old French grange, 'barn', from Latin granum, 'grain'. A grange was first a monastery's granary farm.
hints: A big old country house in a Victorian novel.
Wuthering Heights has a neighbouring house named Thrushcross this.
origin: Old French grange, from Latin grānum

definition: An affectionate word for grandmother.
note: A pet form of 'grandmother', first recorded in the 1600s as 'grannam'.
hints: Her knitting needles and boiled sweets are stereotypes.
A knot that slips, named after an old woman who tied it badly.

definition: To give or allow, or money given for a purpose.
note: From Old French granter, to promise or agree. It also names funds awarded to researchers.
hints: A wish may be this by a genie.
A scholarship is one kind.
origin: Anglo-Norman granter, from Old French granter

definition: A small juicy fruit that grows in bunches on a vine.
note: Via Old French grappe, a cluster, which was originally a hook for picking fruit.
hints: Crushed to make wine.
Dried, it becomes a raisin.
example: Grapes give us whole-fruit snacks, grape juice, raisins, wine, and more.

definition: A diagram showing how quantities relate.
note: A clipping of 'graphic formula', from the 1870s.
hints: Lines and bars on a chart.
Plots one value against another.

definition: To take hold of firmly, or to understand.
note: From Middle English graspen, to grope or feel around. Understanding an idea is likened to getting a hand around it.
hints: What fingers do to a rope.
To finally get what a hard lesson means.

definition: Covered with grass.
note: Built from grass plus -y, and descended from the Old English adjective græsig.
hints: A word for a hillside or meadow in summer.
A famous knoll in Dallas carries this adjective in conspiracy theories.
example: We threw his grassy shorts straight into the washing machine.

definition: To shred against a rough surface, or to irritate.
note: The noun for an iron frame comes from Latin for a hurdle or lattice. The verb for scraping is a separate word.
hints: Cheese is shredded this way.
A noise that does it to your nerves.
example: Grate carrots and onions.

definition: A hole in the ground for a burial, or very serious.
note: From Old English graf, meaning a trench or cave. The serious adjective is a different word, from Latin gravis, heavy.
hints: A churchyard is full of them.
A word to describe a doctor's solemn warning.
example: He put flowers on his mother's grave.

definition: Small stones used for paths.
note: From Old French gravele, 'small gravel'.
hints: Crunches underfoot on a drive.
Pebbles laid on a path.
origin: Old French gravele, from Medieval Latin grava

definition: A sauce made from the juices of cooked meat.
note: Middle English gravey, perhaps from a word for the sediment of melted fat. Its exact origin is uncertain.
hints: Poured over roast dinners.
Turkey's partner at a holiday table.

definition: To feed on grass, or to scrape the skin lightly.
note: The feeding verb comes from the Old English word for grass. The scratching sense is later and may be a separate use.
hints: What cows do in a field.
A scrape on the knee after a fall.

definition: Soft animal fat or an oily lubricant.
note: From Old French craisse, from Latin crassus, 'thick'.
hints: Applied to a squeaky wheel.
Slippery oil in a frying pan.

definition: Covered in or full of grease.
note: From grease plus -y. Chip shops and fry-ups are described this way.
hints: Describes a fried-food cafe's spoon.
What fast food does to your fingers.

definition: Very large, or very good.
note: From Old English great, which meant big, thick or coarse. It only later became a word of praise.
hints: Britain is called this in its formal name.
A word of enthusiastic approval.
example: A great juicy steak.

definition: An excessive desire for more than you need.
note: Back-formed from greedy around 1600.
hints: One of the seven deadly sins.
Wanting more money than you could ever spend.
example: His greed was his undoing.

definition: Wanting more than your share.
note: From Old English graedig.
hints: Eats too much.
Piggish about money.
example: Don't be greedy with the cookies.

definition: The colour of grass and leaves.
note: From Old English grene, related to grow and grass. All three come from the same Germanic root.
hints: Sits between yellow and blue.
Signals go on a traffic light.

definition: To welcome someone with words or a gesture.
note: From Old English gretan, to approach or address. It once carried the sense of coming up to someone.
hints: What you do when a guest arrives.
A handshake or a hello does this.

definition: Deep sorrow, especially after a loss.
note: From Old French grief, heavy, from Latin gravis. Grave is the same root.
hints: What follows a bereavement.
Heavy sorrow, or trouble given to someone.
origin: Old French grief, from Latin gravis; in English since the early 14th century
example: She was worn out from so much grief.

definition: To feel deep sorrow, especially after a loss.
note: From Old French grever, 'to burden', from Latin gravis, 'heavy'. Grief is heaviness of heart.
hints: What the bereaved do after a death.
Sorrow felt at a funeral.
origin: Old French grever, from Latin gravō
example: His behavior grieves his mother.

definition: To cook over direct heat on a metal grid.
note: From French gril, ultimately from a Latin word for a small lattice. It can also mean to question someone intensely.
hints: Used for burgers outdoors.
What police may do in an interrogation.

definition: Dirt that is ground in and hard to remove.
note: Middle English grim meant soot on the face. It is also a London music genre.
hints: What builds up on an unwashed window.
A mechanic's hands might be coated in it.
example: Underneath all that soot, dirt and grime is the true beauty of the church in soft shades of sandstone.

definition: Covered with ground-in dirt.
note: From grime plus -y. Grime comes from Middle Dutch grime, 'soot' or 'dirt'.
hints: How hands look after mechanic's work.
The word for a city window thick with soot.
example: A miner's begrimed face.

definition: To crush into small pieces, or a tiring routine.
note: From Old English grindan. The sense of dull daily labour is likened to turning a mill.
hints: What a coffee mill does to beans.
The daily slog of work.
example: Grind the spices in a mortar.

definition: To complain, especially about small things.
note: From Old English gripan, to seize. It has the same root as grip.
hints: What a grumbler does about the food.
A minor complaint.

definition: Grain that is ready to be ground at a mill.
note: From Old English grist, 'grinding'. 'Grist to the mill' means anything that can be put to useful work.
hints: Wheat for the miller.
Part of the phrase for useful material.

definition: Full of grit; or tough and realistic.
note: From grit, from Old English greot, 'sand'. Crime dramas that avoid glamour are called by this adjective.
hints: How a bite of unwashed spinach can feel.
A realistic police drama set in a hard city.

definition: A low sound made in pain, boredom or disapproval.
note: From Old English granian, to lament or murmur.
hints: How the audience reacts to a bad pun.
Floorboards may make this noise too.

definition: The crease where the thigh meets the lower body.
note: The exact origin is uncertain. Architects also use it for the edge where two vaults intersect.
hints: A muscle strain might occur here.
Part of the body near the hip.

definition: Someone about to marry, or to tend an animal's coat.
note: Short for bridegroom. The verb came from stable servants, who brushed horses.
hints: Stands at the altar beside the bride.
What you do to a horse with a brush.

definition: A long narrow channel.
note: From Dutch groeve, 'ditch'.
hints: A needle follows it on a record.
Feel the beat in funk music.
origin: Old Norse gróf, from Middle Dutch groeve

definition: Excellent, in the style of 1960s slang.
note: From groove plus -y. The slang sense came from jazz, where being 'in the groove' meant playing well.
hints: A flower-power word.
Austin Powers might shout it.

definition: Disgusting, or total before deductions.
note: From Old French gros, big or thick, from Latin grossus. Gross pay is the large full amount.
hints: What a mouldy sandwich is.
Pay before tax comes off.
origin: Old French gros, from Latin grossus
example: I threw up all over the bed. It was totally gross.

definition: The solid surface of the earth.
note: From Old English grund.
hints: Under your feet.
Soil, or reason for a decision.
example: Look, I found a ten dollar bill on the ground!

definition: A number of people or things gathered together.
note: Through French from Italian gruppo, probably a Germanic word. It first meant a cluster in painting.
hints: A band or a team is one.
Friends who meet regularly.

definition: A plump game bird of moors, or to complain.
note: The bird's name is first recorded in the 1530s and its origin is unknown. The complaining sense appeared later, in the army slang of the 1880s.
hints: Shot in Scotland each August on the Glorious Twelfth.
Soldiers did it about food, and so do commuters about trains.

definition: Thin mortar used to fill gaps between tiles.
note: From Old English grut, coarse meal or dregs. The building material kept the sense of a coarse paste.
hints: Fills the lines between bathroom tiles.
It can go mouldy if damp.

definition: A low, rumbling sound of anger, made in the throat.
note: From Middle English groulen, first used of the bowels rumbling.
hints: A dog makes it to warn you off.
A bear's warning noise.
origin: Old French groler, from Old English gryllan

definition: Fully developed; the past participle of grow.
note: From Old English growan. It is also used for adults, as in 'grown-up'.
hints: Describes what an adult is.
What a seed is after it has sprouted.

definition: The process of increasing in size.
note: From grow plus -th, as in length and width.
hints: What a seedling does.
Increase, in plants or an economy.

definition: A lasting feeling of resentment toward someone.
note: From Old French grouchier, 'to murmur', related to grouch. It first meant to complain, then to resent.
hints: 'Hold' it against a friend who wronged you years ago.
What a feuding family keeps alive for generations.

definition: A thin porridge of oats or other grain.
note: From Old French gruel, coarse meal. It was food of the poor and the sick.
hints: What Oliver Twist was served.
A meagre watery meal.
origin: Old French gruel, from Old English grūt

definition: Rough and abrupt in manner or voice.
note: From Dutch grof, coarse or rude, in the 1500s.
hints: A grumpy old man's tone.
Describes the billy goats in a fairy tale.
origin: Dutch grof, from Middle Low German grof

definition: Bad-tempered and easily irritated.
note: From grump plus -y. Grump was an old word for a sulky mood. One of the seven dwarfs is named for it.
hints: One of Snow White's seven dwarfs.
How you feel before your morning coffee.

definition: A short, low sound, or a basic infantry soldier.
note: From Old English grunnettan, imitating the pig's noise.
hints: A pig makes it in a pen.
What a teenager answers in place of words.

definition: Seabird or bat droppings, used as fertiliser.
note: From Spanish via Quechua wanu. Peruvian islands once yielded fortunes in it.
hints: Seabird droppings piled up on islands.
Rich fertiliser, from bats.

definition: To protect, or someone who does so.
note: Through Old French from a Germanic root related to ward and warden.
hints: Stands by the palace gate.
Prisons employ them.
origin: Middle French garder, from Early Medieval Latin wardo

definition: A tropical fruit with pink or white flesh and many seeds.
note: From Spanish guayaba, which came from a Taino word. It was recorded in English in the 1500s.
hints: Grows in warm climates.
Often made into paste or juice.

definition: To estimate without full knowledge.
note: Middle English gessen, probably from a Scandinavian word. It once meant to aim or take aim.
hints: What you do when you don't know.
A try at a riddle.

definition: Someone invited to a home, event or hotel.
note: From Old Norse gestr. It shares a root with Latin hostis, which gave host and hostile.
hints: Arrives when you throw a party.
A visitor who stays the night.

definition: An association of craftsmen or merchants in the Middle Ages.
note: From Middle English gilde, from Old Norse gildi, meaning payment. Members paid dues to join.
hints: A medieval group of weavers or masons.
Often found in fantasy role-playing games.
example: Guilds were an important part of society in the Middle Ages.

definition: Cunning used to deceive.
note: From Old French guile, deception, via a Frankish word for a trick. It is related to wile.
hints: What a fox is said to have.
A trickster wins by it, not force.
origin: Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile

definition: The state of having done wrong, or the feeling that comes with it.
note: From Old English gylt, a crime or fault.
hints: The feeling after a broken promise.
What a jury must decide.

definition: Having done wrong.
note: From Old English gyltig, from gylt, 'crime'.
hints: A jury's possible verdict.
Feeling remorse for a misdeed.
example: Do you have a guilty conscience?

definition: An old British coin worth twenty-one shillings; also a West African country.
note: Named for the Guinea coast, where the gold for the coin came from.
hints: Coin once used in horse sales.
A country in West Africa.

definition: A stringed instrument played by plucking or strumming.
note: From Spanish guitarra, from Greek kithara, an ancient lyre.
hints: Instrument with six strings.
A rock band's main instrument.
origin: Spanish guitarra, from Ancient Greek κῐθᾰ́ρᾱ
example: Learning to strum the guitar rhythmically is essential.

definition: A narrow, steep-sided ravine, often cut by a stream.
note: A word chiefly from American English. Gold-rush stories place prospectors in them.
hints: Prospectors panned in one.
A deep ditch in the mountains.

definition: A narrow channel cut in the ground by flowing water.
note: Origin uncertain, possibly connected with an old word for the throat.
hints: Rain carves one down a hillside.
A narrow ditch beside a road.

definition: A thick Louisiana stew thickened with okra.
note: From Louisiana French gombo, which traces to a Bantu word for okra.
hints: A speciality of New Orleans.
Served over rice with sausage or shrimp.

definition: Sticky or chewy; also a chewy sweet.
note: From gum plus -y. Gum comes from Greek kommi, a tree's sticky sap.
hints: Like a chewy, sticky candy.
Resembling a bear-shaped candy.

definition: A man who uses a gun, especially for crime.
note: Simply gun plus man. News reports use it for an armed attacker.
hints: A bank raider in the news.
Western films show one facing the sheriff at noon.

definition: A soldier or crew member who fires large guns.
note: From gun plus -er. In Britain 'the Gunners' is also a nickname for Arsenal.
hints: A person who operates artillery.
Nickname of a North London football club.

definition: A small, colourful freshwater aquarium fish.
note: Named by mistake after Robert Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad to London.
hints: A beginner's pet fish.
Gives birth to live young.
example: Fred kept a tank of guppies by the windowsill.

definition: A wheeled stretcher used in hospitals.
note: The origin is unknown. One theory ties it to a wheeled horse-drawn cab named after an American inventor called Gurney. It is mainly used in North America.
hints: Paramedics roll one into the ambulance.
Pushed through hospital corridors with a patient lying flat.
example: The death row convict was strapped into the gurney in order to be given the lethal injection.

definition: Hearty enthusiasm in doing something.
note: From Italian gusto, taste, ultimately from Latin gustus.
hints: Eating a meal with it means relishing every bite.
Sung with it means belting it out.
example: He sang with more gusto than talent.

definition: Blowing in sudden strong bursts.
note: Built from gust plus -y. Gust probably came from Old Norse gustr, 'a blast of wind'.
hints: How wind sounds during a storm.
The weather when umbrellas turn inside out.
example: The strong, gusty wind strived to strip the leaves off the trees.

definition: Brave and determined.
note: From guts, long used informally for courage. The y ending turns the noun into an adjective.
hints: Bold in the face of danger.
Having plenty of nerve.
example: People are cool when they're gutsy, doesn't matter if they're men or women.

definition: A channel for carrying away rainwater from a roof or road.
note: From Old French goutiere, from Latin gutta, 'drop'. Bowling lanes have them too, and 'the gutter' also means a low social position.
hints: Clogged with leaves every autumn.
The ball lands in one and scores nothing at a bowling alley.
origin: Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere

definition: A routine you do regularly, often without thinking.
note: From Latin habitus, condition or dress, from habere, to have. A monk's habit is the clothing worn as a routine.
hints: Nail biting can be a bad one.
Something repeated until automatic.

definition: Someone who breaks into computer systems, or an enthusiast who tinkers with code.
note: Originally a woodcutter who hacks with rough blows. The computing sense began with tinkering students at MIT.
hints: A figure in a dark hoodie in the movies.
Can be a black-hat or a white-hat kind.
example: True hackers subscribe to a code of ethics and look down upon crackers.

definition: A Muslim who has memorised the whole Quran.
note: From Arabic for 'guardian' or one who knows by heart.
hints: Someone who knows a holy book by heart.
Arabic title for a memoriser.

definition: A short Japanese poem of three lines.
note: From Japanese haiku. The traditional form has five, seven and five syllables.
hints: A three-line poem of 5-7-5.
A short poem about nature.
example: Early Western haiku often rhymed the first and third lines.

definition: Covered with hair; also risky.
note: From Old English-derived hair plus -y. The informal sense of dangerous is later.
hints: Describes a gorilla's arms.
A tense or scary moment, informally.
example: Jacob was a hairy man.

definition: Permitted under Islamic law, especially of food.
note: Borrowed from Arabic halal, 'permissible'.
hints: Meat prepared according to Muslim practice.
The opposite of haram.

definition: To divide into two equal parts.
note: From Old English words for half. The silent l is kept from the older spelling.
hints: What you do with a cake for two people.
Cut an apple down the middle.
example: The Mediterranean diet halves the risk of heart disease.

definition: A very small village.
note: From Old French hamelet, a little home. Shakespeare's prince of Denmark shares the name but not the origin.
hints: Smaller even than a village.
The Danish prince's play bears the same word.
origin: Old French hamelet, from Old French ham

definition: A tool for driving nails.
note: From Old English hamor.
hints: Thor wielded one.
A judge raises it in court.
example: Bobby used a hammer and nails to fix the two planks together.

definition: Overacted in a showy, exaggerated way.
note: From ham, an old theatre term for an amateur or clumsy actor, plus -y.
hints: What bad stage acting is called.
Describes theatrical overdoing.

definition: A large lidded basket; also to hinder.
note: From Old French hanapier, a case for goblets. As a verb, it is separate and means to hold back.
hints: Packed with food for a picnic.
A Christmas one arrives stuffed with treats and tea.
origin: Anglo-Norman hanaper, from Old French hanapier

definition: The part of an object you hold; or to deal with.
note: From Old English handlian, 'to touch with the hands'.
hints: Part of a mug you grip.
Manage a situation.
example: He grabbed the hammer by the handle.

definition: Useful, or conveniently near.
note: From Middle English handi, formed on hand. It once meant skilful.
hints: A tool within reach is this.
Said of a person good at fixing things.
example: Some people regard duct tape as a handy fix-all.

definition: A large building where aircraft are kept.
note: Borrowed from French hangar, 'shed'. Early aviators took the word from the French, who had it for carriage sheds.
hints: Planes are stored and repaired inside one.
A huge shed at an airfield.
origin: French hangar, from Old French hangart
example: The plane taxied on over to the hangar for repairs.

definition: A shaped frame for holding a garment on a rail.
note: Formed from hang plus -er. The word once also named a person who hangs things, including an executioner.
hints: It keeps a shirt from wrinkling in the wardrobe.
Wire ones from a dry cleaner are often bent into other uses.

definition: To take place.
note: From hap, an old word for luck or chance, plus -en. It is also the root of perhaps and happy.
hints: Events do this.
Come about by chance.
example: Let me tell you how it happened.

definition: Feeling pleasure or contentment.
note: From Middle English hap, meaning luck or chance. To be happy was first to be lucky.
hints: The opposite of sad.
What a smiling face expresses.
example: Music makes me feel happy.

definition: Forbidden under Islamic law.
note: Borrowed from Arabic haram, 'forbidden', the opposite of halal.
hints: The opposite of permitted in Islam.
Arabic for forbidden.

definition: To bother or attack someone repeatedly.
note: From Old French harasser, 'to tire out', possibly from harer, 'to set a dog on'. Workplaces have rules against it.
hints: Constant unwanted contact at work.
To bully with repeated pestering.

definition: A sheltered place for ships; or to shelter.
note: From Old English herebeorg, 'army shelter'.
hints: Boats dock there.
Keep a grudge in mind.

definition: To become or make firm.
note: From Old English heard. Arteries and criminals can both do it.
hints: What concrete does as it sets.
What a tough upbringing does to a heart.

definition: More difficult, or firmer.
note: The comparative of hard, from Old English heard.
hints: Less easy than before.
Tougher or more solid than something else.

definition: Barely, scarcely.
note: From hard plus -ly, which first meant with force.
hints: Almost not at all.
Hints that something is only just so.
example: They hardly ever watch television.

definition: Tough and able to endure difficult conditions.
note: From Old French hardi, bold, probably connected to the word for becoming hard.
hints: Describes plants that survive winter frost.
A word for a sturdy mountain pony.
example: A hardy plant is one that can withstand the extremes of climate, such as frost.

definition: The women's private quarters in a traditional Muslim household.
note: Borrowed from Turkish, from Arabic haram, meaning 'forbidden' or 'protected'. The word carried the idea of a place set apart.
hints: A section of a house set apart.
A word from the Ottoman court.
example: The chieftain possessed a harem of young men and women alike.

definition: A mythical bird-woman, or a nagging woman.
note: From Latin harpyia, from Greek harpuiai, meaning snatchers. The creatures grabbed food and people in myth.
hints: A winged monster in Greek stories.
An insulting term for a shrill, grasping person.
origin: Middle French harpie, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ

definition: A farm tool with teeth that breaks up soil, or to distress deeply.
note: From Middle English harwe, a drag for soil. To harrow someone is to tear at their feelings as the tool tears at the ground.
hints: A farm tool, or a word for an experience that tears at your feelings.
Dragged over a ploughed field to break up clods before sowing.

definition: Rough, severe or unpleasantly strong.
note: From Middle English harsk, linked to Old Norse harskr, which meant rancid. It later widened to cover anything rough or cruel.
hints: Describes a bitter winter or a stern punishment.
A word for grating light or a cruel remark.
example: The harsh cry of a blue jay.

definition: An annoying bother or inconvenience.
note: Origin unknown, possibly from American dialect for panting or from haste. It arrived in the mid-1900s.
hints: Dealing with a cancelled flight is a typical one.
What paperwork and queues amount to.

definition: Spanish for until.
note: Borrowed from Spanish. In English it is mainly seen in hasta la vista.
hints: As in a Terminator farewell.
Spanish preposition for until.

definition: Speed in doing something, often too much of it.
note: Middle English hast, from Old French. A proverb warns that it makes waste.
hints: What a hurried packer shows.
Often followed by 'makes waste'.
example: We were running late so we finished our meal in haste.

definition: To emerge from an egg, or a small door in a floor or deck.
note: The door sense comes from Old English hec, a gate. The egg sense is a separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: What a chick does from its shell.
An opening in a ship's deck.
example: These three chicks hatched yesterday morning.

definition: Someone who dislikes or criticises others out of spite.
note: Built from hate plus -er, and old in English. The slangy modern sense is of a person who sneers at others' success.
hints: The sort who scorns someone's success.
Slang for a negative critic.

definition: To visit a place repeatedly, as a ghost does.
note: From Old French hanter, to frequent. It originally meant just to reside or often visit.
hints: What a ghost does to an old house.
A memory can do it to you.
origin: Old French hanter, from Old English hāmettan
example: A couple of ghosts haunt the old, burnt-down house.

definition: A safe place, or a sheltered harbour.
note: From Old English haefen, meaning harbour. A port and a refuge were the same idea.
hints: A sheltered bay for ships.
Somewhere you feel safe and protected.
origin: Old English hæfen, from Old Norse hǫfn

definition: Widespread destruction and chaos.
note: From Old French in the phrase 'cry havoc', a battle signal for soldiers to seize plunder.
hints: A storm can wreak it.
What a toddler loose in a kitchen causes.
origin: Old French havok, from Old French crier

definition: A danger or risk.
note: From Old French hasard, a dice game, probably from Arabic az-zahr, 'the die'.
hints: A wet floor sign warns of one.
Its first meaning was a game of chance.
origin: Old French hasart, from Arabic اَلزَّهْر; in English since the 16th century
example: Drinking alcohol is a health hazard.

definition: A tree that bears edible nuts, or a light brown-green colour.
note: From Old English haesl, with ancient Germanic roots. The eye colour is named after the nut.
hints: Its nuts are used in spread.
A shade of eye between brown and green.

definition: A line of text at the top of a page, or a headed shot in football.
note: From head plus -er.
hints: Top of a document.
A football goal scored with the forehead.
example: That column should have the header "payment status".

definition: Intoxicating, or exciting to the senses.
note: From Middle English hedi, formed from head plus -y. It first meant headstrong.
hints: Describes strong wine or a thrilling success.
Perfume that goes straight to your head.
example: The cocktail was a heady mixture of spirits.

definition: A person who cures illness, especially by non-medical means.
note: From heal plus -er, from Old English haelan. The word is applied to doctors, faith leaders and herbalists.
hints: A shaman is described this way.
Time is called one in a common saying.
example: The healer says he's able to communicate with the hereafter.

definition: The state of being free from illness.
note: From Old English hælth, from hal, 'whole'. It is related to whole and hale.
hints: What you toast to.
Whole and well, as an old word had it.
example: Her mental health is really affected by stressful environments.

definition: Past tense of hear.
note: From Old English heard, the past form of hieran, 'to hear'. It is spelled like 'herd', and the two sound the same.
hints: What your ears did with a sound.
A word that sounds like a flock of cattle.

definition: The muscle that pumps blood, or the seat of feeling.
note: From Old English heorte, with roots shared across Germanic languages and Latin cor.
hints: It beats in your chest.
The shape on a Valentine's card.
example: He stood still, his heart thumping wildly.

definition: The floor of a fireplace, or the home it stands for.
note: From Old English heorth. Home and hearth are paired because the fire was the centre of a household.
hints: Where Santa's stockings are hung.
The place a family gathers in winter.

definition: Warm, cheerful and wholehearted; or filling, as of food.
note: Heart plus -y. Hearty greetings come from the heart; hearty meals feed you well.
hints: A thick stew on a cold night is this.
A big laugh or a firm handshake.

definition: A device that gives off warmth.
note: From heat plus -er. Space ones are plugged in for cold rooms.
hints: What you switch on in winter.
A device in a car or a bathroom.
example: Turn on the heater; I'm cold.

definition: To lift or throw with great effort.
note: From Old English hebban, to lift. It also means to retch.
hints: What sailors do hauling a rope.
A struggle to move a heavy trunk.

definition: The sky, or the home of God and the blessed.
note: From Old English heofon.
hints: Paradise in the clouds, in belief.
Where angels live.

definition: Weighing a great deal.
note: From Old English hefig, from the root of heave. The heavy thing is what one has to heave.
hints: Metal bands and bags of cement share this quality.
A loaded suitcase might be this.

definition: Very busy and chaotic.
note: From Greek hektikos, 'habitual', used of a persistent wasting fever. The sense of feverish activity came to mean frantic.
hints: A morning with school run and deadlines is like this.
Used of schedules packed full.
origin: Old French etique, from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός
example: The daily life can be busy, hectic and sometimes overwhelming.

definition: To bully or lecture someone in a loud, overbearing way.
note: From Hector, the Trojan warrior in Homer's Iliad. His name came to mean a bully through 17th-century gangs who used it.
hints: What a heckling bully does to a nervous speaker.
The name of Troy's greatest fighter.
origin: Latin Hectōr, from Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ

definition: Large, weighty and powerful.
note: Built from heft, weight, plus -y in the 1800s. The resemblance to German heftig is a coincidence.
hints: Describes a large, weighty parcel.
A burly man with a mighty swing.

definition: How tall something is.
note: From Old English hiehthu, from heah, 'high'.
hints: Measured from base to top.
A tall person's stat.

definition: A very light gas used to fill balloons.
note: Named from Greek helios, 'sun', because it was first detected in sunlight before being found on Earth. Breathing it makes your voice squeak.
hints: Makes party balloons float and voices squeak.
Discovered in the sun before it was found on Earth.
origin: New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος
example: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are noble gases.

definition: A spiral curve like a corkscrew or a coiled spring.
note: Latin helix, from Greek helix, something twisted.
hints: DNA has a double one.
Shape of a spiral staircase.
origin: Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ

definition: A common greeting.
note: First recorded in 1826, from earlier holla and hollo. It became the standard telephone greeting in the late 1800s.
hints: A friendly word when meeting.
What you say when you answer the phone.
example: Every morning they exchanged polite hellos.

definition: A hard hat that protects the head.
note: From Old French helmet, a diminutive of helme, itself Germanic.
hints: Worn by cyclists.
Part of a knight's armour.

definition: Someone who assists another.
note: From Old English helpere. Plain help plus -er.
hints: A person who lends a hand around the house or shop.
Santa's workshop is full of elves doing this job.

definition: From this place or time; for this reason.
note: From Middle English hennes, from Old English heonan, away.
hints: Used in phrases like 'a week from now'.
A formal way of saying therefore.

definition: A collarless knit shirt with buttons at the neck.
note: Named after the English town of Henley-on-Thames, where rowers wore such shirts.
hints: A long-sleeved shirt with a short button placket at the neckline.
Rowing regatta shirts gave it a name.

definition: A reddish dye from a shrub, used for skin and hair.
note: From Arabic hinna. It is used to paint temporary designs on hands.
hints: A red-brown plant dye for hands.
Painted on a bride's hands.

definition: A messenger, or to announce something coming.
note: From Old French heraut, from Germanic words meaning army ruler.
hints: Angels in a carol sing of one.
Announces news.
origin: Latin heraldus, from Old French heraut

definition: Made from plants, especially herbs.
note: From Old French herbal, built from herb plus -al. Herbal teas and remedies are made from leaves and flowers.
hints: Chamomile tea is this type.
A shop sells remedies made from plants.
example: Herbal tea, herbal medicine.

definition: By means of this document or statement.
note: From here plus by. It appears in formal announcements and legal text.
hints: Appears in official announcements and contracts.
A formal opening such as a judge or officiant might use.
example: I hereby declare you husband and wife.

definition: In this document or place.
note: From Old English herinne, meaning here plus in. Common in legal contracts.
hints: Common in contracts, along with 'thereof' and 'whereas'.
A lawyer's way of saying 'in this text'.
example: I shall discuss the question herein.

definition: A belief that goes against the official teachings of a church.
note: From Greek hairesis, 'choice', since a heretic chose their own doctrine. It is also used of any unpopular opinion in a group.
hints: Galileo was accused of it for saying Earth moves around the sun.
Church courts burned people accused of it.
origin: Old French heresie, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις

definition: A person who lives alone, away from society.
note: From Greek eremites, 'person of the desert', through Latin and Old French. Early hermits retreated to the desert for religious reasons.
hints: Lives in a cave or remote cabin.
A crab of this name borrows shells that aren't its own.
origin: Old French eremite, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης

definition: Showing great courage.
note: From hero plus -ic.
hints: Brave in the face of danger.
Like a firefighter's deed.
origin: Middle French heroïque, from Latin hērōicus
example: They took heroic measures to save his life.

definition: A strong, illegal drug made from opium.
note: Coined in German in the 1890s from Greek heros, 'hero', as it made users feel heroic.
hints: A highly addictive narcotic.
Derived from the opium poppy.
origin: German Heroin, from Ancient Greek ἥρως
example: The police searched the house and seized 2 kilograms of heroin.

definition: A tall wading bird with a long neck and sharp bill.
note: From Old French, from a Frankish word of Germanic origin.
hints: Stands motionless in shallow water.
Hunts fish with a quick stab.
origin: Anglo-Norman heiron, from Medieval Latin hairō

definition: A common viral infection that causes sores, especially on the lips or genitals.
note: From Greek herpein, 'to creep', for how the sores spread across skin. It is also the name of a family of viruses.
hints: A cold sore on the lip is caused by this virus.
Its Greek name means creeping.
origin: Latin herpēs, from Ancient Greek ἕρπης

definition: The unit of frequency.
note: Named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. One equals one cycle per second.
hints: A unit used for radio and sound frequency.
What a refresh rate on a screen is measured in.

definition: The period of greatest success or popularity.
note: From the exclamation heyda of the 1500s, probably expressing cheerfulness. It was later reanalysed as the 'day' of success.
hints: The 1920s were jazz's.
A star's career peak.
example: The early twentieth century was the heyday of the steam locomotive.

definition: A pause or gap in a series of events.
note: From Latin hiatus, 'gap, yawning'. A TV show or a band may go on one.
hints: What a band takes between albums.
A series is on this when it pauses production.

definition: A mark on the skin left by a kiss that sucks hard.
note: The origin is unknown. It is American slang, also used for a mark made on skin by a violin chin rest.
hints: A teen might hide one with a scarf.
A love bite.

definition: Out of sight.
note: The past participle of hide.
hints: Concealed from view.
Not easy to find.

definition: To a great degree.
note: From high plus -ly.
hints: Very, as in recommended.
In an elevated way.
example: He is in a highly visible job.

definition: A headscarf worn by some Muslim women.
note: From Arabic hijab, 'cover' or 'curtain'.
hints: Covers hair and neck.
Arabic for a covering.

definition: To seize control of a vehicle, or of anything, by force.
note: Possibly from highway plus jacker, 'one who holds up'. It first appeared in 1920s America.
hints: What pirates did to ships, but with planes.
A conversation, a march or a flight can be taken over this way.
example: They hijacked the judicial process.

definition: A person who walks long distances in the countryside.
note: From hike, a word of uncertain origin that appeared in the early 1800s.
hints: Walks trails with a backpack.
Appalachian Trail traveller.
example: Big black snakes enjoy scaring hikers by hanging from trees.

definition: Having many hills.
note: From Middle English hilly, built from hill plus -y.
hints: A word for rolling countryside.
Not flat; the opposite of a plain.
example: We had to drive on narrow roads through hilly terrain.

definition: To make progress slow or difficult.
note: From Old English hindrian, 'to hold back', related to behind. Hindrance and behind both come from the same root.
hints: What a broken leg does to a runner.
A roadblock does this to a delivery.
example: A drought hinders the growth of plants.

definition: A joint on which a door or lid swings.
note: From Middle English henge, related to hang. A hinge is something a door hangs on.
hints: What a door swings on.
Squeaks if it needs oil.

definition: A person from the 1960s counterculture, associated with peace, long hair and free love.
note: From hip, 'in the know', or from hipster. The name was at first a disparaging label for beatnik imitators.
hints: Wore flowers in their hair at Woodstock.
A VW camper van painted with flowers belongs to one.

definition: A large African river animal; short for hippopotamus.
note: A clipping of hippopotamus, a Greek word meaning 'river horse'.
hints: A massive animal that spends its days in rivers.
Short for a 'river horse'.

definition: A small problem, or a knot or quick fastening.
note: Probably from Middle English hicchen, to move with a jerk. Its origin is obscure.
hints: A snag in the plans.
To thumb a ride, informally.

definition: A person paid to kill someone.
note: Built from hit, used in the sense of 'to murder', and man. The word comes from the world of organised crime.
hints: A figure in crime films, often in a dark suit and sunglasses.
Mob bosses hire one to settle a score quietly.
example: Layla had a dangerous liaison with a hitman.

definition: A person who hits, especially a batter in baseball.
note: From hit plus -er. Heavy ones in baseball or boxing are admired.
hints: Babe Ruth was a famous one.
A clean-up spot in the batting order belongs to a power one.

definition: A small, hairy-footed creature from Tolkien's fiction.
note: Tolkien said he wrote the word on a blank exam paper and invented it from there. He later suggested links to the old word 'holbytla'.
hints: Bilbo Baggins and Frodo are both.
They live in holes in the ground in the Shire.
example: The Misty Mountains are no place for a hobbit.

definition: An activity done for pleasure in spare time.
note: From Middle English hobyn, a small horse. A hobbyhorse was a toy, so the word gradually came to mean a pastime.
hints: Stamp collecting is one.
Something you do for fun after work.
origin: Anglo-Norman hobyn, from Old French hobin
example: I like to collect stamps from different countries as a hobby.

definition: A team sport played with sticks and a ball or puck.
note: Of uncertain origin; it first appears in the early 1500s.
hints: Played on ice or on grass.
Sport with sticks and goals.
example: He helped his team beat the opponent at hockey 11-9 in a high-scoring match.

definition: To trick or cheat someone.
note: A shortening of hocus-pocus, a pseudo-Latin phrase used by conjurers.
hints: Part of a magician's stage phrase.
Conjuror's word that shortened to a verb.

definition: To raise something, especially with ropes or a pulley.
note: An alteration of hoise, from Middle Dutch hisen. It is first a nautical word.
hints: A flag may be pulled up this way.
A crane does it with a heavy load.

definition: Corny or artificially sentimental.
note: From hoke, 'to give an artificial feel', itself from hokum, plus -y.
hints: Contrived and a bit cheesy.
Said of a cheesy trick or gimmick.

definition: A thing that holds, or a person who possesses something.
note: From hold plus -er.
hints: Keeps a candle.
Passport owner.
example: Put your umbrella in the umbrella holder.

definition: Empty inside, or a small valley.
note: From Old English holh, 'cave'.
hints: A tree trunk may be like this.
Sleepy one in a famous legend.

definition: An evergreen shrub with spiky leaves and red berries.
note: From Old English holegn. It is associated with Christmas decoration.
hints: A festive door wreath.
Prickly leaves and red berries.

definition: A show of respect or honour, often by imitating someone's work.
note: From Old French hommage, from Latin homo, 'man', as a vassal became his lord's man. An artist may pay it to a master.
hints: A film that borrows a famous director's style does this.
What a vassal paid to his lord in feudal times.
origin: Old French homage, from Latin homō
example: The American director made an homage to spaghetti western films.

definition: A home run in baseball.
note: Short for 'home run' with an -er ending. It is also the name of an old Hebrew unit of volume.
hints: A big hit that clears the fence.
A baseball hit that sends the runner round all four bases.

definition: Cozy and comfortable, like a home.
note: Formed from home plus -y. It also exists as a slang spelling of homie.
hints: What a warm, welcoming kitchen feels like.
Snug in the way a house can be.
example: Susan added some homey touches to her office.

definition: A close friend.
note: From home plus -ie, meaning a friend from your home area. It began in American slang.
hints: A friend from the neighbourhood.
A slang word for a close friend.
example: Hey there, Francis, my homie!

definition: Truthful and sincere.
note: From Latin honestus, 'honourable'.
hints: Doesn't lie.
The best policy, according to the proverb.
origin: Old French honeste, from Latin honestus

definition: A sweet golden fluid made by bees.
note: From Old English hunig, an ancient Germanic word. As an endearment it has been used for centuries.
hints: Spread on toast.
Made in a hive.
example: The honey in the pot should last for years.

definition: Great respect, or a code of moral integrity.
note: From Old French honor, from Latin honor.
hints: A knight's code of conduct.
To pay it is to show respect.

definition: Cheap or illegal liquor.
note: Short for hoochinoo, a spirit made by the Tlingit people of Alaska.
hints: Moonshine, for example.
Illicit booze in the Prohibition era.
origin: Tlingit Xutsnoowú Ḵwáan, from Tlingit xóots

definition: A sweatshirt with a hood on the back.
note: From hood plus the casual -ie ending. In the 1990s and 2000s British tabloids gave the word a menacing image.
hints: Clothing worn by students and Silicon Valley founders alike.
A cosy top with a kangaroo pocket and drawstrings.
example: You can buy hoodies on the cheap in summer.

definition: A connection of equipment; informally, a casual romantic encounter.
note: From the phrasal verb 'hook up', meaning to connect something.
hints: A caravan park offers one for electricity.
A campervan owner plugs into a utility one.
example: The plumber came to fix the sewer hookup.

definition: Someone who fits hoops around barrels; also an old name for a wild swan.
note: From hoop plus -er. Barrels were once held tight by wooden or iron hoops.
hints: Barrel-making trade and surname.
A wild swan with a trumpet-like call, or a barrel maker.

definition: A shout of joy or approval.
note: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the late 1600s. It may be related to huzzah.
hints: Shouted at a birthday party when the cake appears.
Often follows 'hip, hip'.

definition: A vacuum cleaner in British English; to clean with one.
note: From the Hoover Company, whose name became a generic word. In the UK people say 'hoovering' for any brand.
hints: What British people call any vacuum cleaner.
A brand's name that became the verb for housework.

definition: A funnel-shaped bin that feeds material downward; or one who hops.
note: From hop plus -er. Grain and coal hoppers feed machines from the top.
hints: A funnel-shaped chute for grain or coal.
A grass-dwelling insect that jumps is called this.

definition: Tasting strongly of hops.
note: From hop plus -y. A beer can be described this way.
hints: Bitter flavour in a pale ale.
IPA drinkers like their beer this way.

definition: A huge crowd, often moving noisily.
note: From Polish horda and Russian orda, a nomadic tribe's camp. It entered English in the 1500s.
hints: A swarm of tourists.
Zombies come in these.
origin: Middle French horde, from Russian орда́

definition: A large, stinging wasp, usually striped brown and yellow.
note: From Old English hyrnetu, from a Germanic root also behind German Hornisse. The insect is the largest social wasp in Europe.
hints: Kicking its nest is a bad idea.
Its sting is famously painful, and a fighter jet and a masked radio hero share its name.
example: The Yiddish word for hornet is ferdbin, which means "horse-bee."

definition: Very unpleasant.
note: From Latin horridus, 'bristling'. Originally it described rough, shaggy things before meaning dreadful.
hints: A childish word for a nasty person or thing.
Roald Dahl's Aunts Sponge and Spiker were this.

definition: Intense fear or shock; or a scary genre.
note: From Latin horror, 'a bristling', since fear makes hair stand on end.
hints: Halloween films.
A feeling that makes hair stand up.
origin: Old French horror, from Latin horror

definition: A large hoofed animal used for riding and pulling loads.
note: From Old English hors, an old Germanic word.
hints: Has a mane and gallops.
Ridden in a race.

definition: A cheap place for travellers to sleep, often in shared rooms.
note: From Old French hostel, from Late Latin hospitale, a guest house. Hotel and hospital are close relatives of the same word.
hints: Backpackers share dorms in one for a few pounds a night.
A budget stay where you bring your own towel.
origin: Old French hostel, from Latin hospitalis

definition: A building offering rooms to paying guests.
note: From French hotel, which once meant a town mansion. The word shares a root with hospital and host.
hints: You check into it on holiday.
A porter carries your bags in it.
origin: French hôtel, from Latin hospitālis; in English since the 17th century
example: The bus transports passengers from the hotel to the airport.

definition: In an intense or passionate way.
note: From Old English hatlice, built from hot plus -ly. A hotly debated issue stirs up strong feeling.
hints: How an argument may be waged.
Often follows 'disputed' or 'contested'.
example: Nicolaus Copernicus – German or Pole? This is a hotly debated question.

definition: A hunting dog, or to pursue persistently.
note: From Old English hund, which was once the general word for dog.
hints: A basset or beagle is one.
Reporters do this to a celebrity.

definition: Happening every hour.
note: From hour plus -ly.
hints: Bells that chime at each one.
A wage paid per hour.
example: There are hourly express buses.

definition: A building where people live.
note: From Old English hus, a very old Germanic word.
