hints: Where a family lives.
It has rooms, a roof and a door.
origin: Old English hūs; in English since the 9th century
example: The house was full.

definition: A small, miserable dwelling.
note: From Middle English hovel, a shed or shelter.
hints: A rundown shack.
The opposite of a mansion.

definition: To hang in the air in one place.
note: From Middle English hoveren, to float or linger.
hints: What a helicopter or hummingbird does.
A wasp lingering above a picnic.

definition: An informal cowboy-style greeting.
note: Shortened from how do you do.
hints: What a Texan might say as hello.
A friendly western hello.

definition: A casual word for husband.
note: A pet form of husband plus -y. It sounds fond and informal.
hints: A casual term for a husband.
What a wife might call her partner fondly.
example: Laura thought Jack was the most wonderful hubby in the world.

definition: A tight group; or to crowd close together.
note: From Middle English hudelen, perhaps tied to a word meaning 'to cover up'. The football sense, where players gather to plan, is from America.
hints: Penguins do it for warmth.
Players cluster before a play.

definition: To a very great degree.
note: From huge plus -ly. Huge itself comes from Old French ahuge.
hints: How successful a hit film might be.
A word used to emphasise how big a change was.
example: This new movie is hugely inspired from the 1930s cowboy movies.

definition: A person, or relating to people.
note: From Latin humanus, probably related to homo, man, with a link to humus, earth.
hints: Not an animal or a robot.
Our species.
origin: Middle French humain, from Latin hūmānus m

definition: Showing kindness and compassion, especially towards animals.
note: From Latin humanus, the same root as human. It was once just a spelling variant of that word.
hints: A word on a trap that doesn't hurt the creature.
A society named for protecting animals bears it.
origin: Old French humain, from Latin homō
example: It is no longer considered humane to perform vivisection on research animals.

definition: Modest, not proud.
note: From Latin humilis, 'low', from humus, 'earth'.
hints: A person who doesn't boast.
Its root means close to the ground.
origin: Old French humble, from Latin humilis

definition: In a modest way, without pride.
note: From Middle English humbliche, formed from humble plus -ly.
hints: How a winner might accept an award.
Used when asking a favour with respect.

definition: Damp with water vapour in the air.
note: From Latin humidus, from umere, to be moist.
hints: A tropical summer day feels it.
Weather that makes your clothes cling.
origin: Old French humide, from Latin humidus
example: Near the equator, the weather is hot and humid year-round.

definition: The quality of being funny.
note: An American spelling of humour, from Latin humor, 'fluid'. Medieval medicine held that four body fluids shaped a person's temperament.
hints: What a joke is meant to have.
Said to be what laughter responds to.
example: I fail to see the humor in it.

definition: A grunt that shows doubt or annoyance.
note: An exclamation first recorded in the sixteenth century, an imitation of the sound itself.
hints: A noise of disapproval.
A snort from a grumpy person.

definition: Dark organic matter in soil made from rotted plants.
note: Borrowed straight from Latin humus, meaning earth or soil.
hints: Gardeners love it for rich soil.
Decayed leaves become this.

definition: A feeling about something without proof, or to curve the shoulders.
note: Originally a lump or hump, and the verb meant to push. The feeling sense came later.
hints: A gut feeling.
How you sit over a desk with poor posture.

definition: A need for food.
note: From Old English hungor.
hints: Stomach growls from it.
A strong craving, for food or more.

definition: Needing food.
note: From Old English hungrig, from hungor.
hints: Stomach rumbling.
Wanting a meal.
example: My kids go to bed hungry every night because I haven’t got much money for food.

definition: Attractive and muscular; also chunky.
note: Built from hunk plus -y. Hunk meant a big lump before it became slang for a strong, handsome man.
hints: Describes a muscle-bound film star.
Said of a good-looking and strong man.

definition: A person or animal that hunts.
note: From hunt plus -er.
hints: Pursues prey.
Orion is one in the sky.

definition: A barrier to jump over in a race, or a difficulty to overcome.
note: From Old English hyrdel, a frame of woven twigs used as a temporary fence. Sprinters later leaped over them as athletics barriers.
hints: Runners clear a row of them on the track.
A problem on the path to a goal.
example: He ran in the 100 metres hurdles.

definition: The stick used in the Irish sport of hurling.
note: From hurl, to throw. It is broad-bladed and made of ash wood.
hints: An Irish athlete carries one on the pitch.
Ash-wood stick used to strike a small ball.

definition: To move or act quickly.
note: From Middle English horien, to rush, perhaps imitating a buzzing sound.
hints: What you do when you are late.
Rushing can make waste, says the old proverb.

definition: Hoarse and rough, or a strong sled dog.
note: From husk plus -y. A voice was called husky because it sounds as dry as a husk.
hints: A throaty voice.
A dog that pulls sleds in the Arctic.

definition: A cheeky or shameless woman, in old-fashioned speech.
note: A contraction of housewife; the word once simply meant the woman of a house before it turned into an insult.
hints: An old scolding word for a brazen girl.
Began as a short form of housewife.

definition: To push or hurry; or to work hard to earn money.
note: From Dutch husselen, 'to shake'.
hints: Bustle through a crowd.
A side job to earn extra cash.

definition: A small cage for a pet rabbit, or a cabinet.
note: From Middle English hucche, a storage chest.
hints: A rabbit's home in a garden.
A dresser with shelves on top.

definition: A cross between two different kinds.
note: From Latin hybrida, 'mongrel'.
hints: A car with petrol and electric motors.
A mule is an animal one.

definition: A many-headed monster of Greek myth.
note: From Greek hydra, 'water serpent'. When one head was cut off, two more grew back.
hints: A monster Hercules fought.
A small freshwater creature named after the monster.
example: Hydra was slain by Hercules.

definition: Relating to water; also a name for electricity in Canada.
note: From Greek hydor, 'water'. In Canada it names electricity because early power came from hydroelectric dams.
hints: A prefix about water that also stands alone.
A word for the power bill in Canada.

definition: A doglike African carnivore known for its laughing cry.
note: From Greek huaina, via Latin. The name may come from a word for pig.
hints: Scavenges on the savanna.
Known for a cackling call.
origin: Old French hiene, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα
example: The hyena lost interest in Ziri and ran back into the woods.

definition: A thin membrane at the entrance to the vagina; also, in poetry, marriage.
note: From Greek hymen, 'membrane'. Hymen was also the Greek god of weddings, which is why the word can mean marriage in poetry.
hints: The Greek god of marriage shares its name.
A thin fold of tissue, and a wedding god.
origin: Middle French hymen, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν

definition: Overexcited or overactive.
note: Clipped from hyperactive, with hyper- from Greek huper, 'over' or 'beyond'.
hints: How a child may be after too much sugar.
A word that means 'over'.

definition: In a cold, unfriendly way.
note: Built from icy plus -ly. Icy comes from Old English isig.
hints: How a frosty stare may be given.
Said with no warmth at all.
example: Tom stared at Mary icily.

definition: Widely recognised as a symbol or classic.
note: From icon, from Greek eikon, 'image', plus -ic.
hints: A famous landmark or photograph.
Instantly recognisable by all.
origin: Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός
example: It would be a global tragedy to lose this iconic creature.

definition: A perfect standard, or being perfect for a purpose.
note: From Late Latin idealis, meaning existing in idea. An ideal was first something that exists only as a thought.
hints: Perfect weather for a picnic.
What you aim for but rarely reach.

definition: A phrase whose meaning isn't clear from its words alone.
note: From Greek idioma, a peculiarity. 'Kick the bucket' is one.
hints: 'It's raining cats and dogs' is an example.
A figure of speech particular to a language.
origin: Middle French idiome, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα
example: She often spoke in idioms, pining for salad days and complaining about pots calling the kettle black.

definition: A foolish or stupid person.
note: From Greek idiotes, 'private person', someone with no public role, then an ignorant person.
hints: Calling someone this is an insult.
Its Greek root meant a private citizen.
origin: Old French idiote, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης

definition: A person who does nothing useful with their time.
note: Built from idle plus -er. Idle once meant 'empty' or 'vain'.
hints: Someone lounging about with nothing to do.
A loafer who avoids all work.

definition: A peaceful, charming scene or period, often rural.
note: From Greek eidyllion, a little picture, used for short pastoral poems.
hints: A quiet country summer.
A perfect, pastoral setting.
origin: Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον

definition: A dome-shaped shelter built from blocks of snow.
note: From Inuktitut iglu, which means a house of any kind, not just one of snow.
hints: Built in the Arctic.
Home of ice blocks.
example: The green container is shaped like an igloo.

definition: To set something on fire; or to spark something off.
note: From Latin ignis, 'fire'. Engines ignite fuel and speeches can ignite crowds.
hints: A spark plug does this to the fuel in an engine.
A single match can do this to a heap of dry leaves.

definition: To take no notice of.
note: From Latin ignorare, 'not to know'.
hints: Pay no attention.
Treat as if not there.

definition: A picture, or a likeness of someone or something.
note: From Old French image, from Latin imago, a copy or likeness.
hints: A photo or painting.
What a mirror shows.
origin: Old French image, from Latin imāgō

definition: To fill or saturate with a quality or feeling.
note: From Latin imbuere, to wet or moisten. It first meant to soak, as with dye.
hints: A teacher may do it with curiosity.
To fill with a feeling or idea.

definition: Protected against a disease or penalty.
note: From Latin immunis, 'exempt from duties'.
hints: Vaccines give this.
Safe from infection.
origin: Middle French immun, from Latin immūnis

definition: A strong effect, or a collision.
note: From Latin impactus, 'pressed against'.
hints: Crash of two objects.
Influence on something.
example: His friend's opinion had an impact on his decision.

definition: A graceful African antelope known for its long leaps.
note: Borrowed from Zulu impala. The male has lyre-shaped horns.
hints: Lions hunt it on the savannah.
A Chevrolet car carries its name.
example: Giraffes, zebras, impalas, and elephants are usual neighbors.

definition: To pass on knowledge or a quality.
note: From Late Latin impartire, 'to share'. Wisdom and flavour are both imparted.
hints: A teacher might do it with knowledge.
What spices do to a stew.
origin: Middle French impartir, from Latin partiō
example: The sun imparts warmth.

definition: To get in the way of something and slow it.
note: From Latin impedire, 'to shackle the feet', from pes, 'foot'. It shares a root with pedestrian.
hints: Roadworks might do it to traffic.
Its opposite, in Latin, was to free the feet.

definition: To drive or urge someone to act.
note: Borrowed from Latin impellere, to push against.
hints: A strong sense of duty may do it.
To push forward, as if forced.

definition: To suggest something without stating it outright.
note: From Old French emplier, from Latin implicare, to fold in. The meaning is folded inside what's said.
hints: Hinting rather than saying.
What a raised eyebrow may do.
origin: Old French emplier, from Latin implicare

definition: To bring in goods from abroad.
note: From Latin importare, 'to carry in'.
hints: Customs officers check these crossing the border.
Goods that arrive from overseas.
origin: Old French emporter, from Latin importō
example: Nauru imports foods from Australia because phosphate mining destroyed land for farming.

definition: To force something on someone.
note: From Latin imponere, 'to place upon'.
hints: Set a rule or a tax.
Burden someone with a demand.
origin: Middle French imposer, from Old French emposer

definition: Live comedy or theatre made up on the spot.
note: A clipped form of improvisation.
hints: Performers on stage ask the crowd for a suggestion.
A comedy troupe plays games with no script.
example: She got her start doing improv at The Second City.

definition: Silly and empty of meaning.
note: From Latin inanis, empty or void.
hints: Pointless chatter.
A mindless remark.

definition: The folder where incoming messages arrive.
note: Formed from in plus box. It began as a tray for incoming paper.
hints: Where new email lands.
Often needs clearing to reach zero.

definition: To stir someone up to act, often violently.
note: From Latin incitare, 'to set in motion'. It is related to cite, and to excite.
hints: A speaker accused of provoking a riot might be charged with doing this.
Often followed by the words hatred or violence.
origin: Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō

definition: Money received regularly, especially from work.
note: From Middle English, meaning a coming in.
hints: A paycheque is part of it.
What tax is paid on.
example: With her small income she is having difficulties getting by.

definition: To bring something unwelcome upon yourself.
note: From Latin incurrere, to run into.
hints: What you do when you rack up debt.
A late fee is one you may do.
example: People who smoke incur a great danger to their health.

definition: Truly; in fact.
note: From the phrase in deed, 'in fact'.
hints: A word for emphasis.
Used to confirm something strongly.
example: Indeed, he made several misplays.

definition: An alphabetical list at the back of a book, or a pointing finger.
note: From Latin index, one who points out. The index finger is the one used to point.
hints: Find a topic quickly in a book.
The finger next to the thumb.
example: The index of a book lists words or expressions and the pages of the book upon which they are to be found.

definition: Independent of the big companies; or the music and film made that way.
note: A clipping of independent, used for pop music since the 1980s. It names small-label records and films.
hints: A film made outside a big studio.
A band on a small record label.

definition: A deep blue-violet colour, or the dye that gives it.
note: From Greek indikon, 'from India', where the dye came from. Newton listed it as one of seven rainbow colours.
hints: Sits between blue and violet in the rainbow.
The dye that colours blue jeans.
origin: Spanish índigo, from Ancient Greek ἰνδικόν

definition: Located inside a building.
note: From in plus door.
hints: Inside, not outdoors.
A swimming pool under a roof.
example: These fireworks are not for indoor use!

definition: To bring about or persuade someone into something.
note: From Latin inducere, 'to lead in'. A doctor can induce labour.
hints: What a doctor may do to start labour.
To coax someone into doing something.

definition: Clumsy or unskilled.
note: Via French from Latin ineptus, not fitting. It shares a root with apt.
hints: Said of a bungling beginner.
A juggler dropping every ball earns this label.
origin: Middle French inepte, from Latin ineptus

definition: Without power to move or react.
note: From Latin iners, inactive or unskilled.
hints: Neon and argon are examples of such gases.
A lifeless, still lump.

definition: A baby or very young child.
note: From Latin infans, 'unable to speak'.
hints: A tot in a cradle.
Its Latin root means not speaking.

definition: To pass germs or disease to someone or something.
note: From Latin inficere, 'to dip in', 'to stain'. The root idea was dyeing or tainting.
hints: What a virus does as it spreads through the body.
A cut that is not cleaned may become so.
origin: Middle French infect, from Latin infectus

definition: To conclude from evidence.
note: From Latin inferre, to bring in.
hints: What a detective does with clues.
To work out a conclusion.
origin: Latin inferō, from Latin ferō; in English since the 16th century

definition: A sudden arrival of large numbers of people or things.
note: From Latin influxus, 'a flowing in'. It is common in news about tourists and migration.
hints: A surge of visitors at a festival.
What a sudden flood of applicants might be.
example: Initial readings indicate an influx of toxic chemicals.

definition: To tell someone facts.
note: From Latin informare, 'to shape' or 'to teach'.
hints: Tell someone the facts.
Notify a person of news.
origin: Old French enformer, from Latin īnfōrmō
example: I informed him of his rights.

definition: A block of cast metal, such as gold or iron.
note: Middle English ingot meant a mould for casting metal. Its origin is uncertain.
hints: Poured into a mould.
A bar of gold in a vault.

definition: To breathe air into the lungs.
note: From Latin inhalare, 'to breathe on', built from in- and halare, 'to breathe'.
hints: What you do right after a doctor says 'deep breath'.
Swimmers do it quickly before ducking under the surface.

definition: To force liquid into the body with a needle; or to introduce something new.
note: From Latin injicere, 'to throw in'. Cash or humour can also be injected into a project.
hints: What a nurse does with a syringe.
How a vaccine is often given.
example: Inject hydrogen into the balloon.

definition: To cause physical harm to someone.
note: Back-formed from injury, which comes from Latin injuria, 'wrong' or 'injustice'. The root meaning was a wrong done to someone.
hints: A footballer twists a knee and is out for months.
What a bad fall might do to your wrist.
example: The rugby team's star player got injured in a violent collision.

definition: Harm done to the body.
note: From Latin injuria, 'wrong', from in and jus, 'right'.
hints: A sprained ankle is one.
A footballer may be out with one.
example: The passenger sustained a severe injury in the car accident.

definition: Away from the coast.
note: From in plus land.
hints: Far from the sea.
Not near the shore.

definition: To set a decorative piece into a surface.
note: Formed from in plus lay.
hints: A wooden box with a mother-of-pearl design.
A dentist may fit one into a tooth.

definition: A narrow arm of water leading into land.
note: From Middle English inlete, from the verb to let in.
hints: A small bay or cove.
Where the sea reaches inland.

definition: A person living in a prison, hospital or other institution.
note: From in plus mate, with a possible link to inn. It once meant a lodger.
hints: A person who lives behind bars.
A resident of a cell block.

definition: Present from birth rather than learned.
note: From Latin innatus, 'born in'. Philosophers argue about innate ideas.
hints: Describes a talent a child never had to be taught.
A trait you have from the moment of birth.

definition: Located farther inside.
note: From Old English innera, comparative of inne, within.
hints: A tube in a bicycle tyre, or the peace people seek.
A circle of your closest friends.

definition: British slang tag meaning 'isn't it'.
note: A spoken contraction of isn't it that is now used after almost any statement.
hints: Slang question tag at the end of a sentence.
Short for a very common British question.

definition: What is put into a system, or advice offered to it.
note: Formed from in plus put.
hints: What you type on a keyboard.
Your opinion offered to a group.

definition: Seriously mentally ill, or utterly wild.
note: From Latin insanus, 'not healthy'.
hints: Wildly crazy.
Slang for amazing, too.

definition: A small creature with six legs.
note: From Latin insectum, 'cut into', as the body looks segmented.
hints: Ant or beetle.
Has three body sections.
origin: Middle French insecte, from Latin īnsectum
example: Our shed has several insect infestations, including ants, yellowjackets, and wasps.

definition: To put something into something else.
note: From Latin inserere, 'to join in'.
hints: Slide a coin into a slot.
Place a page in a binder.
example: In order to withdraw money from a cash machine, you have to insert your debit card.

definition: To put in as an addition; or a small picture within a larger one.
note: From in plus set. A map often has one in a corner.
hints: A small map inside a bigger map.
A small panel set into a larger surface.

definition: The inner part, or within.
note: From in plus side.
hints: The opposite of out.
Interior of a building.
example: The inside of the building has been extensively restored.

definition: To demand firmly.
note: From Latin insistere, 'to stand upon'.
hints: Refuse to take no for an answer.
Say strongly that something must happen.
origin: Middle French insister, from Latin īnsistere
example: The Prime Minister insisted on his Chancellor's resignation.

definition: To speak rudely to someone, or a rude remark.
note: From Latin insultare, 'to leap upon'.
hints: What name-calling is.
Offend with a remark.
origin: Middle French insulter; in English since the 17th century
example: He insulted her with his rude remarks.

definition: To pay a company to cover the cost if something goes wrong.
note: From Old French, a variant of ensure. The two are now split: ensure means make certain, insure involves a policy.
hints: Done with a car, a house or a holiday.
A premium is paid for this protection.

definition: Whole and undamaged.
note: From Latin intactus, 'untouched'.
hints: Nothing broken.
Still in one piece.
origin: Middle French intact, from Latin intact(us)
example: I packed my belongings carefully so that they would survive the move intact.

definition: The amount taken in, or an opening where something enters.
note: From in plus take.
hints: How many calories you consume.
A group of new students admitted at once.

definition: To plan to do something.
note: From Latin intendere, 'to stretch toward'.
hints: Have a plan or aim in mind.
To mean to do something deliberately.
origin: Old French entendre, from Latin intendō

definition: Purpose or aim.
note: From Latin intentus, 'stretched toward'.
hints: Something you mean to do.
Plan or purpose.
origin: Old French entent, from Latin intentus

definition: To bury a dead body.
note: Borrowed from Old French enterrer, from Latin in terra, 'in the earth'. Its relative 'interment' is a funeral word.
hints: What a graveyard crew does.
A solemn word for burial.
example: Nikola Tesla's remains are interred in the Tesla Museum in Belgrade.

definition: A trainee who works, often unpaid or low paid, to gain experience; also to confine someone.
note: The trainee sense comes from a doctor who lived in the hospital where they worked, from French interne. The verb means to imprison without trial.
hints: A coffee-fetching newcomer at an office.
Often a student spending a summer learning on the job.

definition: A short form of introduction.
note: Clipped from introduction, which comes from Latin introducere, 'to lead in'.
hints: The opening part of a song or show.
The start of a book or a performance.

definition: To enter a place by force with an army.
note: From Latin invadere, 'to go in'. It is also used for pests and privacy.
hints: What an army does when it crosses a border.
An alien in a sci-fi film may attempt to do this to Earth.
example: Argentinian troops invaded the Falkland Islands in 1982.

definition: To create something that did not exist before.
note: From Latin invenire, 'to come upon, find'. The sense of 'make up' came later.
hints: Edison and Bell are famous for doing this.
A patent is filed to protect what you do.
origin: Old French inventer, from Latin inventus
example: I knew I had to invent an excuse, and quickly.

definition: To put money into something hoping for profit.
note: From Latin investire, 'to clothe', since the money was clothed in something that might grow.
hints: Buy shares in a company.
Spend time or money for a future return.
origin: Middle French investir, from Italian investire

definition: To ask someone to come.
note: From Latin invitare, 'to entertain'.
hints: Send a card for a party.
Ask someone to attend.
origin: Middle French inviter, from Latin invītō

definition: To call on a god, spirit or law for help or authority.
note: From Latin invocare, 'to call upon'. A court may invoke a rule; a wizard may invoke a spirit.
hints: A witch chants to do this to the spirits.
A lawyer can do it with a legal clause.
origin: Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre
example: He invoked the law that would save him.

definition: Toward the inside; or within a person's mind.
note: From Old English inweard, 'in' plus -ward. 'Inward-looking' describes someone focused on themselves.
hints: Doors that open this way swing into the room.
What meditation turns your attention.

definition: A chemical element used as an antiseptic and needed by the thyroid gland.
note: From French iode, from Greek ioeides, 'violet', for the colour of its vapour. Humphry Davy named it in 1814.
hints: Stains skin brown when dabbed on a cut.
Added to table salt to prevent thyroid problems.
origin: French iode, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής

definition: Relating to ions, or to a style of Greek column.
note: From ion, a Greek word for 'going', plus -ic. The other Ionic is an order of Greek architecture marked by scroll-shaped capitals.
hints: A chemistry word about charged particles.
A style of column with scrolls.

definition: Slightly annoyed.
note: Irk is of uncertain origin and once meant to weary or tire of something.
hints: Mildly bothered by a small thing.
Less than furious, more than pleased.

definition: Showing a contrast between what is said and what happens.
note: From irony, from Greek eironeia, 'feigned ignorance'.
hints: Fire station burns down.
Odd in a darkly funny way.
origin: Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός
example: Madness, an ironic fate for such a clear thinker.

definition: A contrast between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and outcome.
note: From Greek eironeia, feigned ignorance. Socrates used the technique in questioning others.
hints: Rain at a weather forecaster's picnic.
When something turns out the opposite of what is expected.
origin: Middle French ironie, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία

definition: A piece of land surrounded by water.
note: The s was added by mistake in the 1500s, as people wrongly thought it came from isle. The Old English word was igland.
hints: Land with water on all sides.
Robinson Crusoe was stranded on one.

definition: A very small island.
note: From Middle French islette, a little isle.
hints: Too small for more than a few trees.
A speck of land in the sea.
origin: Middle French islette, from Middle English holm
example: There is an islet on the other side of this body of water.

definition: A topic of concern, or to send out.
note: From Old French issue, which comes from Latin exire, to go out.
hints: A magazine appears in one each month.
A problem to be resolved.
origin: Old French issue, from Latin exeō
example: She has daddy issues, mommy issues, drug issues, money issues, trust issues, printer issues... I'm just sayin', girl's got issues.

definition: Feeling a need to scratch.
note: From Old English giccig, from itch plus -y.
hints: What a mosquito bite makes you.
Wool jumpers can make skin this way.
example: My nose always gets itchy the moment I put on my face mask.

definition: The thing mentioned, as object or for emphasis.
note: From it plus self.
hints: Used to stress the thing in question.
A reflexive pronoun for a thing.
example: When the opportunity presented itself, no feasible course of action suggested itself (to us).

definition: The hard white material of elephant tusks, or a creamy colour.
note: Through Anglo-Norman from Latin eboreus, from ebur. The colour is named after the material.
hints: Piano keys were once made of it.
A pale shade between white and cream.
origin: Anglo-Norman ivurie, from Demotic Egyptian yb

definition: A short coat.
note: From Old French jaquet, a diminutive of jaque, a short tunic.
hints: Worn over a shirt.
Covers a book too.
origin: Middle French jacquet, from Old French jaque

definition: A big spotted cat of the Americas.
note: From Portuguese jaguar, from a Tupi word for the beast. Its spots have a dot inside, unlike a leopard's.
hints: The largest big cat of South America.
A British car brand has a leaping one on its bonnet.
origin: Portuguese jaguar, from Old Tupi îagûara
example: Kalman photographed exotic wildlife like jaguars and coatis.

definition: Specialised words used by a particular profession or group, hard for outsiders to follow.
note: From Old French jargon, 'chatter', and before that perhaps the sound of twittering.
hints: Lawyers, doctors and programmers each have their own kind.
What a newcomer to a trade has to learn before meetings make sense.

definition: A red or brown opaque quartz stone used in jewellery.
note: From Old French jaspre, from Greek iaspis. It is also a boy's name.
hints: A polished stone in a necklace.
Polished into beads and cabochons for jewellery.

definition: A short trip taken for pleasure.
note: Origin uncertain. It first meant a tiring journey and later a pleasant one.
hints: A quick day out.
A brief pleasure trip.

definition: Flashy and lively; or in the style of jazz.
note: Built from jazz plus -y. The origin of jazz itself is uncertain.
hints: Describes a bright and showy outfit.
Music with a swinging, improvised feel.

definition: A wobbly dessert set from gelatine, sugar and flavouring.
note: Originally a brand name, Jell-O, that spread into everyday use as a general word for the dessert.
hints: A wobbly dessert served at children's parties.
American name for what Britons call jelly.
example: Surprisingly, the starving farm cat ate moldy white bread and lime jello.

definition: A wobbling dessert, or a fruit spread.
note: From French gelee, from Latin gelare, to freeze.
hints: It wobbles on a plate.
Spread on toast with peanut butter.

definition: Moving in sudden starts and stops, or dried strips of meat.
note: From jerk plus -y. The meat sense comes from a different word, charqui, from Quechua.
hints: A bumpy ride feels this way.
A dried beef snack.

definition: A knitted sweater or sports shirt; also a breed of cow.
note: Named after the island of Jersey, famed for knitted garments.
hints: Athlete's top.
A Channel Island gave it a name.

definition: British slang for a man seen as timid or weak.
note: From the girl's name Jessie, used as a mild insult in the sense of a stereotypically feeble person.
hints: Said by one mate to another who won't dive off the rocks.
A British put-down for a nervous chap.

definition: A structure built out into water to protect a harbour or moor boats.
note: From Old French jetee, something thrown out.
hints: Boats tie up at one.
A small pier.
origin: Anglo-Norman geté, from Middle French geté

definition: A precious stone, or a valued ornament.
note: From Anglo-Norman juel. Its ultimate origin is uncertain.
hints: A gem in a crown.
A ruby in a ring.

definition: A very short moment.
note: Origin unknown. It was said to be thieves' slang for lightning.
hints: Promise to return in one and you mean very soon.
A very brief time.
example: I’ll be back in a jiffy.

definition: A power saw with a narrow blade for cutting curves, or a puzzle made of interlocking pieces.
note: From jig plus saw. The puzzle was named after the saw, because early ones were cut from wooden pictures with it.
hints: A tool in a workshop that cuts curved shapes in plywood.
Has a box lid showing the finished picture.

definition: Struggle or striving in the cause of Islam.
note: Borrowed from Arabic jihad, 'struggle' or 'effort'. It can mean inner spiritual effort or armed struggle.
hints: Arabic for striving.
A word for effort in Islamic teaching.

definition: A light ringing sound of small metal objects; also a short catchy tune in an advertisement.
note: Imitates the sound, as with jangle. The advertising sense appeared in the 20th century.
hints: Sleigh bells make it, and so do keys in a pocket.
A radio ad tune that sticks in your head all day.
example: Her tambourine didn't come with any jingles attached.

definition: A person who rides horses in races.
note: From Jock, the Scots form of John, so it first meant a boy or fellow. The riding meaning arose in the 1600s.
hints: Small and light, and wearing silk colours.
One who rides in the Grand National.

definition: A horizontal beam that supports a floor or ceiling.
note: From Old French giste, from gesir, to lie down. A joist lies across the structure.
hints: Floorboards rest on them.
A timber hidden under a floor.

definition: A person who jokes, or a card in a pack.
note: From joke plus -er. The playing card is possibly named from German Jucker, tied to euchre.
hints: A card with a jester on it.
A prankster.

definition: Cheerful and merry.
note: From Old French joli, merry. The word was used for happy people long before it meant extremely.
hints: Santa is described this way.
Full of good spirits.
origin: Old French joli, from Old Norse jól

definition: A combat between two mounted knights with lances.
note: From Old French jouster, from a Latin word meaning near. It means to come together.
hints: A medieval tournament event.
Two horsemen charge each other.
origin: Old French jouster, from Latin iūxta

definition: Full of joy.
note: Simply joy plus -ful. Old French joie came from Latin gaudium.
hints: Describes a wedding crowd or a Christmas carol.
A noise of celebration, not sorrow.
example: The children were joyful on the first day of summer break.

definition: Full of joy.
note: From Old French joieus, from joie. It is a slightly more formal word than joyful.
hints: A formal word for a happy celebration.
Describes a wedding or a glad hymn.
example: Felt a joyous abandon.

definition: A person who decides legal cases, or to form an opinion.
note: From Old French juge, from Latin iudex.
hints: Wears a robe in court.
What you do when you assess someone.
origin: Old French juge, from Latin iūdex

definition: The liquid squeezed from fruit or vegetables.
note: From Old French jus, from Latin ius, which meant broth or sauce.
hints: Squeezed from oranges.
A breakfast drink in a glass.
origin: Old French jus, from Latin jūs
example: Squeeze the orange and some juice will come out.

definition: Full of juice, or full of tempting gossip.
note: Middle English jousy meant drunken, literally full of liquor. The sense of something rich and exciting grew from there.
hints: Ripe peaches are this.
Gossip that is exciting.

definition: Unusually large.
note: Named after Jumbo, a huge African elephant bought by P. T. Barnum in 1882.
hints: A giant-sized pack.
A big jet plane.

definition: A sweater in Britain, or a person or animal that jumps.
note: From jump plus -er, or from an old word for a loose jacket.
hints: Woollen top.
A horse in a show.
origin: Old French jupe, from Arabic جُبَّة

definition: Nervous and easily startled.
note: Built from jump plus -y. It describes someone who jumps at small sounds.
hints: How a person feels after too much coffee.
What a startled cat might be.

definition: A thick tropical forest.
note: From Hindi jangal, 'wasteland' or 'forest'.
hints: Where Tarzan swings on vines.
A tangle of rainforest.

definition: Younger or lower in rank.
note: From Latin junior, 'younger', comparative of juvenis.
hints: Associate-level staff and the school years before the last ones.
A son who shares a father's name.

definition: A drug addict; or a person devoted to something.
note: From junk, a slang word for heroin, plus -ie. It is now also used jokingly, as in 'adrenaline junkie'.
hints: Slang that jokingly follows 'adrenaline' or 'sugar'.
Originally street slang for a heroin addict.

definition: A group of military officers ruling a country after seizing power.
note: Borrowed from Spanish junta, a thing joined, from Latin iungere, to join.
hints: Takes over after a coup.
Military leaders running a state.
example: The brutal military junta was installed by the CIA to protect American business interests.

definition: A member of a jury.
note: From Anglo-Norman jurour, from Old French jurer, to swear. Jurors take an oath.
hints: One of twelve in a trial.
Listens to evidence in court.
example: Sami's lawyer told the jurors that cops arrested the wrong person.

definition: The title of the German emperors, and a word for emperor.
note: From German Kaiser, which like the Russian tsar comes from the Roman Caesar. Wilhelm II was the last to rule Germany.
hints: A German or Austrian emperor before 1918.
A Roman name that became a title for rulers.
example: The kaiser paid tribute to the sultan to avoid being attacked.

definition: Chinese characters used in Japanese writing.
note: From Japanese kanji, 'Han characters'. It is used alongside two syllabic scripts.
hints: A character borrowed from China into Japan.
Part of the Japanese writing system.
example: Japanese is written in a mixture of kanji and kana.

definition: The tenth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek kappa, which came from a Semitic word that meant 'palm' or 'hand'. It is the root of the letter K.
hints: A Greek letter whose Latin cousin is K.
Comes after iota and before lambda.

definition: A Japanese martial art using punches, kicks and open-hand strikes.
note: From Japanese kara, 'empty', and te, 'hand'. It began in Okinawa, and earlier meant 'Chinese hand'.
hints: Practised in a white uniform tied with a coloured belt.
Its practitioners break boards with a bare palm.

definition: The idea that your actions bring matching consequences.
note: From Sanskrit karman, meaning act or deed. It is a concept in Hindu and Buddhist thought.
hints: What goes around comes around.
Good deeds are said to earn it.
example: Everyone will eventually face their own karma someday.

definition: A landscape of caves, sinkholes and limestone dissolved by water.
note: Named for the Karst region of Slovenia and Italy, via German.
hints: Limestone country riddled with sinkholes.
Region that gave its name to a type of terrain.

definition: A small covered boat paddled with a double-bladed paddle.
note: From Inuktitut qayaq, a hunter's boat.
hints: Paddled by one person.
Used in the Arctic and in whitewater.

definition: Pieces of grilled or roasted meat, often on a skewer.
note: From Arabic kabab, by way of Turkish and other languages.
hints: Served in pitta with salad.
Meat roasted on a stick.

definition: With sharp interest or intensity.
note: From Old English cenlice, 'boldly'. Old keen meant brave before it meant sharp.
hints: Felt most strongly after a loss.
Awaiting results with eager interest.
example: The lack of a public sphere in Europe is being felt increasingly keenly.

definition: A person who looks after something.
note: From keep plus -er.
hints: A zoo employee.
A football player who stops shots.

definition: The base unit of temperature in the scientific scale starting at absolute zero.
note: Named after William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, a 19th-century physicist. Zero kelvin is the coldest anything can get.
hints: The unit scientists use when they talk about absolute zero.
Named after a Scottish-based physicist who became a lord.
example: Ice melts above 273.15 kelvins.

definition: A Japanese martial art fought with bamboo swords.
note: From Japanese kendo, 'the way of the sword'.
hints: Fencers wear armour and shout.
Bamboo-sword duelling from Japan.
origin: Japanese 剣道, from Middle Chinese 劍

definition: A shelter for a dog; or a place where dogs are bred or boarded.
note: From Anglo-Norman, northern form of Old French chenil, from Latin canis, 'dog'.
hints: A dog goes in one while its owners are on holiday.
Snoopy sleeps on the roof of his.
origin: Old French chenil, from Latin canis

definition: The softer edible part inside a nut or seed; also the central core of something.
note: From Old English cyrnel, 'little seed', related to corn. In computing the kernel is the core of an operating system.
hints: What is left inside a nut once the shell is cracked.
The core of an operating system shares its name.
example: Black walnut kernels are difficult to get out of the shell.

definition: A container with a spout, used for boiling water.
note: From Old English cetel, from Latin catillus, 'little bowl'. A watched one never boils, the saying goes.
hints: Whistles when the water is hot enough for tea.
An old proverb accuses one pot of blackness while another is just as sooty.
origin: Old English ċietel, from Latin catinus
example: Stick the kettle on and we'll have a nice cup of tea.

definition: A dull yellowish-brown colour, or cloth in that colour.
note: From Hindustani khaki, 'dusty', from Persian khak, 'dust' or 'earth'. British troops in India adopted it for uniforms.
hints: A common colour for army trousers.
A word that literally means dusty.

definition: A person or thing that kicks; in sports, the player who takes kicks at goal.
note: Simply kick plus -er. In American football it is the specialist who attempts field goals.
hints: The specialist who lines up for a field goal.
Also the surprise ending that gives a story its punch.
example: Yanni's goat is a kicker.

definition: A casual word for a child.
note: From kid plus -o. It is used affectionately.
hints: A friendly address to a child.
What a parent may call their son or daughter.

definition: To seize and hold a person unlawfully, often for ransom.
note: Formed from kid and an old slang verb nap, 'to snatch'. It first meant stealing children to work as servants in colonies.
hints: What a villain does to the hero's daughter in a thriller.
A crime in which a demand note is sent.
origin: kid + nap; in English since the 17th century
example: The industrialist's son was kidnapped.

definition: An organ that filters blood; also an edible bean's shape.
note: From Middle English kidenei, of uncertain origin.
hints: You have a pair of them.
Bean shaped like the organ.
example: Ziri will take a test to check if his kidney matches Rima's.

definition: A person or thing that kills.
note: From kill plus -er.
hints: A murderer in a thriller.
A serial one is a sinister figure.

definition: A casual way of saying 'kind of'.
note: A written form of the spoken blend of kind of. It means somewhat.
hints: A spoken way to say 'somewhat'.
A relaxed 'not quite'.

definition: To start a fire, or to stir up a feeling.
note: From Old Norse kynda, 'to light a fire'.
hints: Light dry twigs.
Awaken an interest.

definition: In a caring way; or please.
note: From Old English cyndelic, 'natural'.
hints: How you'd say a polite request.
A warm and gentle manner.

definition: A small booth selling newspapers, snacks or tickets.
note: From Persian kushk, a pavilion, via Turkish and French.
hints: A tiny stall on a street corner.
A self-service ticket machine.
origin: French kiosque, from Middle Persian kwšk'
example: During the fair, there were a lot of kiosks selling food and drinks.

definition: A young cat.
note: From Middle English kitoun, probably from an Old French word for a little cat. Its origin is otherwise obscure.
hints: Playing with a ball of yarn is its idea of fun.
A tiny, mewing pet that grows into a cat.

definition: A pet name for a cat; also a shared pot of money.
note: As a cat name it is from kitten plus -y. The money sense is an older, separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: A cat, in baby talk.
Where friends put money for a shared purpose.
example: Here, kitty kitty! Nice kitty!

definition: A natural talent for doing something easily.
note: From Middle English knak, a sharp sound. How it came to mean skill is unclear.
hints: You either have it or you don't.
A clever trick of doing a job.
example: He had a special knack for getting into trouble.

definition: To go down on your knees.
note: From Old English cneowlian, formed from knee.
hints: What you do to propose or pray.
A knight did this before a king.
example: In church you have to kneel during parts of the service.

definition: The slow sound of a bell, especially at a funeral.
note: From Old English cnyllan, 'to strike'. The silent k was once pronounced.
hints: A funeral bell's sound.
Toll that marks a death.

definition: British informal for knickers, or short cycling shorts.
note: A shortening of knickers, itself from 'knickerbockers', loose breeches named after fictional Dutch New Yorkers. Basketball's New York team uses the name for the same reason.
hints: A short word for undergarments in a British sitcom.
New York's basketball team shares the name.

definition: A mounted soldier of medieval times; also a chess piece.
note: From Old English cniht, 'boy' or 'servant'.
hints: Sir Lancelot was one.
Moves in an L shape.

definition: To strike a door to be let in.
note: From Old English cnocian, likely imitating the sound.
hints: A polite way to announce yourself at a door.
Rap on wood.

definition: A small round hill.
note: From Old English cnoll, a summit.
hints: A grassy rise in a meadow.
Smaller than a hill.

definition: Recognised or familiar; the past participle of know.
note: From Old English cnawen. Something known is something that is not a mystery.
hints: The reverse of a word like 'unfamiliar'.
How a famous person is described to the public.

definition: A grey tree-climbing Australian marsupial that eats eucalyptus.
note: From the Dharug word gula. It is not a bear, despite its look.
hints: Sleeps most of the day.
Cuddly marsupial from Australia.
example: The best known Austrian marsupials are kangaroos and koalas.

definition: Odd or eccentric.
note: From kook, an American slang word for an eccentric, plus -y.
hints: A bit eccentric.
Quirky in an off-beat way.
example: His kooky behavior seemed charming at first, but soon got on our nerves.

definition: Prepared according to Jewish dietary law; or acceptable and honest.
note: From Hebrew kasher, 'fit' or 'proper', via Yiddish. In English, 'not kosher' means dubious.
hints: Rules ban mixing meat and dairy.
If a deal isn't this, it is shady.

definition: Tiny shrimp-like sea creatures eaten by whales.
note: From Norwegian kril, meaning small fish fry.
hints: Baleen whales feed on them.
A swarm in cold southern oceans.
example: Harvesting finfish and krill are potential sources of income.

definition: Praise for an achievement.
note: From Greek kydos, 'glory'. It is singular even though it ends in s.
hints: Praise for a job well done.
Credit given for success.

definition: A tag showing what something is or costs.
note: From Old French label, a strip, from a Frankish word for a rag.
hints: Stuck on a jar or sewn inside a shirt.
What a price sticker is.

definition: Work; or the process of giving birth.
note: An American spelling of labour, from Latin labor, meaning 'toil'. Both work and childbirth were called by this word.
hints: The workers of the world.
A day in September is named for it in the United States.

definition: Hard work, or the process of giving birth.
note: From Latin labor, 'toil'.
hints: What a worker puts in.
Spelled without the u in America.
origin: Old French labor, from Latin labor

definition: A set of rungs for climbing.
note: From Old English hlaedder.
hints: Leans against a wall.
What a painter climbs.

definition: Weighed down with a load.
note: The old past participle of lade, 'to load', from Old English hladan. It is also found in 'fully laden'.
hints: How a donkey with baggage looks.
Burdened with a heavy load.

definition: A deep long-handled spoon for serving soup.
note: From Old English hlaedel, from a root meaning to load.
hints: Used to serve soup from a pot.
A big spoon for punch.

definition: A shallow stretch of water cut off from the sea by a reef or sandbar.
note: From Italian laguna, from Latin lacuna, 'pool' or 'hole'. The Venetian one is the original that gave the word to English.
hints: A ring of calm turquoise water inside a coral atoll.
Venice sits in the biggest one in Italy.
example: We found a beautiful, blue lagoon on the far side of the island.

definition: A Scottish landowner.
note: From Scots laird, a form of lord. It is a title of a landowner in Scotland.
hints: A Scottish lord of the manor.
Owner of a Highland estate.
origin: Scots laird, from Middle English lard

definition: Ordinary church members who are not clergy.
note: From Anglo-Norman laite, ultimately from Greek laos, 'people'.
hints: People in the pews rather than the pulpit.
Everyone in a cathedral who has not been ordained.
origin: Anglo-Norman laite, from Ancient Greek λαός
example: In medieval times, the laity often visited a confessor before major religious festivals.

definition: The eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, or a symbol for wavelength.
note: From Greek lambda, a doublet of Hebrew lamed. Programmers also use it for small anonymous functions.
hints: Appears in physics equations for wavelength.
A logo for the Half-Life games.

definition: To express deep sorrow or regret about something; also a song or poem of grief.
note: From Latin lamentari, 'to wail, weep'. As a noun it often names a mournful piece of music, such as one played on bagpipes.
hints: Often what a bagpiper plays at a funeral.
You might do it over a lost chance or a lost love.
origin: Middle French lamenter, from Latin lāmentor

definition: A long spear used by a mounted knight.
note: From Old French lance, from Latin lancea.
hints: A jousting weapon.
To cut open a boil.
origin: Old French lance, from Latin lancea

definition: A small, sharp surgical knife; or a pointed arch or window.
note: From Old French lancete, 'little lance'. Cathedral windows can have the same name.
hints: A tool for letting blood or lancing a boil.
The medical journal named after it is among the oldest.

definition: A spacecraft built to touch down on another world.
note: From land plus -er, a person or thing that lands. Apollo's lunar module was one, as was the Viking probe on Mars.
hints: Mission control waits anxiously for its signal after the final descent.
Philae was the one that bounced onto a comet.

definition: Tall, thin and a bit awkward.
note: From lank plus -y.
hints: Said of a gangly teenager.
Long-limbed.
example: The lanky teenager towered over his classmates.

definition: The folded flap on the front of a jacket.
note: Formed from lap plus a small ending, meaning a little fold.
hints: A pin may be worn on it.
Part of a suit jacket collar.
example: Did you get a good look at the pin he was wearing on his lapel?

definition: A deep blue stone prized for jewellery and pigment.
note: Short for lapis lazuli, from Latin lapis, 'stone', and a Persian-derived word for the colour blue.
hints: Blue stone in ancient Egyptian jewellery.
Ground to make a precious ultramarine paint.

definition: A brief slip or a gradual passing of time.
note: From Latin lapsus, from labi, to slip.
hints: A moment of poor judgement.
What a membership does if not renewed.
origin: Middle French laps, from Latin lāpsus

definition: A portable computer.
note: Formed from lap plus top, as it sits on your thighs.
hints: Fits in a bag.
A computer used on the sofa.

definition: A conifer that drops its needles in autumn.
note: From German Lärche, an early borrowing from Latin.
hints: A needle-bearing tree that goes bare in winter.
Evergreen-like but deciduous.
origin: German Larche, from Ancient Greek λάριξ

definition: Of great size.
note: From Old French large, from Latin largus, abundant.
hints: A big size on a clothing tag, above medium.
A big size on a clothing tag.
origin: Old French large, from Latin larga
example: Russia is a large country. The fruit-fly has large eyes for its body size. He has a large collection of stamps.

definition: A very slow musical pace.
note: From Italian largo, 'broad'. It is slower than andante.
hints: A direction for a slow tune.
A musical marking, slower than walking pace.

definition: The early, wormlike stage of an insect.
note: From Latin larva, meaning ghost or mask. The larva was seen as a mask hiding the adult.
hints: What a caterpillar is.
Hatches from an egg before pupating.
example: The larva of the small emperor moth feeds on heather plants.

definition: A device that makes a narrow, intense beam of light.
note: An acronym for 'light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation'. The first working one was built in 1960.
hints: A narrow beam of light used in surgery.
A pointer used by a lecturer.

definition: A rope with a loop used to catch cattle.
note: From Spanish lazo, from Latin laqueus, a snare. It is a doublet of lace.
hints: A cowboy swings it overhead.
A looped rope for catching a calf.
example: He managed to catch the runaway bull with a lasso.

definition: As the final point in a series.
note: Simply last plus the adverb ending -ly. Speakers use it to signal that the list is about to end.
hints: A speaker's cue that the finish line is near.
Follows 'firstly' and 'secondly' in a tidy speech.
example: Lastly, cook on low heat for thirty minutes and it's done.

definition: A simple catch that holds a door or gate shut.
note: From Middle English lacchen, to seize or catch.
hints: Lift it to open a gate.
Fastens a garden gate.

definition: In recent times.
note: From Old English laetlice, from late.
hints: In the last few days or weeks.
A word for in recent times.
example: I'd lately returned from Japan.

definition: Present but hidden or not yet active.
note: From Latin latere, 'to lie hidden'. A latent talent shows up only when circumstances call for it.
hints: A talent still undiscovered inside a person.
A virus that sleeps in the body for years.
origin: Old French latent, from Latin latēns

definition: At a time after now.
note: From Old English lator, the comparative of late. It is the adverb you use to put something off.
hints: What you say when you cannot do something now.
The opposite of 'sooner'.
origin: Old English lator, from Old English lætra

definition: Most recent.
note: From Old English latost, superlative of laet, 'late'.
hints: Newest thing.
Last of a series so far.

definition: The milky sap of rubber trees; or a stretchy material made from it.
note: Latin for 'liquid'. Gloves and balloons are often made from it.
hints: What a rubber tree produces.
A stretchy glove material.
origin: New Latin latex, from Latin latex

definition: A machine that spins wood or metal so it can be shaped.
note: Origin uncertain.
hints: Makes table legs round.
Spins material against a cutting tool.
example: He shaped the bedpost by turning it on a lathe.

definition: Coffee made with steamed milk.
note: Short for Italian caffe latte, meaning milk coffee.
hints: Ordered at a cafe.
Espresso topped with foam.
example: I'll have the soup du jour, the Salade Niçoise, and a latte.

definition: The second of two things mentioned.
note: From Old English laetra, comparative of laet, 'late'.
hints: Of two options in a sentence, it picks the one mentioned last.
The second one named.
example: The archaic past participle shapen is only used in misshapen, ill-shapen, and well-shapen (the latter two are much less common, though).

definition: To make sounds that show amusement.
note: From Old English hlehhan, thought to imitate the sound.
hints: The reaction to a joke.
The sound that follows a good joke.
example: There were many laughing children running on the school grounds.

definition: To send off into the air or water, or to introduce.
note: From Old French lancier, 'to throw a lance'.
hints: Send a rocket skyward.
Release a new product.

definition: An evergreen shrub whose leaves were once woven into crowns for victors.
note: From Old French lorier, from Latin laurus. Hence 'resting on your laurels'.
hints: Ancient champions wore a wreath of its leaves.
A cook drops its bay leaf into stew.

definition: An edible red seaweed, eaten especially in Wales.
note: From Old English, where it was a name for a water plant. Welsh laverbread is made from it.
hints: Seaweed turned into a Welsh breakfast item.
A purple seaweed boiled into a paste.
origin: Old English læfer, from Latin laver

definition: Generous or extravagant, with plenty of money spent.
note: From Old French lavasse, a downpour, so lavish was originally pouring something out in torrents.
hints: A banquet with gold plates and endless wine.
A spoiled guest receiving it is showered with gifts.
origin: Old French lavasse, from Middle English laven
example: Distributed gifts with a lavish hand.

definition: Allowed by law.
note: From law plus -ful. Compare 'legal', which is Latin where lawful is English.
hints: Whatever a police officer needs a warrant for must be done this way.
Along with 'good' in an alignment chart.
example: Lawful methods of dissent.

definition: A professional who advises on law and speaks in court.
note: From law plus -yer, as in sawyer.
hints: Argues a case.
An attorney.

definition: A single thickness of something spread over a surface.
note: From lay plus -er.
hints: A cake has several.
Onions have many.

definition: The way things are arranged.
note: From the phrase lay out.
hints: A plan for a page or room.
Arrangement of furniture in a room.
example: The magazine changed its page layout to look more modern.

definition: An easy basketball shot taken close to the hoop.
note: From lay plus up. The player banks or lays the ball up off the backboard.
hints: A close shot in basketball.
An easy shot near the basket.

definition: To drain away by liquid passing through.
note: From Old English words for a muddy stream.
hints: Rain does this to nutrients in soil.
To soak out slowly, as chemicals into water.

definition: Someone who guides or commands others.
note: From lead plus -er.
hints: In charge of the group.
Captain or chief.

definition: Covered with or full of leaves.
note: From leaf plus -y. Leaf comes from Old English leaf, a word shared across the Germanic languages.
hints: Describes a green salad or a shady suburb.
A word for trees in summer.
example: That insect can only be found in very dense leafy forests.

definition: A group of teams that compete, or an old unit of distance.
note: The group sense comes from Italian lega, 'bond'. The distance was about three miles.
hints: Premier one in football.
Twenty thousand under the sea.
origin: Middle French ligue, from Latin ligō

definition: Letting liquid or gas escape through a gap.
note: From leak plus -y. Leak is a word for something that lets water or gas escape, and it can also describe someone who spills secrets.
hints: A boat with a hole might be this.
How a faulty pipe is described.

definition: To gain knowledge or a skill.
note: From Old English leornian. Strangely, learn once could also mean to teach.
hints: What you do at school.
Pick up a new skill.
example: She learned dancing from her sister.

definition: A contract to rent property for a set time.
note: From Anglo-Norman lesser, to let go.
hints: Signed with a landlord.
Often runs for a year.
origin: Old French lesser, from Old High German lāzan

definition: A strap used to hold a dog.
note: From Old French lesse, from a verb meaning to let go.
hints: Walkies need one.
Keeps a pet from running off.

definition: Smallest in amount or degree.
note: From Old English laest, the superlative of less. 'At least' is a way of naming the smallest acceptable amount.
hints: The tiniest portion, as in a phrase about the smallest worry.
Superlative of less.
example: Didn't care the least bit.

definition: To go away from, or to let remain.
note: From Old English laefan, to let stay.
hints: What you do when you depart.
To go away or let something stay.
example: At what time does your train leave?

definition: A narrow shelf jutting out from a wall or cliff.
note: From Middle English legge, from an Old English word for a bar.
hints: A narrow rock shelf.
Where a bird nests on a cliff.

definition: A book recording a business's accounts.
note: From Middle English leger, a book that lies in one place. Double-entry bookkeeping uses debits and credits in it.
hints: An accountant's record of debits and credits.
A bound book listing every transaction.

definition: A blood-sucking worm, or a person who lives off others.
note: From Old English laece, a blood-sucking worm. The old word for doctor is a separate one.
hints: Used by doctors long ago to draw blood.
A freeloader.

definition: Wary and suspicious.
note: First recorded in the 1700s, from an old sense of leer, a sideways glance.
hints: A sideways look of doubt.
Distrustful of a stranger's offer.
example: Since he was bitten by a dog when he was young, he has always been leery of animals.

definition: A left-handed person.
note: From left plus -y. Left descends from Old English lyft, an old word meaning 'weak' or 'worthless'.
hints: A pitcher who throws with the other hand.
Also a nickname for someone on the political left.

definition: Something handed down from the past, or a gift in a will.
note: From Old French legacie, 'office of a deputy', from Latin legare, 'to bequeath'.
hints: What a famous person leaves behind.
Something inherited.
origin: Old French legacie, from Latin lēgātum

definition: Allowed by law.
note: From Latin legalis, from lex, law. Loyal is a doublet of the same word.
hints: What a lawyer is concerned with.
Permitted under the rules of the land.

definition: A traditional story, or a famous person.
note: From Medieval Latin legenda, 'things to be read'.
hints: Robin Hood tales.
A hero of sport or music.
origin: Old French legende, from Latin legenda

definition: Having long legs, or of a plant, tall and spindly.
note: From leg plus -y.
hints: Describes a foal or a stretched houseplant.
Long in the limbs.
example: Fred preferred leggy blondes.

definition: A large unit of Roman soldiers; or a vast number.
note: From Latin legio, 'levy' or 'body of soldiers'.
hints: Caesar commanded several.
Their name is plural in a Bible verse.
origin: Old French legion, from Latin legiō
example: The French Foreign Legion.

definition: Legitimate; genuine.
note: A clipping of legitimate. It is used to say something is the real thing.
hints: Slang for genuine.
What a trustworthy business is.

definition: A helper proposition used in proving a bigger one.
note: From Greek lemma, 'something taken', from the verb for to take. In dictionaries it also means the headword.
hints: A small proof step in mathematics.
Used on the way to a theorem.

definition: A sour yellow citrus fruit.
note: Through Old French from Arabic laymun, a word for citrus.
hints: Squeezed on fish or into tea.
Also a defective car, informally.
origin: Old French lymon, from Sanskrit निम्बू

definition: A long-tailed primate native to Madagascar.
note: From Latin lemures, Roman spirits of the dead. Linnaeus chose the name for animals that come out at night.
hints: Ring-tailed ones live in Madagascar.
A primate with a banded tail.
example: When I was little, people would tease me and call me a "lemur".

definition: A person or bank that lends money.
note: Lend plus -er; from Middle English lenere. The opposite party is the borrower.
hints: What the bank is to a mortgage holder.
A shylock-like figure in fiction, charging interest.
example: Money lenders are enjoying a profitable period.

definition: How long something is.
note: From Old English lengthu, from lang, 'long'.
hints: Measured with a ruler.
The long dimension.
example: A length of timber.

definition: A person with leprosy; or, figuratively, an outcast.
note: From Greek lepra, 'scaly'. The disease is now usually called Hansen's disease.
hints: Sufferer of an old skin and nerve disease.
Figuratively, someone shunned by society.
origin: Latin leprae, from Ancient Greek λέπρα

definition: An area of damaged tissue, such as a wound or sore.
note: From Old French lesion, from Latin laesio, 'a hurting'. Doctors use it for any abnormal patch on skin or organ.
hints: A word on a scan report.
A mark on skin or tissue.
origin: Old French lesion, from Latin laesiō

definition: To make or become smaller in amount or effect.
note: From less plus the verb ending -en. Pain, risk and worry can all be lessened.
hints: What painkillers do to an ache.
A speed limit does it to the danger on a road.

definition: Smaller or of less importance.
note: From Old English laessa, the comparative of little.
hints: What the smaller of two evils is.
The minor of two things.
example: The lesser of two evils.

definition: A period of teaching, or something learned.
note: From Old French lecon, from Latin lectio, 'a reading'.
hints: Taught in class.
What an experience teaches.
origin: Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiō

definition: Capable of causing death.
note: From Latin lethalis, from letum, 'death'.
hints: Capable of causing a death.
Deadly, as a poison can be.

definition: A character of the alphabet, or a written message.
note: From Old French lettre, from Latin littera.
hints: A character in a word or message.
Posted in an envelope.
origin: Old French letre, from Latin littera
example: His grandmother taught him his letters.

definition: An embankment built to stop a river flooding.
note: From French levée, 'raised', from lever. New Orleans relies on them.
hints: A bank built along a river to hold back water.
What failed in New Orleans during Hurricane Katrina.

definition: Flat and even, or a floor of a building.
note: From Old French livel, from Latin libella, a small balance or plumb tool. Its root is libra, scales.
hints: A spirit one shows if a shelf is straight.
A stage in a video game.
origin: Old French livel, from Latin libella f
example: Park the car on the level.

definition: A bar that turns on a fixed point to lift or move something.
note: From Old French leveor, a lifter, from Latin levare, to raise.
hints: Archimedes said he could move the world with one.
Pull it to start the machine.
origin: Old French leveor, from Latin levātor

definition: Legally responsible, or likely to do something.
note: From Old French lier, 'to bind'.
hints: Held responsible for damage.
Prone to a mistake.
origin: Old French lier, from Latin ligō
example: The surety is liable for the debt of his principal.

definition: A woody vine that climbs trees in tropical forests.
note: From French liane, influenced by lier, 'to bind'.
hints: Tarzan swings from one.
A rope-like vine in the jungle.

definition: A false written statement that damages someone's reputation.
note: From Latin libellus, a little book. It first meant any small written document.
hints: Sued in court by a defamed celebrity.
Slander's written counterpart.
origin: Old French libelle, from Latin libellus

definition: Sexual desire or drive.
note: From Latin libido, 'lust'. Freud adopted it for psychic energy in his theory.
hints: Freud made it famous.
Doctors blame stress or medication when it drops.
example: My wife has no libido since she got pregnant. What can I do?

definition: A system that measures distance by timing pulses of laser light.
note: The name began as LIDAR, modelled on radar, with light replacing radio. Self-driving cars use it.
hints: Radar's cousin that uses lasers.
Maps terrain from an aircraft.
example: Lidar is revolutionising archaeology.

definition: A feudal lord to whom loyalty is owed.
note: From Old French liege, probably from a Germanic word meaning free.
hints: A vassal's sworn lord.
Knights swore fealty to this lord.
origin: Anglo-Norman lige, from Middle High German ledic

definition: A person sentenced to life in prison; or a long-time employee.
note: From life plus -er.
hints: Someone serving a very long sentence.
Slang for someone who stays for life.
example: Stefan was locked up with lifers.

definition: Brightness that makes things visible, or not heavy.
note: From Old English leoht, from a root also behind lucid.
hints: Switched on in a dark room.
Feathers have this quality, and so do sunbeams.

definition: Probably going to happen.
note: From Old Norse likligr, from a word for like, meaning having the look of truth.
hints: Odds are in favour.
More probable than not.
origin: Old English ġelīclīċe, from Old Norse líkliga
example: Likely he’ll win the election in this economy.

definition: To compare one thing to another.
note: From Middle English liknen, built on like. It is nearly always followed by 'to'.
hints: Done when you say something is just like another.
A word that often sits before 'to' in a sentence.
example: The physics teacher likened the effect of mass on space to an indentation in a sheet of rubber.

definition: A shrub with fragrant purple blossoms, or a pale purple colour.
note: Ultimately from Persian nilak, bluish, via Arabic and Spanish. The shade is named after the flower.
hints: Blooms in spring with a sweet smell.
A pale shade of purple.

definition: An uncertain in-between state.
note: From Latin limbus, an edge. In medieval belief it was the borderland of hell for souls who could not enter heaven.
hints: Waiting with no decision made.
Also a dance with a low bar.
origin: Latin limbō; in English since the mid 17th century

definition: A boundary that cannot be passed.
note: Through Old French from Latin limes, a boundary path between fields.
hints: What a speed sign shows.
The point beyond which you cannot go.
origin: Old French limit, from Latin līmes

definition: A tree with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant flowers; also called a lime or basswood.
note: From Old English linden, an adjective meaning made of lime wood, from a Germanic word for the tree.
hints: Berlin's famous boulevard is named after this tree.
Its blossoms are brewed into a calming tea.

definition: Arranged in a straight line, or following one step after another.
note: From Latin linearis, from linea, 'line'.
hints: A graph that makes a straight line.
In sequence, step by step.

definition: Cloth woven from flax.
note: From Old English linen, meaning made of flax. The word lin was the plant itself.
hints: Tablecloths and bedsheets.
Woven from the flax plant.

definition: A large passenger ship, or a layer that fits inside something.
note: Built from line plus -er. The ship sense is short for 'ocean liner', a ship that ran regularly on a fixed line of route.
hints: A big cruise vessel.
A bin may have a bag inside as this.

definition: A group of people arranged in a row, or a team's chosen players.
note: From the phrase line up.
hints: Suspects in a row.
A baseball batting order.

definition: To stay longer than needed, or to be slow to leave.
note: From Middle English lengeren, from an old word meaning 'to dwell'. Smells, doubts and guests all linger.
hints: A smell of perfume in a room after someone leaves.
Guests who won't go home at the end of a party.

definition: The specialised language of a particular group.
note: Probably from Latin lingua, tongue, via Portuguese or a similar source.
hints: Jargon of sailors or gamers.
Slang used by a particular profession.
example: They don't speak our lingo.

definition: A fat or oil-like substance in living cells.
note: From Greek lipos, fat.
hints: Cholesterol is one.
A scientific word for fats.
example: The percentage of lipids in an animal cell is about 8%.

definition: A substance that flows, like water.
note: From Latin liquidus, 'fluid'.
hints: Neither a solid nor a gas.
What pours from a jug.
origin: Old French liquide, from Latin liquidus
example: A liquid can freeze to become a solid or evaporate into a gas.

definition: Strong alcoholic drink.
note: From Old French licour, from Latin liquor, 'fluid'.
hints: Whisky or vodka.
Sold in a bottle shop.

definition: A fine, strong cotton thread used in stockings.
note: Named for Lisle, now Lille, in France, where it was first made.
hints: Fabric once used for gloves and socks.
Thread named after a French city.

definition: To pay attention to sound.
note: From Old English hlysnan.
hints: Use your ears.
What students are told to do in class.
example: Please listen carefully as I explain.

definition: Slim, flexible and graceful.
note: From Old English lithe, which meant gentle or mild. The sense of supple came later.
hints: Describes a dancer or a cat.
Moves with easy grace.

definition: A metric unit of liquid volume.
note: From French litre, from an old word for a measure of grain. It is a bit more than a quart.
hints: A bottle of water is often this size.
A metric measure a little under two pints.
origin: French litre, from Ancient Greek λίτρα
example: You should be able to fill four cups with one litre of water.

definition: Rubbish dropped in public, or a group of newborn animals.
note: From Old French litiere, 'bed', from Latin lectus.
hints: Cats have it.
Rubbish on a street.

definition: Small in size or amount.
note: From Old English lytel. It has no relation to the word small.
hints: Fairy-tale heroines such as Red Riding Hood are described this way.
Tom Thumb and Stuart are this by nature.
example: He accepted the little they gave him.

definition: Full of life and energy.
note: From life plus -ly.
hints: Bustling with activity.
A party atmosphere.
example: Lively and attractive parents.

definition: To make or become more lively.
note: Partly from life plus -en, partly a shortening of enliven.
hints: What music might do to a quiet party.
Often followed by up.
example: Let's liven up this party!

definition: The large organ that filters blood and makes bile.
note: From Old English lifer, a very old Germanic word.
hints: Eaten with onions.
Alcohol harms it.
example: Steve Jobs is a famous liver transplant recipient.

definition: A distinctive uniform or colour scheme, as on a servant, a bus or an aeroplane.
note: From Old French livree, 'something handed over', from the verb for deliver. A lord once gave his servants clothing marked with his colours.
hints: What airlines paint on their planes.
A footman's uniform; also a stable for horses.
origin: Anglo-Norman liveree, from Old French livree

definition: Furiously angry, or a bruised bluish colour.
note: From Latin lividus, 'bluish, leaden', the colour of a bruise. 'Livid with rage' described a face gone dark, and the anger outlived the colour.
hints: Furious enough to turn colour.
A very angry parent.
origin: Old French livide, from Latin līvidus
example: Willful stupidity makes him absolutely livid.

definition: A scaly reptile with four legs and a long tail.
note: From Old French lesard, from Latin lacertus. It may be older than Latin.
hints: A gecko is one that climbs walls.
Sun-bathing on a rock is its usual activity.
origin: Anglo-Norman lusard, from Old French lesard

definition: A woolly South American animal related to the camel.
note: From Spanish llama, from Quechua.
hints: Spits when annoyed.
Carries loads in the Andes.
example: The woman is looking at the llama in the field and smiling.

definition: A machine or program that loads things.
note: From load plus -er. A front-end one is a tractor with a scoop; in computing it prepares a program to run.
hints: A tractor with a big bucket at the front.
Piles gravel into a truck.

definition: Having soil rich in clay, sand and decayed matter.
note: From loam plus -y. Loam is an old Germanic word for earth or clay.
hints: The best kind of garden soil.
A word from the garden shed.

definition: Unwilling; reluctant.
note: From Old English lath, which meant hateful or evil.
hints: Describes your feeling about going to a boring meeting.
Reluctant to do something.
origin: Old English lāð, from Old Norse leið
example: I was loath to return to the office without the Henderson file.

definition: To hate something intensely.
note: From Old English lathian, from a Germanic root that gave Old Norse leidhask. The noun loath, 'unwilling', is a close cousin.
hints: Stronger than disliking.
Some people do so to Brussels sprouts or Mondays.
example: I loathe scrubbing toilets.

definition: Belonging to a nearby place.
note: From Late Latin localis, from locus, a place.
hints: A shop in your neighbourhood.
Not from far away.
origin: Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus
example: A local point of view.

definition: To find or to place.
note: From Latin locare, 'to place'.
hints: Find out where something is.
Establish a business.
example: Can you locate your cousins in the Midwest?

definition: A small lockable cabinet.
note: From lock plus -er.
hints: At the gym or school.
Where you store your bag.
example: She was afraid to come out of the locker.

definition: A doctor or other professional who stands in for another.
note: Short for Latin locum tenens, 'holding the place'.
hints: A temporary stand-in for a regular doctor.
From a Latin phrase meaning place-holder.

definition: A particular place or point where something occurs.
note: Borrowed from Latin locus, place.
hints: The scene of a crime.
A central point of activity.

definition: A small house or cabin, or to stay somewhere briefly.
note: From Old French loge, a hut or arbour, from a Germanic root.
hints: A hunting cabin in the woods.
To submit a complaint officially.

definition: Very high, or noble and proud.
note: From Middle English loft, sky or upper room, plus -y.
hints: A mountain peak or an ambition.
Aims that are grand and ambitious.
example: A noble and lofty concept.

definition: Reasoning that follows strict rules.
note: Through Old French from Greek logike, from logos, word or reason.
hints: A step-by-step argument.
What Mr Spock prizes.
origin: Latin logicus, from Ancient Greek λογῐκός

definition: The details or act of signing into a computer system.
note: A noun made from the verb phrase 'log in'. The log is a ship's record book, and recording who entered gave 'log in' its sense.
hints: A username and a password.
What a website asks for before letting you in.
example: I've forgotten my login again.

definition: A sweet on a stick, or in Britain and Australia, a frozen ice treat.
note: Shortened from lollypop. In Australia the word can also mean any sweet or even money.
hints: Sweet that a child might lick.
British word for a frozen treat on a stick.
example: In England a popsicle is called an ice lolly.

definition: Sad from being alone.
note: From lone plus -ly.
hints: Isolated and sad.
No one to talk to.
example: Felt sad and lonely.

definition: A person who prefers to be alone.
note: From lone plus -er. It describes someone who avoids company.
hints: A solitary type.
Someone who avoids parties.
example: I actually enjoy being a loner.

definition: Crazy or very silly.
note: Shortened from lunatic, which came from Latin luna, 'moon', because madness was once blamed on the moon.
hints: Cartoon characters are often described this way.
Daft or wildly eccentric.

definition: Silly or a bit crazy.
note: From loop plus -y.
hints: A word for a scatterbrained idea.
A little off your rocker.

definition: Not tight or firmly fixed.
note: From Old Norse lauss, meaning free or empty.
hints: A wobbly tooth is this.
Not fastened.
example: This wheelbarrow has a loose wheel.

definition: To make or become less tight.
note: From loose plus -en. Old Norse lauss, 'free', is a relative.
hints: What you do with your belt after a big meal.
A screw may do it over time.

definition: A large motor vehicle for carrying goods.
note: Origin uncertain, perhaps from a dialect verb meaning to drag.
hints: What Americans call a truck.
A large goods vehicle on a motorway.

definition: A person or team that does not win.
