note: From Middle English, built from lose plus -er. As an insult it may come from the older word losel, meaning 'worthless fellow'.
hints: The team that comes second.
The unlucky side of a contest.
example: In a two-horse race there is always one winner and one loser.

definition: A liquid cream applied to the skin.
note: From Latin lotio, 'a washing'. Sun tan and moisturiser both come as this.
hints: A bottle of moisturiser.
What you rub on after a sunburn.
example: A lotion for dry skin.

definition: A lottery or a game of chance.
note: Borrowed from Italian lotto, 'lot' or 'destiny'. Players match drawn numbers to win.
hints: A game of picking numbers.
What a draw with a big prize is called.
example: If you win the lotto, what will you do with the money?

definition: A water plant with large pink or white flowers.
note: From Greek lotos, which named several plants. In Asia it is a symbol of purity.
hints: A sacred flower of India.
A yoga pose is named after it.
origin: Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός

definition: At high volume.
note: From loud plus -ly.
hints: Not quietly.
Shouting from a rooftop.
example: He spoke loudly so that his brother could hear him from across the street.

definition: An Irish lake or sea inlet.
note: From Irish loch. It is pronounced like the Scottish word 'loch'.
hints: An Irish lake.
A cousin of the Scottish loch.
origin: Irish loch, from Old Irish loch

definition: To relax lazily; or a room for sitting.
note: Of uncertain origin; it appears in the 1500s.
hints: A hotel's waiting room.
What cats do on a sofa.
example: We like to spend our Sundays lounging about at home in our pyjamas.

definition: A tiny wingless insect that lives on skin or hair.
note: From Old English lus, an old Germanic word. The plural is lice.
hints: Found in hair.
A contemptible person, informally.

definition: Very bad or poor in quality.
note: From louse plus -y. Being infested with lice was a miserable state.
hints: A rotten day.
Terrible service in a restaurant.
example: No offense, but his cooking is lousy.

definition: Beautiful or delightful.
note: From Old English luflic, 'loving', from lufu.
hints: A pleasant sort of word for pretty.
Used for something that gives pleasure.

definition: A person who loves another or loves a thing.
note: From Middle English lovere, built from love plus -er. It can also mean a fan, as in a 'music lover'.
hints: Someone devoted to a hobby, or a sweetheart.
A person who adores books is one of these.

definition: An affectionate way of addressing someone; also a baby's comfort toy.
note: Formed from love plus -y. In Britain it is also associated with theatre people.
hints: A pet name, or a toddler's blanket.
Term of endearment from a shopkeeper.

definition: Further down; or to bring something down.
note: From low plus -er, the comparative form. As a verb it means to move something down gently.
hints: A drawbridge is put into this state to let people cross.
What you do to a flag at sunset.

definition: Humble, or of low rank.
note: Built from low plus -ly. Though it looks like an adverb, it is an adjective meaning of modest standing.
hints: A word for the least important people in a hierarchy.
Describes a peasant, a servant or a worm.

definition: Faithful to a person or cause.
note: From Old French loial, from Latin legalis. Legal is its doublet.
hints: Describes a dog or a friend.
Sticks by you through thick and thin.
origin: Middle French loyal, from Latin lēgālis
example: We must remain loyal to the mission.

definition: Clearly expressed or thinking clearly.
note: From Latin lucidus, bright, from lucere, to shine.
hints: An explanation that is easy to follow.
A dream where you know you are dreaming.

definition: Relating to the lower back.
note: From Latin lumbus, 'loin'. Back doctors talk of the vertebrae in this region.
hints: A type of spinal puncture is named for it.
A cushion for office chairs supports it.

definition: Timber cut into boards; or to move heavily and clumsily.
note: The wood sense is North American; the older sense was cast-off junk, perhaps related to a verb for moving heavily.
hints: Stacked in a timber yard, ready for builders.
The verb is how a bear moves.

definition: A unit measuring the amount of light from a source.
note: From Latin lumen, light. It was adopted as a unit in 1894 by André Blondel.
hints: Printed on a lightbulb box.
A measure of brightness.

definition: Full of lumps; not smooth.
note: From lump plus -y. Lump itself is a Germanic word for a shapeless piece.
hints: How badly mixed gravy might be.
A bad mattress or custard can be this.
example: I don't know which was worse, the lumpy soup or the lumpy bed.

definition: A meal eaten in the middle of the day.
note: First recorded in 1580 as a word for a lump or hunk of food.
hints: Midday meal.
What a sandwich is often for.

definition: A sudden forward thrust, as in fencing.
note: From French allonge, from a Latin root meaning long.
hints: A fencer does it with a sword.
An exercise stepping forward on one leg.

definition: A tall garden flower with spikes of blooms.
note: From Latin lupinus, from lupus, 'wolf'. Its seeds are also eaten.
hints: A tall spiky garden flower.
A plant whose beans are eaten in the Mediterranean.
origin: Old French lupin, from Latin lupīnus

definition: A long-term illness in which the body's immune system attacks itself.
note: Latin for 'wolf'. The disease took the name in the Middle Ages, often explained by its facial sores resembling wolf bites.
hints: A medical term from the Latin for a wild animal.
A condition in which the immune system turns on the body.

definition: To stagger or move suddenly and unsteadily.
note: Originally a nautical word for a ship's sudden roll, of unknown origin.
hints: A boat in rough waves.
Staggering after too many drinks.
example: The truck lurched down the road.

definition: Shocking and sensational, or glaringly vivid.
note: From Latin luridus, pale yellow or wan.
hints: A tabloid's gruesome details.
Harsh and garish colours.
example: The accident was described with lurid detail.

definition: Full of vigour and energy.
note: From Middle English lust, which meant joy or vigour before it narrowed to desire.
hints: A hearty cheer might be described this way.
Robust and enthusiastic.

definition: Great comfort and expense.
note: From Latin luxus, 'excess'.
hints: Five-star treatment.
Costly comfort.
origin: Old French luxurie, from Latin luxuria

definition: Telling untruths; or resting flat.
note: From lie plus -ing. The two meanings come from two different verbs that happen to look alike.
hints: What a witness commits when swearing falsely in court.
What you do when you rest flat on a bed.

definition: To kill someone by mob action without a lawful trial.
note: Probably from the surname Lynch, though which Lynch is uncertain. The practice has a long and shameful history in the United States.
hints: A killing by an unlawful crowd.
An unlawful execution by a mob.

definition: Relating to poetry that expresses a speaker's own feelings, or the words of a song.
note: Via French and Latin from Greek lurikos, 'of the lyre'. Lyric poetry was first the kind sung to a lyre.
hints: Songwriters write these words.
Poetry of personal feeling, or what the singer sings.
origin: French lyrique, from Ancient Greek λυρικός

definition: The words of a song.
note: From Greek lyrikos, 'of the lyre'.
hints: What singers recite.
Words that go with the music.
example: The song’s lyrics were full of nostalgia.

definition: A large, brightly coloured parrot from tropical America.
note: From Portuguese macau, of unknown origin.
hints: A loud, colourful tropical bird.
A big parrot with a long tail and a hooked beak.
example: The blue macaw is on its way to extinction.

definition: Aggressively or showily masculine.
note: Borrowed from Spanish macho, 'male', from Latin masculus, which also gave English 'male'.
hints: Describes a man keen to prove his toughness.
Spanish for male, now a word for swagger.

definition: Large in scale; also a stored set of commands.
note: From Greek makros, 'long' or 'large'. In computing a macro is a short command that stands in for many.
hints: A prefix that points to the big picture.
Economists use it for the study of whole economies.

definition: A polite way to address a woman.
note: From Old French ma dame, 'my lady'. The same word also names a woman who runs a household or a brothel.
hints: How a shop assistant might address a customer.
Polite counterpart to 'sir'.
origin: Old French madame, from Latin mea domina
example: Mrs Grey wondered if the outfit she was trying on made her look fat. The sales assistant just said, “It suits you, madam”.

definition: To drive someone crazy or very angry.
note: From the Old English root of mad. A maddening noise is one that drives you wild.
hints: What a dripping tap at three a.m. does.
To exasperate someone to distraction.

definition: In a wild, frantic, or extreme way.
note: From Middle English madly, built from mad plus -ly. It can also mean extremely, as in 'madly in love'.
hints: How a rushing person moves.
A word before 'in love'.
example: I'm madly in love with you.

definition: A man who is insane, or one who behaves wildly and recklessly.
note: Formed from mad plus man. The word is used both literally and as a jab at reckless people.
hints: Shouted at a driver who cuts across three lanes.
A figure in old stories ranting in the street.
example: The whole country was subject to the caprices of a madman.

definition: A lightweight cotton cloth with a bright plaid pattern.
note: Named for Madras, now Chennai, in India, where the cloth was woven. It is popular in summer shirts.
hints: Preppy summer shirts are often made of this plaid.
Named for a former name of an Indian city.

definition: The use of rituals or supposed supernatural forces to make things happen, or a trick that seems to.
note: Traced back through Greek to Old Persian, where the root referred to the priests known as magi.
hints: Wizards and stage performers both claim it.
Abracadabra is a word for summoning it.
origin: Old French magique, from Ancient Greek μαγικός; in English since the 14th century

definition: Hot molten rock beneath the earth's surface.
note: From Greek magma, 'a kneaded mass', from massein, 'to knead'. It is called lava once it erupts.
hints: What fills a volcano before an eruption.
Rock so hot that it flows.
example: Magma from the mantle or lower crust rises through its crust towards the surface.

definition: An object that attracts iron and some other metals.
note: From Greek Magnetis lithos, 'stone of Magnesia', a region where it was found.
hints: Sticks to a fridge door.
Pulls iron filings towards it.
origin: Old French magnete, from Latin magnēs

definition: A wine bottle holding the equivalent of two standard bottles.
note: Latin for 'great' (neuter), shortened from magnum bonum, 'a great good'. It also names a powerful handgun and an ice cream bar.
hints: Champagne is sometimes served from one to impress.
A bottle size holding 1.5 litres, or a Clint Eastwood handgun.
example: Long Day's Journey into Night is considered to be Eugene O'Neill's magnum opus.

definition: A priest or wise man in ancient Persia.
note: Latin from Greek magos. Its plural, magi, includes the wise men of the nativity.
hints: One of the three in the Christmas story.
Sorcerer or priest from old Persia.
origin: Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος

definition: A young unmarried woman; also first, as in maiden voyage.
note: From Old English maegden.
hints: A girl in a medieval tale.
The first voyage of a ship.

definition: For the most part.
note: From main plus -ly.
hints: For the most part.
Primarily or chiefly.
origin: Middle English maynly; in English since the 17th century
example: He is mainly interested in butterflies.

definition: Corn; the cereal plant Zea mays, or its grain.
note: Borrowed from Spanish maiz, from Taino, the language of the Caribbean people who grew it.
hints: Another name for corn, used in Britain.
A golden crop that the Americas gave the world.

definition: Greater in size, importance or rank.
note: From Latin maior, 'greater'. Its opposite, minor, comes from Latin minor.
hints: The opposite of minor.
A military rank above captain, or a main subject at university.

definition: A person or thing that makes something.
note: From Middle English, built from make plus -er. In religion it can name God as the creator.
hints: Someone who builds things.
A craftsman or the company that builds a product.

definition: Cosmetics, or the composition of something.
note: From the phrase make up.
hints: Lipstick and mascara.
The combination of parts in a team.
example: She is wearing a lot of makeup.

definition: The desire to cause harm or hurt others.
note: From Latin malitia, from malus, 'bad'. In law, 'malice aforethought' is intent to do harm.
hints: A spiteful rumour is spread with it.
Law calls it 'aforethought' when a killer planned in advance.
origin: Old French malice, from Latin malitia

definition: A fast and deadly African snake.
note: Borrowed from Zulu imamba, from a Bantu root.
hints: A fast African snake whose bite is deadly.
Black and green kinds are both feared.
example: The African Black mamba is a large and highly venomous snake.

definition: A lively Latin dance and its music.
note: The dance came from Cuba in the 1940s, from Cuban Spanish mambo. The word itself comes from Haitian Creole, a priestess's title.
hints: A Latin dance with a quick beat.
Number five in a Lou Bega hit.
origin: Haitian Creole manbo, from Spanish mambo; in English since the 20th century

definition: An animal that is warm-blooded, has hair and feeds milk to its young.
note: From Latin mamma, 'breast'. Whales and bats are mammals despite looking unlike the rest.
hints: A whale belongs to this class even though it lives in the sea.
Humans are one.
example: Pangolins are said to be the world's most trafficked mammal.

definition: To run or cope.
note: From Italian maneggiare, 'to handle', from Latin manus, 'hand'.
hints: In charge of a team.
Cope with something difficult.
origin: Early Modern English manage, from Latin manus

definition: A Japanese comic or graphic novel.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, written with characters meaning roughly 'whimsical' and 'picture'.
hints: Read right to left, often in black and white.
Japanese comics with large-eyed characters.
example: Lots of people learn Japanese so they can understand mangas.

definition: A skin disease of animals caused by mites, leaving them itchy and patchy.
note: From Old French manjue, 'itch', from mangier, 'to eat'.
hints: A scruffy stray dog might suffer from it.
Mites cause this itchy hair-loss condition.
origin: Old French manjue, from Latin manducare
example: The stray dog had heartworms, mange, intestinal worms, and a broken leg.

definition: A sweet, juicy tropical fruit with a large stone.
note: Reached English from Portuguese, ultimately from Tamil and Malayalam words for the fruit.
hints: A tropical fruit with orange flesh.
A summer smoothie flavour that is also a chutney.

definition: Scruffy and worn, as if suffering from mange.
note: Formed from 'mange' plus -y, and extended from diseased animals to anything shabby.
hints: Describes a patchy, flea-ridden stray.
Shabby and bald in places.
example: A mangy old fur coat.

definition: An extreme, obsessive enthusiasm, or a state of manic excitement.
note: From Greek mania, 'madness', from the verb mainesthai, 'to rage'.
hints: A craze that sweeps a crowd.
Madness, in Greek; now also a craze.
origin: Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία

definition: A person who behaves wildly or is obsessed with something.
note: From Greek mania, 'madness', through Late Latin. It once named a person with a serious mental disorder.
hints: A reckless driver might be labelled one.
Slasher films love to call their villain this.
origin: French maniaque, from Ancient Greek μανιακός

definition: Wildly energetic or frantic.
note: From Greek mania, 'madness', via the clinical term for the elevated state.
hints: Describes a frenzied burst of activity.
Often paired with 'depressive' in a diagnosis.

definition: Showing qualities thought typical of a man.
note: From Old English manlic, built from man plus -ly. It once simply meant 'befitting a person' and was used for noble conduct.
hints: Describes a deep voice or a firm handshake.
A word for traditionally male traits.

definition: Food that fell from heaven for the Israelites; any unexpected windfall.
note: From Hebrew mān via Greek, in the Book of Exodus. Today a stroke of luck is called manna from heaven.
hints: Bread that appeared in the desert in the Bible.
Often said to come from heaven.
origin: Late Latin manna, from Hebrew מן

definition: A way of doing something, or a way of behaving.
note: From Old French maniere, from Latin manuarius, 'of the hand'.
hints: How someone acts.
Good ones are taught to children.

definition: A large country house with its land, or the estate itself.
note: From Old French manoir, 'dwelling', from Latin manere, 'to stay'.
hints: A lord's country estate in medieval England.
A grand house in the countryside.
origin: Old French manoir, from Latin manēre

definition: A minister's house, especially in Scotland.
note: From Medieval Latin mansa, a dwelling.
hints: A parish minister's home.
Where a Scottish vicar lives.
origin: Medieval Latin mānsus, from Latin manēre

definition: A large ray with wide wing-like fins; also a blanket in Spanish-speaking regions.
note: Borrowed from Spanish manta, 'blanket'. The ray was named for its flat, cloak-like shape.
hints: A giant flat fish that glides through warm seas.
Spanish for a blanket, and a ray named after it.

definition: A long-bodied insect that holds its front legs folded as if praying.
note: From Greek mantis, meaning 'prophet' or 'seer'. The folded forelegs suggested someone in prayer.
hints: Female ones are said to eat their mates.
Often called 'praying' and sits very still.
origin: New Latin mantis, from Ancient Greek μάντις
example: Anna pleaded for someone to remove the mantis from her office.

definition: A cloak, or a role of authority passed to someone; also the layer of the Earth under the crust.
note: From Old English mantel, from Latin mantellum. 'Taking on the mantle' means inheriting a responsibility.
hints: What an heir takes up when a leader steps down.
Also the hot layer of rock between Earth's crust and core.
origin: Old English mæntel, from Latin mantellum; in English since the 9th century

definition: A word or phrase repeated in prayer or meditation; any slogan.
note: From Sanskrit mantra, 'instrument of thought', related to mind. It first meant a sacred Vedic hymn.
hints: What a meditator chants in a quiet room.
A personal motto that someone repeats daily.
example: She repeated `So pleased with how its going' at intervals like a mantra.

definition: Done by hand; or a handbook.
note: From Latin manualis, from manus, 'hand'.
hints: Instruction booklet.
Not automatic.

definition: Animal dung used to fertilise soil.
note: From Middle English manuren, 'to work land', from Old French manouvrer, 'to work by hand'. The sense of spreading dung came later.
hints: A farmer spreads it on fields in spring.
A heap of it steams behind the barn.
origin: Anglo-Norman meinourer, from Old French manovrer

definition: A tree with lobed leaves, known for its syrup and autumn colour.
note: From Middle English mapel, the name of the tree.
hints: Canada's flag features its leaf.
Tree that is tapped for sweet syrup.

definition: A hard stone used in sculpture, or a small glass ball.
note: From Greek marmaros, 'shining stone'.
hints: Statues are carved from it.
A child's glass ball.
origin: Old French marbre, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος; in English since the 12th century

definition: To walk in a steady, regular rhythm, as soldiers do.
note: From Old French marchier, 'to stride, to trample'.
hints: What soldiers do in step.
Also the month after February.
origin: Middle French marcher, from Old French marchier
example: He marched into the classroom and announced the exam.

definition: The blank edge of a page, or a border of difference.
note: From Latin margo, 'edge'.
hints: Notes get written there.
The gap by which one team wins.
origin: Latin marginem, from Old French margin
example: He jotted a note in the margin.

definition: A harbour for small boats and yachts.
note: From Latin marinus, 'of the sea'.
hints: Boats docked in a row.
Where yachts are moored.
example: It's a peaceful marina with not too many boats and yachts.

definition: Of the sea; or a soldier who serves on ships.
note: From Latin marinus, from mare, 'sea'.
hints: Biology of ocean life.
A member of the corps who fights from ships.
origin: Middle French marin, from Latin marinus

definition: A pen with a felt tip, or something that indicates a spot.
note: From mark plus -er.
hints: Draws on a whiteboard.
Sign showing a place.

definition: A place where goods are bought and sold.
note: From Latin mercatus, 'trade', related to merchant.
hints: Stalls full of produce.
Traders sell goods here.
origin: Old English market, from Latin mercātus
example: Without competition there would be no market.

definition: An increase added to cost to set a selling price, or the tags in a web page.
note: A noun from the verb mark up. HTML stands for a hypertext language of this kind.
hints: A shop adds it to the wholesale price.
The language HTML is a kind of this.

definition: A dark brownish red; or to leave someone stranded somewhere remote.
note: The colour comes from French marron, 'chestnut'. The verb, from Spanish cimarron, 'wild', first meant abandoning someone on a deserted island.
hints: Colour of a school blazer or old velvet.
Pirates did this to mutineers on desert islands.

definition: The soft tissue inside bones; also a large green vegetable in Britain.
note: From Old English mearg. The vegetable sense dates from the 1800s.
hints: What donors give to cure leukaemia.
A giant courgette, in British vegetable shows.

definition: To take someone as a husband or wife.
note: From Latin maritare, 'to wed', from maritus, 'husband'.
hints: What happens at a wedding.
To tie the knot.
origin: Anglo-Norman marïer, from Latin marītāre; in English since the 14th century

definition: Low, wet ground with grasses and reeds.
note: From Old English mersc, a word for low wet ground.
hints: Wet land where reeds and herons live.
A boggy lowland, less deep than a swamp.
example: Many animals live in the marsh.

definition: A person killed for their beliefs; or someone who suffers to gain sympathy.
note: From Greek martys, 'witness'. Early Christians who died for their faith were seen as witnesses to it.
hints: Someone who dies for a cause.
An overworked person who complains about it.
origin: Old English martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ

definition: A wonderful thing; or to be amazed.
note: From Old French merveille, from Latin mirabilia, 'wonderful things'.
hints: Something amazing.
Superhero comics publisher.
origin: Old French merveille, from Latin mīrābilia

definition: A person, animal or thing chosen to symbolise a team or group.
note: From French mascotte, from Occitan masco, 'witch', and first meant a lucky charm.
hints: A costumed creature dancing at a sports game.
Originally a good-luck charm.
origin: French mascotte, from Medieval Latin masca
example: Tommy the Tyke is the mascot of Barnsley FC.

definition: A person who builds with stone or brick.
note: From Old French maçon, from Late Latin, 'bricklayer'. The Freemasons take their name from medieval stoneworkers.
hints: Cuts and lays stone for walls.
A jar sharing this name is used for preserves.
origin: Anglo-Norman machun, from Late Latin maciō

definition: Someone with great skill or control.
note: From Latin magister, 'chief' or 'teacher'.
hints: A skilled craftsman, or a ship's captain.
Someone who has fully learned a craft.
origin: Old English mǣster, from Old Latin magester
example: A master of the violin.

definition: Friendly and chummy; also a pirate's way of addressing a shipmate.
note: Built from mate plus -y. Mate is an old word for a companion who eats at the same table.
hints: A pirate might use it for a friend.
Describes a very pally mood.

definition: A grid of numbers, or something in which something develops.
note: Latin for 'womb' or 'breeding female', from mater, 'mother'.
hints: A rectangular array in mathematics.
A sci-fi film with Neo.
origin: Old French matrice, from Latin mātrīx

definition: Dull and not shiny.
note: From French mat, 'dull'. Paint, photos and makeup can have a flat finish.
hints: A flat, non-glossy paint finish.
The opposite of glossy.

definition: Physical substance, or an affair or subject.
note: From Latin materia, 'timber' or 'stuff'.
hints: What everything physical is made of.
A topic, or what is not mind.

definition: Fully grown, or ripe.
note: From Latin maturus, 'ripe'.
hints: Fully grown up.
Cheese that has aged.
origin: Middle French mature, from Latin mātūrus
example: She is quite mature for her age.

definition: A pale, purplish colour.
note: French for 'mallow', the plant with purple flowers. It was also the name of the first synthetic dye, which was this colour.
hints: A pale shade between lilac and violet.
Named for a flowering plant, via French.

definition: An expert or enthusiast in a field.
note: From Yiddish meyvn, from Hebrew, meaning 'one who understands'. A food or wine one knows the subject well.
hints: A wine expert, for instance.
Someone who knows a subject inside out.
example: She is a fashion maven with a lot of influence.

definition: A short saying that states a rule or truth.
note: From Latin maxima, via French, used for a basic principle or axiom.
hints: A pithy line of advice.
'Look before you leap' is one.

definition: Perhaps; possibly.
note: Made from the phrase 'it may be', squashed into one word. Compare the old word mayhap.
hints: A non-committal answer.
Neither yes nor no.

definition: Violent chaos and disorder.
note: From Anglo-Norman mahaim, related to maim. In English law it was the crime of injuring someone so they could not fight.
hints: What a stampede or a school playground at break time looks like.
A word from the old crime of maiming.
example: In all the mayhem, some children were separated from their parents.

definition: The elected head of a town or city.
note: From Old French maire, from Latin maior, 'greater'.
hints: Leads a city council.
Wears a chain of office on formal occasions.
origin: Old French maire, from Latin maior
example: She is said to have had an affair with the mayor of the town.

definition: A field of grass and wildflowers.
note: From Old English maedwe, related to mow. Land that was mown for hay.
hints: Where cows graze and butterflies flutter.
Where wildflowers grow in summer.

definition: Small in amount or quality.
note: From Old French maigre, from Latin macer, 'thin'. The British spelling is meagre.
hints: A scant harvest or a thin wage.
Describes a portion that does not fill you.
example: A meager piece of cake in one bite.

definition: Soft, dry and powdery like ground grain; also, pale.
note: From meal plus -y. Meal is ground grain, from Old English melu. A mealy-mouthed person speaks without frankness.
hints: Describes a mushy, dry apple.
A word that can come before 'mouthed'.

definition: Full of meat; or full of substance.
note: From meat plus -y. Meat once meant food in general, in Old English mete.
hints: A big burger might be said to be this.
A role with much to chew on.
example: Enough of vegetarianism; let's have a meaty meal.

definition: The news and entertainment industries, or means of communication.
note: Latin for 'middle', plural of medium. It became the term for the channels that stand between sender and audience.
hints: Newspapers, television and the internet.
The 'social' kind is all over your phone.

definition: Situated in the middle; relating to an average.
note: From Late Latin medialis, from Latin medius, 'middle'.
hints: An anatomist uses it for a part closer to the body's midline.
The opposite of lateral in a body chart.

definition: The middle value in a sorted list.
note: From Latin medianus, 'of the middle'.
hints: Between the highest and the lowest.
Strip dividing a motorway.
origin: Middle French median, from Latin mediānus; in English since the 19th century

definition: A doctor or someone with medical training, such as one serving with soldiers.
note: From Latin medicus, 'physician'.
hints: Someone shouts for one on a battlefield.
Short for a person who treats the wounded.

definition: The old walled part of a North African city.
note: Borrowed from Arabic madina, 'city'. Marrakech and Fez have famous ones with narrow alleys.
hints: Narrow lanes and souks in Fez or Marrakech.
The old part of the town, contrasted with the new one.
example: Although Hicham usually worked in the new town, he still lived in the medina.

definition: A middle size, or a means of communication.
note: From Latin medium, 'middle'.
hints: Between small and large.
Someone who contacts spirits.

definition: A mixture of different things, especially pieces of music.
note: From Old French medlee, 'mixture' or 'melee'. A swim race with all four strokes is a medley.
hints: Swimmers do all four strokes in one race.
A song that strings together several tunes.
origin: Anglo-Norman medlee, from Medieval Latin misculō

definition: A jellyfish in its free-swimming bell form.
note: From Medusa, the Greek monster with snakes for hair, whose trailing tentacles were likened to snakes. The Greek name means 'guardian'.
hints: Stares turned men to stone in myth.
The jellyfish form takes its name from a snake-haired Gorgon.

definition: A dish of peach, ice cream and raspberry sauce, named after a soprano.
note: Named for Dame Nellie Melba, the Australian opera singer.
hints: Dessert named after an opera singer.
Peach and ice cream together.
example: We are eating melba toast with pink sprinkles because it was a girl.

definition: A confused, close-quarters fight.
note: Borrowed from French melee, from Old French meslee, 'to mix'.
hints: A scrappy brawl in which nobody is in charge.
A tangled fight with everyone mixed up.

definition: Soft, smooth and relaxed.
note: Late Middle English, of uncertain origin, first meaning ripe and sweet. It now describes music, wine and moods.
hints: A relaxed mood after a quiet evening.
Soft golden light at sunset.
origin: Old English melo, from Old English meru

definition: A tune.
note: From Greek melodia, 'singing of songs'.
hints: The part you hum.
Notes forming a recognisable tune.
origin: Old French melodie, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ

definition: A large, sweet fruit with juicy flesh and a thick rind.
note: From Old French melon, from Late Latin and ultimately Greek melopepon, a word that combined 'apple' and 'gourd'.
hints: Cantaloupe and honeydew are types.
A big juicy summer fruit eaten in slices.
origin: Old French melon, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων

definition: A person belonging to a group; also a limb.
note: From Latin membrum, 'limb'.
hints: Belongs to a club.
Part of a body, in old language.
origin: Old French membre, from Latin membrum

definition: An account of the writer's own life or memories.
note: From French memoire, 'memory'.
hints: An autobiography.
A book of personal recollections.

definition: The ability to remember, or a remembered thing.
note: From Old French memorie, from Latin memoria.
hints: Stored in the brain or a computer.
What a photo preserves.

definition: A person or thing that is a threat.
note: From Latin minaciae, 'threats'. A cartoon troublemaker named Dennis made the word a household phrase.
hints: A word from the title of a naughty cartoon boy.
A drunk driver is described as a public one.
origin: Old French manace, from Latin mināx
example: He spoke with desperate menace.

definition: Relating to the mind.
note: From Latin mentalis, from mens, 'mind'.
hints: Happening in the head.
Not physical.
origin: Middle French mental, from Late Latin mentālis

definition: A trusted adviser or teacher.
note: From Mentor, a character in Homer's Odyssey who advised Odysseus's son.
hints: A wise guide to a younger person.
Named for an Odyssey character.
origin: French mentor, from Ancient Greek Μέντωρ

definition: A dealer in fine fabrics such as silk.
note: From Anglo-Norman mercer, from Latin merx, 'wares'. The Mercers' Company is one of London's oldest guilds.
hints: A medieval trader in silk and velvet.
A word that shares a root with merchandise.

definition: Goods sold by a band or brand.
note: A clipping of merchandise, from Latin mercari, 'to trade'. Fans buy it at concerts.
hints: T-shirts sold at a gig.
What a fan buys at a concert stall.

definition: Kindness shown by sparing someone who deserves punishment.
note: From Old French merci, from Latin merces, 'wages, price'.
hints: What a judge might show.
Begged for by a defeated enemy.

definition: Only, and nothing more.
note: From mere plus -ly.
hints: Only, and nothing more than that.
Nothing but.
origin: Middle English mereli; in English since the 16th century
example: I was merely asking.

definition: To combine into one.
note: Borrowed from Latin mergere, 'to dip, plunge, immerse'.
hints: What two lanes of traffic do.
Two companies become one.
example: We merged our resources.

definition: The joining of two companies into one.
note: From merge plus -er, from Latin mergere, 'to dip'.
hints: When two firms combine.
A corporate union.

definition: The quality of being worthy of praise or reward.
note: From Old French merite, from Latin meritum, 'something earned'.
hints: Judged on this rather than favours.
A school badge might reward it.
origin: Anglo-Norman merit, from Old French merite

definition: A small, fast falcon; also the wizard of Arthurian legend.
note: The bird's name comes from Old French esmerillon. The wizard's name is separate and Welsh in origin.
hints: King Arthur's wizard advisor shares his name with a small falcon.
Wears a pointed hat in tales of Camelot.

definition: Cheerful and full of fun.
note: From Old English myrge, meaning 'pleasing, agreeable'.
hints: A word for festive cheer.
Christmas greetings include it.
example: Everyone was merry at the party.

definition: Untidy or chaotic.
note: From mess plus -y. Mess comes from Old French mes, 'a course of food', and later 'a jumble'.
hints: How a teenager's bedroom looks.
The state of a kitchen after baking.
example: Jim ran his fingers through his messy brown hair.

definition: A hard, shiny, conductive material such as iron or copper.
note: From Greek metallon, a word for a mine or quarry, which came to mean what was mined.
hints: Iron and gold are examples.
Conducts heat and electricity well.
origin: Old French metal, from Ancient Greek μέταλλον

definition: A streak of light seen when space rock burns up in the atmosphere.
note: From Greek meteoros, 'high in the air'. Once the word covered all sky phenomena including weather.
hints: A shooting star seen on an August night.
A rock burning in the sky is this.
origin: Middle French météore, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον; in English since the 16th century

definition: A device that measures, such as the amount of gas or electricity used.
note: From Middle English metere, 'one who measures', related to 'mete out'.
hints: The taxi one runs up the fare.
Read monthly by the utility company.

definition: A way of doing something in an orderly manner.
note: From Greek methodos, 'pursuit' or 'way', from meta and hodos, 'path'.
hints: A systematic approach.
A procedure followed step by step.
origin: Middle French methode, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος
example: If one method doesn't work, you should ask a friend to help you.

definition: A chemical group of one carbon atom bonded to three hydrogens.
note: Coined from Greek methy, 'wine', and hyle, 'wood', because methyl alcohol was first got from wood.
hints: Appears in the name of a basic wood alcohol and in many solvents.
Chemists add one to a molecule in a step that takes a name ending in -ation.
example: Methyl is a functional group containing a carbon bonded to three hydrogen atoms, -CH3.

definition: The basic unit of length in the metric system.
note: From French metre, from Greek metron, 'measure'. It was first defined in France in the 1790s.
hints: A unit a bit longer than a yard.
What a ruler of the larger kind measures.
origin: French mètre, from Ancient Greek μέτρον

definition: Relating to a decimal system of measurement, or any standard of measurement.
note: From Greek metron, 'measure'.
hints: Metres and kilograms are part of it.
The system most countries use besides the US.
origin: French métrique, from New Latin metricus

definition: An underground railway system in a city.
note: French, clipped from metropolitain, ultimately from Greek words for 'mother' and 'city'. It was first used for the Paris railway.
hints: The Paris one has art nouveau entrances.
Another name for the subway or tube.
origin: French métro, from Ancient Greek μήτηρ
example: He is going to the stadium by metro.

definition: Short for mezzo-soprano, a singing voice between soprano and contralto.
note: From Italian mezzo, 'middle'. The word is a clipping of mezzo-soprano.
hints: A voice that sits in the middle of a choir's range.
Carmen is a famous role for this voice.

definition: Very small.
note: From Greek mikros, 'small'. It is also short for microwave or microprocessor.
hints: A prefix for tiny things.
Scopes, chips and waves often start with it.

definition: The middle of the day; noon.
note: From Old English middæg, 'mid' plus 'day'. The Spanish siesta once took place at this time.
hints: The sun is highest then.
The Spanish take their siesta around it.
example: One indicates the time as one hour after twelve midday or midnight.

definition: The point equally far from the ends.
note: From Old English middel.
hints: Neither start nor end.
Centre, or halfway.
example: The middle of the war.

definition: A tiny biting or swarming fly.
note: From Old English mycg, a word for a midge, gnat or mosquito.
hints: Clouds of them plague Scottish summers.
A small fly that swarms near water.
example: Midges can be quite bothersome when you're outdoors near water.

definition: A very small thing; a word for a small person that many now consider offensive.
note: From midge, 'small fly', plus -et. It was applied to people in the 1800s and is now avoided; midget submarines remain a term of art.
hints: A tiny submarine in the Second World War.
A word for small people now widely regarded as insulting.
origin: Old English myċġ; in English since the early 19th century

definition: The middle of something; among.
note: From Middle English middes, reshaped from older phrases like 'in middes'. It appears in the phrase 'in the midst of'.
hints: A word for the centre of the action.
Found in 'in the' phrase meaning in the middle of.
example: In the midst of this, it is IT that has made great progress.

definition: In the middle of the distance or time between two points.
note: From Old English midweg, built from mid and way. A fairground's central strip of games and rides borrowed the name after the 1893 Chicago fair's Midway Plaisance.
hints: Halfway between the start and the finish.
Also the name of a carnival strip lined with games and rides.
example: He stopped me midway through the job and told me to put it on hold.

definition: Power or strength; also a word for what is possible.
note: From Old English miht, 'power'. The helping verb is related, since being able is a form of having power.
hints: Strength, as in 'with all your ___ and main'.
A word for great force.

definition: Having great power.
note: From Old English mihtig, from miht, 'might'.
hints: Strong as an ox.
Powerful and impressive.
example: Struck a mighty blow.

definition: To a slight degree; gently.
note: From mild plus -ly, and mild itself goes back to Old English. 'To put it mildly' signals understatement.
hints: Part of the phrase for deliberate understatement.
Said of a curry that isn't spicy.
example: He was mildly interested.

definition: A runner who specialises in the mile.
note: From mile plus -er.
hints: Roger Bannister was this kind of athlete.
A middle-distance racer.

definition: Like milk; pale and cloudy.
note: From Old English meolcig, built from milk plus -y. The Milky Way is named for its pale band of stars.
hints: A galaxy is named after it.
A pale cloudy colour.
example: The milky liquid stains the yarn in a greenish color.

definition: A person who runs a mill that grinds grain.
note: From mill plus -er.
hints: Grinds flour.
A common surname from an old trade.

definition: To copy someone's voice or behaviour, or an animal that copies another's appearance.
note: From Latin mimicus and Greek mimikos, 'belonging to mimes'.
hints: A parrot is good at this.
Copy someone's voice, often to tease.
origin: Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός

definition: To chop very fine; also to walk with small steps.
note: From Old French mincier, from Latin minutia, 'smallness'. 'Mince words' means to soften what you say.
hints: What a cook does with an onion or beef.
Said of walking with tiny steps.
origin: Old English minsian, from Old French mincer
example: Butchers often use machines to mince meat.

definition: A person who digs for coal or metals underground.
note: From mine plus -er. Mine comes from Old French, a word for a tunnel or a vein of ore.
hints: Wears a helmet with a lamp.
Digs for coal or gold.
example: Many miners are afraid that the mine will be closed down soon.

definition: To mix together; to move around and talk with different people.
note: From Middle English menglen, from an older word meaning to mix, with a frequent-action ending.
hints: What you are expected to do at a cocktail party.
Oil and water refuse to.

definition: A servant who follows orders from someone powerful.
note: From French mignon, 'darling' or favourite. Its sense turned from beloved to servile.
hints: A villain's lackey.
Yellow ones in a film are devoted to Gru.
origin: Middle French mignon, from Old French mignon
example: The archvillain deployed his minions to simultaneously rob every bank in the city.

definition: Smaller or less important, or a person under legal adulthood.
note: From Latin minor, 'lesser', which gives the opposite of 'major'.
hints: The opposite of major.
Someone not yet old enough to vote.
origin: Latin minor, from Middle French menor

definition: Tasting or smelling of mint.
note: From mint plus -y. Mint comes from Old English minte, from Latin menta.
hints: How fresh toothpaste tastes.
A chewing gum flavour.

definition: Less, or the sign for subtraction.
note: From Latin minus, the neuter of minor, 'less'.
hints: Takes away rather than adds.
The short horizontal sign in arithmetic.
origin: Latin minus; in English since the 15th century
example: Seven minus two is five.

definition: A sixtieth of an hour; also very small, with a different pronunciation.
note: From Latin pars minuta, 'small part'. The first small division of the hour is the minute.
hints: Sixty seconds.
Hands on a clock face.
origin: Old French minute, from Medieval Latin minūta
example: You have twenty minutes to complete the test.

definition: An optical illusion, like water on a hot road or desert.
note: Borrowed from French mirage in the early 1800s, from mirer, 'to look at'. Light bending in hot air causes it.
hints: A traveller in the desert sees water that isn't there.
A shimmering pool on a hot road.

definition: A glass that reflects an image.
note: From Old French mirour, from Latin mirari, 'to wonder at'.
hints: Reflects your face.
Hangs in a bathroom.
origin: Old French mireor, from Latin mīror
example: I had a look in the mirror to see if the blood had come off my face.

definition: Great unhappiness.
note: From Latin miseria, 'wretchedness'.
hints: Wretched feeling.
What a gloomy mood causes.
origin: Old French miserie, from Latin miseria
example: Ever since his wife left him you can see the misery on his face.

definition: A young girl; also a scolding way to address a girl.
note: From miss plus -y. Miss itself is short for mistress.
hints: How a parent might address a cheeky girl.
A stern name used in a scolding.
example: That's enough out of you, missy!

definition: A courteous title for a man.
note: A form of 'master' that became unstressed. Children also call strangers it.
hints: What a child says to a man in the street.
What you call a man whose name you don't know.

definition: Covered in fine water droplets in the air.
note: From Old English mistig, built from mist plus -y. A morning on a moor can be this.
hints: A morning on the moors.
Vague or tearful, as eyes can be.
example: It's very misty this morning; I can't see a thing!

definition: The wrong or improper use of something.
note: From mis- plus use. It can be the abuse of power or a word used wrongly.
hints: Using a screwdriver as a chisel is one.
What a grammarian sees in 'literally' for emphasis.

definition: A tall pointed hat worn by bishops, or a corner joint cut at an angle.
note: From Greek mitra, 'headband'. The carpenter's joint shares its spelling in British English.
hints: Hat worn by a bishop.
A 45-degree cut for a picture-frame corner.
origin: Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα

definition: A device or person that mixes.
note: From mix plus -er. A kitchen device blends batter, and one at a party is a sociable person.
hints: A kitchen device for batter.
A sociable guest at a party.

definition: Able to move or be moved; also a phone.
note: From Latin mobilis, from movere, 'to move'.
hints: A hanging decoration over a cot.
The British word for a cellphone.
example: A mobile missile system.

definition: A coffee flavoured with chocolate.
note: Named for Mocha, a Red Sea port in Yemen that was a major coffee marketplace under Ottoman rule.
hints: A coffee shop order with chocolate.
Named after a port city in Yemen.

definition: Relating to a mode, or a helper verb such as can or must.
note: From Medieval Latin modalis, from Latin modus, 'measure' or 'manner'. A modal verb shows possibility or necessity.
hints: A grammar word for a kind of helper verb.
Can, must and might are examples.
origin: Middle French modal, from Latin modus

definition: A person who displays clothes, or a small copy or representation of something.
note: From Latin modus, 'measure', through a diminutive form.
hints: Walks a catwalk wearing the designer's clothes.
A scaled-down version of a building or plane.
origin: Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello
example: The supersize model displayed the latest summer shorts fashion, tactfully representing similarly overweight teenagers.

definition: A device that connects a computer to the internet.
note: A blend of 'modulator-demodulator'. It once turned digital signals into sound that could pass down phone lines.
hints: A box with blinking lights near the router.
Old ones screeched when they connected.

definition: Of the present or recent times.
note: From Late Latin modernus, from modo, 'just now'.
hints: Not ancient.
Contemporary.
origin: Middle French moderne, from Latin modo

definition: Humble, or moderate in size.
note: From Latin modestus, 'keeping measure'.
hints: Not boastful.
Small in amount.
origin: Middle French modeste, from Latin modestus

definition: To change slightly.
note: From Latin modificare, 'to limit or measure'.
hints: Alter a design.
Make adjustments.
origin: Middle French modifier, from Latin modificare
example: Her publisher advised her to modify a few parts of the book to make it easier to read.

definition: A self-contained unit of a larger whole.
note: From Latin modulus, 'small measure'.
hints: Part of a course.
Section of a spacecraft.

definition: A rich and powerful person in some industry.
note: Figurative use of Moghul, which meant Mongol and referred to the Mughal Empire of India.
hints: A media tycoon.
A Hollywood boss, or a bump on a ski slope.

definition: Slightly wet; damp.
note: From Old French moiste. Cake, soil and eyes can all be this.
hints: A good sponge cake is this.
Between dry and wet.
origin: Anglo-Norman moist, from Old French moiste; in English since the 14th century
example: Eyes moist with tears.

definition: Covered in mould.
note: Built from mold plus -y. Mold, the fungus, comes from Middle English mowlde.
hints: How old bread ends up.
What forgotten leftovers become.
example: A moldy (or musty) odor.

definition: Turned to liquid by extreme heat.
note: From Old English molten, an old past participle of melt. The word is used for lava, metal and glass.
hints: Lava flowing from a volcano is described as this.
Iron poured into a mould is in this state.
example: A mass of molten rock.

definition: A very brief span of time.
note: From Latin momentum, 'movement', which is also the root of momentum.
hints: A split-second, informally.
Hold on, it won't take long.
origin: Old French moment, from Latin mōmentum
example: Wait a moment, while I lock the front door.

definition: A child's word for mother.
note: From mom plus -y. It is the American form of mummy.
hints: What a toddler calls a parent.
An American child's word for a parent.
example: Remember, never talk to strangers without mommy or daddy around.

definition: What people use to buy and sell things.
note: From Old French moneie, from Latin Moneta, a title of the goddess Juno, in whose temple Roman coins were made.
hints: Coins and notes.
A word whose Roman root names a temple of Juno.

definition: A primate with a long tail.
note: Of uncertain origin; it appears in the 1500s.
hints: Swings in trees.
A cheeky child, in nickname.

definition: One of the twelve parts of a year.
note: From Old English monath, related to 'moon', since months followed the moon's phases.
hints: January is one.
About thirty days.
example: July is my favourite month.

definition: The largest deer, with broad flat antlers, found in North America.
note: From an Eastern Algonquian word such as Narragansett moos, adopted into English.
hints: Large antlered animal of Canadian forests.
Named by Algonquian speakers.
example: We saw a moose at the edge of the woods.

definition: Concerned with right and wrong, or the lesson of a story.
note: From Latin moralis, from mos, 'custom, manner'.
hints: Fables end with one.
Concerned with ethics.
origin: Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis

definition: The confidence and spirit of a group.
note: From French moral, with an e added to tell it apart. Armies and sports teams are said to have high or low levels of it.
hints: What a coach tries to lift after a heavy defeat.
Poor levels in a workplace lead to resignations.
example: After the layoffs, morale was at an all time low; the staff were so dispirited nothing was getting done.

definition: A large eel that lurks in reef crevices.
note: From Portuguese moreia, from Latin muraena. It has sharp teeth.
hints: A fierce eel in a coral reef.
A sea creature that hides in rocky holes.
origin: Portuguese moreia, from Ancient Greek σμύραινα
example: The moray eel isn't as aggressive as it seems.

definition: Having an unhealthy interest in death; or caused by disease.
note: From Latin morbus, 'disease'. A morbid curiosity lingers on unpleasant things.
hints: An interest in graveyards and funerals.
A dark sense of humour about dying.

definition: An edible mushroom with a honeycomb cap.
note: From French morille, ultimately from Germanic words for this fungus.
hints: Prized spring mushroom with a pitted cap.
Foragers look for it in woods.

definition: A place where dead bodies are kept before burial or cremation.
note: From French morgue, which first meant a haughty look. It was the name of a Paris building where bodies were displayed, so the place took the word.
hints: Crime dramas often have a scene in one.
A newspaper's archive is sometimes called this.
example: Rodrigo reached the connecting door leading to the morgue.

definition: A foolish person; once a technical term for mild intellectual disability.
note: Coined in 1910 from Greek moros, 'foolish'; it is now regarded as an insult.
hints: An insult for a dim person.
Used in 1900s psychology before becoming slang.

definition: To change shape smoothly; also a unit of linguistic form.
note: As a verb it is short for metamorphosis, from Greek morphe, 'form'. A film effect of the same name blends one image into another.
hints: A film effect that blends two faces.
A word for transforming.

definition: An old word for tomorrow or the next day.
note: From Middle English morwe, from Old English morgen, 'morning'. It survives mainly in 'good morrow' and 'tomorrow'.
hints: Archaic word for the following day, heard in old-fashioned greetings.
Shakespeare's characters wished each other a good one.
example: Whenever he arrives she leaves on the morrow.

definition: Certain to die; or deadly.
note: From Latin mortalis, from mors, 'death'.
hints: Certain to die one day.
Humans are this, gods are not.
origin: Old French mortal, from Latin mortālis; in English since the 14th century

definition: A mix that binds bricks; or a bowl for grinding; or a short cannon.
note: From Latin mortarium, 'basin'.
hints: Pestle goes with it.
Cement between bricks.
origin: Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium

definition: A picture or pattern made from many small pieces of tile, glass or stone.
note: From Greek mouseion, 'of the Muses', via Latin musaicum, the decoration of grottoes dedicated to them. Roman floors were often covered in them.
hints: Roman villas had floors made of thousands of tiny tiles.
A picture made of coloured tesserae.
origin: Middle French mosaïque, from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον

definition: A Muslim place of worship.
note: From Arabic masjid, 'place of prostration', via Italian and French.
hints: Has a minaret.
Where Friday prayers are held.
origin: Middle French mosquée, from Arabic مَسْجِد
example: There's a mosque near where I live.

definition: Covered with moss.
note: From moss plus -y. Moss comes from Old English mos, 'bog'.
hints: How an old stone wall may look.
A fallen log in a damp wood.

definition: For the most part.
note: From most plus -ly.
hints: Chiefly or for the most part.
Not entirely, but largely.
example: They're mostly good people, although they have made a few mistakes.

definition: A roadside hotel for motorists.
note: A blend of 'motor' and 'hotel'.
hints: Often found beside a highway.
Where the motorist sleeps over.

definition: A female parent.
note: From Old English modor, with cousins across Indo-European languages.
hints: Mum, in full.
The one who bore you.

definition: A recurring theme or pattern in a work of art.
note: From French motif, in the sense of 'main idea', and a doublet of 'motive'.
hints: A repeated pattern on wallpaper.
A theme that keeps returning in a story or song.
example: See how the artist repeats the scroll motif throughout the work?

definition: The act of moving, or a formal proposal.
note: From Latin motio, from movere, 'to move'.
hints: Not standing still.
A proposal put to a meeting.

definition: The reason behind an action.
note: From Latin motivus, 'moving'.
hints: Detectives look for one.
Why a crime was committed.
origin: Anglo-Norman motif, from Late Latin motivum; in English since the 15th century
example: We did not understand his motivation.

definition: Made up of an odd mix of different things.
note: From Middle English motley, 'many-coloured', possibly from the word mote, a speck. Jesters wore motley cloth in patches.
hints: A crew of misfits.
What a jester wears.
origin: Anglo-Norman motteley, from Old English mot

definition: A machine that turns energy into movement.
note: From Latin motor, 'mover', from movere, 'to move'.
hints: Powers a car or a fan.
The thing under the bonnet that makes it go.
example: The door can close by itself because there's a small motor built into it.

definition: A raised mound on which an early castle was built.
note: From French motte, 'mound'. A motte and bailey castle needed one.
hints: Earth hill topped with a wooden keep.
The mound in a Norman castle.
origin: French motte, from Old French motte

definition: A short phrase that states a guiding principle.
note: Borrowed from Italian motto, 'a word, a saying', from Latin muttum, 'a mutter, a grunt'.
hints: Often written under a coat of arms.
A school's Latin slogan.

definition: A furry fungus; or a shape to cast things in.
note: From Middle English molde, from Old French. Bread goes this way, and jelly is set in one.
hints: What grows on old bread.
A form that jelly is set in.
origin: Old French modle, from Latin modulus

definition: To shed feathers, fur or skin so that new ones can grow.
note: From Latin mutare, 'to change', via Old English and Middle English.
hints: What a bird does each year.
Snakes and birds do it.

definition: A raised heap of earth or other material.
note: From a Middle English word meaning a fence or protection, from Old English mund, 'hand, protection'.
hints: A small hill piled up by hand.
A baseball pitcher stands on one.
example: They built small mounds to hide behind.

definition: To climb or get onto something; also a hill.
note: From Old English munt and from Latin mons, 'hill'. A rider mounts a horse, and a picture is mounted on a card.
hints: What a rider does to a horse.
A word before a famous peak's name.

definition: A small rodent, or a handheld computer pointing device.
note: From Old English mus, the same word as in German Maus.
hints: Cats chase it.
You click it beside your keyboard.

definition: The opening in the face used for eating and speaking, or where a river meets the sea.
note: From Old English muth, from a Germanic root.
hints: Where food goes in.
A river has one where it meets the sea.
example: She wiped lipstick from her mouth.

definition: Someone who moves things, or who is in motion.
note: From move plus -er. Movers carry furniture from one home to another.
hints: A job that involves a truck and heavy boxes.
The people who carry your sofa.

definition: A film shown in cinemas or at home.
note: From 'moving picture' plus -ie, attested by 1912 in American English.
hints: Watched with popcorn.
A short form of 'moving picture'.
example: My favorite actor is starring in the new movie.

definition: A machine or person that cuts grass.
note: From mow plus -er. Mow comes from Old English mawan, 'to cut grass'.
hints: What you push across the lawn.
It gets loud on Saturday mornings.
example: Three men jumped out, rolled an old mower down the ramp.

definition: Courage, nerve and spirit.
note: Named after Moxie, an American soft drink first sold in the 1880s whose ads boasted of its effects.
hints: Plenty of this gets you through hard times.
Nerve, or an old soda brand.
example: He's just a small-time thug, but if he had just a little more moxie, he could be a big-time boss.

definition: Spanish for a lot; used in English for emphasis.
note: Borrowed from Spanish. It is not related to English much.
hints: Spanish for 'a great deal'.
Often paired with grande or gracias.

definition: Dirty with muck or mud.
note: From muck plus -y. Muck is from Old Norse myki, 'dung'.
hints: How boots look after a farm walk.
A British word for filthy.

definition: The slippery fluid made by the lining of the nose and throat.
note: Learned borrowing from Latin mucus.
hints: Produced when you have a cold.
A slimy bodily secretion.
origin: Latin mūcus, from Old English slīm
example: The mucus in coryza may vary from runny to viscous.

definition: Covered with or full of mud.
note: From mud plus -y, found in Middle English. It can also describe cloudy water or a dull colour.
hints: How boots look after a wet walk.
A pond stirred up can look this way.
origin: Middle Dutch modde, from Middle Low German modde
example: He slogged across the muddy field.

definition: A small round cake baked in a cup, or a flat British bread roll.
note: Perhaps from Low German Muffe, 'small cake'. English muffins are split and toasted, while American ones are sweet cakes.
hints: Blueberry ones are a bakery favourite.
In Britain a flat yeast type is toasted for breakfast.
origin: Low German Muffe, from Middle Low German muffe

definition: Plain clothes worn by someone who normally wears a uniform.
note: From Arabic mufti, a Muslim legal scholar. British officers used it for civilian dress.
hints: What a soldier wears off-duty.
A day when a school wears no uniform.
origin: Ottoman Turkish مفتی, from Arabic مُفْتِي

definition: Warm, damp and unpleasantly close.
note: From dialect mug, 'mist', from Old Norse mugga, 'drizzle', plus -y.
hints: What a humid summer day feels like.
Close and sticky air.
example: Last night was very hot and muggy, so I didn't sleep so well.

definition: A layer of material spread over soil to protect and feed plants.
note: Probably from Middle English melsche, 'soft', from an Old English word for 'mellow' or 'honeyed'.
hints: Gardeners spread it around plants.
Bark chips on a flowerbed.
example: An organic mulch is a mulch made of natural substances such as leaves or grass clippings.

definition: A preserved dead body wrapped in bandages, or a mother.
note: From Arabic mumiya, 'embalmed body', itself from a Persian word.
hints: Ancient Egyptians preserved them.
Horror films show one lurching in bandages.
origin: Anglo-Norman mumie, from Persian مومیا; in English since the 17th century

definition: A contagious viral illness that swells the glands of the cheeks.
note: From an old verb 'mump' meaning to grimace, a nod to the painful, puffy face of sufferers.
hints: Childhood illness that puffs up the face.
A vaccine protects against it, with measles and rubella.

definition: To chew noisily and with enjoyment.
note: Probably imitative of the sound of chewing, from Middle English monchen.
hints: What you do to crisps.
Chew loudly on a snack.
example: Jim was munching on a biscotti.

definition: A foolish or incompetent person, in British slang.
note: From the Muppets puppets created by Jim Henson. The insult is mild and mostly British.
hints: What you call a mate who locks their keys inside the car.
Kermit and Miss Piggy gave their name to it.
example: Sally is such a muppet, the way she always misses the train.

definition: A large painting made directly on a wall.
note: From French mural, from Latin murus, 'wall'.
hints: Painted on the side of a building.
Wall art on a grand scale.

definition: The unlawful killing of one person by another.
note: From Old English morthor. A group of crows is also called a murder.
hints: The crime at the heart of a detective story.
What a group of crows is called.

definition: Dark, cloudy and hard to see through.
note: From Middle English mirky, built from 'murk' plus -y.
hints: Describes a swamp's water.
Cloudy water you cannot see to the bottom of.
example: Murky rooms lit by smoke-blackened lamps.

definition: Tissue that contracts to move the body; or strength.
note: From Latin musculus, 'little mouse', since flexing a muscle looks like a mouse under skin.
hints: Biceps are one.
Its name suggests a mouse under the skin.
origin: Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus

definition: A building that houses collected objects of interest.
note: From Greek mouseion, 'seat of the Muses'.
hints: A place with exhibits.
Named for the goddesses of art.
origin: Latin mūsēum, from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον
example: They're opening a new coin exhibition at the local museum.

definition: Soft and pulpy.
note: From mush plus -y. Mush may be a variant of mash.
hints: Overcooked peas end up this way.
Overripe fruit can feel like it.
example: The brake pedal is mushy sometimes when I step on it.

definition: Organised sound made for pleasure, using melody and rhythm.
note: From Latin musica and Greek mousike, 'art of the Muses'.
hints: Played by an orchestra.
Named for the nine Greek goddesses of the arts.
origin: Anglo-Norman musik, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα

definition: Having the strong, heavy smell of musk.
note: From musk plus -y. Musk reached English through Late Latin and Greek from Sanskrit, and names a strong-smelling substance from the male musk deer.
hints: A perfume or an animal might smell this way.
Describes a heavy, earthy scent.

definition: To gather together, especially soldiers or courage.
note: From Anglo-Norman mostrer, 'to show', related to monster and demonstrate. Troops were summoned to show themselves for inspection.
hints: A soldier's roll call, or what you must do to 'pass' it.
What you do with courage when you gather every scrap of it.
origin: Anglo-Norman mostrer, from Latin mōnstrō; in English since the 15th century
example: Muster the courage to do something.

definition: Smelling stale and damp.
note: From Late Middle English musty, of uncertain origin. It describes the smell of closed rooms and old books.
hints: How an unopened attic smells.
The smell of a damp, shut-in basement.
origin: Anglo-Norman muste, from Old French moiste

definition: A living thing that has changed because of a genetic mutation.
note: From Latin mutans, 'changing'. X-Men popularised the word for people with strange powers.
hints: Comic-book heroes in Professor X's school are called this.
A being whose DNA has altered, as in a sci-fi movie.

definition: A revolt by sailors or soldiers against their officers.
note: From Old French mutin, 'rebellious', from Latin movere, 'to move'. The famous one aboard HMS Bounty took place in 1789.
hints: The crew of the Bounty rose up against Captain Bligh.
Sailors seize the ship from the captain.

definition: Felt or done by each toward the other.
note: From Latin mutuus, 'exchanged'.
hints: A feeling shared by both.
As in friends you both know.
origin: Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus

definition: An animal's nose and mouth; a strap over it; or the end of a gun barrel.
note: From Old French musel, 'snout', from Latin. To muzzle someone also means to silence them.
hints: A strap over a dog's snout.
The barrel end where a bullet leaves.

definition: A countless number of; or ten thousand.
note: From Greek myrias, 'ten thousand'. Used loosely, it means too many to count.
hints: Describes the stars or the options on a restaurant menu.
Greeks used it as a word for the largest number.
origin: French myriade, from Ancient Greek μυριάς; in English since the 16th century
example: Earth hosts a myriad of animals.

definition: A fragrant, bitter resin from certain trees, used in incense and perfume.
note: From Greek murra, from a Semitic source; compare Arabic murr, 'bitter'.
hints: One of the gifts of the Magi.
Brought to the infant Jesus along with gold and frankincense.
origin: Old English myrre, from Ancient Greek μύρρα
example: Tom and Mary brought frankincense and myrrh.

definition: An evergreen shrub with white flowers and fragrant leaves.
note: From Old French mirtille, from Greek myrtos. In myth, it was sacred to Aphrodite.
hints: Greek brides wore it in wreaths.
Its leaves smell sweet when crushed, and it grows by the Mediterranean.
origin: Old French mirtille, from Ancient Greek μύρτος

definition: Me, as the object of my own action.
note: From Old English me selfum.
hints: Used when I am the one acted upon.
I, in reflexive form.
origin: Old English mē; in English since the 9th century

definition: A person who seeks spiritual truth through meditation; or mysterious in nature.
note: From Greek mystikos, 'secret', from the mystery religions. Related to mystery.
hints: A holy man on a mountaintop in a legend.
One who seeks union with the divine through contemplation.
origin: Old French mistique, from Ancient Greek μυστικός

definition: A tortilla chip topped with cheese.
note: A back-formation from nachos, from a Mexican restaurant waiter's nickname. It is a snack food.
hints: A tortilla chip with cheese.
Eaten at the cinema with dip.
example: Can you melt the cheese for the nachos?

definition: The currency of Nigeria.
note: Formed in 1973 as a contraction of Nigeria.
hints: Money spent in Lagos.
Replaced the Nigerian pound.

definition: Lacking experience and too ready to trust.
note: Borrowed from French naive, the feminine of naif, from Latin nativus, 'native, natural'.
hints: Believing everything you are told.
Innocent, and easy to fool.
example: A teenager's naive ignorance of life.

definition: Without clothes.
note: From Old English nacod. The same word is used for something plainly seen, as in 'the naked eye'.
hints: Without covering.
What the eye is without a microscope.
example: Visible to the naked eye.

definition: That is to say.
note: From name plus -ly, once meaning especially.
hints: Introduces a specific example.
Used to specify precisely.
example: Some of the students — namely Paul, Alice and Jake — seem to have trouble with geometry.

definition: A grandmother, in British and Australian speech.
note: Probably formed from a childish babbling sound, as with many similar words.
hints: A grandmother's pet name.
What a toddler might call a granny.

definition: A person employed to care for children at home.
note: From nan plus -y, where nan is a child's word for grandmother or nursemaid. The goat of the same name is a separate usage.
hints: Looks after the kids while parents work.
Mary Poppins was one.

definition: A cloth or paper square used at the table to wipe the mouth and fingers.
note: From Middle English, formed from nape, 'cloth', and the diminutive -kin. 'Nappe' comes from Old French for tablecloth.
hints: Folded on a plate at a fancy restaurant.
Tucked into a collar to catch drips.

definition: A baby's absorbent undergarment.
note: A shortened form of napkin plus -y. The word is common in British English.
hints: What a baby wears under clothes.
A British word for a baby's diaper.

definition: Narcotics or a drug trafficker, in informal use.
note: Clipping of narcotics.
hints: Slang for a drug lord.
Short for something that numbs.

definition: Of small width.
note: From Old English nearu.
hints: A slim passage.
Gorges and mountain lanes have this feature.

definition: Relating to the nose.
note: From Medieval Latin nasalis, from Latin nasus, 'nose'. A nasal voice sounds as if it comes through the nose.
hints: A kind of voice or a kind of spray.
Describes a voice that hums through the nose.

definition: Very unpleasant, or spiteful.
note: From Middle English nasty, 'unclean, filthy', of obscure origin.
hints: A word for a cruel remark.
Not nice at all.
origin: Middle English nasty; in English since the 15th century

definition: Relating to birth.
note: From Latin natus, 'born'. It is a close relative of words like native and nation.
hints: A word you may see before 'care' in a hospital.
Your chart in astrology is based on when you were born.
example: Sea turtles return to their natal beaches to nest.

definition: A large community of people with a shared land or culture.
note: From Latin natio, 'birth' or 'tribe', from nasci, 'to be born'.
hints: A country and its people.
Its Latin root meant birth.
origin: Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem

definition: Born in a place, or belonging to it by origin.
note: From Latin nativus, 'born'.
hints: From here originally.
A plant that grows naturally in a region.
origin: Old French natif, from Latin nātīvus

definition: Neatly and smartly dressed.
note: Probably a variant of neat, and first used as informal slang.
hints: Said of a sharp dresser.
A jaunty, old-fashioned word for stylish.

definition: The natural world, or the basic character of something.
note: From Latin natura, 'birth' or 'character'.
hints: Forests, rivers and wildlife.
What a naturalist studies.
origin: Old French nature, from Latin nātūra
example: They tried to preserve nature as they found it.

definition: A sick feeling in the stomach, with the urge to vomit.
note: From Greek nausia, 'seasickness', from naus, 'ship'. The word nautical shares the root.
hints: What a rough crossing does to passengers.
Its root is the Greek word for a ship.
origin: Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία
example: He got nausea after two hours of travelling on the plane.

definition: Relating to a navy or to ships.
note: From Latin navalis, from navis, 'ship'. It is not related to the word for the belly button, though the two sound alike.
hints: A battle at sea or an officer's rank.
Describes a force that sails warships.
origin: Middle French naval, from Latin nāvālis
example: Three unidentified naval vessels are heading for the peninsula.

definition: The small scar on the belly where the umbilical cord was attached.
note: From Old English nafola, from a Germanic root.
hints: Also called the belly button.
An orange can be named for this.
example: You were not supposed to show your navel on television.

definition: A Muslim ruler or high official in South Asia under the Mughals.
note: From Hindi and Urdu, ultimately from an Arabic plural meaning 'deputies'.
hints: A historic title in the Indian subcontinent.
A provincial governor under Mughal emperors.
origin: Hindi नवाब, from Arabic نُوَّاب; in English since the 17th century

definition: Close at hand.
note: From near plus by.
hints: Not far away.
In the neighbourhood.
example: Concentrated his study on the nearby planet Venus.

definition: Closer in distance or time.
note: The comparative of near, which comes from Old English neah. A hymn begins 'Nearer, my God, to thee'.
hints: What the finish line gets with every step.
A comparative form of a word meaning not far.
example: I'd like to live nearer the office.

definition: Almost.
note: From near plus -ly.
hints: Close to but short.
Not quite entirely.
origin: near + -ly; in English since the 17th century
example: He left a nearly full beer on the bar.

definition: In a tidy, orderly way.
note: From neat plus -ly. Neat first meant clean and pure.
hints: How a folded shirt is placed in a drawer.
How a tidy writer lines up a column.
example: The washstand drawers were filled with neatly folded towels.

definition: A huge cloud of gas and dust in space.
note: Borrowed from Latin nebula, 'little cloud, mist', which is related to Greek nephele, 'cloud'.
hints: The Orion one is visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch.
Stars are born inside them.

definition: The sweet liquid made by flowers, which bees collect; also a fruit drink.
note: Via Latin from Ancient Greek néktar, the name for the drink of the gods.
hints: Hummingbirds sip it from the base of a blossom.
Bees carry it home to turn into honey.
origin: Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ; in English since the 17th century

definition: A thin pointed tool for sewing, or a pine leaf.
note: From Old English naedl.
hints: Pass thread through its eye.
Pine trees have them.
example: The seamstress threaded the needle to sew on a button.

definition: Lacking what is necessary; or too reliant on reassurance.
note: From Old English nedig, built from need plus -y. It can mean poor or, in slang, someone who wants constant attention.
hints: Describes a person asking for help often.
A friend who always wants reassurance.

definition: The long high call of a horse.
note: From Old English hnaegan, from a Germanic root meaning 'to neigh'.
hints: The sound a horse makes.
A stable sound.

definition: Your sibling's son.
note: From Old French neveu, from Latin nepos, 'grandson' or 'nephew'.
hints: A brother's boy.
Sister's son.
origin: Old French neveu, from Latin nepos
example: Today I picked up my four-year-old nephew from kindergarten.

definition: Like a nerd; keen on studies or technical hobbies.
note: From nerd plus -y. Nerd is a mid-twentieth-century slang word of unknown origin.
hints: Wearing glasses and loving maths, perhaps.
Obsessed with gadgets or comics.
example: That guy is nerdy and weird.

definition: Relating to nerves.
note: From Greek neuron, 'sinew' or 'nerve'.
hints: A network in the brain.
Pathways of the nervous system.

definition: A nerve cell that carries electrical signals.
note: From Greek neuron, 'nerve, sinew'. It is a doublet of nerve.
hints: The brain contains billions of them.
Connected by synapses.
example: In the brain there are around one hundred billion neurons.

definition: At no time; not ever.
note: From Old English naefre, built from ne, 'not', plus aefre, 'ever'. The first part is the same negative seen in 'no' and 'none'.
hints: The opposite of always.
A word for not on any occasion.
example: I have never been to China.

definition: An informal word for a beginner.
note: Formed from new plus -bie. It became popular in online forums and games.
hints: What veterans of a game call a fresh player.
Everyone is one on their first day at work.
example: Most of the online users I play poker with have been newbies.

definition: Very recently.
note: From Old English niwlice, built from new plus -ly. It often goes with a participle, as in 'newly wed'.
hints: Used to describe recent arrivals.
Describes the paint or the married.
example: She smelled the newly budding flowers.

definition: The unit of force.
note: Named after Sir Isaac Newton.
hints: A physicist's unit.
Force that accelerates a kilogram.

definition: A link or connection; or a central point.
note: Latin for 'bond', from nectere, 'to tie'. It names a meeting point.
hints: A connection between things.
A central point where things join.

definition: In a pleasing or polite way.
note: From nice plus -ly.
hints: Pleasantly done.
How you ask for a favour.
origin: Middle English nycely; in English since the 17th century
example: A nicely painted house.

definition: A shallow recess in a wall, or a small specialised area of a market.
note: Borrowed from French niche, from Old French nicher, 'to make a nest'.
hints: A spot in the wall for a statue.
A small market that suits a few buyers well.
origin: French niche, from Old French niche

definition: A silvery metal, or a US five-cent coin.
note: From German Kupfernickel, 'copper demon', as miners cursed the ore that yielded no copper.
hints: Coin worth five cents.
Metal in stainless steel.

definition: The daughter of your brother or sister.
note: From Old French nece, from Late Latin neptia.
hints: Your sibling's daughter.
Her counterpart is a nephew.
example: My niece just celebrated her 15th birthday.

definition: Neat and clever.
note: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the 1860s. It is a cheerful word of praise.
hints: A handy little gadget.
A clever, handy trick.

definition: Quick and light in movement.
note: The -b- crept into Middle English nymel, from Old English namol, 'quick to take'. A nimble thief is quick at grabbing.
hints: A gymnast or a pickpocket.
Jack was this and quick over the candlestick.
origin: Old English nǣmel, from Old English numol
example: He was too nimble for the assailant and easily escaped his grasp.

definition: The number after eighty-nine.
note: From Old English hundnigontig.
hints: Nine tens added up.
Ten less than a century.

definition: A covert warrior of feudal Japan, or anyone stealthy and skilled.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, with an underlying sense of 'hidden person'.
hints: Wears black and moves silently.
A throwing star is its signature weapon.

definition: A silly, foolish person.
note: Its origin is unknown; the related word ninnyhammer appears around the same time.
hints: An old word for a fool.
Silly person, in a gentle jibe.
example: Did you just call me a ninny?

definition: Number nine in order.
note: From Old English nigotha, from nigon, 'nine'. The n was put back in later to match the number.
hints: The one after the eighth.
Beethoven's final symphony is this one.

definition: A veil covering the face except the eyes, worn by some Muslim women.
note: Borrowed from Arabic niqab, 'veil'.
hints: Face covering that leaves eyes visible.
