Arabic for a veil.
example: There are different types of niqab, some of which cover the entire face.

definition: Short for nitroglycerin; or a boost.
note: A clipping of nitroglycerin, a powerful explosive. It is also a fuel booster for racing cars.
hints: An explosive liquid.
A boost in a drag race.

definition: Full of nits, or silly.
note: Formed from nit plus -y. The 'nitty-gritty' phrase is a separate matter.
hints: Part of a phrase meaning the basic details.
Lice eggs make a head this.

definition: Of high birth, or having fine moral qualities.
note: From Old French noble, from Latin nobilis, 'known, famous, of high birth'.
hints: A knight or duke has this rank.
Showing generosity and honour.
origin: Old French noble, from Latin nōbilis

definition: In a way that shows high character.
note: From Middle English, built from noble plus -ly. It is often used for brave or generous deeds.
hints: Describes a kind act or a brave sacrifice.
Acting with honour and generosity.
example: We shall nobly save, or meanly lose, the last best hope of earth.

definition: No person at all.
note: From no plus body.
hints: Not a single person.
The opposite of everybody.
example: Nobody likes him, because he is always blowing his own horn.

definition: Relating to a node or point where lines meet.
note: From node plus -al.
hints: Describes a junction or intersection.
Used for points where things connect.

definition: A loud or unpleasant sound.
note: From Old French noise, 'dispute, wrangle, strife, noise', of uncertain origin.
hints: What neighbours make at night.
Sound you would rather not hear.
origin: Old French noise, from Piedmontese nojé
example: He knew that it was trash day, when the garbage collectors made all the noise.

definition: Making a lot of loud sound.
note: Built from noise plus -y. Noise comes from Old French, though its earlier source is uncertain.
hints: A classroom or street full of racket.
A library should not be this.
example: A small noisy dog.

definition: A person who moves from place to place with no fixed home.
note: From Greek nomas, 'roaming', used of wandering shepherds in search of pasture.
hints: A herder who follows his animals.
Lives out of a tent, travelling.
origin: Middle French nomade, from Ancient Greek νομάς

definition: A long thin strip of cooked dough eaten in soup or stir-fries.
note: Borrowed from German Nudel, whose own origin is uncertain. In slang, your noodle is also your head.
hints: Ramen is a bowl of broth with them.
A pool toy made of floating foam shares the name.
example: She slurped a long noodle up out of her soup.

definition: A loop of rope that tightens when pulled.
note: From Middle English nose, 'noose, loop', of unclear origin.
hints: A rope with a sliding knot.
A hangman's loop.
origin: Old French nos, from Old Occitan nous

definition: Typical or usual.
note: From Latin normalis, 'made according to a carpenter's square', from norma.
hints: Ordinary, as expected.
Not unusual.

definition: An official who witnesses and certifies legal documents.
note: From Latin notarius, 'a scribe or shorthand clerk', related to nota, 'a mark'.
hints: You visit one to have a signature witnessed.
Stamps and seals papers.
example: Instead of the village head, today the meeting was led by the notary.

definition: A small V-shaped cut, or a step upward in level.
note: Recorded since 1577, likely a rebracketing of 'an otch', from Old French ochier, 'to cut a notch'.
hints: Cut into a stick to count days.
A belt is tightened one of these at a time.

definition: To become aware of; or a sign giving information.
note: From Latin notitia, 'being known', from noscere, 'to know'.
hints: See and take note.
A sign pinned to a board.
origin: Middle French notice, from Latin nōtitia; in English since the 17th century
example: Did you notice the flowers in her yard?

definition: To inform someone formally.
note: From Latin notificare, 'to make known'.
hints: Send word of a change.
Tell someone officially.
example: The airport was closed and emergency services were notified.

definition: An idea or belief.
note: From Latin notio, 'concept'.
hints: A vague thought.
Something you've taken into your head.

definition: A long work of fiction, or something new and original.
note: From Old French novel, 'new', from Latin novellus, a diminutive of novus.
hints: A book of invented story.
An idea that has never been tried.
origin: Italian novella, from Latin novella; in English since the 17th century
example: His bookcases were filled with nothing but novels.

definition: A beginner with little experience.
note: From Latin novicius, 'newly arrived', from novus, 'new'. It first named a person newly entering a religious order.
hints: A first-time skier on the nursery slope.
A person newly admitted to a convent, on probation.
origin: Anglo-Norman novice, from Latin novīcius; in English since the 14th century

definition: A narrow spout at the end of a hose or pipe that directs a flow.
note: From Middle English noselle, a 'little nose', a diminutive of nose.
hints: A petrol pump has one you squeeze.
Twist it on a garden hose to switch from mist to jet.

definition: A small difference in meaning, tone or colour.
note: Borrowed from French nuance, 'shade', which is distantly from Latin nubes, 'cloud'.
hints: What a blunt argument lacks.
Subtle shades of a colour or a meaning.
example: Without understanding the finer nuances you can't enjoy the humor.

definition: A gentle push, often with the elbow.
note: Dating from around the seventeenth century, perhaps from a Scandinavian word meaning 'to push' or 'to rub'. It is also used for a small push towards a choice.
hints: What an elbow gives to get your attention.
A light poke that suggests an action.

definition: A small lump of something, such as gold; also a bite-sized piece of food.
note: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in Scotland and in Australian goldfields.
hints: Prospectors in the Gold Rush hoped to find one in a stream.
Fast food chicken often comes in this shape.

definition: A count or quantity expressed in figures.
note: From Latin numerus. The word reached English via Old French.
hints: Digits make this up.
Used for counting.

definition: A person trained to look after the sick.
note: From Old French norrice, from Latin nutrix, 'a woman who nourishes'. It once named a woman who suckled a child.
hints: Works with a doctor on a ward.
Wears scrubs in a hospital.
origin: Old French norrice, from Latin nūtrīcius

definition: A spice from the seed of a tropical tree.
note: From Middle English notemuge, a partial translation of Latin nux muscata, 'musky nut'.
hints: Grated over eggnog.
Once so valuable that nations fought over the islands that grew it.
origin: Medieval Latin nux muga, from Medieval Latin nux muscata

definition: Tasting of nuts; also, informally, crazy.
note: From nut plus -y. Nut comes from Old English hnutu. The crazy sense is a 1900s slang use.
hints: The taste of a brown, toasted flavour.
Also slang for someone a bit mad.

definition: A strong, stretchy synthetic fibre.
note: Coined by DuPont in 1938, formed from a random syllable plus a common fibre ending.
hints: Used for stockings and ropes.
The first fully synthetic fibre.

definition: A female nature spirit in Greek myth, or a young insect.
note: From Greek numphe, which meant 'bride' or 'young woman'. The insect sense is for a young form that has not yet grown wings.
hints: A spirit of rivers and woods.
A young dragonfly before it takes wing.
origin: Old English nymphē, from Ancient Greek νύμφη
example: The ancient Greeks believed that nymphs inhabited forests and bodies of water.

definition: Made of oak.
note: From Old English acen, 'of oak', built from oak plus -en. It is a poetic word for sturdy wooden things.
hints: Describes a bucket or a door.
A type of strong timber, in poems.
example: A solid oak table.

definition: A fertile spot in a desert.
note: From Greek oasis, probably from an Egyptian word. Palm trees grow around a spring there.
hints: A green spot in the Sahara.
A peaceful retreat from a busy place.
origin: Late Latin Oasis, from Egyptian wḥꜣt

definition: Extremely overweight in a way that affects health.
note: From Latin obesus, 'having eaten away', from ob- plus edere, 'to eat'.
hints: Clinical term for being very overweight.
A health risk measured by BMI.

definition: A thing you can see or touch; or to disagree.
note: From Latin objectum, 'something thrown in the way'.
hints: A physical item, or a goal.
To protest against a proposal.
origin: Old French object, from Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον
example: It was full of rackets, balls and other objects.

definition: To force someone to do something, or to do them a favour.
note: From Latin obligare, 'to bind'; the old sense was creating a duty. It is a doublet of obligate.
hints: An invitation you feel bound to accept.
A host who happily helps a guest.
origin: Old French obligier, from Latin obligō
example: Your carelessness obliges firmness on my part.

definition: To get or acquire.
note: From Latin obtinere, 'to hold on to'.
hints: Get hold of something.
Secure a permit.
origin: Anglo-Norman obtenir, from Latin obtinēre; in English since the 15th century
example: Applicants must obtain a permit before construction.

definition: Slow to understand; or, in geometry, an angle over ninety degrees.
note: From Latin obtusus, 'blunt', from obtundere, 'to beat'. A dull mind is blunt like the angle.
hints: An angle between a right angle and a straight line.
Describes someone who misses the obvious hint.

definition: Relating to hidden supernatural forces; or hidden from view.
note: From Latin occultus, 'hidden'. The word became linked with magic, astrology and secret knowledge.
hints: Tarot cards and séances belong to it.
Horror films often draw on this world of dark rituals.

definition: To fill or take up space or time, or to seize.
note: From Latin occupare, 'to seize'.
hints: Take a seat.
Take over a building in a protest.
origin: Old French occuper, from Latin occupāre
example: The historic mansion occupied two city blocks.

definition: To happen, or to come to mind.
note: From Latin occurrere, 'to run to meet'.
hints: What an accident does.
When an idea does this, it comes to mind.
origin: Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō
example: The liftoff will occur in exactly twelve seconds.

definition: A vast body of salt water covering much of the Earth.
note: From Greek Okeanos, the great river believed to circle the world, via Latin and Old French.
hints: The Atlantic and the Pacific are examples.
Bigger than any sea.
origin: Old French occean, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός

definition: A yellowish-brown earth pigment, or the colour itself.
note: From Greek ochra, 'pale yellow'. People have used it as paint for tens of thousands of years.
hints: A warm earthy yellow paint from the ground.
Used in cave art, and a shade of orange-yellow.
origin: Old French ocre, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα

definition: A fuel hydrocarbon whose rating shows how well petrol resists knocking.
note: From oct-, 'eight', plus -ane, as it has eight carbon atoms. Petrol grades are labelled with its number.
hints: Pump labels give a number for it.
High-performance fuel boasts a higher rating.

definition: The gap between a note and the next note of the same name.
note: From Latin octavus, 'eighth'. It spans eight notes of the scale.
hints: On a piano, the same note repeats at one.
Eight white keys from do to do.

definition: A group of eight, especially eight musicians.
note: From oct-, 'eight', plus the ending -et.
hints: A chamber piece for eight players.
A group of eight.
example: An octet of waiters sang her "Happy Birthday".

definition: A round opening at the top of a dome; also a circular window.
note: Borrowed from Latin oculus, 'eye'.
hints: The Pantheon in Rome has a famous one that lets in light and rain.
A round window shaped like an eye.
example: One can glimpse the sky through the oculus of the Pantheon in Rome.

definition: More strange or unusual.
note: The comparative of odd, which came from Old Norse oddi, 'point of land', and later 'third or uneven number'.
hints: Comparing two peculiar things.
Stranger than strange, when set beside another.

definition: In a strange or unexpected way.
note: From odd plus -ly. Odd goes back to Old Norse oddi, a triangle's point, which led to the sense of 'uneven'.
hints: How a strange noise can seem.
Used before 'enough' to introduce a surprise.
example: For December, it was oddly warm.

definition: A theatre or concert hall; originally a small Greek building for music.
note: From Greek oideion, from ode, 'song'.
hints: Ancient building for music, and a cinema name.
A cinema chain borrowed it.

definition: The organs of an animal, such as liver and kidney, used as food.
note: From Middle English offal, built from 'off' and 'fall': what falls off in butchering.
hints: Liver and kidneys are examples.
Butcher's leftovers that some cooks prize.
example: In Mary's butcher shop, you can also find an offal shop.

definition: To hurt someone's feelings or break a rule.
note: From Latin offendere, 'to strike against'. An offence was a stumbling.
hints: What a rude joke may do to a listener.
To break the law is to commit an offence.
origin: Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō
example: Your accusations offend me deeply.

definition: To hold out something for someone to accept.
note: From Old English offrian, 'to make a sacrifice'.
hints: What a shop does with a discount.
Put forward for acceptance.
origin: Old English offrian, from Latin ob

definition: A place where people work at desks; also a public position.
note: From Latin officium, 'service or duty'.
hints: A cubicle farm.
A job role and a place of work.
origin: Old French office, from Latin officium
example: He rented an office in the new building.

definition: To balance one thing against another.
note: From off plus set.
hints: Cancel out carbon emissions.
A printing method or a compensation.
example: There is a small offset between the switch and the indicator which some users found confusing.

definition: Many times; frequently.
note: From Middle English ofte, with an -n added by analogy with 'seldom'.
hints: Its opposite is seldom.
Happens again and again.
example: I often walk to work when the weather is nice.

definition: Of old; from a past time.
note: From Middle English olden, probably an old plural form of old. It remains mostly in the phrase 'olden days'.
hints: Used for times long gone by.
Often paired with 'days'.
example: The legend has come down in this district from olden times.

definition: Having lived or existed longer.
note: The comparative of old, from Old English ald. Elder is a related older form.
hints: Comparing two ages.
A sibling born first is this.

definition: Of the greatest age.
note: The superlative of old.
hints: Eldest in a family.
Most ancient.

definition: An old song, film or thing from the past.
note: Formed from old plus -ie.
hints: A radio station might play a golden one.
A classic hit from decades ago.
example: We were listening to oldies music on the car radio.

definition: A small oval fruit eaten or pressed for oil, or a dull green colour.
note: From Old French olive, from Latin oliva.
hints: A martini garnish.
Pressed to make a Mediterranean cooking oil.
origin: Old French olive, from Latin olīva

definition: A shading of colour from light to dark; also an old card game.
note: From French, meaning 'shaded'. The card game came from Spanish hombre, 'man'.
hints: A gradient on hair, nails or fabric.
A colour that fades gradually.

definition: The last letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek o mega, 'great o', to tell it apart from the short omicron.
hints: Watches and ohms both borrow this letter.
The final letter, meaning the end.

definition: A round vegetable with layers that makes people cry when cut.
note: From Old French oignon, from Latin unio.
hints: Cutting one brings tears.
A layered bulb with a sharp smell.
origin: Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem

definition: Connected to the internet.
note: Formed from on and line, from older uses for being connected to a power or telephone line.
hints: Not offline.
Where you are when you browse the web.

definition: The beginning of something, usually something unwelcome.
note: Formed from 'on' plus 'set'.
hints: The start of a fever or a storm.
The first moment a symptom appears.
example: The onset of pneumonia.

definition: Moving forward in space or time.
note: From Old English on plus -weard. 'Christian soldiers' march in a hymn.
hints: A cry to troops to continue the advance.
A command to a team trailing in a race.
example: There was an onward rush as the gates opened.

definition: Energy, power or appeal.
note: Imitates the sound of a sudden effort.
hints: What a dull dish needs.
Zest and vigour.

definition: Not letting light through; or hard to understand.
note: From Latin opacus, 'shaded'. A rule written in confusing jargon is said to be opaque.
hints: A frosted window is not clear but this.
Unclear jargon in a contract.
example: Opaque windows of the jail.

definition: Something that opens, or the first of a series.
note: From open plus -er.
hints: Takes the lid off a can.
The first song in a concert.

definition: Without hiding anything.
note: From open plus -ly.
hints: Frankly and in public.
Speaking with nothing concealed.
example: Sami talked to Layla openly about other girls that he liked.

definition: A drama in which the words are sung to an orchestra's accompaniment.
note: Borrowed from Italian opera, 'work'. It is a doublet of 'opus'.
hints: Sung in grand theatres, often in Italian.
A fat lady is said to end it by singing.

definition: To give or state an opinion.
note: From Latin opinari, 'to think or suppose'. Today it is often used with a slightly formal or mocking tone.
hints: What a pundit does on television.
To give your two cents, in a stuffy way.
origin: Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor

definition: A drug that acts on pain receptors, such as morphine or heroin.
note: Coined in the 1960s from opium plus -oid, 'like'. It covers both natural and synthetic painkillers.
hints: A class of drugs behind a modern addiction crisis.
Morphine and fentanyl belong to this group.

definition: A narcotic drug made from the juice of the poppy.
note: From Greek opion, from opos, 'juice'.
hints: Made from a flower's sap.
Source of morphine and heroin.
origin: Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον
example: What can bound feet, essay-writing and opium have in common?

definition: To resist or be against.
note: From Latin opponere, 'to set against'.
hints: Vote against.
Act against an idea.
origin: Old French opposer, from Latin opponere
example: There is still time to oppose this plan.

definition: Relating to the eye or sight.
note: From Greek optikos, 'of sight'. It appears in 'optic nerve', which carries signals from the eye to the brain.
hints: A nerve that joins the eye to the brain.
A word in a kind of fibre that carries light.
origin: Middle French optique, from Ancient Greek ὀπτῐκός

definition: A choice that may be taken.
note: From Latin optio, 'choice'.
hints: One of several things you may select.
A menu item you could pick.

definition: A priest who gave wise advice from gods, or a source of wisdom.
note: From Latin oraculum, from orare, 'to speak'.
hints: The one at Delphi.
A wise source consulted.
origin: Old French oracle m, from Latin ōrāculum n

definition: By mouth, or spoken rather than written.
note: From oral plus -ly. Oral comes from Latin os, 'mouth'.
hints: How medicine is taken if it is not an injection.
An exam taught by speaking, not writing.
example: He was administered the drug orally.

definition: A citrus fruit, and its colour.
note: From Old French orenge, from Arabic naranj, from Sanskrit. The fruit was named long before the colour.
hints: Fruit with peel.
The fruit gave the colour its name.
origin: Old French pome orenge, from Sanskrit नारङ्ग

definition: A plant with showy, intricately shaped flowers.
note: From Greek orkhis, 'testicle', after the shape of the plant's paired root tubers. English picked it up in the 1800s via New Latin.
hints: A prized houseplant with a long arching stem of blooms.
Vanilla comes from the pod of one.
origin: New Latin Orchideae, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις

definition: A painful or difficult experience.
note: From Old English ordal, 'judgement'. In medieval times it was a trial by fire or water to test guilt.
hints: What a long dental procedure might feel like.
Once a medieval trial by hot iron or water.
origin: Medieval Latin ordālium, from Old English ordēl

definition: A command; or an arrangement in sequence.
note: From Old French ordre, from Latin ordo, 'row' or 'rank'. The word later stretched to cover commands and religious brotherhoods.
hints: What a waiter writes down.
Alphabetical is a type of it.
origin: Old French ordre, from Latin ōrdinem

definition: A part of the body with a particular job, or a large keyboard instrument with pipes.
note: From Greek organon, 'tool, instrument', via Latin and Old French.
hints: The heart or liver is one.
A church instrument with pipes and pedals.
origin: Old French organe, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον

definition: A bay window that sticks out from an upper wall.
note: From Old French oriol, meaning a porch or gallery.
hints: A window projecting from a building's face.
Found on old college and manor houses.
origin: Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus

definition: To align or position something relative to a direction or situation.
note: From the Latin oriens, 'rising', meaning the east where the sun comes up. To orient yourself was once literally to face east.
hints: What you do with a map and compass before setting off.
A new hire gets an induction session to help with this.
example: We had to orient ourselves in the forest.

definition: The point where something begins.
note: From Latin origo, 'beginning'.
hints: Where it all started.
A source or root.
origin: Old French origine, from Latin orīgō

definition: Richly decorated, often to excess.
note: From Latin ornatus, 'equipped, adorned', from ornare.
hints: Baroque churches are covered in this kind of detail.
A gilded mirror frame carved with swirls and leaves.
example: It takes a skilled craftsman to carve a handle that ornate.

definition: A child whose parents are both dead.
note: From Greek orphanos, 'bereaved', related to a word for bereft. Dickens' Oliver Twist is the classic fictional example.
hints: Oliver Twist and Annie are both this.
A child in a Dickens novel with no parents to care for him.
origin: Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός

definition: Different from the one already mentioned.
note: From Old English other, from a root that meant 'second'. It is related to the Germanic word for 'either'.
hints: A word for not this one.
The remaining one of two.
example: Today isn't any other day.

definition: A playful, water-loving mammal with webbed feet and a long body.
note: From Old English otor, from a Germanic root that is related to the word 'water'.
hints: It slides down muddy riverbanks.
Sea ones hold hands while they sleep.

definition: Indicates duty or what is right to do.
note: From Old English ahte, the past of agan, 'to own'. What you ought to do was once what you owed.
hints: A helping verb of obligation.
Used before 'to' with duties.
origin: Old English āhte, from Old English āgan
example: I ought to vote in the coming election.

definition: A unit of weight equal to one sixteenth of a pound.
note: From Latin uncia, a Roman unit that was a twelfth part of something.
hints: A small unit used in cooking and mail.
Sixteen make a pound.
origin: Middle French once, from Latin ū̆ncia

definition: A period when a service such as power is not working.
note: From out plus -age, on the pattern of shortage. Storms cause power ones.
hints: The lights go dark after a storm.
A website goes down for hours.

definition: A loud public protest or sudden uproar.
note: Formed from out plus cry, and already in Middle English.
hints: A scandal or an unpopular law often triggers one.
The crowd's angry response to an unfair decision.
example: His appearance was greeted with an outcry of jeering.

definition: To do better than someone else.
note: Built from out- plus do, from Old English. To outdo is to go beyond another's effort.
hints: What rivals try to do to each other.
To surpass a competitor.

definition: On the outside; farther from the centre.
note: From Old English utera, a comparative of ut, 'out'. It is the opposite of inner.
hints: Space is this kind, beyond Earth.
Its space is where satellites orbit.

definition: A set of clothes, or an organisation.
note: From out plus fit, a word for equipping.
hints: What you wear for a party.
A group, in a rough sense.
example: She wore a fashionable outfit with matching purse and shoes.

definition: To go beyond or surpass; also, money spent.
note: From Old English utgan, built from out and go. As a noun it means money going out, the opposite of income.
hints: Money that leaves your account.
A financial word that is the reverse of 'income'.

definition: A person living outside the protection of the law; or to ban something.
note: From Old Norse utlagi, 'one outside the law'. In medieval England an outlaw could be killed without punishment.
hints: Robin Hood and Jesse James fit the description.
Someone with a price on their head in the Wild West.
origin: Old English ūtlaga, from Old Norse útlagi
example: The main character in the play was a bit of an outlaw who refused to shake hands or say thank you.

definition: A passage for release, or a shop selling brand goods or a power socket.
note: From out plus let.
hints: Plug something into it.
Discount shopping centre.
example: He blocked the way out.

definition: The amount produced.
note: From out plus put.
hints: What a factory or a computer yields after its work.
What a factory yields.

definition: The closing section of a song, film or video.
note: A blend of out and intro, first attested in a 1967 Bonzo Dog Doo-Dah Band song title.
hints: Where a song winds down at the end.
The opposite of an intro.

definition: The very beginning of something.
note: Built simply from out and set. It appears almost always in the phrase 'at the outset'.
hints: Appears in the phrase 'from the' plus this word, meaning from the start.
A good essay states its aim right here.
example: He agreed and understood from the outset, so don't bother explaining again.

definition: The organ in which eggs are made, or the part of a flower that holds the ovules.
note: From New Latin ovarium, from Latin ovum, 'egg'.
hints: Where eggs are produced.
The base of a flower's pistil.
origin: New Latin ovarium, from Latin ovum
example: The male testicles are homologous to the female ovaries.

definition: Shaped like an egg.
note: From Latin ovatus, from ovum, 'egg'. Botanists use it for leaves wider at the base.
hints: A leaf shape in botany.
Like an egg outline.

definition: To an excessive degree.
note: From over plus -ly.
hints: More than is wise.
More than is wise or needed.
example: Parents can be overly protective of their children.

definition: Done openly, not hidden.
note: From Old French overt, 'open'.
hints: Done in plain sight.
Hidden actions are its opposite.
origin: Anglo-Norman overt, from Old French overt

definition: Relating to sheep.
note: From Late Latin ovinus, from ovis, 'sheep'. It is the sheepish counterpart to bovine for cattle.
hints: A formal word about a woolly animal.
Cousin of the adjective that describes cows.
origin: Late Latin ovīnus, from Latin ovis

definition: Shaped like an egg.
note: From Latin ovum, 'egg', plus -oid, 'resembling'. It is a geometry word for an egg-like shape.
hints: Like an egg or a rugby ball, roughly.
A rounded shape, longer than a circle.

definition: A person who owns something.
note: From Old English agnere, from the verb agan. 'Own' is actually a back-formation from it in the sense of owner.
hints: The person with the deed or the receipt.
A dog's human.
example: The police recovered the stolen car and returned it to its owner.

definition: A compound of oxygen and another element.
note: From Greek oxus, 'sharp, acid', the same root that gave 'oxygen'.
hints: Rust is one.
A chemical made by burning something with air.
example: Nitrous oxide stopped being used as an anaesthetic a long time ago.

definition: The gas we breathe to live.
note: Coined in French by Lavoisier from Greek roots meaning 'acid-former', since he mistakenly thought all acids contain it.
hints: Gas in the air.
A flame needs it to burn.
origin: French oxygène, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς
example: Without oxygen, all animals would have disappeared long ago.

definition: A shelled mollusc eaten raw or cooked, some of which make pearls.
note: From Old French oistre, from Greek ostreon. 'The world is your oyster' comes from Shakespeare, where it means opportunity is there for the taking.
hints: A shellfish served on ice with lemon.
Where a pearl grows.
origin: Old English ostre, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον

definition: A form of oxygen with three atoms, found in a protective layer high above the Earth.
note: Coined in 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schonbein, from Greek ozon, 'smelling', because of its sharp smell.
hints: A layer high up shields us from ultraviolet rays.
Its hole over the poles worried the world.
origin: German Ozon, from Ancient Greek ὄζον

definition: Someone who sets the speed in a race, or a horse that paces.
note: From pace plus -er.
hints: Runner who sets the tempo.
Keeps others at a steady speed.

definition: A person or machine that packs goods.
note: From pack plus -er. The Green Bay football team's name comes from a meat-packing company.
hints: A worker filling boxes in a warehouse.
An American football team in Wisconsin has a name for them.

definition: A small container or parcel.
note: From Anglo-French pak, 'pack', with a diminutive ending.
hints: Crisps come in one.
A paper sachet of seeds.
example: Don't throw the crisp packet on the floor!

definition: A short oar with a broad blade; or to wade in shallow water.
note: From Middle English padell, a small spade, mixed with a verb meaning to splash. Kids do the second at the seaside.
hints: What a canoeist dips into the river.
What children do at the water's edge on a beach.
origin: Medieval Latin padela, from Latin patella

definition: A flooded field in which rice grows.
note: Borrowed from Malay padi, 'rice plant'.
hints: Rice grows in one.
A wet field in Asia.
origin: Malay padi; in English since the 20th century

definition: A military chaplain; or a priest.
note: From Italian, Spanish and Portuguese padre, 'father'. A soldier calls the unit's chaplain this.
hints: A priest in the army.
A Spanish word for father.

definition: A follower of an old or non-mainstream religion.
note: From Latin paganus, 'rural' or 'civilian', from pagus, 'village'. The Church used it for those who did not join Christianity.
hints: A word from early church history.
Once meant someone from the countryside.
origin: Latin pāgānus, from Middle English payen
example: This community has a surprising number of pagans.

definition: A small device that beeps to summon someone.
note: From page plus -er. Doctors once carried them.
hints: A beeper from before mobile phones.
Hospital staff wore these to be called quickly.
example: Yanni turned his pager off.

definition: Coloured liquid that dries to coat a surface.
note: From Latin pingere, 'to paint', via Old French.
hints: Applied with a brush or roller.
An artist mixes it on a palette.
origin: Old French peintier, from Latin pingō
example: Artists use `paint' and `pigment' interchangeably.

definition: The large home of a ruler.
note: From Latin Palatium, the Palatine Hill in Rome where emperors lived.
hints: Buckingham is one.
Residence of a monarch.
origin: Old French palais, from Latin palātium

definition: The roof of the mouth; also a person's sense of taste.
note: From Latin palatum. People used to think taste lived in the roof of the mouth, so the word came to mean taste.
hints: A cleansing sorbet resets it between courses.
The soft and hard parts form the roof of the mouth.
origin: Latin palātum; in English since the 14th century
example: Y is pronounced with the tongue approximating the hard palate.

definition: A wooden platform for stacking goods, or a simple straw bed.
note: From Middle English paillet, 'bundle of straw', from Old French paille, 'straw'. The straw bed is the older sense; the shipping platform came later.
hints: A forklift slides its prongs beneath one.
Goods wait on it in a warehouse.

definition: A condition of paralysis, often with shaking.
note: From Old French and Latin paralysis, from Greek, meaning 'loosening'. Bell's palsy is a modern named example.
hints: An old name for paralysis.
Bell's is a famous kind.
origin: Anglo-Norman paralisie, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις

definition: A black and white bear from China.
note: Borrowed from French, of unclear origin. It eats bamboo.
hints: A bear that eats bamboo.
A black and white animal that the WWF uses as its emblem.
origin: French panda, from Nepali निँगाले; in English since the 20th century

definition: A flat section of a surface, or a group of people chosen to discuss something.
note: From Middle English panel, which could mean a piece of cloth or a list of jurors, from Old French.
hints: A door can have one set in it.
A group of experts on a show.

definition: A small room or cupboard where food is kept.
note: From Old French paneterie, a place for bread, from Latin panis, 'bread'.
hints: Tins, flour and pasta are stored there.
Originally the bread room of a great household.
origin: Old French paneterie, from Latin panis
example: I'm wondering if I could get a referral to your food pantry.

definition: Trousers.
note: Short for pantaloons, named after a comic character of old Italian theatre called Pantalone. Americans use it for trousers.
hints: What you wear on your legs.
A word for trousers in America.
origin: French pantalon, from Italian Pantalone; in English since the 19th century

definition: Relating to the pope.
note: From Medieval Latin papalis, from papa, 'father'.
hints: Describes a pope's decree.
A bull issued from Rome.
origin: Old French papal, from Medieval Latin pāpālis
example: Papal Audiences are held on Wednesdays if the Pope is in Rome.

definition: A father, in folksy speech; or soft and mushy.
note: From pap, a soft food, or an alteration of papa.
hints: Southern name for dad.
A folksy name for a dad.

definition: A public procession.
note: From French parade, from Spanish parada, 'a halt'.
hints: A march through streets.
Floats and bands go by.
example: The Parade of the Marksmen at the Hanover Schützenfest each July is one of the longest regular parades in the world.

definition: A package wrapped for sending.
note: From Old French parcelle, 'a small piece', from Latin particula. A parcel of land is a small plot.
hints: What a courier leaves on the porch.
Also a piece of land, or the thing passed around in a children's game.
origin: Old French parcelle, from Latin particula
example: I saw a brown paper parcel on my doorstep.

definition: Forgiveness, or an official release from punishment.
note: From Old French pardoner, 'to forgive'.
hints: What a president can grant a convict.
Said when you did not hear something.

definition: A mother or father.
note: From Latin parens, 'begetter', from parere, 'to bring forth'.
hints: The person who raises a child.
Mother or father, in one word.
origin: Anglo-Norman parent, from Latin parentem; in English since the 15th century

definition: A tool for peeling or trimming.
note: Built from pare, 'to trim off the outer layer', plus -er. A paring knife is its close cousin.
hints: A tool for peeling fruit.
Used to trim the skin off an apple.

definition: A local church district, or in Louisiana a county-like area.
note: From Old French paroisse, from Greek paroikia, 'neighbourhood'.
hints: The area a vicar serves.
A local division of a church.

definition: Equality, especially of pay, status or level.
note: From Latin par, 'equal'. In computing, a parity bit is a check that counts whether the number of ones is odd or even.
hints: Campaigners demand it between men's and women's pay.
In computing, a bit checks for it to catch errors.
origin: Middle French parité, from Latin pār

definition: A hooded jacket for cold or wet weather.
note: Reached English by 1780 through Russian and Aleut, ultimately from a Tundra Nenets word.
hints: A hooded coat for the Arctic.
A hooded coat with a fur-trimmed edge for the Arctic.
origin: Tundra Nenets парка, from Russian па́рка
example: What do you think about this parka?

definition: A sitting room used to receive guests; also a shop for certain services.
note: From Old French parleor, from parler, 'to speak'. The room was for talking.
hints: A Victorian family kept their best furniture in one.
An ice cream shop calls itself an ice cream one.
origin: Old French parleor, from Medieval Latin parlātōrium

definition: An imitation meant to mock or amuse.
note: From Greek paroidia, 'a song sung beside another'.
hints: A funny copy of a famous film.
A mocking copy of a serious work.
origin: Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία

definition: Early release of a prisoner on conditions.
note: From French parole, 'word', since a prisoner gave his word.
hints: Granted after good behaviour.
Given before serving the full sentence.
origin: Middle French parole, from Ancient Greek παραβολή; in English since the 17th century
example: He will be on parole for nearly two more years.

definition: A colourful bird that can imitate speech; or to repeat without understanding.
note: From Middle French perrot, perhaps a pet form of Pierre. To repeat someone else's words is to do this.
hints: A pirate's traditional shoulder companion.
What a bird does when it copies your speech.
example: I bought a wonderful parrot at the pet store.

definition: To ward off an attack or a question.
note: From Italian parare, 'to ward off' via French.
hints: A fencer's defensive move.
Deflect a question without really answering it.
origin: Old French paree, from Medieval Latin parāta

definition: To break a sentence into its grammatical parts, or to analyse code.
note: Probably from Middle English pars, 'parts of speech', from Latin pars, 'part'.
hints: Done to a sentence in a grammar lesson.
A computer does it to a line of code.

definition: In some part.
note: From part plus -ly.
hints: Not totally.
To some degree.
example: They had partly finished the house, so they could move in before winter.

definition: A social gathering, or a group or person involved in something.
note: From Old French partie, 'part, side, share'.
hints: Held with music and cake.
A political group, or a person in a lawsuit.
example: I'm throwing a huge party for my 21st birthday.

definition: The standard unit of pressure.
note: Named after Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician who studied fluids and pressure. A programming language shares his name.
hints: What pressure is measured in, in physics.
Named after a 17th-century French thinker.

definition: A high-ranking Ottoman official.
note: From Turkish pasa. It was a title for governors and generals.
hints: An Ottoman governor.
A Turkish title of rank.
origin: Ottoman Turkish پاشا, from Persian بچّه

definition: Outdated or no longer fashionable.
note: The unaccented form of French passé, 'past'.
hints: Out of style.
Fashion words say it for old hat.

definition: A person who passes something, such as a ball or an exam.
note: Formed from pass plus -er.
hints: A quarterback is described as a good one.
Someone who succeeds in a driving test.

definition: A food made from wheat dough, shaped and boiled.
note: Borrowed from Italian pasta, 'paste, dough', from Greek.
hints: Spaghetti is one kind.
Eaten with sauce, from Italy.
origin: Italian pasta, from Ancient Greek πάσσω

definition: A soft, sticky mixture, or to stick something with glue.
note: From Old French paste, 'dough', from Greek.
hints: A soft, sticky mixture.
Copy, then do this on a computer.
origin: Old French paste, from Ancient Greek παστά

definition: A soft, pale shade of a colour; also a chalky crayon or a drawing made with one.
note: Via French from Italian pastello, from the Latin word for 'paste', because the crayons were made from a pressed paste of pigment.
hints: Easter eggs and baby-room walls are often painted in these shades.
A chalky art stick in this family is used for soft drawings.
origin: French pastel, from Ancient Greek πάστη

definition: A minister who leads a congregation.
note: From Latin pastor, 'shepherd', since a pastor tends a flock of believers.
hints: Leads a church flock.
Its Latin root meant shepherd.
origin: Old French pastor, from Latin pāstor

definition: Baked dough made with fat, used for pies and tarts.
note: From Old French pastaierie, from paste. Croissants and eclairs are examples.
hints: What a pie is wrapped in.
A baker's window is full of these.
origin: Old French pastaierie, from Ancient Greek παστά
example: That pastry shop sells not just pastries, but all kinds of baked goods.

definition: Pale and unhealthy-looking; or a baked meat pie.
note: The adjective is from paste plus -y. The pie is a separate word, from Old French paste, 'pastry'.
hints: A sickly complexion.
A Cornish miner's lunch.
example: Are you feeling OK? You look a bit pasty.

definition: A piece used to cover a hole, or a small area.
note: From Middle English patche, of uncertain origin.
hints: Sewn on a worn elbow.
A pirate might wear one over an eye.
example: His sleeves had patches on the elbows where different fabric had been sewn on to replace material that had worn away.

definition: An official right to be the only maker of an invention.
note: From Latin patere, 'to lie open', since patents were open letters.
hints: Protects an invention.
Obvious, in a different sense.

definition: Father, in Latin and old British slang.
note: From Latin pater, meaning father.
hints: The Latin for dad.
Old school slang for a father.

definition: A paved outdoor area beside a house.
note: From Spanish patio, 'courtyard', of uncertain origin.
hints: Where a barbecue might be set up.
A paved spot outside the back door.
origin: Spanish patio, from Old Occitan patu
example: Something fell on the patio, but I could not see what it was.

definition: A regular round made by guards or police to keep watch.
note: From French patrouiller, 'to paddle in mud', a word from soldiers' slang.
hints: Police car on a regular round.
A guard walking the grounds at night.
origin: French patrouille, from Old French patrouille

definition: A supporter or regular customer.
note: From Latin patronus, 'protector', from pater, 'father'.
hints: Gives money to the arts.
A regular at a pub.
origin: Old French patron, from Latin patrōnus
example: This car park is for patrons only.

definition: A small flat cake of minced food, such as meat.
note: Earlier meant 'small pie', from French pate.
hints: The meaty part of a burger.
A flat round of ground beef.
example: The cook fried the hamburger patty, then put it in a bun.

definition: A short stop or rest.
note: From Latin pausa, from Greek pausis, 'stopping'.
hints: A button on a video player.
A brief silence.
origin: Middle French pause, from Ancient Greek παύω

definition: Covered with a hard surface.
note: From Middle English paven, from Old French. A road or path with asphalt is this.
hints: A road with a smooth top.
The opposite of a dirt track.

definition: The day on which wages are paid.
note: Simply pay plus day. Many workers get one weekly, fortnightly or monthly.
hints: The day your bank balance briefly looks healthy.
Often the last Friday of the month for salaried staff.
example: I don't think I should buy anything else until after payday.

definition: The person receiving a payment.
note: From pay plus -ee, the ending for a person who receives. A cheque is written to this person.
hints: Whose name goes on a cheque.
The one who gets the money.
example: Tom wrote Mary's name as the cheque payee.

definition: A person who pays.
note: From pay plus -er. In law, the payer of a bill is the person responsible for settling it.
hints: Who hands over the money.
On a cheque or invoice, the debtor takes this role.
example: The company is the largest tax payer in the region.

definition: The reward or result at the end of an effort, or a payment that settles something.
note: Formed from the phrasal verb 'pay off', which first meant to settle a debt in full.
hints: What a long gamble or a long wait finally delivers, if you're lucky.
A bribe handed over in an envelope goes by this name.

definition: A sum of money paid to someone, such as a prize or settlement.
note: From the phrasal verb pay out. A lottery winner receives a big one.
hints: What a casino gives you if you win at slots.
An insurance company sends it after an approved claim.
example: The maximum payout from this fruit machine is £20.

definition: Freedom from war, or a state of calm.
note: From Old French pais, from Latin pax.
hints: What a treaty aims for.
The dove is its symbol.
example: May there be peace in our time.

definition: A soft, juicy, downy-skinned fruit with a large stone.
note: From Latin persicum, 'Persian apple', via Old French peche.
hints: A fuzzy summer fruit.
Its Latin name points to Persia.

definition: Looking pale and unwell.
note: From peak, in the sense of pinched or sickly, plus -y.
hints: How a person looks when they're coming down with something.
British word for sickly in appearance.
example: Are you all right, mate? It's just you look a bit peaky.

definition: A legume eaten as a snack, grown underground.
note: From pea plus nut, since it resembles both.
hints: A butter is made from it.
Eaten roasted at a ball game.
example: He always liked eating peanuts along with tea before biscuits came into his life.

definition: A smooth, round gem formed inside an oyster.
note: From Old French perle, of uncertain origin.
hints: Found inside an oyster.
A string of these is a classic necklace.
origin: Old French perle, from Latin perula

definition: A small stone made smooth by water.
note: From Old English papolstan, 'pebble-stone', of unknown origin. Beaches covered with them are called shingle.
hints: What you skim across a lake.
Smooth ones line a stream bed.
origin: Old English papolstān, from Old English stān

definition: A sweet, buttery nut from an American tree.
note: From French pacane, from an Algonquian word.
hints: The nut in a Southern pie.
Related to the walnut.

definition: A foot-operated lever, as on a bicycle or piano.
note: From Latin pes, 'foot', via French pedale.
hints: Pushed round by a cyclist.
A piano has two or three at the bottom.
example: There are three pedals on manual cars, two on automatics.

definition: A small annoyance that irritates you.
note: A back-formation from peevish, so the noun came after the adjective.
hints: As in pet this?
Something that gets on your nerves.

definition: A small, hard ball of compressed material.
note: From Old French pelote, 'small ball', from Latin pila, 'ball'. It is related to the word pill.
hints: Fed to hamsters or fired from an air gun.
What an owl coughs up.
origin: Old French pelote, from Latin pila

definition: Relating to the hips and the bony basin they form.
note: From pelvis, Latin for 'basin'. Physiotherapists teach pelvic floor exercises.
hints: A fracture in the hip bones is this.
Fish have fins named after this area.

definition: The bowl-shaped bone structure at the base of the spine.
note: Latin for 'basin', for the shape. It connects the spine to the legs.
hints: Elvis swivelled this part of his body.
The bones your hips are attached to.
origin: Latin pēlvis, from Old Latin pēluis

definition: Relating to punishment, especially by law.
note: From Latin poenalis, from poena, 'punishment'.
hints: Relating to punishment under the law.
A criminal code or a prison colony may carry this word.
origin: Old French peinal, from Ancient Greek ποινή

definition: A writing tool with a graphite core.
note: From Old French pincel, 'paintbrush', from Latin penicillus, 'little tail'.
hints: Has an eraser on the end.
Sharpened with a blade.
origin: Old French pincil, from Latin pēnicillum; in English since the 16th century

definition: A short pasta shaped like quills.
note: Borrowed from Italian, where it is the plural of penna, 'feather' or 'quill'. The tube ends are cut diagonally like a pen nib.
hints: A type of pasta served with sauce.
A tubular Italian pasta.
example: Can you pick up a few boxes of penne?

definition: A garden plant with large, fragrant, pink or white flowers.
note: From Latin paeonia, from Greek, which comes from the name of a legendary healer, Paeon.
hints: Big, ruffled blooms in late spring.
Peachy blossoms with a sweet scent.
origin: Old English peonie, from Old French peone
example: My favourite flower is the peony.

definition: Human beings in general, or the members of a nation or community.
note: From Old French people, from Latin populus. It is related to the word popular.
hints: More than one person.
What a crowd is made of.
example: People don't like it when you tweak their noses.

definition: A hot spice made from dried berries, or a vegetable of the same name.
note: From Latin piper, from Sanskrit pippali. It was once worth a fortune in Europe.
hints: Grinder at a dinner table.
Spice that goes with salt.
origin: Old English piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι

definition: Full of energy and cheerfulness.
note: From pep, a shortening of pepper, plus -y.
hints: A cheerleader's mood.
Bouncy and lively.
example: Cedric was not feeling peppy when he woke up two hours before dawn.

definition: A place to sit; also a freshwater fish.
note: From Old French perche, 'pole', from Latin pertica. The fish is named from a Greek word, perke.
hints: Where a bird sits on a branch.
A spiny freshwater fish.
origin: Old French perche, from Ancient Greek πέρκη

definition: Serious and immediate danger.
note: From Old French peril, from Latin periculum, 'trial' or 'danger'. It gives us the adjective perilous.
hints: What a hero in a film is in.
A grave kind of danger.
origin: Old French peril, from Latin perīculum
example: Your life is in peril.

definition: A length of time, or a full stop.
note: From Greek periodos, 'a going round'.
hints: An era, or punctuation.
A full stop in American writing.
origin: Middle French periode, from Ancient Greek περίοδος; in English since the 17th century

definition: To die, or to rot away.
note: From Old French perir, from Latin perire, 'to pass away'. It is a formal word for dying, especially in disasters.
hints: Food that spoils quickly is said to be like this.
Mountaineers sometimes do this in a storm.
origin: Old French perir, from Latin perīre
example: You will go, you will never return, in war you will perish.

definition: Cheerful and lively.
note: From perk plus -y. Perk is a verb meaning to brighten up.
hints: How a morning person may seem.
Describes a bright, bouncy mood.
example: She answered with a perky smile and bounced off.

definition: To allow, or an official document of permission.
note: From Latin permittere, 'to let pass'.
hints: A licence to do something.
To give leave or allow.
origin: Middle French permettre, from Latin permittō; in English since the 15th century
example: Children are not permitted beyond this point.

definition: A drink made from fermented pears.
note: From Old French pere, from Latin pirum, 'pear'. It is similar to cider, which is made from apples.
hints: The pear cousin of cider.
An alcoholic drink from fruit trees in Gloucestershire.
origin: Old French peré, from Latin pirum

definition: An individual human being.
note: From Latin persona, which first meant a mask worn by an actor.
hints: A single human being.
Its Latin ancestor was an actor's mask.
origin: Anglo-Norman parsone; in English since the 13th century

definition: Annoying; causing trouble.
note: Possibly a US alteration of pest or pesty, with an uncertain history.
hints: What a swarm of flies can be.
A mild word for irritating.
example: Stay out of my yard, you pesky kids!

definition: A green sauce made from basil, nuts, cheese and oil.
note: From Italian pesto, 'pounded', because the ingredients are crushed together. It comes from Genoa.
hints: A sauce for pasta.
Basil-based and green.
example: The diced courgette will be added to the pesto just before serving.

definition: One of the coloured parts of a flower.
note: From Greek petalon, 'leaf'. Roses and daisies are ringed with them.
hints: Plucked in 'he loves me, he loves me not'.
The soft coloured part of a bloom.

definition: Small, in French.
note: From Old French petit, 'small'. It appears in terms like 'petit four' and in law.
hints: A French word for small.
A small cake, in 'four'.

definition: Small and slim, said of a woman.
note: Borrowed straight from French, the feminine form of petit, 'small'. Clothes shops use it as a size category.
hints: A clothing-label size for shorter, slimmer frames.
Borrowed from French, where the masculine form is petit.

definition: Fuel for cars, in Britain.
note: From French petrole, from Latin petroleum, 'rock oil'.
hints: Filled at a pump.
What Americans call gas.

definition: Small and unimportant; or mean over trivial things.
note: From Old French petit, 'small'. 'Petty cash' means a small fund for minor spending.
hints: Describes a spat over something trivial.
Cash is the small kind in an office drawer.
origin: Anglo-Norman petit, from Old French peti; in English since the 16th century
example: Limited to petty enterprises.

definition: A virus that infects bacteria.
note: Short for bacteriophage, 'bacteria eater', from Greek phagein, 'to eat'.
hints: A virus that preys on microbes.
Viruses that attack germs, researched as medicine.

definition: The drug-making industry.
note: A clipping of 'pharmaceutical', ultimately from Greek pharmakon, 'drug'. It is often used in news about big companies.
hints: Business headlines call the big companies this.
Lobbyists for the industry that makes your medicines.
example: We're investing in pharma and biotech.

definition: One stage in a series of changes.
note: From Greek phasis, 'appearance'. The Moon goes through four of these each month.
hints: A stage the moon goes through.
A teenager's passing stage.

definition: An intense irrational fear of something.
note: Abstracted around 1790 from words ending in -phobia, from Greek phobos, 'fear'. The word is rarely used alone in Greek.
hints: Fear of spiders, heights or enclosed spaces each has a Greek-based name ending in this.
Fear of heights or enclosed spaces.
example: I know someone with a strange phobia of ladders.

definition: A device for talking to people far away.
note: Short for telephone, from Greek tele, 'far', and phone, 'sound'. It is now often a pocket computer.
hints: Rings or buzzes in your pocket.
A device you tap, swipe and call from.
example: Daragh's on the phone at the moment. He'll call you when he's finished.

definition: Fake or insincere.
note: Of unknown origin, though it may come from an old slang word for a swindlers' brass ring. It is used for anything pretending to be real.
hints: A word for a fraud.
Describes a smile that is not genuine.

definition: A single particle of light.
note: From Greek photos, 'light', plus -on. The name was proposed in the 1920s, shortly after Einstein's idea of light quanta.
hints: What a laser beam is made of.
Particle that travels at the speed of light.
example: Gamma rays are composed of very energetic photons.

definition: A short group of words, or a musical passage.
note: From Greek phrasis, 'speech' or 'diction'.
hints: Group of words.
Turn of speech.
origin: Late Latin phrasis, from Ancient Greek φράσις

definition: A large keyboard instrument played with hammers striking strings.
note: Short for pianoforte, Italian for 'soft-loud', because it could play both quietly and loudly. Earlier keyboards could not vary volume with touch.
hints: Has black and white keys.
A concert grand is a big one.
example: The piano in his house takes up a lot of space.

definition: A public square in an Italian town.
note: Borrowed from Italian. It is a doublet of place, plaza and platz.
hints: St Mark's in Venice is the most famous one.
Cafes with outdoor tables surround one in Rome.
example: Almost all of Rome's famous piazzas have fountains.

definition: A pointed stake; also, protesters standing outside a workplace.
note: From French piquet, 'pointed stake'. A picket line is a row of striking workers.
hints: A line of striking workers at a factory gate.
White fence made of pointed wooden stakes.

definition: A vegetable, usually a cucumber, preserved in vinegar or brine; or a tricky spot.
note: From Middle Dutch pekel, 'brine'. Being 'in a pickle' means in a difficult position.
hints: Sits in a burger next to the onions.
Someone in trouble is said to be in a fix like this.
example: A pickle goes well with a hamburger.

definition: A small truck, or the act of collecting something.
note: From pick up.
hints: Truck with an open back.
Collection of goods from a shop.

definition: Fussy about what you will accept.
note: From pick plus -y. A picky eater chooses carefully among what is offered.
hints: A child refusing vegetables may be this.
One who is hard to please at dinner.
example: I am very picky about the way my kitchen is laid out.

definition: A meal eaten outdoors.
note: From French pique-nique, of uncertain origin.
hints: Sandwiches on a blanket.
Lunch in the park.

definition: A part broken or cut from something larger.
note: From Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, of uncertain origin. It also names a single item in a set, such as a chess man.
hints: A slice of cake or a chess man.
One part of a jigsaw.
origin: Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia
example: I’d like another piece of pie.

definition: To make a hole through something.
note: From Old French percier.
hints: A needle can do it to cloth.
Make a hole for an earring.
origin: Old French percier, from Latin pertūsus

definition: Deep devotion to religion or duty.
note: From Latin pietas, meaning dutiful respect. It shares a root with pity.
hints: A word for being religious.
Sister word of 'pity'.
origin: Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās
example: Colleen's piety led her to make sacrifices that most people would not have made.

definition: A plump, short-legged bird common in towns and cities.
note: Through Old French from Latin pipio, a young chirping bird. Homing ones carried messages for centuries.
hints: A city bird that pecks crumbs in the square.
Trained ones carried messages across battlefields.
origin: Old French pyjon, from Latin pīpiāre

definition: A little pig, or a pet name for one.
note: From pig plus -y. It is used in 'piggy bank', a savings pot shaped like the animal.
hints: What a child may call a young swine.
A bank with a coin slot in its back.

definition: A tall upright support for a building, or a person who supports a group.
note: From Old French pilier, from Latin pila, 'pillar'. Figuratively, a pillar of the community is someone others lean on.
hints: Greek temples have rows of these holding up the roof.
A trusted figure in a town is described as one of the community.
origin: Old French pilier, from Latin pila

definition: A cushion for the head.
note: From Old English pyle.
hints: Found on a bed at night.
Where you rest your head at night.
origin: Old English pyle, from Latin pulvīnus

definition: A person who flies an aircraft or steers a ship.
note: From Middle French pilot, from Italian pilota. It first meant a ship's guide into harbour before being used for aircraft.
hints: Sits in the cockpit.
A first episode of a series is called this.
origin: Middle French pilot, from Ancient Greek πηδόν

definition: The smallest finger on the hand.
note: From a Dutch word for 'little', pink or pinkje, and the -y ending. The shade pink is a different word.
hints: The finger you swear a promise with.
The little one on your hand.

definition: A type of grape or the wine it makes.
note: From French pinot, from pin, 'pine', for the shape of the cluster. Noir and grigio are two kinds.
hints: A kind of grape for a red or white wine.
Noir and grigio are two kinds.

definition: A horse or bean with a patchy, spotted coat.
note: From Spanish pinto, 'painted' or 'mottled'. It names piebald horses and a speckled bean.
hints: A spotted horse in a western.
A kind of bean in chilli.

definition: Deeply religious.
note: From Latin pius, 'dutiful'. A churchgoer may be called this.
hints: Devout and faithful.
Describes a monk at prayer.
example: Sami and Layla's pious marriage was hiding a multitude of sins.

definition: A person who plays a pipe or bagpipes.
note: From pipe plus -er. The Pied one in the old tale lured rats and children.
hints: A famous one led rats out of a town.
Plays the bagpipes at a Scottish parade.

definition: Irritation caused by hurt pride; or to stir interest.
note: From French piquer, 'to prick'. Curiosity can be this, in the phrase 'to ___ someone's interest'.
hints: A feeling after a slight to your pride.
A fit of this makes someone storm off.
origin: French piquer, from Old French piquer

definition: Robbery at sea; or copying copyrighted material illegally.
note: From Greek peirates, 'brigand'. Software and film copying also take the name.
hints: Sea bandits off Somalia, or illegal downloads.
The crime of Blackbeard and of bootleg DVDs.
origin: Medieval Latin pīrātia, from Ancient Greek πειρατεία
example: How should the international community respond to Somali piracy?

definition: A robber on the seas.
note: From Greek peirates, 'attacker', from peiran, 'to attempt'.
hints: Captain Hook is one.
Plunders ships.
origin: Old French pirate, from Ancient Greek πειρατής

definition: A small handgun.
note: From French pistole, probably from German via Czech pist'ala, a pipe.
hints: Weapon in a holster.
A cowboy's sidearm.

definition: A cylinder that moves up and down inside an engine.
note: From French piston, from Italian pistone, 'a large pestle'. It is the heart of a petrol engine.
hints: The part driven by an explosion in a car engine.
A brass-instrument valve also has this name.

definition: A black sticky substance; also to throw, or the tone of a sound.
note: The tar sense is from Old English pic, from Latin pix. The throwing sense is a separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: What a baseball player throws.
How high or low a note sounds.
origin: Old English piċ, from Latin pix

definition: Short and full of meaning.
note: From pith plus -y. Pith is the spongy centre of a plant stem, and by extension the core of an idea.
hints: Describes a short, sharp remark.
A quip is this.
example: Welcomed her pithy comments.

definition: The smallest dot of a digital image.
note: A blend of 'pix', for pictures, and 'element'. A screen is built from millions of them.
hints: A tiny square on a screen.
A camera rating is counted in millions of them.
example: The greater the number of pixels per inch the greater the resolution.

definition: A small mischievous fairy.
note: The word is first recorded in the seventeenth century in the folklore of south-west England. Its origin is uncertain.
hints: A mythical creature with pointed ears.
Associated with Cornish folklore.

definition: A round flat bread baked with tomato and cheese.
note: Borrowed from Neapolitan, first recorded in Naples in 1590. It reached English in 1931.
hints: Often delivered in a box.
Naples is its famous home.
example: Want to go out for pizza tonight?

definition: A particular spot or position.
note: From Old English place and Old French place, both from Latin platea, 'broad street'. It can name a position, a home, or a rank.
hints: Where something is located.
What you take at the table.
origin: Old English plæċe, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα

definition: A deadly epidemic disease, or a pest infestation.
note: From Latin plaga, 'blow' or 'wound'.
hints: The Black Death.
Locusts in an Old Testament story.
origin: Old French plage, from Latin plāga

definition: Cloth with a pattern of crossing stripes.
note: From Scots plaid, of uncertain origin, and ultimately from Scottish Gaelic plaide, 'blanket'. In North America it names any tartan-like pattern.
hints: A pattern on a lumberjack shirt.
Tartan is a close cousin.

definition: Simple and without decoration; also a flat stretch of land.
note: From Old French plain, from Latin planus, 'flat'. Both senses come from the idea of something smooth and even.
hints: A white wall or an unseasoned bowl of rice has this look.
A great, flat grassland.
origin: Anglo-Norman pleyn, from Latin plānus; in English since the 17th century
example: Would you like a poppy bagel or a plain bagel?

definition: A braid of hair or straw.
note: From Old French pleit, from Latin plectere, 'to weave'. A pleat is a related form.
hints: A braid in a girl's hair.
Three strands woven together.

definition: Lying in a flat plane.
note: From Late Latin planarius, from Latin planus, 'flat'. Engineers use it of circuits and graphs.
hints: A graph is this if it can be drawn without crossing lines.
Flat, two-dimensional shapes.
origin: Late Latin plānārius, from Latin plānus

definition: A large body that orbits a star.
note: From Greek planetes, 'wanderer', since planets drift against the fixed stars.
hints: Mars or Venus.
Its Greek name meant a wanderer.
origin: Old French planete, from Ancient Greek πλανάω

definition: A long, flat piece of timber.
note: From Old Northern French planque, from Latin planca. It also names a sport exercise and a part of a political platform.
hints: A pirate victim walked off one.
A flat board used to build a deck.
origin: Old French planke, from Old Northern French planque

definition: A flat plate of metal or stone, usually inscribed, fixed to a wall or given as an award.
note: Borrowed straight from French, where it meant a plate or slab. The same word also names the sticky film that builds up on teeth.
hints: Something a landmark wears to say who once lived there.
A dentist wants you to scrape this off your teeth.
origin: French plaque, from Middle Dutch placken

definition: The fluid part of blood, or an ionised gas.
note: From Greek plasma, 'something molded'.
hints: What lightning is made of.
Fluid part of your blood.
origin: Late Latin plasma, from Ancient Greek πλάσμα

definition: Someone who plays a game or an instrument.
note: From play plus -er; Old English plegian was the verb.
hints: Member of a team.
Someone on the pitch or the stage.

definition: A public square in a town.
note: From Spanish plaza, from Latin platea, 'broad street'. It is a word for an open gathering space.
hints: Where people meet in a city centre.
A Spanish word for a town square.
origin: Spanish plaza, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα
example: Tourists gathered in the central plaza.

definition: To beg earnestly; or to enter a response in court.
note: From Old French plaidier, 'to bring a legal case'. A defendant pleads guilty or not guilty.
hints: What a child does for a treat.
A defendant makes one in court.
origin: Old French plaider, from Medieval Latin placitum
example: He pleaded with me not to leave the house.

definition: To make someone happy; also a polite word added to requests.
note: From Old French plaisir, from Latin placere, 'to be agreeable'.
hints: The magic word of good manners.
A polite request word.
origin: Old French plaise, from Latin placeō
example: Her presentation pleased the executives.

definition: A fold pressed into cloth.
note: From Middle English, a variant of plait. A kilt is full of them.
hints: A crease sewn into a skirt.
Folds in a kilt.

definition: Ordinary common people, often said with disdain by those who think themselves above them.
note: From Latin plebs, the common people of ancient Rome as opposed to the patrician nobles. Later also taken as the plural of 'pleb'.
hints: What a snob calls everyone outside his exclusive circle.
Ancient Rome split its citizens into these and patricians.

definition: A solemn promise.
note: From Old French plege, 'surety'.
hints: Oath of loyalty.
Promise to donate.
origin: Anglo-Norman plege, from Old French plege

definition: A large amount.
note: From Old French plente, from Latin plenitas, 'fullness'.
hints: More than needed.
More than you could possibly need.
example: We are lucky to live in a land of peace and plenty.

definition: A person who plies; also a tool, in the plural.
note: From ply plus -er. You are far more likely to see it as 'pliers', a gripping tool.
hints: Singular of a gripping tool's name.
You rarely see this form without an s.
example: My toolbox contains only pliers, a hammer, and a screwdriver.

definition: A difficult or unfortunate situation; also an old word for a solemn promise.
note: From two words that merged: one meaning danger, another a pledge, as in 'plight your troth'. It survives in both senses.
hints: What refugees and stranded travellers face.
An old betrothal phrase promised to pledge your troth in this way.
origin: Old English pliht, from Latin plicitum; in English since the 14th century
example: The woeful plight of homeless people.

definition: To pull sharply; also courage.
note: From Old English pluccian, 'to pull'. The sense of courage is figurative, as in 'having the pluck to try'.
hints: What you do to a guitar string.
Courage, as in having plenty of it.

definition: Exactly vertical; also a lead weight on a line.
note: From Old French plombe, from Latin plumbum, 'lead'. A plumber originally worked with lead pipes.
hints: A builder checks a wall is this.
Weight hanging from a string.
example: The tower of Pisa is far out of plumb.

definition: A large feather, or a rising column of smoke.
note: From Latin pluma, 'feather'. Smoke or water rising in a feathery shape is named after it.
hints: A feather on a hat.
What smoke rising from a chimney can form.

definition: Pleasantly rounded or chubby.
note: From Middle Dutch plomp. It was once also used to mean 'blunt', as in 'a plump refusal'.
hints: A cheek or a fruit might be this.
Round and well-fed.
origin: Middle Dutch plomp, from Middle Low German plump

definition: To dive or drop suddenly into something.
note: From Old French plongier, 'to throw into', from a Latin word for lead weight. Prices and divers both do it.
hints: What a diver does from a cliff.
What the stock market does in a crash.
origin: Anglo-Norman plungier, from Old French plongier
example: The stock market plunged.

definition: To drop or place with a dull sound.
note: Imitative of the sound. The noun is recorded earlier than the verb.
hints: A sound like a pebble landing in water.
How a heavy coin lands in a jar.

definition: A grammatical form meaning more than one.
note: From Latin pluralis, from plus, 'more'. Most English nouns add -s.
hints: What 'geese' is to 'goose'.
Most English nouns make this by adding -s.
origin: Old French plurel, from Latin plūrālis
example: The plural of 'cat' is 'cats', but the plural of 'child' is 'children'.

definition: Luxurious and soft; or a soft fabric.
note: From French peluche, 'fluff'. Toy bears made of it are called by the same word.
hints: A soft toy bear's fabric.
A velvet-like fabric, or very luxurious.

definition: To cook gently in simmering liquid, or to hunt illegally.
note: The cooking sense comes from Old French pocher, 'to put in a pocket', as egg white forms around the yolk. The hunting sense comes from a different root meaning to poke.
hints: An egg can be cooked this way.
Doing what a trespasser does after dark in someone's woods.
origin: Old French pocher, from Old French poche

definition: A small pouch sewn into clothing.
note: From Old North French poquet, 'little bag'.
hints: Keep coins in it.
Part of trousers.
origin: Anglo-Norman poket, from Old Northern French poquet

definition: A raised platform for a speaker, conductor or winner.
note: From Greek podion, 'little foot', from pous. Roman amphitheatres had a podium wall for VIP seats.
hints: What an Olympic medallist stands on.
Where a conductor stands before the orchestra.
origin: Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον

definition: An old word for poetry.
note: From Old French poesie, from Greek poiesis, 'a making'. It has a bookish, old-fashioned feel.
hints: A dusty word for verse.
What a bard composes.
origin: Middle French poesie, from Ancient Greek ποίησις

definition: Having to do with poetry, or having the beauty and feeling of it.
note: From Greek poietikos, 'creative', from poieo, 'to make'. A poet was literally a maker.
hints: Said of a sunset described in lovely, rhythmic words.
'Justice' is often said to be this when it is neatly ironic.
origin: Middle French poetique, from Ancient Greek ποιητικός
example: Iambics are one form of poetic meter.

definition: Writing arranged in lines with rhythm or imagery.
note: From Greek poiesis, 'making', from poiein, 'to make'.
hints: Verse written by poets.
Sonnets and haiku are examples.
origin: Old French pöeterie, from Ancient Greek ποιητής

definition: A sharp end; also a purpose or a score.
note: From Old French point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick'. It covers a tip, a dot, a score and the main idea.
hints: The sharp end of a pencil.
The idea behind an argument.
origin: Old French point m, from Latin pūncta f; in English since the 14th century
example: He stuck the point of the knife into a tree.

definition: Having a sharp tip or tips.
note: From point plus -y. It is informal for pointed.
hints: What a witch's hat is.
Describes the end of a sharpened pencil.

definition: Calm balance and self-assurance.
note: From Old French pois, 'weight'. Balanced weight became balanced bearing.
hints: A graceful and steady manner.
What a ballerina has on one foot.
origin: Anglo-Norman pois, from Middle French pois

definition: Calm and balanced; or ready to act at any moment.
note: From Old French peser, 'to weigh', so poised means weighed in balance. Dancers and ambitious politicians are both described this way.
hints: A cat before a pounce is this, hovering on the edge of action.
A calm, collected person in a tense interview.

definition: A substance that can kill or harm.
note: From Old French poison, from Latin potio, 'a drink', the same root as potion.
hints: What a snake's venom may contain.
Snow White's apple held it.
origin: Old French poison, from Latin pōtiōnem

definition: A card game of betting and bluffing; also an iron rod.
note: The card game is American, of uncertain origin. The tool for stirring a fire is a separate word, from poke.
hints: A game where you hold your cards close.
What you stir the fireplace with.

definition: Cramped and small, or very slow.
note: Derived from poke plus -y.
hints: Describes a tiny room or a slow driver.
Cramped rather than roomy.
example: Passed a series of poky little one-horse towns.

definition: Relating to the Earth's poles.
note: From Latin polus, from Greek polos, 'pivot'. Bears and ice caps are described with it.
hints: A bear that lives in the Arctic.
A cold region at the top of the globe.
example: A polar air mass.

definition: The force that keeps order and enforces the law.
note: From French police, from Greek politeia, 'government of a city'. It shares its root with politics.
hints: Officers on patrol.
Shares a root with politics.
origin: Middle French police, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία; in English since the 18th century

definition: A course of action chosen by a government or company; also an insurance contract.
note: From Old French policie, from Greek politeia, 'government'.
hints: A set of rules, or an insurance contract.
Insurance document or government plan.
origin: Old French policie, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία; in English since the 15th century
example: The Communist Party has a policy of returning power to the workers.

definition: A disease that can cause paralysis.
note: Short for poliomyelitis, from Greek polios, 'grey', and myelos, 'marrow'. A vaccine nearly wiped it out in the 1950s.
hints: A disease once feared worldwide.
A disease defeated by a vaccine.
example: Having autism is much better than dying of polio or measles.

definition: A city-state of ancient Greece.
note: Greek for 'city'. Politics and police both grew from it.
hints: Athens or Sparta, for example.
Root of politics and police.

definition: To make shiny by rubbing; or a substance for doing so.
note: From Old French polir, from Latin polire.
hints: Shine your shoes.
Applied to nails.
example: He polished up the chrome until it gleamed.

definition: Showing good manners.
note: From Latin politus, 'polished'.
hints: Saying please and thank you.
Well mannered.
example: It's not polite to use a mobile phone in a restaurant.

definition: A lively dance from Bohemia.
note: From Czech, probably from pulka, 'half', for the half-step. It spread across Europe in the nineteenth century.
hints: Spotted pattern as well as a dance.
Dots, in the name of a pattern.

definition: The fine powder that flowers produce for reproduction.
note: From Latin pollen, 'fine flour'. Linnaeus adopted it for plants. It causes hay fever.
hints: A sneeze-making dust in spring.
What a bee carries from flower to flower.

definition: A small growth; or a tubelike sea creature.
note: From Greek polypous, 'many-footed'. Coral is made of colonies of these.
hints: A tiny animal that builds a reef.
A word for a growth with many feet, in Greek.
origin: Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους

definition: To think about something carefully.
note: From Latin ponderare, 'to weigh', from pondus, 'weight'. To ponder is to weigh an idea in your mind.
hints: Rodin's Thinker sits in this pose.
A chess player might do it over a tricky move.
origin: Old French ponderer, from Latin ponderāre

definition: A pet dog.
note: Its origin is uncertain. It has been used as a friendly term for a dog since the early twentieth century.
hints: A friendly name for a dog.
What you walk each evening.

definition: In a bad way, or unwell.
note: From poor plus -ly.
hints: Done in a bad or weak way.
British word for sick.

definition: A tall, fast-growing tree, often planted in rows.
note: From Old French poplier, from Latin populus, the Latin name of the tree.
hints: Lines French country roads.
Its leaves flutter in the slightest breeze.
origin: Anglo-Norman popler, from Old French poplier

definition: A father, in informal speech.
note: An alteration of papa.
hints: A folksy word for dad.
Used affectionately for a father.

definition: A bright red flower; also its colour.
note: From Old English popig, from Latin papaver. Red ones are worn on Remembrance Day.
hints: A red flower worn in November.
Its seeds go on a bagel.
origin: Old English popiġ, from Latin papāver

definition: A covered entrance or veranda at the front of a house.
note: From Old French porche, from Latin porticus, 'portico'. It is where you may sit on a swing.
hints: Where a rocking chair sits.
The covered part by a front door.
example: He sat on his porch, waiting for his friend to come over.

definition: Fat, or like pork.
note: From pork plus -y, and pork itself comes from Latin porcus, 'pig'.
hints: Piggish in appearance.
Slang for pork, or something fat.

definition: Full of tiny holes that let liquid or air pass through.
note: From Latin porus, 'opening'. A sponge is porous; a leaky border is metaphorically so too.
hints: A sponge or limestone is this.
A leaky security barrier is also called this.
origin: Old French poros, from Latin porus
