example: Sponges are porous so they can filter water while trapping food.

definition: A grand entrance, or an internet gateway.
note: From Medieval Latin portale, from Latin porta, 'gate'.
hints: A grand doorway or entrance.
A website acting as a gateway.
origin: Old French portal, from Medieval Latin portāle
example: The portals of the cathedral.

definition: A person who carries luggage, or a dark beer; also a doorkeeper.
note: From Latin portare, 'to carry'.
hints: Carries your bags at a hotel.
A dark ale named after workers.
example: By the time I reached the train station I was exhausted, but fortunately there was a porter waiting.

definition: A hard puzzle; or someone who pretends.
note: From pose plus -er. It also means a person who acts in a false way to impress.
hints: A brain-teaser.
Someone who acts like what they are not.

definition: To put forward as a basis for argument.
note: From Latin positus, 'placed'. Philosophers posit theories before testing them.
hints: To suggest an idea for debate.
What a scientist does with a hypothesis.

definition: A group summoned to chase a criminal.
note: Short for Latin posse comitatus, 'the power of the county'. It is now a casual word for a group of friends.
hints: In old westerns, a sheriff gathers one.
A band of friends, in slang.
example: The sheriff gathered the posse together.

definition: Relating to the mail; or slang for crazy.
note: From post plus -al.
hints: A service that delivers letters.
What a worker is when furious, in slang.
example: He's a postal worker, and has been in the postal industry for decades.

definition: A large printed sheet for display.
note: From post plus -er, as originally pasted on posts.
hints: Hangs on a bedroom wall.
Advertises a film.

definition: An edible tuber.
note: From Spanish patata, from Taino batata, a sweet potato.
hints: Chips are made from it.
A tuber grown underground.

definition: Powerful.
note: From Latin potens, 'being able'.
hints: A strong drink.
Strongly effective.

definition: A drink with medicinal, magical or poisonous effects.
note: From Latin potio, 'a drink'. It is common in fairy tales and fantasy.
hints: A witch stirs it in a cauldron.
Harry Potter studies making them in Snape's class.
origin: Old French pocion, from Latin pōtiō
example: He hoped to win the princess's heart by mixing the love potion the witch gave him into her drink.

definition: A person who makes pottery; or to wander about aimlessly.
note: From Old English pottere, one who makes pots.
hints: Works at a wheel with clay.
Idle around the garden.

definition: A small bowl for toilet training; or silly.
note: From pot plus -y. In British English it also means mad or crazy.
hints: What a toddler learns to use.
British slang for crazy.

definition: A small bag; or a kangaroo's pocket.
note: From Old French pouche, from a Frankish word. Marsupials carry their young in one.
hints: Where a kangaroo carries its baby.
A small bag on a belt.
origin: Old Northern French pouche, from Old French poche

definition: A unit of weight or of British money; also to hit repeatedly.
note: From Old English pund, from Latin pondo, 'weight'. The hitting sense is a separate word.
hints: Sterling money unit.
What a hammer does to a nail.
origin: Old English pund, from Latin pondō

definition: Tending to pout.
note: Built from pout plus -y. Pout is a verb for pushing out the lips in sulkiness.
hints: How a sulking child's lips look.
Sticking out the lower lip.

definition: Fine, dry particles.
note: From Old French poudre, from Latin pulvis, 'dust'.
hints: Talc, flour or ground spice.
What a cannon needed, in gun form.
origin: Old French poudre, from Latin pulvis

definition: The ability to do something, or control over others.
note: From Old French povoir, from Latin potis, 'able'. It covers strength, authority, and electricity.
hints: What a strong engine produces.
What a ruler holds over a country.
origin: Old French poeir, from Latin posse

definition: To express approval or worship.
note: From Old French preisier, 'to value'.
hints: Compliment someone.
What a choir might offer in church.
origin: Old French proisier, from Late Latin pretiō
example: The parents praised their children for their academic performance.

definition: A mischievous trick played for fun.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may be linked to an old verb meaning to show off or dress up. 1 April is the day it is most expected.
hints: A whoopee cushion on a chair.
A harmless trick on April Fools' Day.
example: He pulled a gruesome prank on his sister.

definition: A large edible shellfish like a shrimp.
note: First recorded in the early fifteenth century in several spellings. It has no clear relatives in other languages.
hints: Often served in a cocktail.
A seafood close to a shrimp.

definition: A spoken request or thanks to a god.
note: From Old French preiere, from Latin precari, 'to ask earnestly'.
hints: Said at bedtime.
Spoken to a deity.
origin: Old French preiere, from Latin precem

definition: To deliver a sermon, or to lecture others on how they should behave.
note: From Latin praedicare, 'to proclaim'. Preaching to the choir means lecturing people who already agree.
hints: A pulpit is where it happens.
Nobody likes being on the receiving end of this from a know-it-all.
example: The minister is not preaching this Sunday.

definition: To tidy feathers, or to admire yourself.
note: From Middle English, from an old word for a pin. Birds preen to keep their feathers neat, and people preen to look good.
hints: A bird does it to its feathers.
What a vain person does before a mirror.

definition: To like one thing more than another.
note: From Latin praeferre, 'to carry before'.
hints: Choose one over the other.
Would rather have this one.
origin: Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō; in English since the 14th century
example: I prefer tea to coffee.

definition: A group of letters added to the start of a word to change its meaning; also an initial code number.
note: From Latin praefixum, 'fixed in front'.
hints: 'Un-' and 'pre-' are examples.
The 'tele' that begins telephone and television.
origin: Late Latin praefīxum, from Latin praefīxus

definition: To push firmly; also newspapers or a printing machine.
note: From Old French presser, from Latin pressare, 'to press'. The newspapers sense comes from the printing press.
hints: What you do to a doorbell.
A collective word for journalists.

definition: Pleasing to look at.
note: From Old English prættig, which once meant crafty. It slowly shifted from cunning to charming.
hints: Attractive, but not stunning.
Its oldest sense meant crafty.
origin: Old English prættiġ; in English since the 15th century

definition: The cost of something.
note: From Old French pris, from Latin pretium, 'worth'. Price and prize were once the same word.
hints: What a tag shows.
What a shopper checks before buying.
origin: Old French pris, from Latin pretium
example: They say that every politician has a price.

definition: Expensive.
note: From price plus -y, a casual word from the 1930s.
hints: How you describe a restaurant bill that stings.
Said when a menu makes you wince.
example: I think that hotel is going to be a little pricey for you.

definition: A feeling of satisfaction in your own worth; also a group of lions.
note: From Old English pryde, from an older word for 'proud'. A group of lions is called a pride, a poetic use.
hints: A feeling after a big win.
A group of lions.
example: He swelled with pride as he held the trophy. His family watched with pride from the bleachers.

definition: A religious figure who leads worship.
note: From Old English preost, from Greek presbyteros, 'elder'.
hints: Leads worship at a church altar.
Serves in a church.
origin: Old English prēost, from Old French prestre
example: The priest at the Catholic church heard his confession.

definition: First; chief.
note: From Italian and Latin prima, 'first'. It is used in 'prima donna' and 'prima facie'.
hints: A word meaning first in a stage title.
A Latin word for first, in 'facie' and 'donna'.

definition: Relating to the earliest, most basic instincts.
note: From Latin primus, 'first'. A primal scream expresses raw feeling.
hints: A fear of the dark is an instinct of this kind.
What a therapist's scream is named after.
example: Primal eras before the appearance of life on earth.

definition: Best in quality; or first in importance.
note: From Latin primus, 'first'. A prime number has only itself and one as factors.
hints: A number such as seven, in maths.
The highest quality, as of beef.
origin: Old French prime, from Latin prīmus
example: Our manhood's prime vigor.

definition: A first book on a subject; also a base coat of paint.
note: From Medieval Latin primarius, 'first'. A prayer book for beginners was the original sense.
hints: A painter applies it before the colour goes on.
A short introduction to a topic.

definition: First-rate; excellent.
note: Borrowed from Italian primo, 'first'. It is a doublet of prime.
hints: Slang for top quality.
An Italian word for 'first'.

definition: A son of a king, or a ruler.
note: From Latin princeps, 'first man'.
hints: Son of a monarch.
Machiavelli wrote a book of advice for one.
origin: Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps; in English since the 14th century
example: The crown prince is the one who is to succeed to the throne.

definition: To mark letters onto paper; or a mark left behind.
note: From Middle English prenten, shortened from emprinten, 'to imprint'. It names text, pictures and a fingerprint.
hints: What a machine does with ink.
A mark left by a thumb.

definition: A misfolded protein that can cause brain diseases.
note: Coined from the letters of proteinaceous infectious particle.
hints: The cause of mad cow disease.
An infectious protein, not a virus.
example: I advise you not to eat the meat, it may have prions still.

definition: Coming before in time; also a monastery official.
note: From Latin prior, 'earlier'. In law it describes a previous conviction.
hints: Earlier in time, as in a previous commitment.
A head of a small monastery.
example: His prior residence was smaller than his current one.

definition: A religious house led by a prior or prioress.
note: From Anglo-Norman priorie. It ranks below an abbey.
hints: Smaller than an abbey.
Many English ruins date from Henry VIII's dissolution of these.

definition: A glass shape that splits light into colours.
note: From Greek prisma, 'something sawn off'. Newton used glass ones to show light breaking into a spectrum.
hints: Used to make a rainbow of light.
A shape with triangular ends.
origin: Late Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρίσμᾰ

definition: A place where criminals are locked up.
note: From Old French prisun, from Latin prensio, 'a seizing'.
hints: Where convicts serve sentences.
A jail, by another name.
origin: Old English prisūn, from Latin prehensiōnem
example: The cold stone walls of the prison had stood for over a century.

definition: Sharing in secret knowledge; also an outhouse.
note: From Old French prive, 'private'. 'Privy to' means let in on a secret.
hints: Told in confidence, you are said to be this to it.
A word for an old outdoor toilet.
origin: Old French privé, from Latin prīvātus; in English since the late 14th century
example: Privy to the details of the conspiracy.

definition: To explore or investigate; or a tool or craft for exploring.
note: From Latin probare, 'to test'. It names a doctor's instrument and a spacecraft.
hints: What space agencies send to far planets.
A journalist might do it into a scandal.

definition: Gain after costs are paid.
note: From Latin profectus, 'progress'.
hints: Money left over.
What a business hopes to make.

definition: A short for promotion; an advert for something.
note: A clipping of promotion. A trailer or a discount can be called one.
hints: A trailer for an upcoming film.
An advert or discount.

definition: Done without delay, or a cue.
note: From Latin promptus, 'brought forth'.
hints: On time and ready.
Reminder for an actor.
origin: Middle French prompt, from Latin prōmptus
example: He was very prompt at getting a new job.

definition: Lying face down; or likely to suffer something.
note: From Latin pronus, 'bent forward'. People are prone to colds, or lie prone on the ground.
hints: Lying face down on the floor.
Likely to suffer something, as in 'accident-___'.

definition: A pointed tip of a fork.
note: From Middle English pronge. A trident has three.
hints: One tip on a fork.
A tooth of a pitchfork.

definition: Evidence that shows something is true.
note: From Old French prove, from Latin probare, 'to test'. It is also the strength of alcohol.
hints: What a lawyer must show a court.
What a maths exercise ends with.
origin: Old French prove, from Latin probō

definition: To drive or push something forward.
note: From Latin propellere, from pro-, 'forward', and pellere, 'to push'.
hints: A boat's engine turns a screw to do it.
What a rocket's burning fuel does.
example: Steam propels this ship.

definition: Correct or suitable.
note: From Latin proprius, 'one's own'.
hints: Done the right way.
Fit for the occasion.

definition: A tiny positively charged particle found in an atom's nucleus.
note: From Greek protos, 'first'. The name was chosen by Rutherford for the nucleus of the simplest atom, hydrogen.
hints: Together with neutrons it forms the nucleus of every atom.
The number of them in an atom sets which element it is.
example: Gluons glue quarks together to form particles such as protons.

definition: Feeling deep satisfaction in yourself or others.
note: From Old English prud, 'proud' or 'haughty'. The word moved from vanity towards healthy satisfaction.
hints: How a parent feels at a graduation.
Said of someone pleased with an achievement.
example: Proud to serve his country.

definition: To show that something is true.
note: From Old English profian and Old French prover, from Latin probare, 'to test'. It once meant to try or test something.
hints: What evidence does to a claim.
Show that a claim is correct.
origin: Old English prōfian, from Latin probō
example: I will prove that my method is more effective than yours.

definition: Shown to be true or reliable.
note: A past participle of prove, common in Scots.
hints: Demonstrated beyond doubt.
As in a track record.
origin: Late Latin probō, from Latin probus

definition: To move quietly in search of prey.
note: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin. Cats and burglars prowl.
hints: What a tiger does at night.
A burglar might do it around a house.
example: Watch the lioness prowling in the shrubbery for zebras.

definition: A person or thing authorised to stand in for another.
note: From Middle English, a contraction of procuracie, from Latin procuratio, 'management'. In computing it relays web traffic.
hints: One who votes in your place.
A server that relays web traffic.

definition: A dried plum; also to cut back a plant.
note: The fruit is from Old French prune, from Latin prunum. The cutting verb is separate, from Old French proignier.
hints: A wrinkled dried fruit.
What a gardener does to a rose bush.
origin: Old French prune, from Ancient Greek προῦνον

definition: A sacred song or poem of praise.
note: From Old English psealm, from Greek psalmos, 'song sung to a harp'. The Bible contains 150 of them.
hints: A song in the Bible.
Sung by choirs in church.
origin: Old English psealm, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός

definition: Fake or pretending to be something it is not; also a pretentious person.
note: From the Greek prefix pseudo-, 'false', which comes from pseudes, 'lying'. Used on its own as a put-down.
hints: A put-down for someone faking cleverness.
Prefixed to 'science' or 'nym' to mean not genuine.

definition: To mentally prepare; or to trick.
note: A clipping of psychology or psychiatry. 'Psych up' means to prepare oneself mentally.
hints: What a team does before a big match.
A word you shout when fooling someone.

definition: A person's mind or deepest inner self.
note: From Greek psyche, 'soul' or 'breath'. In myth, Psyche was a mortal woman who married the god Eros.
hints: Psychologists study the human one.
The Greek word that began words like psychology.
origin: Latin psychē, from Ancient Greek ψυχή

definition: A crazy or dangerous person, in slang.
note: Shortened from psychopath.
hints: A Hitchcock film title.
A deranged person in a thriller.
example: She complained that he was a psycho for driving at such a high speed in heavy traffic.

definition: Of the lower front part of the pelvis.
note: From pubes, Latin for the groin or private parts.
hints: Relating to a pelvic bone.
A word for part of the pelvis.
example: Would it bother you if your boyfriend had pubic hair?

definition: Open to everyone, or relating to the people at large.
note: From Latin publicus, which is related to populus, 'people'.
hints: Not private.
A park or a library is this.
origin: Anglo-Norman public, from Old French public; in English since the 14th century
example: Performers and members of royal families are public figures.

definition: A small pool of water on the ground.
note: From Middle English podel, a diminutive of Old English pudd, 'ditch'. Children love to jump in them.
hints: Left on the pavement after rain.
Splashed in by children in wellies.
origin: Old English pudd; in English since the 14th century
example: There were puddles of muddy water in the road after the rain.

definition: Short and plump.
note: From pudge, a word of uncertain origin, plus -y. It is often used affectionately for children's fingers.
hints: A chubby baby's hands.
Round and soft.
example: The pudgy child had a difficult time running the mile.

definition: A town or village in Spanish-speaking regions; also a Native American village of stacked adobe houses.
note: Borrowed from Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus. It is a doublet of people.
hints: A cluster of sun-baked clay homes in New Mexico.
Taos is a famous example in the American Southwest.
origin: Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus; in English since the 19th century

definition: Swollen or full, as if inflated.
note: From puff plus -y. It describes eyes after crying or a jacket full of down.
hints: What eyes look like after crying.
A jacket filled with down.

definition: The raised stand in a church from which a preacher speaks.
note: From Latin pulpitum, 'platform'.
hints: A preacher climbs a few steps to reach it.
Where a Sunday sermon is delivered from, high above the pews.
origin: Old French pulpite, from Latin pulpitum
example: From the pulpit, he preached about love and forgiveness.

definition: Soft and fleshy; or in a cheap sensational style.
note: From pulp plus -y. Pulp is the soft inside of fruit, and cheap magazines were once printed on pulp paper.
hints: Orange juice with bits.
Like the cheap fiction of old magazines.

definition: A blow with the fist; also a fruity drink.
note: The blow is from Old French ponchonner, 'to punch'. The drink is a separate word, likely from Hindi.
hints: A boxer throws one.
A bowl at a party with fruit juice.
origin: Old French ponchonner, from Latin punctio

definition: A person who gives expert opinions, especially in the media.
note: From Hindi pandit, a learned man, from Sanskrit pandita. In English it came to mean a commentator.
hints: Pops up on news panels after an election.
Sports ones offer opinions from the studio.
origin: Hindi पंडित, from Sanskrit पण्डित; in English since the 19th century
example: Pundits consider him one of the best passers in the league.

definition: To penalise for wrongdoing.
note: From Latin punire, from poena, 'penalty'.
hints: Detention is one.
Give a penalty.
example: That is a criminal offense, and you will surely be punished!

definition: A person who places a bet, or in British slang any paying customer.
note: From punt plus -er. The betting sense comes from punt, 'to gamble'; the boat and football senses are separate.
hints: Studies the racecard before putting money on a horse.
In British slang, the ordinary customer of any business.

definition: Relating to the stage between larva and adult insect.
note: From pupa plus -al. Pupa is Latin for 'girl' or 'doll'.
hints: A stage in a butterfly's life.
The chrysalis phase.

definition: A student; also the dark centre of the eye.
note: From Latin pupillus, 'orphan' or 'ward'. The eye sense is from Latin pupilla, 'little doll', after the tiny reflection seen in it.
hints: A student in a class.
The black centre in the middle of the iris.

definition: A model moved by hand or strings.
note: From Old French poupette, 'little doll'.
hints: Kermit is one.
Pulled on strings.
origin: Middle French poupette, from Latin pupa

definition: A young dog.
note: From earlier puppie, once a woman's pet dog, of uncertain origin. It was probably from French poupee, 'doll'.
hints: A young dog that chews your shoes.
Eight weeks old and full of play.

definition: Food blended to a smooth paste.
note: Borrowed from French puree. Baby food is often this.
hints: A smooth blend of cooked vegetables.
What a blender makes of soup.
example: Tomato sauce is generally a puree.

definition: Entirely, or only.
note: From pure plus -ly.
hints: Without any mixture.
Solely, simply.
origin: Middle English purely; in English since the 14th century
example: I wish to resign from my work for purely personal reasons.

definition: To rid of something unwanted.
note: From Old French purgier, from Latin purgare, 'to make pure'. It is used for cleansing and for removing members of a group.
hints: To clear out what is unwanted.
A political clearing out of rivals.
origin: Old French purgier, from Latin pūrgō
example: After the process, the machine purges the chamber before venting it to remove toxic gases.

definition: To remove impurities from something.
note: From Old French purifier, from Latin purus, 'clean'.
hints: What a filter does to water.
Rituals do it to the soul.
origin: Old French purifier, from Latin pūrificō

definition: The state of being free from anything that spoils or dilutes.
note: From Latin puritas, from purus, 'clean'. Used of gold, water, and moral character alike.
hints: What a jeweller measures in karats.
A quality claimed by spring water and by saints.
origin: Old French purete, from Latin puritas
example: The purity of the water was tested in a laboratory.

definition: A colour made from red and blue.
note: From Old English purpul, from Greek porphyra, the shellfish dye.
hints: Colour of royalty.
Violet-like shade.
origin: Old English purpul, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα

definition: A small bag for money; or to tighten the lips.
note: From Old English purs, from Latin bursa, 'bag'. Lips are said to be pursed when pressed tight.
hints: A handbag or coin holder.
What lips do when puckered.

definition: To chase, or to follow a goal.
note: From Old French poursuivre, from Latin prosequi, 'to follow forward'.
hints: Run after something in order to catch it.
Seek a career or a dream.
origin: Anglo-Norman pursure, from Latin prōsequor; in English since the 14th century

definition: Aggressively assertive.
note: From push plus -y. A pushy salesperson does not take no for an answer.
hints: A salesman who will not accept refusal.
A person who shoves forward to get ahead.
example: A pushful insurance agent.

definition: A soft paste that sets hard, used to fix window glass.
note: From French potee, 'potful', originally a polishing powder. It stays soft until it dries.
hints: What holds a pane in its frame.
Clay-like stuff for sealing cracks.

definition: A problem or toy that tests your skill.
note: Origin uncertain; it appears in the 1500s.
hints: A jigsaw is an example.
Something that confuses you.

definition: A very small person or animal; also a legendary race of tiny people.
note: From Greek pygme, 'a fist', as a measure of length, so the pygmies were fist-high. The word is now considered offensive when used for people.
hints: A dwarf hippo is called by this name.
From a Greek word for a fist-length.
origin: Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος

definition: A tall steel tower holding up electricity cables.
note: From Greek pylon, 'gateway'. It first named the entrance towers of Egyptian temples.
hints: Tall steel frame in a field.
Holds up the power lines across hills.

definition: Heat-resistant glass used for cookware and labs.
note: Originally a trademark, now widely used for any borosilicate glass.
hints: Baking dish that survives the oven.
Brand name that became everyday word.

definition: A large non-venomous snake; also a programming language.
note: From Greek Python, a serpent slain by Apollo. The language was named after a comedy group.
hints: Squeezes its prey.
A popular coding language.
origin: Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων

definition: The cry of a duck; or a fake doctor.
note: Imitative of the duck's call. The fraud sense is short for quacksalver, someone who boasts of remedies.
hints: What a duck says.
A fraudulent healer.

definition: To shrink back in fear; also a small game bird.
note: The verb is from Middle Dutch queilen. The bird is a separate word, from Old French quaille.
hints: What a coward might do before a bully.
A small game bird with speckled feathers.
origin: Middle Dutch queilen; in English since the 15th century

definition: Charmingly old-fashioned.
note: From Old French cointe, 'clever' or 'pretty', from Latin cognitus. It once meant skilled or cunning before it came to mean pleasingly odd.
hints: A village with thatched cottages.
Teashops on a cobbled lane.
origin: Anglo-Norman cointe, from Latin cognitus; in English since the 18th century
example: Houses with quaint thatched roofs.

definition: A financial analyst who uses mathematical models.
note: Short for quantitative analyst.
hints: Wall Street number cruncher.
Short for the type of analyst who builds models.

definition: A tiny particle that makes up protons.
note: Coined in 1963 by physicist Murray Gell-Mann, apparently an arbitrary word. It is also a fresh cheese in German.
hints: A tiny part of a proton.
Up and down are two flavours.
example: Quarks have not been observed directly but theoretical predictions based on their existence have been confirmed experimentally.

definition: A place where stone is dug; also an animal being hunted.
note: The pit sense comes from Medieval Latin quarreria, a place where stones are squared. The prey sense is a separate word from Old French, meaning the parts of a hunted animal fed to hounds.
hints: A deep pit where limestone is dug out.
What a hunter pursues, for another sense of the word.
origin: Medieval Latin quarreria, from Latin quadrō
example: A British term for `quarry' is `stone pit'.

definition: A quarter of a gallon.
note: From Old French quarte, from Latin quartus, 'fourth'. It equals two pints.
hints: Two pints of milk.
A fourth of a gallon.
origin: Old French quarte, from Latin quartus

definition: A hard crystalline mineral.
note: From German Quarz, of unclear origin.
hints: Clear stone in watches.
A common crystal.

definition: To put an end to; to annul.
note: From Old French quasser, from Latin quassare, 'to shake'. Courts quash verdicts and rebels are quashed.
hints: What a judge does to a conviction.
To crush a rebellion.
origin: Old French quasser, from Latin quatiō
example: The government quashes any attempt of an uprising.

definition: Seemingly; almost but not quite.
note: Latin for 'as if'. It is used as a prefix, as in 'quasi-official'.
hints: A Latin word meaning 'as if'.
Used as a prefix, as in '-official'.
example: Putin's passport was found on the quasi drone attack scene.

definition: A female monarch, or the wife of a king.
note: From Old English cwen, 'woman' or 'wife'. It is also a chess piece and a card.
hints: Wears a crown.
The strongest piece on a chessboard.

definition: Strange or odd; also an inclusive term for people who are not heterosexual or cisgender.
note: From a word possibly of German origin that first meant strange. It was once an insult but has been reclaimed by many.
hints: Old word for peculiar, now also an identity.
Strange, in older use.

definition: To calm or put down.
note: From Old English cwellan, 'to kill'. It now means to suppress, as of riots or fears.
hints: What police do to a riot.
To calm fears.
origin: Old English cwellan; in English since the 10th century

definition: A question.
note: From Latin quaere, 'ask'. It is a word for a database request.
hints: Typed into a search box.
A question put to a database.
example: There was a question about my training.

definition: A long search for something.
note: From Old French queste, from Latin quaerere, 'to seek'. Knights went on one for the Holy Grail.
hints: What knights set out on.
A game mission with a reward.

definition: A line of people waiting.
note: From Old French cue, 'tail', from Latin cauda. British people are famed for joining one.
hints: What people form at a bus stop.
A British word for a line.
origin: Anglo-Norman queue, from Latin cauda; in English since the 19th century

definition: Fast; taking little time.
note: From Old English cwic, which meant 'alive'. The old sense survives in 'the quick and the dead' and in 'quicksand'.
hints: A fox in the famous typing sentence is this and brown.
Once meant 'alive' in Old English.

definition: Making little or no noise.
note: From Old French quiet, from Latin quietus, 'at rest'. It is related to the word quit.
hints: What a library asks for.
What a room is when everyone is silent.
origin: Old French quiet, from Latin quiētus
example: I can't hear the music; it is too quiet.

definition: A large feather, or a pen made from one.
note: First recorded in the early fifteenth century for a reed fragment and a feather shaft. Porcupines also have these sharp spines.
hints: A pen dipped in ink, long ago.
A spine on a porcupine.

definition: A padded bed covering stitched in layers.
note: From Old French cuilte, from Latin culcita, 'mattress'. Patchwork ones are sewn from scraps.
hints: A patchwork bed covering.
Grandma may have sewn one.
origin: Anglo-Norman quilte, from Old French coilte
example: My grandmother is going to sew a quilt.

definition: A peculiar habit or twist of character.
note: First recorded in the 1540s, of uncertain origin. It is possibly from an old Norse word for a bend or angle.
hints: A small oddity of someone's character.
A habit that makes a person unique.

definition: Charmingly odd or unconventional.
note: From quirk plus -y. A quirk was a sudden twist or oddity in behaviour.
hints: A word for an indie film's offbeat heroine.
What describes a person with unusual habits.
example: I'm shy at first, but once I trust you I become a quirky goofball.

definition: Fairly, or completely.
note: From Middle English quite, from Old French quite, 'free' or 'clear', from Latin quietus. It once meant 'completely'.
hints: A word that can mean fairly or entirely.
As in 'it's ___ cold'.
origin: Anglo-Norman quite; in English since the 14th century

definition: The minimum number of members needed for a meeting to make decisions.
note: From Latin quorum, 'of whom', from the wording of old commissions naming those who had to be present.
hints: Without enough people, the vote cannot go ahead.
A committee fails to reach it when too many are absent.
example: We can discuss the issue tonight but cannot vote until we have a quorum.

definition: An old word meaning 'said'.
note: From Old English cwæth, the past tense of cwethan, 'to say'. The raven in Poe's poem is famously 'quoth' nevermore.
hints: An old past tense of say.
Poe's raven did it.

definition: A Jewish teacher and religious leader.
note: From Hebrew, meaning 'my master', and later passed into Greek and Latin. It was a title of respect for scholars.
hints: Leads a synagogue.
A title meaning 'my master' in Hebrew.
origin: Ecclesiastical Latin rabbi, from Hebrew רַבִּי

definition: A small mammal with long ears.
note: From Middle English rabet, probably from Old French.
hints: Lives in a burrow.
Pulled from a magician's hat.
origin: Latin rabettus, from West Flemish robbe
example: The pioneers survived by eating the small game they could get: rabbits, squirrels and occasionally a raccoon.

definition: Infected with rabies; or fanatical.
note: From Latin rabidus, 'raging', from rabies. It is often used of fierce supporters.
hints: How a mad dog might be described.
Fanatical, as in a very eager fan.

definition: A deadly viral disease of mammals, spread by bites.
note: Borrowed directly from Latin rabies, 'rage, madness'. It is a doublet of rage.
hints: Pasteur is famous for the vaccine against it.
Foaming at the mouth is a classic symptom in a dog.
example: A stray dog bit me on the street and gave me rabies.

definition: Someone or something that takes part in races.
note: Built from race plus -er. Race itself came from Old Norse ras, 'a running'.
hints: Drives a fast car on a track.
What a runner is in a sprint.

definition: Relating to race.
note: From race plus -al.
hints: Concerning groups of people.
A discrimination based on it is illegal.

definition: Prejudice against people because of their race.
note: From race plus -ism.
hints: Discrimination by ethnicity.
Belief that some groups are inferior.

definition: A person who believes some races are better than others, or showing such bias.
note: From race plus -ist.
hints: Someone who discriminates by race.
Bigotry of this kind is condemned under many laws.

definition: A bat with strings for tennis; also a loud noise or a dishonest scheme.
note: From Old French rachette, perhaps from Arabic for 'palm of the hand'. The noise and fraud senses are separate words.
hints: Strung and swung at Wimbledon.
Neighbours' loud party makes a terrible one.
example: He bought a new tennis racket two days ago.

definition: A system that finds objects by bouncing radio waves off them.
note: An acronym for 'radio detection and ranging'. It was developed in the 1930s and 1940s.
hints: Used by air traffic controllers.
Something that is 'under' it goes unnoticed.

definition: Arranged like rays spreading from a centre; also a type of tyre.
note: From Latin radius, 'ray' or 'spoke'. Most cars ride on radial tyres.
hints: Lines like spokes spreading from a hub.
The kind of tyre most cars have.
origin: Medieval Latin radiālis, from Latin radius
example: The spokes on most modern bicycle wheels are tangential to the hub rather than radial.

definition: A device or system that broadcasts sound by waves.
note: Short for radiotelegraphy, with radio- from Latin radius, 'ray'. It carries music and talk.
hints: Plays music in the car.
A device with a tuning dial.

definition: A line from the centre of a circle to its edge, or a bone in the forearm.
note: Latin for 'ray' or 'spoke of a wheel'.
hints: Half the diameter.
A bone in your arm.
example: Fatima claims to have visited all the bars within a five-mile radius of her Manhattan apartment.

definition: A radioactive gas given off by rocks.
note: From radium, since it comes from the decay of that element. It can build up in basements.
hints: A gas that seeps into basements.
A colourless radioactive gas.
example: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are noble gases.

definition: A fundraising draw where ticket holders can win prizes.
note: From Old French rafle, a dice game, also 'plundering', from a verb 'to snatch'.
hints: Tickets are pulled from a bucket at a school fair.
A number called out by a person on a stage wins a hamper.
example: He entered a raffle to win a lifetime supply of toothpaste, but he did not win.

definition: A person who makes a sudden attack to steal.
note: From raid plus -er. In business, a corporate raider buys up companies to break them apart.
hints: A Viking approaching a coast.
An Indiana Jones film is about the lost ark's ones.

definition: Having a lot of rain.
note: From Old English reginig, built from rain plus -y. People save money 'for a ___ day', meaning for hard times.
hints: A day to take an umbrella.
The sort of weather that fills puddles.
example: Due to the rainy weather, we decided not to play in the park.

definition: To lift up or increase.
note: From Old Norse reisa, 'to raise'. It is the causative of rise.
hints: What you do with your hand to ask a question.
To bring up a child or lift a flag.

definition: An Indian prince or king.
note: From Hindi raja, from Sanskrit rajan, 'king'. It is a relative of the Latin rex.
hints: A ruler in India.
A prince of old India.
example: After a long reign, the rajah abdicated in favor of his son.

definition: Wheat noodles served in broth.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, which took it from Chinese la mian, 'pulled noodles'. Instant packets are a cheap staple.
hints: A noodle soup from Japan.
Instant packets feed students.

definition: A large farm for cattle or horses.
note: From American Spanish rancho, 'small farm'. It was recorded in English in 1808.
hints: Cowboys work on one.
Also a creamy salad dressing.

definition: Without pattern or purpose.
note: From Old French randon, 'rush' or 'speed', from randir, 'to run'.
hints: Happening by chance alone.
Not planned.
origin: Old French randon, from Old Norse rend

definition: Sexually aroused, in British slang.
note: First recorded in the 1600s; its origin is uncertain.
hints: A cheeky British adjective.
Slang for being in the mood.
example: If you're feeling randy, give me a call and I'll come round and give you some hot lovin'.

definition: A line of mountains; or the extent of something.
note: From Old French rengier, 'to arrange in a row', from renc, 'rank'. It also names a stove and a shooting area.
hints: A line of mountains.
A big cooker in a kitchen.
example: The valley was between two ranges of hills.

definition: A person who looks after a park, or a roamer.
note: From range plus -er.
hints: Guards a national park.
Texas has a famous lawman with this title.

definition: Money demanded for the release of a captive.
note: Through Old French from Latin redemptio, 'a buying back'. It shares a root with redemption.
hints: What kidnappers ask for in the movies.
A king's famous one was paid for Richard the Lionheart.
origin: Old French raençon, from Latin redēmptiō

definition: Very fast.
note: From Latin rapidus, 'swift', from rapere, 'to seize'. Rivers have these, in the plural.
hints: White water in a river.
Very quick in motion.
origin: Middle French rapide, from Latin rapidus

definition: A bird of prey, such as an eagle or hawk.
note: From Latin raptor, 'kidnapper' or 'plunderer', from the verb meaning 'to seize'. Hunting birds are named for snatching their prey.
hints: Falconers keep them; so do some museums of birds.
Sharp talons and a hooked beak, or a film dinosaur.
example: Nowhere in the Bible does it state that Jesus wasn't a raptor.

definition: Not often.
note: From rare plus -ly.
hints: Not occurring often at all.
Not frequently at all.
example: Brothers have the same blood, but rarely the same character.

definition: The quality of being uncommon; or an uncommon thing.
note: From Latin raritas, from rarus, 'thin' or 'sparse'. A rarity is something thinly spread in the world.
hints: A collector prizes a coin that only a few were minted.
In a trading card game it grades how scarce a card is.
origin: Middle French rarité, from Latin rāritās

definition: A mischievous or cheeky person.
note: From Old French rascaille, 'rabble'. It once meant the common soldiers of an army, then a rogue.
hints: What you call a naughty puppy.
Said fondly to a cheeky child.
example: That little rascal bit me!

definition: Rough and scratchy in sound.
note: From rasp plus -y. A rasp is a coarse file, and by extension a harsh sound.
hints: A voice after shouting all day.
Hoarse and scratchy.
example: His incessant coughing made his voice sound raspy.

definition: Somewhat, or preferably.
note: From Old English hrathor, comparative of hrathe, 'quickly'.
hints: Fairly, or would sooner.
Used when you prefer one thing.
origin: Old English hraþor; in English since the 16th century
example: It's been rather/quite a good meal overall, but this melon is rather too tasteless.

definition: A fixed share of a scarce supply; to limit something to fixed amounts.
note: From French ration, and before that Latin ratio, 'reckoning'. It is a doublet of reason.
hints: Wartime brought books of coupons for it.
Explorers measure out food this way on a long trek.

definition: To make quick, short knocking sounds; or to unsettle someone.
note: Probably imitates the sound; the word appears in Middle English. A rattlesnake is named after its tail.
hints: A baby shakes one for fun.
Loose parts in an old car do this over bumps.

definition: Shabby or run down; or in a bad mood.
note: From rat plus -y. It can mean worn-out and rodent-like.
hints: A worn-out old sweater.
British slang for irritable.

definition: To tangle up, or oddly, to untangle.
note: From Dutch ravelen, 'to tangle'. It ended up as its own opposite, meaning both to knot and to unknot.
hints: Can mean to snarl or to pull apart.
Sweaters do this at the edges.

definition: A large black bird with a deep croak.
note: From Old English hraefn. Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem is about one.
hints: A big black bird in a Poe poem.
A bird kept at the Tower of London.

definition: A deep, narrow valley carved by running water.
note: Borrowed from French ravin, from Old French meaning 'a violent rush of water'. The name remembers the water that cut it.
hints: A hiker might cross it by a rope bridge.
Smaller than a canyon, steeper than a valley.
example: It took them several hours to make their way down the ravine.

definition: A soft fabric made from cellulose fibre.
note: The name was chosen in 1924 in the United States, probably from French for 'ray of light', because of its shine.
hints: A silky cloth made from wood pulp.
A fabric first made as artificial silk.

definition: A sharp blade used for shaving.
note: From Old French rasour, from raser, 'to scrape'. It is also the name of a thin shell.
hints: What a barber uses.
Used on a beard.

definition: To stretch out to touch something; or to arrive at.
note: From Old English raecan, 'to stretch out'. It covers extending a hand and getting to a place.
hints: What you do for a top shelf.
What an arm does to grab something.
example: Government reaches out to the people.

definition: To respond to something.
note: From re- plus act. In chemistry, substances do it when mixed.
hints: What you do when startled.
Chemicals do it when mixed.

definition: A person who reads.
note: From read plus -er.
hints: Someone with a book.
Often has a library card.

definition: Prepared and set to go.
note: From Old English raede, 'prepared'. It is the starting word in 'set, go'.
hints: Said before the starting gun.
The first word in a countdown.
example: She is ready to resign.

definition: Truly, or very much.
note: From real plus -ly. It has long been used to add emphasis.
hints: Used to add emphasis to an adjective.
Stronger than just 'quite'.

definition: A kingdom or domain.
note: From Old French reaume, of unclear origin, possibly from Latin regalis, 'royal'. It is used for fantasy lands too.
hints: A kingdom in a fairy tale.
A word for a field of activity.

definition: Real estate; land and buildings.
note: From Middle French realite, 'property', a doublet of reality. It is mostly seen in names of estate agencies.
hints: Appears on estate agents' signs.
A word on an estate agent's board.
example: In English common law, realty is owned land plus the physical structures associated with it.

definition: A person or machine that cuts and gathers a crop.
note: From Old English ripere, from the verb reap. The 'Grim' version is a figure of Death carrying a scythe.
hints: Cuts the wheat at harvest time.
Death is pictured as a grim one, with a scythe.

definition: To supply with weapons again.
note: From re- plus arm. A rebuilding army or nation does it.
hints: What a disarmed country might do.
To load up weapons again.
example: After the war, the defeated country was not rearmed by the victors.

definition: A cause or explanation; also the power of thinking.
note: From Latin ratio, 'calculation'.
hints: The why behind an act.
Logic as a human ability.
example: The reason a steady state was never reached was that the back pressure built up too slowly.

definition: Steel rods used to strengthen concrete.
note: A blend of 'reinforcing' and 'bar'. It gives concrete the tensile strength it lacks.
hints: Hidden inside concrete.
Steel bars inside a wall.

definition: A partial refund of money paid.
note: From Old French rabatre, 'to beat down', related to abate. Companies offer them to encourage purchases.
hints: A cashback offer on a new appliance.
A refund of part of the money from a tax bill.

definition: A person who resists authority.
note: From Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis, 'waging war again'. Teenagers are often called one.
hints: One who defies those in charge.
The sort who defies a government.
origin: Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis
example: A group of rebels defied the general's orders and split off from the main army.

definition: To restart a computer, or to relaunch a film series.
note: From re- plus boot, the computer sense of starting up, itself from 'pulling oneself up by the bootstraps'. Hollywood uses it for fresh retellings.
hints: What tech support says to try first.
What a studio does to a tired franchise.

definition: Born again, in a literal or spiritual sense.
note: Re- plus born. It is used for religious conversions and for revived brands.
hints: What a phoenix is after the flames.
A revived franchise is said to be this.

definition: A sharp expression of disapproval; or to scold.
note: From Anglo-Norman rebuker, 'to beat back'. A scolding was imagined as driving someone back.
hints: A teacher's stern reply to a rude pupil.
The Bible says to do it to a wise man and he will love you.
example: He had to take the rebuke with a smile on his face.

definition: A puzzle that uses pictures to stand for words.
note: From French, from Latin rebus, 'by things'. A picture of an eye plus a can might spell something.
hints: A picture puzzle.
A wordless word game.

definition: To remember, or to call back.
note: From re- plus call.
hints: Bring to mind.
A maker may order one for a faulty product.
origin: re- + call; in English since the 16th century

definition: A short summary of what happened.
note: Short for recapitulation. It is often shown at the start of a TV episode.
hints: A summary at the start of a TV show.
What an announcer gives of the story so far.

definition: Having happened not long ago.
note: From Latin recens, 'fresh' or 'new'.
hints: Not long past.
Near in time.

definition: A break in school; or a hollow space in a wall.
note: From Latin recessus, 'a going back'. Courts and parliaments also have them.
hints: The playground bell rings for this.
A niche for a statue or shelf.
example: Students who do not listen in class will not play outside during recess.

definition: Instructions for making a dish.
note: Latin for 'take!', the opening word of old medical prescriptions.
hints: Ingredients and steps.
What a cook follows.
origin: Middle French récipé, from Latin recipiō; in English since the 18th century
example: Whenever he found a new recipe, he wrote it in his notebook.

definition: To repeat something aloud from memory.
note: From Latin recitare, 'to read out'. Pupils once recited poems in front of the class.
hints: A child reads a poem out loud at school.
Pupils once stood to do this to a poem in class.
origin: Old French reciter, from Latin recitō
example: Janice is able to recite pi to 100 decimals.

definition: To think or calculate.
note: From Old English gerecenian, 'to explain'.
hints: Guess that something is so.
Work out a sum.

definition: To spring or shrink back; also the kick of a gun when fired.
note: From Old French reculer, 'to move backward', itself from Latin roots meaning 'backside'.
hints: A rifle does it against your shoulder.
You might do it from a snake or a bad smell.

definition: Short for reconnaissance; a scouting mission.
note: A clipping of reconnaissance, from French, 'a recognising'. Soldiers send a unit ahead to gather information.
hints: A scouting trip before an attack.
Soldiers gathering information before moving in.

definition: A written account or a best-ever achievement.
note: From Latin recordari, 'to remember'.
hints: Vinyl disc, or an athletic best.
The best mark ever set.
example: The heat and humidity were both new records.

definition: A priest in charge of a parish; or the head of a school or university.
note: From Latin rector, 'ruler', from regere, 'to rule'. Scottish universities elect one to chair their court.
hints: An Anglican minister in some parishes.
In Scotland, students elect one.
origin: Old French rector, from Latin rēctor
example: In April 1933, Heidegger was appointed rector of the University of Freiburg.

definition: To happen again.
note: From Latin recurrere, 'to run back'. A recurring dream is one you have often.
hints: A dream that repeats.
Said of events that come around again.
example: This is a recurring story.

definition: To cut again.
note: From re- plus cut. A film can be this when editors reshape it.
hints: What an editor may do to a film.
Trimming something a second time.

definition: To buy back, exchange a voucher, or save from a fault.
note: From Latin redimere, 'to buy back'. A coupon is one you can this.
hints: What you do with a coupon at the till.
What a hero does after a bad mistake.
origin: Old French redimer, from Latin redimō

definition: Describing a chemical reaction in which one substance loses electrons and another gains them.
note: A blend of reduction and oxidation, the two halves that always happen together.
hints: A chemistry word for electron transfer.
Rusting is an example.

definition: To make smaller.
note: From Latin reducere, 'to lead back'.
hints: Cut down the amount.
What a sauce does when simmered.
origin: Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō

definition: Brought back or revisited.
note: Latin for 'returning', from reducere. Often tacked on after a title, as in a film revival.
hints: Placed after a title to say it's back.
Latin for returned.
example: The Victorian era redux.

definition: Thin and high in sound; or full of reeds.
note: From reed plus -y. Reed instruments can have this tone.
hints: A high, thin tone.
A marsh grown over with tall grass.

definition: A medieval official; or the head of a township.
note: From Old English gerefa, 'steward'. The sheriff was a shire-reeve.
hints: A medieval steward.
The first part of the word sheriff came from its shire.

definition: To mention, or send to another source.
note: From Old French referer, from Latin referre, 'to carry back'. It is a doublet of relate.
hints: What a doctor does for a specialist.
To point to a source.
origin: Old French referer, from Latin referre
example: To explain the problem, the teacher referred to an example in another textbook.

definition: To fill something again; also a new supply to replace what is used.
note: Formed from re-, 'again', and fill.
hints: A coffee shop might offer a free one if you bring your cup back.
Pens, printers and prescriptions all need one eventually.
example: Can you refill my cup please? I've finished my coffee.

definition: To purify or improve something.
note: From re- plus fine. Oil and sugar are refined; so are manners and ideas.
hints: Crude oil goes through a plant to get this treatment.
Sugar is processed this way to turn white.

definition: To repair or fit out again.
note: From re- plus fit. Ships are said to get one in dock.
hints: What a ship gets in a dock.
A makeover of a vessel.

definition: An automatic reaction the body makes without thinking.
note: From Latin reflexus, 'bent back'. A reflex is a signal that bounces straight back as a movement.
hints: A doctor taps your knee with a small rubber hammer to test one.
Snatching your hand from a hot pan happens before you decide to.

definition: To improve by changing.
note: From Latin reformare, 'to form again'.
hints: Make better.
Change a law for the better.
origin: Old French reformer, from French réforme

definition: Shelter from danger.
note: From Latin refugium, 'a flying back'.
hints: A safe haven.
Where people flee for protection.
origin: Old French refuge, from Latin refugium

definition: To pay money back.
note: From Latin refundere, 'to pour back'.
hints: Return a faulty item.
Money returned.
origin: Old French refondre, from Latin refundere
example: Please refund me my money.

definition: To say no; or rubbish, pronounced differently.
note: The verb is from Old French refuser. The noun refuse, meaning rubbish, comes from the same source.
hints: Decline an offer.
Garbage collected from bins.
origin: Old French refuser, from Latin refūtāre

definition: To prove a claim wrong.
note: From Latin refutare, 'to repel' or 'drive back'. Strictly, it means to show something is false, not merely deny it.
hints: A lawyer does this to the witness's story.
Evidence can do this to a theory.

definition: To get back something lost.
note: From re- plus gain.
hints: Win back control.
Recover your strength.
example: She regained control of herself.

definition: Fit for a king or queen.
note: From Old French regal, from Latin regalis, from rex, 'king'. A stately posture is called it.
hints: Like a royal.
Stately, like a monarch.
origin: Old French regal, from Latin rēgālis

definition: To consider, or a feeling of esteem.
note: From Old French regarder, 'to look back at'.
hints: Look upon with respect.
Esteem or concern.
origin: Old French regarder; in English since the 16th century

definition: Someone who rules on behalf of a monarch who is too young or ill.
note: From Latin regere, 'to rule'. A famous London street and an era are named after one.
hints: The ruler when a king is a child.
A prince who governed for his unwell father.
origin: Anglo-Norman regent, from Latin regēns; in English since the 15th century

definition: A Jamaican style of music with an offbeat rhythm.
note: From Jamaican rege, meaning rags or a quarrel. It rose in the late 1960s and Bob Marley made it global.
hints: The sound of Bob Marley.
A style with a laid-back off-beat guitar chop.
example: I heard some reggae music playing in the distance.

definition: A system of government or its leaders.
note: From French regime, from Latin regimen, 'rule'.
hints: Often comes with the word military.
A government in power.
origin: Middle French regime, from Latin regimen

definition: A large area or district.
note: From Latin regio, 'direction' or 'district', from regere, 'to rule'.
hints: Part of a country.
Tuscany, for example.
example: Penguins inhabit the polar regions.

definition: To feel sorry about something.
note: From Old French regreter, 'to lament'.
hints: Wish you hadn't.
Feeling of sorrow over the past.

definition: Treatment to recover from addiction or injury.
note: A clipping of rehabilitation. It is used for treatment centres.
hints: A place to recover from addiction.
Treatment after an injury.

definition: A Japanese practice in which healers hold their palms over a person to channel energy.
note: From Japanese for 'spiritual energy'. Scientists have found no proof that it works.
hints: Hands-on healing from Japan.
Alternative therapy using the palms.

definition: To refuse or turn down.
note: From Latin reicere, 'to throw back'.
hints: Say no to an offer.
A publisher might do it to a manuscript.

definition: To join again; also to answer sharply.
note: From Middle English rejoynen, from French re- plus joindre, 'to join'.
hints: A hiker does it with the group after a short break.
A river does it with another after splitting around an island.

definition: To tell, or to connect.
note: From Latin relatus, 'carried back'.
hints: Tell a story.
Connect to another thing.
example: The captain related an old yarn.

definition: To become calm and less tense.
note: From Latin relaxare, 'to loosen', from laxus, 'loose'. It is a command many give to the anxious.
hints: What a spa promises.
What you do on a sofa.
origin: Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre
example: Tensions between the two countries have relaxed somewhat in recent weeks.

definition: A race in which team members pass a baton; or to pass on.
note: From Old French relaier, 'to exchange tired animals for fresh'. It first named fresh hounds or horses along a route.
hints: A track race passing a baton.
To pass a message along.
origin: Middle French relai, from Old French relaier; in English since the 19th century

definition: An old object that survives from the past.
note: From Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae, 'remains'. It also names a saint's remains kept in a church.
hints: An ancient artefact.
Part of a saint kept in a church.
origin: Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae

definition: The easing of pain or worry; or a raised carving.
note: From Old French relever, 'to raise again'.
hints: What you feel when exams end.
A sculpture that juts from a flat surface.
origin: Old French relief, from Latin relevare
example: He asked the nurse for relief from the constant pain.

definition: A tangy sauce; or enjoyment of something.
note: From an old word meaning 'taste' or 'smell', related to release. To relish a challenge is to enjoy it.
hints: Put on a hot dog with pickles.
To do this to an opportunity is to savour it.
origin: Anglo-Norman reles, from Old French reles

definition: To experience something again, especially in memory.
note: Formed from re- plus live. The older sense was to bring something back to life.
hints: What old photographs and anniversaries invite you to do.
Veterans and sports fans both talk about doing this with big moments.
example: I relive that horrible accident every night and wake screaming.

definition: To load again, as a gun or a web page.
note: From re- plus load. Refresh your browser and it will do this.
hints: A gunslinger stops to do it after emptying the chamber.
Pressing refresh makes a web page do it.

definition: To stay behind or continue to be.
note: From Latin remanere, 'to stay behind'.
hints: Be left after others have gone.
What is left over.
example: Promise me you will always remain my good little girl.

definition: To make again, or a new version of a film.
note: From re- plus make.
hints: Hollywood loves one.
A new take on an old movie.
example: You'll need to remake that cake, as it's completely burned.

definition: A comment or short statement; also to notice or say something.
note: From French remarquer, 're-' plus 'marquer', to mark. To remark was originally to mark or observe.
hints: What you make in passing at a dinner party.
Something that may be passing, witty, or offensive.
origin: Middle French remarquer, from Old French remarquer

definition: A cure or solution.
note: From Latin remedium, 'a cure'.
hints: Medicine for a cold.
A fix for a problem.

definition: To help someone remember.
note: From re- plus mind.
hints: Nudge a memory.
What a note on the fridge does.

definition: A new version of a song made from the original recording.
note: From re- plus mix. A producer rearranges a track's parts in it.
hints: A DJ's take on a pop song.
A new version of a track.

definition: Far away or isolated; also a controller.
note: From Latin remotus, 'moved back'.
hints: Hard to reach.
Changes the television channel.
origin: Old French remot, from Latin remotus

definition: To take away.
note: From Latin removere, 'to move back'.
hints: Take off or out.
Pull away from a place.

definition: Relating to the kidneys.
note: From Latin ren, 'kidney'. Doctors use it in terms like 'renal failure'.
hints: A medical adjective for an organ.
Doctors use it for kidney matters.
origin: Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs
example: Renal failure leads to disturbed water homoeostasis.

definition: To give something a new name.
note: Formed from re- plus name.
hints: A file on a computer can be changed with it.
A company does it after a rebrand.
example: Many streets in the former East Germany were renamed in 1990.

definition: To cause to become, or to provide or give.
note: From Old French rendre, 'to give back'.
hints: Make something look different in digital graphics.
Melt fat to make lard.
origin: Old French rendre, from Latin reddere

definition: To make new again, or extend.
note: From re- plus new. You do it to a library book or a passport.
hints: What you do to a subscription.
What you do to a library loan.
example: We renewed our friendship after a hiatus of twenty years.

definition: Fame for something notable.
note: From Old French renoun, from re- and noun, 'name'. To be renowned is to be named again and again.
hints: Said of a scientist or chef whose name is known across the world.
Earned by achievement, then spread by word of mouth.

definition: Something hired out, or the fee paid for it.
note: From rent plus -al.
hints: A car hired at an airport.
A holiday flat you pay for weekly.

definition: To open again.
note: Simply re- plus open. Shops, cases and old wounds can all be reopened.
hints: Shops did it after a long closure.
A detective can do this to a cold case.
example: They reopened the theater.

definition: To fix something broken.
note: From Latin reparare, 'to make ready again'.
hints: Mend a broken thing.
What a garage does.
origin: Middle French reparer, from Latin reparō
example: She repaired her TV set.

definition: To pay back what you owe.
note: From Old French repaier, from re- plus paier, 'to pay'. It covers debts and kindnesses.
hints: What you do with a loan.
Return a favour.
origin: Old French repaier, from Latin pācāre
example: I finally repaid my student loans, just before sending my kids to college.

definition: To officially cancel a law.
note: From Old French rapeler, 'to call back'.
hints: Parliament may do it to a statute.
Revoke a law.

definition: To say or do again.
note: From Latin repetere, 'to seek again'.
hints: Say it once more.
Do it once more.
origin: Old French repeter, from Latin repetō
example: The scientists repeated the experiment in order to confirm the result.

definition: To drive back or push away.
note: From Latin repellere, 'to drive back'. Insect sprays do it to mosquitoes, and magnets of the same pole do it to each other.
hints: What a spray does to mosquitoes.
Like poles do it to each other.
origin: Latin repellere; in English since the 15th century

definition: To feel deep regret for wrongdoing and want to change.
note: From Old French repentir, from Latin paenitere, 'to cause regret'. Preachers use it as a call for sinners.
hints: A street preacher might cry 'turn' and do this.
To be sorry for sin and seek forgiveness.
origin: Old French repentir, from Classical Latin paenitēre

definition: To play again; or a repeat showing of an event.
note: From re- plus play.
hints: Referee checks it on video.
Watch the goal once more.

definition: An account of something; or to tell it.
note: From Latin reportare, 'to carry back'.
hints: A school one comes at the end of term.
A news item or a gunshot sound.
example: A report by the telecommunications ministry on the phone network revealed a severe capacity problem.

definition: To share something on social media again.
note: From re- plus post. It spread with social networks.
hints: What you do with someone else's tweet.
A button on social media shares it again.

definition: A repeat of a television show.
note: From re- plus run. Summer schedules are often full of them.
hints: A repeat broadcast.
TV in summer is full of them.
example: I'm not a fan of the new Simpsons episodes, but the old reruns have me in stitches, although I've seen them countless times.

definition: The selling of something already bought.
note: From re- plus sale. 'Resale value' is what a car will fetch later.
hints: The price a car fetches after years of use.
An online market for used trainers.
example: They bought the contents of the locker for resale.

definition: To save from danger.
note: From Old French rescourre, 'to shake off'.
hints: A lifeguard does this.
Save someone from harm.
example: The well-trained team rescued everyone after the avalanche.

definition: To feel bitter about something you consider unfair.
note: From French ressentir, 'to feel strongly again'. It once meant simply to feel deeply, good or bad.
hints: A sibling might do this about a brother's favoured treatment.
Bitter feelings about an unfair promotion.
origin: Middle French ressentir, from Old French resentir
example: The bride greatly resented being left at the church.

definition: To set back to the starting state.
note: From re- plus set. A button on a device often does this.
hints: What a button on a router does.
To restore a clock to zero.

definition: To live in a particular place.
note: From Latin residere, 'to sit back, remain'. A resident is someone who stays put.
hints: A formal verb on forms asking about your address.
Power can also be said to do this in someone.
origin: Old French resider, from Latin resideō

definition: To give up a post.
note: From Latin resignare, 'to unseal'.
hints: Hand in your notice.
Quit a job formally.
origin: Anglo-Norman resigner, from Latin resignāre; in English since the 14th century

definition: A sticky substance from trees, or a synthetic one like it.
note: From Greek retine, through Latin and Old French. Amber is fossilised tree resin.
hints: What amber was before it hardened.
Sticky sap used to make glue and varnish.
origin: Old French résine, from Latin resīna
example: Pine trees produce a sticky resin.

definition: To fight against or refuse to give in.
note: From Latin resistere, 'to stand against'.
hints: Fight off a temptation.
Refuse to yield.
origin: Middle French resister, from Latin resistere

definition: A holiday destination; or a recourse.
note: From Old French resortir, 'to go out again'.
hints: Beach hotel complex.
The last one is a final option.

definition: The outcome of something.
note: From Latin resultare, 'to leap back'.
hints: What happens in the end.
Final score or consequence.

definition: To begin again after a pause.
note: From Latin resumere, 'to take up again'.
hints: Pick up where you left off.
Start again after an interruption.
origin: Middle French resumer, from Latin resumere
example: Normal service has resumed.

definition: The selling of goods to the public.
note: From Old French retailler, 'to cut off a piece'.
hints: Shops do this.
Shopping malls and high streets sell in this way.

definition: To keep or hold on to.
note: From Latin retinere, 'to hold back'.
hints: Keep in memory.
Hold on to something you have.
origin: Anglo-Norman reteiner, from Old French retenir

definition: To take again, such as an exam or a film shot.
note: From re- plus take. A film director calls for one when a scene goes wrong.
hints: A director shouts for one when an actor fluffs a line.
A student who fails an exam sits it again as a this.

definition: To strain as if about to vomit.
note: From Old English hraecan, 'to clear the throat, cough up'. It describes the heaving without the result.
hints: What a bad smell may make you do.
A dry heave.

definition: The layer at the back of the eye that senses light.
note: From Medieval Latin tunica retina, 'net-like tunic', because its blood vessels look like a net.
hints: The screen on which the eye's lens focuses an image.
Apple uses its name for high-resolution displays.
example: This could cause irreversible damage to Damiano’s retina.

definition: To stop working, or to go away to rest.
note: From Old French retirer, 'to withdraw'.
hints: Leave a job for good.
Go to bed for the night.
origin: Middle French retirer, from Old French retirer
example: Having made a large fortune, he retired.

definition: Styled after the past.
note: Borrowed from French retro, from Latin retro, 'backwards'. It names fashions that deliberately look old.
hints: A throwback style from decades ago.
Old-school fashion that is back in style.

definition: To try again.
note: From re- plus try. Software offers a button for it after a failure.
hints: What a failed upload invites.
What a court may do in a second trial.

definition: To come or go back.
note: From Old French retourner, 'to turn back'.
hints: Come home again.
What you press after typing.
origin: Anglo-Norman returner, from Medieval Latin retornare
example: Although the birds fly north for the summer, they return here in winter.

definition: To use something again.
note: From re- plus use. It sits alongside reduce and recycle.
hints: Part of a green slogan, with reduce and recycle.
Using a bag a second time.

definition: To renovate or give something a fresh, improved form.
note: From re- plus vamp, 'to patch up'. The noun arrived later from the verb.
hints: A shop might do this to its look before a grand reopening.
A tired website gets an overhaul.
origin: re-; in English since the early 19th century
example: They revamped their old house before selling it.

definition: To make known or show.
note: From Latin revelare, 'to unveil'.
hints: Uncover a surprise.
A twist unveiled at the end of a film.
origin: Old French reveler, from Latin revēlāre
example: The actress won't reveal how old she is.

definition: To take great delight; or a noisy celebration.
note: From Old French reveler, 'to be disorderly', from Latin rebellare, 'to rebel'. It is a doublet of rebel.
hints: What partygoers do at a feast.
To take joy in something.
origin: Old French revel, from Latin rebello

definition: To feel deep respect and admiration for.
note: From French reverer, from Latin revereri, 'to fear' and respect. It is related to reverent.
hints: How believers feel about a saint or a great teacher.
Stronger than respect, short of worship.

definition: To go back to an earlier state or habit.
note: From Latin revertere, 'to turn back'. In law, property can revert to its original owner.
hints: What a frog in a fairy tale does when it turns back into a prince.
Use the undo command and a document will do this to an earlier version.
origin: Old French revertir, from Latin revertō
example: We reverted to the old rules.

definition: A critical assessment, or to look at again.
note: From Old French reveue, 'viewed again'.
hints: A film critic writes one.
Look over once more.
origin: Old French reveüe, from Latin revideō

definition: To go back over something to improve it, or to study again before an exam.
note: From Latin revisere, 'to look at again'. British students revise for exams where Americans say review.
hints: What you do to a draft after feedback.
What a British student does the night before a test.
origin: Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō

definition: To bring back to life, consciousness or use.
note: From Latin revivere, 'to live again'. A paramedic, a theatre company and a dying fire can all be given this.
hints: What a defibrillator or a fresh breeze might do.
Old musicals get this on stage decades later.
origin: Anglo-Norman reviver, from Old French revivre
example: Interest in ESP revived.

definition: To officially cancel something.
note: From Latin revocare, 'to call back'. A licence can be revoked for misbehaviour.
hints: A court strips someone of a driving licence.
An invitation is taken back.
origin: Middle French révoquer, from Latin revocare
example: Your driver's license will be revoked.

definition: To rise up against authority, or to disgust.
note: From French revolter, from Italian rivoltare, 'to turn around'.
hints: Peasants rising against a ruler.
What rotten food does to your stomach.
example: The farmers had to revolt against the government to get what they deserved.

definition: A stage show of sketches, songs and dances.
note: Borrowed from French revue, literally 'review'. It parodied the events of the year.
hints: A show of comic sketches and songs.
Often mocks the news of the year.

definition: Something given in return for good work or help.
note: From Old French rewarder, 'to take notice of'.
hints: Offered for a lost pet's return.
Prize for effort.
example: For catching the thief, you'll get a nice reward.

definition: To wind back to an earlier point, as with a tape or film.
note: Formed from re- plus wind, as in winding a spool.
hints: What you did with a cassette to hear a song again.
A button with two left-pointing arrows.
example: Let's rewind the clock to an earlier time.

definition: A large horned animal; short for rhinoceros.
note: A clipping of rhinoceros, from Greek words for 'nose' and 'horn'. In British slang the word has also meant money.
hints: A thick-skinned horned beast.
A threatened animal of Africa and Asia.
origin: Clipping of rhinoceros; in English since the 19th century
example: Giraffes, rhinos, hippos, and elephants are prehistoric relics.

definition: Words that end in the same sound; or a short verse.
note: From Old French rime, with the spelling later influenced by Greek rhythmos. Nursery verses are called it.
hints: Cat and hat do it.
A nursery verse.

definition: A regular beat or pattern in sound.
note: From Greek rhythmos, 'flow' or 'measure'.
hints: A drummer keeps it.
Its spelling has no ordinary vowels.
origin: Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός
example: Dance to the rhythm of the music.

definition: A narrow strip of fabric.
note: From Old French riban, of uncertain origin.
hints: Tied around a gift.
Cut at an opening ceremony.

definition: In a lavish or abundant way.
note: From Old English riclice, from rice, 'powerful', plus -lice. Rich once meant powerful.
hints: 'Deserved' often follows this word.
A tapestry in deep reds and golds.

definition: Full of or plagued by something unpleasant.
note: The past participle of ride, used as a suffix to mean oppressed or overrun, as in 'guilt-' or 'bug-'.
hints: Tacks on to 'bug' or 'debt' to mean overrun with it.
What a horse has been after a day on the trail.

definition: A puzzling question with a clever hidden answer.
note: From Old English rædels, linked to words for 'counsel' and 'advice'. The Sphinx of Greek myth is the most famous riddle-asker.
hints: Bilbo trades them with Gollum in the dark.
The Sphinx posed one about creatures walking on four, two and three legs.

definition: A person who rides.
note: From Old English rideri, 'knight' or 'horseman'. It is also a clause added to a document.
hints: Sits on a horse or a bicycle.
Someone on a bike or horse.
origin: Old English rīdere; in English since the 14th century

definition: A long narrow raised strip of land.
note: From Old English hrycg, 'back' or 'spine'. The word started as the back of an animal.
hints: A narrow crest at the top of a hill.
The top line of a roof.

definition: A long gun fired from the shoulder.
note: Short for 'rifled gun', after the spiral grooves in the barrel. As a verb it also means to rummage through.
hints: A hunter's long gun.
To search roughly through a drawer.
origin: Old French rifler, from Old High German riffilōn
example: He lifted the rifle to his shoulder and fired.

definition: Correct; or the opposite of left.
note: From Old English riht, 'straight' or 'just'. It also names a legal entitlement.
hints: A legal entitlement, like free speech, goes by this name.
The side of the body opposite the left.

definition: Stiff and not bending.
note: From Latin rigidus, from rigere, 'to be stiff'. It also describes inflexible views.
hints: A steel bar is this.
A strict rule that cannot bend.
origin: Latin rigidus, from Middle English rigged

definition: Strictness; harsh exactness.
note: From Latin rigor, 'stiffness', from rigere, 'to be stiff'. It also shows in 'rigor mortis'.
hints: Hard, exact discipline.
The stiffness after death, in Latin.

definition: A bell-ringer, or a substitute who looks like someone else.
note: From ring plus -er. A dead ringer is a double, a phrase possibly from horse racing.
hints: Sounds the church bells on Sunday.
A fake who takes the place of a champion.

definition: To wash with clean water.
note: From Old French rincier, 'to rinse'. It often removes soap.
hints: What you do after shampooing.
A quick wash that leaves no soap.
origin: Old French rincier, from Latin recentare

definition: To grow ready to eat.
note: From ripe plus -en, from Old English ripian. Fruit left in the sun does it.
hints: What a banana does on the counter.
To become fully mature, as fruit.
example: Grapes ripen in the sun.

definition: Something or someone that rips; in slang, an excellent thing.
note: Formed from rip plus -er. The slang approval is especially Australian.
hints: A nickname of a notorious Victorian-era London killer.
Down under, a great day at the beach might earn this praise.

definition: A small wave on the surface of water.
note: Perhaps altered from an older word rimple, 'to wrinkle'. It also names effects that spread outward from one event.
hints: Spreads in rings when you drop a pebble into a pond.
A small event with far-reaching consequences is said to have one 'effect'.

definition: Having gone up; the past participle of rise.
note: From Old English risen, past participle of risan. It is the word for dough that has done its job.
hints: What bread dough has done after proving.
The past participle of a word about going up.

definition: Something that goes up; or a step on stairs.
note: Built from rise plus -er. 'An early riser' is someone who wakes at dawn.
hints: Someone who is up at dawn.
The upright part of a stair.

definition: Likely to cause harm or loss.
note: From risk plus -y. Risk came into English from French, which took it from Italian risco.
hints: A gamble might be called this.
Describes a dangerous bet.

definition: A set of actions performed in a fixed way.
note: From Latin ritualis, from ritus, 'rite'.
hints: A ceremony repeated each year.
A habit performed the same way each time.

definition: A person or group competing against another.
note: From Latin rivalis, 'one who uses the same stream'. Neighbours who shared water were often in dispute.
hints: A competitor for the same prize.
A business that sells to the same customers.
example: Chris is my biggest rival in the 400-metre race.

definition: Torn apart or split.
note: The past participle of the old verb rive, 'to split', related to Old Norse rifa.
hints: Split in two by a quarrel or a lightning bolt.
Describes a party divided by dissent.

definition: A large natural stream of water.
note: From Old French riviere, from Latin ripa, 'bank'. It flows to the sea.
hints: The Thames or the Nile.
Water flowing to the sea.
example: Occasionally rivers overflow their banks and cause floods.

definition: A metal pin used to join sheets of metal.
note: From Old French rivet, from river, 'to fasten'. It is hammered flat at one end.
hints: Used to build ships and bridges.
A metal pin on a pair of jeans.
origin: Old French rivet, from Latin ripa

definition: A cockroach; or a freshwater fish.
note: The insect word is short for cockroach, from Spanish cucaracha. The fish is an older, different word from Old French.
hints: A pest in the kitchen.
A pest that survives anything.

definition: To cook in an oven; or to mock in good fun.
note: From Old French rostir, from a Frankish word. A comedy event named for it features jokes at the guest's expense.
hints: A Sunday dinner meat.
A comic event of friendly insults.

definition: A person who steals by force or threat.
note: From Old French robeor, from a Germanic root related to 'rob' and 'rape'. Robin Hood is the best-known folk example.
hints: Waves a gun at a bank teller.
Robin Hood is said to have been one.
example: The robbers came out from behind the trees and attacked him.

definition: A machine that carries out tasks automatically.
