note: From Czech robota, 'forced labour', used in Karel Capek's 1920 play. It entered English soon after.
hints: A mechanical worker.
A machine from a Czech play of 1920.
origin: Czech robot; in English since the 20th century
example: We have a robot in the house that does the vacuuming.

definition: Strong and healthy.
note: From Latin robustus, 'strong as oak', from robur.
hints: Strong enough to withstand hard use.
Sturdy and hardy.
example: He was a robust man of six feet four.

definition: A curved piece beneath a chair; also a rock musician.
note: From rock plus -er. The curved base on a cradle or chair is called a rocker as well.
hints: A curved strip on the bottom lets a chair sway.
A fan of loud guitars and leather jackets.

definition: A projectile or spacecraft driven by exhaust; also a salad leaf.
note: From Italian rocchetta, 'spool', from the shape of the first fireworks. The leaf comes from a separate word, ruccola.
hints: Takes astronauts to orbit.
A peppery salad green.
origin: Italian rocchetta, from Lombardic rocko; in English since the 20th century

definition: Full of rocks; or unsteady.
note: From rock plus -y. A relationship or a road can be this.
hints: A road of boulders and stones.
A shaky start to a project.
origin: Anglo-Norman roc, from Medieval Latin roca

definition: A gnawing mammal such as a mouse, rat or squirrel, with front teeth that never stop growing.
note: From Latin rodens, 'gnawing', from rodere, 'to gnaw'.
hints: Mice, rats, beavers and squirrels all belong to this group.
Pest controllers deal with the kind that raid pantries.

definition: A show of cowboy skills like bull riding.
note: From Spanish rodeo, from rodear, 'to surround', since it was a cattle roundup. It is now a sport.
hints: A show with bucking broncos.
Cowboys ride bulls in it.

definition: Radio word meaning 'message received'.
note: In 1940s military radio it stood for the letter R, short for 'received'. It was later replaced by 'romeo' in the spelling alphabet.
hints: What a pilot says to confirm.
Used in radio chat to say 'got it'.

definition: A cylinder that rolls, or a large wave.
note: From roll plus -er.
hints: Paint applied with it.
Curl worn in hair.

definition: A hard, sharp Italian-style cheese for grating.
note: Borrowed from Italian romano, 'Roman'. It is a doublet of Roman.
hints: Often sprinkled over pasta.
Named for the capital city.

definition: A piece of music where the main theme keeps returning.
note: From Italian rondo, 'round', related to rondeau. Classical composers used it for finales.
hints: A piece in which a theme returns.
A lively form often ending a sonata.

definition: A samurai with no master.
note: From Japanese, literally 'wave person', someone drifting like waves.
hints: A wandering swordsman in feudal Japan.
A samurai who has lost his lord.

definition: A beginner, especially in sport or the police.
note: Possibly an alteration of recruit, though this is not certain.
hints: A first-year player in a league.
A newcomer to the team.

definition: Having plenty of space.
note: From room plus -y. Room comes from Old English rum, 'space'.
hints: A big car interior.
Like a spacious closet.
example: A roomy but sparsely furnished apartment.

definition: A perch where birds rest or sleep.
note: From Old English hrost, which meant 'perch' and also the framework of a roof. 'Rule the roost' means to be in charge.
hints: Where chickens sleep.
A perch where a hen settles for the night.

definition: A string of beads used for counting prayers; also a rose garden.
note: From Latin rosarium, 'garland of roses'.
hints: Catholic worshippers run the beads through their fingers.
A string of beads with a crucifix on its end.
example: Jonas isn’t interested in the rosary because he’s an atheist.

definition: A hard resin rubbed on violin bows and used by gymnasts for grip.
note: From Old French raisine, a variant of resine, and a doublet of resin.
hints: Rubbed on a bow's hair.
Stops a hand from slipping.

definition: A list of names, often showing duties or team members.
note: From Dutch rooster, 'gridiron', after the ruled lines of the list.
hints: Names on a team sheet.
A work schedule.
origin: Dutch rooster, from Middle Dutch roosten
example: I'm number 12 on the roster for tonight's game.

definition: Turning around a centre, like a wheel; also a roundabout in the US.
note: From Latin rota, 'wheel', through Medieval Latin. A rotary phone had a dial you turned.
hints: An old telephone had one you spun with your finger.
A circular junction in New England is called this.
origin: Medieval Latin rotarius, from Latin rota
example: The accident blocked all traffic at the rotary.

definition: To turn around a fixed centre.
note: From Latin rotare, 'to turn like a wheel', from rota. Earth does it once a day.
hints: What the Earth does every twenty-four hours.
What you do to tyres to wear them evenly.
example: The lamb roast rotates on a spit over the fire.

definition: The turning part of a machine.
note: From a clipping of rotator, coined by William Kingdon Clifford. A helicopter has blades on one.
hints: The spinning blades on a helicopter.
The turning part in a motor.

definition: Decayed, or very bad.
note: From Old Norse rotinn.
hints: What old fruit becomes.
Of poor quality.
example: The floors were damaged and the walls were rotten.

definition: A red powder for the cheeks.
note: Borrowed from French rouge, from Latin rubeus, 'red'. It means 'red' in French.
hints: Makeup applied for colour in the cheeks.
French for the colour red.

definition: Not smooth; or approximate.
note: From Old English ruh, 'rough' or 'hairy'. It is spelled with a gh but sounds like f.
hints: Sandpaper has a surface like this.
Like a draft that is not polished.

definition: Shaped like a circle or ball.
note: From Old French rond, from Latin rotundus, 'wheel-shaped'. It also names a turn in a game or a drinks order.
hints: Like a ball or a coin.
A turn in a boxing match.
origin: Old Northern French roünt, from Old French ront
example: The ancient Egyptian demonstrated that the Earth is round, not flat.

definition: A device that directs internet traffic around a network; also a woodworking tool.
note: From route plus -er. Most homes have one blinking in a corner.
hints: The blinking box that gives your house wi-fi.
A woodworker's power tool that cuts grooves.

definition: A wanderer; or a vehicle that explores a planet.
note: From rove plus -er. Spacecraft that explore planets are named after it.
hints: A vehicle that explores Mars.
A wanderer who never settles.

definition: A tree with red berries, also called the mountain ash.
note: From a Scandinavian word, perhaps related to Old Norse reynir. Folklore said it protected against witches.
hints: A tree with bright red berries.
The mountain ash, as it is also known.
example: The rowan tree is sometimes known as the mountain ash tree.

definition: Noisy and disorderly.
note: Possibly from row, in the sense of 'noisy argument'. It started in the United States for a rough person.
hints: A noisy crowd after a match.
Loud and out of control.

definition: A person who pulls oars.
note: From row plus -er. Oxford and Cambridge race each other each spring.
hints: Sits in a boat and pulls hard.
A person in a university boat race.
example: The rower blames his oar.

definition: Belonging to a king or queen.
note: From Old French roial, from Latin regalis, from rex, 'king'. It is a doublet of regal.
hints: A family with a crown.
A word for a monarch's household.
origin: Old French roial, from Latin rēgālis

definition: A stretchy material made from latex.
note: From rub plus -er, since the material was first used to rub out pencil marks.
hints: Tyres are made of it.
An eraser in Britain.

definition: Broken pieces of stone or brick, as from a ruined building.
note: From Anglo-Norman, probably meaning 'bits of broken stone', and likely related to rubbish.
hints: What is left after an earthquake or demolition.
Rescuers dig through it looking for survivors.
origin: Old Norse rubba, from Old French robe

definition: The currency of Russia.
note: From Russian rubl, probably related to a word meaning 'to chop', as lumps of silver were once cut.
hints: Money spent in Moscow.
Russian currency, in 100 kopeks.

definition: A flat blade at the back of a boat or aircraft, turned to steer.
note: From Old English rothor, 'oar for steering', related to row.
hints: The pilot's foot pedals move one on the tail of a plane.
A captain turns the wheel and a hinged blade below the stern responds.

definition: Healthy reddish in colour.
note: From Old English rudu, 'redness', plus -y. In British speech it is also a mild swear word.
hints: A healthy red complexion.
The glow of a fire on a face.

definition: A team sport played with an oval ball.
note: Named for Rugby School in Warwickshire, where the game developed in the nineteenth century.
hints: A game of tries and scrums.
Played with an oval ball.

definition: A person who governs; or a straight measuring strip.
note: From rule plus -er. A schoolchild has one in a pencil case.
hints: A king or queen, or a strip for drawing straight lines.
Marked in centimetres.

definition: A Cuban ballroom dance with a slow rhythm.
note: Borrowed from Spanish rumba, of Cuban origin. It is danced in pairs.
hints: A Latin dance.
Cuban, and danced in pairs.

definition: A low, heavy, rolling sound.
note: From Middle English rumblen, probably an imitation of the sound. In American slang it also means a street fight.
hints: Distant thunder or a hungry stomach.
In West Side Story the gangs stage one.
example: They heard the rumbling of thunder.

definition: An unproven story going from person to person.
note: An American spelling of rumour, from Latin rumor, 'common talk'. It spreads without proof.
hints: Gossip with no source.
What spreads in an office without proof.
origin: Old French rumeur, from Latin rūmor

definition: A person who runs, or a long thin carpet.
note: From run plus -er.
hints: Athlete on a track.
Long strip on a table.
example: He sent a runner over with the contract.

definition: Flowing easily; or dripping.
note: From run plus -y. A nose or an egg yolk may be this way.
hints: A cold gives you a nose like this.
A soft egg yolk.
example: Yanni says whenever he washes his face, his nose gets runny.

definition: Rainwater flowing over land into streams; or a final deciding vote.
note: From run off. Fertiliser in it can pollute rivers.
hints: What storm drains carry to the river.
A second election when nobody wins a majority.

definition: A strip where planes take off and land.
note: From run plus way.
hints: Airport strip.
Where models walk in fashion shows.

definition: The currency of India and several nearby countries.
note: From Hindustani rupiya, a coin introduced by Sher Shah Suri in the sixteenth century. It is also used in Pakistan and Nepal.
hints: Money in India.
Currency in Nepal and Sri Lanka.

definition: Relating to the countryside.
note: From Latin ruralis, from rus, 'countryside'. It is the opposite of urban.
hints: Tractors and barns mark this kind of landscape.
Farms and villages.
origin: Old French rural, from Latin rūrālis

definition: Simple and rural in style.
note: From Latin rusticus, from rus, 'countryside'. It describes both country people and the cosy, rough-hewn look of wooden furniture.
hints: A cabin with log walls and a stone hearth.
Interior-design word for a farmhouse look.

definition: A small dark-furred animal; or the colour black in heraldry.
note: From Old French sable, from a Slavic word for the animal. Its fur was prized.
hints: A weasel-like animal valued for its coat.
The black colour in a coat of arms.
origin: Old French sable, from Middle Low German sabel

definition: A curved cavalry sword.
note: From French sabre, from Hungarian szablya. It is also a fencing weapon.
hints: A sword used by horsemen.
A fencing weapon with a curved blade.

definition: Holy or worthy of reverence.
note: From Latin sacrare, 'to consecrate'.
hints: Treated as holy.
A temple is thought to be so.

definition: A seat on a horse or bicycle.
note: From Old English sadol.
hints: Placed on a horse's back.
A bike seat.

definition: In a sorrowful way; or unfortunately.
note: From sad plus -ly. 'Sad' once meant 'full' or 'satisfied' in Old English.
hints: How a person might say goodbye.
Used to introduce unwelcome news.
example: “Only when we climb up can we see it,” he said sadly.

definition: An expedition to see or hunt wild animals, especially in Africa.
note: Borrowed from Swahili safari, 'journey', itself from Arabic safar. A very ordinary word for a trip.
hints: Tourists in jeeps look for lions on this.
Where you go to see elephants in the wild.
example: We're going on a safari in Kenya.

definition: Without risk.
note: From safe plus -ly.
hints: Without harm.
Arrive without trouble.
example: He watched a video on how to pierce his belly button safely.

definition: Being protected from danger.
note: From Old French sauvete, from Latin salvus, 'unharmed'.
hints: A helmet provides it.
A lock on a gun is named for it.
origin: Old French sauveté, from Latin salvus

definition: Hanging loosely or drooping.
note: From sag, probably from a Scandinavian word, plus -y.
hints: What old socks and mattresses become.
Droopy and slack.

definition: A person who works on or sails a ship.
note: From sail plus -or, an old variant of -er.
hints: Popeye was one.
Serves aboard a ship.

definition: A person recognised by a church as holy.
note: From Old English sanct and Old French saint, from Latin sanctus, 'holy'. Churches name many after them.
hints: A holy person with a feast day.
Patrick and George are two.
origin: Old English sanct, from Latin sānctus
example: The Roman Catholic Church proclaimed Kateri Tekakwitha a saint in 2012.

definition: A greeting meaning peace, often with a low bow.
note: From Arabic salam, 'peace'. It is a doublet of Hebrew shalom.
hints: A greeting, sometimes with a low bow and a hand to the forehead.
Its Hebrew cousin is shalom.

definition: A dish of raw vegetables, often with a dressing.
note: From Old French salade, from Latin sal, 'salt', because the greens were once dressed with salt. It reached English around the fifteenth century.
hints: A bowl of greens.
Lettuce, tomato and cucumber.
origin: Old French salade, from Latin saliō
example: We'd like a couple of cheese salads and two Pepsis, please.

definition: A fixed regular payment for work.
note: From Latin salarium, 'salt money', an allowance for Roman soldiers to buy salt, according to a popular account.
hints: Monthly pay.
Pay that gets deposited every month.

definition: Containing salt, or a salty solution used in medicine.
note: From Latin sal, 'salt'. A saline drip is a salt-water solution given by a vein.
hints: A hospital drip bag holds this solution.
Contact-lens solution is this.
origin: Medieval Latin salīna, from Latin sal

definition: The watery fluid made in the mouth that helps with chewing and digestion.
note: A Latin word for 'spit', borrowed into English in the 1600s.
hints: Makes your mouth water at the smell of food.
Pavlov's dogs produced it when a bell rang.
origin: Latin salīva, from Middle English salive
example: The highly contagious virus was spread through blood and saliva.

definition: A pink-fleshed fish that swims upstream to spawn.
note: From Latin salmo, perhaps from salire, 'to leap'.
hints: Leaps up waterfalls.
Fish that returns to its birth river.

definition: A place where hairdressers or beauticians work; or a grand reception room.
note: Borrowed from French, which took it from Italian salone, 'large hall'. In the 1700s a salon was also a gathering for talk and ideas.
hints: A place for a haircut or a manicure.
A gathering of thinkers in an eighteenth-century drawing room.

definition: A bar in the Old West; also a car with a closed body.
note: From French salon, a big hall, which itself comes from Italian sala, 'room'. The car sense is British; Americans say sedan.
hints: Cowboys swing through its doors in Westerns.
A four-door car in British English.

definition: A spicy sauce; also a Latin dance and its music.
note: From Spanish salsa, 'sauce', from Latin salsus, 'salted'. The music style took the same word.
hints: A dip to go with tortilla chips.
A Latin dance with quick steps.

definition: A greeting or gesture of respect.
note: From Latin salutare, 'to greet'.
hints: Soldiers do it.
Raise a hand to your brow.
origin: Latin salūtō; in English since the 15th century
example: The soldiers greeted the dignitaries with a crisp salute.

definition: A healing ointment.
note: From Old English sealf, from an old Germanic word for 'ointment'. It is also used for anything that soothes, such as a salve for guilt.
hints: A cream for a minor burn.
Anything that eases a conscience.
example: He needed a salve for his conscience.

definition: A burst of gunfire; or a sudden round of applause or criticism.
note: From Latin salvo, 'safe' or 'reserved', first used in law for an exception. It later came to mean a volley of guns fired together.
hints: A volley of cannon fire.
An opening attack in a dispute.

definition: A lively Brazilian dance.
note: From Portuguese samba, of African origin. It is the music of Rio's carnival.
hints: A dance of Rio's carnival.
A Brazilian rhythm.

definition: A small part to show what the whole is like.
note: From Old French essample, 'example'.
hints: A taste at a supermarket.
A free taste.
origin: Old French essample, from Latin exemplum

definition: The state of being sound of mind.
note: From Latin sanitas, 'health'. It is the root of sanitary.
hints: What a tough toddler can test.
What a person is said to lose when driven mad.
origin: Middle French sanité, from Latin sānitās
example: Gaslighting can cause victims to question their own sanity.

definition: Too sentimental; or full of tree juice.
note: From Old English saepig, 'full of sap', built from sap plus -y. The sentimental sense is figurative, like something too sweet.
hints: A movie that is too soppy.
A tree full of sticky sugar.

definition: A clingy plastic film used to wrap food.
note: A trade name coined by the Dow Chemical Company. The plastic is a chlorine-based polymer.
hints: Wrap that clings to a bowl.
Brand name of kitchen film.

definition: Informal name for a sergeant.
note: A clipping of sergeant, which comes from Old French.
hints: What soldiers call their drill leader.
Short for a certain army rank.

definition: A deadly nerve agent used as a chemical weapon.
note: Named from the initials of its German creators Schrader, Ambros, Rüdiger and Van der Linde.
hints: A poison gas banned by international treaty.
Its name is built from the initials of its inventors.

definition: Bold, cheeky and lively.
note: An American alteration of saucy, first recorded in 1799. It describes a confident tongue.
hints: A cheeky answer to an elder.
A bold, spirited retort.
example: William became really talkative and sassy.

definition: A smooth fabric with a glossy surface.
note: From French satin, which may trace to the Arabic name of a Chinese port city. It reached Europe through trade.
hints: A glossy fabric for evening wear.
Sheets or gowns that feel silky.

definition: Writing, comedy or art that mocks human folly or public figures to expose and criticise them.
note: From Latin satura, from lanx satura, 'a full dish' or mixed platter. Swift's A Modest Proposal is a famous example.
hints: Gulliver's Travels and late-night political sketches share this tradition.
A newspaper that invents absurd headlines to poke fun at the powerful.
origin: Middle French satire, from Latin satira
example: He was not aware that the praise was a satire in disguise.

definition: A half-man, half-goat spirit of Greek myth.
note: From Greek satyros, through Latin and French. In myth satyrs followed the god Dionysus.
hints: A creature from Greek myth with a goat's legs.
A woodland follower of the god of wine.
origin: French satyre, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος

definition: A liquid served with food.
note: From Old French sauce, from Latin salsa, 'salted'. Salt was the original seasoning.
hints: What pasta is served with.
Tomato or soy, perhaps.
origin: Old French sause, from Latin salsus

definition: A small dish for a cup, or a flat disc shape.
note: From Old French saussier, a dish for sauce. UFOs are often called flying ones.
hints: Sits under a teacup.
Aliens' vessel in 1950s films.

definition: Cheeky; or a little bit rude in a fun way.
note: From sauce plus -y. A sauce adds spice, so a saucy remark has a bit of spice.
hints: A cheeky remark with a bit of spice.
Slightly rude, but in a fun way.

definition: A small room heated to high temperatures for sweating.
note: Borrowed from Finnish sauna. Finland has a long tradition of them.
hints: A hot Finnish steam room.
A hot wooden room people sit in to sweat.
example: The hotel has a sauna in the basement.

definition: Wild, fierce or brutal.
note: From Old French sauvage, from Latin silvaticus, 'of the woods'.
hints: A fierce beast.
Untamed and cruel.
origin: Old French sauvage, from Latin silvāticus

definition: A person who puts money aside; or something that saves.
note: From save plus -er. A bank pays interest to this kind of customer.
hints: Someone who puts money in the bank.
A person who saves up.

definition: A person who rescues others from danger or ruin.
note: From Old French sauveour, from Late Latin salvator. With a capital S it names Jesus in Christianity.
hints: A hero who arrives at the last moment.
The British spelling has a 'u'.
origin: Old French sauveour, from Late Latin salvātor

definition: Shrewd and well-informed.
note: Probably from creole forms of Portuguese sabe, 'he knows', from saber. It began as a pidgin word for 'to know'.
hints: What a tech-literate person is.
Streetwise and clever.

definition: A person who saws timber for a living.
note: From saw plus -yer, the same ending as in lawyer. Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's famous boy.
hints: Mark Twain's famous boy bears the same name.
A worker at a sawmill or in a pit.

definition: To burn with hot liquid or steam.
note: From Old Northern French escalder, from Latin excaldare, 'to wash in hot water'. Milk is scalded by heating it almost to boiling.
hints: What boiling water does to skin.
A burn from steam.
origin: Old Northern French escalder, from Late Latin excaldāre
example: She scalded her hands when she turned on the faucet and hot water came out.

definition: A set of marks for measuring; also a device for weighing; or a small plate on a fish.
note: From Latin scala, 'ladder', for the measuring sense, and from a separate Old French word for the plate on a fish.
hints: A bathroom device for weighing yourself.
A fish's armour plate.

definition: The skin on top of the head, under the hair.
note: From Middle English scalp, probably from a North Germanic word. It once meant the skull's crown.
hints: Where dandruff forms.
The skin under your hair.
example: They wanted to take his scalp as a trophy.

definition: Covered with small flat plates.
note: From scale plus -y. Fish and snakes are covered with them.
hints: A lizard's skin.
What a fish's skin is covered in.

definition: A mischievous rascal.
note: From Middle Dutch schampen, 'to slip away', via Old French escamper, 'to run away'. It first meant a rogue and is now used affectionately of a naughty child.
hints: A cheeky child.
A little rascal.
origin: Middle Dutch schampen, from Old French escamper

definition: A leafless flower stalk growing straight from the root.
note: From Latin scapus, 'shaft', and a distant doublet of shaft.
hints: Part of a daffodil or hosta.
A flower stem with no leaves.
origin: Latin scāpus, from Doric Greek σκᾶπος

definition: Not enough in supply; hard to find.
note: From Old Northern French escars, meaning stingy or sparing. 'Make yourself scarce' means leave.
hints: Resources become this in a drought.
What you do not want food to be in a famine.

definition: To frighten; or a fright.
note: From Middle English skerren, 'to frighten', from Old Norse. As a noun it names a sudden fright or public alarm.
hints: What a ghost story tries to do.
A sudden fright.

definition: Frightened.
note: From scare plus -ed. Scare is from Old Norse skirra.
hints: Afraid of the dark.
Frightened out of your wits.
example: I’m scared I’ll miss the train.

definition: A long strip of cloth worn around the neck.
note: Probably from Old Northern French escarpe, 'pilgrim's purse hung from the neck'. It then came to mean cloth worn around the neck.
hints: Worn around the neck in winter.
Keeps your neck warm.

definition: Causing fright.
note: From scare plus -y. It is the usual word for a horror film.
hints: A horror film is this.
Makes your heart race on a dark night.
example: The tiger's jaws were scary.

definition: Offering beautiful views of the landscape.
note: From Greek skene, 'stage'. The word first related to theatre scenery before it described natural views.
hints: A road tourists choose over the fast motorway.
A route winding past mountains and lakes.
origin: Middle French scénique, from Ancient Greek σκηνικός
example: We have plenty of time: let's take the scenic route.

definition: A smell, especially a pleasant one.
note: From Old French sentir, 'to feel or smell', from Latin sentire. Hounds follow a trail by it.
hints: A perfume's fragrance.
A trail a hound follows.
origin: Old French sentir, from Latin sentiō

definition: A plan or outline showing how something is structured.
note: Borrowed from Latin and Greek skhema, 'form' or 'shape'. It is a doublet of scheme.
hints: A database designer draws one before building tables.
Psychologists use it for a mental framework.
origin: Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα

definition: A plan, often a sly one.
note: From Greek schema, 'form' or 'shape'.
hints: A clever or crafty plan.
A plot hatched in secret.
origin: Medieval Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα; in English since the 18th century

definition: A place where children are taught.
note: From Greek skhole, which first meant leisure, then the place where leisure was spent learning.
hints: Pupils go there on weekdays.
Its Greek ancestor meant free time.
origin: Old English scōl, from Ancient Greek σχολή
example: The school was built in 1932.

definition: A descendant of a notable family; also a cutting for grafting.
note: From Old French cion, from a Frankish word meaning 'shoot' or 'twig'. Gardeners graft one onto a rootstock.
hints: A young heir of a famous family.
A twig grafted onto a tree.
example: Daniel covered the scion with grafting tape to protect it from drying.

definition: To mock someone; or to eat greedily.
note: The mocking sense is from Middle English, probably of North Germanic origin. The eating sense is a separate British slang word.
hints: What a rude person does to a poor idea.
British slang for wolfing food down.

definition: To tell someone off angrily.
note: From Middle English scolde, first recorded around the twelfth or thirteenth century. It was once a noun for a quarrelsome person.
hints: What an angry parent does.
A telling-off for a child who misbehaved.
example: I advise that you refrain from using that kind of language at home, lest your mother scold you.

definition: A small baked quick bread eaten with jam and cream.
note: Originally Scots, possibly from a Dutch or Low German word for 'fine bread'. It is the centre of cream tea.
hints: Eaten with clotted cream and jam.
Part of an English afternoon tea.
origin: Middle Low German schö̂ne, from Scottish Gaelic sgonn

definition: A tool for lifting loose material; also an exclusive news story.
note: From Middle Dutch schope, 'bucket for bailing water'. In journalism it is a story that a rival lacks.
hints: What you use to serve ice cream.
A reporter's exclusive news story.
origin: Middle Dutch scoep, from Middle Dutch schoppe
example: She kept a scoop in the dog food.

definition: To move quickly or slide sideways.
note: Of uncertain origin, possibly from Old Norse skjóta, 'to shoot'.
hints: Make room on the bench.
Quick word for sliding over.
example: Do you mind scooting a bit to the left?

definition: The extent of something; or an aiming device.
note: From Italian scopo, 'aim', from Greek skopos, 'target'. It is also a short form of words like microscope.
hints: How wide a project reaches.
A sight on a rifle.
origin: Italian scopo, from Ancient Greek σκοπός
example: Environmental impacts lie outside the scope of this report.

definition: A player who gets points, or someone who records them.
note: From score, which began as a notch cut in a stick to keep count. The word comes from Old Norse skor.
hints: The striker who nets the winning goal.
The official who writes down runs in cricket.

definition: Deep contempt for someone or something.
note: From Old French escharnir, 'to mock'. To scorn something is to treat it as beneath you.
hints: A curl of the lip showing contempt.
What you may feel for a bad idea.
origin: Old French escharnir, from Old French escarn

definition: To put a decisive end to a rumour or plan; also a whisky from Scotland.
note: The verb comes from Middle English scocchen, 'to cut', probably via Anglo-Norman. Shakespeare's Macbeth says 'We have scotched the snake, not killed it', meaning wounded it.
hints: Stamping out a rumour is said to do this to it.
Also a whisky from the Highlands, or a kind of tape.
origin: Latin ex-, from Old French coche

definition: To scrub hard; or to search thoroughly.
note: From Middle Dutch scuren, 'to polish'. The search sense comes from rough, hurried movement over an area.
hints: What you do to a burnt pan.
What a detective does to a crime scene.
example: Scour the counter tops.

definition: Someone sent ahead to gather information.
note: From Old French escoute, 'listening', from Latin auscultare, 'to listen'. It is also a young member of a youth movement.
hints: A soldier sent ahead of an army.
A talent-spotter at a football match.
origin: Old French escoute, from Latin auscultō

definition: To frown angrily.
note: From Middle English scowlen, probably of North Germanic origin. It is used for dark, unfriendly looks.
hints: The face of a grumpy person.
A dark, angry frown.

definition: To go away quickly.
note: Possibly a clipping of scramble, or from German schramm. It is commonly shouted at someone unwelcome.
hints: What you tell a stray cat.
What you shout to shoo away a pest.
example: What are you kids doing on my lawn? Scram!

definition: A small piece left over; or to discard.
note: From Old Norse skrap, 'trifles'. It also means a minor fight, in British speech.
hints: A bit of leftover paper.
A bit of metal bound for the junkyard.
example: She jotted it on a scrap of paper.

definition: To drag something rough over a surface, removing a layer.
note: From Old Norse skrapa, 'to scratch'. A scrape is also a minor injury or a tight spot.
hints: What you do to ice off a car windscreen.
A graze on a child's knee.
origin: Old Norse skrapa, from Old English scrapian

definition: A loud, piercing cry of fear or excitement.
note: From Middle English screamen, probably imitating the sound.
hints: What a person does on a roller-coaster.
A cry from a horror film.
origin: Middle Dutch scremen, from Old Norse skræma
example: Her screaming attracted the neighbors.

definition: A slope of loose stones on a hillside.
note: Probably from Old Norse skridha, 'landslide'. Climbers find it tiring because it slides underfoot.
hints: Stones sliding on a mountain.
Loose rock that slips under a climber.

definition: A flat surface for display or a partition.
note: From Old French escren, a shield against heat.
hints: Where a film is shown.
A divider in a room.
origin: Anglo-Norman escren, from Old French escren

definition: A threaded metal fastener you twist in.
note: From Old French escroue, 'nut'. It is driven in with a turn.
hints: What you drive with a driver.
A threaded fastener for wood.
origin: Old French escroue, from Latin scrōfa

definition: A person who copied documents by hand.
note: From Latin scriba, 'secretary', from scribere, 'to write'.
hints: A monk in a scriptorium.
Wrote for people who could not read or write.

definition: A certificate or token used in place of money.
note: From Middle English scrippe, a small bag for carrying food or coins, so the word began as a purse.
hints: A voucher used instead of cash.
Company towns once paid workers in it.

definition: The written text of a play or film, or a style of handwriting.
note: From Latin scriptum, 'something written'.
hints: Lines that actors read.
Joined-up handwriting.
origin: Old French escrit, from Latin scriptum

definition: A rolled-up document; or to move text on a screen.
note: From Middle English scrowle, from Old French escroue.
hints: Ancient writing roll.
What you do with a mouse wheel.

definition: To rub hard to clean; or low bushes.
note: From Old English scrybb, a variant of shrub. The cleaning verb is separate.
hints: What you do to a dirty floor.
The low bushes of a dry plain.
example: She scrubbed his back.

definition: A tight huddle of players or people.
note: A shortening of scrummage, a variant of scrimmage. Rugby players push against each other in one.
hints: Packed forwards pushing in rugby.
A crush of reporters around a politician.
example: A scrum developed around the bar when free beer was announced.

definition: Underwater breathing gear.
note: An acronym for 'self-contained underwater breathing apparatus'. It lets a diver breathe without a hose to the surface.
hints: What a diver wears to breathe.
Gear with an air tank.
example: This year, Carlos wants to learn how to scuba dive.

definition: A sailor, or the lowest naval rank.
note: From Old English saeman, formed from sea and man.
hints: Found on the crew list of any merchant ship.
A common rank below able-bodied in a navy.

definition: To look for something carefully.
note: From Old French cerchier, from Latin circare, 'to go round'.
hints: Hunt for what is lost.
Googling is a modern form of it.
origin: Anglo-Norman sercher, from Late Latin circō

definition: One of the four parts of the year; or to add flavour to food.
note: From Old French seison, 'sowing time', from Latin satio.
hints: Summer, winter and two others.
What salt and pepper do to food.
origin: Old French seson, from Latin satiō
example: This invasive species reproduces so rapidly that it can completely take over an area in just a couple seasons.

definition: Coming right after first; also a sixtieth of a minute.
note: From Latin secundus, 'following'. The time unit is the second small division of an hour.
hints: Next after number one.
A unit of time shorter than a minute.
origin: Old French second, from Latin secundus

definition: Something kept hidden from others.
note: From Latin secretus, 'set apart'.
hints: Do not tell anyone.
Hidden information.
origin: Latin sēcrētum; in English since the late 14th century
example: The combination to the safe was a secret.

definition: A distinct part of an area or economy.
note: From Latin sector, 'cutter', from secare, 'to cut'.
hints: A slice of a circle or industry.
The banking one is part of finance.

definition: Safe from danger, or to fasten firmly.
note: From Latin securus, 'free from care'.
hints: Locked down tight.
To fix something so it will not come loose.

definition: A closed car with a separate trunk.
note: The word first meant a covered chair carried by two men, from 1634. The car body style borrowed it.
hints: A four-door family car.
A chair carried by two porters.

definition: The ritual meal held at the start of the Jewish festival of Passover.
note: From Hebrew for 'order', since the meal follows a set sequence.
hints: A meal with matzo and bitter herbs.
Passover supper.
example: You'll never guess who showed up at my seder.

definition: To lead someone astray, often by charm or tempting offers; to attract strongly.
note: From Latin seducere, 'to lead apart or astray', from se-, 'aside', and ducere, 'to lead'.
hints: Casanova's name is tied to it.
A tempting sale might do it to your wallet.

definition: Shabby and a little disreputable.
note: From seed plus -y. The shabby sense dates to the 1700s and referred to worn-out appearance.
hints: A rundown bar in a bad district.
A squalid-looking hotel.
example: He was soiled and seedy and fragrant with gin.

definition: Someone who looks for something.
note: From Old English, built from seek plus -er. It combines in words like 'job seeker' and 'asylum seeker'.
hints: In Quidditch it hunts the Golden Snitch.
Goes before 'thrill' or 'truth' to name a type of person.

definition: To move smoothly from one thing to another.
note: From Italian segue, 'it follows', a musical direction. It now describes smooth transitions in talk.
hints: A smooth shift between topics.
Moving from one song to the next without a pause.
example: I can tell she’s going to segue from our conversation about school to the topic of marriage.

definition: A large fishing net hung vertically in the water.
note: From Old English segne, from Latin sagena. It is also a river in Paris.
hints: A fishing net with floats.
A river in Paris.
origin: Old English seġne, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη

definition: To grab or take by force.
note: From Old French seisir, 'to take possession'. It is also used for grabbing a chance, as in 'seize the day'.
hints: What a customs officer does to contraband.
To grab hold of a chance.
origin: Old French seisir, from Early Medieval Latin sacīre

definition: Rarely; not often.
note: From Old English seldan, later changed by analogy with words like 'whilom'. It is the opposite of often.
hints: 'Once in a blue moon' says the same.
A cousin of 'rarely' that few people use out loud.
example: Anger is never without a reason, but seldom with a good one.

definition: To choose, or chosen with care.
note: From Latin selectus, 'picked out'.
hints: Pick from a list.
Exclusive or choice.
example: He looked over the menu, and selected the roast beef.

definition: A person who sells.
note: From sell plus -er.
hints: The owner of a shop or stall.
Estate agents and market traders play this part.
example: Sellers and buyers are anonymous and very hard to recognize.

definition: A governing body, often the upper house of a legislature.
note: From Latin senatus, 'council of elders', from senex, 'old man'.
hints: Part of the US Congress.
A council of elders in ancient Rome.
origin: Old French senat, from Latin senātus

definition: A person or device that sends something.
note: Formed from send plus -er.
hints: Name written in the top corner of an envelope.
Return to ___ is stamped on a letter that couldn't be delivered.

definition: Older or higher in rank.
note: From Latin senior, 'older', the root of senate and senator.
hints: A final-year student.
Discounts for pensioners often carry this word.

definition: A plant whose leaves are used as a laxative.
note: From Arabic sana, a plant. Its pods and leaves have long been used in medicine.
hints: A herb used in traditional medicine.
A plant from the cassia family.

definition: A way of perceiving, such as sight or smell; or good judgement.
note: From Latin sensus, 'feeling'. Humans have five of them, by tradition.
hints: Sight and smell are two of the five.
A word for good judgement.
origin: Old French sens, from Latin sēnsus
example: The dictionary gave several senses for the word.

definition: A teacher, especially of a martial art.
note: Borrowed from Japanese sensei, 'teacher' or 'elder', literally 'one born earlier'.
hints: The title for a karate master.
Mr Miyagi was one.

definition: A device that detects changes.
note: From sense plus -or.
hints: Detects motion for a light.
Your phone has a lot of them.
example: The smoke sensor triggered the alarm.

definition: A soldier posted to guard a place.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from sentinel or an old word for path. Sentry boxes are small huts for the guard.
hints: Stands in a little box outside a palace.
Challenges anyone who approaches at night.
example: The sentry demanded the password from everyone.

definition: A reddish-brown colour of old photographs.
note: From Latin sepia, 'cuttlefish', whose ink gave the pigment. Old prints have this tint.
hints: The tint of a faded old photograph.
A pigment from a sea creature's ink.
origin: Latin sēpia, from Ancient Greek σηπία

definition: Infected with harmful bacteria; also relating to a buried waste system.
note: From Greek septikos, 'putrefying', from sepein, 'to rot'.
hints: A dirty wound can turn this way.
A buried tank for household waste is named with it.

definition: A story that follows an earlier one.
note: From Latin sequi, 'to follow'.
hints: Film number two.
Comes after the original.
origin: Middle French sequele, from Latin sequēla

definition: Calm, peaceful and untroubled.
note: From Latin serenus, 'clear', first used of the sky. A cloudless sky is serene.
hints: A still lake at dawn.
Titles such as 'Most ___ Highness' once went to European princes.
example: She looked at her students with joviality and a serene mentality.

definition: Happening in a series.
note: From Latin series, 'row'.
hints: Describes a killer in thrillers.
Occurring one after another in order.

definition: A run of things in order, such as episodes.
note: From Latin series, 'row' or 'chain'. The word has the same form in singular and plural.
hints: A show with many episodes.
A chain of things in order.
example: They were investigating a series of bank robberies.

definition: A small stroke at the end of a letter.
note: From earlier ceriph, of obscure origin. Times New Roman has them; Arial does not.
hints: A feature of Times New Roman.
A typeface style with tiny feet.

definition: A talk on religion or morals given in church.
note: From Latin sermo, 'discourse'. A long lecture of any kind can be called one.
hints: A pulpit speech on Sunday.
Anything long and preachy may be called one.

definition: The clear fluid part of blood; or a treatment made from it.
note: From Latin serum, 'whey'. It is now also a cosmetic liquid.
hints: A clear fluid from blood.
A face treatment in a small dropper bottle.
example: The serum was responsible for the horrible disfiguration.

definition: To work for someone; or to put food on a plate.
note: From Old French servir, from Latin servire, 'to be a slave'. Tennis players do it to start a point.
hints: What a waiter does with food.
What you do to open a game of tennis.
origin: Old French servir, from Latin servus; in English since the 13th century
example: May I serve you?

definition: A computer that provides data to others; or a person who waits tables.
note: From serve plus -er.
hints: Hosts a website.
A waiter in a restaurant.

definition: A motor that adjusts a mechanism.
note: A clipping of servomotor, from Latin servus, 'servant'. It moves robot arms.
hints: A small motor in a robot arm.
A part that controls a model plane's flaps.

definition: A small seed used in cooking and oil.
note: From Greek sesamon, from a Semitic source. 'Open!' says the magic password in Ali Baba's tale.
hints: Dotted on hamburger buns.
The magic word that opens a cave in Ali Baba.
example: Mayonnaise and sesame paste go really well together.

definition: To resolve, or to make a home.
note: From Old English setlan, 'to seat'.
hints: Put an end to a dispute.
Make a new home somewhere.
origin: Old English setlan, from Old English setl

definition: The way something is arranged or organised; or a trick arranged in advance.
note: A noun made from the verb phrase 'set up'. It names an arrangement of equipment, or a plot arranged to frame someone.
hints: How a desk and monitors are arranged.
A rigged situation meant to trap someone.
example: It takes time to learn the setup around here.

definition: The number after six.
note: From Old English seofon, shared by nearly all Indo-European languages. It was long regarded as a lucky number.
hints: One more than six.
The number of days in a week.

definition: To cut apart; to end a connection.
note: From Old French sevrer, from Latin separare, 'to separate'. It is a doublet of separate.
hints: What a surgeon or a quarrel can do to a tie.
To cut off completely.
origin: Old French sevrer, from Latin separāre
example: After he graduated, he severed all links to his family.

definition: Very serious or harsh.
note: From Latin severus, 'strict'.
hints: Strict and harsh, as in a storm.
Grave in extent.

definition: Waste water and human waste carried away in drains.
note: From sewer plus -age. The treatment of it is a vital public health service.
hints: What treatment plants clean up.
What flows through the pipes beneath the street.
example: Untreated sewage can pollute rivers.

definition: An underground channel that carries away waste water.
note: From Anglo-Norman sewere, 'water course', from Old French. It is the sort of place where alligators are said to live in urban legend.
hints: Below the street, carrying waste away.
Where city drainage ends up.
example: There was a blockage in the sewer after an item of clothing was flushed down the toilet.

definition: Prejudice or discrimination based on sex.
note: From sex plus -ism, coined in the 1960s on the pattern of racism.
hints: What a gender pay gap may reflect.
A word that grew out of the women's movement.

definition: Treating people unfairly because of their sex.
note: From sex plus -ist, after sexism, which came into use in the 1960s.
hints: What an unfair 'jokes about women' comment is called.
A person with prejudice based on gender.

definition: A church worker who looks after the building and may dig graves.
note: From Old French segrestien, from Medieval Latin sacristanus. It is a doublet of sacristan.
hints: Rings the bell and tends the churchyard.
Hamlet has a gravedigger who could be this.
origin: Old French segrestien, from Latin sacer

definition: Relating to sex or to the two sexes.
note: From Latin sexualis, from sexus, 'sex'.
hints: Describes reproduction involving two parents.
Related to the biology of male and female.
origin: By surface analysis; in English since the 17th century

definition: Worn out and run-down.
note: From the old word shab, 'scab' or scaly skin disease, plus -y. It describes clothes, houses and unkind treatment.
hints: A threadbare coat with frayed cuffs.
Treatment that is mean and unworthy of a friend.

definition: A small, crude hut.
note: Its origin is unknown; some scholars suggest Mexican Spanish jacal, from Nahuatl. It is a roughly built shelter.
hints: A rickety hut by the shore.
Like a cabin that needs repair.

definition: A dark area out of the sun; or a variety of a colour.
note: From Old English sceadu. It also names a lampshade and a small variation of a colour.
hints: A cool spot under a tree.
Dark green or light green, as a variation.

definition: A dark shape cast when light is blocked.
note: From Old English sceadu, related to shade.
hints: What follows you in the sun.
Peter Pan lost his.
example: My shadow lengthened as the sun began to set.

definition: Giving shade; or suspicious and dishonest.
note: Built from shade plus -y. A shady deal is one done out of sight.
hints: A park bench under a big tree.
A dodgy business deal.
example: The shady side of the street.

definition: A long narrow rod or passage.
note: From Old English sceaft, 'pole' or 'spear shaft'. It is also a vertical passage in a mine or lift.
hints: The long body of an arrow.
A narrow vertical passage in a mine.

definition: Having long, rough, untidy hair or fur.
note: Formed from shag, 'rough hair', plus -y.
hints: A sheepdog or a yak looks this way.
A cartoon dog and his friend with a goatee share the name.
example: Junipers with shagged trunks.

definition: To move quickly to and fro.
note: From Old English scacan, 'to shake'. It also names a drink made from milk and ice cream.
hints: What you do to a snow globe.
What a dog does after a bath.

definition: Disturbed or upset; or moved rapidly back and forth.
note: The past participle of shake. James Bond's martini is shaken, not stirred.
hints: How a scared person looks after a close call.
What Bond wants his martini to be.
example: We were left shaken by the revelations of abuse.

definition: A container or device that is shaken, as for seasoning or cocktails.
note: Formed from shake plus -er.
hints: A bartender uses a metal one for mixing drinks.
Sits on the table with holes in its top for sprinkling.

definition: Trembling, or not firm.
note: Built from shake plus -y. A shaky voice or a shaky argument both lack steadiness.
hints: A voice that wavers when nervous.
An argument that might not hold.

definition: A soft, finely layered rock.
note: From Old English sceal, 'shell' or 'husk'. It splits into thin flakes and is a source of oil and gas.
hints: A rock that splits in thin layers.
A soft rock that gas is extracted from.

definition: A helping verb for the future or duty.
note: From Old English sceal, 'I must'. The earlier sense of obligation survives in 'thou shalt not'.
hints: Used with I and we in formal futures.
An old word of obligation in commandments.
example: I shall sing in the choir tomorrow.

definition: A spiritual healer or go-between who is said to communicate with the spirit world.
note: Borrowed through German and Russian from the Evenki language of Siberia.
hints: Drumming and trance are used in rituals led by one.
Siberian peoples gave this title its name.
example: The shaman performed the ritual rain dance.

definition: A painful feeling of having done something wrong.
note: From Old English scamu, 'shame' or 'disgrace'. It is also used for a pity, as in 'what a pity'.
hints: What a blush may show.
The feeling after doing something embarrassing.

definition: The part of the leg between knee and ankle.
note: From Old English sceanca, 'leg'. It also names the shaft of a tool and, in prison slang, a homemade blade.
hints: A cut of lamb from the lower leg.
The long part of a tool between handle and tip.

definition: The outer form of something.
note: From Old English gesceap and sceap, meaning 'creation' or 'form'. It also means condition, as in 'in good ___'.
hints: A circle or a square.
Fitness, as in 'in good form'.
origin: Old English ġesceap, from Old English scieppan

definition: A broken fragment, usually of glass or pottery.
note: From Old English sceard, 'a gap' or 'broken piece'. Archaeologists find pottery ones.
hints: A sliver of broken pottery.
A sharp fragment of broken glass.

definition: A portion; or to give a part to others.
note: From Old English scearu, 'a cut' or 'division'. It also names a unit of ownership in a company.
hints: A slice of the pie.
A unit of stock in a company.
example: Each of the robbers took a share of the loot.

definition: Islamic religious law, based on the Quran and the example of the Prophet.
note: From Arabic shari'a, 'path' or 'way to water'. It is interpreted differently across schools and countries.
hints: The legal framework of Islam.
An Arabic word that means a path to water.
example: Do you want sharia to be implemented in your country?

definition: A large predatory sea fish; or a cunning swindler.
note: From Middle English, first recorded in 1442 for the fish. Its origin is uncertain. A card shark is a swindler at cards.
hints: A big fish with a dorsal fin.
A cunning card-player who cheats.

definition: Having a fine cutting edge; or clever.
note: From Old English scearp, 'cutting'. It is also a musical note raised a half step.
hints: What a knife must be to cut well.
A music note raised a half step.
example: A pencil with a sharp point.

definition: To cut hair off the skin with a razor.
note: From Old English scafan, 'to scrape'. A narrow miss is a 'close one'.
hints: What you do with foam and a blade.
Done to a beard each morning.

definition: A bundle of grain stalks tied together, or a bunch of papers.
note: From Old English sceaf. Its plural is sheaves.
hints: Farmers bound stalks of wheat in one.
A bundle of papers held together.

definition: To cut off wool from a sheep.
note: From Old English sciran, 'to cut'. Sheep farmers do it each spring.
hints: What a farmer does to a flock in summer.
To clip a fleece.

definition: A close covering for a blade, or a similar protective case.
note: From Old English sceath, from a Germanic word for splitting or dividing.
hints: A dagger rests in one at the belt.
A knight draws his sword from this leather case at his hip.

definition: A gentle shine on a surface.
note: From Old English sciene, 'beautiful' or 'bright'. The adjective became a noun for a glossy brightness.
hints: The glow on polished wood.
A soft glossy shimmer.
example: The thin layer of oil at the top of the soup produced a mesmerizing sheen.

definition: A woolly farm animal.
note: From Old English sceap. The plural is the same as the singular.
hints: What a shepherd tends.
A word whose plural looks identical.

definition: Complete; or very thin.
note: From Old English scire, 'bright' or 'clear'. It describes pure, unmixed things and also near-transparent cloth.
hints: A very thin curtain.
A cliff that drops straight down.
origin: Old English sċǣre, from Old Norse skírr
example: Got the job through sheer persistence.

definition: A flat piece of cloth, paper or metal.
note: From Old English sciete, 'cloth'. A bed has one, and so does a printer tray.
hints: Linen on a bed.
A page in a printer tray.
origin: Old English sċīete, from Old English sċēat

definition: An Arab tribal leader or Muslim religious teacher.
note: From Arabic shaykh, 'elder'. A romantic-lover sense came from a 1921 film.
hints: A respected elder in the Gulf.
Also the title of a religious leader in Islam.
example: My grandfather is a Bedouin sheikh, chief of one of the most powerful tribes of the desert.

definition: Australian slang for a woman.
note: From the Irish girl's name Sheila, used in Australia for any young woman. It is informal.
hints: A word in the 'G'day, mate' vocabulary.
What Australians once called a woman, from a girl's name.

definition: A hard outer covering.
note: From Old English sciell. Eggs, nuts and snails all have one.
hints: The covering of an egg or a snail.
A seaside find for a collector.

definition: Covered with or made of shells.
note: From shell plus -y. Describes beaches strewn with shell fragments.
hints: A beach littered with broken bits of clam.
Describes sand mixed with fragments from the sea.

definition: A fortified wine from southern Spain.
note: An English back-formation from 'sherris', which was taken for a plural. It came from Xeres, the old spelling of Jerez.
hints: Offered to guests before Christmas dinner in Britain.
It is named for the Spanish town of Jerez.
example: Gabriel took nothing but the hot soup and a little sherry.

definition: A piece of armour held up for protection.
note: From Old English scield.
hints: Knights carried one.
Protect from harm.

definition: To move or change position; or a period of work.
note: From Old English sciftan, 'to divide' or 'arrange'. It also names a work period, as in 'the night ___'.
hints: A change of position.
The hours someone works at a factory.
example: She shifted slightly in her seat.

definition: A person who secretly promotes something while pretending to be unconnected.
note: Its origin is unknown; it first appears in American fairground slang around 1914.
hints: A fake bidder at an auction.
Plant in the crowd to praise a product.

definition: To give out light.
note: From Old English scinan, 'to shine'. Shoes and the sun do it.
hints: What the sun does.
What polished shoes do.

definition: Bright and reflecting light.
note: From shine plus -y. New coins are this way.
hints: New coins and polished shoes.
What a polished car looks like.

definition: An English county.
note: From Old English scir, 'district'. It is the ending in county names such as Lancashire.
hints: Where Tolkien's hobbits lived.
The final part of several English county names.

definition: To avoid a duty.
note: First recorded around 1633, possibly linked to the verb shark. It describes dodging work.
hints: What a lazy worker may do with chores.
To avoid a responsibility.

definition: A garment for the upper body, with sleeves and a collar.
note: From Old English scyrte, from a Germanic root meaning 'short'. It is a cousin of skirt.
hints: Worn with a tie.
Buttoned up the front.
example: He went to the mall to find a decent shirt for his interview.

definition: The seven-day mourning period in Judaism after a death.
note: From Hebrew shiv'a, 'seven'.
hints: Mourners sit at home for a week.
Hebrew for seven, for a week of grief.
example: The family is sitting shiva.

definition: To tremble, usually from cold or fear.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may be a changed form of an old word for 'chatter'. 'Shiver my timbers' is pirate talk.
hints: What a wet swimmer does on land.
A ghost story might send one down your spine.
example: They stood outside for hours, shivering in the frosty air.

definition: A group of fish; or a shallow area of sea.
note: The fish sense is from Middle Dutch scole, 'troop'; the shallow-water sense is from Old English sceald, 'shallow'. The two words sound alike by accident.
hints: Fish swimming together.
A sandbank near a coast.

definition: A sudden upsetting surprise.
note: From Middle French choquer and Middle Dutch schokken, 'to jolt'. It also means an electric jolt.
hints: What bad news can be.
What an electric jolt delivers.
origin: Middle Dutch schokken, from Middle French choquer

definition: Poorly made or low in quality.
note: Origin unknown; it may come from an old word for loose stone fragments. In the 1800s shoddy was also cheap cloth made from recycled wool.
hints: A cheaply built house that falls apart.
Workmanship that cuts corners.

definition: To fire a weapon; or a new plant growth.
note: From Old English sceotan. It also covers filming a movie and a young plant sprout.
hints: What an archer does with an arrow.
A new plant growth.

definition: The land at the edge of a sea or lake.
note: From Middle English schore, perhaps from a Germanic word for a cliff. The beach lies on it.
hints: Where waves meet the land.
A coast in a sailor's view.

definition: Cut off; having had hair or wool clipped.
note: The old past participle of shear, from Old English scoren. Sheep farmers cut their wool in spring.
hints: A sheep after its spring cut.
Having lost one's locks.
example: Picked up the baby's shorn curls from the floor.

definition: Not long or not tall.
note: From Old English sceort, from a Germanic root. It is cousin to skirt and shirt.
hints: The opposite of tall.
A kind of trousers worn in summer.

definition: Slang for a short person, or an affectionate word for a girlfriend.
note: From short plus -y. In hip-hop slang the word can also be a term for a young woman or friend.
hints: Nickname for someone not very tall.
A word that turns up in rap lyrics.

definition: Used to say what is right or expected.
note: Originally the past tense of shall, from Old English sceolde, 'owed'.
hints: Advice, with less force than must.
The word for moral duty.

definition: To call out loudly.
note: From Middle English shouten, of uncertain origin. In Britain a 'shout' is also a round of drinks.
hints: What a fan does in a stadium.
To yell across a field.

definition: To push roughly.
note: From Old English scufan, 'to push'. It is a rougher form of a push.
hints: What you do in a crowded lift.
A rough push.
example: The people pushed and shoved to get in line.

definition: A tool with a broad blade for digging or scooping.
note: From Old English scofl, related to shove. Snow and earth are moved with it.
hints: What you use to clear a driveway after a blizzard.
A gravedigger's best-known tool.

definition: A brief fall of rain, or a spray of water for washing.
note: From Old English scur, 'rain shower'.
hints: April brings them.
Where you wash standing up.
example: Today there will be frequent showers and some sunny spells.

definition: Flashy and attention-seeking.
note: From show plus -y. A showy outfit is meant to be noticed.
hints: A peacock's feathers might be called this.
A loud, bright outfit.

definition: A thin strip torn or cut off; or to cut into strips.
note: From Old English screade. A cook might do it to cheese, and an office to old papers.
hints: What you do to old documents.
A thin strip of cheese.

definition: A tiny mouse-like animal; or a nagging woman.
note: From Old English screawa, 'shrew'. Shakespeare's play about taming one is a comedy.
hints: A tiny insect-eating mammal.
The Shakespeare play about one being tamed.
origin: Old English sċrēawa, from Norwegian skrugg

definition: Clever and sharp, especially in practical or financial matters.
note: From Middle English shrewed, meaning 'wicked' or 'accursed', from shrew, 'a villain'. Over time the cunning sense lost the wickedness.
hints: A trader who spots a bargain before others.
Shares an origin with a scolding woman in a Shakespeare play.
example: He was too shrewd to go along with them on a road that could lead only to their overthrow.

definition: A small sea creature with a curved body, or a small person.
note: From Middle English shrimpe, of uncertain origin.
hints: Grilled on a skewer.
A small crustacean eaten as seafood.

definition: A holy place or a memorial.
note: From Old English scrin, from Latin scrinium, 'chest for papers'.
hints: Pilgrims visit one.
Place devoted to a saint.
origin: Old English scrīn, from Medieval Latin scrīnium

definition: To become smaller; or a slang word for a psychiatrist.
note: From Old English scrincan.
hints: Wool does it in a hot wash.
A therapist, informally.

definition: A cloth wrapped around a dead body; anything that covers or hides.
note: From Old English scrud, 'garment'. It first meant clothing in general.
hints: A cloth wrapped around a body for burial.
Fog can form one over a hilltop.

definition: A woody plant smaller than a tree.
note: From Old English scrybb, 'bushy plant'. It has several stems, unlike a tree.
hints: Smaller than a tree, bigger than a flower.
A bush in the garden.

definition: To raise the shoulders to show doubt or indifference.
note: From Middle English schruggen, probably from a Scandinavian word. A shrug can say 'I don't know'.
hints: A gesture meaning 'who cares'.
Raising both shoulders in doubt.

definition: Became smaller; the past form of shrink.
note: From Old English scruncan, 'to shrivel'.
hints: What a wool jumper does in a hot wash.
Hollywood put a film's kids through a machine that did this to them.

definition: To remove a husk or shell.
note: Its origin is unknown. It is what you do to corn and oysters.
hints: What you do to an ear of corn.
What you do to an oyster.

definition: To push aside or move elsewhere.
note: From Middle English schonten, 'to jerk or swerve'. A train is shunted onto another track.
hints: A train moved onto a side track.
Moving someone out of the way.
origin: Old English sċunian, from Old English sċyndan

definition: To tell someone to be quiet.
note: Imitative of the hissing sound used to quiet someone. It resembles hush.
hints: What a librarian does.
The sound of a finger to the lips.
example: As Dmitri was talking, the teacher suddenly shushed him.

definition: In a timid, bashful way.
note: Built from shy plus -ly. Shy comes from Old English sceoh, 'timid'.
hints: How a child waves hello.
A way of smiling that avoids eyes.
example: "That's a Christmas present for you, Anne," said Matthew shyly.

definition: A hand tool with a curved blade used to cut grain or long grass.
note: From Old English sicol, borrowed very early from Latin. Paired with a hammer, it formed a famous communist emblem.
hints: It is crossed with a hammer on a red flag.
Reapers swung it by hand before machines took over the harvest.
origin: Old English sicol, from Latin sēcula

definition: Often ill and weak; or unpleasantly sweet.
note: From sick plus -ly. A sickly smell or taste turns the stomach.
hints: A child with weak health.
Describes cloying syrup.
origin: Old English sīcle, from Old Norse sjúkligr

definition: Slang for a person with unpleasant or twisted tastes.
note: From sick plus the informal -o ending.
hints: A slang term for someone considered disturbing.
Informal name for a perverse person.

definition: A long attack in which a place is surrounded.
note: From Old French sege, 'seat', from Latin sedere, 'to sit'. Besiegers sit down outside.
hints: An army camped around a castle.
Troy endured a famous one.

definition: A rugged mountain range.
note: Spanish for 'saw', from the jagged shape.
hints: Nevada has one.
Spanish mountains, saw-toothed.

definition: A tool with small holes for separating fine from coarse bits.
note: From Old English sife. Flour is passed through one, and the phrase 'a memory like one' means forgetful.
hints: A kitchen tool with a mesh for flour.
Said of a poor memory that lets things fall through.

definition: The ability to see; or something seen.
note: From Old English gesihth, 'vision'. It also names the aiming device on a gun.
hints: One of the five senses.
What a tourist attraction is called.

definition: The eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek sigma. In mathematics it stands for a sum, and in statistics for standard deviation.
hints: A Greek letter used for summing.
Written as an angular capital or a looping small letter.

definition: A sign that conveys information.
note: From Latin signalis, from signum, 'sign'.
hints: A flag or light used to communicate.
Bars on a phone.
origin: Old French segnal, from Latin signum

definition: Making no sound.
note: From Latin silens, 'being still'.
hints: Making no noise at all.
What the k in knight is.

definition: A hard mineral compound found in sand and quartz.
note: From Latin silex, 'flint'. It is the main ingredient of glass.
hints: Sand is mostly this, and so is glass.
Sachets of it keep new shoes dry.
origin: New Latin silica, from Latin silex
example: It has high percentage of silica and alumina.

definition: Soft and smooth, like fine fabric.
note: From silk plus -y. Silk was prized as a luxury import from China.
hints: A smooth, glossy hair or voice.
Soft as a fabric made by caterpillars.

definition: Foolish or playful.
note: From Old English saelig, 'happy' or 'blessed'. Its meaning slid from lucky to innocent to foolish over centuries.
hints: A clown's behaviour.
Once meant 'blessed' in Old English.

definition: A shiny white metal and the colour of it.
note: From Old English siolfor, a word shared across Germanic languages.
hints: Element number forty-seven.
What second place wins.

definition: To cook gently just below boiling.
note: From a dialect word simper, probably imitating the soft bubbling. Anger can simmer too.
hints: A stew left on low heat is doing this.
A quiet fury that hasn't boiled over.

definition: Easy, or not complicated.
note: From Latin simplex, 'one-fold'.
hints: Not hard to follow.
Plain and uncomplicated.
origin: Old French simple, from Latin simplex

definition: In an easy way, or merely.
note: From simple plus -ly.
hints: Merely, or in plain fashion.
Plain and uncomplicated.

definition: From a past time up to now; or because.
note: From Middle English sithens, from Old English sith tham, 'after that'. It can start a time clause or a reason.
hints: A word used with dates, as in 'from then'.
Can also mean 'because'.
example: I met him last year, but haven't seen him since.

definition: Wicked, or against religious law.
note: From Old English synful, built from sin plus -ful. It can also jokingly describe rich desserts.
hints: A chocolate cake described on a menu as decadent is this.
A rich dessert is jokingly called this on a menu.
example: He said it was sinful to wear lipstick.

definition: To burn slightly at the surface.
note: From Old English sengan, 'to burn slightly'. Hair and fabric are easily scorched this way.
hints: What a match might do to hair.
A light scorch, not a full burn.

definition: A person who sings.
note: From sing plus -er.
hints: Performs with a voice.
Performs songs in a band.

definition: One only; or not married.
note: From Latin singulus, 'one by one'.
hints: Alone, or one at a time.
Not in a relationship.
origin: Old French sengle, from Latin singulus
example: Single chrysanthemums resemble daisies and may have more than one row of petals.

definition: A person who breaks religious or moral law.
note: From sin plus -er. Church language divides people into saints and these.
hints: Preachers warn it to repent.
Common word in hymns and sermons.
example: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

definition: A hollow space in the bones of the face.
note: Latin for 'curve' or 'bay'. A cold can block them.
hints: What gets blocked in a cold.
A cavity in the skull near the nose.

definition: A loud warning device; also a mythical sea singer.
note: From Greek Seiren, the sea women whose song lured sailors to their doom. The warning device took the name for its wail.
hints: Wails on an ambulance.
A mythical singer who lured sailors.
origin: Old French sereine, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν

definition: A timid or unadventurous person, used mockingly.
note: From sis, short for sister, plus -y.
hints: A schoolyard taunt.
From a childish word for sister.

definition: A female sibling.
note: From Old English sweostor, and related words appear across many languages.
hints: Brother's counterpart.
A girl in your family tree, born of the same parents.
example: My sister is always driving me crazy.

definition: A comedy series built around a regular set of characters in everyday situations.
note: Short for situation comedy, formed in the 1950s. Friends and Fawlty Towers are well-known examples.
hints: Friends and Fawlty Towers are examples.
A TV show with a laugh track.

definition: A person paid to look after children, pets or a house while others are away; also someone posing for a portrait.
note: Formed from sit plus -er. Baby-sitters were so called because they stayed seated in the house.
hints: Parents call one when they plan a night out.
An artist's model holding still for a painting.

definition: Number six in a sequence.
note: From Old English siexta, built on six plus the ordinal ending. It follows the fifth.
hints: The one after the fifth.
A year of school in Britain, before university.

definition: The number after fifty-nine.
note: From Old English sixtig, 'six tens'. It marks the number of minutes in an hour.
hints: Minutes in an hour.
A ripe age for a retirement party.

definition: To glide on a blade or wheels; also a flat fish.
note: From Dutch schaats, from a word for a stilt. The fish is a separate word, from Old Norse.
hints: A blade fixed to a boot.
A flat ray-like fish.
origin: Dutch schaats, from Middle Dutch schāetse

definition: A person who skates.
note: From skate plus -er; skate itself came from Dutch schaats. Ice and roller varieties exist.
hints: Glides on a rink in winter.
A teenager at a half-pipe on a board.
example: I like skating, but I'm not a very good skater.

definition: A quick, rough drawing; or a short comic scene.
note: From Dutch schets, from Italian schizzo.
hints: Pencil drawing.
Comedy troupe performs it.
origin: Dutch schets, from Ancient Greek σχέδιος

definition: A person who glides down snow on long runners.
note: From ski plus -er. Ski is a Norwegian word meaning 'stick of wood'.
hints: Wears goggles on a mountain.
Moves down a slope on boards.
example: The professional skier liked to "hot-dog" down the mountain.

definition: A small light boat.
note: From Middle French esquif, from Italian schifo. It is the same root as the word ship.
hints: A small rowing boat.
A little boat for one or two.
origin: Middle French esquif, from Lombardic skif

definition: The ability to do something well.
note: From Old Norse skil, 'distinction' or 'discernment'. It is gained through practice.
hints: What practice builds.
Something an expert has and a beginner lacks.
example: Where did you pick up that skill?

definition: Very thin; or gossip as in the skinny.
note: From skin plus -y.
hints: Lattes can be made with this kind of milk, and jeans can be cut this way.
Tight jeans style.
example: A child with skinny freckled legs.

definition: A garment that hangs from the waist.
note: From Old Norse skyrta, 'shirt'. It is a cousin of the word shirt.
hints: Worn at the waist, falling below.
Also to avoid a topic by going around it.

definition: To move around stealthily.
note: From Middle English sculken, from a North Germanic word. A group of foxes is also called one.
hints: To sneak around.
What a fox does in the dark.
example: The lonely man skulks down the main street all day.

definition: The bony frame of the head.
note: From Middle English sculle, probably of Scandinavian origin. A pirate flag shows one.
hints: The bone that shelters the brain.
The symbol on a pirate flag.

definition: A small black-and-white animal that sprays a foul-smelling fluid.
note: From an Algonquian word, from a root meaning 'one who squirts'. It reached English in the 1630s.
hints: An animal with a bad smell.
A black animal with a white stripe.

definition: Loose; not taut; or lazy.
note: From Old English slaec, 'lazy' or 'loose'. A rope can be this, and so can a worker.
hints: A rope that hangs loose.
Lazy in doing duties.

definition: Killed, especially in battle.
note: The past participle of slay, from Old English slean, 'to strike'. It belongs to epic poetry.
hints: What a dragon-killer's victim was.
A dragon, once the knight was done.

definition: A skiing race that zigzags between gates, or any twisting course.
note: From Norwegian sla, 'sloping', and lam, 'track'. It now covers canoes and water-skiing too.
hints: A skiing event where racers weave between flags.
Canoeists do this on rapids.
example: Slalom is her strongest Olympic sport.

definition: Casual, informal language.
note: First recorded around 1756 for the special talk of thieves. Its origin is unknown.
hints: Words like 'cool' and 'bro'.
Casual words that dictionaries record later.
example: Their speech was full of slang expressions.

definition: A slope; or a point of view.
note: From Middle English, probably from a Scandinavian word. In news it can mean a particular bias in how a story is told.
hints: A tilt, like a roof.
A bias in a news story.
example: The house was built on a bit of a slant and was never quite level.

definition: To cut with a sweeping stroke; or the symbol /.
note: From Late Middle English, of uncertain origin. It is also the key above the Enter key.
hints: A sword stroke.
The key beside the full stop.
example: They slashed at him with their swords, but only managed to nick one of his fingers.

definition: A grey rock used for roofs; or a list of candidates.
note: From Old French esclate, 'splinter'. 'A clean slate' is a fresh start, from the writing tablets that were wiped.
hints: A grey roofing tile.
What you wipe clean to start over.

definition: A person who covers roofs with slates; or a woodlouse.
note: From slate plus -er. Woodlice are also called slaters in some regions.
hints: A tradesman who fixes slates to a roof.
A little grey creature found under garden stones.

definition: A person owned by another and forced to work.
note: From Medieval Latin sclavus, from the name of the Slavic peoples, many of whom were enslaved in the Middle Ages. It is also used for a device controlled by another.
hints: A person held in bondage.
A device controlled by a master.
origin: Old French esclave, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος

definition: A person who kills, especially in legend.
note: From Old English slaga. Buffy was a vampire one.
hints: Buffy is the vampire kind.
A hero who kills a dragon.
example: Ziri was a powerful demon slayer.

definition: Cheap, seedy and morally dubious.
note: Origin unclear; it first meant flimsy cloth. The sense of being disreputable grew later.
hints: A dingy bar or a dishonest salesman.
A politician caught in a scandal.
example: Sleazy characters hanging around casinos.

definition: A vehicle on runners for sliding over snow, or a heavy hammer.
note: From Middle English slegge, a hammer, though the snow sense is a different word, related to sled. In cricket, to sledge means to taunt.
hints: Dogs pull one across snow.
Santa's ride, in British English.
origin: Dutch sleedse, from Middle Dutch sleedse
example: The sledge ran far better upon the ice; I cannot say the same for the dogs.

definition: Smooth and glossy.
note: A late variant of slick. It is used for hair, cars and designs.
hints: Describes a polished car or an otter's coat.
Smooth, shiny and elegant.

definition: To rest with your eyes closed.
note: From Old English slaepan. People do it for about a third of their lives.
hints: What you do at night.
What a dormouse does all winter.

definition: Tired and ready for bed, or quiet and slow-moving.
note: Simply sleep plus -y. A sleepy town is one where nothing much ever seems to happen.
hints: What a yawn and heavy eyelids suggest.
One of the seven dwarfs.
example: Beginning to feel sleepy.

definition: The part of a garment covering an arm, or a protective cover.
note: From Old English slieve.
hints: Part of a shirt.
What a vinyl record comes in.
origin: Old English slīef; in English since the 10th century
example: The sleeves on my coat are too long.

definition: A thin piece cut from something.
note: From Old French esclice, 'splinter'. It is what you cut from a cake.
hints: A piece of bread.
A wedge of pizza.
example: Jim was munching on a slice of toast.

definition: Smooth and slippery; or polished and clever.
note: From Old English slic, 'smooth'. An oil spill is one on water.
hints: Oil on water may make one.
A clever, too-polished salesman.
example: This rain is making the roads slick.

definition: To glide smoothly; or a playground structure.
note: From Old English slidan. It names a playground feature and a presentation page.
hints: Children go down one at the park.
A page in a presentation.

definition: A small hamburger; also a control moved along a track, or a baseball pitch that breaks sideways.
note: Formed from slide plus -er. The small burger sense is said to come from burgers sold at White Castle.
hints: On a volume control you push it up and down.
A pitcher throws a breaking one to fool the batter.
example: We ordered five sliders.

definition: Small in degree, or to insult by ignoring.
note: From Old Norse slettr, 'smooth'.
hints: A minor change.
To snub someone by ignoring them.
example: There's slight chance that it will work.

definition: A thick slippery goo.
note: From Old English slim, 'mud' or 'sticky stuff'. Snails leave a trail of it.
hints: What a snail leaves behind.
Green ooze in a children's show.

definition: Covered in slime; or repulsively insincere.
note: From slime plus -y. A slimy person is an oily flatterer.
hints: Like a wet frog.
A used-car salesman, in a rude description.
example: The frog's body was all slimy.

definition: To throw; or a strap for holding something.
note: From Middle English slyngen, probably from Old Norse slyngva, 'to hurl'. David used one against Goliath.
hints: What David used against Goliath.
A band that supports a broken arm.

definition: To move quietly and guiltily.
note: From Old English slincan, 'to creep'. A cat that has done wrong may do it.
hints: How a guilty dog leaves the room.
To creep away, ashamed.

definition: A catchy phrase used in advertising or politics.
note: From Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm, 'army cry'.
hints: Used on posters.
A war cry that became a marketing tool.
origin: Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm, from Old Irish slóg
