example: We need a campaign slogan that'll really energize the base.

definition: A single-masted sailing boat.
note: Borrowed from Dutch sloep. It is a doublet of chalupa and shallop.
hints: A one-masted sailboat.
A small ship in the age of sail.

definition: A surface that tilts upward or downward.
note: From the adjective aslope, 'at an angle'. A hill side or a ski run is one.
hints: A hillside that tilts, good for skiing.
Not flat; running at an angle.
example: The road has a very sharp downward slope at that point.

definition: Careless or messy; or wet and runny.
note: From slop, liquid mud, plus -y. Both the wet and the careless senses grew from it.
hints: A teacher's word for an untidy essay.
A 'joe' served in a bun is this kind.
example: The carpenter did a sloppy job of building the staircase.

definition: To splash noisily.
note: Imitative of the sound of liquid moving. Compare splash and splosh.
hints: What water in a bucket does when carried.
The noise of boots in puddles.
example: The water in his bottle sloshed back and forth as he ran.

definition: Laziness; or a slow tree-dwelling animal.
note: From Middle English slouthe, 'laziness', built from slow. One of the seven deadly sins.
hints: One of the seven deadly sins.
An animal that hangs from branches.
example: Hot summer days inspire a sense of sloth in me.

definition: To shed a layer of skin; or a muddy bog.
note: From Middle English slogh, perhaps related to a Germanic word for slipping. The bog sense is a separate old word, said slow.
hints: What a snake does with its old skin.
In Pilgrim's Progress, Christian struggles through a muddy bog of Despond that shares the word.
example: This skin is being sloughed.

definition: Less fast.
note: The comparative of slow.
hints: Not as quick.
A tortoise compared with a hare.

definition: At a low speed.
note: From slow plus -ly.
hints: Not quickly.
Like a tortoise.
example: Please go slow so I can see the sights.

definition: Thick, soft, wet mud or waste.
note: From Middle English slugge or sluche, 'mud, mire', perhaps altered from an older word for slush.
hints: Collects at the bottom of a sewage tank.
Old engine oil turns into this black gunk.

definition: Past tense of slink.
note: The past tense of slink, from Old English slincan, 'to creep'. It is used for sneaking away.
hints: What a thief did on leaving.
What a cat did after being caught.

definition: To drink or eat noisily.
note: From Middle Dutch slurpen, 'to sip'. It is considered polite with noodles in Japan.
hints: The noise of soup eaten with relish.
What you do with a straw at the end of a drink.
example: They sat in the kitchen slurping their spaghetti.

definition: Half-melted snow.
note: Possibly a variant of sludge, or imitative of the sound. It makes city streets messy.
hints: Grey snow in a street.
Wet snow in thaw.
example: As the skiing season drew to an end, there was nothing but slush left on the piste.

definition: In a sneaky or cunning way.
note: From Middle English sleighly, built from sly plus -ly. It suggests a secretive smile.
hints: A secretive smile, as of a fox.
Doing something while hoping no one notices.
example: Everyone was staring at Daniel strangely and smiling slyly.

definition: A sharp slap; or a slight taste.
note: The slap is imitative. The taste sense is from Old English smaec, 'taste'.
hints: A sharp blow with a flat hand.
A touch of flavour or trace of something.

definition: Little in size.
note: From Old English smael, 'narrow' or 'slender'. It is the opposite of large.
hints: The opposite of big.
Tiny, like a mouse.

definition: Clever; or to sting.
note: From Old English smeortan, 'to hurt'. The sense of clever evolved from being sharp or stinging.
hints: What a bright student is.
What a stinging cut does.

definition: To break violently; or a big hit.
note: Probably imitative of the sound. A tennis shot is named for it.
hints: What a hammer does to glass.
A hit show or film.
example: The demolition team smashed the buildings to rubble.

definition: To spread something messy across a surface.
note: From Old English smerian, 'to anoint with fat'. It also means to damage someone's name.
hints: What jam does on a cheek.
To blacken a rival's reputation.
example: The artist smeared paint over the canvas in broad strokes.

definition: The sense that detects odours.
note: From Middle English smellen, of unknown earlier origin. It is the sense of the nose.
hints: What your nose picks up.
Fresh bread has a good one.

definition: Having an unpleasant odour.
note: From smell plus -y. The word for a bad smell is more casual than 'malodorous'.
hints: Gym socks left in a bag.
Gym socks forgotten at the bottom of a bag.

definition: To melt ore to extract metal; also a small silvery fish.
note: From Middle Low German smelten, 'to melt', and it is also the past tense of smell. The fish is a separate word in the same spelling.
hints: What a furnace does to ore.
A small fish in the same family as a salmon.
origin: Middle Dutch smelten, from Old Saxon smeltan

definition: To turn up the corners of the mouth in pleasure.
note: From Middle English smilen, probably from Middle Low German. It is a common show of happiness.
hints: What a joke or a greeting often brings.
A happy curve of the mouth.
origin: Middle High German smielen, from Old High German smielēn

definition: Cheerful and smiling; also a face symbol.
note: From smile plus -y. The yellow smiley face of the 1960s and the emoji both took the name.
hints: The yellow circle with two dots and a curve.
A text message can make one from a colon and bracket.

definition: A self-satisfied, half-hidden smile.
note: From Old English smearcian, 'to smile'. It suggests smugness rather than warmth.
hints: A smug grin after winning.
The expression of someone who knows a secret.

definition: To strike hard; to punish severely.
note: From Old English smitan, 'to smear or daub'; the sense of striking came later. It appears in the Bible when God punishes.
hints: What a god or a hero might do to an enemy.
An old word for a heavy blow.

definition: A person who works metal; also a common surname.
note: From Old English smith, 'craftsman'. It survives in blacksmith and goldsmith.
hints: The one who shapes iron on an anvil.
The most common surname in England.

definition: A loose garment worn over clothes to protect them.
note: From Old English smocc, 'a garment slipped into'. Painters and children wear them.
hints: What a painter wears over clothes.
A loose protective shirt.

definition: The cloud given off by something burning.
note: From Old English smoca. It rises from chimneys and campfires.
hints: What billows from a chimney.
Where there is this, there may be fire.

definition: A person who smokes tobacco; or a device for smoking food.
note: From smoke plus -er. In cooking, a smoker is a box that cooks meat slowly in smoke.
hints: Hangs outside the office door on a break.
Barbecue fans slow-cook brisket in a box of this name.

definition: Filled with smoke, or tasting of it.
note: From smoke plus -y. Smoky bacon and whisky carry this flavour.
hints: A bar in the days before indoor bans.
A flavour of barbecue sauce or whisky.

definition: Having an even surface, free of bumps.
note: From Old English smoth, of unknown origin.
hints: Like polished stone.
Not rough or lumpy.
example: Water as smooth as a mirror.

definition: A small bit of food eaten between meals.
note: From Middle Dutch snacken, 'to snap at'. It is lighter than a meal.
hints: Crisps or fruit between meals.
What you grab when you are peckish.

definition: A slow animal with a spiral shell.
note: From Old English snegel. It carries its home on its back.
hints: A slow animal with a house on its back.
A creature that leaves a slimy trail.

definition: A long limbless reptile.
note: From Old English snaca. A person who betrays is also called one.
hints: A long, legless reptile that hisses.
A traitor, in a rude sense.

definition: Twisting like a snake; or sly.
note: From snake plus -y. A winding road can be this.
hints: A winding mountain road.
Twisting and treacherous.

definition: A trap; also a type of drum.
note: From Old English sneare, 'noose'. The drum takes its name from the wires stretched across the head.
hints: What a hunter sets with a loop of wire.
A drum with a rattling sound.

definition: Sarcastic, mocking remarks.
note: Back-formed from snarky, which came from an old verb meaning to snort or snore. Lewis Carroll used Snark for an imaginary creature in 1876.
hints: Sharp and sarcastic commentary online.
Lewis Carroll's poem hunts one.

definition: To growl angrily; or a tangle.
note: The tangle is from Middle English snarlen, 'to trap', built on the word snare. The growl is a separate word.
hints: A dog baring its teeth.
A tangle in your hair.

definition: To move quietly and secretly.
note: From Old English snican, 'to creep or crawl'. A sneak preview is an early secret showing.
hints: What a burglar does through a house.
An early look at a film.

definition: Acting in a secret, underhanded way.
note: From sneak plus -y. Sneak may be from an old word for creeping.
hints: A cat stealing food from the table.
How a fox is traditionally described.

definition: To show scorn by curling the lip.
note: From Middle English sneren, 'to mock'. It is a scornful expression.
hints: A curled lip of scorn.
A look of contempt at a poor effort.

definition: To burst air out of the nose suddenly and uncontrollably.
note: From Middle English snesen, an altered form of fnesen, from Old English fneosan, 'to sneeze, snort'. The initial f became s.
hints: Dust or pepper might cause one.
What follows a loud 'ah-choo'.
example: Pepper makes me sneeze.

definition: Mockingly critical in a sly way.
note: Probably from a dialect word meaning 'sharp' or 'cutting'. A snide remark is a cheap shot.
hints: A sly, nasty comment.
A cheap jab from the back row.
example: Don't make snide remarks to me.

definition: To breathe in through the nose in short, audible breaths.
note: From Middle English sniffen, imitative of the sound. A cold or a smell can make you do it.
hints: What a dog does at a lamp post.
What a person with a cold does.

definition: To shoot from hiding; also a wading bird.
note: From Old Norse snipa, the bird. Hunters who shot the elusive bird were 'snipers', and the verb followed.
hints: A hidden shooter's act.
A long-billed bird of the marsh.

definition: A shooter who fires from a hidden spot.
note: From snipe, a bird hard to hit, so hunters of snipe were skilled marksmen.
hints: A long-range marksman.
Hunter of a wading bird gave it its name.
example: This game has no sniper rifles, so you can't snipe in it.

definition: To inform on someone; or a person who does so.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to snatch. In Harry Potter, the Golden one is a small winged ball in Quidditch.
hints: A word for a classmate who tells the teacher.
Honour among thieves forbids being one.

definition: A game fish of warm Atlantic waters; also cocking a snook at someone.
note: From Dutch snoek, 'pike'. The rude gesture of thumbing your nose is a separate word.
hints: Fish prized by Florida anglers.
To cock one is to thumb your nose.

definition: To pry into other people's affairs.
note: From Dutch snoepen, 'to eat in secret'. It now suggests prying.
hints: What a nosy neighbour does at a window.
To spy on a private matter.
origin: Dutch snoepen, from Old Norse snópa
example: If I had not snooped on her, I wouldn't have found out that she lied about her degree.

definition: A loud rough breath through the nose.
note: From Middle English snorten, earlier fnorten. Pigs and bulls do it, and so do amused people.
hints: A pig's noise.
What a stifled laugh may turn into.

definition: The long nose of an animal such as a pig.
note: From Middle English snute. Pigs root in the ground with one.
hints: A pig's nose.
A part of a crocodile's face.
example: The pig rooted around in the dirt with its snout.

definition: To put out a candle; or powdered tobacco.
note: The tobacco sense is from Middle Dutch snuffen, 'to sniff'. A candle is put out by pinching its wick.
hints: What you do to a flame.
Ground tobacco taken through the nose.

definition: Covered in or like soap.
note: From soap plus -y. Bath water, bubbles and dishes may be this.
hints: Water full of bubbles.
How hands feel before the tap.
example: His skin was still soapy after the shower.

definition: The game of association football.
note: Shortened from association, with an -er ending added, in the late 1800s.
hints: What Americans call football.
Played with a round ball and goals.

definition: Relating to society, or fond of company.
note: From Latin socialis, 'allied', from socius, 'companion'.
hints: A word for sociable or concerning the community.
Describes media like Instagram.
origin: Middle French social, from Latin sociālis
example: Teresa feels uncomfortable in certain social situations.

definition: A hollow fitting that holds something, such as a plug, bulb or eye.
note: From Anglo-Norman soket, a small spearhead. Your eye sits in one.
hints: What a plug goes into on the wall.
The bony hollow around the eyeball.
origin: Anglo-Norman soket, from Old French soc

definition: A soft, reactive metal and part of table salt.
note: Coined in 1807 by Humphry Davy from soda.
hints: Chemical symbol Na.
Found in salt.
example: Sodium reacts vigorously and exothermically with water.

definition: To make or become softer or gentler.
note: From soft plus the verb ending -en. Voices, butter and blows can all be softened.
hints: Butter left out on a counter will do this.
To lessen a blow with kind words.

definition: Gently or quietly.
note: From soft plus -ly.
hints: Not harshly.
Speak in a whisper.
example: The masseuse was rubbing my back too softly for my liking, so I asked her to go harder.

definition: Wet and heavy.
note: From dialect sog, 'soaked', plus -y. Neglected cereal and sandwiches often end up so.
hints: Cereal left in milk too long.
A sandwich left in the rain.

definition: Comfort in sadness or loss.
note: From Old French solas, from Latin solacium, 'comfort'. People find it in music, friends or faith.
hints: Found in a hot drink after a bad day.
Comfort offered at a funeral.
origin: Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium

definition: Relating to the sun.
note: From Latin solaris, from sol, 'sun'. Panels turn sunlight into power.
hints: Panels on a roof turn sunlight into electricity.
Our system is named for this star.

definition: A metal alloy melted to join other pieces of metal.
note: From Old French soudure, from souder, 'to solder'. The word comes from Latin solidare, 'to make solid'.
hints: An electronics hobbyist heats it with an iron.
Fixes wires onto a circuit board.
origin: Old French soldure, from Old French souder

definition: Only; alone.
note: From sole plus -ly.
hints: Exclusively.
Not shared with anyone.
example: They need to be able to irrigate without relying solely on rain.

definition: Serious and dignified, without any joking.
note: From Latin sollemnis, 'celebrated at fixed times', so first used for annual religious rites.
hints: The mood at a funeral.
Describes a promise or an oath taken with weight.
origin: Old French solempne, from Latin sōlemnis
example: The judge was solemn as he pronounced sentence.

definition: Firm and not liquid or gas.
note: From Latin solidus, 'firm'. Ice is one, but steam is not.
hints: What ice is, compared with water.
A state of matter that holds its shape.
origin: Old French solide, from Latin solidus
example: Almost all metals are solid at room temperature.

definition: To find the answer to a problem.
note: From Latin solvere, 'to loosen or untie'. A mystery or puzzle can be settled by it.
hints: What you do with a puzzle.
What a detective does to a case.
example: Did you solve the problem?

definition: Dark, serious and gloomy in mood.
note: From French sombre, 'dark', from Latin sub umbra, 'under shade'. Sombre is the British spelling.
hints: Suits worn at a funeral.
A tone of mourning.
example: A suit of somber black.

definition: A way of finding objects underwater using sound.
note: An acronym for 'sound navigation and ranging'. Submarines and fishing boats rely on it.
hints: A submarine's ping.
How a ship finds the seabed.
example: They were able to detect the sunken wreck using sonar.

definition: A piece of classical music for one or two instruments.
note: From Italian sonata, 'sounded', as opposed to a cantata, which is sung. Beethoven's 'Moonlight' is a famous piano one.
hints: Beethoven wrote thirty-two for piano.
Played, not sung, as opposed to a cantata.
example: I've just listened to a beautiful Beethoven sonata.

definition: Relating to sound.
note: From Latin sonus, 'sound'. A sonic boom is made by an aircraft passing the speed of sound.
hints: A boom from a fast jet.
Having to do with noise.

definition: Earlier; or preferably.
note: From soon plus -er.
hints: Earlier than expected.
Preferably, in the phrase would rather.

definition: An old word for truth.
note: From Old English soth, 'true'. It survives in 'forsooth' and in 'soothsayer', one who tells the truth of the future.
hints: An archaic word for truth.
A person who foretells the future was named for it, with 'sayer'.
example: "Thou speakest sooth." "Why are you talking like that, Tom?"

definition: To calm or comfort; to ease pain.
note: From Old English sothian, 'to prove true', from soth, 'true'. It once meant to agree with someone, then to flatter, and finally to calm.
hints: Aloe on sunburn does it, and so does a lullaby for a crying baby.
What a warm bath does to tired muscles.

definition: Covered in soot.
note: From soot plus -y. A chimney sweep would be this.
hints: A chimney sweep's face.
A black smudge from a fire.

definition: Very greatly; painfully.
note: From Old English sarlice, formed from sore plus -ly.
hints: Used with 'missed' or 'tempted'.
How a team needs a good striker when losing.
example: I missed him sorely.

definition: Deep sadness.
note: From Old English sorg.
hints: Grief after a loss.
A feeling of great sadness.

definition: Feeling regret; or poor and pitiful.
note: From Old English sarig, 'sore' or 'grieved', related to sore. It is not related to sorrow.
hints: What you say after stepping on a toe.
A word that begins an apology.

definition: A casual way of saying 'sort of'.
note: A written form of the spoken reduction of sort of. It means somewhat.
hints: A spoken way to say 'in a way'.
A relaxed way to hedge.
example: The portraits on the wall aren’t that good, but they’re just sorta cool to have around.

definition: Noise; also healthy or reliable.
note: The noise sense is from Latin sonus. The healthy sense comes from Old English gesund, 'healthy'.
hints: What an ear picks up.
As in 'safe and ___', in good shape.

definition: The place where something begins.
note: From Old French sourse, from Latin surgere, 'to rise'.
hints: Where a river starts.
A reporter protects this.
origin: Old French sorse, from Latin surgō
example: The accused refused to reveal the source of the illegal drugs she was selling.

definition: The direction opposite north.
note: From Old English suth. It is the way to Antarctica from the equator.
hints: Penguins live near the pole at this end of the map.
The way swallows go in winter.

definition: A person who scatters seed.
note: From Old English sawere, built from sow plus -er. A famous parable features one.
hints: A farmer scattering grain.
The farmer in a famous parable.

definition: The area beyond Earth; or an empty area.
note: From Old French espace, from Latin spatium. It can also be a gap between words.
hints: Where the stars are.
The gap between words on a page.

definition: A digging tool with a flat blade; also a card suit.
note: From Old English spadu. The card suit is a different word, from Italian spada, 'sword'.
hints: What a gardener uses to dig.
A black card suit.

definition: To slap, especially on the bottom as punishment.
note: Probably imitative of the sound of a slap.
hints: What a parent might do to a naughty child.
Smack on the bottom.

definition: Thinly spread; scarce.
note: From Latin sparsus, 'scattered', from spargere, 'to scatter'. Hair, crowds and furniture can be sparse.
hints: A beard patchy and thin is described so.
A desert with few trees has this kind of vegetation.
example: It makes things easier if your matrix is sparse.

definition: A sudden involuntary muscle contraction.
note: From Greek spasmos, from spaein, 'to draw or pull'. It also means a sudden burst of activity.
hints: A twitch in a muscle.
A sudden painful clench.
origin: Old French spasme, from Ancient Greek σπασμός
example: Jessica went into spasms after eating a peanut.

definition: A sudden rush or large number of things at once.
note: Originally a Scots and Northern English word for a river in flood.
hints: Rivers do this in heavy rain, and so do events.
Burglaries, for example, can come in one.

definition: To talk.
note: From Old English specan, probably an altered form of an older word sprecan. It is what you do with your voice.
hints: What you do to give a talk.
What a person does at a podium.

definition: A long pointed weapon for thrusting or throwing.
note: From Old English spere. Hunters and soldiers carried them for thousands of years.
hints: A weapon thrown by hunters.
A long shaft with a sharp point.

definition: A tiny spot.
note: From Old English specca, 'small spot'. Dust leaves one.
hints: A tiny dot of dust.
A dot barely visible on a window.

definition: The act or ability of speaking, or a talk.
note: From Old English spaec, related to speak.
hints: A politician gives one.
Spoken communication.

definition: How fast something moves.
note: From Old English sped, which meant 'success' or 'prosperity'. 'Godspeed' wished a traveller good luck.
hints: What a gauge on a dashboard shows.
How fast a car goes.

definition: Moving or done quickly.
note: From Old English spedig, 'successful, prosperous', since speed once meant good fortune. A 'speedy recovery' is wished to sick friends.
hints: Wished to someone in a get-well card.
A fast courier or a quick reply fits this description.
example: A speedy errand boy.

definition: A magic formula; or a short period of time.
note: From Old English spel, 'story' or 'speech'. A word spoken with power became a charm.
hints: What a wizard casts.
A short stretch of weather.
origin: Old English spell; in English since the 16th century
example: He whispered a spell as he moved his hands.

definition: An ancient grain; or past tense of spell.
note: The grain is from Old English spelt, a kind of wheat. The past tense form is a British spelling of spelled.
hints: An old variety of wheat.
The British past of a word about letters.
origin: Old English spelt, from Late Latin spelta

definition: To pay out money; or to pass time.
note: From Old English, partly from Latin expendere, 'to weigh out'. You can do it with money or hours.
hints: What a shopper does.
What you do with a holiday week.
origin: Old English spendan, from Latin expendere
example: I've already spent hundreds of dollars buying dog chow.

definition: The male reproductive cell; also the sperm whale's waxy oil.
note: From Greek sperma, 'seed'.
hints: Reproductive cell of a male.
The whale named after this fluid.
origin: Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα
example: A sperm is mostly a nucleus surrounded by little other cellular material.

definition: A perfectly round solid shape, like a ball.
note: From Greek sphaira, 'ball'.
hints: The shape of a globe.
A basketball is one.
origin: Old French sphere, from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα; in English since the 14th century

definition: A strong flavouring from a plant.
note: From Old French espice, from Latin species, 'kind'. Pepper and cinnamon are famous ones.
hints: Pepper and cinnamon.
What makes a curry hot.
origin: Old French espice, from Latin speciēs

definition: Hot with flavourings.
note: From spice plus -y. Chilli peppers make food this way.
hints: A hot curry.
A food with a kick.

definition: An eight-legged creature that spins webs.
note: From Old English spithra, from spinnan, 'to spin'.
hints: Makes a web.
Itsy bitsy one in a rhyme.

definition: A long, practiced sales speech.
note: Borrowed from German Spiel, 'game' or 'play', perhaps via Yiddish. It describes a patter delivered with practice.
hints: A salesperson's patter.
A well-rehearsed pitch.
origin: German Spiel, from Old High German spil

definition: A sharp pointed piece of metal; or a sudden sharp rise.
note: From Old Norse spik, 'nail'. Sprinters wear shoes with them, and a graph can show a sudden one.
hints: What a runner wears on shoes for grip.
A sudden jump on a chart.
example: The trap was lined with spikes.

definition: Covered with sharp points.
note: From spike plus -y. Hedgehogs and punk hair are this.
hints: A hedgehog's coat.
Hair styled with gel.
origin: Middle Dutch spiker, from Latin spīca
example: The leaves of this ivy are very spiky.

definition: To let liquid fall out by accident.
note: From Old English spillan, 'to destroy or waste'. The word shifted from killing to wasting to letting fall.
hints: What you do to a cup of tea.
Something to avoid crying over, in a proverb.

definition: Poured out accidentally; the past form of spill.
note: The past form of spill. A proverb warns not to cry over milk in this state.
hints: The state of milk in a proverb about regret.
A British past form of a word about accidents with drinks.

definition: Relating to the backbone.
note: From Latin spinalis, from spina, 'thorn'.
hints: Concerning a column of vertebrae.
Cord running through your back.

definition: Covered in sharp spines.
note: From spine plus -y. Cacti and sea urchins are this.
hints: A cactus or an urchin.
Prickly all over.

definition: A curve winding around a point.
note: From Latin spiralis, 'coiled'.
hints: Shape of a snail shell.
A staircase may wind this way.
origin: Middle French spirale, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα

definition: A tall pointed tower on a church.
note: From Old English spir, 'stalk' or 'shoot'. A church steeple reaches skyward like one.
hints: The pointed top of a church tower.
Salisbury's is famously tall.
origin: Old English spīr; in English since the 16th century
example: The spire of the church rose high above the town.

definition: The soul, or a ghost, or strong liquor.
note: From Latin spiritus, 'breath'.
hints: A ghost, or a team's morale.
Whisky and gin are called this.
origin: Old French espirit, from Latin spīritus

definition: A kind of dog with a pointed muzzle, thick fur and curled tail.
note: From German Spitz, meaning pointed. Pomeranians and Samoyeds are spitz breeds.
hints: A fluffy dog breed type.
Group that includes the Pomeranian.

definition: To scatter water, or the sound of it.
note: Probably an imitation of the sound.
hints: A child jumping in a puddle.
A small amount of something added.

definition: The sound of a soft thing hitting a flat surface.
note: Imitative, related to an older verb meaning to spread flat. It is the noise of a tomato landing.
hints: A tomato hitting the floor.
A wet slap of a dropped pie.
example: I didn't see the egg fall, but I heard the splat when it hit the floor.

definition: An organ near the stomach that filters blood, or a mood of bitter anger.
note: From Latin splen and Greek splen. Old medicine held that this organ produced bad temper, so venting your spleen means releasing anger.
hints: Sits on the left side, under the ribs.
Ancient doctors blamed it for gloom.
origin: Anglo-Norman espleen, from Ancient Greek σπλήν

definition: To divide; or to break along a line.
note: From Middle Dutch splitten, recorded since about 1567. You can do it to a log, a bill, or a banana dessert.
hints: What you do to a bill among friends.
What an axe does to a log.
origin: Middle Dutch splitten, from Middle Low German splitten

definition: To ruin; or to pamper.
note: From Latin spolium, 'plunder'. Food goes off, and children can be overindulged by it.
hints: What happens to milk left out.
What you do to a grandchild with sweets.
origin: Old French espoillier, from Latin spoliō; in English since the 16th century

definition: Past of speak; also a rod in a wheel.
note: The verb is the past tense of speak. The wheel part is from Old English spaca, a different word.
hints: Joins the hub of a bicycle wheel to the rim.
What a person did at a podium.

definition: Expressed in words aloud.
note: The past participle of speak.
hints: Said out loud.
Not written.

definition: A soft, absorbent material or sea animal used for washing; also a light cake.
note: From Greek spongos, via Latin. Real ones are sea animals.
hints: Found at the kitchen sink and on the sea floor.
A cake as light as it is airy.
origin: Old English spunge, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά

definition: A light-hearted parody; or a trick.
note: Coined in 1884 by the English comedian Arthur Roberts as the name of a card game of trickery. It then came to mean a hoax.
hints: A comic imitation of a film.
A hoax played for laughs.

definition: A ghost; or to frighten.
note: Borrowed from Dutch spook, 'ghost'. It can also name a secret agent.
hints: What a ghost story might feature.
To startle a horse.
origin: Dutch spook, from Middle Dutch spooc
example: The building was haunted by a couple of spooks.

definition: Eerie and ghostly.
note: From spook plus -y. Spook came from Dutch for ghost.
hints: What Halloween is meant to be.
A graveyard at midnight.
example: When there are no men around, the night is somewhat spooky.

definition: A tiny reproductive cell of a fungus or plant.
note: From Greek spora, 'seed'. Mushrooms and ferns release them.
hints: What a mushroom scatters to reproduce.
A tiny seed-like particle from a fern.
origin: New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά

definition: A competitive physical activity.
note: Short for disport, from Old French, 'to amuse oneself'. It originally meant any pastime.
hints: Football or tennis.
What the Olympics celebrates.
origin: Old French desporter, from Latin deportāre
example: Basketball is her favorite sport, and she also enjoys various other sports as well.

definition: Fond of sport, or stylish in a way suited to it.
note: From sport plus -y. It can also describe a small, fast car.
hints: A word for a child who joins every team.
What a two-seater convertible might be called.
example: He's perfect for me, as he's both studious and sporty.

definition: A husband or wife.
note: From Old French spous, from Latin sponsus, 'betrothed'.
hints: A marriage partner.
Wife or husband.
origin: Anglo-Norman espus m, from Latin spōnsus m

definition: A tube from which liquid pours.
note: From Middle English spouten, from Middle Dutch. A kettle has one, and so does a whale.
hints: The part of a teapot for pouring.
What a whale blows through its blowhole.
example: I dropped my china teapot, and its spout broke.

definition: A fine mist of liquid.
note: From Middle Dutch spraeyen, 'to sprinkle'. It also names a bunch of flowers.
hints: What an aerosol can does.
A cluster of flowers in a bouquet.
example: The sailor could feel the spray from the waves.

definition: To open out over a surface, or a soft food for bread.
note: From Old English spraedan.
hints: Butter on toast.
Cover a wide area.
origin: Old English sprǣdan; in English since the 13th century

definition: A short period of unrestrained activity, especially shopping.
note: Of uncertain origin; it was first recorded in the early nineteenth century. It suggests wild abandon.
hints: A shopping binge.
An outing of reckless indulgence.

definition: A small twig or shoot.
note: From Middle English sprigge, of uncertain origin. A cook adds a small one of parsley.
hints: A small piece of parsley.
A little twig used to garnish a dish.

definition: A season, a coil of metal, a water source, or a leap.
note: From Old English springan, 'to leap or burst forth'.
hints: A coil in a mattress, or a season of blossoms.
Where a stream begins, or a jump.
origin: Old English spring, from Old English spryng

definition: A short fast run.
note: From Old Norse spretta, 'to jump up'.
hints: A 100-metre race.
A burst of speed.

definition: A small elf-like spirit; also a lemon-lime soda brand name and a graphic image in a game.
note: From Old French esprit, from Latin spiritus. It is a doublet of spirit.
hints: Fairies and pixies belong to the same family.
In an old video game, a small moving picture of a character.
origin: Old French esprit, from Latin spīritus

definition: A new shoot growing from a seed or plant.
note: From Middle English sproute; related Dutch and Low German forms exist. Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like buds.
hints: Beans do this on damp paper.
The little green things in a Christmas dinner.
origin: Middle Dutch sprute, from Middle Low German sprûte

definition: A tall conifer; or neat and smart in appearance.
note: The tree name comes from 'Pruce', an old name for Prussia, where the wood was imported from. The adjective sense came a bit later and may be related.
hints: Many families put one up at Christmas.
As an adjective, describes someone smartly turned out.

definition: The past participle of spring; or fitted with springs.
note: From the verb spring, an Old English word. 'Sprung' also means a mattress or floor with springs inside.
hints: A trap that has been triggered has been this.
A well-cushioned bed or dance floor is described this way.

definition: To gush out suddenly; or a short burst of effort.
note: From earlier spirt, 'to sprout'. A runner makes one to overtake near the finish.
hints: What water does from a cut hose.
A final dash near the finish line.

definition: A small group working together.
note: From French escouade, from Spanish escuadra, 'square'. It first named a troop drawn up in a square.
hints: A football team's group of players.
A group of soldiers or police.

definition: A four-sided shape with equal sides.
note: From Old French esquarre, from Latin quadra, 'a square'.
hints: Four right angles.
A plaza in a town.
example: A checkerboard has 64 squares.

definition: To crush flat; also a vegetable, a racket sport, and a fruit drink.
note: The verb comes from Old French esquacher, 'to crush'. The vegetable is unrelated, from a Narragansett word.
hints: What you do to a bug, a hat or a plan.
A pumpkin's relative, or a game played in a walled court.
origin: Old French esquacher, from Latin ex

definition: To crouch low; or short and wide.
note: From Old French esquatir, 'to crush or flatten'. It also names a gym exercise and settling in an empty building.
hints: A deep knee bend at the gym.
What a short, stocky shape is called.
origin: Old French esquatir, from Latin coāctus

definition: A small firework that fizzes; or a short satire.
note: Possibly imitative of a small explosion. A damp one fizzles without going off, which gave the word its sense of a weak joke.
hints: A firework that fizzles.
A short, witty satirical piece.
example: English Navy squibs set fire to two dozen enemy ships in a Dutch harbor during the 16th-century battle against the Spanish Armada.

definition: A sea creature with ten arms.
note: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the seventeenth century. It squirts ink.
hints: A sea creature that squirts ink.
Served as calamari.

definition: A knight's attendant; or a landowner in the English countryside.
note: From Old French escuier, 'shield-bearer', from Latin scutum, 'shield'. A squire carried a knight's shield before becoming a knight himself.
hints: Sancho Panza served Don Quixote in this role.
The big landowner of a village in Austen's England.
origin: Old French escuier, from Latin scūtārius

definition: To shoot out liquid in a thin quick stream; also a small jet, or a small or annoying person.
note: From Middle English squirten, of uncertain origin and probably imitating the sound.
hints: A lemon does it in your eye if you squeeze it badly.
A water pistol or a ketchup bottle can do it.

definition: Steady and not likely to change; or a building for horses.
note: From Latin stabilis, 'standing firm'.
hints: Where a racehorse sleeps.
Not likely to wobble or change.
example: He was in a stable relationship.

definition: A tidy pile.
note: From Old Norse stakkr, 'haystack'. Pancakes and plates are piled in them.
hints: A pile of pancakes.
A tall pile of books.

definition: The employees of a business; or a long stick.
note: From Old English staef, 'stick' or 'letter'. It also names the lines on which music is written.
hints: The workers at a shop.
A stick used by a wizard.

definition: Serious, steady and rather dull.
note: An old spelling of 'stayed', the past participle of stay. It describes someone settled in their ways.
hints: A sober, conventional person.
The opposite of wild.
example: Tom's a fine babysitter, just very serious, almost staid, and the kids think he's a bore.

definition: A step in a flight.
note: From Old English staeger, 'step', from a word meaning 'to climb'. You go up a flight of them.
hints: One step in a flight.
What you climb in a house.
example: As the elevator is out of order, we must go down the stairs.

definition: A set of steps connecting floors.
note: From Old English staeger, with an -s ending added later.
hints: Climbed to reach the bedrooms.
Steps between two floors.
example: There're two cats at the top of the stairs.

definition: No longer fresh.
note: From Old French estale, 'in place', as in standing too long. Bread and jokes both go this way.
hints: Bread left out for days.
A joke told too many times.

definition: The stem of a plant; or to follow someone secretly.
note: From Middle English stalke, of uncertain earlier origin. The following sense is a different word, from Old English.
hints: The stem of celery.
What a predator does to its prey.

definition: A market table; or to delay.
note: From Old English steall, 'standing place'. A car engine can do it, and so can a speaker buying time.
hints: A table in a market.
What an engine does when it cuts out.

definition: The way someone stands, or a stated position.
note: From Italian stanza, 'standing'.
hints: Feet apart in a batting position.
Political position.

definition: To be upright on your feet.
note: From Old English standan. It also names a stall, a position, or a platform.
hints: What you do when the anthem plays.
A position taken on an issue.

definition: Past tense of stink.
note: From Old English stanc, the past of stincan, 'to smell'. It describes a foul smell.
hints: What rotten eggs did in the fridge.
A past form of a word about foul smells.

definition: A common bacterium that can infect skin.
note: Short for staphylococcus, from Greek for a bunch of grapes, after how it clusters.
hints: Bacteria that cause boils.
A clump of germs that look like grapes.
example: Staph infections in hospitals pose a significant threat to the health of postoperative surgical patients.

definition: A basic food or main item always kept in supply; also a small wire fastener for papers.
note: The goods sense comes from Old French estaple, a market town. The fastener sense is a separate word, from Old English stapol, 'post'.
hints: Rice in many kitchens, or the wire in an office desk.
A wire pushed through a stack of office paper.
origin: Anglo-Norman estaple, from Late Latin stapula
example: Rice is a staple in the diet of many cultures.

definition: A white carbohydrate in potatoes, rice and bread; also stiffener for fabric.
note: From Old English words meaning 'stiff'. Laundry starch makes collars hold their shape.
hints: Stiffens a shirt collar after ironing.
Found in bread, rice and pasta.

definition: To look fixedly.
note: From Old English starian, 'to gaze'. It is considered rude when done at strangers.
hints: What you do at an eclipse you should not look at.
To gaze rudely.
example: The students stared at the teacher with amazement.

definition: Severe or plain; or complete.
note: From Old English stearc, 'stiff' or 'strong'. A bare room or a sharp contrast can be this.
hints: A bare white room.
An obvious, harsh contrast.

definition: Full of stars, or shaped like one.
note: From star plus -y, first seen in Middle English. A famous painting by Van Gogh uses it in its title.
hints: Describes a clear night far from city lights.
Van Gogh gave it to a night in Saint-Rémy.
example: Despite a starry cast, the film performed poorly at the box office.

definition: To begin.
note: From Old English styrtan, 'to leap up'. A sudden jump gave the word its sense of beginning.
hints: What you do at the line of a race.
The opposite of finish.

definition: To suffer or die from lack of food.
note: From Old English steorfan, which meant to die of any cause. It narrowed to hunger.
hints: What a famine does to a population.
Originally meant simply to die.
example: The political prisoners starved to death.

definition: A hidden supply.
note: Of unknown origin. It may blend 'stow' and 'cache'. People keep one of treats or cash.
hints: A hidden hoard of sweets.
A secret store.
example: They had quite a stash of food saved up for emergencies.

definition: A condition; or a country's government and territory.
note: From Latin status, 'condition'. It can also mean to say something formally.
hints: What a nation is called politically.
The condition something is in.
origin: Old French estat, from Latin stātus

definition: Not moving or changing; also crackling electricity.
note: From Greek statikos, 'causing to stand'.
hints: Crackles on a radio.
A balloon sticks to a wall because of it.
origin: Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός

definition: Statistics.
note: A clipping of statistics. Sports fans quote them.
hints: Numbers a sports fan cites.
Figures that describe a game.

definition: A carved or cast figure of a person or animal.
note: From Latin statua, from stare, 'to stand'.
hints: Stands in a town square.
Bronze or marble likeness.
origin: Old French statue, from Latin statua

definition: Standing or position, or the current state of something.
note: Latin for 'standing', from stare, 'to stand'.
hints: Your rank in a hierarchy.
Update shown on a social profile.
example: Superstition is highly correlated with economic status.

definition: A narrow strip of wood; or to fend off.
note: A back-formation from staves, the plural of staff. 'Stave off' means to hold danger at a distance.
hints: A strip of wood in a barrel.
To keep hunger or danger away for a while.

definition: The place or role of another.
note: From Old English stede, 'place'. It survives in 'in his stead' and in 'homestead'.
hints: A word in an old phrase about taking another's place.
The tail end of the word for a farm and its buildings.
example: Can you go in my stead?

definition: Firm and not shaking.
note: From stead, 'a place', plus -y.
hints: Not wobbling.
Calm and reliable.
example: Hold the ladder steady while I go up.

definition: A thick slice of meat.
note: From Old Norse steik, 'roast on a stick'. Beef is the best known.
hints: A thick cut of beef on a plate.
What a grill sizzles.

definition: To take something that is not yours.
note: From Old English stelan. In baseball, a runner can do it to a base.
hints: What a thief does.
What a runner does to a base.

definition: Hot water vapour.
note: From Old English steam, 'vapour'. Engines once ran on it.
hints: What rises from a kettle.
What drove old trains.

definition: Hot and misty; or erotic.
note: From steam plus -y. A steamy bathroom has fogged mirrors, and a steamy novel is racy.
hints: What a bathroom is after a hot shower.
A romance novel might be described this way.

definition: A strong alloy of iron.
note: From Old English stiele. It builds bridges and skyscrapers.
hints: A strong alloy for bridges.
Iron mixed with carbon.

definition: Rising sharply; or to soak in a liquid.
note: From Old English steap, 'high' or 'lofty'. Tea leaves are soaked, and a high price is also called it.
hints: A hill hard to climb.
What tea does in a pot.
example: The steep attic stairs.

definition: To guide a vehicle; or a young bull.
note: From Old English steoran, 'to guide'. The animal sense is separate, from Old English steor.
hints: What you do with a wheel.
A young bull raised for beef.
origin: Old English stēoran, from Old English stēor

definition: A large beer mug.
note: From German Stein, 'stone', short for stoneware jug. It is associated with Oktoberfest.
hints: Raised at Oktoberfest.
A mug for beer.

definition: A strong, nasty smell.
note: From Old English stenc, which oddly could mean any smell, including a pleasant one. The bad sense won out over time.
hints: Rotten eggs give it off.
A landfill in summer.

definition: A tiny tube placed inside a blood vessel to hold it open.
note: Its origin is unclear; it may be named after the dentist Charles Stent.
hints: Surgeons insert one to keep an artery from narrowing.
A small mesh tube used in heart procedures.

definition: A sound system with two channels.
note: Short for stereophonic, from Greek stereos, 'solid'.
hints: Speakers on the left and right.
A hi-fi with left and right speakers.

definition: Strict and severe; or the back of a ship.
note: The strict sense is from Old English styrne. The ship sense is a separate word, from Old Norse.
hints: A teacher who allows no nonsense.
The rear of a boat.

definition: A thin piece of wood; or to attach.
note: From Old English sticca, 'twig'. As a verb, it describes glue doing its work.
hints: A twig from a tree.
What glue does.
example: A stick of dynamite.

definition: Adhesive, or awkward.
note: From stick plus -y.
hints: Covered in glue or syrup.
A difficult situation.

definition: Rigid and hard to bend.
note: From Old English stif. A neck after a long drive can be so.
hints: How your neck feels after a long drive.
Not flexible.

definition: A mark of shame or disgrace attached to a person or condition.
note: From Greek stigma, a mark pricked or branded into skin, such as one put on slaves. The meaning moved from the physical brand to the social one.
hints: What society hangs on people it looks down on.
Once a literal brand burned into the skin.
origin: Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα

definition: Not moving; or even so.
note: From Old English stille, 'quiet' or 'motionless'. It is also a distilling apparatus.
hints: Motionless, like a pond.
A word meaning 'nevertheless'.
example: Sit there and stay still!

definition: A tall pole with a footrest for walking high off the ground; or a post holding up a building.
note: From Middle English stilte. Circus performers walk on them, and some houses stand over water on them.
hints: What a circus performer walks on to look tall.
A post that raises a house above a flood.
example: He was so tall I thought he was on stilts.

definition: To pierce skin with a sharp point, as a bee does; or a police trap.
note: From Old English sting, 'a piercing'. A sting can also mean a police operation to catch criminals.
hints: What a bee or a nettle does.
A police trick to catch a crook.

definition: Unwilling to spend or share.
note: Of uncertain origin; perhaps from a dialect form of sting. Scrooge was the classic example.
hints: Scrooge before his night of ghosts.
Leaves a tiny tip.
example: She practices economy without being stingy.

definition: To give off a strong foul smell.
note: From Old English stincan, which originally meant just 'to smell', pleasant or not. Only later did it turn bad.
hints: What rotten eggs do.
A bad smell.

definition: Smelling bad.
note: From stink plus -y, found in Middle English. Dutch and Low German have near-identical words.
hints: A word for gym socks.
Cheese or feet may earn it.

definition: A fixed period of work.
note: From Old English styntan, 'to make blunt', which led to the sense of limiting. You may do a stint abroad.
hints: A short spell in a job.
A spell on duty, like a tour.

definition: The stalk of a mushroom or similar plant.
note: From Latin stipes, meaning a post or stock.
hints: Part of a mushroom between cap and ground.
The part between cap and ground.

definition: A single loop of thread in sewing, knitting or stitching up a wound; also a sudden pain in the side.
note: From Old English stice, 'a prick or stab'. The painful kind in your side comes from running.
hints: A doctor may use several after a deep cut.
A runner clutches a sharp pain in the ribs with this name.
example: I cut myself badly while cooking and needed to go to hospital to get stitches.

definition: A supply of goods; or a share in a company; or a flavoured broth.
note: From Old English stocc, 'tree trunk' or 'post'. It has many senses, from shop inventory to soup base.
hints: Goods on a shop's shelves.
Soup is built on a good one.
example: We have a stock of televisions on hand.

definition: A person who endures pain without complaint.
note: From Greek Stoikos, after the Painted Porch in Athens where the philosophers taught. They preached calm acceptance of fate.
hints: Someone who bears hardship without complaint.
A philosopher like Marcus Aurelius.
origin: Latin stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός

definition: To tend a fire by adding fuel.
note: From Middle Dutch stoken, 'to poke'. You can also stir up feelings with it.
hints: What you do to a furnace with coal.
To fuel a fire or an argument.
origin: Dutch stoker, from Middle Dutch stoken

definition: Past tense of steal; also a long wrap worn over the shoulders.
note: The past tense is from Old English stal. The garment is from Latin stola, a different word.
hints: What the thief did to the jewels.
A fur wrap for a lady's shoulders.

definition: Taken without permission.
note: The past participle of steal.
hints: What a thief takes.
Not paid for.

definition: To step down heavily.
note: A variant of stamp, first recorded in 1803. A foot pounding the floor does it.
hints: What an angry child does.
A heavy walk that shakes the floor.
example: The men stomped through the snow in their heavy boots.

definition: A hard piece of rock.
note: From Old English stan. It is also a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds.
hints: A pebble on a beach.
A British measure of weight.
example: He wanted a special stone to mark the site.

definition: Slang for a person who often smokes cannabis.
note: From stone, to be 'stoned' meaning intoxicated. It was first slang in the 1960s.
hints: A character in a comedy film who lounges on a sofa.
A slang term for someone fond of getting high.

definition: Full of rocks; or cold and unfeeling.
note: From stone plus -y. A stare can be this way as can a field.
hints: A field full of rocks.
An unfriendly, cold silence.

definition: A seat with no back.
note: From Old English stol, 'seat' or 'throne'. A bar often has high ones.
hints: A seat in a bar.
What a milkmaid sat on.

definition: To bend forward and down; also the steps at a building's front door.
note: The verb is from Old English stupian. The porch sense is American, from Dutch stoep.
hints: What you do to pick up a coin.
The steps at a New York brownstone.
example: He stooped to tie his shoe-laces.

definition: A place where goods are sold; or to put away for later.
note: From Old French estorer, 'to build or furnish'. It is both a shop and a verb for saving.
hints: Where you buy groceries.
What a squirrel does with nuts.
example: This building used to be a store for old tires.

definition: One floor of a building.
note: From Medieval Latin historia, perhaps because early buildings had painted tiers telling stories. The American spelling drops the e.
hints: A skyscraper has many of these.
What a building has more of when it is tall.
origin: Medieval Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορίᾱ
example: For superstitious reasons, many buildings number their 13th storey as 14, bypassing 13 entirely.

definition: A large wading bird with long legs and bill.
note: From Old English storc. Folklore says it brings babies.
hints: A bird said to deliver babies.
A tall bird nesting on chimney tops.
example: When the clock tower struck ten, the stork flew off to Africa.

definition: A violent disturbance of the weather.
note: From Old English storm. It describes wind, rain, snow and thunder.
hints: Thunder and lightning.
A hurricane or a blizzard.

definition: Full of storms, or turbulent.
note: From storm plus -y. Relationships and weather can both be stormy.
hints: What the night was in the opening line of a famous cliché.
Dark clouds and thunder.
example: Wide and stormy seas.

definition: A tale told for entertainment; or a floor of a building.
note: From Old French estoire, from Latin historia, the same source as history. The meaning of a floor in a building is a separate sense of uncertain origin.
hints: A tale before bedtime.
One level of a skyscraper.
origin: Anglo-Norman estorie, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔στορῐ́ᾱ

definition: A device for cooking or heating.
note: From Middle Dutch stove, 'heated room'. It first meant a hot room before the cooking sense.
hints: A cooker with burners.
What you boil a pot on.
origin: Middle Dutch stove, from Middle Low German stove

definition: To stretch tightly, or pressure; also a variety.
note: From Old French estreindre, 'to bind tightly'.
hints: Put too much effort.
A type of virus.
example: The rope strained when the weight was attached.

definition: A narrow channel connecting two bodies of water.
note: From Old French estreit, 'narrow', from Latin strictus. 'Dire straits' means narrow trouble.
hints: Gibraltar and Hormuz are famous ones.
Dire ones are what a band sang about, and what a hard luck case is in.
origin: Old French estreit, from Latin strictus

definition: A single thread or hair; also to leave someone stuck in a place.
note: The verb comes from the old word for a shore, meaning to run a ship aground. A beach and a thread of hair share the spelling by coincidence of English history.
hints: One piece of hair or rope fibre.
What happens to a traveller when the last bus has gone.

definition: A narrow band of leather or cloth.
note: From strop, a variant of an old word for a loop on a harness. It holds a watch or a bag.
hints: What holds a watch on your wrist.
A band that holds a rucksack on a shoulder.
origin: Old English strop, from Ancient Greek στρόφος

definition: Layers, especially of rock or of society.
note: Latin, the plural of stratum, 'something spread out', from sternere, 'to spread'.
hints: Geologists read them in the face of a cliff, like pages of a book.
Sociologists use it for the ranked layers of a society.

definition: Dried stalks of grain; or a thin tube for drinking.
note: From Old English streaw. The tube was first made of actual stalks.
hints: What a scarecrow is stuffed with.
What you sip a milkshake through.

definition: To wander off; or a lost animal.
note: From Old French estraier, 'to roam'. A lost dog or cat is called one.
hints: A lost cat without a home.
A dog roaming without an owner.
origin: Anglo-Norman estray, from Old French estrai
example: The child strayed from the path and her parents lost sight of her.

definition: A long thin line or a run of luck.
note: From Old English strica, 'line'.
hints: A mark across glass.
A winning run.

definition: A small river, or a continuous flow.
note: From Old English stream.
hints: A small flowing watercourse.
Continuous flow of data online.

definition: A public road with buildings alongside.
note: From Latin strata via, 'paved way'.
hints: Lined with houses.
Where a road meets pavements.
example: I live on the street down from Joyce Avenue.

definition: Short for streptococcus, the bacteria that cause a sore throat.
note: A clipping of streptococcus, from Greek words for 'twisted chain' and 'berry'.
hints: A common infection of the throat.
Bacteria in chains that cause tonsil trouble.

definition: Pressure or strain, or emphasis.
note: Shortened from distress, from Old French.
hints: Feeling under pressure.
The strong syllable in a word.
origin: Old French destrecier, from Latin strictus

definition: Scattered about untidily.
note: The past participle of strew, from Old English streowian, 'to scatter'.
hints: What a teenager's bedroom floor is with clothes.
Petals are scattered at a wedding.

definition: Demanding obedience; exact.
note: From Latin strictus, 'drawn tight'.
hints: A teacher with firm rules.
Exact in rules.

definition: To walk with long, confident steps.
note: From Old English stridan, 'to straddle'. A stride is the distance covered between planting one foot and the next.
hints: A long, confident step; also what a runner's gait is made of.
Hit your own while working and everything flows smoothly.
example: He strode confidently across the hall.

definition: Bitter conflict or disagreement.
note: From Old French estrif, 'quarrel', from a Frankish root. It appears in phrases like 'civil strife'.
hints: Headlines mention it in a country torn by unrest.
Marital disputes and street rioting both get this label.

definition: To hit, or a refusal to work.
note: From Old English strican, 'to go or stroke'.
hints: Workers walk out, or a bowler's perfect throw.
A bat hitting a ball.
example: He struck the table with his elbow.

definition: A thin cord, or a sequence of characters.
note: From Old English streng.
hints: Tied to a kite.
What a guitar has six of.

definition: A long narrow piece; or to remove clothing or covering.
note: From Middle Low German strippe, 'strap', of uncertain origin. It names a comic page, an airfield, and the act of undressing.
hints: A long, thin piece of paper.
A runway for aircraft.
example: He felt a flat strip of muscle.

definition: A long narrow band of colour.
note: From Middle Dutch stripe. A zebra and a barber's pole both have them.
hints: What a zebra wears.
A sergeant's sleeve badge shows them.
example: A green toad with small black stripes or bars.

definition: To try very hard.
note: From Old French estriver, 'to quarrel'.
hints: Make a great effort.
Work towards a goal.
example: We strive for the truth.

definition: A hit, a caress, or a sudden loss of blood to the brain.
note: From Old English strac.
hints: A swimmer's movement.
A cat likes this.

definition: A slow, relaxed walk.
note: Probably from German strollen, related to a word for a vagabond. It arrived in English in the 1600s.
hints: What couples do along a promenade at sunset.
The opposite of a march or a dash.
origin: German strollen, from Alemannic German strollen

definition: Having great power.
note: From Old English strang.
hints: What a tower, tea or an athlete can be.
Able to lift heavy loads.
example: A strong radio signal.

definition: To play a guitar by sweeping a hand across its strings.
note: Probably imitating the sound, possibly a variant of thrum.
hints: What a campfire guitarist does.
Sweep across the strings of a guitar.

definition: To walk proudly; or a supporting bar.
note: From Middle English strouten, 'to bulge'. A peacock does it. The bar sense is related.
hints: A peacock's walk.
A brace in a roof.
example: He struts around like a rooster in a hen house.

definition: Unable to move or progress.
note: The past tense of stick, from Old English stician. A cork can be this, and so can a crossword solver.
hints: What a car may be in mud.
How a puzzler feels without ideas.

definition: A room where an artist works, or a place where films are made.
note: From Italian studio, 'study', from Latin studium, 'zeal'.
hints: A painter's workspace.
Where music is recorded.
example: His studio was cramped when he began as an artist.

definition: To learn about a subject.
note: From Old French estudier, from Latin studium, 'zeal'. It also names a room for reading.
hints: What a student does before an exam.
A room with a desk and books.
origin: Old French estudier, from Latin studium

definition: Things or material; or to fill tightly.
note: From Old French estoffe, 'material'. It also means to cram a turkey with a filling.
hints: Odds and ends.
What you do to a turkey before roasting.
origin: Latin stuffa, from Old High German stoffōn

definition: Lacking fresh air, or overly formal.
note: From stuff plus -y. A stuffy nose is blocked, and a stuffy person is stiff.
hints: A closed-up room in summer.
A cold gives you a nose like this.
example: Hot and stuffy and the air was blue with smoke.

definition: What remains of a cut tree.
note: From Middle English stumpe. A politician's campaign speech is a 'stump speech'.
hints: What is left of a felled tree.
A short, thick remainder of something.
origin: Middle Low German stump, from Middle Dutch stomp

definition: A daring feat; or to hold back growth.
note: Its origin is unknown. It first appeared in American slang in the late nineteenth century for a feat of skill. A separate verb sense means to hold back growth.
hints: A dangerous move in a film.
What a lack of food can do to growth.

definition: Lacking sense or intelligence.
note: From Latin stupidus, 'amazed' or 'dazed', from stupere, 'to be numb'.
hints: Lacking good sense or judgement.
Its Latin root meant to be stunned.
origin: Middle French stupide, from Latin stupidus

definition: Strongly built and not easily damaged.
note: Once meant bold or fierce in Middle English, from Old French. The sense shifted from fierce people to solid things.
hints: Describes a table or boots that will last for years.
A ladder you can trust your weight to is this.

definition: A manner of doing things; or fashion.
note: From Latin stilus, 'pointed writing tool'. The writing tool gave its name to a way of writing, and then to any manner.
hints: How someone dresses or writes.
A fashionable quality.
origin: Old French estile, from Latin stilus

definition: Smooth and charming in manner.
note: From Latin suavis, 'sweet'. It is a doublet of sweet.
hints: A debonair, polished gentleman.
Charming, like a film spy.

definition: To overcome and bring under control.
note: From Old French souduire, from Latin subducere. The Latin may have been influenced by subdere, 'to place under'.
hints: A guard might do it to a prisoner.
What a dimmer does to the lights.
origin: Old French souduire, from Latin subdūcō

definition: To yield, or to hand in.
note: From Latin submittere, 'to lower'.
hints: Give in to authority.
Hand in an essay.

definition: A smaller set whose members all belong to a larger one.
note: From sub- plus set. In maths, all squares are a subset of rectangles.
hints: Squares compared to rectangles in geometry.
A group inside a larger group in maths.
example: We asked a subset of the population of the town for their opinion.

definition: So slight or delicate that it is hard to notice.
note: From Old French soutil, from Latin subtilis, 'fine' or 'woven finely'. The b is a later spelling.
hints: Not obvious or loud.
A hint rather than a shout.
origin: Anglo-Norman sotel, from Old French sotil

definition: In a way that is delicate and hard to notice.
note: From Middle English sotilly, from subtle. The b in the spelling was added later to match Latin.
hints: Hinting rather than saying outright.
A shade of colour that changes so gently you barely see it.
example: Mary believes Tom is subtly using her gender to discredit her.

definition: A residential area on the edge of a city.
note: From Latin suburbium, 'under the city'.
hints: Homes with lawns outside the centre.
Commuters live there.
origin: Old French suburbe, from Latin suburbium
example: The other day something horrible happened in a Tokyo suburb.

definition: An underground railway or an underpass.
note: From sub- plus way.
hints: New York's metro.
Called the Tube in London.

definition: A person easily fooled; or a part that clings by suction.
note: From suck plus -er, first for a suckling animal. The gullible sense is an American use from the 1800s.
hints: One who falls for a con.
An octopus has rows of them on its arms.
example: One poor sucker had actually given her his life’s savings.

definition: Happening quickly and without warning.
note: From Old French sodain, from Latin subitaneus.
hints: An abrupt change.
Without any warning.
example: The sudden drop in temperature left everyone cold and confused.

definition: Soft leather with a velvety surface.
note: From French gants de Suede, 'gloves from Sweden'. It is brushed on the inside.
hints: What a velvety shoe is made of.
A soft, napped leather.

definition: To feel pain or endure hardship.
note: From Latin sufferre, 'to bear'.
hints: Experience pain.
Endure something bad.

definition: A group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning.
note: From Latin suffixus, 'fastened underneath', from sub- and figere, 'to fasten'.
hints: -ness and -ing are examples.
Added at the tail of a word, like 'ful' on a cup.
example: The suffix "-able" changes "sing" into "singable".

definition: A sweet crystalline food.
note: Ultimately from Sanskrit sarkara, 'gravel' or 'grit', through Arabic and Italian. Cane and beets are the main sources.
hints: What goes in tea.
A sweet crystal from cane.

definition: Full of sugar, or sickeningly sweet.
note: From sugar plus -y. The word traces back through Arabic and Persian to Sanskrit sharkara, 'grit'.
hints: Cereal and fizzy drinks earn the label.
A film that is too sentimental gets it too.
example: He eats too much sugary food.

definition: A set of rooms; or a set of musical pieces.
note: From French suite, 'following'. It is a doublet of suit.
hints: A fancy hotel room set.
A set of musical movements.
origin: Middle French suite; in English since the 18th century
example: The Presidential suite is well appointed and allows for good security.

definition: A yellow chemical element that smells of rotten eggs when burned in some forms.
note: Latin sulpur, spelt with ph in older English. In the Bible it is 'brimstone', fuel for hell.
hints: Matches and volcanoes both involve it.
Rotten-egg smell gives it away.

definition: Silent and moody after being upset.
note: From sulk plus -y. A sulky is also a light cart for harness racing that seats just one rider.
hints: A child quietly pouting.
A one-seat racing cart.

definition: To stain or spoil.
note: From Old English sylian, 'to soil'. It is most often used of reputations.
hints: What a scandal does to a good name.
To tarnish something clean.
example: He did not wish to sully his hands with gardening.

definition: A Muslim ruler, especially of the Ottoman Empire.
note: Borrowed through French from Arabic sultan, 'power' or 'authority'. Ottoman rulers held the title for centuries.
hints: Ruler in Istanbul's palace in the Ottoman era.
Saladin held this title.
origin: Middle French sultan, from Arabic سُلْطَان
example: The sultan does not like the badger and the badger the sultan.

definition: A shrub, and the tangy red spice made from its berries.
note: From Middle English sumac, from Arabic summaq, from a word meaning 'red'. It is used in Middle Eastern cooking.
hints: A tangy red spice.
A shrub whose leaves turn red in autumn.
origin: Anglo-Norman sumak, from Classical Syriac ܣܘܡܩܐ

definition: The warmest season of the year.
note: From Old English sumor.
hints: Season between spring and autumn.
Long, hot days.
example: Gradually, the end of summer hove into sight.

definition: The highest point of a mountain, or a top-level meeting.
note: From Old French sommette, from Latin summus, 'highest'.
hints: Reaching Everest's peak.
A meeting of world leaders.
origin: Anglo-Norman sumet, from Middle French sommet
example: In summer, it is possible to hike to the summit of Mount Shasta.

definition: To call someone to come, often with authority.
note: From Latin summonere, 'to remind secretly'. Courts and wizards both do it.
hints: What a court does to a witness.
What a wizard does to a demon.

definition: Having sunk or lying below the surrounding level.
note: An old past participle of sink. Sunken treasure and sunken cheeks are examples.
hints: Treasure lying on the sea floor.
Cheeks hollowed by illness.
example: Hunger gave their faces a sunken look.

definition: Bright with sunshine.
note: From Old English sunnig, built from sun plus -y. It also describes a cheerful nature.
hints: A clear, bright day.
A cheerful disposition.
example: A gay sunny room.

definition: The time when the sun goes down.
note: From sun plus set.
hints: Evening glow.
Beach at dusk.

definition: Excellent; or above and beyond.
note: From Latin super, 'above'. It is used as a prefix and on its own as slang.
hints: A slangy word for great.
The word before 'man' for a flying hero.

definition: Excellent.
note: From Latin superbus, 'proud' or 'grand'.
hints: A truly wonderful performance.
Of the highest standard.

definition: An evening meal.
note: From Old French soper, 'to sup', related to soup.
hints: Dinner by another name.
Last meal of the day.
example: We normally have supper at 7.

definition: To provide what is needed; or a stock of something.
note: From Old French soupleer, from Latin supplere, 'to fill up'.
hints: Economists pair it with a curve that slopes upward.
What a shop keeps on its shelves.
origin: Old French soupleer, from Latin suppleo

definition: Certainly, or without doubt.
note: From sure plus -ly.
hints: Used to express confidence.
Without a doubt.
example: Surely, you must be joking.

definition: Someone who rides waves on a board.
note: From surf plus -er. The sport spread from Hawaii in the 20th century.
hints: Waits in the water for the next big wave.
Californian beaches are full of them.
example: The surfer tried to ride the crest of the wave.

definition: Rude and bad-tempered.
note: A sixteenth-century alteration of sirly, 'lordly', from sir plus -ly. It once meant haughty before it meant gruff.
hints: A grumpy waiter.
Unfriendly and short-tempered.
example: The receptionist at the hotel was surly and not at all friendly.

definition: A light four-wheeled carriage.
note: Named after Surrey, the English county, where a similar cart was first made.
hints: Old open-topped carriage.
Fringe on top is in a musical.

definition: To look over or measure; also a set of questions.
note: From Old French surveeir, 'to look over'.
hints: Questions given to many people.
A land measurer does one.
origin: Old French sourveoir, from Latin videre
example: He surveyed his new classmates.

definition: A Japanese dish of vinegared rice with fish or other toppings.
note: Borrowed from Japanese. The word originally referred to the sourness of the rice.
hints: Raw fish on rice.
Rolled with seaweed and eaten with soy sauce.
example: For the vegetarians, she served cucumber sushi.

definition: A short scripture or aphorism in Indian tradition.
note: From Sanskrit sutra, 'thread'. The Kama one is famous, as are Buddhist ones.
hints: A short text in an Indian tradition.
Literally a thread in Sanskrit.
example: The rubber sutra neti strings I ordered from India have finally arrived.

definition: An old word for a young man, especially a country suitor.
note: From Old Norse sveinn, 'boy' or 'servant'. A poet might call a lover this.
hints: A country lover in a poem.
An old poetic term for a suitor.
origin: Old English sweġen, from Old Norse sveinn

definition: A Hindu religious teacher.
note: From Hindi svami, from Sanskrit svamin, 'master' or 'lord'. It is used as a title of respect.
hints: A Hindu teacher.
A title meaning 'master'.

definition: Wet, spongy land with trees.
note: Early records from 1624 are from North America, with uncertain earlier roots. Alligators live in them.
hints: Wet land where alligators live.
A soggy, muddy marsh.
origin: Old English swamm, from Middle Low German sump

definition: Stylish in a flashy, expensive way.
note: Probably from a dialect verb meaning to strut or swagger.
hints: A posh hotel might be called this.
Elegant in a showy manner.

definition: A large flying or moving group of insects.
note: From Old English swearm. Bees and locusts do it, and so do crowds.
hints: Bees leaving a hive.
A large crowd moving together.

definition: The rush of water up a beach after a wave breaks.
note: Of Scandinavian origin; compare Swedish and Norwegian dialect words for splashing. It is the opposite of backwash.
hints: Water running up a beach.
Where the surf spreads out on the sand.
example: The swash of waves on the beach.

definition: A broad strip or sweep.
note: From Old English swaeth, 'track'. A farmer cuts a wide one with a scythe.
hints: A wide strip of cut grass.
A broad band of land.
example: A large swath of the population is opposed to this government policy.

definition: To make a solemn promise; or to use rude words.
note: From Old English swerian, 'to take an oath'. Both senses grew from the idea of invoking something sacred.
hints: What a witness does in court.
To curse when angry.

definition: Damp with perspiration.
note: From sweat plus -y. Gym kit and summer tubes are good examples.
hints: What a runner is after a marathon.
How your palms feel before an interview.

definition: To clean with a brush; or a long arc.
note: From Middle English swepen. It also names a chimney cleaner and a clean win in a series.
hints: What you do to a floor with a broom.
A win of every game in a series.
example: Please sweep the floor.

definition: Tasting like sugar; or pleasant and kind.
note: From Old English swete. It also names a candy in British speech.
hints: What honey tastes like.
A kind, endearing nature.

definition: To grow larger; or a rolling wave.
note: From Old English swellan. An ankle can do it, and so can the ocean.
hints: What a sprained ankle does.
A long wave out at sea.

definition: Past tense of sweep.
note: The past tense of sweep, from Middle English swepen. It describes a floor cleared with a broom, or someone carried away.
hints: What a broom did to the floor.
How a romantic hero treats someone off their feet.

definition: Fast; or a type of bird.
note: From Old English swift, 'quick'. The bird is named for its fast, darting flight.
hints: Quick and rapid.
A fast bird with sickle-shaped wings.
example: Swift flight of an arrow.

definition: Liquid kitchen scraps fed to pigs; or to drink greedily.
note: From Old English swillan, 'to wash'. It also means cheap, poor-quality drink.
hints: What a farmer pours into the pig trough.
To gulp down drink in large amounts.

definition: A pig; or a contemptible person.
note: From Old English swin. It is an old plural-looking word that is also singular.
hints: An old word for hogs.
A rude name for an awful person.
example: H1N1 got very poor marks from Gallup on the job they did on swine flu.

definition: To move back and forth; or a seat on ropes.
note: From Old English swingan, 'to beat or whip'. It also names a playground seat and a jazz style.
hints: A seat on chains at the playground.
What a golfer does with a club.

definition: To twist round and round.
note: From Middle English swirlen, probably from a Scandinavian word. Water in a drain does it.
hints: What milk does when stirred into tea.
The spiral of water in a plughole.
example: The leaves swirled in the autumn wind.

definition: A soft rustling sound; or smart and fashionable.
note: Imitative of a sound like a brush or a skirt. In British slang it means stylish.
hints: The sound of a basketball through the net.
A silk skirt's soft rustle.

definition: A device that turns something on or off, or to change.
note: Of uncertain origin, possibly from Low German.
hints: Flick to turn on a light.
Change one thing for another.

definition: To dive down suddenly.
note: From Old English swapan, 'to sweep'. Eagles do it onto prey.
hints: What a hawk does to catch a mouse.
A sudden dive from above.
example: The raptor swooped down on its prey.

definition: A long blade for fighting.
note: From Old English sweord. Knights carried them.
hints: A knight's weapon.
A long blade with a hilt.
origin: West Midland Middle English sword, from Old English sweord
example: He took out his sword and stabbed the man in the stomach.

definition: Declared under oath.
note: The past participle of swear, from Old English sworen. An enemy may be one of these.
hints: What a witness's statement is.
Bound by an oath, as an enemy.
example: His sworn statement convinced the judge.

definition: A sign standing for something else.
note: From Greek symbolon, 'token' or 'sign'.
hints: A dove is one for peace.
A mark such as an ampersand.
origin: French symbole, from Ancient Greek σύμβολον

definition: A church council.
note: From Greek sunodos, 'meeting', from sun, 'together', and hodos, 'way'. It is a gathering of church leaders.
hints: A gathering of bishops.
A formal church meeting.
example: As a young priest, Father Thomas attended his first synod.

definition: The rules for arranging words into sentences, or code into valid programs.
note: From Greek syntaxis, 'arrangement'. A compiler complains about an error in it.
hints: What a compiler checks before running your code.
Word order in a grammar class.
origin: Late Latin syntaxis, from Ancient Greek σύνταξις

definition: An electronic musical keyboard.
note: A clipping of synthesizer. It is a key instrument in pop music of the 1980s.
hints: A keyboard that makes electronic sounds.
What a band uses for beeps and swoops.

definition: A thick sweet liquid.
note: From Old French sirop, from Arabic sharab, 'drink'. Pancakes are often poured with maple.
hints: What goes on pancakes.
Maple is a sweet tree one.
origin: Old French sirop, from Arabic شَرَاب

definition: A set of connected parts forming a whole.
note: From Greek systema, 'organised whole'.
hints: Things working together.
A network of connected parts, as in a body or computer.
origin: Middle French sisteme, from Ancient Greek σύστημα; in English since the early 17th century
example: Exercise helped him get the alcohol out of his system.

definition: A cat with striped or mottled fur.
note: From French tabis, 'striped silk', named from a district in Baghdad where it was made. The cat took the name from the pattern.
hints: A striped house cat.
A cat with dark swirls on grey fur.

definition: A piece of furniture with a flat top.
note: From Latin tabula, 'board'. It is also a grid of data.
hints: Where you eat dinner.
A grid of rows and columns.
origin: Old English tabele, from Old French table
example: It was a sturdy table.

definition: A slab for writing, a pill, or a handheld computer.
note: From Old French tablete, 'small table'.
hints: Take one with water.
An iPad is one.

definition: Something forbidden by social custom.
note: Borrowed from Tongan tapu, 'sacred' or 'prohibited'. Captain Cook introduced it to English in the 1770s.
hints: A subject you do not raise at dinner.
A word from the Pacific meaning forbidden.

definition: A small drum played with one hand while the other plays a pipe.
note: From Old French tabour, which came from Persian via Arabic.
hints: A small medieval drum.
Played alongside a pipe by wandering musicians.
origin: Old French tabour, from Arabic طُنْبُور

definition: To grapple, or the gear used for fishing.
note: From Middle Dutch taken, 'to seize'.
hints: Bring down a player.
Fishing equipment.

definition: Sticky; or cheap and in poor taste.
note: From tack plus -y. Wet paint is the first kind.
hints: Wet glue or paint.
A garish, cheap decoration.
example: This paint isn't dry yet; it's still a bit tacky.

definition: A planned action to reach a goal.
note: From Greek taktika, 'matters of arrangement'.
hints: Part of a strategy.
A chess manoeuvre.
origin: New Latin tactica, from Ancient Greek τακτικός

definition: A chewy candy.
note: Probably related to tafia, a kind of rum. It is pulled until it is soft.
hints: A sweet pulled at the seaside.
A candy that sticks to your teeth.
example: Do you like saltwater taffy?

definition: The vast northern forest of conifers that spans Russia and Canada.
note: From Russian taiga, borrowed from Turkic languages of Siberia.
