hints: Biome of firs and spruces.
The snowy forest south of the tundra.

definition: A person who makes or fits clothes, especially suits.
note: From Old French tailleur, from tailler, 'to cut'. Savile Row is famous for them.
hints: Savile Row is full of them.
Takes your measurements before cutting the cloth.
example: He works as a tailor on Swanston Street.

definition: To spoil or contaminate.
note: From Old French teint, 'dyed', through the idea of tinging with something. A scandal may do it to a name.
hints: What a scandal does to a reputation.
Rotten food has this kind of spoil.
origin: Middle French teint, from Latin tinctum

definition: The past participle of take; also in a romantic relationship.
note: From Old Norse tekinn. It can mean seized, or, in casual speech, no longer single.
hints: What a seat is if someone else is in it.
Describes someone who has a partner.
origin: Old English tacen, from Old Norse tekinn

definition: One who accepts or grabs something.
note: From take plus -er. It is the opposite of a giver.
hints: A phrase about a generous partner warns of a giver and this.
Someone who accepts the bet.

definition: A natural gift or ability.
note: From Greek talanton, an ancient weight or sum of money, which became a metaphor for gifts through a biblical parable.
hints: Gift for singing, perhaps.
Parable of coins gave it its meaning.
origin: Old English talente, from Ancient Greek τάλαντον
example: He has a real talent for drawing.

definition: A running count.
note: From Latin talea, 'stick', for the notched stick used to keep records. Votes are counted by it.
hints: A running count of votes.
To add up scores.

definition: A sharp claw of a bird of prey.
note: From Old French talon, 'heel'. Eagles grip with them.
hints: An eagle's claw.
What an owl grips a mouse with.
origin: Old French talon, from Latin tālus
example: The eagle's talons were exposed like huge meat hooks.

definition: A person who trains wild animals.
note: From tame plus -er. A circus lion one is a familiar figure.
hints: Someone in a circus who trains lions.
A person who calms wild creatures.

definition: A bicycle for two riders; or two things working one behind the other.
note: From Latin tandem, 'at length', used as a joke for horses hitched one behind the other. 'In tandem' means working together.
hints: A bike with two seats and two sets of pedals.
Originally a pun on 'at last' about harnessed horses.
origin: Latin tandem; in English since the late 19th century

definition: A snarled mass; or to twist together in a knot.
note: From Middle English tanglen, probably Scandinavian, from a word linked to seaweed. Fishing line and hair both do it.
hints: Hair after a windy day.
Headphone cables in a pocket.
example: They carved their way through the tangle of vines.

definition: A passionate dance from Argentina; or the letter T in radio code.
note: Borrowed from Rioplatense Spanish. The dance began in Buenos Aires in the late nineteenth century.
hints: A dance of sharp steps and close hold.
The word for T in the spelling alphabet.

definition: Sharp and zesty in flavour.
note: From tang plus -y. Lemon and vinegar are this way.
hints: A sharp, citrus flavour.
Describes yoghurt or barbecue sauce.
example: My dad's tangy barbecue sauce recipe is a well-kept family secret.

definition: A ship or truck built to carry liquids in bulk.
note: From tank, itself a word that came into English via Portuguese from the languages of India. Oil tankers are among the largest ships afloat.
hints: A huge ship that may spill crude oil at sea.
A lorry on the motorway carrying milk or fuel.

definition: A person who turns animal skins into leather; also an old British sixpence.
note: From tan, the bark used to treat hides. The coin sense is separate slang.
hints: A worker in a smelly leather yard.
One who treats hides with bark.
origin: Old English tannere, from Old French tannour

definition: A short Japanese dagger.
note: Borrowed from Japanese tanto, 'short blade'. It was carried by samurai as a backup to the katana.
hints: Samurai kept one as a secondary blade.
Short Japanese blade.
origin: Japanese 短刀, from Middle Chinese 短刀

definition: Small Spanish snacks or starters.
note: Spanish for 'lids' or 'covers'. A popular story says bars once laid a slice of bread over a drink to keep flies out.
hints: Little plates in a Spanish bar.
Patatas bravas and olives.

definition: To narrow to a point; or a thin candle.
note: From Old English tapor, 'candle', of uncertain origin. Candles narrow towards the top.
hints: A thin candle.
To grow gradually narrower.
origin: Old English tapor, from Latin papyrus

definition: A pig-like animal with a short trunk.
note: From Tupi tapi'ira, through French. It lives in forests of South America and Asia.
hints: A hoofed animal with a flexible snout.
A relative of the rhinoceros and horse.
origin: French tapir, from Old Tupi tapi'ira
example: A tapir is a mammal with prehensile lips for eating tree foliage.

definition: Something aimed at.
note: From Old French targette, 'little shield', as the thing aimed at was once a small shield.
hints: Aim here with an arrow.
A goal that has been set.

definition: A tax on imports or exports; or a list of fees.
note: From Italian tariffa, from Arabic ta'rif, 'notification'. Trade wars are fought with them.
hints: What a government adds to imported steel.
What a trade war puts on foreign goods.

definition: A road or airfield surface made from tar and stones.
note: A clipping of tarmacadam, from tar and macadam, the crushed-stone road named for the Scot John McAdam. It was once a trademark.
hints: Where a plane waits before takeoff.
Planes taxi across it.

definition: A deck of cards used for fortune-telling.
note: From French tarot, from Italian tarocchi. The deck was first used for a card game.
hints: Cards read by a fortune teller.
A deck with 'The Fool' and 'The Tower'.
example: She predicts the future with tarot cards placed on the floor.

definition: The sense of flavour; or to try food.
note: From Old French taster, 'to touch or try'. It is the sense used by the tongue.
hints: What a chef samples.
What the tongue does.
origin: Old French taster, from Classical Latin taxāre

definition: Pleasant to eat.
note: From taste plus -y. It is a casual word for delicious.
hints: A chef hopes diners will use this word of a dish.
Cake and ripe strawberries earn this praise.
example: You could make this tasty meal for breakfast.

definition: A potato, informally.
note: A clipped form of potato, like 'mater for tomato.
hints: Slang for a spud.
Hash browns are made from them.
example: We ate them taters up real good.

definition: A permanent design inked into skin; also a military display.
note: The body art word is from Tahitian tatau. The military sense, from Dutch taptoe, is a separate word.
hints: Inked picture on an arm.
A military show with drums and bagpipes.

definition: Worn out and shabby.
note: A British word of uncertain origin, in use since the 1500s; it may be linked to tatters. A different, dialect word clips potato.
hints: A scruffy old coat.
Faded and frayed.
example: The tramp wore a tatty old overcoat.

definition: A greyish-brown colour.
note: From French taupe, 'mole', via Latin talpa, since the colour matches the animal's fur.
hints: Colour of a mole's fur.
A neutral shade between brown and grey.

definition: An old-fashioned pub or inn.
note: From Latin taberna, 'hut' or 'shop'. Taverns served wine to travellers.
hints: Where travellers on a medieval road might rest.
A place for ale and a bed in fantasy games.
origin: Old French taverne, from Latin taberna
example: There are several cozy taverns in the old part of the city.

definition: Yellowish-brown in colour.
note: From Old French tane, 'tanned'. A kind of owl shares the name.
hints: A lion's coat colour.
A brown owl is named after it.
origin: Anglo-Norman taune, from Old French tané

definition: A group of organisms classified together, such as a species or family.
note: Back-formed from taxonomy, from Greek taxis, 'arrangement'.
hints: A category in biology.
Genus and species are examples.

definition: To pass on knowledge.
note: From Old English taecan, 'to show'. It is what a professor does.
hints: What a professor does.
To instruct a class.

definition: Filled with tears.
note: From tear plus -y. A farewell may leave you so.
hints: Eyes at a sad goodbye.
About to cry.
example: Ziri's eyes were getting teary.

definition: To mock playfully; or to comb out fibres.
note: From Old English taesan, 'to pluck apart'. A friend does it with gentle jokes.
hints: What siblings do to one another.
To make fun lightly.
example: The flirting man teased the young woman.

definition: A short preview meant to tempt; or someone who teases.
note: From tease plus -er. A film trailer is one, as is a brain puzzle.
hints: A short film trailer before the main one.
A brain one is a puzzle that challenges you.

definition: A style of electronic dance music with a driving, repetitive beat.
note: Clipped from technology. It grew in 1980s Detroit.
hints: A genre that grew out of Detroit warehouses.
The sound of a Berlin nightclub.
example: What's the difference between trance, house, and techno music?

definition: Very small.
note: An alteration of tiny, with a childish feel. It is an informal word.
hints: A very small amount.
Tinier than small.
example: We make a teeny bit of progress, then we go back to square one.

definition: The plural of tooth.
note: From Old English teth, an irregular plural. Dentists look after them.
hints: Brushed twice a day.
What a dentist inspects.

definition: A telecommunications company.
note: Short for the older Tel. Co., as in names of local telephone companies.
hints: A company that sells phone and broadband service.
Short for a phone or broadband provider.

definition: A bank worker who handles cash; or someone who tells a story.
note: From tell plus -er, from the old sense of counting. A fortune one reads palms.
hints: The person behind the glass at a bank counter.
One who counts money, and one who tells fortunes.

definition: A British word for television.
note: A shortened form of television plus -y. It is the British casual term.
hints: What you watch in the evening.
A box in the living room.
example: The British call a tv set a telly.

definition: A person's mood, or to moderate or toughen.
note: From Latin temperare, 'to mix in proportion'.
hints: Lose it and you shout.
What a blacksmith does to steel.
origin: Old English ġetemprian, from Latin temperō

definition: A building for worship; also the side of your head.
note: The building from Latin templum. The head part comes from a different word, Latin tempora.
hints: Place of worship in many religions.
Where your glasses arm rests.
origin: Old English templ, from Latin templum

definition: To lure someone into doing something wrong.
note: From Old French tempter, from Latin temptare, 'to test'. A dessert menu can do it.
hints: What a dessert does to a dieter.
To lure into doing something naughty.
origin: Old French tempter, from Latin temptare
example: She tempted me to eat the apple.

definition: A person who rents a home or land.
note: From Old French tenant, 'holding', from tenir.
hints: Pays the landlord monthly.
Lives in a rented flat.
example: The landlord can evict a tenant who doesn't pay the rent.

definition: Soft and gentle, or to offer.
note: From Latin tener, 'soft'. The offering sense is a separate word, from tendere.
hints: A steak that is easy to cut.
Offer a formal bid.

definition: A strong cord that joins muscle to bone.
note: From Medieval Latin tendo, from Greek tenon, 'sinew'. The Achilles is the largest in the body.
hints: Connects muscle to bone in your leg.
Achilles' weak spot was named after one.
origin: French tendon, from Ancient Greek τένων
example: Tendons and ligaments are more fragile than you might think.

definition: A principle that a group believes.
note: Latin for 'he holds'. A core belief is something held.
hints: A guiding principle.
A core belief of a faith.
example: Bouteflika violated basic tenets of democracy to maintain power.

definition: A racket sport played over a net.
note: A popular explanation says it comes from Old French tenez, 'take this', called by the server, though this is not certain.
hints: Wimbledon is devoted to it.
Games, sets and matches.

definition: A high male singing voice; or the general sense of something.
note: From Old French tenour, from Latin tenere, 'to hold'. In music it held the main melody in early choral works.
hints: A singer like Pavarotti.
The overall tone of a speech.

definition: Stretched tight; or the form of a verb showing time.
note: The grammar sense is from Latin tempus, 'time'. The tight sense is from Latin tensus, 'stretched'.
hints: What nerves feel before an exam.
Past, present or future.

definition: A mathematical object that generalises vectors and matrices, or a muscle that tightens a part.
note: From New Latin tensor, 'that which stretches'. Einstein's relativity relies on them.
hints: General relativity is written in the maths of this object.
Google's machine-learning library is named after it, with 'flow'.
origin: New Latin tensor, from German Tensor; in English since the 18th century

definition: Number ten in order.
note: From Middle English tenth. Old English used teotha, which gave 'tithe'.
hints: The one after the ninth.
One part in ten.

definition: The holding of a position, or secure academic employment.
note: From Old French tenir, 'to hold'.
hints: A professor's job security.
The length of time in a role.
origin: Old French tenure, from Latin tentus

definition: Barely warm.
note: From Latin tepidus, 'lukewarm'. A bath left too long gets this way.
hints: Water that has cooled down.
An unenthusiastic reception.
example: I'm drinking a cup of tepid water.

definition: Earth or land, in Latin.
note: Borrowed from Latin terra, 'earth'. It shows up in words like terrace and terrain.
hints: A Latin word for soil.
Think of the 'firma' that follows it.

definition: Extreme fear.
note: From Latin terror, from terrere, 'to frighten'.
hints: What a horror film aims for.
Dread of a high order.
origin: Old French terreur f, from Old Latin tr̥reō
example: He used terror to make them confess.

definition: A thick cotton cloth with small loops, used for towels.
note: Of uncertain origin. It is the soft loop-piled fabric of towels and bathrobes.
hints: What many bath towels are made from.
A looped cotton cloth that soaks up water.

definition: Brief and abrupt.
note: From Latin tersus, 'wiped clean', used of neat and polished style. It now suggests curtness.
hints: A one-word reply.
A short, curt message.
example: Short and terse and easy to understand.

definition: A person or device that tests something; also a sample for trying out, or a bed canopy.
note: The sense of one who tests is simply test plus -er. The bed canopy is a different word, reaching English through Old French.
hints: A sample pot of paint in a hardware shop is called one.
A four-poster bed has a roof of fabric with this name.

definition: Easily annoyed.
note: From Old French testu, 'headstrong', from teste, 'head'. Someone who is short of sleep may be this way.
hints: Short-tempered and snappish.
Describes someone about to snap.
example: He gets really testy when he doesn't get his way.

definition: A small, colourful freshwater aquarium fish.
note: Short for a former genus name based on Greek for 'four-angled'.
hints: Neon is a famous one.
A little shoaling fish from South America.

definition: A noble in early England or Scotland.
note: From Old English thegn, 'servant' or 'warrior'. Macbeth was one.
hints: A title in Shakespeare's Scottish play.
A lord of old Scotland.

definition: To show gratitude.
note: From Old English thancian. It is related to the word think, from the idea of a thought of kindness.
hints: What you say after a gift.
To express appreciation.
example: Thanks to your help, I could understand the book quite well.

definition: The act of stealing.
note: From Old English thiefth, related to thief. It is a crime of taking someone's property.
hints: What a burglar commits.
A crime against property.
example: Bike theft is on the rise.

definition: Belonging to them.
note: From Old Norse their(r)a. It replaced the older English word hira.
hints: A word for what belongs to more than one person.
Often confused with a place word.

definition: The main subject or idea.
note: From Old French teme, from Greek thema, 'something laid down'. A story, a party or a piece of music has one.
hints: The central idea of a story.
A party's chosen topic for costumes.

definition: From that place or from that time.
note: From Middle English thennes, built on thenne with an adverbial -es ending. It is a close cousin of whence.
hints: Old maps and travel diaries say 'and ___ to Rome'.
Its question-word twin is whence.
example: Cross fix at 6000 feet, thence descend to 3000 feet and fly direct to MAP (missed approach point).

definition: An idea that explains how something works.
note: From Greek theoria, 'a looking at' or 'contemplation'.
hints: Darwin proposed one about evolution.
A reasoned explanation awaiting testing.

definition: In or at that place.
note: From Old English thaer. It is the opposite of here.
hints: The opposite of here.
A word that points to a place.

definition: A long essay for a degree, or a main claim.
note: From Greek thesis, 'a placing'.
hints: What a PhD student writes.
A proposition to be argued.
origin: Latin thesis, from Ancient Greek θέσῐς

definition: The eighth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek theta. Mathematicians use it for an angle.
hints: A Greek letter used for angles.
Written with a horizontal bar in an oval.
example: Theta is the ninth letter of the Greek Alphabet.

definition: Having great depth; or dense.
note: From Old English thicce. Soup and fog can be this way.
hints: Porridge and pea soup can be like this.
A fog you can barely see through.

definition: A person who steals.
note: From Old English theof, shared across the Germanic languages. A shoplifter or burglar is one.
hints: A burglar by another name.
Takes what belongs to someone else.
example: A thief steals for a long time, but eventually he will hang.

definition: The part of the leg above the knee.
note: From Old English theoh. A drumstick on a chicken is the lower part, but this is above.
hints: The upper leg.
A cut of meat between hip and knee.
origin: Old English þēoh; in English since the 8th century

definition: An old word for 'yours'.
note: From Old English thin. It was used with thou and appears in old prayers and poems.
hints: An old word for belonging to you.
A word in Shakespeare for 'yours'.

definition: An informal word for something you cannot name or have forgotten.
note: Formed from thing plus -y, a casual stand-in for a name that won't come.
hints: What you call the gadget when the proper name escapes you.
Heard in 'pass me that, you know, the whatsit'.

definition: To use your mind to reason.
note: From Old English thencan. It is related to the word for 'thank', both from an old sense of 'thought'.
hints: What you do before answering.
What a brain does.
example: I've been thinking all day and getting nowhere.

definition: In a thin layer or a sparse way.
note: From Middle English thinnelich, from thin plus -ly. 'Thinly veiled' means barely hidden.
hints: Sliced finely, as with garlic.
Describes an insult that is barely disguised.

definition: Number three in order.
note: From Old English thridda. It follows the second.
hints: The bronze medal place.
What comes after second.
example: The third tree from the left is my favorite.

definition: The need to drink, or a strong craving for something.
note: From Old English thurst, from the same root as 'dry'. It extends to hunger for success or knowledge.
hints: What a long walk in the desert gives you.
Water is meant to quench it.
example: We developed a great thirst during our hike.

definition: The number after twenty-nine.
note: From Old English thritig, 'three tens'.
hints: Three tens added together.
A decade of ages.

definition: A narrow strip of leather; or a sandal held by a strap.
note: From Old English thwong, 'strip of leather'. It was used for binding and for whips.
hints: A leather strip for tying.
A beach sandal held on by a strap.

definition: A sharp spike on a plant.
note: From Old English thorn. Roses have them.
hints: What a rose has along its stem.
A prickle on a bush.

definition: Despite the fact that; however.
note: From Old Norse tho, replacing the older Old English theah.
hints: A word to express contrast.
A word that signals contrast.
example: Though it is risky, it is worth taking the chance.

definition: To beat hard, or to defeat completely.
note: A variant of thresh, from Middle English; beating grain with a flail and beating a person were the same motion. To thrash around is to flail wildly.
hints: What a swimmer in trouble does with their arms.
A sports score of ten-nil would be described this way.

definition: A thin cord of twisted fibre.
note: From Old English thraed, from thrawan, 'to twist'.
hints: Used with a needle.
A spool is wound with it.

definition: A warning of harm to come.
note: From Old English threat, 'oppression or pressure'.
hints: What a bully makes.
A sign of danger.

definition: The number after two.
note: From Old English thri, shared across Indo-European languages. It is a number of many sayings.
hints: One more than two.
A crowd, they say, when added to two.

definition: Three times.
note: From Middle English thries, with a once, twice, thrice pattern. The -ce ending is an old genitive form that became fixed.
hints: Used by poets and witches, rarely by anyone else.
The witches in Macbeth chant that the brindled cat has mewed this many times.
origin: Old English þriwa, from Old English -es
example: I called you thrice last night.

definition: Careful, sparing use of money and resources.
note: From Old Norse thrift, 'prosperity', related to thrive. A thrift shop sells second-hand goods for charity.
hints: Describes the habit of saving instead of spending.
Second-hand charity stores in America carry its name.
example: His thrift can be seen in how little the trashman takes from his house.

definition: A sudden wave of excitement.
note: From Old English thyrlian, 'to pierce'.
hints: What a roller-coaster gives.
Excite greatly.
example: The thrills of space travel.

definition: To grow strongly and do well.
note: From Old Norse thrifask, 'to grasp for oneself'.
hints: Plants do it in sunshine.
Flourish and prosper.
example: Not all animals thrive well in captivity.

definition: The passage at the front of the neck.
note: From Old English throte.
hints: Where a sore feeling is felt.
Cleared before a speech.
example: The wild pitch bounced and hit the catcher in the throat.

definition: To beat with a strong pulse.
note: From Middle English throbben, possibly imitative. A bruised thumb does it.
hints: What a headache does.
A beat of pain, in time with the heart.

definition: A ceremonial chair for a king or queen.
note: From Greek thronos, 'seat'.
hints: Where a monarch sits.
The seat of power.
origin: Old French trone, from Ancient Greek θρόνος

definition: To hurl through the air.
note: From Old English thrawan, 'to twist or turn'. A pitcher does it from a mound.
hints: What a pitcher does with a ball.
To toss a ball.

definition: Hurled through the air.
note: The past participle of throw.
hints: What a ball is after it leaves your hand.
Tossed or flung by someone.

definition: A low, steady humming sound.
note: Imitative of a continuous vibration. A guitar string or an engine can do it.
hints: The sound of a purring engine.
A low, steady strumming.
example: He could hear the thrum of a banjo.

definition: To push suddenly, or the force that moves a rocket.
note: From Old Norse thrysta, 'to push'.
hints: Jab a sword forward.
Force generated by a jet engine.

definition: The short, thick digit on the hand.
note: From Old English thuma. The word has a silent b, added later in spelling.
hints: What a hitchhiker sticks out.
The finger that gets an upturn for approval.

definition: A heavy dull blow or its sound.
note: Probably imitative, from the mid sixteenth century. A dropped book makes one.
hints: The sound of a book dropped on a floor.
A dull knock on a door.

definition: A dull sound of something heavy landing; also a jocular past tense of think.
note: Imitates the sound, and the past tense form follows words like sunk.
hints: A book dropped on a carpet makes this sound.
A hollow thud.

definition: To block someone's plan.
note: From Old Norse thvert, 'across'. Something laid across your path stops you.
hints: What a detective does to a robbery.
A bridge troll tried to do this to billy goats.

definition: A small herb used in cooking.
note: From Old French thym, from Greek thymon. It sounds like 'time'.
hints: A herb sounding like a clock's word.
Often paired with parsley and sage.
origin: Old French thym, from Ancient Greek θύμον

definition: A small jewelled crown.
note: From Latin tiara, 'Persian headdress', from Greek. A beauty queen or a bride might wear one.
hints: A jewelled headpiece for a princess.
What a pageant winner is crowned with.
origin: Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα
example: The queen’s tiara was a masterpiece of craftsmanship.

definition: The shin bone.
note: From Latin tibia, 'shinbone' or 'flute'. It is the larger bone in the lower leg.
hints: The bone below the knee.
The shinbone.
example: I dislocated my ankle, and I also broke my tibia and fibula bones.

definition: A device or display showing live information, or slang for the heart.
note: From tick plus -er. A stock one printed prices on paper tape; a ticker-tape parade showers confetti.
hints: Stock prices scroll past on a tape or a news channel's bottom strip.
Slang for the heart in your chest.
example: The ticker was showing an increased rate of flow.

definition: A slip that gives you entry or travel.
note: From Old French estiquet, 'label', from a word meaning to stick.
hints: Needed to board a train.
What a cinema box office sells.
origin: Middle Scots tikkat, from Old French estechier

definition: To touch someone lightly so that they squirm or laugh.
note: From Middle English tiklen, of uncertain origin; it may be a repeated form of an older word for touching lightly.
hints: Feet, ribs and underarms are the usual targets.
A feather is the classic tool.

definition: Relating to the ebb and flow of the sea.
note: From tide plus -al. A wave of this kind is caused by the moon's pull.
hints: Water that comes and goes twice a day.
A wave named for the ocean's rise and fall.
example: The tidal barrier and flood walls need to be reinforced.

definition: A large cat with orange fur and black stripes.
note: From Greek tigris, through Latin and Old French. It is native to Asia.
hints: A striped big cat.
What Tony the Frosted Flakes mascot is.
origin: Old English tigras, from Ancient Greek τίγρις

definition: Firmly fixed; not loose.
note: From Middle English tight, a variant of thight, 'dense'. A rope or a schedule can be this.
hints: A rope pulled firm.
A close-fitting pair of jeans.

definition: Pieces of meat marinated in spices and cooked, as in chicken tikka masala.
note: Borrowed from Hindustani tikka, 'piece' or 'bit'.
hints: Curry house favourite with marinated chunks.
A menu word for a piece of grilled meat.

definition: The wavy line over a letter, as in n with a wave.
note: From Spanish tilde, from Latin titulus, 'inscription'. It marks Spanish letters and Portuguese vowels.
hints: A wavy mark over a letter.
The squiggle on a Spanish n.
example: The tilde is used in math to denote equivalence.

definition: Wood prepared for building.
note: From Old English timber, 'building' or 'wood'.
hints: Logs cut into planks.
Shouted when a tree falls.

definition: Happening at a good time.
note: From time plus -ly.
hints: Arriving at the right moment.
Happening at just the right moment.
example: With timely treatment the patient has a good chance of recovery.

definition: A device that counts down time.
note: From time plus -er. Ovens and eggs often need one.
hints: What you set when baking.
A kitchen device that rings.

definition: Shy and lacking confidence.
note: From Latin timidus, from timere, 'to fear'. A mouse is a classic example.
hints: Describes a nervous mouse.
Not bold; easily scared.
origin: Middle French timide, from Latin timidus
example: John's a very timid person. I doubt he'll be brave enough to face his brother.

definition: Dry, easily lit material used to start a fire.
note: From Old English tynder, related to 'tendan', to kindle. Today also the name of a dating app.
hints: A campfire builder collects this with kindling.
A spark falling on it is enough to start a flame.

definition: A slight touch of colour or feeling.
note: From Latin tingere, 'to dye'. A hint of sadness or colour is this.
hints: A hint of colour.
A slight touch of sadness.

definition: A travelling mender of pots and pans; also to fiddle with something.
note: From Middle English tynkere, maybe from the sound of hammering on tin. To tinker is to tweak a machine until it works.
hints: Fiddling with an engine on a Sunday.
A craftsman once travelled from village to village mending pots.

definition: Likely to tip over.
note: From tip plus -y. An old sense meant stylish.
hints: A wobbly canoe might feel this way.
Easily toppled.
example: Get up on your tippy toes.

definition: Slightly drunk.
note: From tips, an old word, plus -y. It describes the unsteady stage before outright drunkenness.
hints: A little unsteady after a glass or two.
Slightly drunk.

definition: Needing rest.
note: From Old English tyrian, 'to become weary'. A long day makes you this.
hints: How you feel after a long day.
What a yawn shows.

definition: Thin soft paper; or a mass of cells in the body.
note: From Old French tissu, 'woven', from tistre.
hints: Used to wipe your nose.
Muscle is one kind.
origin: Old French tissu, from Latin texō

definition: A giant; or someone of huge power.
note: From the Titans of Greek myth, the giants who ruled before the Olympian gods. It now describes a person of great power.
hints: A giant of industry.
One of the old gods overthrown by Zeus.

definition: This present day.
note: From Old English to daege, 'on this day'. It is the opposite of tomorrow or yesterday.
hints: Not yesterday, not tomorrow.
The current date.
example: Did you see today's newspaper?

definition: A hot sweetened drink with whisky.
note: From Hindi tari, the fermented palm sap, brought to Britain through India. The British drink took the name.
hints: A hot drink for a cold.
Whisky with honey and hot water.

definition: A switch that flips between two states, or a short peg used as a fastener.
note: Of uncertain origin; the nautical meaning was a pin through a rope's loop. The computing sense is a switch that changes between two settings.
hints: A button on a duffle coat.
Phone settings have one to turn wifi on and off.

definition: A fixture for waste; or the act of washing and dressing.
note: From French toilette, a cloth used for dressing.
hints: The loo, in polite speech.
Its French source was once a cloth.
origin: Middle French toilette; in English since the 19th century
example: My toilet got clogged. Now the bathroom's flooded.

definition: A red fruit eaten as a vegetable.
note: From Spanish tomate, from Nahuatl tomatl.
hints: Used in ketchup.
Salad ingredient.
origin: Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl
example: He was chopping a tomato to put in the salad.

definition: Relating to tone or pitch.
note: From tone plus -al. It can describe music or the overall mood of a piece.
hints: About the pitch of music.
How colours or sounds are balanced.

definition: Powder used in a printer; or a skin lotion.
note: From tone plus -er. A cartridge holds the first, and a bottle holds the second.
hints: What a laser printer uses up.
A lotion after cleansing.
example: The printer needs more black toner.

definition: The muscle in the mouth used for tasting and speaking; also a language.
note: From Old English tunge.
hints: Helps you taste.
Your mother one is your first language.
example: He spoke with a thick tongue.

definition: A restorative; or fizzy water flavoured with quinine.
note: From Greek tonikos, 'of stretching'. Gin is often mixed with it.
hints: What goes with gin.
A medicine that refreshes.

definition: A metric unit of mass of 1,000 kilograms.
note: From French tonne. It is a doublet of ton and tun.
hints: A thousand kilos.
A unit used for freight and emissions.
example: This bridge has a weight-bearing capacity of just ten tonnes.

definition: One of the hard white structures in the mouth.
note: From Old English toth. A saw has them as well.
hints: What a dentist fills.
A bit of the cutting edge of a saw.

definition: A yellowish gemstone.
note: From Old French topace, from Greek topazos. It is the birthstone for November.
hints: A golden-yellow jewel.
A November birthstone.

definition: A subject of conversation or writing.
note: From Greek topika, 'matters of place', the title of a work by Aristotle. It now means a subject.
hints: The subject of a talk.
What an essay is about.
origin: Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός
example: A society where a topic cannot be discussed, does not have free speech.

definition: Something that sits on top, or a top hat.
note: From top plus -er in Middle English. It is also used for a cake decoration.
hints: A wedding cake might have a pair of figures as one.
A magician might pull a rabbit from it.

definition: A handheld light; or a burning stick.
note: From Old French torche, 'twisted', since the first ones were twisted straw or rope. In British English it also means a flashlight.
hints: What an Olympic runner carries.
What you use in a power cut.

definition: A twisting force that causes something to rotate.
note: Borrowed from Latin torquere, 'to twist'. A torque wrench measures it when tightening bolts.
hints: A figure car makers quote beside horsepower.
A wrench set to a precise setting measures this on a wheel nut.

definition: The trunk of the body.
note: From Italian torso, 'stump', from Latin thyrsus. A statue without limbs is often called this.
hints: A statue with no head or limbs.
The body between neck and hips.
origin: Italian torso, from Ancient Greek θύρσος
example: The word goy likely is derived from gev, meaning body or torso.

definition: A doughnut shape in geometry.
note: Latin for 'swelling' or 'cushion'. Mathematically it is a ring made by spinning a circle.
hints: A shape like a ring doughnut.
A tyre-like geometrical form.

definition: The whole amount; or complete.
note: From Medieval Latin totalis, from totus, 'whole'. You reach it by adding.
hints: The sum of all the parts.
What a bill adds up to.
origin: Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis

definition: A natural object that represents a family or clan.
note: Borrowed from Ojibwe, from a word for a clan relative. Totem poles carved by Pacific Northwest peoples display them.
hints: A carved pole with animal faces.
An emblem of a clan.

definition: To make contact with the hand.
note: From Old French touchier, of Germanic origin. It is also one of the five senses.
hints: One of the five senses.
What a fingertip does.
origin: Old French tochier; in English since the 14th century
example: I touched his face softly.

definition: Easily offended, or awkward to deal with.
note: A variant of older tetchy, influenced by the sense of 'touch'. A touchy subject is one you hesitate to handle.
hints: A topic you steer around at dinner.
Describes a person who takes a joke the wrong way.
example: He can be very touchy when you talk about his estranged son, so be as tactful as possible.

definition: Strong and hard to damage; or difficult.
note: From Old English toh, 'tenacious'. Both steak and a hard problem can be this way.
hints: A chewy steak.
A hard problem to solve.
example: The tent, made of tough canvas, held up to many abuses.

definition: In the direction of.
note: From Old English toweard, 'facing'.
hints: Heading that way.
Facing a given direction.
example: She moved toward the door.

definition: A cloth for drying.
note: From Old French toaille. You use one after a bath.
hints: What you use after a shower.
Thrown in to give up in boxing.
example: He needed a towel for wiping the slippery floor.

definition: A tall narrow building or structure.
note: From Old English torr and Old French tur, from Latin turris. Churches and castles often have them.
hints: The Eiffel one is famous.
A tall part of a castle.
origin: Old English tūr, from Ancient Greek τύρρις

definition: Poisonous.
note: From Greek toxikon, 'poison for arrows', from toxon, 'bow'. It now describes harmful chemicals or behaviour.
hints: Describes a poisonous chemical.
A harmful, bad relationship.
origin: French toxique, from Ancient Greek τοξικόν
example: Keep the cat away from any cleaning products, they're toxic.

definition: A poison made by a living thing.
note: From the same Greek root as toxic. Snake venom and bacteria produce them.
hints: A poison made by a snake.
What bacteria can produce to harm the body.
example: Plants produce toxins to defend themselves from predators.

definition: A small sign of something; or to follow.
note: From Old French trace, 'track'. You can follow one, or draw over a picture.
hints: A tiny amount left behind.
To copy a drawing through thin paper.

definition: A bullet that leaves a glowing trail; also a substance used to follow a process.
note: Formed from trace plus -er.
hints: Gunfire at night looks like streaks of light thanks to it.
Doctors inject a radioactive kind to follow blood flow.

definition: An area of land; or a short pamphlet.
note: From Latin tractus, 'a drawing out'. A digestive passage is called by it too.
hints: A large expanse of land.
A short religious pamphlet.
origin: Old English traht, from Latin tractus

definition: To buy and sell; or a skilled craft.
note: From Middle Low German trade, 'track' or 'course'. A carpenter has one, and so does a merchant.
hints: What merchants do.
A skilled job such as plumbing.
origin: Middle Low German trade, from Old Saxon trada

definition: A person who buys and sells.
note: From trade plus -er.
hints: Works at the stock exchange.
A seller at a market.
example: A rich trader felt that the hour of his death was approaching.

definition: Causing great sorrow.
note: From Greek tragikos, 'of tragedy'.
hints: A sad ending in a play.
Terribly sad.
example: Her father's early death was tragic.

definition: A line of linked railway carriages; or to teach.
note: From Old French trainer, 'to drag', from Latin trahere. It also names the long trailing part of a gown.
hints: What runs on rails.
What a coach does with athletes.
origin: Old French train, from Latin trahō; in English since the 19th century
example: Express trains don't stop at Princeton Junction.

definition: A distinguishing characteristic.
note: From French trait, 'line' or 'feature', from Latin tractus. Eye colour is inherited this way.
hints: Something like generosity or bravery.
A feature passed in genes.
origin: Middle French trait, from Latin trahō
example: Generosity is an important trait in today's selfish society.

definition: To walk heavily; or a vagabond.
note: From Middle Low German trampen, 'to stamp'. It names a wanderer who walks long distances.
hints: A long, heavy walk through mud.
A wanderer without a home.
origin: Middle Low German trampen, from Middle Dutch trampen

definition: A half-conscious state, as in hypnosis or deep concentration.
note: From Old French transe, 'fear' or 'passage', from a verb meaning to pass over. Also a dance-music genre.
hints: What a hypnotist puts a subject into.
What a spiritual medium goes into.

definition: Across or beyond; also short for transgender.
note: From Latin trans, 'across'.
hints: A prefix meaning across.
A short word for those who live a gender different from the one assigned at birth.

definition: Rubbish.
note: From Middle English trasch, probably a dialect word for broken twigs. It is what you put in a bin.
hints: What goes in a bin.
Waste to be thrown out.

definition: Of poor quality or tasteless, like cheap fiction or TV.
note: From trash plus -y. Often used for entertainment people enjoy anyway.
hints: A paperback sold at an airport kiosk.
A reality show you watch as a guilty pleasure.

definition: A serious injury, or a deeply distressing experience.
note: From Greek trauma, 'wound'.
hints: What an emergency department treats.
An emotional wound that lingers.
example: We're not talking about paper cuts or sprains here — we're talking about trauma.

definition: To go from one place to another.
note: From Old French travailler, 'to toil', so journeys were once seen as hard work. It is a doublet of travail.
hints: Journey abroad.
Once meant labour.

definition: To fish by dragging a large net.
note: From Dutch tragelen, 'to drag'. It also means to search through a large amount of material.
hints: What a fishing boat does with a big net.
To search through a mass of records.

definition: To walk on; or the pattern on a tyre.
note: From Old English tredan, 'to step'. A tyre has a grooved one for grip.
hints: What you do carefully on thin ice.
The grooves on the sole of a boot.

definition: To behave towards someone; or a special pleasure.
note: From Old French tretier, 'to handle', from Latin tractare. It covers medicine, behaviour, and a small gift.
hints: What a child gets at Halloween.
What a doctor does for an illness.
origin: Anglo-Norman treter, from Latin tractāre; in English since the 14th century
example: You treated me like a fool.

definition: A formal agreement between nations.
note: From Old French traite, from Latin tractare, 'to handle'.
hints: Signed by two countries.
Versailles was one.
origin: Anglo-Norman treté, from Old French traité

definition: Three times as much; or the highest part in music.
note: From Old French, from Latin triplus. In music the high voice was the third added above the main tune.
hints: Turn up the bass and down this on a stereo.
A boy soprano sings in this range.
origin: Old French treble, from Latin triplus

definition: A small shaking, from the ground or the body.
note: From Latin tremor, 'a shaking'; Middle English used it for fright.
hints: Seismologists measure these before a quake.
A shaky voice or hand.
example: The optometrist has been losing patients ever since he developed tremors in his hand.

definition: A long narrow ditch.
note: From Old French trenchier, 'to cut'.
hints: Soldiers in the First World War lived in them.
Ditch dug in the ground.
example: The trenches for installing the underground cables were dug with a trencher.

definition: A general direction of change.
note: From Middle English trenden, 'to roll about'. It now names what is fashionable or on the rise.
hints: What goes viral for a while.
A line that slopes upward on a graph.

definition: Fashionable at the moment.
note: From trend plus -y. Trend first meant to turn or bend.
hints: A cafe in a hip neighbourhood is called this.
What this season's clothes are.

definition: A group of three.
note: From Greek trias, 'three'. In music it is a chord of three notes.
hints: Three things grouped together.
A chord made of three notes.
origin: Latin triad-, from Ancient Greek τριάς

definition: A test; or a legal hearing.
note: From Old French trier, 'to try'. A new medicine goes through one, and a defendant faces one.
hints: What a defendant faces in court.
A test of a new medicine.

definition: Relating to a tribe.
note: From tribe plus -al; tribe is from Latin tribus, a division of the Roman people.
hints: Concerning a group with shared ancestry.
Loyalties to one's own group.

definition: A social group sharing ancestry and customs.
note: From Latin tribus, which originally meant one of three divisions of Rome's early people.
hints: A group with a shared chief and customs.
A Native community, or an ancient Hebrew clan.
origin: Old French tribu, from Latin tribus
example: She found her tribe among fellow cross-stitchers.

definition: A very short moment.
note: From Middle English trisen, 'to pull sharply'. In the phrase 'in a trice' it means in an instant, as quickly as a tug.
hints: A moment, in the phrase 'in a'.
A blink of time.

definition: A cunning act meant to fool someone.
note: From Old Northern French trique, 'deceit'. A magician performs them.
hints: What a magician performs.
A cheeky deceit at Halloween.

definition: Difficult to deal with, or deceitful.
note: From trick plus -y.
hints: A fiddly problem.
Sly in manner.
example: They were in a tricky situation.

definition: Past tense of try.
note: From Middle English, built from try plus -ed. It can also mean tested, as in 'tried and true'.
hints: What you did when you attempted.
A word that goes with 'true'.

definition: A quick fluttering of two notes, or a sound like that.
note: From Italian trillo, imitating the sound.
hints: A bird's rapid warble.
Singers decorate a long note with one.
example: He pronounced his R's with a distinct trill.

definition: The stomach lining of a cow, eaten as food; or nonsense.
note: From Old French tripe, 'entrails'. Calling an idea this means it is rubbish.
hints: A Lancashire dish from a cow's stomach.
A word for nonsense.
origin: Old French tripe, from Spanish tripa

definition: Three times as large or made of three parts.
note: From Latin triplus, 'threefold'.
hints: Three of something.
A jump in athletics has this name.

definition: A three-legged stand, especially for a camera.
note: From Greek tripous, 'three-footed', from tri- and pous, 'foot'.
hints: A photographer sets one up for a long exposure.
Three legs keep a telescope steady on uneven ground.
origin: Latin tripod-, from Ancient Greek τρίποδ-
example: Cameras often have tripod attachments, which help when taking steady photographs.

definition: Overused and unoriginal.
note: From Latin tritus, 'worn out'. A cliche is this.
hints: A cliche is this.
A phrase worn out from overuse.

definition: Unimportant facts and details; also a quiz game.
note: From Latin trivium, 'crossroads', since common gossip was heard where three roads met. Pub quizzes are full of it.
hints: What a pub quiz is based on.
Facts so small they come up only on quiz night.
example: Today's trivia corner! Today it's about the origin of Calpis.

definition: A group of soldiers; or to move in a group.
note: From French troupe, recorded in English since 1545. It can also name a group of scouts or monkeys.
hints: A unit of soldiers.
A group of monkeys.
origin: French troupe, from Old French trope

definition: Soldiers, as a body.
note: From French troupe, 'band' or 'company'.
hints: Army members.
Soldiers in a group.

definition: A recurring theme or device.
note: From Greek tropos, 'turn'. A familiar figure of speech or storytelling pattern is called one.
hints: A familiar plot device in films.
A cliche of a genre.
origin: Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος

definition: A prize awarded for victory.
note: From Greek tropaion, 'monument of an enemy's defeat'.
hints: A cup for the winner.
Placed on a shelf.
origin: Middle French trophée, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον

definition: A long open container that animals drink or eat from.
note: From Old English troh. The word also means a low point between waves or economic peaks.
hints: Pigs crowd around one at feeding time.
Sailors dread the dip between two big waves.
example: One of Harriet's chores was to slop the pigs' trough each morning and evening.

definition: A group of performers who travel and work together.
note: Borrowed from French in the 1800s. It is a doublet of troop, the two words coming from the same source.
hints: A circus or a travelling theatre company has one.
Dancers, jugglers and clowns might belong to the same one.

definition: A freshwater fish related to the salmon.
note: From Old English truht. Anglers prize them.
hints: A fish caught by fly fishers.
Spotted and found in cold streams.
origin: Old English truht, from Ancient Greek τρώκτης
example: Many anglers consider trout to be the archetypical quarry.

definition: A valuable collection of things found.
note: From Anglo-Norman tresor trouve, 'found treasure'. It is most often used in 'treasure ___'.
hints: A hoard of valuables found.
A hidden store of valuable things.
example: Tatoeba is a treasure trove of wisdom and world knowledge.

definition: An agreement to stop fighting.
note: From Middle English trewes, 'pledges', from Old English treow, 'faith'. Soldiers in 1914 held a famous one at Christmas.
hints: A pause in a war.
A white flag signals a wish for one.

definition: A large road vehicle for goods.
note: Perhaps from Greek trochos, 'wheel'. It was first a small wheel, then a cart.
hints: A big lorry.
A vehicle that carries cargo.
origin: Latin trochus, from Ancient Greek τροχός

definition: Really; genuinely.
note: From Old English treowlice, 'faithfully'. It is used at the end of a letter.
hints: The word before a signature in 'yours ___'.
Said when you mean it sincerely.
example: That is truly all I know.

definition: A winning card suit; or to beat.
note: Possibly from French triomphe, 'triumph'. A trump beats the other suits.
hints: A card that beats the rest.
To outdo a rival's play.

definition: The main stem of a tree; or an elephant's nose; or a car's boot.
note: From Old French tronc, 'alms box' or 'tree trunk'. Travellers also pack their belongings in a large box of the same name.
hints: An elephant's long nose.
The back storage area of an American car.
origin: Old French tronc, from Latin truncus

definition: A framework of beams; or to tie up tightly.
note: From Old French trousse, 'bundle'. Bridges and roofs use them, and cooks tie up a bird with string.
hints: A triangle framework in a roof.
To tie up a chicken before roasting.
origin: Old French trousse, from Classical Latin tortus

definition: Belief that someone is reliable.
note: From Old Norse traust, 'confidence'. It also names a legal arrangement for managing assets.
hints: What a bridge of friendship needs.
What you put in a reliable friend.

definition: Reliable and dependable.
note: From trust plus -y. It often precedes steed or sword.
hints: A faithful old horse in a Western.
Used of a long-serving knife or car.
example: She's been using the same trusty sewing machine since she started out, thirty long years ago.

definition: What is true.
note: From Old English triewth, 'faithfulness'. It is related to the word true.
hints: The opposite of a lie.
What a witness swears to tell.

definition: Relating to a tube.
note: From tube plus -al. It is a medical word, as in tubes of the body.
hints: A medical word about a duct.
Describes a passage like a tube in the body.

definition: Short and plump.
note: From tub plus -y. It is not related to chubby, though the two overlap.
hints: Plump, like a barrel.
Rounded and stout, in a cuddly way.

definition: A thick underground stem of a plant, like a potato.
note: From Latin tuber, 'swelling'. Potatoes and yams are examples.
hints: A potato is one.
A fleshy root vegetable.

definition: A cup-shaped spring flower.
note: From Middle French tulipe, from Turkish tulbent, 'turban', since the flower looks like a turban. The Dutch grew a mania for them in the 1600s.
hints: A flower tied to the Netherlands.
A spring bulb in many colours.
origin: Middle French tulipe, from Classical Persian دلبند
example: My mother likes tulips very much and so does my sister.

definition: A fine netting used for veils and ballet skirts.
note: Named after the French town of Tulle, where it was made. Bridal veils use it.
hints: The airy fabric of a tutu.
A fine net for a bride's veil.
example: She walked down the aisle in style, wearing her gorgeous mermaid-cut tulle wedding gown.

definition: To fall over, often rolling or flopping.
note: From Old English tumbian, 'to dance about'. It came to mean falling in a heap, and a tumble dryer turns clothes over and over.
hints: What a toddler does on the playground.
A dryer called by this name spins your laundry.

definition: A child's word for the stomach.
note: A child's version of stomach, via an old colloquial form stummy. It is used for the belly.
hints: What a baby rubs after feeding.
What aches after too much cake.

definition: An abnormal lump of tissue.
note: From Latin tumor, 'a swelling'. It is the American spelling of tumour.
hints: A medical growth that a scan can show.
A lump a doctor may remove.
origin: Old French tumour, from Latin tumor
example: I don't think it's true that cell phones cause tumors, Esther.

definition: A cold, flat Arctic region with no trees.
note: Borrowed from Russian tundra, which came from a Sami word for a treeless plain.
hints: Permafrost lies beneath it.
Reindeer wander it.
example: Are there many arctic foxes in the tundra?

definition: A person or device that tunes an instrument or radio.
note: From tune plus -er. A piano technician is one.
hints: A technician for a piano.
The dial on an old radio.

definition: A long loose garment worn over the body.
note: From Latin tunica. Roman soldiers wore one under their armour.
hints: A Roman soldier's garment.
A long shirt reaching to the thighs.
origin: Middle French tunique, from Latin tunica

definition: An underground passage.
note: From Old French tonnel, 'cask'.
hints: Under a hill.
A train goes through it.
example: The tunnel reduced congestion at that intersection.

definition: A turbine; or a booster in an engine.
note: Short for turbine or turbocharger, from Latin turbo, 'whirl'. It forces extra air into an engine.
hints: A booster for a car engine.
A fast speed setting.

definition: A large bird eaten at Christmas and Thanksgiving; also a country.
note: The bird was confused with guinea fowl, which came through Turkey, and so took the country's name.
hints: Roasted at Thanksgiving.
Bird named after a country by mistake.
example: All week after Thanksgiving, I had turkey sandwiches for lunch.

definition: A small tower on a castle wall or building corner.
note: From Old French torete, 'little tower', itself from Latin turris. Warships and tanks have rotating gun ones.
hints: Where an archer in a fortress might stand watch.
The rotating part of a tank that holds the gun.
origin: Old French torete, from Latin turris
example: Their Victorian house had three turrets and a large amount of gingerbread trim.

definition: A reptile with a shell that can swim.
note: Probably an alteration of French tortue.
hints: Slow moving shell-wearing animal.
Lays eggs on a beach.

definition: A private teacher.
note: From Latin tutor, 'guardian'. Students hire one for extra help.
hints: Someone hired to help with homework.
A university teacher guiding a few students.

definition: A musical direction for everyone to play together.
note: Italian for 'all', from Latin totus.
hints: Orchestras follow it after a solo.
Italian for 'everyone' on a score.

definition: A man's formal black jacket, or the whole suit.
note: Named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where the fashion is said to have started. The place name likely comes from an Algonquian language.
hints: James Bond wears one.
Worn with a bow tie.
example: He wore a tuxedo for his sister's wedding.

definition: An old word for two.
note: From Old English twegen, 'two'. It survives in 'never the twain shall meet'.
hints: A poetic word for a pair.
The first part of a famous author's pen name.

definition: A sharp ringing sound; or a nasal accent.
note: Imitative of a string being plucked. A banjo string and a country voice both have one.
hints: The sound of a guitar string plucked.
A nasal accent in a country song.

definition: To adjust slightly.
note: From Old English twiccian, 'to pluck'. It started as a pinch and became a small adjustment.
hints: A small adjustment.
What you do to settings.
example: If we tweak the colors towards blue, it will look more natural.

definition: The short chirp of a bird; or a post on a social network.
note: Imitative of a bird's call. It also names a short social media post.
hints: A bird's short call.
A short online post.

definition: The number after eleven.
note: From Old English twelf, meaning 'two left over' after ten.
hints: Two times six.
A clock's top number.

definition: The number after nineteen.
note: From Old English twentig, 'two tens'.
hints: Two tens added together.
One more than nineteen.
example: She looks like she's in her early twenties, perhaps 21 or 22 years old?

definition: To dance with fast hip-shaking movements.
note: Probably a blend of twitch and jerk; the dance became widely known from the early 2000s.
hints: A hip-hop dance move.
A dance featuring rapid hip motion.

definition: Two times.
note: From Old English twiges, from twi, 'two'. It is the adverb for doing something once more.
hints: One more time than once.
Said of doing it double.
example: You should brush your teeth twice a day.

definition: Cloth woven with diagonal ridges.
note: From Old English, meaning 'two-threaded'. Denim and chinos are examples.
hints: Fabric with a slanted weave.
Used in jeans and jackets.
origin: Old English twilīċ, from Latin bilix

definition: Strong string made of twisted threads; or to wind.
note: From Old English twin, 'double thread'. A gardener ties plants with it.
hints: String for tying a parcel.
What a vine does round a post.

definition: To spin round and round.
note: Of Scandinavian origin. A dancer or baton does it.
hints: What a ballerina does.
A fast spin.

definition: To turn round; or an unexpected turn in a story.
note: From Middle English twist, from Old English, a pair of things. A story or a rope can have one.
hints: What you do to open a jar.
A surprise at the end of a film.

definition: A sudden small movement.
note: From Middle English twicchen, 'to pluck'.
hints: An eyelid does it.
A small spasm.
example: I saw a little twitch in the man's face, and knew he was lying.

definition: An old word meaning 'between'.
note: A shortened form of betwixt, from Old English. It is found in the phrase 'twixt and between'.
hints: An old poetic word for in between.
A short version of a longer old preposition.

definition: A very rich and powerful businessperson.
note: Borrowed from Japanese taikun, 'great lord', a title for the shogun.
hints: Monopoly's mascot is dressed as one.
A railway or oil magnate of the 1800s.
example: Investors were impressed by the real estate tycoon's strategy.

definition: The act of fastening with a knot.
note: From tie plus -ing, from Old English tigan. A shoelace or a knot can be involved.
hints: What you do to shoelaces.
Fastening with a knot.

definition: A ruler who uses power cruelly and without limit.
note: From Greek tyrannos. The Greek word first meant a ruler who seized power, not necessarily a cruel one.
hints: A king who silences all opposition.
Tyrannosaurus rex was named as the king of these lizards, with this word at its root.

definition: A southern African philosophy that a person is a person through other people.
note: From the Zulu and Xhosa word for humanity. Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu helped spread the idea; it also names a Linux system.
hints: Desmond Tutu often spoke of this idea of shared humanity.
A free operating system took its name from it.

definition: The milk gland of a cow.
note: From Old English uder. It hangs below the cow.
hints: What a farmer milks.
The bag under a cow.
example: Yanni cleans his goat's udder very well before he milks it.

definition: Freedom, in Swahili.
note: Borrowed directly from Swahili. It was a rallying cry during African independence movements.
hints: Swahili word chanted at independence.
The summit of Kilimanjaro bears this name.

definition: An open sore.
note: From Latin ulcus, 'sore'. Stomach ones were once thought to be caused by stress.
hints: A sore in the stomach lining.
An open sore on the skin.
origin: Old French ulcere, from Latin ulcus

definition: A long, loose overcoat; also a province of Ireland.
note: Named for the coat's original maker, a Belfast company. Sherlock Holmes is shown wearing one.
hints: A heavy coat Sherlock Holmes might wear.
A province split between the Republic and the UK.

definition: Extreme; beyond the usual.
note: From Latin ultra, 'beyond'. It is used as a prefix, as in ultrasound.
hints: A prefix meaning beyond.
A race longer than a marathon is named with it.

definition: The official who enforces the rules in games such as cricket or baseball.
note: A misdivision of 'a noumper' into 'an oumper', from Old French non per, 'not equal', a third party who breaks ties.
hints: Raises a finger in cricket to give a batter out.
At Wimbledon, the one in the high chair calls the score.
origin: Old French nonper, from Latin par

definition: Not capable.
note: From un- plus able.
hints: Lacking the means to do something.
Can't do it.

definition: Not yet born.
note: From Old English unboren. It is used of a baby in the womb and, more poetically, of future generations.
hints: A mother-to-be is carrying such a child.
Speeches talk about the generations yet to come.

definition: A brother of one's parent.
note: From Old French oncle, from Latin avunculus, 'little grandfather'. It is a family member on one side.
hints: A parent's brother.
Said to be what Bob is, in a saying.

definition: Not cut; or not edited.
note: From un- plus cut. A rough gemstone or a film not trimmed may be it.
hints: A rough diamond.
A film with nothing removed.

definition: Not alive but not truly dead either, as zombies and vampires.
note: From un- plus dead, but the sense became popular after Bram Stoker's Dracula in 1897.
hints: Dracula's world is full of them.
Zombies and vampires belong to this category.

definition: Below or beneath.
note: From Old English under. It is the opposite of over.
hints: The opposite of over.
Found beneath a bed or a bridge.
example: The under parts of a machine.

definition: Not done; untied; or ruined.
note: From un- plus done. It has three meanings: unfinished work, unfastened laces, or a person brought to ruin.
hints: Shoelaces left this way cause trips.
Tasks left on a to-do list.
example: The work could be done or undone and nobody cared.

definition: Excessive or unwarranted.
note: From un- plus due. It describes something beyond what is right.
hints: Beyond what is called for.
Needless, as in worry.

definition: Anxious or uncomfortable.
note: From un- plus easy. The word once also meant difficult.
hints: How you feel walking home alone at night.
A truce between rivals that might not hold.
example: Was always uneasy with strangers.

definition: Not level or regular.
note: From Old English unefen. It can describe ground or a score.
hints: What a pitted road is.
What a rocky path or a mismatched contest feels like.

definition: Not just or equal.
note: From un- plus fair.
hints: Not treating everyone the same.
Cheating at a game is like this.
example: It was unfair for the boss to give larger bonuses to his friends.

definition: Not suitable; or out of shape.
note: From un- plus fit. A person who rarely exercises may be it.
hints: Not up to the standard.
Out of condition.

definition: To open out or develop gradually.
note: From Old English unfealdan. A map and a story can both do it.
hints: What a map does when you open it.
What a story does chapter by chapter.

definition: Wicked, or outrageously bad.
note: From Old English unhalig, 'not holy'. 'An unholy row' uses it for sheer excess.
hints: An alliance between enemies might be called this.
Horror films have rituals of this kind.

definition: To make into one.
note: From Late Latin unificare, 'to make one'. A nation or group can be brought together this way.
hints: What a leader does for a divided country.
To bring parts into a whole.
origin: Middle French unifier, from Late Latin unificare

definition: A joining together; or a group of workers.
note: From Late Latin unio, from unus, 'one'. A marriage is one, and so is a trade body.
hints: A workers' association.
A marriage, in a formal word.
origin: Old French union, from Latin ūnus

definition: One of a kind.
note: From French unique, from Latin unicus, 'single'.
hints: No other like it.
Without equal anywhere.
example: The unique existing example of Donne's handwriting.

definition: Sounding or acting together at the same time or pitch.
note: From Medieval Latin unisonus, 'having the same sound'. A choir sings 'in unison' when everyone sings the same note.
hints: A choir all singing the same note.
Soldiers marching in step move this way.
origin: Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus; in English since the 15th century

definition: To join together as one.
note: From Latin unire, 'to make one', from unus, 'one'. Countries and teams do it.
hints: What a common cause does to people.
To bring separate things together.

definition: The state of being as one.
note: From Old French unite, from Latin unitas, 'oneness'. It is what a team strives for.
hints: Agreement and togetherness.
What 'strength in numbers' relies on.
origin: Old French unité, from Latin ūnitās

definition: Not fair or right.
note: From un- plus just, which comes from Latin justus. It describes laws, wars and punishments.
hints: Said of a verdict that sends the wrong person to prison.
A law that treats people differently for no good reason.
example: The solution was very unjust.

definition: Except if.
note: From Middle English on lesse, 'on a less condition than'.
hints: Introduces a condition.
A word that sets an exception.

definition: Not similar to.
note: From un- plus like.
hints: Different from.
Not at all alike.
example: The disgust I felt after watching last weekend's horror movie was unlike anything I had felt before.

definition: Not lit.
note: From un- plus lit. A dark path or a fire never lit is this.
hints: A dark street at night.
A candle before the match.

definition: To take a load off a vehicle or container; also to get rid of something.
note: Formed from un- plus load.
hints: What a delivery driver does on arriving at the shop.
A dock worker does it to a cargo ship, crate by crate.

definition: To open something with a key.
note: From un- plus lock.
hints: Turn a key in a door.
Release a hidden feature.
example: I unlocked the door and walked in.

definition: Not fulfilled or not yet encountered.
note: From un- plus met. Needs and conditions can be this.
hints: A condition that has not been satisfied.
A goal not reached.

definition: To take things out of a suitcase or box.
note: From un- plus pack. A holiday ends with this chore.
hints: The first job after you get home from a trip.
Also to analyse an idea in detail.
example: I've just arrived. I haven't even unpacked my suitcases yet.

definition: Not yet paid for, or done without wages.
note: From un- plus paid.
hints: A bill left outstanding.
Work done for free.

definition: Not real; or amazing, in slang.
note: From un- plus real. Teens use it as praise for something astonishing.
hints: What a dream feels like on waking.
Said by a teenager of a stunning goal.

definition: A state of public disturbance or dissatisfaction.
note: From un- plus rest. Often used in news about protests and uprisings.
hints: A word from the news when streets fill with protesters.
A curfew may be imposed during it.

definition: Hard to control or manage.
note: From un- plus rule plus -ly. Middle English ruly meant disciplined.
hints: Describes a classroom of bored children.
Hair that will not stay flat.

definition: Likely to cause harm or danger.
note: From un- plus safe. As a verb it can mean to release a weapon's safety catch.
hints: What a wobbly bridge is.
A word on a warning sign near thin ice.

definition: Not seen or noticed; invisible.
note: From Old English ungesewen. It is also what examination passages not studied beforehand are called.
hints: The kind of translation passage nobody has prepared.
Ghosts and gravity are described this way.

definition: Not fixed or not yet placed.
note: From un- plus set. Jelly that has not firmed up is this.
hints: Jelly that is still runny.
A gem not yet put in a ring.

definition: Not certain.
note: From un- plus sure.
hints: Hesitant about a decision.
Not confident.

definition: To loosen a knot.
note: From Middle English untien, from un- plus tie. A shoelace or a rope can be loosened this way.
hints: What you do to a shoelace.
To free a rope from its knot.

definition: Up to the time of.
note: From Middle English until, probably a northern variant built from Old Norse und, 'up to'. It marks a limit in time.
hints: A word marking an end point in time.
Up to the moment when.

definition: Too many to count; or never told.
note: From Old English unteald, 'not counted'. Both senses survive: untold riches and an untold story.
hints: Riches beyond measure.
A secret that nobody has ever shared.
example: There is no greater agony than bearing an untold story.

definition: Not true; false.
note: Built from un- and true. Old English treowe meant 'faithful', so untrue can mean disloyal as well as wrong.
hints: Said of a rumour that has been disproved.
Old usage also describes a faithless lover.
example: She says that I stole her necklace, but that's completely untrue.

definition: Not yet put to use.
note: From un- plus used. In one sense it also means unaccustomed, as in being 'to' something.
hints: A brand-new item still in its wrapper.
What a gym membership often is.
example: We bought an unused car for a change.

definition: To remove a covering and reveal; to show publicly for the first time.
note: Formed from un- plus veil, ultimately from Latin velum, 'cloth, sail'.
hints: A statue is shown to the public by pulling away a cloth.
A company does it to a new product at a launch event.

definition: Not married.
note: From un- plus wed. It is a bit formal for single.
hints: Not yet married.
Said of an unmarried person.

definition: Not feeling healthy; ill.
note: From un- plus well. It is a polite, understated way to say sick.
hints: The polite word in an absence note to school.
A mild sickness, often cited by people calling in to work.
example: If the parrot seems sick or unwell, let me know immediately.

definition: To loosen something wound, or to relax.
note: From Old English unwindan, 'to unwrap'. Relaxing after work is like a spring losing tension.
hints: What you do on a Friday evening.
Thread coming off a spool.
example: Could you unwind about a foot of ribbon so I can finish the package?

definition: Not showing good sense.
note: From Old English unwis, 'foolish', from un- plus wise.
hints: Texting a former partner at midnight might be this.
A poor decision.
example: An unwise investor is soon impoverished.

definition: To open a fastener with teeth.
note: From un- plus zip. A jacket or a file can be this way opened.
hints: What you do to a jacket.
To open a compressed computer file.
example: Gabriel frantically unzipped his tent and called for help.

definition: Cheerful and optimistic.
note: From up plus beat. In music, the upbeat is the unstressed beat before the downbeat.
hints: A word for a positive forecast.
How a good-news speech sounds.

definition: A new version or the act of making something current.
note: From up plus date.
hints: News bringing you up to speed.
What your phone asks you to install.
example: The server update ran overnight.

definition: Going up a slope; or hard and demanding.
note: Simply up plus hill. An uphill battle is a struggle against odds.
hints: What Sisyphus pushes his boulder.
A tiring walk that makes your legs burn.

definition: To maintain or support, especially a rule or decision.
note: From up plus hold. Courts uphold or overturn verdicts.
hints: What an appeals court may do to a verdict.
To defend a principle.

definition: The work and cost of keeping something in good condition.
note: Formed from up plus keep, in the sense of maintaining.
hints: A big old house with a leaky roof demands plenty of it.
Garden, car or castle, it is the ongoing bill after you buy.
example: I would enjoy having a swimming pool, but I don't want to deal with the upkeep.

definition: High ground inland, away from the coast or valleys.
note: From Old English upland, which meant the countryside as opposed to town. The adjective grew later.
hints: Sheep graze across moors of this kind.
Hills and plateaus, the opposite of lowland.

definition: To raise up, physically or in spirit.
note: From up and lift. It can mean a lift in mood or a rise in standards.
hints: A bra is sometimes advertised as giving this.
A rousing speech can give listeners this.
example: Music can uplift your spirits.

definition: To send a file to the internet.
note: From up plus load.
hints: Pushing photos from your phone to a cloud service.
Post a video online.

definition: Higher in position.
note: From Middle English, the comparative of up. It is the opposite of lower.
hints: A class or a hand, in two familiar phrases.
The top deck of a bus.
example: In the upper center of the picture.

definition: A loud, confused outburst of noise or anger.
note: A loan translation of Dutch oproer or German Aufruhr, from up and roar.
hints: Parliament can fall into one over a heated debate.
A crowd's response when a goal is disallowed.

definition: To disturb or overturn; or unhappy.
note: From Middle English upsetten, 'to set up'. A stomach, a cart and a person can all be this.
hints: A tipped glass of water.
Distressed after bad news.

definition: The positive side of a situation.
note: From up plus side.
hints: The silver lining of a bad situation.
Investors weigh it against the downside of a risk.
example: What was the idea of leaving the cup upside down last time?

definition: How quickly something is taken up or absorbed.
note: Formed from up and take. It describes absorption of nutrients and take-up of new products.
hints: Doctors measure oxygen use by athletes with its name.
Being quick on it in conversation means grasping things fast.

definition: The residential or upper part of a city, away from the centre.
note: Formed from up plus town, first in American English. In New York it means the northern part of Manhattan.
hints: In New York it lies north of midtown.
Billy Joel sang about the girl from this district.

definition: Toward a higher place.
note: From Old English upweard.
hints: Heading to the sky.
The direction of a rising graph or a hot-air balloon.
example: A general upward movement of fish.

definition: Relating to a city.
note: From Latin urbanus, from urbs, 'city'. It is the opposite of rural.
hints: City skylines and street art are of this kind.
Of a big town.

definition: Needing immediate action.
note: From Latin urgere, 'to press'.
hints: Needing immediate attention.
Pressing, as a deadline.
origin: Middle French urgent, from Latin urgēns
example: An urgent appeal was sent out for assistance.

definition: Liquid waste from the kidneys.
note: From Latin urina. A medical sample for a test is often of it.
hints: A sample a doctor may test.
Waste water made by the kidneys.

definition: Fit to be used.
note: From use plus -able. Software designers talk of how easily something is.
hints: What a broken tool is not.
What a good user interface is.
example: The lawnmower is a bit rusty but still usable.

definition: The way something is used.
note: From Old French usage, from user, 'to use'. A dictionary records it.
hints: How a word is commonly employed.
The amount of data or power consumed.
origin: Old French usage; in English since the 14th century

definition: Able to be used for a purpose.
note: From use plus -ful.
hints: Handy and practical.
Worth having around.

definition: A person who shows people to their seats.
note: From Old French ussier, 'doorkeeper', from Latin ostiarius. It also means to guide someone in.
hints: Works at a wedding or cinema.
To guide in, as to show guests in.
origin: Anglo-Norman usser, from Old French ussier

definition: Normal; as expected.
note: From Latin usualis, 'of use'. It is what happens most of the time.
hints: The standard order at a cafe.
What is customary.
origin: Old French usuel, from Latin ūsuālis

definition: To seize power wrongfully.
note: From Latin usurpare, 'to take over'. A rebel might do it to a throne.
hints: What a pretender does to a king.
To take a throne with no right.
origin: Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō
example: He usurped my rights.

definition: The lending of money at an unfairly high interest rate.
note: From Latin usura, 'use', since the lender charges for the use of money.
hints: Medieval churches condemned it.
Loan sharks practise it.

definition: The organ in which a baby develops before birth.
note: Latin for 'womb', a word used in anatomy for over two thousand years.
hints: Also called the womb.
Medical word for where a foetus grows.
example: How do you expect me to have children when I don't have a uterus?

definition: Useful.
note: From Latin utilis, 'useful'. It is an old, learned word.
hints: An old word for useful.
A cousin of the word utility.
origin: Middle French utile, from Latin ūtilis

definition: The greatest possible; extreme.
note: From Old English utmest, 'outermost', from ut, 'out'. 'Do your utmost' means try as hard as you can.
hints: 'Of the importance' in a solemn warning.
What your best effort is stretched to.
example: He tried his utmost.

definition: An imagined perfect society.
note: Coined by Thomas More in 1516 from Greek ou 'not' and topos 'place', so it literally means 'no place'.
hints: More used it for the title of his book.
Its opposite is dystopia.
origin: New Latin Ūtopia, from Ancient Greek οὐ

definition: To say aloud; or complete.
note: From Middle English utteren, 'to speak out', and as an adjective, 'outermost'. 'Utter nonsense' is total nonsense.
hints: To say a word aloud.
Total, as in nonsense.

definition: Empty or unoccupied.
note: From Latin vacans, 'being empty'.
hints: A room with no guest.
Without anyone in it.
origin: Old French vacant, from Latin vacāns

definition: To leave a place or a position empty.
note: From Latin vacare, 'to be empty'. Early English use was legal: to annul something so that it stood empty.
hints: Tenants must do it when the lease ends.
Hotel guests do so by checkout time.
example: He vacated his coaching position because of the corruption scandal.

definition: A space empty of matter; also a cleaning appliance.
note: From Latin vacuus, 'empty'.
hints: Outer space is an example.
Cleaner that sucks up dust.
origin: New Latin vacuum, from Classical Latin vacuum
example: Without their support he'll be ruling in a vacuum.

definition: A person who parks cars or attends to a man's clothes.
note: From Old French vaslet, 'young man'. It now describes a car-parking service.
hints: Takes your car at the hotel door.
A gentleman's personal servant.
origin: Middle French valet, from Late Latin vassallus

definition: A low area between hills.
note: From Old French valee, from Latin vallis.
hints: Often has a river at the bottom.
Lowland between two ridges.
origin: Anglo-Norman valey, from Old French valee
example: The Indus River valley was the site of an ancient civilization.

definition: Great courage, especially in battle.
note: The American spelling of valour, from Latin valere, 'to be strong'. It is awarded in medals.
hints: Bravery on the battlefield.
What a medal may honour.
example: He received a medal for valor.

definition: How much something is worth.
note: From Old French value, 'worth'. It can be money or principles.
hints: What a price shows.
What you hold dear.
