origin: Old French value, from Latin valēre

definition: A device that controls the flow of liquid or gas.
note: From Latin valva, 'leaf of a door'. The heart has four.
hints: A tap-like part in a pipe.
A part of the heart that controls flow.

definition: To disappear suddenly.
note: Aphetic form of evanish, from Latin evanescere, 'to fade away'. Magicians vanish coins and assistants.
hints: What a magician makes a coin do.
Ghosts do it at dawn.
origin: Old French esvanir, from Latin ēvānēscō
example: The money vanished in las Vegas.

definition: Excessive pride in looks, or a dressing table.
note: From Latin vanitas, 'emptiness'.
hints: A bathroom unit with a mirror.
Admiring yourself in a mirror.
origin: Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas

definition: Dull and lacking interest.
note: From Latin vapidus, 'flat' or 'stale', used of wine. Conversation can be this way.
hints: A dull conversation.
Lacking spark.

definition: A mist or gas from a liquid.
note: The American spelling of vapour, from Latin vapor, 'steam'. It rises from a kettle.
hints: What rises from a hot bath.
The gas form of a liquid.

definition: Showing differences or many kinds.
note: From vary plus -ed.
hints: Showing many different kinds.
A diet with lots of different foods.

definition: To a very great extent.
note: From vast plus -ly. Vast comes from Latin vastus, 'empty, immense'.
hints: How much bigger a galaxy is than a planet.
An adverb that stresses a huge difference.
example: He had vastly overestimated his resources.

definition: An arched ceiling; or a strong room; or to leap.
note: From Old French volte, 'turned'. It names a bank room, a church ceiling, and a pole jump.
hints: A bank's secure room.
To leap over using a pole.
origin: Old French volte, from Latin volūta

definition: To boast.
note: From Old French vanter, from Latin vanus, 'vain'. It survives in 'much vaunted'.
hints: To brag about something.
What a boastful person does with achievements.

definition: A quantity with magnitude and direction; or an organism that carries disease.
note: From Latin vector, 'carrier'.
hints: Arrow in physics.
A mosquito spreading malaria.

definition: Someone who avoids all animal products.
note: Coined in 1944 from the first and last letters of vegetarian. It excludes dairy and eggs.
hints: Eats no meat, dairy or eggs.
Stricter than a vegetarian.
example: Our vegan-friendly shaving brush is made with synthetic bristles instead of badger hair.

definition: Casual word for a vegetable or vegetarian.
note: A clipping of vegetable or vegetarian, plus -ie. 'Veggie burger' uses the second sense.
hints: A burger with no meat.
A casual name for carrots and broccoli.

definition: A soft fabric with a thick, smooth pile.
note: From Old French veluotte, from Latin villus, 'shaggy hair'.
hints: Curtains in a theatre.
Smooth and soft to touch.
origin: Old Occitan veluet, from Latin villus

definition: A person or company that sells.
note: From Anglo-Norman vendour, from Latin vendere, 'to sell'.
hints: Hot dog seller.
Stall seller at a market.

definition: A thin decorative layer of wood, or a false outward show.
note: From German Furnier, 'to inlay', from French fournir, 'to furnish'. A veneer of politeness is a thin layer over something less nice.
hints: Cheap furniture often has a thin layer of this over chipboard.
Of civilisation, it is said to be thin.
origin: German Furnier, from Old French fornir

definition: The place where an event happens.
note: From Old French venue, 'a coming'. A concert is held at one.
hints: Where a concert is held.
A place booked for a wedding.

definition: Spoken, or relating to words.
note: From Latin verbalis, from verbum, 'word'.
hints: Not in writing.
A spoken agreement is this.
origin: Old French verbal, from Late Latin verbālis

definition: The edge of something; or to be close to.
note: From Old French verge, 'rod'. It also names the grass at the road's edge.
hints: The grass at a road's edge.
Close to tears, on the brink.
origin: Middle French verge, from Latin virga

definition: To confirm that something is true.
note: From Latin verificare, 'to make true'.
hints: Check a fact.
Prove that it's accurate.
origin: Old French verifier, from Latin vērus

definition: Against, as in a contest.
note: Latin for 'turned toward' or 'against'. It is often abbreviated vs.
hints: Team A is placed against Team B.
Shown with a v between two names.

definition: The highest point of something; the corner where lines or edges meet.
note: Borrowed from Latin vertex, 'whirl, top'. It is a doublet of vortex.
hints: A triangle has three of them.
The sharp tip of a cone.

definition: Energy and enthusiasm.
note: From French verve, 'caprice' or 'rapture'. A performer can play with it.
hints: Liveliness in a performance.
A burst of spirited energy.
example: Her verve stayed with her well into her old age.

definition: A ship or boat, or a container for liquid.
note: From Old French vaissel, from Latin vascellum, 'small vase'.
hints: A craft on the sea.
A jug or a vein could be called this.

definition: A short match made of wax or wood.
note: Named after Vesta, the Roman goddess of fire and hearth.
hints: Old name for a match.
Roman goddess whose flame was tended by priestesses.

definition: Capable of working or surviving.
note: From French vie, 'life', from Latin vita.
hints: A plan that might succeed.
A newborn that can live alone.

definition: A parish priest in the Church of England.
note: From Old French vicaire, from Latin vicarius, 'substitute'. He stood in for a bishop or rector.
hints: A priest in an English village.
A church leader in a parish.

definition: A person harmed by a crime or accident.
note: From Latin victima, 'sacrificial animal'.
hints: One who suffers harm.
Its Latin ancestor was an animal offered in sacrifice.
origin: Middle French victime, from Latin victima

definition: The winner of a contest.
note: From Latin victor, 'conqueror'.
hints: Takes the spoils.
Champion at the end.

definition: A recording of moving images.
note: From Latin video, 'I see'. It also names a recorded film.
hints: What a camera records.
A clip on a phone.
example: She is a star of screen and video.

definition: A person watching something.
note: From view plus -er.
hints: Sits in front of a screen.
Audience member at home.

definition: A Norse seafarer who raided and traded across Europe from the late 700s.
note: The origin is debated; it may come from Old Norse vik, 'bay'. Horned helmets in pictures are a modern myth.
hints: A raider in a longship with a dragon prow.
Horned helmets were a later artist's invention.
example: Viking helmets with horns aren't in style in Scandinavia anymore.

definition: A large house in the country or by the sea.
note: From Latin villa, 'country house'. Holiday ones are rented abroad.
hints: A holiday home in the sun.
A Roman country house.

definition: A stringed instrument slightly larger than a violin.
note: From Italian viola, from a Latin word for fiddle. It is played under the chin.
hints: An instrument a bit bigger than a violin.
A flower, a cousin of the pansy.
origin: Italian viola, from Medieval Latin vitula

definition: A small purple flower, or the colour.
note: From Old French violete, from Latin viola.
hints: Colour at the end of a rainbow.
Roses are red, these are blue.
origin: Old French violette, from Latin viola

definition: A stringed instrument played with a bow.
note: From Italian violino, 'little viola'.
hints: A bowed instrument with four strings.
A fiddle, in folk music.
example: When I play it like this, it's a fiddle; when I play it like this, it's a violin.

definition: A venomous snake.
note: From Latin vipera, 'snake that gives birth to live young'. An adder is one.
hints: A poisonous snake.
The adder is a British one.
origin: Middle French vipere, from Latin vīpera
example: Gaboon vipers have unique horns on the tip of their noses.

definition: Relating to a virus; or spreading quickly online.
note: From virus plus -al. A video can be called it if shared widely.
hints: A video shared by millions.
Caused by a germ.

definition: Someone who has not had sex; or something pure or untouched.
note: From Latin virgo, 'maiden'.
hints: As in olive oil.
Untouched or new.
origin: Old French virgine, from Latin virginem

definition: A good quality of character.
note: From Latin virtus, 'manliness' or 'excellence', from vir, 'man'.
hints: Patience is said to be one.
A moral quality such as honesty.

definition: A tiny infectious agent; or a harmful computer program.
note: From Latin virus, 'poison'. It is smaller than bacteria.
hints: A cause of colds and flu.
Harmful code on a computer.

definition: The ability to see; or an imagined image.
note: From Latin visio, 'sight', from videre, 'to see'.
hints: What opticians test.
A dream of the future.

definition: To go and see someone.
note: From Latin visitare, 'to go to see'. You can pay one to a friend or a museum.
hints: What you do to see a friend.
A trip to a place.
origin: Old French visiter, from Latin vīsitō; in English since the 13th century

definition: A front part of a helmet or cap that shades the eyes.
note: From Anglo-Norman viser, from Old French vis, 'face'. A knight's one lifted to show the face.
hints: A knight's face guard.
A cap's brim that shades the eyes.
origin: Anglo-Norman viser, from Old French visiere

definition: A long view, especially a scenic one.
note: From Italian vista, 'sight'. A mountain top offers one.
hints: A scenic outlook.
A wide view over a valley.

definition: Relating to sight.
note: From Latin visualis, from visus, 'sight'.
hints: Seen with the eyes.
A chart or picture.
origin: French visuel, from Late Latin vīsuālis

definition: Essential; or full of life.
note: From Latin vitalis, from vita, 'life'. Vital signs show life.
hints: Essential for life.
Pulse and breathing are called this sign.
origin: Old French vital, from Latin vītālis
example: Blood and other vital fluids.

definition: Bright and clear.
note: From Latin vividus, 'lively'. A dream or a colour can be this.
hints: A bright colour.
A memory so clear it feels real.

definition: A female fox.
note: From Old English fyxen, 'she-fox'. It is also an old insult for a bad-tempered woman.
hints: A she-fox in the wild.
A reindeer in the Christmas song.

definition: Short for vocabulary, the words you know.
note: A clipping of vocabulary.
hints: What students memorise before a language test.
Words you know.

definition: Relating to the voice; or speaking out.
note: From Latin vocalis, from vox, 'voice'. A singer has them, and a campaigner can be this.
hints: A singer's part of a song.
Someone who speaks out loudly.
example: Organized a vocal group to sing his compositions.

definition: A clear strong spirit, usually from grain or potato.
note: From Russian vodka, a diminutive of voda, 'water'. It means 'little water'.
hints: A clear spirit from Russia.
Used in a Moscow mule.
example: My head is throbbing because of all the vodka I had last night.

definition: A burst of many things sent at once, such as arrows or shots; in tennis, a hit before the ball bounces.
note: From Middle French volee, 'flight', and ultimately from Latin volare, 'to fly'.
hints: Archers loose it on the order 'fire'.
A tennis player strikes the ball with no bounce.
origin: Middle French volée, from Late Latin volatus

definition: The amount of space something takes up, a book, or loudness.
note: From Latin volumen, 'a roll', as books were scrolls.
hints: A single book from a set.
What a dial adjusts on a radio.
origin: Old French volume, from Latin volūmen
example: The gas expanded to twice its original volume.

definition: To throw up the contents of the stomach.
note: From Latin vomere. It is a medical and a plain word.
hints: What seasickness may cause.
What a queasy stomach may lead to.
example: After drinking too much, the students vomited.

definition: A religion from West Africa and the Caribbean, often wrongly linked to pins in dolls.
note: From Louisiana Creole voudou, from Haitian Creole, from the Fon word vodun, meaning spirit or deity. The movie stereotype hardly resembles the real faith.
hints: Haiti and New Orleans are linked with this religion.
Films show pin-stuck dolls, a stereotype of the real practice.
origin: Louisiana Creole voudou, from Fon vòdún

definition: A whirling mass of water or air, such as a whirlpool or tornado.
note: From Latin vortex, a variant of vertex, from vertere, 'to turn'. It also describes a situation that sucks you in.
hints: What a draining bathtub forms.
A swirling storm of wind shaped like a funnel.

definition: A person who casts a ballot.
note: From vote plus -er. In many countries you must register to be one.
hints: Someone at the polls.
Casts a ballot in an election.
example: Obviously the Republicans are scared to death of the voters.

definition: To confirm that someone or something is reliable.
note: From Middle English vouchen, 'to summon as a witness', from Old French. A friend can do it for your character.
hints: What a reference does for a job seeker.
To speak up for someone's honesty.

definition: A speech sound made without blocking the breath; or the letter for it.
note: From Old French vouel, from Latin vocalis, 'sounding'. In English they are a, e, i, o and u.
hints: A, E, I, O or U.
What a consonant is not.

definition: A long journey, especially by sea.
note: From Old French veiage, from Latin viaticum, 'provisions for a journey'.
hints: Columbus made a famous one in 1492.
A long trip across the ocean.

definition: The sound of a revving engine.
note: Imitative, like the noise it names.
hints: Sound a sports car makes.
What a child says while pushing a toy car.

definition: Crude, coarse or lacking good taste.
note: From Latin vulgus, 'the common people'. The Vulgate was the common Latin Bible.
hints: A rude joke at a posh dinner.
Also describes a fraction, once called common.
example: Appealing to the vulgar taste for violence.

definition: Competing for something.
note: The present participle of vie, from Old French envier, 'to challenge'. Rivals are said to be doing it for a prize.
hints: Two rivals competing for a title.
Competing eagerly for first place.

definition: Funny in a crazy way.
note: From whack plus -y. It describes zany people and ideas.
hints: A zany, eccentric idea.
Like a comedy full of bizarre antics.

definition: A thin crisp biscuit; or a thin disc of bread used in communion.
note: From Anglo-Norman wafre, from a Germanic word for 'honeycomb', because of the pattern. Ice cream is often served between them.
hints: A thin crisp biscuit for ice cream.
A thin disc of bread in church.

definition: A crisp batter cake with a grid pattern; also, to talk on without saying much.
note: From Dutch wafel, related to wafer. The verb 'waffle', to ramble, is a separate word that appeared in the 1600s.
hints: Syrup pools in its square dimples.
What a politician does when avoiding a straight answer.
origin: Dutch wafel, from Middle Dutch wafel

definition: A four-wheeled cart for goods.
note: Borrowed from Dutch wagen. Settlers crossed America in covered ones.
hints: What settlers rode across the prairie.
A child's pull-along toy cart.
origin: Middle Dutch wagen; in English since the late 15th century

definition: A fast, slender tropical game fish; also a cry of joy.
note: Perhaps named after Oahu, an obsolete spelling of which was Wahoo.
hints: A game fish related to the mackerel.
Fast ocean predator.

definition: The narrow part of the body between ribs and hips.
note: From Middle English wast, probably from Old English. A belt goes round it.
hints: Where a belt sits.
The narrow part of an hourglass figure.

definition: A person who serves food and drink at tables.
note: From Middle English waiter, once a watchman, from wait. The restaurant sense came later, from one who attends on diners.
hints: Brings the menu and later the bill.
Someone who says 'Table for two?'
example: Waiter! There's a fly in my soup.

definition: To give up a right or a claim.
note: From Middle English weyven, 'to abandon'. A bank might do it to a fee.
hints: What a landlord may do to a late fee.
To choose not to enforce a rule.
origin: Anglo-Norman weyver, from Old French waif

definition: A document in which someone gives up a right or claim.
note: From Anglo-Norman weyver, 'to abandon'. You sign one before bungee jumping.
hints: What you sign before a risky activity.
A legal form giving up a claim.
example: I had to sign a waiver when I went skydiving, agreeing not to sue even if something went wrong.

definition: A person who goes on foot; also a frame that helps someone walk.
note: From walk plus -er.
hints: One who takes a stroll.
A frame for support on the move.
example: The park was full of morning walkers enjoying the fresh air.

definition: A small case for money and cards.
note: Of uncertain origin; it appears in Middle English.
hints: Kept in a pocket.
Holds cash and cards in a pocket.
example: The thief stole all the money and credit cards out of the old man's wallet.

definition: A wrinkled nut with a hard shell that grows on a tree; also its dark wood.
note: From Old English wealhhnutu, 'foreign nut', since it came from lands beyond. Wealh meant foreign or Celtic.
hints: A nut that looks like a tiny brain.
Prized for its dark, handsome wood in furniture.

definition: A ballroom dance in three-beat time.
note: From German Walzer, from walzen, 'to roll or turn'. Vienna made it famous.
hints: A ballroom dance with a one-two-three beat.
Strauss wrote famous ones.
origin: German Walzer, from Old High German walzan

definition: To walk about without a fixed route or purpose.
note: From Old English wandrian, related to 'wend' and 'wind'. A mind that drifts off topic is said to do this as well.
hints: What a daydreaming tourist does down side streets.
Also what your attention does in a dull lecture.

definition: A casual way of saying 'want to'.
note: A contraction of want to, recorded as early as 1824.
hints: A relaxed way to ask what you desire.
A spoken blend of two words.

definition: A person responsible for guarding or supervising a place or people.
note: From Anglo-Norman wardein, related to 'guardian'. Prisons, parks and colleges have them.
hints: A prison's boss in the movies.
A park ranger or a game keeper may hold this title.
origin: Anglo-Norman wardein, from Old French guarder

definition: Less cold.
note: The comparative of warm.
hints: More toasty than before.
A device to keep drinks hot.

definition: In a friendly way; also in a way that keeps in heat.
note: Formed from warm plus the adverb ending -ly.
hints: How a good host greets you at the door.
Wrapped up this way, you can stay out in winter.

definition: Mild heat, or friendliness.
note: From warm plus -th.
hints: What a fire gives.
Kindness in a person's manner.

definition: A network of rabbit burrows, or a crowded maze of passages.
note: From Anglo-Norman warenne, a piece of land kept for game.
hints: Rabbits live in one.
A maze of narrow streets.

definition: Covered in small hard growths.
note: From wart plus -y. A toad's skin is this way.
hints: A toad's skin.
Lumpy and rough.

definition: A machine for washing clothes; or a small flat ring that seals a joint.
note: From wash plus -er. The metal ring sits under a bolt or inside a tap.
hints: A cycle of spin and rinse happens in this machine.
A small rubber one stops a tap from dripping.

definition: Weak, thin or watery.
note: From wash plus -y.
hints: What an overly diluted drink tastes.
Insipid or pale.

definition: To use carelessly; or rubbish.
note: From Old French guast, from Latin vastus, 'empty'. It names both throwing things away and what is thrown away.
hints: What you do with money you squander.
Rubbish thrown out.
example: Waste a joke on an unappreciative audience.

definition: To look at carefully; or a timepiece on the wrist.
note: From Old English waecce, 'wakefulness'. A guard keeps one at night.
hints: What you wear on your wrist.
What a lifeguard does at the beach.
example: Watching the clock will not make time go faster.

definition: The clear liquid that falls as rain.
note: From Old English waeter. Rivers, rain and oceans are made of it.
hints: What you drink when thirsty.
A chemical made of hydrogen and oxygen.

definition: Like water; thin and weak, or full of water.
note: From Old English wateriġ, formed from water and -ig.
hints: A thin, bland soup earns this description.
Eyes can look this way when you have a cold.

definition: To be unsteady or unsure.
note: From Middle English waveren, 'to move unsteadily'. A flame or a decision can do it.
hints: What a voice does when nervous.
To be torn between choices.

definition: Made of wax; or pale like wax.
note: From Old English weaxen, 'of wax'. A pale face may be called it.
hints: A pale, smooth face like a candle.
Made of the stuff candles are formed from.
example: Careful, the floor is waxy.

definition: To make or become less strong.
note: From weak plus -en. Illness, doubt and lack of food can each do it.
hints: What a long illness does to a body.
What a leak does to a dam.
example: The prisoner's resistance weakened after seven days.

definition: Less strong.
note: The comparative of weak, from Old Norse veikr.
hints: Not as powerful as before.
Less sturdy than another.

definition: Without strength or force; also, frail and sickly.
note: From Old English waclice, formed from weak plus -ly.
hints: How a tired patient might whisper.
A handshake of this kind gives a bad impression.

definition: A great amount of money or possessions.
note: From Middle English welthe, related to well, as in well-being.
hints: Riches and abundant possessions.
Its old root meant well-being.
example: Money talks, but true wealth whispers.

definition: A tool for fighting or defence.
note: From Old English waepen.
hints: A sword or a gun.
Armed forces carry them.
example: He was licensed to carry a weapon.

definition: A small, slender, quick predator related to stoats and ferrets; also a sly person.
note: From Old English weosule. The origin before that is uncertain.
hints: A song says it goes pop.
A shifty person who dodges blame has the name.

definition: To make cloth by crossing threads.
note: From Old English wefan. A loom is used.
hints: What a loom does.
What a spider does with a web.
example: The ambulance weaved its way through the heavy traffic.

definition: A person who makes cloth on a loom.
note: From Old English wefan, 'to weave'. A weaverbird also builds elaborate nests.
hints: Works at a loom turning thread into fabric.
Also a bird that makes a hanging nest.

definition: A camera attached to a computer for video calls.
note: Blend of web and camera. The first well-known one watched a coffee pot at Cambridge in 1991.
hints: The little camera above a laptop screen.
What you cover for privacy.

definition: A tapering piece of material used to split or hold.
note: From Old English wecg. A door may be held open by one.
hints: What keeps a door open.
A piece of cheese cut like a triangle.

definition: Full of weeds; or thin and weak.
note: From weed plus -y. A neglected garden is this way.
hints: An overgrown flowerbed.
A puny, thin person.
example: Weedy plants that take over a garden.

definition: Once a week.
note: From week plus -ly.
hints: A magazine that comes out every seven days.
Happening every seven days.

definition: To find how heavy something is.
note: From Old English wegan, 'to carry or lift'. A scale does it.
hints: What a scale does.
To consider options before choosing.

definition: How heavy something is.
note: From Old English wiht, related to weigh.
hints: A scale shows it.
What a gym bar adds.

definition: Strange or unusual.
note: From Old English wyrd, 'fate'. The word first meant destiny, then something uncanny.
hints: Odd and unsettling.
Once meant fate in Old English.
example: There are lots of weird people in this place.

definition: An odd or eccentric person.
note: From weird plus -o, first recorded in American English in the 1950s. Weird itself once meant 'fate'.
hints: A schoolyard insult for the strange kid.
Said of someone who talks to their plants.

definition: An old word for a girl or young woman, often a servant.
note: From Middle English wenchel, 'child', which was neutral before it became patronising.
hints: Tavern server in a historical drama.
Medieval word for a young lass.

definition: To hit sharply.
note: Uncertain in origin; it is probably imitative of the sound of a blow. 'Out of whack' means out of order.
hints: A hard blow with a stick.
The sound of a bat hitting a ball.
example: The bat whacked the baseball.

definition: A huge sea mammal.
note: From Old English hwael. Blue ones are the largest animals ever.
hints: The largest animal in the sea.
A mammal that sings in the ocean.

definition: A structure where ships dock.
note: From Old English hwearf, 'bank' or 'shore'. Boats load and unload at one.
hints: A place for ships to tie up.
A landing stage beside the water.

definition: A cereal grain from which flour is made.
note: From Old English haete, probably related to white. Bread is baked from it.
hints: What bread is made from.
A golden field crop.
example: They bought a sack of wheat and a sack of rye with the intent to try their hand at milling and baking.

definition: A round part that turns on an axle.
note: From Old English hweol. Bicycles and cars roll on them.
hints: A round part on a bicycle.
What you turn to steer a ship.

definition: A puppy; or a cheeky young man.
note: From Old English hwelp. Dogs and wolves have them.
hints: A baby dog or wolf.
A rude word for a young upstart.

definition: From where.
note: From Middle English whennes, from Old English hwanon plus an -s ending. It already includes the meaning 'from', so 'from whence' is technically redundant.
hints: Archaic for from where.
Poets pair it with thence, meaning from there.
example: She has reddish hair, whence comes her nickname "Carrot".

definition: At what place.
note: From Old English hwaer. It starts a question about location.
hints: A question about a location.
What a map answers.

definition: What one of several.
note: From Old English hwylc, 'of what kind'. It asks a choice.
hints: A question word for choosing.
A word to pick between two.

definition: A faint smell.
note: Imitative, first recorded for a puff of air. A bit of perfume or smoke is one.
hints: A hint of cooking in the air.
A faint trace of perfume.

definition: A period of time; or during the time that.
note: From Old English hwil, 'time'. It can also mean 'although'.
hints: A short period of time.
A word meaning 'although' or 'during'.
example: He was here for a little while.

definition: A British word for while.
note: From while plus the old adverb ending -s, with a t added later.
hints: A formal way to say meanwhile.
Old-fashioned British version of a conjunction.

definition: To complain in a high, drawn-out tone.
note: From Old English hwinan, 'to whistle through the air'. A dog or a child may do it.
hints: What a puppy does at the door.
A child's long complaint.

definition: Complaining in a fretful tone.
note: From whine plus -y. It describes a child who keeps grumbling.
hints: A child grumbling in the back of a car.
Constantly moaning.
example: She is very whiny; she keeps complaining about trivial things.

definition: To spin rapidly.
note: From Middle English whirlen, from a Scandinavian word. A dancer or a tornado can do it.
hints: What a dancer does.
A spinning motion.
origin: Old English hweorfan, from Old Norse hvirfla
example: The dancer whirled across the stage, stopped, and whirled around to face the audience.

definition: A strong spirit distilled from grain, especially in Scotland.
note: Shortened from Gaelic uisge beatha, 'water of life'. Scotch is the famous Scottish kind.
hints: A Highland distillery's famous product.
'Water of life' in Gaelic, aged in oak barrels.
origin: Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha, from Medieval Latin aqua vitae
example: "I'll have whisky, please!" "All I've got is tea or nothing."

definition: The colour of snow or milk.
note: From Old English hwit. It is the colour of clean paper.
hints: The colour of fresh snow.
The opposite of black.

definition: Complete; not divided.
note: From Old English hal, 'healthy', also source of hale and heal. A loaf or a number may be this.
hints: Every bit of it, not in parts.
The opposite of a fraction.
example: This variety of fascinating details didn't fall together into an enjoyable, coherent whole.

definition: Completely.
note: From whole plus -ly.
hints: To the full extent, in total.
In every part, completely.
example: He was wholly convinced.

definition: A loud cry of joy.
note: From Middle English whopen, imitative. It is a sound of excitement.
hints: A shout of excitement.
What a crowd gives at a win.

definition: A spiral or circular pattern, like a fingerprint ridge.
note: An alteration of whirl. The word is also used for a ring of leaves around a stem.
hints: Pattern at the tip of your finger.
A swirl of leaves around a stem.

definition: Of which person.
note: From Old English hwaes, the genitive of who. It asks about ownership.
hints: A word asking who owns it.
The possessive of who.

definition: Evil, or slang for excellent.
note: From Middle English wikked, meaning evil. Slang uses it as high praise.
hints: A villain in a fairy tale.
Boston slang for very.

definition: The set of stumps and bails in cricket, or a small gate.
note: From Old Northern French wiket, 'small door'. In cricket the batter defends it.
hints: What a bowler tries to knock down.
Also a small gate set in a larger door.
origin: Old Northern French wiket, from Old Norse víkjask
example: The umpire placed the wickets 10 minutes before the match started.

definition: Over a large area or to a great extent.
note: From wide plus -ly.
hints: Commonly or broadly.
Known by many.
example: Wandered wide through many lands.

definition: To make or become wider.
note: From wide plus -en. A road or a gap can be this way.
hints: What a road project does.
What your eyes do in surprise.

definition: A woman whose husband has died.
note: From Old English widuwe. It is the same word in many Indo-European languages.
hints: A woman who has lost her husband.
A spider with a famous black name.

definition: How wide something is.
note: From wide plus -th, on the pattern of length. A ruler can measure it.
hints: Side to side measure.
What a door's frame has.
example: Cut the bread into diagonal slices the width of a finger.

definition: To hold and use a tool or weapon.
note: From Old English wealdan, 'to rule'. A king can do it to power, and a knight to a sword.
hints: What a knight does with a sword.
To exercise power over others.
origin: Old English wealdan, from Old English wieldan

definition: A sausage, typically a hot dog.
note: A shortening of German Wienerwurst, 'Vienna sausage'.
hints: Served in a bun with mustard.
Named for a European capital.

definition: To move quickly from side to side.
note: From Middle English wiglen, probably from a Dutch or Low German word for rocking. Worms and toddlers do it.
hints: A worm does it across the pavement.
Toes in the sand.
origin: Middle Dutch wigelen, from Middle Low German wigelen
example: Her hips wiggle as she walks.

definition: An old word for a living creature.
note: From Old English wiht, 'creature'. It also names ghostly beings in fantasy.
hints: An archaic word for a being.
A ghostly figure in fantasy.

definition: Radio shorthand meaning 'I will comply'.
note: A blend of will and comply, used in radio and military talk.
hints: Said in reply to a command by radio.
Pilots and soldiers say it to confirm.

definition: In an uncontrolled way, or extremely.
note: From wild plus -ly.
hints: Without restraint.
Crazily, without any control.
example: He swung wildly at the guy's head, but ended up on the floor.

definition: A graceful tree with slender, drooping branches that grows near water.
note: From Old English welig. The wood is used for cricket bats, and the tree gives its name to the weeping kind.
hints: A cricket bat is often cut from its wood.
The 'weeping' kind droops over ponds.

definition: Weak or cowardly.
note: From wimp, of uncertain origin, plus -y. It describes feeble people or things.
hints: The opposite of brave.
A weak, timid manner.

definition: To flinch in pain.
note: From Anglo-Norman wincier, 'to bend aside'. A sharp pain makes you do it.
hints: What you do at a sharp pain.
To flinch at a sudden sting.

definition: A machine that hauls with a drum and cable.
note: From Old English wince, 'reel'. A tow truck often has one.
hints: A tow truck's cable drum.
A crank for hauling a heavy load.

definition: An opening in a wall fitted with glass.
note: From Old Norse vindauga, 'wind eye'.
hints: Lets light into a room.
Its name once meant wind eye.

definition: With a lot of wind.
note: From Old English windig, built from wind plus -y. A kite flies best on such a day.
hints: A day for flying a kite.
Chicago is nicknamed the city of this.

definition: A place where wine is produced.
note: From wine plus -ery. Vineyards grow the grapes and wineries turn them into wine.
hints: Tours and tastings take place at one in Napa.
Where grapes get crushed and barrelled.
example: Their Napa Valley winery was built in 1958 on the site of a former vegetable farm.

definition: A player on the flank of a team in football, rugby or hockey.
note: From wing plus -er. The wings of a pitch are the sides.
hints: A fast player who hugs the touchline.
A footballer who whips in crosses.

definition: The one who comes first.
note: From win plus -er.
hints: Takes the trophy.
The champion of the contest.

definition: The coldest season.
note: From Old English winter, perhaps related to a word meaning wet.
hints: Season of frost and snow.
Comes after autumn.

definition: Something that wipes, especially a blade clearing a car windscreen.
note: A plain agent noun from wipe, from Old English wipian.
hints: Swishes rain from a windscreen.
Found on the front of a car in the rain.

definition: Good judgement gained from experience.
note: From Old English wisdom, from wis, 'wise'.
hints: What a sage has.
Kind of tooth that arrives late.

definition: In a sensible way, showing good judgement.
note: From Old English wislice. Wise is related to 'wit' and 'wisdom'.
hints: How an owl is said to act.
How a prudent person invests.
example: She wisely decided to re-check her homework before submitting it.

definition: Thin and light, like a wisp.
note: From wisp plus -y. Hair or cloud can be this.
hints: Fine, thin hair.
A cloud thin and light.
example: The wispy smoke rose from chimneys all around town.

definition: A woman said to have magical powers.
note: From Old English wicce. Fairy tales feature them with broomsticks and cauldrons.
hints: A fairy-tale figure on a broomstick.
Hunted in Salem in 1692.

definition: Inside, or not beyond.
note: From Old English withinnan, 'on the inside'.
hints: Contained by.
Not further than.

definition: Clever and amusing.
note: From Old English wittig, 'clever' or 'wise', built from wit. A good one has a sharp, quick tongue.
hints: Quick with a clever remark.
Like Oscar Wilde's quips.
example: His speech was both witty and informative.

definition: A man with magical powers; or a very skilled person.
note: From Middle English wys, 'wise', plus -ard.
hints: Merlin was one.
Someone brilliant at a skill.

definition: Unsteady and shaky.
note: From wobble plus -y. Wobble itself imitates the movement.
hints: A table with one short leg.
A toddler's first steps.

definition: Past participle of wake.
note: From Old English wacan, with the -n of an old participle. It is what you are after the alarm rings.
hints: What you are after the alarm goes off.
A past form of a word about sleep.

definition: An adult human female.
note: From Old English wifman, 'wife-person'. The first part is wif, 'woman', which gave wife.
hints: An adult female person.
Its Old English root came from a word for wife.

definition: More than one woman.
note: From Old English wifmen, the plural of wifman. The vowel change is a relic of old plurals.
hints: The plural of an adult female.
The group of people in a ladies' room.

definition: A feeling of amazement, or to ask oneself.
note: From Old English wundor, 'marvel'.
hints: Awe at something great.
One of seven ancient ones is the pyramids.

definition: Crooked or unsteady.
note: From a dialect word, possibly an alteration of an old word for 'shaky'. A table with uneven legs is this.
hints: A table with an uneven leg.
A crooked picture frame.

definition: Made of wood, or stiff and awkward.
note: From wood plus -en.
hints: A spoon, or a stiff actor's performance.
Not flexible or natural.
example: An ancient cart with wooden wheels.

definition: Like or made of wood.
note: From wood plus -y. A scent or a plant stem can be this.
hints: A forest smell.
A plant with a hard stem.

definition: One who courts a lover.
note: From woo plus -er, from Old English wogere. Romeo was one.
hints: A suitor in a romantic story.
Someone who pursues a sweetheart.

definition: Covered in wool, or vague and unclear.
note: From wool plus -y. A woolly argument is as fuzzy as a sheep.
hints: A mammoth is this.
A jumper in winter, or a hazy argument.

definition: Using too many words.
note: From Old English wordig, built from word plus -y. An essay padded with extra phrases can be this.
hints: A rambling speech.
Padded with extras.
example: The story was long and very wordy.

definition: A person who does a job.
note: From work plus -er.
hints: An employee.
A bee in a hive.

definition: The Earth and all that lives on it.
note: From Old English weorold, 'age of man'. It combined words for man and age.
hints: The Earth, as a whole.
What a globe represents.
example: All the world loves a lover.

definition: To feel anxious.
note: From Old English wyrgan, 'to strangle', later 'to harass'. The sense of fretting arrived in the 1800s.
hints: What you do before an exam.
What a parent does when you're late.
example: I worry about my job.

definition: Of lower quality; more bad.
note: From Old English wiersa, a comparative that has no connection with bad. It is the irregular form of bad.
hints: What a bad situation becomes if it deteriorates.
The comparative of bad.

definition: To become or make worse.
note: From worse plus -en, in Middle English. Wounds and weather worsen.
hints: What a cold does without rest.
Said of a storm that intensifies.

definition: The most bad.
note: From Old English wierresta, the superlative of the same root as worse. It is the extreme of bad.
hints: The opposite of best.
The lowest of all.

definition: The value of something; or deserving of.
note: From Old English weorth, 'valuable'. Things are said to be it or not it.
hints: What a thing's price is meant to match.
What an old coin is, in money.
example: 10 dollars worth of gasoline.

definition: Deserving respect or attention.
note: From worth plus -y.
hints: Deserving of respect.
A noble foe.

definition: The past of will; or a polite request word.
note: From Old English wolde. The L is silent in speech.
hints: A helping verb used in polite requests.
A word with a silent L.
origin: Old English wolde; in English since the 9th century

definition: An injury to the body; or past tense of wind.
note: The injury is from Old English wund. The other word, rhyming with found, is from wind.
hints: A cut on the skin.
What a clock did once it was cranked.

definition: Made by weaving.
note: The past participle of weave, from Old English wefan. A basket or blanket can be this way.
hints: What a basket or rug is.
A cloth made on a loom.
example: The incidents woven into the story.

definition: Wreckage; or destruction.
note: From Middle English wrak. It is also seaweed washed ashore, and in 'wrack and ruin'.
hints: Seaweed thrown on a beach.
A word in the pair 'and ruin'.
origin: Old English wracu, from Old English wrǣċ

definition: A ghost, especially one seen just before or after a death.
note: First recorded in Scots in 1513, with no certain origin. Tolkien's Ringwraiths are cursed kings.
hints: In Tolkien, the Nazgul are called Ring ones.
A pale figure from the mist.
example: His voice was drowned out by the wraith's sudden howl.

definition: To cause damage or harm.
note: From Old English wrecan, 'to drive' or 'avenge'. Storms and rivals do it.
hints: What a storm may do to a coastline.
To bring about havoc.
example: The earthquake wreaked havoc in the city.

definition: A ring of leaves or flowers woven together.
note: From Old English wriða, 'something twisted'. Wreaths were worn on the head by Olympic champions and hung on doors at Christmas.
hints: Hung on a front door in December.
Placed at a war memorial on Remembrance Day.

definition: A ruined vehicle or building; or to destroy.
note: From Anglo-Norman wrec, from an Old Norse word for something washed ashore. A shipwreck is an old example.
hints: A ruined ship at the bottom of the sea.
What a bad crash makes of a car.
example: The house was a wreck when they bought it.

definition: A tool for gripping and turning nuts; or a sharp twisting pull.
note: From Old English wrencan, 'to twist'. British people call the tool a spanner.
hints: A plumber tightens a pipe with one.
To twist an ankle painfully is to do this to it.
origin: Old English wrenċ; in English since the 18th century

definition: To pull away by force.
note: From Old English wraestan, 'to twist'. A rival may do it to control.
hints: To take control by force.
To twist something away.
example: He wrested the remote control from my grasp and changed the channel.

definition: To squeeze and twist, to get liquid out.
note: From Old English wringan. A wet towel gets it.
hints: What you do to a wet cloth.
To twist a towel dry.

definition: The joint between the hand and forearm.
note: From Old English wrist. A watch or bracelet goes on it.
hints: Where a watch is worn.
A bendable joint by the hand.
example: With a flick of the wrist, he threw the frisbee to a team-mate.

definition: A person who writes.
note: From write plus -er.
hints: Pens novels or articles.
An author or journalist.
example: Has your girlfriend written you another letter already? She’s quite a writer!

definition: Incorrect or unfair.
note: From Old English wrang, 'twisted' or 'crooked'. It first meant bent before it meant not right.
hints: The opposite of right.
A mistaken answer.
origin: Old English wrang, from Old Norse rangr

definition: In a dry, mocking way.
note: From wry plus -ly. Wry comes from Old English wrigian, 'to turn'.
hints: With a twisted, dry smile.
How an ironic comment is delivered.

definition: A heavy, colourless gas used in lamps.
note: From Greek xenos, 'strange', because it was found as a rare gas. Some car headlights use it.
hints: A gas in bright headlights.
A noble gas named for strangeness.
example: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are noble gases.

definition: A luxury sailing or motor boat.
note: From Dutch jacht, from jachtschip, 'hunting ship'. It was first a fast light vessel used for chasing pirates.
hints: A boat for the very rich.
A sleek vessel in a harbour.
example: Would you like to go sailing on my uncle’s yacht?

definition: A loud, rowdy person.
note: From Gulliver's Travels by Jonathan Swift, where Yahoos are brutish creatures. It is also a cry of joy.
hints: A boorish, loud person.
A cheer of joy.

definition: A member of a Japanese organised crime gang.
note: Borrowed from Japanese. The name is often explained as from a losing hand in a card game, though that is folklore.
hints: Known for full-body tattoos and strict codes.
Japan's equivalent of the mafia.

definition: A person from the northern US, or any American in the eyes of foreigners.
note: The origin is unclear; one theory points to the Dutch name Jan Kees. It first meant a New Englander.
hints: A name for a person from New England.
A New York baseball team bears the name.

definition: Once a year.
note: From year plus -ly.
hints: Occurring once in a twelvemonth.
Happening every twelve months.

definition: The colour of lemons and sunflowers.
note: From Old English geolu, related to the word gold.
hints: Banana colour.
Shares a root with gold.
origin: Old English ġeolwe, from Old English ġeolu

definition: To give way; or to produce.
note: From Old English gieldan, 'to pay'. A farm gives one, and a driver gives way.
hints: What a crop gives at harvest.
What a road sign tells a driver.

definition: An exclamation of alarm.
note: First recorded in mid-twentieth century America. It is a mild cry of shock.
hints: A cry when you see a spider.
What you say at a nasty surprise.
example: Then she told me I was ‘beautiful, for a black girl’. —Yikes!

definition: A thick, tangy food made from fermented milk.
note: Borrowed from Turkish yogurt, from a verb meaning 'to thicken'. Live bacteria turn the milk sour.
hints: Often sold with fruit at the bottom of the pot.
A breakfast food with probiotic cultures.
example: Cheese, butter, cream, yogurt and kefir are dairy products.

definition: A cricket ball pitched right under the batter's bat.
note: Possibly from the old slang phrase about tricking someone 'Yorkshire'. A fast one is deadly.
hints: The most dangerous delivery for a tail-ender.
A ball that pitches at the batter's toes.
example: He bowled forty-seven toe crushing yorkers that resulted in the wickets of 6 batsmen.

definition: Not old.
note: From Old English geong. It is the opposite of old.
hints: The opposite of old.
A child or a cub.

definition: The time of being young; or a young person.
note: From Old English geoguth. It is the period before adulthood.
hints: Teenage years.
A young person.

definition: A spiky evergreen plant of dry regions with tall flower spikes.
note: The English word began as a variant of yuca, the name for cassava, and was later applied to this plant.
hints: A desert plant with sword-like leaves.
Often grown as a houseplant or in dry gardens.

definition: Disgusting.
note: From yuck, an exclamation of disgust, plus -y.
hints: How a child describes cooked greens.
Gross or unpleasant.
example: The food that I ate today was very yucky.

definition: Tasty.
note: From the sound of 'yum', an exclamation of enjoyment. It is a child's word for delicious.
hints: A child's word for delicious.
Said after a nice bite.

definition: A horse-like African animal with black and white stripes.
note: From Italian zebra, from Portuguese, of uncertain origin. Each has its own stripe pattern.
hints: A striped animal on the savannah.
A black and white animal.
example: Giraffes, zebras, impalas, and elephants are usual neighbors.

definition: The highest point, or the point in the sky directly overhead.
note: Via Medieval Latin from Arabic samt, 'direction' or 'path'. A mistaken copying of the Arabic letters in Europe turned the m into 'ni'.
hints: Where the midday sun sits at the equator.
The peak of an empire's power, or what a mountaineer aims for.
origin: Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت
example: His fame was at its zenith at that time.

definition: Full of lively flavour.
note: From zest plus -y. Zest is the outer rind of a citrus fruit. A tangy sauce is this.
hints: A lemony, tangy flavour.
Bright and punchy in taste.

definition: Nothing at all.
note: Probably from Joe Zilch, a placeholder name in a 1930s humour column.
hints: Zero, in American slang.
Absolutely nothing.

definition: A fastener made of interlocking teeth that you slide shut.
note: Named in 1925 by B.F. Goodrich for boots that used one; it is now the common American word, while British English says zip.
hints: Gets stuck on your jacket on a cold morning.
Two rows of tiny teeth lock together with a slider.
example: He got his T-shirt stuck in the zipper of his jacket.

definition: Lively and quick.
note: From zip, a sound of rapid movement, plus -y.
hints: Describes a nimble small car.
Speedy and energetic.

definition: The belt of sky divided into twelve signs, such as Aries and Leo.
note: From Greek zoidiakos kyklos, 'circle of little animals', since most of the signs are creatures.
hints: Astrologers use its twelve houses to read your birth chart.
Gemini, Taurus and Capricorn are among the signs.
origin: Old French zodiaque, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός [κύκλος]

definition: A corpse brought back to life; or a person who seems lifeless.
note: From a West African word, via Haitian Creole, for a spirit or revived body.
hints: A walking horror-film corpse.
Someone moving with no energy at all.

definition: Relating to a zone.
note: From zone plus -al. Weather and defence in sport can be this.
hints: About an area or zone.
A kind of defence in football, not man-to-man.

definition: Chaotic and crowded like a zoo.
note: From zoo plus -ey.
hints: An airport at Christmas.
Messy and noisy, as an animal enclosure.
